name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Career Pathways Commission releases draft, seeks public input
text:
Imagine being a high school student in Connecticut entering junior or senior year. You are unsure of what the future looks like and college doesn’t feel like the best fit. Between classes, extracurriculars and other obligations, you have your hands full. What happens after graduation, whether it is an apprenticeship, entry-level work or a deferred college degree, is an open question.  
This is the experience of some students in the state and it is being further complicated by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, rising college costs and limited exposure to jobs before graduation.
But a coalition of state leaders, educational representatives, advocates and business leaders hope that this experience changes in the coming years through the work of the Connecticut Career Pathways Commission. The body is tasked with developing a plan for work-based learning and career exposure in the state that will better prepare students of all ages for in-demand careers, creating pathway opportunities beginning in kindergarten through adulthood.
The commission was first discussed publicly in the spring, when Gov. Ned Lamont issued an executive order establishing the creation of group, charging it with crafting a plan to help prepare students not only for the jobs of today, but also for the  “jobs of the future.”
“We must have a system where students and job seekers can see the full arc of opportunity, a system where employers help shape the programs that prepare their future workforce, and a system where everyone — from classrooms to campuses to companies — is aligned around shared goals and shared outcomes,” Lamont said in a statement released earlier this year.
The commission, a 40-member body made up of representatives from workforce boards, higher education, labor, business, the legislature, student bodies and more, must create a five-year strategic plan that offers recommendations for a system that can help students across the state, creating clear and effective opportunities for students of all ages to access the information, skills and experience related to career pathways. 
The commission — led by former U.S. Education Secretary and previous state education official Miguel Cardona — must complete a draft report by the end of the year, with a final report due to the governor and the legislature by February 2027.
It must also make drafts of its proposals available to the public and collect feedback, incorporating public suggestions into future drafts of the report. It released its first draft of proposed recommendations for the creation and  structure of the pathways system earlier in October, with public comments being accepted online until Saturday, Oct. 17. On that day, the commission will also hold its final virtual comment sessions at 10 a.m. 
The current comment period is the first opportunity for the broader public to interact with the work of the commission, which has been meeting since May. Additional comment periods will be opened in future, as the body continues its work and prepares to submit its draft report later this year. 
In interviews with The Connecticut Mirror, commission members said the comment period is a key chance for them to show the progress they’ve made in recent months, and for the public to weigh in on the further direction of the work.
The goal
On paper, Connecticut has a vast network of resources and opportunities available to students looking to find a career path. By one count, there are more than 90 career pipeline-related programs, all of which are spread across more than a dozen state agencies — from the Department of Labor to the Department of Economic and Community Development.  
But these programs are disconnected and spread out across the state, creating a situation where students in one part of Connecticut may have access to opportunities that are walled off from students living elsewhere. 
“A lot of what’s going on across the state is pockets of opportunity based off of leadership interests, and that means it’s also ebbs and flows budget-wise based on the district’s priorities,” said Kate Dias, president of the Connecticut Education Association teacher union and a member of the commission. “It’s not necessarily the systemic commitment that we are really looking for.” 
Closing that gap and ensuring that students across the state not only have access and exposure to different career pathways, but can also develop clear skills that directly track with what local businesses and employers are looking for, is the central focus of the commission. 
“What the commission is really trying to do is ensure that opportunities are available to everyone and that they’re not based on where you live and what institutions you go to,” said commission member Kelli-Marie Vallieres, who serves as the state’s chief workforce officer and leader of the Office of Workforce Strategy. 
The Office of Workforce Strategy is also joining with the Governor’s Workforce Council to help coordinate with the Career Pathways Commission on the development and implementation of the career pathways plan.
The aim is for the commission’s work to build off already existing state programs, while also creating new opportunities for student engagement and learning. The pathways are also intended to closely connect with industry needs, giving students of all ages the ability to connect with career opportunities repeatedly over time. 
The focus on career pathways arrives at a key time for the state. There are more than 86,000 job openings in Connecticut, with employers reporting that they are having difficulty filling open roles. The Connecticut Business and Industry Association’s annual business survey, released in September, found that some 72% of respondents reported having difficulty finding and retaining workers, with skill gaps being a notable part of the problem. 
“We heard from businesses over and over, and we continue to hear, that they’re just not seeing the type of pipeline that they need in order to meet the 86,000 job offerings that we currently have in Connecticut,” said Chris DiPentima, president and CEO of CBIA and a member of the commission. “The students coming out of high school are not well enough prepared either from a technical point of view or just durable human skills.”
But rather than view that gap as an impediment, members of the commission say that it presents an opportunity: a chance for educators, industry and government to come together and create a better system, one that is more closely aligned with not only employer needs, but student interests.
That’s especially relevant amid a national resurgence in interest in skilled trades, an interest that has grown in recent years as college costs rise, and artificial intelligence threatens the type of work often done by entry-level administrative and white collar workers. According to a 2026 survey funded by a high school trades group and conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, 1 in 6 students reported trying to enroll in trades courses but being turned down due to a lack of space.
And that limited availability could further reduce the workers available for industries that are projected to be among the fastest growing in the state. Data from the Connecticut Department of Labor suggests that the state expects to experience a notable increase in employment between 2022 and 2032, with a significant portion of that growth expected to be in jobs that do not require a bachelor’s degree. That includes industries like hospitality, health care, transportation and manufacturing. 
These roles could account for more than 55% of job growth by 2034, with a CBIA Foundation report released earlier this year  arguing that the state must create a better pathways system that will help students connect and prepare not only for these fields, but for jobs that could exist in the future. 
“We have to have a transformational change, or we will continue to not see businesses stay in Connecticut and the economic growth and will miss the prosperity that this state can absolutely realize,” DiPentima said. 
Unpacking recommendations
There are many ways to create a career pathways system, however. 
The goal is to create a framework that “maintains the ability to stay current,” said Vallieres.  “We’re building the processes and the systems to make sure that we are updating these credentials and these pathways on a timely basis, so that we’re keeping pace with what industry demands are.” 
In its first set of draft recommendations, the commission is focusing on how it will structure that deeper work. The recommendations released this month focus on two broader objectives: creating a pathways system that is accessible to all learners in the state and building out the system that will support the work.
The recommendations offered in the report have been broken down into four “pillars.”
In the first pillar, the focus is on giving students a strong foundation, with the draft suggesting things like a statewide system for career readiness that includes clear skill building opportunities, career advising and job exploration opportunities. 
The second pillar calls for better preparing learners with industry-aligned skills and credentials, recommending that the state not only create clear dual credit and credential systems for students, but also improve the training pipeline for instructors, include community colleges in pathways work, and create clear sequences of studies that can be adapted to different groups of learners depending on age and skill level. 
The third and fourth pillars focus on work-based learning opportunities and the establishment of a clear unified system capable of managing the entire career pathways network, respectively. 
The draft document so far suggests that the task before the commission is a large one, requiring not only the creation of the career pathways system itself, but also of the evaluation, data collection, and broader management structures that will support what is ultimately created. 
A complicated process
With just a few months to go before the final report is due, commission members say that public input is incredibly important to the process, adding that the career pathways system that is created in the coming years will only be as effective as the engagement and participation that students and other stakeholders have with it.  
Dias of the CEA notes that teachers in particular will play a significant role, adding that with so many responsibilities already on their plates, the career pathways discussion will require a fundamental rethinking of the state’s education system to ensure that teachers can handle the new responsibilities expected of them. 
“At the end of the day, we’re talking about programmatic shifts that are going to involve transportation, bringing in different experts, creating regional resource networks for both industry and as well as school districts to create the network that is necessary to provide every student in Connecticut some sort of work-based experience,” she said. 
“You can’t keep adding to our system without subtracting,” she added. “There just aren’t enough hours in a day.”
But if the state can successfully pull the transformation off, it is a shift that Dias says will be worthwhile. “Our goals are ambitious, our ideas are not small, but I believe that if we do this well, the impact can be really important in terms of changing the outcomes for students,” she said. 
For Shannon Marimón, executive director of ReadyCT, a CBIA affiliate that focuses on providing career pathways support to students across the state, the commission has a tremendous opportunity before it. 
“We need to have the education system speaking to our employer community so that it can really align with where the workforce is currently and where it’s headed, because we want to make sure we’re setting young people up for the opportunities to be prepared and successful,” she said. 
But the actual implementation of the final recommendations will be out of the commission’s hands and will instead be up to the governor and the Legislature. The commission has not yet publicly released its specific policy recommendations or put a clear number on the amount of funding that will be needed to turn the career pathways plan to life. 
As the work continues, members of the commission are hopeful that their report will have an impact, saying that the state needs to make a change to give students a real shot at success. 
“We’re really working hard to set up something that we think is transformative,” Dias said. “I think that was always the goal: what can we do that supports the economic growth and development of the state of Connecticut that increases opportunities for our students?”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Freedom Caucus lawmakers vote to sponsor election bills, reject dark money resolution
text:
In some of the last votes they’ll make as state lawmakers, several Wyoming Freedom Caucus members and allies voted Thursday to sponsor a slate of legislation to revamp the state’s election system. 
At a legislative committee meeting in Casper, the group of Republican lawmakers also rejected a resolution intended to combat dark money — a political force the caucus has blamed for voters overwhelmingly rejecting their candidates in the 2026 primary election. 
Since the Freedom Caucus rose to power, a core part of its mission has included reshaping how elections are carried out in Wyoming. That focus has largely been aimed at restricting how and when people can vote. Some of those proposals succeeded at the statehouse, including 2025 legislation that added proof of residency and citizenship to the documents needed to register to vote. 
Other bills, however, including a ban on ballot drop boxes and measures to count votes by hand, have failed time and again. And after the caucus lost its House majority and backslid in the Senate in the primary election, those bills are unlikely to succeed in the 69th Wyoming Legislature.  
“One delicate issue is that there’s been an election in the intervening time between when these bills were proposed,” Joint Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions Committee Co-Chairman Cale Case said at Thursday’s meeting. The Lander Republican won his primary election against a caucus-aligned challenger.
“I believe that has real implications on how these bills will be received in the 2027 session,” Case said, adding that he did not think they would clear initial hurdles in the session’s process. 
Republican Sen. Cale Case of Lander during the 2025 legislative session. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
While Case is not associated with the caucus, most of the committee’s current membership is. His comments came in the late afternoon as lawmakers had reached the election portion of the agenda, which included consideration of 13 bills. When Case asked the committee how it would like to proceed, Casper Republican Rep. Tony Locke, a Freedom Caucus member who lost his reelection, asked for each bill to be heard and voted on. 
Lyman Republican Rep. Joe Webb, another Freedom Caucus member who lost in August, also asked that the committee forge ahead. 
“If another Legislature deems that these bills are not necessary, that is their responsibility and that falls upon their shoulders and not ours,” he said. “But I think we have the due diligence to proceed,” he said. 
Altogether, the committee voted to sponsor eight bills and move four more to its November meeting for consideration. The sponsored measures would ban drop boxes, restrict how ballots can be delivered and revise acceptable forms of voter ID, among other things. 
Ten Sleep Republican Sen. Ed Cooper, who is not on the committee, brought a resolution for the panel to consider sponsoring. 
“I do believe we have an election integrity problem in Wyoming and it comes down to money,” Cooper said. 
More specifically, he said, dark money, or political spending where the source of funds is not publicly disclosed, is affecting elections across the country, including in Wyoming. 
A large volume in dark money, in fact, was spent ahead of Wyoming’s 2026 primary election, including by groups both opposing and supporting the Freedom Caucus. 
Make Liberty Win, a Virginia-based political action committee, for example, spent $549,000 largely backing caucus candidates, as WyoFile previously reported. However, the PAC’s funding is obscured since it largely relies on funding from its nonprofit, Young Americans for Liberty, and is not required by federal law to publicly disclose its underlying individual donors. 
Meanwhile, opposition to the caucus was better organized and funded than it was during the last election cycle, as WyoFile reported in August. That included the PAC for a Better Wyoming, which spent about $191,000 opposing the caucus, according to campaign finance reports. Details about the PAC’s funding remain unknown to the public since it reported that Wyoming Donor Alliance, a nonprofit, was the single source of its funding. The caucus recently blamed this type of spending for its election defeat. 
At the meeting in Casper, Mills Mayor Leah Juarez told the committee dark money is no longer just a problem for statewide or national races. 
“I’m here today because the mayoral election in Mills, Wyoming, a community of 5,000 people, has become the target of organized political activity funded through a political action committee from Wisconsin,” Juarez said.
“The public has a legitimate right to know who is paying to influence its mayoral elections as well as everybody else’s elections in this room,” she said. 
Afton Republican Sen. Dan Dockstader brought a motion to move the legislation to the committee’s next meeting for a full discussion, public comment and notice. 
No one spoke against the motion, or the bill’s concept, but it failed on a voice vote when the committee’s caucus associates opposed it. 
Though Casper Republican Sen. Bill Landen did not run for reelection and is concluding his last term in January, he told the committee he’s hoping to see the state strengthen its campaign finance laws. 
“I think there’s a lot of work to do in the Secretary of State’s office on this front. I don’t think that our disclosure methods are adequate enough,” he said.
The committee’s next meeting is scheduled for November.

name: VTDigger
title: In his third congressional race, Republican Gerald Malloy is looking for middle ground
text:
Gerald Malloy, Republican candidate for Vermont’s U.S. House of Representatives seat. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger
It’s been six years and two big losses since “Deploy Malloy” first entered Vermonters’ vocabulary — but this time he’s taking a different tack.    
The slogan belongs to Gerald Malloy, a U.S. army veteran, former defense contractor at Lockheed Martin, Bowhead and Raytheon, and perennial congressional candidate in the Green Mountain State since 2022. He previously lost to two liberal U.S. senators in landslide races, and he’s now seeking a congressional office for a third time, challenging U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. 
His message? Lower bureaucratic barriers for business to develop in Vermont and bring balanced representation back to Vermont — representation that reflects red parts of Vermont as well as blue.
Malloy arrived on the Vermont political scene in 2022 with an endorsement from President Trump and conservative stances on issues like immigration and abortion, according to Middlebury College political science professor Matt Dickinson. He positioned himself to the right of Christina Nolan, the moderate Republican candidate whom Gov. Phil Scott endorsed, Dickinson added. Malloy also expressed his support for a border wall and disclosed that he had voted for Trump in past elections.
Now, political experts say Malloy may be changing his tune. He said he has broken with Trump on certain issues, such as the tariff war with Canada, the government’s military strategy in the Iran war and some current immigration enforcement tactics.
Despite some disagreements with Trump, Malloy said he still considers himself a conservative Republican. This time his platform centers around affordability and business. Vermont’s young people are leaving the state, he said, due to issues with affordability, and he wants to turn the tide.
Balint, the Democratic incumbent, is the third member of the Vermont congressional delegation that Malloy will face off against. First elected to national office in 2022, Balint champions issues like affordable housing, healthcare, climate action and reproductive rights. She is a vocal opponent of the Trump administration as well, encouraging Democrats to stand up against the White House. 
Polls indicate Balint is the clear favorite, with one recent survey from Vermont Public showing that if the election was held on the day of the survey, 43% of poll respondents would vote for Balint and 28% for Malloy.
It is notoriously hard to unseat incumbents in House races, Dickinson said, especially as a Republican in a blue state. Malloy’s previous opponents, U.S. Sens. Peter Welch and Bernie Sanders, won in landslides, with Welch taking 68% of the vote in 2022 and Sanders taking 63% of the vote in 2024. 
And Vermont is a special case, Dickinson added, noting that the last time an incumbent governor was ousted was in 1962.
“Vermonters generally stick with what they know,” he said.
Malloy disagreed. He’s been going door-to-door and talking to people all over the state, he said, and he’s heard a different message.
“Vermonters want change,” Malloy said. “They want balance. They want results, and they want accountability. We don’t have that right now.”
And Malloy has shown grit and connection with people on the ground throughout his campaigns, according to Paul Dame, chair of the Vermont Republican Party.
“I think Malloy is somebody who, even during his first run, was somebody who went everywhere to talk to everybody,” Dame said. “I mean that’s one of the reasons he was sort of the surprising win in the first primary, you know, against Christina Nolan, is he just puts in the work and he goes to people.” 
Malloy has always been a strong candidate in the primaries, according to Nicholas Charyk, the manager of government and public affairs at Downs Rachlin Martin — the largest law firm in Vermont — and a past campaign manager for multiple Vermont Democrats, adding that his win against Nolan came as a surprise to many in Vermont’s political community. He drew a comparison between Malloy’s 2022 campaign and Democrat Amanda Janoo’s recent gubernatorial primary win against Ali Richards, whom many political experts expected to win.

READ MORE

But after the primaries, the two candidates’ roads diverged, Charyk said.
“I think Amanda has continued to surprise people by gaining real traction and making it a real race,” Charyk said. “Malloy was unable to do that.”
Dickinson described Malloy’s 2022 platform as “hawkish,” with an emphasis on foreign policy and Malloy’s military experience, which inspired the slogan “Deploy Malloy.” He embraced Trump’s endorsement, Dickinson said. Malloy also expressed support for a nationwide abortion ban in June 2022, but he reversed course after Roe v. Wade was overturned.
“The problem is, as he found out when he was beaten easily by Peter Welch, is there’s a ceiling to being a MAGA type Republican in Vermont,” Dickinson said. “You’re not going to get more than 30% of the vote.”
Since 2022, Dame said there has been an effort from Vermont’s Republican party at large to bridge the gap between Gov. Phil Scott’s moderate stances and the more conservative national GOP. 
Supporting Gov. Scott has been a core facet of Malloy’s campaign platform in 2026, Dickinson said. Malloy argued that Scott has not been receiving the support he needs from Balint, Sanders and Welch, pointing out in an interview that all three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation endorsed Janoo, Scott’s opponent.
Balint countered that argument, highlighting collaborations between herself and Scott on housing, infrastructure, rural health care and the impacts of the tariff war with Canada.
“We certainly don’t agree on everything, but we do work together to get results for our state,” Balint wrote in a text to VTDigger.
It is difficult for her to “tease out” the exact reason why Malloy was running for a seat in the national congressional body, Balint said.
“He’s very focused on state issues, which I totally get,” Balint said. “We have a lot of them here, and a lot of the stuff he talks about is focused on state-level issues, which we in Congress don’t get to weigh in on.”
Malloy has drawn attention to expletives in statements made by Balint in previous cycles, which he argued are “disgraceful,” and called on Balint to resign.
“She’s committed misconduct and should not be in office,” Malloy said in the interview. 
Balint, for her part, said she’s seen a “different side” of Malloy, who she said has been quite “affable” over the years. She said she was surprised by the tactics in his campaign ads and his emphasis on her instances of “coarse language,” adding that she has a large body of work in healthcare, housing and other issues that shows her dedication to Vermonters. 
“You can make a case around policy for why you might not support what I believe,” Balint said in an interview, “but he is openly supporting a president who has said absolutely horrible things about women, about immigrants, about trans people — really horrific things.”
Some Vermonters remain skeptical about Malloy’s allegiances with Trump, and whether he will be willing to break with the president on key issues. Charyk said he sees clear evidence that Malloy’s stance has moderated lately, but he does not know if it will be enough for Vermonters.
“He was pretty full-throated in his support historically,” Charyk said, “but whether sort of a nuanced, slight differentiation is going to be meaningful to Vermont voters, I’m very, very skeptical.” 
Balint agreed, arguing that Vermonters have experienced real harm in the past few years through the decisions of the federal government.
“I think that Vermonters can see directly how this president’s initiatives have really hurt them, from, you know, the cuts to Medicaid, to letting the Affordable Care Act subsidies lapse, to the cuts to SNAP,” she said. “And so he doesn’t seem to have a clear case that he’s making to Vermonters that he will be a check on this president, because I think he’s still very much in support of this president.”
Charyk and Dickinson both emphasized one thing: Malloy has an uphill battle ahead of him. But Malloy said he likes his chances, and he will continue to fight for the Vermont he wants to see.
“I want Vermont to be a place to stay, live, and thrive,” Malloy said. “It’s not on that path right now.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota secretary of state office targeted amid probes into mailed election threats across US
text:
Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon received a threatening letter with an unidentified powder in the mail. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said Friday that a package containing a threatening letter and an unidentified white powder was intercepted before reaching his office, as federal investigations continue into similar packages mailed to election administrators and congressional offices across the U.S. amid midterm campaigning. 
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service is currently testing the material sent to Simon’s office, the secretary of state said in a statement.
“Threats against election workers are unacceptable and should not be tolerated,” Simon’s statement said. “Our office will not be deterred and will continue to support the thousands of election officials across the state as they administer elections to their communities.”
Similar packages have prompted responses in other states, including Arizona, Wisconsin and Nebraska. Election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma were evacuated after receiving suspicious mail containing powdery substances, while the U.S. Postal Service intercepted a similar package intended for Ohio’s secretary of state. 
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement expressing concern over the incidents, saying that threats against election officials “have no place in our democracy.”
The investigations come less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 general election. Early, in-person voting started Friday in Minnesota.
Simon said earlier this month that his office will be operating with “a war room mentality” on Election Day, coordinating with election administrators in all 87 counties and local law enforcement to prepare for potential threats and to combat misinformation.
In recent months, Minnesota has faced heightened federal scrutiny regarding its elections. In August, the U.S. Department of Justice sent election monitors to polling sites in two Minnesota counties. President Donald Trump has also made claims, without evidence, of election fraud in the state, and federal prosecutors recently charged 10 people with illegally voting or registering to vote in Minnesota elections.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: On the campaign trail for Republicans, Trump changes course and advocates for mail-in voting
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting in this year’s midterm elections, the president is calling on voters to vote early and by mail as he campaigns in support of Republican candidates nationwide.
National polling has indicated that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting in this year’s elections than Republicans are, and control of the U.S. House and U.S. Senate is at stake in the election. If Democrats take control of one or both bodies, Trump and members of his administration likely will face investigations and could be impeached. 
“So vote early, vote by mail, or vote on Election Day, Nov. 3rd,” Trump said at a rally in Wasilla on Tuesday, urging voters to track their mailed ballot to ensure it is received.
Alaska has a limited ballot tracking service online; voters cannot tell until after the election whether their ballot was counted or rejected, and current state law does not allow voters to fix any technical problems that cause a ballot to be rejected.  
“Sort of follow your vote if you’re going to do mail-in,” Trump said.
Trump’s comments in Alaska followed a video he posted Oct. 3 that urged Republicans to vote early and by mail. 
“If your state has early voting, do not wait. Go out and vote. Vote early, vote by mail or vote in person on Election Day, Nov. 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left Dumb-ocrats in a midterm victory that is too big to rig,” Trump said in the video.
A week later, in New York on Oct. 9, Trump again urged voters to cast ballots by mail.
“We’re in the golden age of America. And if you’re voting by mail, make sure that you request your ballot by Oct. 24th, remember that, and have it postmarked by Election Day. I don’t know, I always like Election Day better, but what do I know about things like that?” he said.
While Trump has repeatedly tried to deter Americans from voting by mail, a voting method he attributes to his loss in 2020, he has also reversed course before. In 2024, he urged Republicans to vote by mail ahead of that year’s election despite denigrating mail-in voting for months beforehand.
Trump himself frequently votes by mail in Florida elections. 
Last week in Tennessee and in Ohio on Monday for a rally, Trump didn’t mention mail-in voting but noted that early voting is underway. “So get out and vote. And if you have to, you do it Nov. 3rd. I don’t care how you do it, but we have to do it,” he said in Ohio.
At rallies in Montana and Arizona on Wednesday, Trump did not mention mail-in voting but did note that early voting is already under way in both states. He did not say, as in Ohio, that supporters should vote early.
“For some reason, when you have a president, Republican or Democrat, it’s just brutal,” Trump said on Oct. 10 in Tennessee. “They don’t seem to win the midterms. But we’re gonna turn that tradition around.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana renews deals with 4 Medicaid providers; lawmakers want better health outcomes
text:
Louisiana has approved renewing the contracts of four managed care organizations that offer Medicaid healthcare plans to some 1.2 million state residents. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/The Missouri Independent)Louisiana lawmakers renewed state contracts Thursday with four private managed care organizations that provide Medicaid coverage, calling on state health officials to ensure the money results in better health outcomes. 
Louisiana will spend more than $16 billion on its managed Medicaid contracts in calendar year 2027, according to numbers shared at Thursday’s meeting of the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget. The deals range between $3.2 billion to $5.8 billion and cover some 1.2 million of the 1.3 million people in the state who use Medicaid. 
The four organizations are Atena, AmeriHealth Caritas, Humana Health and Louisiana Healthcare Connections. Two other providers — UnitedHealth and an Elevance Health-Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana joint venture — chose this year to pull out of the state.  
Most of the time spent on the contracts involved discussion about continued health struggles across the state.  
Sen. Regina Barrow, D-Baton Rouge, said her Google search before the meeting showed her Louisiana’s health ranking among states went from 49th in 2010 to 50th last year.
“We don’t need to continue to invest money in something that’s not working,” Barrow said.
Committee member Rep. Tony Bacala, R-Prairieville, shared his concerns about the state having spent more on Medicaid in recent years in direct payments to hospitals independent of the cost for its managed care contracts. Louisiana has raised its reimbursement rates for caregivers and facilities who accept Medicaid patients. But Bacala noted that more than half of Louisiana’s Medicaid enrollees are children, who tend to have fewer health issues   
“It just boggles my mind that we’re doing it,” Bacala said about needing to spend more on Medicaid.
Seth Gold, Medicaid director for the Louisiana Department of Health, told committee members the state’s higher Medicaid costs can also be attributed to healthcare inflation and the worsening health of enrollees.
“The average member is relatively sicker than they used to be, which means that we spend more per member than we used to,” Gold said.
Other lawmakers stressed to state health officials that Medicaid expenditures should be tied to better health outcomes. 
Barrow requested that the health department establish metrics for the four Medicaid providers so that lawmakers can track how they spend public dollars and whether the money improves the health of enrollees. 
Gold said the state Medicaid program will place more emphasis on accountability from providers and preventative health measures, such as well-baby visits. He also mentioned that providers would be directed to increase the availability of prescription medications to treat substance abuse. 
“We’re not going to pay anymore for bad outcomes,” Gold said.  
The federal government covers more than 75% of the cost of Medicaid in Louisiana, which is higher than the national average of just under two-thirds, according to Kaiser Family Foundation data. 
Some states could soon have to pay a larger share if they don’t fall in line with Trump administration policy changes, which include coverage limits for noncitizens legally in the U.S. that took effect this month and work requirements. Higher reimbursement rates for hospitals and doctors who accept Medicaid patients are also expected to increase state costs.
Just before the committee approved the Medicaid contract renewals, its members learned Louisiana Health Connections and Ochsner had reached terms to keep the health system’s affiliated caregivers and facilities in the Medicaid provider’s network. As recently as last week, Ochsner told the health department there was still no deal in place that included coverage for the 70,000 LHC enrollees who get their care through Ochsner.
Also at the meeting, lawmakers approved a three-year, $4.3 billion contract for health insurance through the state’s Office of Group Benefits, which covers state employees, retirees, K-12 public school teachers and their dependents. The plan also includes those who work at state colleges and universities as well as participating school districts and political subdivisions.
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana was the only bidder for the contract and will be paid 3% of the total value, which comes to $140 million. The other 97% of state dollars will cover plan participants’ claims over the contract period.

name: VTDigger
title: A free press under pressure: New York Times’ Eric Lipton speaks in Vermont
text:
Eric Lipton, a four-time Pulitzer Prize winner and investigative reporter for The New York Times, talks to an audience at the Delta Hotel in South Burlington on 9 October 2026. Photo by Daria Bishop for Vermont Digger.

Eric Lipton, an investigative journalist for the New York Times, spoke Friday, Oct. 9, at Delta Hotels in South Burlington about his reporting on profiteering within the Trump administration. More than 180 people attended the sold out event, hosted by VTDigger and Seven Days.
Lipton described how he and his colleagues investigated the Trump family’s pursuit of personal profit across the world, including an estimated $2.2 billion earned by President Trump during the first year of his second term. He also recounted how federal agents arrived at his and his colleagues’ homes with subpoenas seeking phone records and information about their confidential sources and how The New York Times fought back.
Lipton reflected on the critical role of a free press in a democracy and the importance of vigorous, innovative news organizations, including Seven Days and nonprofits like ProPublica and VTDigger. He ended with a promise, “We will not be intimidated.” 
The talk capped a two-day visit to his alma mater, University of Vermont, where Lipton met with students and delivered a free masterclass in investigative reporting to Vermont journalists.
A full recording of the event, produced by CCTV, is available online. VTDigger thanks CCTV, Seven Days and the Delta Hotels for helping make the event possible.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware LIVE Weekend Top 10: Festivals, music, Halloween fun and more across the First State
text:
Jazz in Rehoboth, Crafts at Hagley, Children at the Zoo and fun in Middletown. Image created with AI on 10/16
From Hagley’s popular craft fair and the Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival to Halloween celebrations, live opera and community events, Delaware offers something for nearly everyone Oct. 16-18.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Fall is in full swing, and Delaware is serving up a weekend packed with entertainment, family adventures, cultural experiences and opportunities to enjoy the outdoors.
Whether you’re looking for a scenic afternoon shopping for handmade crafts, a night of live music, a family trip to a pumpkin patch or something a little spooky, this weekend offers plenty of reasons to get out and explore the First State.
Delaware LIVE has selected 10 events worth considering for your weekend plans, with activities stretching from the Brandywine Valley to the beaches of Sussex County.
1. Hagley Craft Fair brings artisans to the Brandywine Valley
One of Delaware’s favorite fall traditions returns to the scenic grounds of Hagley Museum and Library this weekend.
The annual Hagley Craft Fair brings together artisans from across the Mid-Atlantic region, offering handmade jewelry, pottery, woodworking, leather goods, textiles, fine art and specialty foods.
The event transforms Hagley’s upper property and Soda House into a marketplace where visitors can meet craftspeople, discover one-of-a-kind gifts and enjoy the natural beauty of the Brandywine Valley.
It’s an ideal outing for those looking to get an early start on holiday shopping while enjoying a Delaware autumn tradition.
To Go: Saturday, Oct. 17, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Sunday, Oct. 18, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington. Advance admission is $10 for adults and $8 for children ages 6-14. Children younger than 6 and Hagley members are admitted free. Tickets are valid both days. Information: hagley.org.



2. ConCon Expo offers an unusual look at conspiracy theories and pop culture


For something completely different, ConCon Expo arrives in Wilmington on Sunday with a convention exploring conspiracy theories, curiosity and the stories people believe.
Inspired by the mockumentary The Conspiracists, the event features an expo and an evening movie presentation followed by a discussion with cast and crew.
Organizers describe the gathering as an inclusive event that focuses less on whether conspiracy theories are true and more on why people find them fascinating.
Hosted by King Creative and Uncultured Swine, ConCon promises one of the weekend’s more unconventional entertainment experiences.
To Go: Sunday, Oct. 18, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. for the expo, followed by a film presentation and discussion from 5 to 7 p.m. Siegel Jewish Community Center, 101 Garden of Eden Road, Wilmington. Tickets and details: theconspiracists.com/concon.



3. Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival fills the coast with music
The beach isn’t just for summer. This weekend, Rehoboth Beach and neighboring coastal communities become destinations for music lovers as the 37th Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival continues through Sunday.
The annual celebration attracts nationally recognized performers and jazz enthusiasts for several days of concerts, intimate performances and special events.
This year’s featured artists include Boney James, Brian Culbertson, Najee, Gerald Albright and other leading performers.
From smooth jazz to high-energy contemporary performances, the festival offers an opportunity to enjoy world-class music while exploring coastal Delaware during one of its most pleasant seasons.
To Go: Thursday through Sunday, Oct. 15-18, at venues throughout the Rehoboth Beach area. Performance times and ticket prices vary. Information and tickets: rehobothjazz.com.
4. Fifer Orchards Fall Fest celebrates the harvest
For families looking to make the most of fall, Fifer Orchards in the Camden-Wyoming area continues its annual Fall Fest.
Visitors can explore a sprawling corn maze, pick pumpkins and apples, enjoy outdoor attractions and sample seasonal favorites, including apple cider, kettle corn and fresh cider doughnuts.
The farm’s harvest celebration combines traditional agricultural experiences with activities designed to entertain children and adults.
With fall colors, pumpkins and plenty of opportunities for family photographs, Fifer’s remains a popular destination for autumn outings.
To Go: Saturday, Oct. 17, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with final entry at 4:30 p.m. Fifer Orchards, Camden-Wyoming. Admission is $18 online or $24 at the gate for ages 3 and older. Additional charges apply to some activities. Closed Sundays. Information: Fifer’s Fall Fest details.



5. Emo Night Brooklyn brings Halloween energy to The Queen




Wilmington’s nightlife gets an early Halloween celebration Friday when Emo Night Brooklyn arrives at The Queen.

The Halloween Edition transforms the venue’s Crown room into a dance party featuring emo, pop-punk and alternative favorites.
Guests are encouraged to dress in costume and enjoy a high-energy evening filled with the songs that defined a generation of alternative music fans.
The event offers a change of pace from traditional Halloween parties, combining nostalgia with a spirited dance-floor atmosphere.
To Go: Friday, Oct. 16, at 8:30 p.m. Doors open at 8 p.m. The Crown at The Queen, Wilmington. Event listed as 18-plus. Tickets: thequeenwilmington.com.



6. OperaDelaware brings Mozart’s ‘Don Giovanni’ to The Grand


Opera lovers and newcomers alike have an opportunity to experience one of Mozart’s most celebrated works as OperaDelaware presents Don Giovanni at The Grand Opera House.
The production blends drama, romance, dark comedy and supernatural themes in the story of a charming but reckless nobleman whose actions eventually catch up with him.
Featuring music by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, the opera offers audiences a chance to experience a major classical production without traveling to Philadelphia or New York.
The performances are sung in Italian with English supertitles.
To Go: Friday, Oct. 16, at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, Oct. 18, at 2 p.m. The Grand Opera House, 818 N. Market St., Wilmington. Tickets listed from $15 to $109. Information: operade.org.



7. Wilmington Rugby hosts Brandywine in regional showdown


For sports fans looking for something beyond football and soccer, Wilmington Rugby Club takes the field Saturday against regional rival Brandywine Rugby Football Club.
Delaware’s oldest men’s rugby club has developed a dedicated following, with its home matches providing an opportunity to experience the fast-paced and physical sport up close.
Rugby combines the movement and endurance of soccer with the contact and strategy of football, creating an exciting atmosphere for spectators.
The fall matchup is a chance to support local athletes and discover a sport that continues to build a following in Delaware.
To Go: Saturday, Oct. 17. The club’s home-match schedule lists Brandywine as the opponent, with a 1 p.m. kickoff indicated in event information supplied to Delaware LIVE. Alapocas Run State Park, 4351 Weldin Road, Wilmington. Confirm kickoff details at wilmingtonrugby.com.



8. Boo at the Zoo offers Halloween fun for families


Halloween arrives early at the Brandywine Zoo, where families can combine a visit with the animals and seasonal activities.
Boo at the Zoo encourages children and adults to wear costumes while enjoying the zoo’s exhibits and Halloween atmosphere.
Unlike some evening Halloween attractions, the zoo’s daytime celebration is designed to be welcoming to younger children.
Families can also take advantage of the opportunity to learn about the animals and participate in educational experiences offered throughout the day.
To Go: Friday through Sunday, Oct. 16-18, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Brandywine Zoo, 1001 N. Park Drive, Wilmington. Activities are included with regular zoo admission unless otherwise noted. Information: brandywinezoo.org.
9. NAMIWalks Delaware brings community together for mental health
One of the weekend’s most meaningful community events takes place Saturday along Wilmington’s Riverfront.
NAMIWalks Delaware brings families, volunteers, mental health advocates and supporters together to raise awareness and funds for programs serving people affected by mental illness.
Organized by the National Alliance on Mental Illness in Delaware, the event emphasizes inclusion, understanding and the importance of community support.
Participants will walk a 3-kilometer route along the Riverwalk, with live entertainment, food trucks and family-friendly activities adding to the experience.
The gathering also offers an opportunity for individuals and families to connect with an organization that provides education, advocacy and support throughout the state.
To Go: Saturday, Oct. 17, with registration beginning at 7:30 a.m. and the 3K walk starting at 9 a.m. Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park, 80 Rosa Parks Drive, Wilmington. Information, registration and donations: namiwalks.org/delaware.


10. Dark Dover Lantern Tours explore the capital’s mysterious past


History takes a spooky turn in Dover as First State Heritage Park offers its Dark Dover Lantern Tour.
The guided evening experience takes participants through the historic heart of Delaware’s capital, sharing stories of murders, mysterious events and characters whose legends remain part of the city’s past.
Against the backdrop of historic buildings and lantern-lit streets, visitors discover a different side of Dover’s long history.
The walking tour offers an alternative to traditional haunted attractions, combining historical storytelling with the atmosphere of an October evening.
To Go: Friday, Oct. 16. First State Heritage Park, Dover. Tickets are listed at $15 per person. Advance registration is required, and space is limited. Confirm tour times and availability through Delaware State Parks reservations or call 302-739-9194.
More weekend fun: Middletown Family Fun Fest
Families in southern New Castle County have another option Saturday when downtown Middletown hosts its Family Fun Fest.
The free community celebration features games, crafts, live music and face painting, offering an affordable outing for families with children.
To Go: Saturday, Oct. 17, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Downtown Middletown, with visitor entrance at 19 W. Green St. Free admission. Information: Middletown Main Street.




















Make the most of a Delaware fall weekend
With festivals, live entertainment, outdoor recreation and community gatherings scheduled across all three counties, the Oct. 16-18 weekend offers something for almost every interest and budget.
For families, Fifer Orchards, the Brandywine Zoo and Middletown Family Fun Fest offer opportunities to spend time together. Music lovers can choose between the Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival, OperaDelaware and a lively night at The Queen.
Those looking for something different can explore ConCon Expo, experience Wilmington Rugby or discover the darker side of Dover’s history.
And for Delawareans seeking to support an important cause, NAMIWalks provides an opportunity to make a difference while enjoying the Wilmington Riverfront.
Whatever your plans, it’s a good weekend to get out, explore and enjoy Delaware.

name: VTDigger
title: Popular Brousseau Mountain trail in Essex County conserved for peregrine falcons and future generations
text:
The view looking southeast from Brousseau Mountain in Norton on September 4, 2021. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger
A remote, scenic hike in the border town of Norton has been permanently preserved for public access.
Ann Sage, who grew up in the tiny Essex County town, and her husband, Victor Peters, sold a 21-acre parcel to the town of Norton this summer, Vermont Land Trust announced earlier this month. The town conserved the parcel, which hosts a quarter mile of the popular Brousseau Mountain Trail, with the land trust.
“We wanted it left for generations to come” and “for the moose and the deer and bear that travel through there and the peregrine falcons that nest on the cliff, just a little ways up from the property,” said Sage, who now lives in Chittenden County, in an interview last week.

The Brousseau Mountain Trail in Norton on September 4, 2021. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

Vermont Land Trust holds the conservation easements on more than 650,000 acres, covering over 11% of the state. The easements are permanent legal agreements limiting development and protecting land for farming, forestry, nature, clean water or recreation. Such easements sometimes qualify the owner for reduced property or income taxes.
The Brousseau Mountain Trail, which Sage said has been open since the 1970s, is a short, moderate hike with a round-trip distance of 1.6 miles and around 600 feet of elevation gain. After leaving the now-town-owned parcel, it traverses an already-conserved working forest to reach the 2,723-foot peak.
A cliff lookout near the top provides extensive views to the southeast over Little Averill Lake and into New Hampshire. The cliff is also host to the nests of peregrine falcons, one of the fastest creatures on the planet. The raptors almost went extinct due to pesticide poisoning in the middle of the 20th century. Visitors are advised to avoid nesting areas during the birds’ incubation period of March through August.
Views across the border into Canada are visible on the hike back down.
“We wanted to keep the magical, pristine peacefulness of the whole area intact,” Sage said.
The property directly connects to thousands more acres of conserved forestland that is open for non-motorized, recreational public access.
“We just didn’t want to take the chance of selling the land to individuals that might consider closing the trail,” Sage said. “I adore the idea that nothing is going to happen to it because Vermont Land Trust has stewardship of the property.”
Norton voters approved the acquisition at this year’s Town Meeting, according to the meeting minutes. The cost of acquiring and conserving the property — assessed at $43,000 — was covered by the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and private donations, said Kerry O’Brien, project director for the land trust, in an email.
The town’s acquisition of the property means it will lose $983 annually in tax revenue, a tradeoff voters found worthwhile for its permanent protection.
Brousseau Mountain (on right) as seen from the south on September 4, 2021. Peregrine falcons nest on the mountain’s cliffs. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger
The trail will continue to be managed by the NorthWoods Stewardship Center in East Charleston. NorthWoods runs summer camps and outdoor programs that regularly include the hike up Brousseau Mountain. It also runs the Northeast Kingdom Mountain Challenge, a hiking challenge checklist that consists of 20 mountains in northeastern Vermont — including Brousseau Mountain.
“The Brousseau Mountain Trail is such an important part of our community,” said Stephanie Thibault, Norton Selectboard member, in a press release. “It’s a great hike and a beautiful view. We are thrilled that it’s protected and will be enjoyed for generations.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Original governor’s mansion in Helena to reopen to tours
text:
An interior room at the Original Governor's Mansion in Helena. (Montana Historical Society photo)Following the completion of exterior restoration work, the original governor’s mansion has been reopened to the public, the Montana Historical Society said in a press release.
Built in 1888, the 21-room mansion will be open, with registration, for tours at 1:30 p.m. and 2:30 p.m., every Saturday. The state bought the property in 1913 and it served as the home for nine Montana Governors and their families. The building was closed in 2025 for repairs.
The Original Governor’s Mansion. (Montana Historical Society photo)
Workers repaired and repainted the upper balustrade, main level deck, and front porch, the press release said.
“The restoration gave the mansion’s exterior the care it deserved, and now visitors can see the results firsthand,” Darby Bramble, museum education officer with the Montana Historical Society said in a press release. “Our tours bring the Victorian era to life through artifacts and stories from the families who lived here, and now we have the added dimension of talking about what it takes to preserve a historic home like this one.”
The Montana Historical Society is also hosting two upcoming special events at the mansion. From 5 p.m., to 7 p.m., on Oct. 31, the museum will have Halloween-themed tours. And on Nov. 27, the original governor’s mansion will host a holiday-themed event.
Registration is required for both of those events, the release stated.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Proposed Mason County data center could get $50 million annual tax break, think tank estimates
text:
Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill says the data center developer would get "the bulk" of its water from the Ohio River. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)A proposed Mason County data center campus for the technology company Meta could avoid paying about $50 million a year in local taxes through a tentative agreement between the county and Meta, according to a new analysis from a progressive think tank. 
In its Friday analysis, the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy estimates the local property tax break offered by the county to Meta would “dramatically reduce” the company’s taxes to the county government and local schools, even when accounting for smaller annual payments Meta would make directly to the county and schools as a substitute for paying the local taxes. 
Jason Bailey, the executive director of the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, told the Lantern the think tank doesn’t want the “enormous” local tax break offered in Mason County to become “a template for other data center projects across the state.” 
“What Meta is giving or providing in payments to Mason County is a small fraction of what they would pay if they were taxed fully in the way that other businesses and residents of Mason County are,” Bailey said. “That is supposed to be one of the draws or attractions of data centers, but we’re already seeing much of that being evaded away.” 
The think tank, pulling from details provided in the community benefits agreement, estimates the county and local schools would receive about $59 million annually in local property taxes without the bonds. In contrast, the agreement calls for Meta to pay the county about $5 million annually and the local school district about $2 million annually as a substitute for paying the taxes.
Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, recently settled a multistate lawsuit over whether its products harmed young people; Kentucky will get $358 million in that deal. A Meta spokesperson did not immediately provide a response Friday afternoon to an emailed Lantern request for comment about the analysis. 
Democratic Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill did not immediately respond to emails and text messages sent Friday afternoon requesting a phone interview about the analysis. McNeill, a backer of the project, revealed Meta’s involvement during a fiscal court meeting this month after it had been a secret to the public for over a year. 
The think tank’s analysis primarily focuses on what are known as industrial revenue bonds offered by the county that will exempt the data center campus from paying local property taxes. 
The Lantern reported a tentative community benefits agreement between the county and a subsidiary of Meta states that it will invest billions of dollars into the project’s initial phase but will also receive those bonds from the county that are set to last 40 years.
The detailed local tax breaks also do not account for the state-level sales tax break on data center equipment passed by the GOP-controlled state legislature, which the think tank estimates could give an additional $400 million-plus tax break for the initial phase of the Meta data center. 
Some Republican state lawmakers have hinted at rolling back that sales tax break when lawmakers reconvene next year. That sales tax break would have to be approved by a state economic development board that meets later this month. 
Bailey said their latest analysis is a “rough estimate” that makes “a lot of assumptions”, including how much of the value of taxed property of the data center campus will be the equipment — the computers, for example — and how much value will be the land and buildings on the campus.
But he said the think tank wanted to get an initial understanding of the scale of the local tax break, arguing it deserves as much scrutiny as state-level tax breaks that could benefit data center developers. 
“I think as much attention, if not more, needs to go to the local taxation,” Bailey said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: ‘I want to live now’: Indiana death row inmate makes clemency plea ahead of execution
text:
Jeffrey Weisheit answers questions during his Oct. 16, 2026, clemency hearing at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. Board members questioned him about the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch and whether he could safely serve a life sentence. (Screenshot from livestream)Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit asked Indiana’s parole board Friday to let him live out his life in prison, but repeatedly struggled to explain why anger at his girlfriend led him to kill her two young children.
During 64 minutes of questioning at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City, Weisheit apologized for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb.
He described placing a phone book on an electric stove burner, turning it on and leaving the house with both children still inside. He also spoke of his religious conversion and said he wants to keep helping others behind bars.
Alyssa Lynch, 8, and her brother, Caleb, 5, were killed in a 2010 house fire set by Jeffrey Weisheit. Weisheit is seeking clemency ahead of his scheduled Nov. 5 execution. (Courtesy photo)
Board members pressed him on his account of the killings, his prison disciplinary record and his reluctance to seek mental health treatment while incarcerated. They repeatedly asked whether his struggles to manage anger, cope with stress and resolve conflicts could endanger other prisoners or correctional staff if his death sentence were commuted to life without parole.
“There is no excuse or explanation for what I did,” said Weisheit, 50, who appeared with attorney Joseph Perkovich.
The livestreamed interview opened the board’s consideration of his clemency request ahead of his scheduled Nov. 5 execution. Public testimony is scheduled Monday in Indianapolis. The five-member panel will then make a nonbinding recommendation to Gov. Mike Braun, who will decide whether to spare the inmate’s life.
Weisheit became noticeably emotional and cried while discussing Bible passages about Jesus healing and helping others, including the account of a Roman centurion whose servant Jesus healed.
But much of the hearing centered on the murders and what board members could rely on in assessing his request for mercy.
“The word sorry cannot be enough, but I am so sorry to Lisa Lynch and her family, and Steve Lynch and his family,” Weisheit said.
He said he thinks about the children every day and hopes to remain a son, brother and uncle to relatives who have continued supporting him.
 Board members press for answers about killings
Weisheit was caring for the children while their mother, Lisa Lynch, worked the night of April 9, 2010. Firefighters found their bodies after responding to the burning Evansville home early the next morning.
A jury convicted him of two counts of murder and arson in 2013 and recommended a death sentence.
On Friday, Weisheit described financial strain, disagreements over caring for the children and his belief that Lisa Lynch had betrayed him. He said he had become consumed with thinking about the issue in the weeks before the killings.
He told the board that the children had watched a Disney movie and fallen asleep before he sent them to bed. He later spoke with their mother by phone.
Afterward, he said, he grew increasingly angry.
Caleb got out of bed wanting to play, Weisheit said. He acknowledged binding the boy with duct tape, putting a rag in his mouth to keep him from screaming and placing him on his bed.
Alyssa remained in her own bed, he said.



Quotation







I don’t understand why I got so mad ... I can’t explain it.


– death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit


Weisheit said he packed belongings into his car and decided to set the fire just before leaving. He denied setting the fire during his 2013 trial, court records show.
Court records also detail preparations he made before the killings: He stopped payments on an engagement ring, told the jeweler he was leaving the country, quit his job and withdrew the money in his bank account.
He fled to Kentucky, where police apprehended him following a high-speed chase.
Board members Friday questioned him about road flares found under and around Caleb’s body. Weisheit acknowledged buying flares and keeping them in the house but denied placing them near the boy.
He offered no explanation for how they got there. At one point, he speculated that police or emergency responders could have been responsible, without providing evidence for that suggestion.
One board member asked why he had not simply left the house without hurting the children. Another asked why he directed his anger toward them rather than their mother.
Weisheit said he could not hurt Lisa Lynch because she was pregnant with his child.
He repeatedly said he could not explain his actions. He also denied being under the influence of alcohol or drugs at the time.
“I don’t understand why I got so mad,” he said. “I just, I don’t know, I don’t know why, why I can’t explain it.”
A life beyond death row
Board members devoted much of the hearing to whether Weisheit could safely spend the rest of his life in prison.
Weisheit said he takes pride in his sanitation duties in the prison, focuses on keeping his surroundings clean and tries to help other prisoners. He described buying snacks for others on his unit and said he wants to continue contributing to the prison community.
“I want to live now,” he said. “I want to try to make things better as much as I can, especially in prisons, because I see how bad, like this prison, it’s managed.”
Still, board members questioned how he would manage conflict if he moved out of death row and into the prison’s general population, particularly if he had to share a cell.
Weisheit said he generally tries to find common ground with others and retreats to his cell when tensions rise.
Board member Mia Kelsaw asked what he would do if the source of conflict was his cellmate. Weisheit said he would try talking to the person and seek help from a correctional officer.
Chairwoman Gwendolyn Horth also questioned how statements about his Christian faith fit with his prison disciplinary record.
She noted an incident involving fecal matter. Weisheit denied throwing it at anyone, saying he had kept it in a cooler in his cell because he feared another prisoner would attack him. He said officers required him to empty it into a toilet.
Outside the Indiana State Prison on Monday, May 19, 2025, in Michigan City. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
He also disputed the circumstances of other incidents, including possessing a broken squeegee handle and blocking his cell’s lock with cardboard. He said he intended to repair the cleaning tool and used the cardboard because he feared other prisoners could enter his cell.
Those explanations prompted another board member to question how he would handle pressure in a different prison setting — and how the board could be assured he would not harm someone during another episode of distress.
Weisheit maintained that being around more people could be better than spending years with the same small group on death row. He said he gets along with the prisoners currently housed there, although they sometimes get on one another’s nerves.
“We’re the same five people,” he said. “We don’t get to see much of anybody else other than (correctional officers). And COs don’t like coming in because we talk them to death.”
Later, Kelsaw questioned why Weisheit had spent so much time discussing his relationship with Lisa Lynch and comparatively little describing the steps he took to kill the children. She also questioned why he had not taken advantage of available mental health services in prison.
Weisheit said he was afraid to discuss personal matters with counselors. By the end of the hearing, though, he said he would like to speak with someone.
“I wish you had have taken the opportunity to get some help, so that you could be able to figure out what in the world was going on with you,” Kelsaw said. “Every opportunity you have, you take what’s offered, and you work on you.”
Questions remain over brain injuries
Weisheit repeatedly attributed difficulties throughout his life to problems with his brain. He described childhood head injuries, trouble concentrating and fears about medication.
He said he was not taking psychiatric medication. When a board member asked about his bipolar disorder diagnosis, he continued to emphasize his belief that brain damage was the underlying problem.
His attorneys are seeking additional brain imaging and a two-week execution delay. They contend that evidence of brain injuries, mental illness and childhood trauma was not adequately developed in earlier proceedings.

The lawyers want MRI and PET scans and further analysis to help establish whether abnormalities preceded the murders. Weisheit also suffered a head injury when police used a Taser during his arrest and he fell. The extent and timing of earlier injuries have been disputed in court.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker approved funding for further investigative work Sept. 16 but denied the transportation request Oct. 7. His attorneys have since turned to the Indiana Supreme Court, asking that his execution move from Nov. 5 to Nov. 19.
The state Supreme Court set deadlines for both sides to submit additional arguments on the transportation and scheduling requests. The state’s response is due at 4:30 p.m. Friday, and Weisheit’s attorneys have until 4:30 p.m. Monday to reply.
The court has not yet ruled on either request. Weisheit’s execution remains scheduled for Nov. 5.
Tears over Scripture
Asked about his faith, Weisheit said he had been baptized and had read the Bible seven times from beginning to end. He said he’s currently reading it again.
“I’ve made my peace with God,” he said. “I’ve talked to Him. I’ve got baptized.”
When Horth asked his favorite book, he described passages about Jesus helping people.
‘Jeffrey, I forgive you’: Father of slain children supports clemency for Indiana death row inmate

“My favorite parts are mainly when Jesus is helping somebody,” he said.
Weisheit became visibly emotional and cried while talking about his faith.
“I’m still learning,” Weisheit said.
He said he has cut back on swearing and tries to watch his words and behavior as he continues learning about his faith.
Horth acknowledged that faith near the hearing’s close.
“I love that you have found the Lord,” she said. “We all live in a broken world, but we will be in paradise.”
“But I want you to know that I do believe, from what I heard from you, that you have transformed and have that relationship right now,” she continued “I’m grateful for that.”
The board did not announce a clemency recommendation Friday and does not expect to before Oct. 23.
Public testimony scheduled for Monday
Friday’s interview followed a plea for clemency from the children’s father, Steven Lynch, who signed an affidavit supporting life imprisonment without parole.
“What good does it do the memory of my children to put this man to death?” Lynch wrote before concluding his affidavit with “Jeffrey, I forgive you.”
Perkovich previously emphasized that Lynch speaks for himself and does not represent the views of all the children’s relatives.
Weisheit was the first Indiana death row prisoner to personally answer the board’s questions in a clemency interview since Benjamin Ritchie in May 2025.
Joseph Corcoran did not seek clemency before his December 2024 execution. Roy Lee Ward declined a prison interview with the board last year, although his attorneys presented his clemency case during the public hearing in Indianapolis.
The board recommended against clemency for Ritchie, and Braun allowed his execution to proceed. Braun also denied Ward’s clemency request.
Weisheit’s execution would be Indiana’s fourth since the state resumed executions in December 2024 after a 15-year pause.
Under the current schedule, the board will hear public testimony Monday, Oct. 19, in conference rooms 1 and 2 at the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis. Testimony supporting clemency is scheduled from 9 to 11 a.m., followed by testimony opposing it from 1 to 3 p.m.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: On Connecticut bear hunt, Gov. Lamont and GOP challenger Fazio find common ground
text:
A black bear tagged by the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection to track the species' population. (Courtesy CT DEEP)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
When it comes to Connecticut’s increasingly troublesome relationship with black bears, both candidates in this year’s governor’s race are in agreement on a somewhat controversial solution.
Gov. Ned Lamont, the Democratic incumbent, and his opponent, Republican Sen. Ryan Fazio, have both supported measures in recent years to allow the hunting of black bears. Those efforts have been repeatedly defeated by opponents of hunting who argue that non-lethal means can be effective at reducing conflicts with people.
Connecticut is home to between 1,000 and 1,200 black bears, with the population concentrated largely in the state’s northwest corner. Encounters with people — including home break-ins and attacks on livestock — have risen in recent years, according to wildlife officials.
However, Connecticut is one of only two states in the Northeast that does not allow bear hunting. The other, Rhode Island, has fewer than a dozen bears. A Coventry, Rhode Island, resident recently posted a video of a bear walking onto her front steps and tearing at her home’s siding shingles, apparently trying to reach a wasp nest underneath the shingles.
The state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, which tracks and helps manage the state’s bear population, has repeatedly sought support from lawmakers to establish a regulated hunting season, with Lamont’s backing. Lamont was also asked about the idea during a Democratic primary debate in July, saying he supported a hunt. His opponent in the primary, Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden, said he was opposed.
“The governor supports a limited and carefully regulated bear hunt because Connecticut’s bear population is continuing to grow and we’re seeing more and more conflicts between bears and people every year,” Lamont campaign spokesperson Lauren Gray said in a statement. “Bears are now in all 169 towns, and residents are dealing with bears getting into homes, damaging property and threatening pets and livestock. We’ve tried education, prevention and other measures, and those efforts will continue, but the governor believes we also need to have additional tools available to manage the population and keep people safe.”
Gray added, “That doesn’t mean an unlimited hunt. Any hunt should be regulated and based on the best available science, with DEEP determining the appropriate limits.”
The most recent serious effort to enact a bear hunt came in 2025, when a bill dealing with the killing of nuisance bears was amended in the Senate to give the governor the ability to order DEEP to schedule a hunting season if the number of conflicts rise to a level that poses “a threat to public safety.” Fazio voted for the amended bill, which passed the chamber on a bipartisan vote of 34-2.
In the House, however, opponents amended the bill again in the final hours of the legislative session to remove the language permitting a hunt. The bill died upon returning to the Senate.
In an interview last week, Fazio said that having a “controlled and regulated bear hunt” is necessary to protect public safety. He specifically pointed to an incident in 2022, when a black bear attacked and injured a 12-year-old boy in Morris.
“We know the bear population is increasing at an unsustainable rate, especially in northwest and north-central and western Connecticut,” Fazio said. “Bears are smarter animals than most, and they have no fear of human beings because of our state policy currently.”
Fazio also criticized the governor’s lack of success in getting a bear hunting bill through the legislature, despite having a 2-1 majority of Democrats in both chambers.
“I think if you can’t get it done in eight years and you think it should get done, then you have a problem, and you deserve some criticism for it,” Fazio said.
In the absence of a hunt, DEEP has focused its efforts to reduce conflicts on a public awareness campaign encouraging residents to take steps such as removing bird feeders and keeping trash cans indoors between the spring and fall, when bears are most active.
In this July 25, 2014, file photo, a black bear in captivity awaits handouts at the the Maine Wildlife Park in Gray, Maine.
DEEP also hired a team of researchers from Mississippi State University this summer to conduct the first scientific survey of the state’s bear population in more than a decade. The results of that survey are expected to be released in the spring.
Sen. Christine Cohen, D-Guilford, a former chair of the legislature’s Environment Committee who has been an outspoken opponent of bear hunting, said state officials lack the data on bear population growth they’d need to determine whether a hunt is necessary. In the meantime, she said, more can be done to condition bears to avoid humans.
“I still contend that if the problem we’re trying to solve is bears coming into neighborhoods, which is what we hear over and over again, killing them doesn’t address the underlying cause — which is really the availability of human food,” Cohen said.
In 2023, Lamont signed a measure passed by lawmakers clarifying the circumstances in which bears may be killed in self-defense and allowing DEEP to issue permits to farmers whose crops or livestock were damaged by nuisance bears. The law also made it illegal to intentionally feed “potentially dangerous animals,” including bobcats, coyotes and bears.
DEEP has since issued 21 permits stemming from agricultural damage, resulting in the lawful killing of 36 bears.
The agency has also charged at least seven people with unauthorized killings of black bears since 2012. The majority of those cases involved claims of self-defense or defense of animals, according to a review published in CT Insider.
