name: Connecticut Mirror
title: More CT landfills are being topped with solar panels
text:
From their perch overlooking a busy stretch of Interstate 95 in New Haven, the 1,900 solar panels that sit atop the city’s old landfill are a prominent display of a growing trend in Connecticut.
The solar array, built by Greenskies Clean Energy, is one of at least 29 large arrays that have been built or approved to be built on top of closed, capped landfills — a number that will likely increase in the coming years, according to state officials and developers.
That number is from the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, which must approve permits to construct projects on top of capped landfills. Those caps are designed to prevent the spread of leachate and other pollutants into the environment. The agency is currently reviewing permit applications at four other capped landfills, according to a spokesman.
Ryan Linares is the vice president of land acquisition at Greenskies, a solar energy company that opened its first two solar landfills in 2016 in Meriden and North Haven. Since then, its portfolio has grown to include landfills in Fairfield, West Haven and East Haven.
Its newest facility, the one in New Haven, opened in July.
While many of the state’s 294 closed landfills are candidates for solar fields, not all are.
Linares said that his company typically looks for landfills with a flat “plateau” of about 5 acres, which he said is large enough for a 1 megawatt facility. Proximity to existing electrical infrastructure is also essential to allow the solar array to connect to the local power grid.
One of the benefits that solar developers see in landfills is that they are usually town-owned and have limited opportunities to be sold or put to other productive uses. Companies can also make use of state incentives for the redevelopment of brownfield sites. 
“It’s a very good argument to say that this is the highest and best use, and we typically don’t see much pushback on that,” Linares said.  
Because landfills are contaminated areas, penetration of the cap, or the material sealing the landfill, is usually not permitted. It’s for that reason that large, shady trees are often prevented from growing over the cap — allowing plenty of access for sunlight. 
The number of solar fields on landfills has increased in the past decade. Since 2023, six projects have been approved by the Connecticut Siting Council, which has jurisdiction over projects with a capacity over 1 megawatt. (Smaller projects, such as those developed by Greenskies, are subject to local jurisdictions).
Linares said that Greenskies’ own portfolio of landfill arrays will likely double in size by the end of next year as it wraps up projects that are under active development.
“The programs in the state of Connecticut [are] really incentivizing development on brownfield or landfill properties, as opposed to other vacant pieces of property that aren’t brownfields or landfills,” he said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan engineer who helped expose Flint Water Crisis files for injunction to block EPA policy
text:
Elin Warn Betanzo, president and founder of Safe Water Engineering LLCAfter filing a lawsuit seeking the reinstatement of her position on the Environmental Protection Agency’s National Drinking Water Advisory Council, Elin Warn Betanzo is aiming to block the EPA policy it used to justify her dismissal.
Warn Betanzo is the head of a Detroit-based drinking water consulting firm and is among the individuals who helped to uncover the Flint water crisis. After signing on to a declaration of dissent along with hundreds of other EPA employees in July 2025, Warn Betanzo was removed from her role on the advisory council.
The declaration argued President Donald Trump’s Administration had undermined the agency’s mission of protecting human health and the environment. Employees who signed it were placed on leave, with the EPA saying in a statement that it has a “zero-tolerance policy for career bureaucrats unlawfully undermining, sabotaging, and undercutting the administration’s agenda as voted for by the great people of this country last November.”
In June 2026, Warn Betanzo filed a lawsuit against the EPA and its administrator, Lee Zeldin, arguing they had violated her First Amendment rights by suspending her for criticizing agency leadership.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Wednesday, Warn Betanzo filed a request for a preliminary injunction, ordering Zeldin and the EPA to cease enforcement of its dissent policy and reinstate her to her position on the National Drinking Water Advisory Council.
“There is no way to interpret the ‘zero tolerance’ policy as constitutionally valid,” Warn Betanzo’s attorneys wrote in their request to U.S. District Court Judge Susan K. DeClercq. 
“The policy’s broad, standardless language and the EPA’s pattern of unconstitutional enforcement leave no room for reinterpretation,” the attorneys wrote, later stating “If left intact, the policy will continue to intimidate employees into silence.”
The EPA said it does not comment on pending litigation “in keeping with a longstanding practice.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Kosta Diamantis’ second criminal trial delayed until 2027
text:
A second criminal trial for Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis, the former Connecticut budget director turned federal fugitive, has been delayed until June 2027.
U.S. District Judge Stefan Underhill held a status conference with federal prosecutors and Diamantis’ defense attorney on Friday morning to decide how to handle his second criminal case, in which he is accused of accepting bribes in return for helping to cancel a state audit into suspected Medicaid fraud.
Diamantis’s second corruption trial had been scheduled to begin in early December, but after he fled to Greece last month in order to avoid imprisonment, the parties in the case have agreed that the case should be delayed until next year.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Francis told Underhill on Friday that the legal arguments leading up to the second trial could change based on whether Diamantis is apprehended and returned to the United States before June.
But it was suggested on the conference call that the trial would move ahead regardless of whether Diamantis is in the courtroom or not. 
Diamantis has drawn international media attention in recent months after he obtained a Greek passport and fled the United States to avoid being sentenced to seven years in prison for soliciting bribes from school construction contractors.
During his first criminal trial last year, Diamantis was convicted of 21 counts of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and lying to federal investigators, after the jury agreed that he used his public office to financially benefit himself and his family.
Diamantis is expected to face similar allegations in his second criminal trial. In that case, prosecutors have alleged that Diamantis assisted Helen Zervas, a Connecticut eye doctor who was being investigated for potential Medicaid fraud. 
According to the indictment in the case, Diamantis pressured other state officials to cancel an audit of Zervas’ optometry practice, and later accepted $95,000 in payments from her and her fiancé, former state lawmaker Chris Ziogas.
In court records, prosecutors cited several communications they obtained between Zervas and Diamantis. In one of those messages, Diamantis asked Zervas to calculate what it was worth to her to “avoid criminal fraud charges.” 
Both Zervas and Ziogas have already pleaded guilty in federal court. 
Federal prosecutors told Underhill on Friday that they expected the criminal trial in June to take roughly a week. 
Whether Diamantis is in attendance during that week, however, is still a question. 
During his criminal sentencing hearing in September, prosecutors clarified that Diamantis had obtained dual citizenship in Greece, which could make it more difficult  to extradite him to the United States. 
Prosecutors said that Diamantis had been in contact with federal officials and had made plans to meet with a federal agent at the airport in Athens in order to voluntarily return to the United States. 
But Diamantis never arrived for that rendezvous, they said. 
Since then, Diamantis has conducted dozens of interviews with Connecticut media outlets, including the Connecticut Mirror, during which he has asserted that he is the victim of a political prosecution.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Cincinnati Public Schools has served hundreds with first-in-the-nation sleep lot for families
text:
The modular unit and playground at Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot at William Howard Taft Elementary School. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).Cincinnati Public Schools is the first school district in the nation to own and operate a parking lot where families experiencing homelessness can go to at night and sleep in their cars.
Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot opened April 30 at William Howard Taft Elementary School and more than 300 people have slept in the lot so far, said Megan Rahill, shelter and housing specialist with Project Connect.
“A lot of times, when you’re sleeping in your car, it’s because you’ve exhausted all your social avenues of people you can stay with, and so they’re often feeling so isolated and like nobody cares anymore, and they’re on their own,” Rahill said. “If they’ve already been sleeping in their car, it’s just on a dead-end street and it’s scary, so we’ve got a space you can come to where other people and other kids are there, there’s food and you don’t have to worry about where you’re going to the restroom.”
Project Connect is a program that provides support to students in the district experiencing homelessness under the federal McKinney-Vento Act that supports the enrollment and education of homeless students by making sure homeless youth have access to a public education.
Nearly 8% of Cincinnati Public School students — about 2,650 — experienced homelessness during the 2025-26 school year, according to data from the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce.
The number of students experiencing homelessness in the district has mostly been on the rise in the last five years — up from about 2,000 students experiencing homelessness during the 2021-22 school year, according to ODEW data.
The district also noticed a “pretty significant increase” of families experiencing homelessness sleeping in their cars, said Project Connect Manager Rebeka Beach.
Families sleeping in their cars often do not know where to safely park their car overnight. Sometimes, they would park somewhere and feel unsafe or the police would ask them to move, Rahill said.
“It was hard to have a consistent spot or they’re parked in the Kroger parking lot, but then you’re worried maybe someone I know will see me,” she said.
People staying in their cars often don’t have a place to go to the bathroom, shower, access water, or cook food.
“I had a parent tell me ‘We feel like we’re just like animals. We don’t have facilities that we can use. We’re trapped in this little vehicle,” Rahill said.
A street outreach worker from Greater Cincinnati Behavioral Health Services has to see someone sleeping in their car in order to have them verified to be put on a homeless shelter waiting list.
“We were hearing so often from parents that it was taking so long to get verified just to get on the waiting list for shelter because they moved so much throughout the night they couldn’t connect with the street outreach worker,” said Beach, who has been working for the district for nearly twenty years.
“In one week we had two parents who came in and said they had lost their employment because they’d fallen asleep just because they were up watching their children during the night and couldn’t sleep.”
That’s when the district started looking into some ideas to help families.
Project Connect discovered San Diego’s Safe Sleeping Program and Long Beach City College’s Safe Parking Program, so they went on a research trip to California.
“We decided we wanted to open our own safe sleep lot,” Beach said.
Once Project Connect had the idea for the Safe Sleep Lot, it took just under a year for the lot to open.
“One of the reasons that we created the lot was that that the process (to get verified) can be quite cumbersome for a family,” Rahill said.
“It’s so early in the morning that they’re coming. Oftentimes our families are going to work, they’re taking the kids to school, they’ve been ships passing in the night.”
When a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, they are automatically verified and added to a shelter waiting list.
“The Safe Sleep Lot serves as a bridge to shelter, so families sleep in the lot, they’re verified within 24 hours,” Beach said.
  How the Safe Sleep Lot operates 

The Safe Sleep Lot has 12 spaces and is open daily from 9:30 p.m. to 6:30 a.m. There are typically between three to eight families that stay in the lot every night.
A family gets referred to the Safe Sleep Lot and then Project Connect does an intake appointment. Once they are accepted, families receive a bag with pillows, towels, blankets, and laundry pods. The kids also get to pick out a stuffed animal.
Each family that stays in the lot gets a parking pass with a unique code that security scans when they arrive for the night to help keep track of who is staying in the lot.
After a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, Rahill is able to get them on the shelter waiting list. She also gets the family a hotel stay.
Project Connect can put a family in a hotel for up to two weeks if they have CareSource as their health insurance provider. A family will still get a hotel stay if they don’t have CareSource, but instead it’s for four to six nights.
“We are quite transparent with them that it’s unlikely that the shelter placement will come through while you’re in the hotel,” Rahill said.
She encourages families to use that time in the hotel to try to find somewhere to stay.
“Most of the families are on that trajectory of Safe Sleep Lot, emergency hotel stay back to the Safe Sleep Lot on a waiting list,” Beach said.
There is no limit on how many nights a family can stay at the Safe Sleep Lot and the average wait time to get into a shelter typically ranges from one to two months, Beach said.
The Safe Sleep Lot has security, a library, wifi and a tutoring program will soon be available to families on Wednesday nights.
The Safe Sleep Lot is open March through November.
“We’re not really comfortable having people there when it’s really cold,” Rahill said.
Christ Church Cathedral will be able to host families during the winter months.
Project Connect built a modular unit through grant funds complete with a kitchen area, showers, bathrooms, and room for security. There are frozen meals, snacks, breakfast items, and hygiene items. A local nonprofit has also partnered with the Safe Sleep Lot to provide laundry services to families.
Project Connect is going to build a pergola so families can have a place to sit and stretch their legs.
The Safe Sleep Lot has led to more students being enrolled in school and some students are now enrolled at Taft Elementary School.
“We do have quite a few students who now go to (Taft Elementary) because we were able to use the address of the Safe Sleep Lot,” Rahill said. “They’re just taking their kids to school in the morning from the Safe Sleep Lot.”
“Once they get into shelter or to a more stable address, then the next step is we we set up transportation for them, so that they can stay at the same school. The closer we get to that really stable point, the attendance starts to rise.”
For students experiencing homelessness, Beach likened it to Maslow’s hierarchy of needs.
“If your basic needs are not being met, you’re not positioned to learn,” she said.
“Our goal is for families to be able to sustain jobs that provide for livable wages and be able to sustain housing and exit shelter.”
She hopes other school districts will be able to create their own version of the Safe Sleep Lot and was, at one point, receiving calls daily asking how the district made the lot.
“I really want to build a blueprint out of how we did it, so that it’s replicable,” Beach said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Coastal regulators OK revised Cliff Walk repair plan; path could reopen as soon as 2028
text:
A fence and barrier close off access to Newport's Cliff Walk and detour signs point the way on Narragansett Avenue in this May 2025 photo. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)The rocky road to restoring Newport’s Cliff Walk has cleared a significant obstacle after the city secured permission from Rhode Island coastal regulators.
The Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council (CRMC) approved a revised repair plan at its meeting Tuesday. The unanimous vote, made with little discussion, paves the way to restore the public walking path and reopen as early as 2028. Sections of the Cliff Walk have been closed for more than four years due to structural collapses during severe weather. 
The CRMC previously considered, but opted not to issue a decision, on the $23 million repair project, which is funded through a $13.8 million federal grant, a $6.25 million congressional appropriation and a $3 million state bond.
At its initial hearing in July, the CRMC instead told city engineers and the adjacent private property owners to consider alternatives. At issue was proposed restoration work on a 25-foot sliver of bluffs situated in the middle of the repair site spanning the path between Webster Street and Narragansett Avenue. While the Cliff Walk is public, this section is flanked by a private overlook included with the Gilded Age mansion behind it. 
CRMC staff concluded that the stone work proposed below the private overlook was unnecessary, with no public benefit to stabilizing private property. Attorneys and engineers representing the Ochre Point estate known as “Southside” initially resisted, insisting the riprap was critical to stabilizing the public pathway on either side of it, and an adjacent stone arch bridge.
Mandated by the CRMC at its July 13 meeting to consider alternatives, the team came up with seven options, settling on one that satisfied all the parties involved.
The revised repair plan uses a few dozen steel bars to anchor the bedrock below the overlook, a process known as rock doweling, without requiring a special exception from the CRMC at all.
“This alternative removes the prohibited activity — fill in tidal waters — and provides the best option to protect not only the bridge and the overlook, but the public accessible cliff walk itself,” Richard Lucia, CRMC engineer, wrote in a Sept. 16 memo, recommending the CRMC approve the revised plan.
The stone bridge will be secured with foundational drilling at its base, Lucia wrote.
Who will pay for ongoing maintenance of the bridge — the price for which was not specified — remains unclear. 
Girard Galvin, Newport city solicitor, told coastal regulators at Tuesday’s meeting that he expected Ochre Point owners to continue to be responsible for maintenance. But Turner Scott, the attorney for Ochre Point, replied that his client was not going to cover the cost, suggesting it could be taken from the public funds for the renovation project.
The public funding for the project may restrict spending on private property, council members pointed out. But the rules governing state and federal funding are not part of the CRMC’s purview, Mark Hartmann, CRMC counsel, said during the meeting.
Thomas Shevlin, a spokesperson for the city, said in an interview Friday that maintenance costs for the private bridge would likely be a shared responsibility between the city and the property owners, much like other aspects of the pedestrian walkway, for which ownership remains unclear.
“I don’t know that we can really weigh until there’s an actual instance where we need to think about who’s responsible for what piece of the bridge work,” Shevlin said. “A lot of it would depend on individual circumstances.”
The timeline for repairs will depend on the success of the city’s competitive solicitation for engineers and construction firms to do the work, and an outstanding permission from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Shevlin said. The city needed CRMC approval before seeking the Army Corps of Engineers’ permit.
“I think we’d need one good working season to get this thing done,” Shevlin said, suggesting the walkway could reopen sometime in 2028.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma state superintendent candidates seek more unified approach to education
text:
Democrat Jennettie Marshall, left, and Republican Robert Franklin, right, are running in the Nov. 3 general election for Oklahoma state superintendent. (Photos provided)OKLAHOMA CITY — Two candidates hoping to lead a more collaborative Oklahoma State Department of Education are running for superintendent of public instruction.
Voters will choose between Republican Robert Franklin and Democrat Jennettie Marshall in the Nov. 3 general election. The winner will govern the state’s public schools system as the head of both the Education Department and the Oklahoma State Board of Education.
While Marshall touted her administrative experience in law enforcement and as a member of the Tulsa Board of Education, Franklin said his 45 years working as a teacher and leader in K-12 schools, CareerTech and higher education make him the most qualified candidate for the role. 
Both candidates said they want to improve Oklahoma’s poor academic outcomes and support teachers rather than focus on political divisions.
“That seems to be something that we’re hand in hand on,” Franklin said. “So now, what’s the differentiating factor? To me, it goes down to the experience.”
Franklin, 66, of Sand Springs, said his top priority would be to unify school districts, higher education institutions, tribal nations and other key stakeholders to address Oklahoma’s teacher workforce shortage. Boosting the pipeline of future teachers with programs like Union High School’s educational leadership course could be scaled statewide, he said.
State superintendent candidate Robert Franklin speaks at a campaign event in Edmond on Aug. 3. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma could keep teachers in the classroom with regionally competitive pay, he said, and by hiring more counselors and behavioral health specialists to help address classroom disruptions.
Franklin also proposed opening regional service centers at higher education campuses across the state where Education Department staff could bring professional development, particularly in early literacy and math, and other resources to nearby public schools.
Marshall, 68, of Tulsa, suggested hosting regional problem-solving sessions each month to more quickly address local concerns. 
She said Oklahoma must do better than aim for the regional average in teacher pay. Respect for teachers’ professional skills must be restored, she said.
“In reality, what we see is teachers not being paid what they should be paid in the state, and we see teachers feeling devalued by the fact that they’re not able to teach because they are placed in the confines of cookie-cutter curriculums,” Marshall said.
The state superintendent has limited influence over teacher salaries, state funding levels for public schools and classroom lesson plans. But, both candidates said they hope to enact change by improving the Education Department’s relationships with districts and other state entities, which they said suffered during former Superintendent Ryan Walters’ turbulent tenure.
Walters, a Republican, resigned in September 2025 to lead a nonprofit. Neither he nor his governor-appointed successor, Superintendent Lindel Fields, filed to run this year for elected office. 
The Education Department must hold districts accountable for their academic results, Marshall said, but the agency should offer help and resources rather than punishment. While Marshall served on the Tulsa school board, Walters threatened a state takeover of the district if it didn’t quickly improve its academic scores.
“When people are operating under a punitive umbrella, they’re less productive,” she said. “Rather than being focused on the business at hand, they are busy looking over their shoulders, seeing when the hammer’s going to fall. Who’s coming after me? What are they coming after me for next? And that’s where we were with Ryan Walters. We were in a very combative and volatile season, and that was statewide. Educators can’t teach while walking on eggshells.”
Tulsa Board of Education member Jennettie Marshall speaks to the Oklahoma State Board of Education before a vote on Tulsa Public Schools’ accreditation on Aug. 24, 2023, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Brent Fuchs/For Oklahoma Voice)
Providing schools with more immediate and usable state testing data could help drive academic improvement, Franklin said. He suggested changing Oklahoma’s method of state testing from once-a-year exams in the spring to benchmark assessments, which students would take incrementally throughout the school year.
Some states, such as Indiana, already have switched to benchmark-style tests to give schools and parents more up-to-date information on students’ academic progress. Walters called for a similar change shortly before he left office.
Unlike Walters, who claimed state testing could be overhauled in less than a year, Franklin said it’s “going to take us a while” to develop a plan and earn federal approval.
Many Oklahoma districts pay for benchmark assessments and deliver them internally to inform instructional decisions. 
State test scores, on the other hand, typically aren’t revealed in Oklahoma until the following school year.
“That is nothing but a bureaucratic process that is supporting no one, and we’re spending millions doing it and making ourselves miserable all the month of April and May,” Franklin said.
Although she didn’t call for a new state testing system, Marshall echoed that education data is often provided and acted upon too late.
“If we have a teacher that’s not making the mark or we have a child that’s not making the mark, why are we waiting?” she said. “If something is not working to get that child across the finish line, change it then.” 
Early voting will take place Oct. 28-31. Polls will open on Election Day Nov. 3 from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Making daylight saving time permanent is a bad idea
text:
A bill to make daylight saving time permanent in New Jersey is another example of Trenton lawmakers wasting time on bad ideas. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A measure state lawmakers advanced on Thursday is an example of what I’m calling the Trenton Trifecta.
It’s dumb. It’s bad. And it’s pointless.
We very often get bills that are one of those, but it’s rare for them to qualify for all three.
I’m talking about the bill to make daylight saving time permanent if Congress authorizes states to do so.
Look, I get it. Changing clocks twice a year can be annoying. But there are more annoying chores I have to do far more often; it would not occur to me to seek a change in state law so I can avoid doing them.
Dark afternoons are also a bummer. But we would not gain any sunlight by making daylight saving time permanent, because we cannot command the sun to give us more daylight. Yes, our afternoons would stay brighter longer but our mornings would stay darker later. Winter sunrises would largely happen after 8 a.m., and in some places in the U.S. the sun would rise closer to 9 a.m. All the grumbling about commuting home in the dark would be replaced by grumbling about commuting to work in the dark.
So that’s why this is dumb. Here’s why it’s bad: We’ve already tried this and we hated it so much Congress reversed course within a year.
In December 1973, Richard Nixon signed a bill, approved overwhelmingly by Congress, that made daylight saving time permanent, part of a push to save energy. Not only was it unclear that goal was achieved — the U.S. Department of Transportation did a study and indicated energy savings of 0.4% to 1.5% — but the shift created panic among parents when they realized they had to send their kids to school in predawn darkness for months at a time. From December 1973 to February 1974, public approval of year-round daylight saving time plummeted from 79% to 42%.
“I think we have to recognize that we may have made a mistake,” Iowa Sen. Dick Clark said in February 1974, two months after voting yes to make daylight saving time year-round.
This was such a bone-headed move, it took just two months for a U.S. senator to admit he erred by supporting it. In September 1974, Congress voted to bring back standard time for four months out of the year.
Now for the pointlessness of all this. The only bill in Congress with enough support to make it to a vote — this is the one that led daylight saving time fan President Donald Trump to publicly release Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton’s phone number to get Cotton to end his opposition — would make daylight saving time permanent in New Jersey. There’s no reason for our lawmakers to waste any time considering this bill; if Congress acts, we have to make the shift.
The Legislature has countless bills on deck that would be wiser uses of their time. Let’s focus on those.

title: Mississippi State, Ole Miss and USM combine to host prestigious men’s golf tourney at Fallen Oak
text:

BILOXI – Ole Miss, Southern Miss and Mississippi State men’s golf teams will combine to host the Fallen Oak Collegiate Invitational this weekend for what has become one of the most prestigious autumn tournaments in college golf.
Rick Cleveland
Joining the three Mississippi teams at the highly acclaimed Tom Fazio-designed Fallen Oak course will be top-ranked Arkansas, No. 4 Alabama, Florida State, No. 14 Georgia, No. 12 Illinois, No. 20 Ohio State, Iowa, LSU, South Carolina, No. 9 Tennessee, Wake Forest and Wisconsin. Ole Miss coach Chris Malloy says there is a long waiting list of teams that want to get into the Fallen Oak field.
All 15 teams in the field are ranked in the top 100 in the NCAA Division I rankings. Mississippi State is No. 34, Ole Miss No. 37 and Southern Miss No. 57.
“You won’t find a better college golf field anywhere in the country this fall,” said Southern Miss golf coach Eddie Brescher, whose Golden Eagles qualified for the NCAA Tournament last spring for the first time in school history.
“This tournament just keeps growing in stature, This is a post-season quality field for a fall tournament.”
Árni Sveinsson 
LSU and Alabama tied for the team title at Fallen Oak last fall, and LSU’s Gunnlaugur Arni Sveinsson, from Iceland, won the individual championship and returns to defend his title. Sveinsson, the world’s No. 8 ranked amateur golfer, shot rounds of 66, 70 and 67 for a 54-hole total of 13-under-par 203 for the victory, one shot better than Alabama’s William Jennings, who also will return to Fallen Oak.
Said Iowa coach Tyler Stith a year ago at Fallen Oak, “I have been coaching college golf for 15 years, and this is one of the best tournaments I’ve ever been a part of. The tournament operations and hospitality is first-class and the golf course itself is as good as any we play in college golf. This is our third year to play here, and I sure hope we get invited back.”
Championship play for the 54-hole event begins Saturday and continues through Monday. Admission is free to the public, and large-screen televisions will be strategically placed around the course so that football fans can keep up with their favorite teams on a big college football Saturday and with NFL games on Sunday.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware high school football weekend features major matchups with playoff implications
text:
Photo: Salesianum vs. Smyrna at the University of Delaware Stadium on Friday October 10, 2026. Photo by Dave Reeder.
Smyrna-Cape Henlopen, St. Georges Tech-Caesar Rodney and Milford-Red Lion highlight a Friday night schedule that could reshape the postseason picture, while No. 1-ranked Salesianum returns to action Saturday.
WILMINGTON, Del – Delaware’s high school football season reaches an important stage this weekend, with several games carrying playoff positioning, district implications and statewide bragging rights.
The marquee matchup comes in Lewes, where unbeaten Cape Henlopen hosts Smyrna in a meeting of two of the state’s highest-ranked Class 3A programs. But it is hardly the only game worth watching.
St. Georges Tech travels to Caesar Rodney in another matchup between highly ranked 3A teams, while Milford visits Red Lion Christian Academy in a game featuring two 4-1 teams near the top of the Class 2A rankings.
One change from an earlier version of the weekend schedule: Salesianum is not playing Appoquinimink on Friday. The Sals instead visit Hodgson Vo-Tech at 11 a.m. Saturday, while Appoquinimink hosts Souderton of Pennsylvania on Friday. Milford also plays at Red Lion Christian, not Polytech. delawaresportsmedia.com
Cape gets another major test:  Smyrna (4-1) at Cape Henlopen (5-0)
Friday, 7 p.m., Legends Stadium, Lewes
This may be the most important game in Delaware this weekend.
Cape Henlopen enters unbeaten after surviving a 24-21 test from Appoquinimink last week. Smyrna comes in ranked among the state’s best despite a 32-26 loss to Salesianum. MaxPreps.com
The matchup gives Cape another opportunity to demonstrate that its undefeated start is built for the postseason, while Smyrna has a chance to respond immediately after its first loss.
With the teams ranked No. 2 and No. 3 in Class 3A by Delaware Sports Media, the result could have significant consequences for seeding and home-field positioning later in the season. delawaresportsmedia.com
St. Georges and Caesar Rodney collide:  St. Georges Tech (4-1) at Caesar Rodney (5-2)
Friday, 7 p.m., Rider Stadium, Camden
This matchup has the feel of a playoff game before the playoffs arrive.
St. Georges Tech enters ranked No. 7 in Class 3A, while Caesar Rodney is No. 6, making this one of the weekend’s most evenly matched games on paper. delawaresportsmedia.com
For both programs, the opportunity is straightforward: A win over another quality opponent strengthens the résumé and helps build momentum heading into the final weeks of the regular season.
Milford faces major road test: Milford (4-1) at Red Lion Christian Academy (4-1)
Friday, 7:30 p.m., Red Lion Christian Academy
Milford gets one of its toughest tests of the season against another 4-1 team.
Delaware Sports Media lists Red Lion Christian as the No. 3 team in Class 2A and Milford at No. 5, giving the game immediate significance for postseason positioning. delawaresportsmedia.com
Milford has become one of the more closely followed programs in southern Delaware, and a road win here would strengthen the Buccaneers’ standing as the season moves toward November.
Sussex Central looks to keep building: Dover (1-4) at Sussex Central (4-1)
Friday, 7 p.m., Sussex Central High School, Georgetown
Sussex Central has positioned itself among the better teams in Class 3A and enters Friday ranked No. 5 in the division. Dover, meanwhile, comes in at 1-4. delawaresportsmedia.com
For Sussex Central, this is the kind of game a playoff contender cannot afford to overlook. Another victory would keep the Golden Knights firmly in the postseason discussion.
Middletown looking for traction:W illiam Penn (0-5) at Middletown (1-3)
Friday, 7 p.m., Cavalier Stadium, Middletown
The records make this matchup different from some of the weekend’s headline games, but the stakes remain significant for a Middletown program accustomed to postseason football.
The Cavaliers are 1-3, while William Penn enters 0-5. delawaresportsmedia.com
For Middletown, the remainder of the schedule offers little room for error if the Cavaliers hope to build momentum and remain relevant in the playoff conversation.
Lake Forest carries top ranking into Delmar: Lake Forest (4-1) at Delmar (2-3)
Friday, 7 p.m., Delmar High School
Lake Forest has quietly built one of the state’s stronger résumés and enters the weekend ranked No. 1 in Class 2A by Delaware Sports Media. delawaresportsmedia.com
Delmar is 2-3 but remains the kind of opponent capable of making a road trip difficult.
For Lake Forest, the challenge is maintaining its position as the regular season enters its second half.
Salesianum returns Saturday: Salesianum (4-1) at Hodgson Vo-Tech (1-4)
Saturday, 11 a.m., St. Georges Tech High School
Salesianum enters the weekend ranked No. 1 in Delaware by MaxPreps after consecutive wins over Sussex Central and Smyrna. MaxPreps.com
The Sals defeated Smyrna 32-26 last week and now begin district play against Hodgson. The game is scheduled for 11 a.m. Saturday. MaxPreps.com
Salesianum’s upcoming schedule also includes Appoquinimink, Middletown, Caravel and William Penn, giving the Sals several opportunities to reinforce their position as one of the teams to beat in Class 3A.
Other games to watch
Appoquinimink, 3-2, hosts Souderton Area of Pennsylvania at 6:30 p.m. Friday, while Polytech, 4-1, hosts St. Mark’s at 7 p.m. Howard visits Tatnall at 4 p.m., and Laurel travels to Indian River at 6 p.m. delawaresportsmedia.com
The weekend should provide a clearer picture of where Delaware’s contenders stand as district schedules intensify and the race for playoff positioning begins to take shape.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Mixed signals on Medicaid ballot question have serious implications for South Dakota
text:
The federal government's website for Medicaid, a health insurance program for people with low incomes. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)There’s something unclear about Constitutional Amendment I, a question on the Nov. 3 ballot that would change South Dakota’s Medicaid expansion program.
Medicaid expansion covers healthcare costs for South Dakotans making less than $22,000 a year. The federal government covers 90% of the cost. The state covers the remaining 10%.
For years, the Legislature refused that deal. So, in 2022, South Dakota voters approved it themselves by placing it in the state constitution.
Medicaid expansion coverage is crucial for 31,000 of our friends and neighbors. That’s especially so for those struggling to make ends meet. Housing and grocery costs have soared recently, and wages have not kept up.
Ballot measure could auto-repeal Medicaid expansion, attorney general says in contrast to lawmakers

Backers of Amendment I want to change the language, by saying if the federal government lowers its funding match, the state should get the flexibility to decide whether expansion is worth the new cost.
“It would NOT automatically end Medicaid expansion,” say Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen, Sen. Casey Crabtree and Rep. Will Mortenson, all Republicans, in the ballot questions pamphlet distributed by the Secretary of State’s Office.
Here’s where it gets confusing.
Their statement contradicts Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley’s explanation of the amendment.
“This proposed Constitutional Amendment ends the expanded Medicaid coverage if the federal funding for expansion drops below 90%,” reads the explanation, which is printed on the ballot.
The attorney general’s statement reads more like a trigger law to overturn Medicaid expansion, rather than a maneuver to give lawmakers more flexibility.
When asked about the discrepancy between lawmakers’ interpretation and his own, Jackley doubled down.
“When you look at what the legislative proposal was that the title is based upon and the language is, it’s very straightforward of how this would occur,” Jackley said to South Dakota Searchlight. “And again, the Legislature made that decision.”
So which one is it?
Amendment I is one of four amendments placed on the ballot by the Republican-controlled Legislature. Another asks voters to raise the threshold for approving constitutional amendments to 60%, which some lawmakers say would protect the constitution (voters have rejected similar measures twice already).
Urging voters to support one ambiguous constitutional amendment while asking them to protect the constitution with another feels incongruent.
Regardless of either interpretation, Amendment I opens the door to repealing Medicaid expansion — a program voters supported in 2022.
Proponents of Amendment I argue they’re safeguarding the state budget from a financial hit if the current presidential administration lowers the federal match.
Another safeguard against the feds changing the funding match could be reminding the administration about the effect Medicaid expansion has on states like ours. It’s brought $870 million to South Dakota since implementation.
But it’s about more than dollars. It’s about keeping rural hospitals open, communities thriving and South Dakotans healthy.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Justices uphold law allowing certain overseas voters to cast ballots for Nebraska elections
text:
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John  Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)LINCOLN — A Republican-led challenge to overturn a state voting law allowing certain overseas voters to vote in Nebraska is over after a Nebraska Supreme Court ruling Friday.
In an unsigned, 6-1 decision, the justices said challengers — the Republican National Committee and two Lancaster County voters, Jack Riggins and Pam Dingman — “failed to prove the statute is unconstitutional on its face.” 
The RNC needed to prove that the statute had no constitutional applications. However, Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen and Attorney General Mike Hilgers offered one: a voter born in South America to Saunders County missionaries who intended to return home.
“This and other courts have previously recognized that children acquire their parents’ domicile at birth and that such domicile ‘continues until a new one, a ‘domicile of choice,’ is acquired,” the Friday opinion states.
Justices consider appeal in challenge to Nebraska overseas voter law

The challenged 2005 law allows U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but who have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in that county. It would be a felony to register or vote in multiple states or counties.
The RNC argues the law “dilutes the votes of lawful Republican voters” and violates Article VI, Section 1 of the Nebraska Constitution, which defines a qualified voter as a U.S. citizen who “has resided within the state and the county and voting precinct for the terms provided by law.”
In 1895, 20 years after the constitutional provision was adopted, the high court said “residence” and “domicile” were synonymous. On Friday, justices stuck with that interpretation and agreed that a child could adopt a parent’s “domicile” under certain circumstances.
Justice William Cassel dissented from the majority’s opinion because he said he would have dismissed the case outright. He disagreed with the majority’s ruling that Dingman had standing to sue as the elected Lancaster County engineer. She is running unopposed for reelection. A Lancaster County District Court judge and the other justices said the RNC and Riggins did not have standing.
Nebraska Supreme Court Justice William Cassel of O’Neill, center, greets lawmakers after the 2026 “State of the Judiciary” address. Jan. 22, 2026 (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Cassel said that while a recent U.S. Supreme Court case could give Dingman standing, he agreed with the Hilgers’ office that the decision is “not binding” and refers to federal law.
Citing the small percentage of voters registered to vote under the challenged statute who cast a ballot compared to the number of voters in total, Cassel said they “establish that the claimed harm is neither actual, imminent nor palpable.” 
For example, in the 2024 general election, 72 individuals registered under the challenged law voted, among 965,236 total voters, or 0.007%.
As of July, 116 overseas Nebraska voters were registered under the targeted statute, six of whom voted in the May 12 primary, according to data from Evnen’s office. That includes one voter in Lancaster County. In total, 30 of the 116 voters are registered in Lancaster County.
“The purported harm resembles a droplet in a deluge. I acknowledge that under other circumstances, standing might exist. But not here,” Cassel said. “I would dismiss the appeal, and, therefore, I respectfully dissent.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Donald Trump to campaign in Fort Myers next week
text:
President Donald Trump points into the crowd after headlining a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)President Donald Trump will campaign in the Sunshine State next week, just as early voting is set to expand throughout Florida.
The president will campaign in Fort Myers on Friday, Oct. 23. The physical location of the event has not yet been announced.
Doors will open at 10:30 a.m. The program will begin at 12:30 p.m., with Trump scheduled to speak at 2 p.m.
Early voting begins in many counties in Florida starting Monday, Oct. 19. State law mandates that all counties must provide early voting by Saturday, Oct. 24.
The president himself said in a social media post last month that he would appear twice in Florida before the election.
“Two Rallies are already scheduled in Florida for Byron and, will be, as always, “SOLD OUT!” he wrote in a lengthy post that included his reaction to published reports that Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds had scrubbed any mention of him from his website.
“This was a Fake Story, with no sources, and the only justification for it is they want to stop my ever upward momentum,” Trump said.
The president’s endorsement of the Naples U.S. House member in early 2025 made him the early favorite in the Republican primary race for governor, which he won by 23 points over Lt. Gov. Jay Collins on Aug. 18.
In September, Vice President J.D. Vance made a campaign appearance in Lakeland in Central Florida. That event included appearances by Donalds, U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, and several congressional candidates.
Meanwhile, the campaign for Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly announced this week that former President Bill Clinton will appear with Jolly on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in Hollywood. It would be Clinton’s first public campaign event of the 2026 election cycle.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Supreme Court upholds validity of Fairness for Girls ballot measure
text:
Former State Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar leads a news conference for the Fairness for Girls campaign that seeks to constitutionally designate sex-separate athletics for K-12 and collegiate sports on June 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Julie Slama/Fairness for Girls)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Friday unanimously upheld the validity of a 2026 ballot measure seeking to cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the Nebraska Constitution.
Justice Derek Vaughn of Omaha, in a 7-0 opinion, agreed with a lower district court’s ruling that the Fairness for Girls campaign had enough detail on its petition pages under state law.
“Section 32-1401 does not require an object statement to summarize all major provisions of an initiative,” Vaughn wrote.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Voters will see the item on their ballots as Initiative Measure 442. A hearing on the measure was held in Lincoln this week, and public hearings will be held in Kearney and Omaha next week.
The Fairness for Girls proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and teams as male, female or coed. Male students couldn’t play on female-only teams.
The ballot measure would not define “sex” in the constitution. State law defines sex as whether someone “naturally has, had, will or would have, but for a congenital anomaly or intentional or unintentional disruption, the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports and utilizes” either eggs (female) or sperm (male) for fertilization.
A Lincoln voter, Cara Ullman, argued that the petitions lacked specificity in their “object statement,” so she signed to place the issue on the ballot without fully knowing what it would do. 
Ullman’s attorney, Sydney Hayes, had argued before Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret that if object statements could be so broad, it could be “open season for vague, incomplete and misleading” statements.
Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret ruled against all of Ullman’s points. The Supreme Court noted that if a voter wanted to know exactly what a measure would do, they “need only flip over the page to read the proposed initiative’s full text.”
Lancaster County judge dismisses challenge to Nebraska K-12, collegiate sports ballot measure

Vaughn said the court could not read additional meaning into the law and that the court’s interpretation is supported not just by what’s in the law but also by what’s excluded.
For example, in Arizona, petitioners must describe the “principal provisions of the proposed measure” and a disclaimer that the description “may not include every provision contained in the measure,” Vaughn wrote.
The justices said a ballot measure’s object statement needs to say what type of measure it is.
“The language ‘legal effect of the filing of the petition’ contained in § 32-1401 does not require an initiative’s object statement to set forth every consequence that would result from the initiative measure should it be adopted by voters,” Vaughn wrote. “Instead, based on its plain language, it requires only that the object statement informs potential petition signers whether the legal effect of the petition is a referendum, enactment of a law or a constitutional amendment.”
Justice Jason Bergevin did not participate in the decision. Court of Appeals Judge PaTricia Freeman rounded out the court in his absence.
The general election is Nov. 3.



Initiative Measure 442 ballot language
A vote “FOR” will amend the Nebraska Constitution to provide: (1) Schools must expressly designate each athletic team or sport as one of the following based on biological sex: (a) Males, men or boys; (b) females, women or girls; or (c) coed or mixed; and (2) Athletic teams or sports designated for females, women or girls shall not be open to students of the male sex. The amendment would apply to all athletic teams or sports sponsored by public schools or postsecondary educational institutions, and private schools or educational institutions whose athletic teams or sports compete against public schools or institutions.
A vote “AGAINST” means the Nebraska Constitution will not be amended in this manner.
Shall the Nebraska Constitution be amended to provide: (1) Schools must expressly designate each athletic team or sport as one of the following based on biological sex: (a) Males, men or boys; (b) females, women or girls; or (c) coed or mixed; and (2) Athletic teams or sports designated for females, women or girls shall not be open to students of the male sex. The amendment would apply to all athletic teams or sports sponsored by public schools or postsecondary educational institutions, and private schools or educational institutions whose athletic teams or sports compete against public schools or institutions.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Visit Jackson unveils 5-year plan to boost tourism amid funding challenges
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Visit Jackson has unveiled a five-year strategy aimed at attracting more visitors to Mississippi’s capital city, but the agency acknowledged serious obstacles: inadequate lodging, poor perceptions of the city’s attractions and uncertainty over funding.
Visit Jackson, which laid out the plan during a two-hour meeting earlier this week, has operated on a $5.4 million budget since October 2024 — but officials said $1.8 million of that came from federal pandemic relief funds that are no longer available.
To fill that gap, Visit Jackson hopes voters approve a financing measure on the Nov. 3 ballot that would increase taxes on restaurants by 0.5% and lodging by 1%.
Jackson saw over 1 million travelers in fiscal year 2025 and increased its overnight retention by 4% from 2024, according to Visit Jackson data. The city also brought in $80 million in tourism-driven revenue. 
A sign welcomes in audience members during Visit Jackson’s State of Tourism address on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.  Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The report highlights many positives, such as Jackson’s most popular attraction being the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum.
But a chief concern is Jackson’s lack of lodging. 
The city of Jackson has 3,775 units within the city limits — including hotels and Airbnb rentals.
Tourism officials note that 60% of the city’s accommodations are motels and other budget-style facilities similar to Super 8 and OYO brands.
Other concerns voiced a large lack of knowledge about the city and its offerings. In a pool of 220 respondents who had not visited the city, 47% said they were disinclined to visit because of the lack of resources available to learn about the city’s recreational offerings.“Our success will not be measured solely by how many people we bring to our city, but also by what their presence makes possible for the people who live here,” Visit Jackson spokesperson Yolanda Clay-Moore said. 
Nichols Tourism Group and Destination Consultancy Group drafted the five-year blueprint that reflected information from surveys and tourism data. 
The focus of the strategy is a five-step revitalization plan that advocates refer to as “RESET” –  refine, enhance, strengthen, expand and thrive.
The proposal calls for the formation of a new tourism council, strengthening marketing strategies and working toward improving city facilities.
During the plan unveiling, Mayor John Horhn again floated the potential for a convention center hotel.
Jackson Mayor John Horhn gives a speech during Visit Jackson’s State of Tourism Address at the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The idea is not new. The long-discussed hotel project was at the center of a federal corruption case that ensnared former Mayor Chokwe Lumumba, who is now awaiting sentencing along with two others after pleading guilty to a bribery charge.
Visit Jackson CEO Ricky Thigpen acknowledged that details were still being developed. A more comprehensive plan, which he jokingly said was contained in a thick three-ring binder, includes monthly goals, meetings and regular check-ins to keep the effort on track.

name: Delaware
title: New Dover transitional home opens doors to veterans, community
text:
Saving A Place For You will host a Nov. 8 Friendsgiving open house to introduce its new veterans housing program and build community support.
DOVER, Del. — A new transitional home for veterans experiencing homelessness is opening its doors in Dover, offering up to a year of stable housing while helping residents connect with services and work toward independent living.
Saving A Place For You, Inc., a Delaware nonprofit founded last year, will introduce the home to the broader community during a Friendsgiving Open House from 3 to 6 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 8, at 21 S. Saulsbury Road.
The event will give veterans, families, nonprofit organizations, businesses, potential donors and other community members an opportunity to tour the home, meet the organization’s leaders and learn about housing and support available to veterans.
“Our veterans have given so much in service to our country, and they deserve to know that their service is remembered and that their community has not forgotten them,” founder Electa Thompkins said.
“This home represents more than a roof over someone’s head,” she said. “It represents hope, dignity, and an opportunity for a fresh start.”
A path toward independence
Saving A Place For You was founded in October 2025 by Thompkins and Sadé Truiett in response to the need for safe housing and additional support for veterans navigating the transition to civilian life or experiencing housing instability.
The organization says eligible veterans may stay in its transitional housing program for up to one year. During that period, residents can be connected with supportive services, community resources and personal-development opportunities intended to help them establish longer-term stability.
The organization also announced that it will waive its application fee for veterans seeking transitional housing, an effort intended to reduce one potential barrier for those seeking help.
Building a community of support
Truiett, the organization’s co-founder, said opening the home is only one part of a broader effort to establish partnerships among organizations, businesses and individuals interested in supporting veterans.
“Opening the doors to our transitional home is an important milestone, but our vision extends far beyond the walls of this building,” Truiett said.
“We want to build a community of people and organizations who are willing to stand alongside veterans as they navigate their next chapter.”
The Friendsgiving gathering is intended in part to build that network.
Guests will be able to tour the residence, meet board and leadership members and learn about opportunities to volunteer, donate, share resources or establish community partnerships.
For veterans who may need housing, organizers will also provide information about eligibility, the application process and available resources.
Honoring service, providing hope
The timing of the open house, shortly before Veterans Day and the Thanksgiving season, offers an opportunity to recognize veterans’ service while drawing attention to the need for stable housing and community support.
Saving A Place For You describes its mission with the phrase “Honoring Service, Providing Hope,” emphasizing both immediate housing needs and the longer-term goal of helping veterans regain independence.
Thompkins said the goal is to create a place where veterans feel supported while determining what comes next.
“We want veterans to know that there is a place where they can feel welcomed, supported and encouraged as they take their next steps,” she said.
TO GO

What: Saving A Place For You Friendsgiving Open House
When: Sunday, Nov. 8, 3-6 p.m.
Where: 21 S. Saulsbury Road, Dover
What to expect: Tours of the new veterans transitional home, refreshments, information about housing and support services, meetings with organizational leaders and opportunities to learn about volunteering, donations and community partnerships.
Who can attend: Veterans, community members, veteran-serving organizations, prospective partners, donors and supporters.
Veterans seeking housing: Saving A Place For You is waiving its application fee for veterans seeking transitional housing.
