name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico state Rep. Reeb resigns following ruling in Alec Baldwin case
text:
New Mexico state Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) on Oct. 15, 2026, announced her resignation from her seat following a ruling by a federal judge that her role in the House represented a conflict with her work as a special prosecutor in the involuntary manslaughter case against Alec Baldwin. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico state Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) on Thursday announced her resignation from the state House of Representatives following a ruling by a federal judge that her role in the House represented a conflict with her work as a special prosecutor in the involuntary manslaughter case against Alec Baldwin.
First Judicial District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies brought that case following the October 2021 death of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins on the set of the film Rust after a bullet discharged from a gun held by Baldwin. Former Judge Mary Marlowe Sommer dismissed the case in July of 2024.
Baldwin subsequently sued Carmack-Altwies, Reeb and others. In decision Thursday, U.S. District Judge Kea W. Riggs ruled against many of Baldwin’s claims due to prosecutorial immunity, but he also found that Reeb violated the state’s separation of power provision when she “simultaneously exercised the sovereign power of two distinct branches of New Mexico state government by holding two public offices.”
In a news release issued Thursday, Reeb said she “respectfully” disagrees with the Court “but I respect our Constitution and the institutions that uphold it.” As such, she said she was resigning to continue her work as a special prosecutor and resigning, effective immediately.
“There are victims and families across this state who have trusted me with their cases, and many of them have already waited too long for justice,” Reeb said in a statement. “I made a commitment to stand with them in the courtroom, and I owe it to them to keep that commitment.”
Reeb also noted that she had “relied” on guidance from both the State Ethics Commission and the New Mexico Attorney General to continue serving in both roles.
State Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), with whom Reeb serves on a special investigatory committee examining Jeffrey Epstein’s activities in the state, also cited Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s opinion when she was criticized for taking a job in Carmack-Altwies’ office while serving in the Legislature. She subsequently resigned after Torrez issued a letter that his 2024 opinion had :been read more broadly than intended.” He instructed any DA’s office employing a lawmaker to rectify the situation immediately and noted that he would not pursue legal action against any office that had previously hired a lawmaker “based on an honest misunderstanding of our 2024 opinion.”
This is a developing story and will be updated as needed.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Lisa Demuth says she voted to cap insulin prices. She voted against it at least twice.
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the GOP nominee for Minnesota governor, and her running mate Ryan Wilson spoke at a Capitol press conference on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)In recent election questionnaires, House Speaker Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, said she voted to cap the price of insulin for Minnesotans — an example of how she says she has worked throughout her legislative career to make life in the state more affordable.
But Demuth, alongside nearly every other Minnesota Republican, voted against capping the price of co-pays for prescription drugs that treat chronic illnesses, such as diabetes, at $25 per month in 2023. This was one of the many pieces of legislation the Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta passed without the help of GOP lawmakers. In 2019, Demuth also voted against cost-sharing limits on insulin that would have reduced the price for consumers.
Demuth did vote in favor of an insulin pricing law in 2020 that allows people to acquire a one-time, 30-day supply of insulin for $35 on an emergency basis.
It’s unclear whether Demuth’s claim of voting to cap insulin prices in questionnaires from WCCO and AARP Minnesota is related to her 2020 vote regarding emergency insulin. Demuth’s campaign did not immediately respond to the Reformer’s request for comment.
The 2020 law was called the Alec Smith Insulin Affordability Act after a 26-year-old man who was unable to afford the $1,300 monthly cost of insulin and supplies died in 2017. Smith aged out of his parents’ health insurance, and he rationed his insulin because of the cost. His family lobbied the Minnesota Legislature to support the bill.
When the 2020 law was first proposed, it included a cap on insulin co-pays, said Rep. Mike Howard, DFL-Richfield, who was the chief author of the legislation.
Republicans controlled the Minnesota Senate and Democrats controlled the House, and Howard said Republicans in 2020 did not want to pass the bill with the cap on insulin, so lawmakers had to compromise.
A cap only passed when Democrats took full control of state government.
Howard said it’s misleading for Demuth to claim she voted for an insulin cap, even if she voted in favor of one for emergency supplies. He said that’s not what an average person thinks when they read of a cap on insulin prices.
“I can totally understand the need in an election that is being fought on the grounds of who is going to make your life more affordable — prescription drugs are a big driver of costs,” Howard said in an interview. “But it’s pretty disingenuous when your entire legislative record is on the side of Big Pharma and big insurance companies that are amassing large profits.”
Howard said he spent years meeting with and negotiating with representatives of the three  pharmaceutical companies that manufacture the vast majority of the nation’s insulin: Eli Lilly, Sanofi and Novo Nordisk.
One of the people he met with was lobbyist Ben Golnik, whose largest client is Novo Nordisk. Howard said he believes the insulin price-capping legislation would have passed earlier if it wasn’t for the opposition of the pharmaceutical companies.
Golnik is a top advisor to Demuth’s campaign for governor, and he’s doing the work without receiving a paycheck from the campaign. Golnik also represents the tobacco industry and the horse-racing track Running Aces.
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic nominee for governor, voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, which included a $35 monthly co-pay cap on insulin and several measures to reduce prescription drug costs.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ‘No Kings’ rallies on Saturday focusing on early voting
text:
Connecticut will be host to dozens of “No Kings” rallies on Saturday, but this time, the focus is on early voting. 
Organizers are billing it as a nationwide day of action focused on helping voters make a plan for the upcoming general election on Nov. 3.
Organizers include Indivisible, League of Women Voters, CT 50501 and General Strike Connecticut. 
Early voting runs from Monday to Nov. 1. Every town must have at least one early voting location, open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with extended hours to 8 p.m. on Oct. 27 and 29.
Those dates are the backbone of Saturday’s message, and organizers say the point is giving voters time. 
“The reason the emphasis is on voting early is because it gives everyone more time to fix any issues, such as being purged from the voter rolls or having trouble getting to the polls,” said Joanna Swomley, co-leader and co-founder of Indivisible Greenwich.
In Hartford, protesters plan to meet on the South Lawn of the Capitol at 11 a.m. Other events Saturday are scheduled to take place at New London’s Parade Plaza at 10 a.m., Stratford’s Paradise Green at 11 a.m. and Middletown’s City Hall at 9 a.m. 
Saturday’s rally marks the fourth “No Kings” effort in Connecticut since its first organized demonstrations in June 2025. Police officials estimated 12,000 people attended Hartford’s rally in October 2025 and 5,500 people in March 2026.
Some towns are inviting participants to dress in black to honor victims of ICE, while other events will encourage banging pots and pans to make noise, a popular non-violent protest known as “Cacerolazo”.
Organizers said the event is more than just standing up against the Trump administration. Online webinars from the program have covered topics such as the importance of early voting, polling issues that may arise and protesters’ roles.
“We are going to have a voting table with QR codes to official websites. We’re going to make that information available to people who want to check their registration, get the hours and places to vote and things like that,” said Swomley.
Organizers issued reminders that Saturday’s “No Kings” events are meant to be nonviolent, nonpartisan protests.
Organizers say the movement isn’t tied to one party, and Swomley said that is central to why they want everyone to show up. She described the concern behind the protests as one that crosses party lines. 
“Everyone should be concerned about an authoritarian takeover, regardless of your party or your affiliation. It’s irrelevant to what kind of government you want to have,” she said.

name: California
title: People — not computers — should be deciding if my family can rent a home
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Dillon Forst
Dillon Forst, a logistics coordinator, is studying psychology, sociology and business at California State University, San Marcos.


My wife and I are preparing for a baby, and like any parents trying to get their lives in order, we need a place to bring our child home. 
During various rental application processes, I expected to provide proof of income, answer questions and follow application requirements. I did not expect to find myself questioning whether the people responsible for reviewing our information understood the process they were requiring us to use.
At one apartment community in San Diego County, we received an approval email and signed lease documents. Yet income verification continued to be an obstacle. We supplied documentation. We followed up. 
An employee acknowledged a calculation error, and our housing navigator questioned why verification remained unresolved. 
Having encountered application problems at another local property, I began paying closer attention to the distance between what we were being told and what was actually happening. 
An approval should have meant we could move forward. Instead, we were still trying to understand what was wrong and who could fix it. After all, I had spent eight years as a licensed mortgage banker, so reading W2s and 1099s, calculating income, auditing files, processing loans and supporting underwriting were part of my work experience. 
When the income calculations didn’t make sense, I had a professional reason to question them. I couldn’t inspect the software the apartment community was using, but I knew how to read our income documents and how to check the calculations myself. 
If someone with my background couldn’t get a clear resolution, what happens to an applicant who doesn’t understand how all this works?
That’s where my concern about artificial intelligence begins.
I’m Google AI-certified, and I use technology every day. I see its value. My concern is not that the technology should disappear. It is that a company should never let a system become the final answer for a rental decision when the evidence says otherwise. 
When a result conflicts with the information in front of an employee, someone needs both the authority and the responsibility to examine it, explain it and correct it. 
Otherwise, what purpose does the employee serve? Relinquishing our faculties to software leaves the person affected trying to reason with people who have stopped exercising their own judgment — their God-given ability to think — in favor of a machine.
As I looked beyond our experience, I found reasons to take that concern seriously. 
In 2022 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reported more than 26,700 complaints by renters, including those who faced inaccurate screening information and lengthy, confusing correction processes. 
That does not establish what caused our problems, but it shows that the difficulty of getting errors corrected extends beyond our application. 
In a landmark national class-action lawsuit, Louis v. SafeRent, Black applicants using housing vouchers alleged SafeRent’s algorithmic screening system disadvantaged Black and Latino applicants through its treatment of credit information and housing assistance data. 
The case settled in 2024 for $2.275 million without an admission of wrongdoing. 
Consider what reaching a courtroom requires of someone still trying to find a home. The ability to keep fighting a decision depends partly on what a person has left to fight with. 
Someone with savings may be able to absorb another application fee or a delay. Someone already stretched thin may not. 
Where financial disadvantage overlaps with racial inequality, an unresolved screening error can reinforce barriers that already exist. A family’s private struggle becomes a social problem when institutions control access to housing without providing an effective way to challenge data mistakes.
And who answers for these mistakes? The owners or managers of a property can point to the software provider. The provider can point back to the company making the housing decision. And its staff can point to company policy. 
Each explanation sends the applicant somewhere else. Follow that reasoning long enough and accountability seems to disappear, despite people having made decisions at every step. 
In their eyes, it can function like a liability shield, whether or not it offers any actual legal protection. Everyone can explain their limited role. But applicants are still left without a resolution.
I’d rather people be empowered to examine the evidence, explain the disputed result and correct an error before a housing opportunity disappears. 
Companies adopting these systems should train their staff and provide an alternative when the technology fails. Verifying income and preventing fraud are reasonable goals, but accuracy and accountability need to remain part of achieving that. 
Because a correction that arrives after a family has lost an apartment is hardly a workable solution.

name: California
title: Big Tech and Big Business are spending millions to block progressives on the California ballot
text:
In summary
Voters in these nine legislative districts are weighing in on particularly competitive races, made even more competitive by the flood of outside money pouring in to sway public opinion.  


With less than three weeks until Election Day, outside groups are pouring millions of dollars into two types of state legislative races: purple districts featuring a Democrat and a Republican, and safely Democratic districts featuring Democrats of different ideological stripes.
Political action committees backed by politically powerful groups such as unions and business have spent over $100 million on California legislative races so far this election cycle, eclipsing 2024 spending. Groups can spend unlimited amounts on “independent expenditures” to boost or oppose a candidate, providing they don’t coordinate with the campaign. 
Since they came on the scene in January, two new tech-backed groups have dominated spending in legislative races. Grow California, funded by cryptocurrency investor Chris Larsen and venture capitalist Tim Draper as a “counterforce” to union spending, has spent $17.5 million this cycle. California Leads, funded by Meta and Google, has spent close to $14 million this year to support candidates who are focused on “real-world solutions rather than ideological fights.”
Legislative Action PAC, which Republican strategists founded in 2025 at the request of Republican lawmakers amid frustration with the official state Republican Party, is also spending for the first time this cycle. It aims to help Republicans hold seats they flipped in 2024, and its major funders include Google, AT&T and oil and gas companies. The PAC and its offshoots, Legislative Action Victory PAC and Legislative Bipartisan Action PAC, have spent at least $6 million to support Republican candidates since April.
A CalMatters analysis of spending since the June 2 primary found that these are the nine most expensive competitive general election contests in the Legislature. Total spending in each race includes campaign spending from the primary through Sept. 19, the most recent reporting period, and independent expenditures from the primary through Oct. 13.
$5.6 million: David Penaloza (D) v. Jessie Lopez (D) – Assembly District 68
The priciest race so far is between two millennial Democrats who both serve on the Santa Ana City Council in Orange County. Lopez is the more progressive of the two: She helped pass a rent control ordinance in 2021 and faced a recall attempt by the local police union after she voted to create a police oversight commission in 2022. Tech money is flowing to help her opponent: In recent weeks, California Leads has spent $1.4 million and Grow California has spent $1.3 million on ads supporting Penaloza. 
Several powerful unions, including those representing public employees, nurses and California State University faculty, have spent a combined $1.4 million on ads supporting Lopez and attacking Penaloza.
$5 million: John Erickson (D) v. Brian Goldsmith (D) – Senate District 24
In the battle to succeed Sen. Ben Allen, Brian Goldsmith, an entrepreneur and former senior adviser for the pro-Israel advocacy group Democratic Majority for Israel, faces John Erickson, a West Hollywood city councilmember. The coastal Los Angeles district includes Malibu and Santa Monica. The two candidates are sharply divided on renter protections. Erickson supports repealing both the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act and the Ellis Act, which limit local rent control and allow landlords to evict tenants to leave the rental business. That’s likely driving the influx of money supporting Goldsmith from the California Apartment Association, which has spent $450,000 on independent ads attacking Erickson. The California Realtors Association is the main funder of a PAC that’s spent over $600,000 backing Goldsmith. 
Criminal justice reform advocates and organized labor, including the carpenters and school employees association, have bankrolled ads supporting Erickson.
$4.7 million: Greg Wallis (R) v. Leila Namvar (D) – Assembly District 47
Republican Assemblymember Greg Wallis is again fighting hard to retain his seat representing a purple district that includes both deep-blue Palm Springs and Cathedral City as well as conservative suburbs around Redlands and Yucaipa. Wallis has a significant fundraising advantage over his opponent, Democrat Leila Namvar, a former local labor leader and city planner. His campaign has outspent hers 6-to-1 and independent expenditures supporting him are more than 5-to-1. A moderate with a pro-business record, Wallis has been a favorite of California Leads, which has spent $1.1 million supporting him. A PAC funded by oil and gas companies has spent about $450,000. Legislative Bipartisan Action PAC spent about the same. 
Amid the flood of outside spending, the Democratic Party has backed Namvar. Since mid-September, the party and its county committees have given her committee about $1.8 million. 
$4.6 million: Sara Hernandez (D) v. Sarah Rascón (D)  – Senate District 26
Two Democrats are vying to replace departing progressive Sen. María Elena Durazo in this deep blue Los Angeles-based district. Sara Hernandez, a community college trustee, faces Sarah Rascón, a planning commissioner for East Los Angeles. Grow California and California Leads are backing Hernandez to the tune of about $3 million, even though her campaign website says she will “fight for strict rules with real enforcement” on Big Tech profits. Cardrooms near this district, including Hawaiian Gardens Casino and Commerce Casino, which are in a perennial battle with tribal casinos over gaming rights, have spent about $500,000 on independent ads supporting Hernandez. 
Rascón, whose top priorities include advancing environmental and social justice, has rejected corporate money. Her campaign had spent about $34,000 as of mid-September, and the Working Families Party and California Environmental Voters have spent over $100,000 on ads supporting her.
$3.8 million: Eric Lucan (D) v. Jackie Elward (D) – Assembly District 12
This seat, which encompasses all of Marin County and some of Sonoma County, is another target of Grow California. The group has spent about $1.8 million on ads supporting Marin County Supervisor Eric Lucan. Lucan’s positions are more moderate than those of progressive Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward, who said in a KQED questionnaire that she supports moratoriums on “all things AI,” including data centers, and that “protecting workers is the priority.” 
Elward’s support comes chiefly from the California Labor Federation, AFL-CIO, Consumer Attorneys of California and SEIU California State Council, which have spent over $1 million to support her race.
$3.2 million: Jeff Gonzalez (R) v. Ida Obeso-Martinez (D) – Assembly District 36
Outside groups have spent $2.7 million to back Republican Assemblymember Jeff Gonzalez. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Traditionally Democratic, this Latino-majority district along the California-Mexico border voted for Trump by 1.3 percentage points in 2024. The same year, Republican Jeff Gonzalez flipped it. Democrat Ida Obeso-Martinez, a nurse practitioner and Imperial County councilmember, is now challenging him to take it back. Oil and gas companies, a California Chamber of Commerce PAC and Legislative Bipartisan Action PAC are among the outside groups that have spent $2.7 million on mailers, polling, and TV and digital ads supporting Gonzalez and attacking Obeso-Martinez. 
No outside groups have spent on behalf of Obeso-Martinez, but the California Democratic Party and its central committees recently gave Obeso-Martinez over $1.5 million for the final weeks of the race.
$2.8 million: Josh Hoover (R) v. Amy Slavensky (D) – Assembly District 7
Incumbent Republican Josh Hoover faces Democrat Amy Slavensky, a retired teacher and superintendent, in this competitive Sacramento-area district, which shifted rightward after redistricting in 2022. Hoover’s allies, including business groups, cardrooms, and the Legislative Action PAC, have spent at least $2.3 million, chiefly on digital ads and mailers supporting him and opposing Slavensky. 
No independent groups have spent to support Slavensky, but Democrats have contributed close to $1 million to Slavensky since mid-September.
$2.6 million: Leticia Castillo (R) v. Clarissa Cervantes (D) – Assembly District 58
Assemblymember Leticia Castillo at her desk during a floor session at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Jan. 23, 2025. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Republican Assemblymember Leticia Castillo flipped this Latino-majority seat in Riverside County in 2024, defeating Democrat challenger Clarissa Cervantes by 596 votes. This year is a close rematch. Cervantes, a Riverside city councilmember whose sister is Sen. Sabrina Cervantes, received just 24 more votes than Castillo in the June primary. In a rare move, Cervantes has outspent the incumbent Castillo in the general election. Much of her spending — close to $1 million — has been from her campaign account, compared to Castillo’s $80,000. 
Legislative Action Victory PAC has spent about $650,000 on ads attacking Cervantes, and a coalition of unions spent about $530,000 supporting her. Both parties have been pouring in money to their respective candidates in the last few weeks.
$2.6 million: Guillermo Gonzalez (R) v. Melissa Hurtado (D) – Senate District 16
Incumbent Democratic Sen. Melissa Hurtado won this district by 13 votes in 2022 even as Gov. Gavin Newsom lost it by more than 10 percentage points, making her the only Democrat to represent a state Senate district that President Donald Trump won in 2024. She faces a challenge from Republican Guillermo Gonzalez, a small business owner and former aide to Rep. David Valadao. Legislative Action PAC has spent over $1.7 million supporting Gonzalez and opposing Hurtado. 
The Democratic Party and various county central committees have donated $4.8 million to Hurtado’s campaign war chest this election cycle, allowing her to spend close to $1 million between the primary and mid-September’s filing deadline.

name: California
title: California falls short on Medi-Cal fraud, state report says
text:
In summary
The state has not investigated 26,000 of its 28,000 highest-risk Medi-Cal providers, the report says. Health officials dispute it.


Is California doing enough to curtail Medi-Cal fraud?
The state auditor doesn’t think so.
A report released Thursday by Grant Parks, the state auditor, suggests the Department of Health Care Services is ill-equipped to stop pervasive abuse in Medi-Cal, a program that serves about 14 million Californians and pays out $200 billion annually.
The report described a “history of concern” about the department’s oversight of Medi‑Cal providers and classified it as “high-risk” for fraud, waste and abuse. The Department was first given the designation in 2007 for other reasons, including concerns about organizational restructuring and policymakers’ calls for increased accountability and program effectiveness.
In its response, the department disagreed with the auditor’s findings, saying the report “omits critical information and context, resulting in an incomplete analysis” and that it highlights “isolated anecdotes while ignoring system-wide data showing effective systems and controls.”
The report listed several concerning examples:

Two medical providers billed almost $1.6 million in Medi-Cal services in 2024-25, despite having been deemed ineligible to participate in the program several years earlier.
One transportation provider claimed to have driven 35 people in a single day, nine of them traveling more than 340 miles apiece. If this info was legitimate, the report said, the transportation provider would have traveled more than 3,000 miles on a single day in a single vehicle for those nine trips alone, not to mention the other 26. The provider took in more than $11 million in 2024-25.
Of the 28,000 Medi-Cal providers considered at highest risk of fraud or abuse, the report said, the Department had not begun investigations into 26,000.

name: California
title: Republicans are spending millions to oust a Democrat who won by 187 votes. Should he worry?
text:
In summary
Rep. Adam Gray, a Democrat from Merced, won the closest House race in 2024 by just 187 votes. Now the GOP, which is hungry for a win in California, is spending millions to try and oust him.


Democratic Rep. Adam Gray knows all too well that every vote makes a difference.
Two years ago, it took The Associated Press more than a month after Election Day to declare Gray won the race to represent California’s 13th Congressional District, the tightest U.S. House race in the country. By a mere 187 votes, Gray unseated incumbent Republican Rep. John Duarte, to whom Gray lost by just 564 votes two years earlier. 
This year Gray will likely benefit from the blue wave that polls show is sweeping the nation, as well as the pro-Democratic redistricting California voters approved last fall. The odds look favorable and the well-respected Cook Political Report moved the race from “toss-up” to “lean Dem” back in January. 
But Gray and House Democrats – who recently sent their campaign committee chair to rally support in Modesto – aren’t leaving anything to chance.
“It’s always competitive, because people aren’t looking to rubber stamp the political parties. They’re looking for somebody who actually puts them first,” Gray said in an interview.
The 13th District, which stretches from Stockton down State Route 99 to Merced, was one of the country’s closest swing seats until voters last year approved Proposition 50, the congressional redistricting plan designed to oust five California Republican incumbents and shore up support for vulnerable Democrats. 
Despite the district’s Democratic advantage on paper, Republicans are bullish about their candidate, former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln, who in 2021 unseated a progressive Democrat mayor in the heavily liberal city. Part of the GOP’s hopefulness also likely stems from having few other prospects for winnable races in California after last year’s redistricting. 
Republican groups have poured money into the race, and House GOP leadership even sent Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana to Chowchilla to rally support for Lincoln. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with House Republican leadership, already spent more than $4.34 million on the race this year as of Oct. 11, the most recent campaign filing available. The money is buying ads that paint Gray as tainted by his years in the Legislature and in Congress.
In contrast, campaign finance records show the House Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with House Democrats, has spent less than $400,000 this year on the race. 
Lincoln, a Marine Corps veteran who once served on the presidential helicopter Marine One, is emphasizing the need to cut costs for everyday people, such as by reducing taxes and limiting wasteful government spending. He frequently blames Gray for voting in 2017 to raise California’s gas tax. But Lincoln does not outline specific suggestions for how he would cut taxes and curb allegedly wasteful government programs. 
He wants to boost public safety by investing in law enforcement and ensuring the U.S. does not return to Biden-era immigration policies at the Southern border. His campaign website also highlights support for policies to boost the American artificial intelligence industry in its race against Chinese competitors, including President Donald Trump’s plan to let developers police themselves. 
“My message resonates with the voters regardless of a party,” Lincoln said, stressing that issues like affordability and access to water aren’t partisan. “They’re not red or blue — they’re red, white and blue.”
The Valley’s most independent voice?
The race largely boils down to who can win among the ‘Valleycrats’ — voters who are registered as Democrats but historically have been willing to vote for some Republicans. Proving they’re not beholden to their party is key for both Gray and Lincoln. 
“The Democrat who owns a gun, the Democrat who’s in the union but drives a truck, these are the kind of voters that are gettable for Republicans in that district,” said Paul Mitchell, a Democratic consultant and data aficionado who drew the Prop. 50 congressional maps. 
Lincoln’s political breakout came in 2020 when he won the race for mayor. He unseated Michael Tubbs, a progressive Democrat who grabbed national attention for piloting a two-year guaranteed income program that gave $500 per month, no strings attached, to 125 randomly selected city residents from low-income neighborhoods. That victory alone, Lincoln argues, proves he has cross-party appeal. 
Lincoln also touts his record on law enforcement, pointing out that Stockton’s violent crime rate hit a 15-year low by the time he left office in 2025, a reflection of a nationwide downward trend in violent crime. He did not seek reelection as mayor and instead in 2024 ran unsuccessfully for Congress against Rep. Josh Harder.
Democrats highlight staffing shortages in Stockton’s police department during Lincoln’s tenure, which led the department to cut the types of calls officers responded to. Lincoln said the department faced the same recruitment and retention issues as law enforcement departments across the country in the wake of George Floyd’s killing and social justice protests.
Rather than focus on Gray’s actions in Congress, Lincoln’s campaign has primarily attacked Gray for votes he took during the decade he served in the California Legislature. 
“Regardless of what party’s in power, you should be focused on putting the American people first and putting money back into the pockets of the hardworking American people,” Lincoln said in an interview. He said Gray was “complicit in the cost of living crisis” because he voted for legislation that increased state taxes and fees on transportation.
Advertisements funded by the House GOP-aligned super PAC highlights Gray’s 2017 vote for a state transportation bill that included a 12-cent per-gallon increase to the state’s gas tax and higher vehicle registration fees. The bill passed with the minimum two-thirds supermajority needed to increase taxes in California, a feat possible only because all Democrats supported it — making any of them effectively the deciding vote. 
Gray and other on-the-fence legislators were promised a collection of eleventh-hour “sweeteners” for their votes — state funding for projects in their districts that lawmakers can tout among their accomplishments. Gray’s district received $100 million to build 4.5 miles of road connecting Highways 99 and 140 in Merced County, the so-called Campus Parkway Project that takes drivers from the highway east to UC Merced.
Republicans accuse Gray of improperly profiting from those projects after a construction business that his cousin owns, and in which he holds a minority stake, was awarded a contract to construct a 133-room Hilton Garden Inn that now anchors a business plaza near the new segment of road.
“Adam Gray — you pay more, he gets rich,” says an advertisement by the Congressional Leadership Fund, which alleges Gray “pocketed” $400,000 of the $100 million allocated to the project in his district.
Gray disclosed receiving more than $366,000 from Marvulli, the construction company, in 2023 and 2024, according to House financial reports. He also disclosed owning a stake in the company valued between $250,000 to $500,000 which generated income between $50,000 and $100,000.
Political gravity favors Democrats
Despite the investment from national Republicans, Lincoln faces an uphill battle. 
Gray brands himself as a bipartisan champion and frequently promotes legislation he’s worked on with Republican colleagues. Earlier this year the House passed the telehealth access bill that Gray introduced with Republican Rep. David Valadao of Hanford and a measure to streamline geothermal energy projects he authored with Republican Rep. Young Kim of Orange County. 
“He’s taken some votes where he’s kind of, like, split from Democrats and become more of a point person for being able to do things across the aisle,” said Mitchell, the Democratic data and map guru. 
The California Farm Bureau, which rarely backs Democrats, endorsed him in April, citing his ability to work across party lines to deliver on water access and grants to improve farm technology.
“When results matter, Adam is the one who puts politics aside and makes sure that farmers and ranchers benefit from the decisions happening in Washington, D.C.,” said Shannon Douglass, the group’s president, in a statement. 
Even the Madera County Young Republicans club appeared to endorse Gray over Lincoln, drawing an admonishment and disciplinary action from the California Young Republicans leadership.
Gray has slammed his opponent for working for the California Republican Party, where Lincoln previously served as a finance director in 2025 before he opted to run for Congress again. 
“They’re literally running him so that they can get another yes-man for Trump,” Gray said. “With me, voters get somebody that actually puts the Valley first.”
Gray said even though Republican groups are far outspending Democratic ones in the race, he’s confident his campaign has built enough trust through its person-to-person canvassing to overcome the difference with voters. 
At a canvassing launch on Saturday inside a Modesto union hall, a few dozen volunteers gathered to knock doors for Gray, some traveling from their homes in the overwhelmingly liberal San Francisco Bay Area in the hopes of boosting Democrats in the Central Valley’s battleground districts.
Among them was Ann Merrill, a San Francisco-based organizer who emphasized to fellow volunteers how important it is to not take a single vote for granted, even if Democrats continue to perform well in polls nationwide. To drive home her point, Merrill held up a small jar with a handful of glass beads inside. 
“These are the 187 votes,” Merrill said, referring to Gray’s previous razor-thin margin of victory, shaking the jar so its contents rattled. 
“You may feel like, ‘Oh gosh, I only talked to five people today.’ Well, multiply those five people by everyone who’s out talking to five people, and doing that day after day after day,” Merrill said. 
Gray said he and his team have held door-knocking events nearly every weekend since he took office. He thanked the volunteers and introduced a special guest: House Democrats’ campaign chair Rep. Suzan DelBene who, as Speaker Johnson did for Lincoln, traveled from Washington, D.C. to convey party leadership’s support for and investment in Gray.
“I promised Suzan we’re going to win by at least 188 votes in this election,” Gray joked, eliciting laughter from the crowd.

name: California
title: There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know
text:
In summary
Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it.


For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.
It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 
A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.
Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. 
A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.
What would Prop. 1 do?
If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.
Where would the money go?
Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down:

$7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
$1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes.
$1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes.
$500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. 
$450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. 
$350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students.
$200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation.
$200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. 

How would California pay for it?
It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. 
Have we done anything like this before?
California voters approved (by the slimmest of margins) another bond in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1.
What do supporters say?
Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. 
Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. 
Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that.
Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. 
“Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.”
What do opponents say?
When this measure came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers.
Sen. Tony Strickland, a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets.
“It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. 
And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said.
Opponents have not reported receiving any contributions.

name: California
title: New California laws arise from latest legislative skirmishes in endless ‘tort wars’
text:
The state Capitol is an arena where lobbyists for thousands of interest groups battle over issues that mostly involve money — very often big money. The Legislature and the governor can, and often do, write into law new provisions that financially benefit one interest or are costly for another.
One of the longest-running conflicts, dubbed “tort wars,” pits lawyers who file personal injury lawsuits and their allies against business interests and their insurers.
They fight over laws that specify which actions cause damages, known as “torts,” which can be the subject of liability lawsuits and what compensation can be collected if such cases prevail.
The stakes can be immense, involving many billions of dollars, so for tort warriors it’s a perpetual game of defining new, legally actionable acts; expanding or shrinking those already on the books, or devising tactics to thwart those employed by the other side.
The dynamics of tort politics were demonstrated one night in September 1987, as that year’s legislative session was nearing adjournment.
Veteran lobbyists for major tort war interests had been exploring a potential multi-point deal to resolve some long-simmering issues with key legislators behind closed doors. The negotiators took a break for dinner and drinks at what was then Sacramento’s famous political watering hole, Frank Fat’s restaurant.
Spontaneously, as the liquor flowed and food was consumed, negotiations restarted right there, as  Willie Brown, then the much-celebrated speaker of the state Assembly, bounced from table to table.
The result was the infamous “napkin deal” that gave everyone involved at least part of what they wanted. It was jotted down on a napkin, quickly drafted into legislation and passed with no public input.
One provision — which years later haunted Brown and other politicians — protected the tobacco industry from lawsuits by disease-stricken former smokers. (Footnote: I and the late Jay Michael, a lobbyist for medical interests who was one of the participants,  co-wrote a book about lobbying that includes a detailed account of how the napkin deal came about.)
This brief history of tort wars sets the stage for what has been happening recently, including in the just-concluded 2026 legislative session.
Two years ago, the business side scored a significant victory with passage of two bills that narrowed the scope of the Private Attorneys General Act, which allows workers to sue their employers in the name of the state for alleged violations of workplace laws.
Employer groups had qualified a ballot measure to overhaul PAGA, as the law is known, which prodded lawyers and other rival interests to agree to a compromise in return for dropping the measure.
The 2026 session, as usual, featured a couple of other tort-related measures.
One, Assembly Bill 1776,  is a significant expansion of the Cartwright Act, California’s long-standing law prohibiting monopolistic arrangements among businesses.
The state’s Law Revision Commission proposed extending it to actions by a single corporation that had monopolistic effects and allowing private parties to file suits under the revised law.
Business interests opposed the entire concept, saying it was unneeded, and they particularly disliked the private right of action. Before the bill received final approval that part was stricken, limiting enforcement to the attorney general or a local prosecutor.
The second measure, Senate Bill 690, arose out of an American Bar Association publication describing how some California attorneys were using, or misusing, California’s law against secret wiretaps to demand payment from corporations for using website tracking software to gather information.
Business groups depicted the practice as extortion, and SB 690 was drafted and enacted to make using the wiretap law this way much more difficult.
This year’s legislative session is over, but tort warriors already are gearing up for the next one.

name: Nevada Current
title: Disciplined judge defends family court seat against challenge from disciplined attorney
text:
Mary Perry, Jennifer Isso. (Candidate photos)Family Court Judge Mary Perry is hoping to win reelection after agreeing in 2024 to be publicly censured for her actions on the bench. She’ll face attorney Jennifer Isso, whose own discipline by the State Bar was stayed by the Nevada Supreme Court, allowing her to run for the bench.
“I’m probably in one of the best places I’ve been in in a long time,” Perry told the Current. “My discipline is behind me.” 
Perry says the behavior that resulted in her agreement to be censured by the Judicial Discipline Commission (JDC) was the result of a breast cancer medication that brought on hormonal changes. “It took about a year for it to run through the system and for me to level off and get used to it,” Perry said.  
In two court cases cited by the JDC, Perry, an Air Force veteran, displayed “a needlessly disrespectful tone of voice, obvious changes in her mood, the use of profanity, personally demeaning comments about the litigants, and generally, her overall demeanor and lack of professional decorum to all litigants…”  
Videos of Perry yelling at litigants have circulated on social media. 
Perry is a member of UNLV Boyd School of Law’s charter class. She  hears child custody and divorce cases, and was first elected in 2020. 
Of the 97 attorneys who evaluated Perry in the Las Vegas Review Journal’s Judging the Judges survey, only 35% recommended that she be retained. 
“I attribute a lot of it to my being abrupt,” she said, adding that “after eight and a half years in the military, I learned that as long as I say what I’m thinking straightforward, not try to sugarcoat it, people cannot state that they misunderstand me. You gotta make sure people understand what you say when you’re a judge.”
Of 16 cases appealed, Perry’s ruling has been found in error on 11 cases, according to Our Nevada Judges, a website that tracks the state’s judiciary.  
“I’m not afraid to make judgment calls when there’s not necessarily any guidance on it,” she said. “I’ve been appealed in those areas where there’s not necessarily guidance.”
She says her “learning curve is picking up a lot. I’ve passed the part where everything is brand new, and I’m having to learn every little thing. It’s been a pleasure to be doing what I’m doing.”
Perry raised about $101,000 through the third quarter and has just under $16,000 in the bank. Endorsements on her website include the Western States Carpenters, the Clark County Deputy Marshals Association, SEIU Nevada, Culinary Local 226, and community groups, including Hispanics in Politics and the Asian American Group.  
She is also endorsed by the Third Branch PAC, which states it’s a bipartisan organization but is funded solely by the Nevada Republican Club. Judicial races are nonpartisan.  
Isso, who obtained her law degree from UNLV’s Boyd School of Law, raised no money and is $1,938 in the hole, according to her campaign contribution and expense report for the third quarter. She has no endorsements listed on her website. 
In an automatic review earlier this year of the Nevada Bar’s recommendation that Isso be suspended, the Nevada Supreme Court approved the suspension, but stayed the discipline, allowing Isso to seek the seat in Departt. P. 
“Isso admitted to failing to demonstrate respect for the court, witnesses, opposing litigants, and opposing counsel,” the order said.
She also “admitted to making statements she knew were false or with a reckless disregard for the truth” regarding Judge Stephanie Charter, Judge Mari Parlade, and then-Judge Paul Gaudet, who is now running for the bench under the name Michel Gaudet. 
“The Court stayed her suspension for 18 months and ordered us to monitor her on probation with several conditions,” State Bar Counsel Dan Hooge said earlier this year, “If she stays out of trouble and completes her conditions, then she will not serve the suspension. If she doesn’t, then we will revoke her probation. If revoked, she would serve the suspension and have to petition for reinstatement after.” 
Isso, who did not respond to the Current’s request for an interview for the general election, is also the subject of videos on social media. 
In one undated video on YouTube, an emotional Isso is seen crying and bemoaning her appearance before the court. 
“I was visibly upset in that particular hearing,” she said before the primary election, noting the judge sanctioned her client for missing a deposition. 
“I have to protect clients, and that’s going to cause friction. I’m very direct, very honest, and I’m willing to challenge authority,” Isso said. “I’m being an advocate rather than causing controversy.”
The video, Isso said, was posted by Steve Sanson of Veterans in Politics after Isso filed her candidacy. 
Perry, who is endorsed by VIP, paid the organization more than $2,000 for advertising, and paid more than $12,000 since July to Veterans in Politics International, a consulting company owned by Sanson and Stephanie Phillips, who finished 6th in the Nevada U.S. Senate Republican primary in 2024.

name: Nevada Current
title: Why the Republicans’ voter fraud messaging may backfire
text:
Study after study has shown voter fraud happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels. Nonetheless, rhetoric from the Trump administration about voter fraud has been pervasive.(Official White House Photo by Molly Riley)
With Election Day 2026 just weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the results will almost certainly hinge on voter turnout, just as they did in 2024.
Given that genuinely undecided voters are scarce — as little as 5% to 7% of the electorate, according to major polls — both Democrats and Republicans must look to mobilize their rank-and-file supporters. To do so, the Republican Party has bet strongly this year on a strategy of convincing people that voter fraud is rampant.
As a scholar of U.S. politics, I see this as a high-risk strategy for Republican candidates and American democracy. That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can reduce motivation to vote – even if based on flawed information. But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November.
 Voter fraud vs. reality

Voter fraud is not a real problem in the United States. Study after study, by public officials and think tanks, has shown that voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels.
Nonetheless, rhetoric from the Trump administration about voter fraud has been pervasive. Consider the recent claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls – a number reduced to 185 when state authorities pressed for details, and reduced to zero when the state investigated the names provided.
There is comparable behavior from Congress. My own research on political communication has shown that a substantial number of members of Congress, strongly skewing Republican, make frequent use of rhetoric that undermines democratic norms and delegitimizes political institutions.
The strategy ties readily into President Donald Trump’s persistent false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election. It also ties into his administration’s strongly anti-immigrant agenda, which spreads fear of noncitizens corrupting U.S. politics.
How does this uncertain political environment influence voters?
There is clear data showing that voter confidence in elections has fallen across party lines: Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable. Conventional wisdom suggests such discouraging numbers would depress turnout.
It’s not as simple as that, however.
 What motivates voters

Extensive research confirms the axiom that a sense of civic duty is the strongest predictor of whether someone will vote. It supersedes trust, partisanship and policy preferences.
Any campaign’s quest to mobilize additional voters, therefore, must find them among citizens without a strong sense of civic duty. But among these people, diminished trust in democratic processes can play out in counterintuitive ways.
Recent research on German voters is relevant to the U.S.: It shows that among more passive voters – those following cues from political elites – reduced trust in elections can depress motivation to vote. That’s because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm.
Conversely, among voters with greater skepticism about elite messaging, reduced trust can motivate increased turnout as an attempted corrective for a flawed system.
What does this mean for potential voters in the U.S.? Among Republicans, it appears that the party’s strategy carries a strong risk of backlash.
Findings from MIT’s Election Lab confirm that cues from political elites are a powerful factor in voter behavior. Specifically, cues setting expectations of a disappointing or untrustworthy result will reduce motivation. Why vote if you don’t expect it to help achieve the desired result?
The same study finds Republican voters broadly inclined to believe GOP leaders’ cues about voter fraud and to frame their expectations accordingly. And once they’ve made that shift, they cling firmly to the belief, even in the face of contrary empirical evidence or messaging from within the party.
In the current election cycle, 50% of Republicans surveyed distrust mail-in voting, and 51% fear voting by noncitizens. They expect election results to be fraudulent. This likely won’t mobilize them, as there’s no positive result they can expect to affirm. The Republican Party’s messaging has painted its voters into a corner.
Democrats, meanwhile, are less inclined to believe claims of voter fraud. But they are more inclined to be concerned about attempts to undermine the midterms by political elites making such claims. Examples include the Trump administration’s efforts to sow doubt about voting by mail and about alleged noncitizen voting.
These efforts increase motivation to vote among Democrats. Unlike GOP voters, they see the capacity to correct for the system’s vulnerabilities – the potential and urgency to overwhelm attempts at voter suppression through higher turnout.
 Truth and trust

Opponents of Trump and the GOP may find these diverging effects encouraging. No matter the results this November, however, we’re left with a precarious dynamic. Increasing numbers of voters lack trust in elections and make their decisions to vote – or not – based on limited or flawed information.
Fortunately, there are signs of hope.
Although voters in general are poorly informed about how elections are conducted, they can and do respond to clear information familiarizing them with election processes.
I’ve seen this myself over the years, working with nonpartisan efforts to register young adults and train them as poll watchers. And in the current election cycle, there have already been widespread efforts to broaden public awareness about the fact that state officials, not federal ones, have authority over voter rolls and election security.
Meanwhile, fewer Americans are expected to vote by mail this year – whether due to fear of fraud or fear of the Post Office. If they instead vote in person, a silver lining is that positive personal experiences with poll workers are also associated with increased voter trust.
Looking beyond November, what Americans can hope for is a cycle in which clear election outcomes provide an opportunity to inform voters of how and why the system works. That’s the way to motivate more political engagement and voter turnout in the future.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico reports 2 more New World screwworm cases
text:
The New Mexico Department of Agriculture on Oct. 15, 2026, reported the state's third and fourth cases of New World screwworm (pictured above) in Grant County. (Image via Texas A&M)The New Mexico Department of Agriculture on Thursday reported two more New World screwworm cases in the state, both in Grant County, inflicting a horse and a calf.
“We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” State Veterinarian Dr. Samantha Holeck with the New Mexico Livestock Board said in a statement.
The cases mark the third and fourth for the state, which in September expanded surveillance for the pest following the detection of the second case in a horse, also in Grant County. New Mexico reported its first case in June — in a Lea County dog — just days after the first U.S. incursion of the devastating parasitic fly in a south Texas calf.
Named for the maggot’s behavior of feeding on live tissue, the New World screwworm Thas advanced rapidly through Mexico after being mainly contained in Central America for several decades. The state launched a one-stop website in mid-May to track cases.
A Thursday news release says state and federal officials continue to expand surveillance and fly-trapping to identify possible additional cases, with a minimum 12.4-mile radius infested zone established around each animal’s location, and the most northern zones combined into one.
“We appreciate the continued cooperation of livestock producers, veterinarians and animal owners as we respond to these additional cases,” New Mexico Secretary of Agriculture Jeff Witte said in a statement. “Early detection and prompt reporting are critical to limiting the spread of this pest. We encourage everyone to remain vigilant and work closely with animal health officials.”

Officials encouraged animal owners to monitor them for: un-healing wounds, wounds with maggots and other abnormal signs of injury and to contact the Livestock Board if they suspect the presence of New World screwworm.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ jail guards push to expand isolated confinement. Critics call for ‘humane’ alternatives.
text:
Antonne Henshaw, who served 30 years in New Jersey prisons, urged legislators to not pass a bill that would expand isolated confinement for people who assault correctional officers. Beside him is Brittany Bower, a Pemberton teacher who also opposes the plan. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey lawmakers and prison officials have tried multiple strategies to stop inmates from assaulting officers behind bars, from installing “splashguards” in cells’ food ports to prevent troublemakers from hurling bodily fluids at staff to heightening penalties against attackers and requiring them to be tested for contagious diseases.
But a state legislator who wants to further punish abusive inmates by expanding isolated confinement encountered impassioned pushback Thursday — about two hours’ worth from prison justice advocates, civil rights defenders, and former inmates who testified against the proposal at a public hearing at the Statehouse in Trenton.
The common theme from critics: isolated confinement is torture and those held there, especially for prolonged periods, suffer mental damage that shapes the person they are when they eventually leave prison.
“Your humanity gets stripped away from you. You start losing sense of who you are,” said Antonne Henshaw, who spent 30 years in prison before being released in 2018. “We bring this home with us, and this not only makes the officers unsafe; it makes the community unsafe. Isolated confinement as currently running in New Jersey Department of Corrections is one of the biggest public health threats to people being released.”
Bill sponsor Sen. Linda Greenstein (D-Middlesex), who chaired the Senate law and public safety committee where the bill was heard Thursday, said she would use the testimony to further shape the bill before putting it up for a vote. She said she did not know when that would be.
Union leaders implored lawmakers to act soon.
William Sullivan heads the New Jersey Policemen’s Benevolent Association Local 105, which represents nearly 4,500 correctional and parole officers.
He told the committee assaults on officers have risen over 300% since 2018, with bodily-fluid assaults spiking more than 700% in that time. Nearly half of all attacks involved bodily fluids and more than 10% of the prison workforce was out on leave in 2024 because of assaults, Sullivan said. He attributed the bulk of assaults to a small group of repetitively violent inmates and brought with him more than two dozen photos of officers bruised and bloodied or soiled from inmate assaults.
Jason Cook, the union’s vice president and a correctional officer at New Jersey State Prison in Trenton, shared his experience as someone hit by bodily fluids.
“Your natural reaction is to immediately get it off you. You want to wash yourself. You want to take your contaminated uniform off. You want to get into clean clothes. But you are a correctional police officer. You cannot simply walk away,” Cook said. “You still have a unit to secure, you still have inmates to supervise, you still have responsibilities to your fellow officers.”
Sullivan blamed the Isolated Confinement Restriction Act, the 2019 state law Greenstein’s bill would amend, for contributing to the rise in attacks.
“We now encounter inmates who deliberately assault officers because they believe doing so will get them removed from the general population. Think about that: an inmate afraid of another inmate assaults a corrections officer to escape the situation,” Sullivan said.
On the flip side, he added, some incarcerated people fake a vulnerability to dodge discipline for assaulting officers.
William Sullivan, a correctional officer who heads the New Jersey Policemen’s Benevolent Association Local 105, testifies on Oct. 15, 2026, in support of legislation that would expand isolated confinement in New Jersey prisons. Beside him is Jason Cook, who’s also a correctional officer and the union’s vice president. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
The Isolated Confinement Restriction Act prohibits isolated confinement altogether for vulnerable people, defined as those who are young or elderly, pregnant or postpartum, LGBTQ, mentally ill, developmentally disabled, significantly visually or hearing impaired, or diagnosed with serious medical conditions. It also restricts it for everyone else to no more than 20 hours a day, 20 consecutive days, or 30 days during a 60-day period.
Greenstein’s bill would amend the law to allow prison officials to isolate more people for longer periods of time by:

Expanding how many hours anyone can be held in isolation in state prisons from 20 to 22 hours a day.
Creating a new definition of “repetitively violent inmate” as someone who’s already served two or more stints in solitary or close custody or who’s believed to pose “substantial risk of serious harm” to themselves or others.
Removing restrictions on how many days repetitively violent inmates can remain in isolated confinement.
Requiring people who say they’re LGBTQ to be proven so by a medical or mental health examination, or a judicial determination that they’re in imminent danger of being abused or harassed because of their sexual orientation.
Allowing officials to isolate vulnerable people if staff believes they will seriously harm an officer, other staffers, or themselves, or if the inmates want to be placed there and provide informed, voluntary, written consent.

The bill’s critics complained that Department of Corrections officials never fully implemented the law, due to pandemic-related challenges, ongoing staffing shortages, and cramped facility conditions. A state prisons watchdog revealed in 2023 that officials routinely flout its requirements.
Thursday, the legislation’s supporters and opponents disagreed so much that Greenstein began asking each if they had any “creative” ideas to solve the problem.
They did.
The Rev. J. Amos Caley, a pastor at Reformed Church of Highland Park and an organizer with New Jersey Prison Justice Watch, suggested expanding mental health treatment and restorative justice interventions between staff and people in their custody, saying such approaches have worked in other states.
“Officer safety and humane treatment are not competing priorities. They are mutually reinforcing responsibilities. If we want safer prisons, we need to make the prisons more functional, not increase the practices that further erode that safety, which isolation is documented to do,” Caley said.
Ron Pierce, a former prisoner who now works in the state corrections ombudsperson’s office, suggested lawmakers do nothing, for now.
Besides the splashguards, officials have implemented a mail-scanning system to prevent drugs — a common instigator of assaults — from entering prisons, and legislators should wait to see if those reduce assaults, which would render Greenstein’s bill unnecessary, Pierce said.

Jim Sullivan of the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey urged legislators to require fuller public reporting on out-of-cell time, create independent oversight of county jails (which now have none), invest more in staffing and de-escalation training, and hold regular oversight hearings to ensure Isolated Confinement Restriction Act compliance.

Sean Washington was exonerated in 2020 after spending 25 years in prison for a Camden double murder he didn’t commit. He urged legislators to visit the prisons — especially New Jersey State Prison in Trenton, with wings dating back to the early 1800s — before considering anything that could worsen confinement for those in state custody.
“Go look at them cells. That’s not good for human beings,” Washington said. “If they had animals in there, PETA would be protesting and filing lawsuits against New Jersey for the way those cells look.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington energy debate centers on clean energy deadlines, rising utility costs
text:
Washington Policy Center Vice President of Research Todd Myers, left, joins “Inside Olympia” host Austin Jenkins, right, to discuss whether the state should make it easier for utilities to meet its clean energy mandates. (Photo courtesy of TVW)Washington’s rising utility rates have exposed a central policy divide: Should the state make it easier for utilities to meet its clean energy mandates, or relax those mandates to contain costs and protect reliability?
Former Democratic State Sen. Reuven Carlyle, an architect of Washington’s landmark climate laws, argues the state must remove barriers to building new energy resources while preserving its climate goals. Washington Policy Center Vice President of Research Todd Myers contends the mandates themselves are driving up costs and should be revised to give utilities more time and greater flexibility to use natural gas.
The two offered competing prescriptions in interviews with Austin Jenkins on TVW’s “Inside Olympia,”but found significant common ground.
Carlyle acknowledged lawmakers failed to adequately address permitting and infrastructure barriers when adopting the Clean Energy Transformation Act and Climate Commitment Act. He said he would address those shortcomings if writing the legislation today and expressed openness to economically sensible flexibility.
Myers advocated extending the 2030 clean electricity deadline and allowing additional natural gas generation when reliability is threatened.
Their differences over natural gas contrast with shared enthusiasm for nuclear power. Carlyle reluctantly accepts that additional natural gas peaking plants may be necessary but strongly prefers small modular nuclear reactors or geothermal energy. Myers sees natural gas as an affordable, reliable bridge while supporting nuclear technology, potentially financed by data center developers.
Both endorsed faster permitting and saw opportunities for data centers to finance new generation, although Carlyle emphasized their growing electricity demands while Myers questioned their current impact on Washington’s consumption.
Both advocated greater efficiency and consumer engagement to reduce peak demand. Carlyle emphasized grid modernization and distributed battery storage; Myers favored time-of-use pricing and financial incentives.
Their competing prescriptions leave lawmakers and utility regulators confronting the same challenge: maintaining affordable, reliable electricity while determining how much flexibility Washington’s clean energy transition requires.
