name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Demystifying mental health inpatient stays
text:
Getty Images.I am one of the 68 million Americans living with a mental illness and one of the over 10 million Americans who have been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Living with these diseases and seeking treatment is highly stigmatized — and newly precarious under the policies of the current federal administration. The best way to break stigma and advocate for better care is to share personal experiences.
In my youth, there was minimal mental health education in school. Any that was taught focused on depression only. I learned more details of how my great-grandfather died on his farmstead from my family than any insights on why he was never treated for depression and post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Mental health diagnoses are as complicated and diverse as our own brains and environments. Everybody deserves to feel well, and modern medications, support groups and therapy treatments have vastly improved over the past few decades. It is also true that feelings like anxiety helped us survive in a dangerous world before modern medicine, but we don’t have to accept those stressful symptoms as an everyday fact of life.
We are very lucky to live in 2026 for the abundance of mental health medications, community peer support groups and therapy options, often covered by health insurance. Less than a century ago, the regular course of action was to be locked in an asylum and not actively treated with any currently-prescribed medication. 
Lithium carbonate (a salt that improves brain activity) was first federally approved to treat bipolar disorder in 1970, just 56 years ago. The first selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (often known by their acronym, SSRIs, which treat depression) arrived a decade later. There are millions of Americans who could benefit from these prescribed medications that have been proven to be safe and effective in clinical trials, even going years into ongoing treatment. Taking medication, attending a peer support group, benefiting from therapy and prioritizing healthy habits like sleep are never something to be ashamed of. Caring for your mental health helps you and everybody you care about.
I have been diagnosed with bipolar depression since 2013. I have also been diagnosed with PTSD since 2020. Past trauma was rekindled by the early pandemic. Now with medication, those PTSD symptoms have been effectively treated for six years. If you or your loved ones have noticed ongoing depression, swings in mood or productivity, or the night terrors of PTSD, all of those can be treated by a provider with prescribed medication, peer support groups like those at the VA and therapy that is covered by health insurance.
The experience of an in-hospital stay has remained hidden from the general public, except in often inaccurate depictions in film and television. By the nature of these places, the media does not take photographs or interview patients when they are in a mental health unit, which can give them an undeserved, negative aura.
Getting admitted isn’t easy. People must exhibit suicidal thoughts or threatening behaviors, be experiencing psychosis (false thoughts or beliefs), or be unable to take care of themselves. Depending on their insight into their illness, they can be admitted voluntarily or under a “72-hour hold” that can lead to a civil commitment, where a court requires treatment under state law.
A psychiatric unit is different from other medical units. There are locked doors and restrictions on what clothing can be worn or gifts brought in. There are often limited visiting hours. It’s hard to stay connected because patients are separated from their devices and common-area phones have limited hours.
Inpatient mental health units are the safest place for a patient. There are separate units for children and adults. Depending on the size of the hospital, there may be different levels of care, or separate units for young adults and older adults. If a loved one is clinically lucid (with clear, rational thoughts), then the hospital can be boring. Television is restricted to certain channels and content. You may spend a whole afternoon watching reruns of “Roseanne,” which had its last season (aside from a brief reboot) nearly three decades ago. There may also be a nature slideshow channel during quiet hour (shift change). There often are newspapers or old magazines. 
These can be a good test of how patients are able to read and function. If you see a patient reading the entire A section over their morning coffee, they are probably being medicated just fine and are waiting to discharge. Many units also feature individual and group therapy, occupational therapy, art therapy and medication management.
The most fun part of the day are the meal times. In my experiences at the University of Minnesota, we marked our paper menus with a stub pencil and turned them in for the next day. You learn the secret menu from other patients, like asking for hot sauce or having your provider prescribe double portions. One patient tried to trade me his second hamburger for a single chocolate chip cookie. I lost 30 pounds in three months instead.
While hospitals are required by law to limit the use of restraints, seclusion and sedatives, these are employed at times when a patient is lashing out and in danger of hurting themselves or others. I have been restrained and sedated several times, which is traumatic and humiliating. Avoiding this experience is one of the reasons why I have always taken my medication as prescribed. I have also marked “allergies” on my chart for medications that did not work, leading to my inpatient stay being extended by weeks when these were prescribed by accident.
When you are ready to be discharged, it’s important to be connected to the services you will need to continue to heal and recover. For some it may be therapy, support in the community or specialized housing.
The best way to continue your recovery is to start with self-care like regular exercise, eating healthy, making sleep a priority and other healthy habits. Taking medication and working with your prescriber to address side effects can help. Engaging in other therapies often makes a significant improvement. Joining a peer support group with other people living with a mental illness helps ease the isolation many feel. Finally, follow up and chart progress. 
People with mental illness are able to live more healthy and fulfilling lives today because of the sacrifices of patients and advocates. From Nellie Bly to the Affordable Care Act, we have made progress. But there is a retrenchment underway that is increasing stigma and denying care.
Medicaid is the single largest payer of mental health services in the United States and Minnesota, and it’s under threat after the Republican trifecta cut nearly $1 trillion from the program for low-income Americans and people with disabilities. Congress introduced new bureaucratic hurdles with the express intent of reducing the Medicaid rolls, which could be especially difficult for people suffering from mental illness. 
Under Trump-appointed U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. the administration has worked to reduce funding for federal agencies that publicly subsidize mental health research, including the National Institute of Mental Health, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration and Health Resources and Services Administration. 
Under Kennedy’s leadership, SAMHSA also announced a Make America Healthy Again initiative this past May to wean patients — both adults and youth — off of prescribed mental health medication in favor of nonmedication treatment options. Patient advocacy groups and medical professionals have pushed back. They highlight the “robust” depth of clinical research showing safety and efficacy, and the need for more patients to have access to professional, evidence-based care. Using words like “overprescribing” only stigmatizes medication treatments that in most cases are not habit-forming.
Despite these policy headwinds, there is hope. Many mental health symptoms are treatable. And no matter how people lived in the past, we all deserve to live happy, healthy and fulfilling lives. 
To learn more, NAMI Minnesota has a booklet explaining inpatient hospitalizations and how families can help. If you or somebody you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call or text the suicide and crisis lifeline at 988. Caring counselors are here for you. You are not alone. In life-threatening situations, call 911.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Education leaders ‘disappointed’ with latest charter school grades
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
For yet another year, Mississippi’s charter schools posted a substandard performance on their Mississippi Department of Education report cards. 
None of Mississippi’s charter schools scored a B or higher on the accountability grades this year. Only one was rated C — Ambition Preparatory Charter School in Jackson — while most of the others were rated D. The lowest rated charter school was Instant Impact Global Prep Charter School in Natchez, which received an F.


Three of the state’s 12 charter schools weren’t graded. One lacked complete data because of the limited grades it served this past school year, while the other two started operations this year.
State education leaders said they were “disappointed” with the continued lack of progress. 
“I’m a little annoyed with some of the directions they’re going in,” said state Rep. Rob Roberson, a Republican from Starkville who chairs the House Education Committee. “I’m not going to say I’m not interested in having a conversation to make them better, but I’m having a lot of heartburn with how they’re set up and where they’re at right now.”
Rep. Rob Roberson, R-Starkville, listens as Teresa Jackson, former superintendent of the Winona-Montgomery Consolidated School District, speaks during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
According to state law, charter schools can only be established in areas where the local school district is rated C or above if the local school district’s board approves. There’s no appeal process, so if the school board denies the request, the process ends. 
New charter schools can only be established without local school board approval in areas where the local district is failing or receives a D rating on the accountability model.
Mississippi charter school researchers and leaders have maintained that it’s difficult to perform under the strict rules the state has imposed, and that charter schools require flexibility and freedom to flourish. This past year, they lobbied lawmakers to loosen these restrictions, allowing charters to open in more places. 
But state lawmakers — especially in the Senate — have been hesitant to grant the board more power as schools performance falters.
“It’s a hard one for me,” Roberson said. “I expect better.” 
Lisa Karmacharya, executive director of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, listens during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Lisa Karmacharya, executive director of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, said on Tuesday that she understands Roberson’s frustration but highlighted the progress of Ambition Prep, calling it the charter board’s “flagship” school. 
Since its first grade in 2023, Ambition has gained 30 points on the accountability scorecard, marking academic progress. 
She recommended that instead of pushing for charter school growth during the new year, the board should focus on outcomes and go back to the original promise of charter schools in Mississippi: that they would be afforded more flexibility than traditional public schools in exchange for better outcomes. 
Despite current standings, Karmacharya still believes the sector has an important place in Mississippi’s education system.
“Although the scores aren’t where we want them to be, we know that families choose these options and opportunities because they feel it’s what their child needs,” she said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s ‘constitutional sheriff’ push reaches voters with Amendment 8
text:
State Sen. Jill Carter speaks to the media surrounded by local sheriffs from around the state and a handful of GOP senators on April 5, 2023, regarding SJR 42. The goals of the legislation “would be to provide local sheriffs with the legal backing to defy COVID-era lockdowns, protect concealed carry information and oversee federal investigations,” the accompanying news release stated (Jason Hancock/Missouri Independent). When MyPillow founder Mike Lindell visited the Missouri Capitol in January 2023, the conversation was focused on election security.
Lindell, a Donald Trump ally who has repeatedly promoted false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen, offered a suggestion to lawmakers and activists: Contact your “constitutional sheriff.”
Craig and Linda Rantz, who were there that day, pointed out a problem. Missouri’s Constitution doesn’t establish the office of sheriff. State law does.
Nearly four years later, Missouri voters will decide whether to change that — and whether to make the state attorney general the only official who can initiate proceedings to remove a county sheriff.
Amendment 8 would make the elected office of county sheriff a constitutional requirement and place certain duties already spelled out in state law into the Missouri Constitution. That would prevent lawmakers from eliminating the office or changing those constitutional duties without voter approval.
But the proposal would also change how sheriffs can be removed from office. Under current law, a county prosecutor or the state attorney general can initiate a legal action known as quo warranto seeking a sheriff’s removal. Amendment 8 would reserve that authority to the attorney general, with a court ultimately deciding whether a sheriff should be removed. The amendment would not apply to St. Louis city, St. Louis County or St. Charles County.
The final proposal is narrower than earlier versions, which sought to give sheriffs authority to oversee federal and state investigations. But the debate surrounding it has continued to reflect a broader political movement that sees county sheriffs as a check on government overreach.
Craig and Linda Rantz recalled meeting with Lindell and then-Secretary of State Jay Ashcroft on Jan. 5, 2023, to discuss a method they had developed for hand-counting election results. The Rantzes and Lindell then walked to the Capitol, they said, and met with lawmakers, including Republican state Sen. Jill Carter of Granby. 
A few weeks after the meeting, Carter introduced legislation for the first time to amend the Missouri Constitution and enshrine a provision already in state law: that each county elect a sheriff to serve as its chief law enforcement officer. 
But her initial proposal also included a provision not found in state law that would have required sheriffs to “oversee all federal and state investigations in his or her county.”
Carter argued during an April 2023 Senate hearing that sheriffs should serve as “a hedge of protection” against violations of civil liberties and what she considered unconstitutional actions by the federal government. Her news release that April further stated the goal of the legislation “would be to provide local sheriffs with the legal backing to defy COVID-era lockdowns, protect concealed carry information and oversee federal investigations.” 
That broader vision of sheriffs’ authority didn’t survive the legislative process. Lawmakers eventually stripped out the provision giving sheriffs oversight of federal and state investigations.
“We’re not giving them any more power, any more authority than they currently statutorily have,” Carter said of Amendment 8.
The question appearing on the ballot as Amendment 8 asks voters whether they want to “support law enforcement by preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff, prohibiting the removal of a county sheriff except by a writ of quo warranto, and recognizing the office of sheriff as part of the administration of justice.”
 Constitutional sheriffs

For Osage County Sheriff Michael Bonham, the fight to take Missouri from statutory to constitutional sheriffs started before the meeting with Lindell. He said more than 30 states already enshrine the sheriff’s authority in their constitutions and argued that Missouri should do the same. 
But, he said, he struggled to get a legislator to “pick up” the issue. 
“It is a pure motive to be able to protect the legitimate office of the sheriff in the state of Missouri,” he said, “that legislators can’t come in and [say] ‘We’re mad at the sheriffs’ and that’s it. We’re going to make a state police.”
From Bonham’s perspective, a 2023 showdown between Illinois sheriffs and the governor also helped propel the legislation into the spotlight.
On Jan. 10, 2023, Gov. JB Pritzker signed the Protect Illinois Communities Act, which banned the sale of new assault weapons, high-capacity magazines and devices known as switches. The law also required existing owners to register their weapons or face criminal penalties.
The legislation followed a mass shooting at an Independence Day parade in Highland Park, Illinois, in July 2022.
Dozens of Illinois sheriffs announced they would not enforce the new restrictions or check compliance. Bonham supported their stance.
“I live in a rural area that is very pro-Second Amendment,” he said, “and to go to their house and say, ‘Look, you need to give up all your guns.’ That’s not going to happen.”
The Illinois law allowed people who already owned covered weapons to keep them, if they complied with registration requirements. But if they didn’t comply, a court could order them to surrender their covered firearms.
The Illinois sheriffs gained strong support from the Constitutional Sheriffs and Peace Officers Association, a national organization that promotes the belief that sheriffs have the authority to refuse to enforce laws they consider unconstitutional.
The group was founded by Richard Mack, a former Arizona sheriff and Oath Keepers board member who has been a prominent figure in the national constitutional sheriff movement. 
Bonham said his support for Missouri’s measure was not inspired by Mack’s work or the association. 
This spring, the term “constitutional sheriffs” was used repeatedly during hearings and debates in both Missouri legislative chambers, but what that term truly represented wasn’t discussed until Republican State Rep. Bryant Wolfin of St. Genevieve raised the issue right before the House passed the measure in May.
State Rep. Bennie Cook, a Republican from Houston, speaks on the Missouri House floor May 5, 2025 (Tim Bommel/House Communications).
Wolfin asked Republican state Rep. Bennie Cook of Houston, who handled Carter’s bill in the House, why lawmakers call this the “constitutional sheriff” bill. 
“That’s what basically we’ve been calling it for the past three to four years,” Cook replied, “is a constitutional sheriff bill to ensure it’s in the Constitution. 
Wolfin said he understood the term to mean how sheriffs are not only defending the constitution but also “defending our rights from the federal government or from state overreach.”
Cook said that Wolfin was “hitting the nail on the head.” 
“The sheriff is there to protect us from other entities,” Cook said. “They’re the chief law enforcement of the state or of the county, so they’re there to protect us from any type of overreach and kind of what you’re talking about there. That’s already in statute. This just moves it into the constitution to ensure that our sheriffs can never, never be taken away from us.” 
Wolfin ultimately voted against the amendment, saying that it didn’t go far enough to empower constitutional sheriffs. 
In an interview with The Independent last month, Wolfin said the bill does not align with what the grassroots conservatives movement has been pushing and why many wanted this legislation in the first place.
“Quite frankly, I think most of the people in our (legislature) were a little confused by what we were trying to do and why we were doing it,” he said. 
He also objected to the provision that would take away local prosecutors’ authority to seek a sheriff’s removal.
Carter told The Independent the attorney general has been the one to initiate a quo warranto process in the most recent cases when a sheriff has been removed in St. Louis and Ray County. Amendment 8 essentially solidifies the process that is currently in place. Bonham said county prosecutors can and have asked the attorney general to initiate the proceedings.
“Right now, as far as removal, it defers to the AG’s office because prosecutors have a strong relationship, usually with their sheriffs in prosecuting criminals,” Carter said.  
During the House debate in May, other lawmakers raised concerns about the duties that Amendment 8 would elevate from state law into the Constitution.
Among them is a requirement that sheriffs “apprehend and commit to jail all felons and traitors,” language already found in Missouri statute. Putting it into the Constitution would mean lawmakers could no longer change that requirement without voter approval.
Several Democrats questioned the wording, particularly the reference to “traitors.”
Democratic state Rep. Aaron Crossley of Independence noted that the word “traitor” isn’t defined in state statute.
“Is a traitor a protester?” he said. “Is it a political dissenter? Is it someone who disagrees with whoever is in power? I’m already uncomfortable with it being a statute, but putting it in our constitution where it can never be changed – or it can be but with a lot of hassle – I think that we’re really treading down a dangerous, dangerous road.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: How Missouri almost lost an experienced physician associate
text:
A healthcare worker places a bandage on a child after giving a vaccination shot (Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention).When I considered practicing in Missouri in late 2020, I expected the licensing process to evaluate my education, training, experience and professional credentials. What I did not expect was to be asked to reconstruct more than three decades of my personal preprofessional history.
After six months of unemployment due to the COVID-19 pandemic, I was offered a job and needed a Missouri physician assistant/associate (PA) license. Having practiced in other states, I assumed the process would focus on the qualifications most relevant to patient care: accredited education, national certification, clinical experience and any disciplinary record.
Instead, Missouri requires applicants to submit a complete curriculum vitae covering every year from high school graduation through the application date, including the names and addresses of all employers and supervisors, employment dates, job titles and all professional and nonprofessional activities.
I was 59 years old when I applied to practice in Missouri, more than 40 years after graduating from high school. In essence, the application process required me to document every employer, supervisor and activity dating back more than three decades before I became a certified PA at 49. It was time-consuming, frustrating and daunting. A 25-year-old PA applicant, only eight years removed from high school, likely wouldn’t find this extraordinary. But reconstructing eight years of work history is vastly different from reconstructing 30 years.
More importantly, I struggled to understand how this requirement improved patient safety or measured clinical competence. Missouri can verify meaningful indicators of readiness to practice through accredited education, national certification, professional references, clinical employment history and disciplinary records maintained by licensing authorities.
These safeguards protect the public while providing a meaningful assessment of a clinician’s qualifications. They are also the most relevant factors for determining whether a PA is prepared to care for patients.
In my case, the requirement nearly discouraged me from pursuing licensure in Missouri. After months of unemployment, I had little choice but to complete the process. But if I had been offered a comparable position in a state with a less cumbersome process, I might have chosen to practice there instead. That raises an important question: How many qualified healthcare professionals have chosen to practice elsewhere because of unnecessary licensing requirements?
Even a small loss of clinicians can have significant consequences in a state already facing workforce shortages. I was just one licensing applicant, but my experience may reflect that of an unknown number of PAs who have faced a similar experience.
No one is suggesting Missouri abandon its rigorous licensing standards. Patients deserve confidence that healthcare professionals are competent, ethical and qualified to practice. Thorough background checks, verification of education and certification and review of disciplinary history are the safeguards most relevant to evaluating a clinician’s fitness to practice, not unrelated employment from decades before entering the profession.
Healthcare delivery has changed dramatically over the past several decades. Clinicians today are educated to nationally accredited standards, maintain certification, complete continuing medical education and practice under extensive regulatory oversight. Licensing boards now have faster, more reliable ways to verify qualifications and disciplinary histories. Requirements focused on irrelevant preprofessional employment do not contribute to patient care.
Notably, Missouri licensing requirements for physicians do not include such demands, and nurse practitioners (NPs) are governed by the Board of Nursing, which has no similar requirement. This discrepancy raises a fundamental question: Why are PAs uniquely burdened with requirements that neither physicians nor NPs must meet?
The Missouri Board of Healing Arts, in collaboration with Missouri lawmakers, should streamline licensing requirements by eliminating the requirement to document preprofessional work history unrelated to healthcare when applying for initial PA licensure.
Passing the PA Licensure Compact was an important step toward improving interstate mobility for qualified PAs, but it does not change initial licensure requirements for PAs.
Missouri is seeking clinicians. Communities need providers. Patients need timely access to care. The question is whether the state wants experienced healthcare professionals to invest their time caring for patients or reconstructing employment records that play no role in patient care. The path forward is clear: reform PA licensing requirements and remove obligations that serve no public purpose.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: ‘Antithesis to that chaos’: 15-petition effort will soon launch, seeking Nebraska’s 2028 ballot
text:
Eric Underwood of Lincoln, leader of the groups Advocates for All Nebraskans and Make Nebraska Even Better, sits in a downtown bar and grill on Sept. 29, 2026. In front of him are a variety of documents for petitions he aims to file and run for the 2028 general election. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Before announcing a statewide 2028 petition last month to suspend Nebraska’s fuel tax for two months each year, Eric Underwood had spent a week to 10 days finalizing the idea.
That same day, on Sept. 24, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen allowed Nebraska agricultural producers to request refunds on state taxes for diesel fuel until Dec. 23, unless extended. The refunds in the executive order include one on a new 0.25-cent-per-gallon tax on dyed diesel signed into law this year. President Donald Trump issued a similar order for federal diesel taxes when he visited Grand Island on Oct. 5.
Underwood’s idea, by contrast, would extend relief to all drivers in Nebraska between Sept. 1 and Oct. 31. The proposal would also cap the maximum state fuel tax at 35 cents per gallon in perpetuity. 
The state tax is currently 31.8 cents, but Underwood expects an effort to increase it.
“State statutes can be a lot like Shakespeare when you’re diving into them,” Underwood told the Nebraska Examiner. “Amending them can be even worse, trying to edit Shakespeare or try to be the CliffsNotes of Shakespeare.”
Gov. Jim Pillen announces a pair of executive orders aimed at easing cost burdens on Nebraska agriculture producers on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Governor’s Office)
But the “Harvest Fuel Tax Holiday,” aimed at a period of more local travel for harvesting and school activities, is just the opening salvo to a multi-act “statutory audit” aimed for 2028.
Just days after announcing his first petition, Underwood sat down with the Examiner at the steakhouse he manages in downtown Lincoln to explain a network of 15 petitions. The petitions are united under the label “Make Nebraska Even Better.”
Among the topics Underwood is pursuing — a collection he says goes from relief to reform — are property taxes, local unfunded mandates, education and election administration.
“You can’t have the conversation if it’s not on paper, and if it’s not going to be willed into paper form at the Legislature, now it is,” Underwood said.
The statutory ‘audit’
This isn’t the first time Underwood, a former chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, has led a multipronged petition effort. 
Last year, Underwood and a small team announced “Advocates for All Nebraskans” with three property tax petitions, which are the same this time around: cap annual property valuation growth at 3%, halve taxable valuations by 50% and create a $50,000 minimum base salary for all public school teachers by repurposing state funds already going to K-12 schools.
Eric Underwood, former chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, center, leads a news conference with his new nonprofit Advocates For All Nebraskans to announce two ballot measures intended to lower property taxes and cap annual increases to property valuations. Aug. 25, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The 2026 petition effort also sought to return Nebraska to a “winner-take-all” system for awarding Electoral College votes at the 2026 election, which is returning for the 2028 cycle. If passed, the earliest it could affect a presidential election is 2032, unless the Legislature steps in sooner. The 2026 effort would have also required hand-counting of paper ballots, which isn’t returning in the 2028 crop at this time.
Supporters ultimately did not submit signatures for any of its 2026 statewide petitions.
For 2028, Underwood said, he met with local taxing authorities and is now proposing to:

Lower maximum property tax levy limits for the largest taxing authorities while increasing authority for smaller subdivisions, such as natural resource districts, rural fire departments, and airport authorities.
Cement voter approval before any political subdivision could exceed certain property tax limits in law. 
Legally block state lawmakers from shifting state costs to local property taxpayers. A similar legislative effort to let the voters decide the fate of future unfunded mandates has repeatedly failed to move forward. It fell short 23-20 in January.

A stack of petitions led by Eric Underwood of Lincoln, leader of the groups Advocates for All Nebraskans and Make Nebraska Even Better, sits in a downtown bar and grill on Sept. 29, 2026. The petitions are for the 2028 general election. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“For any elected official, I don’t care who you are, to say that it is not within state statutes to solve these problems is either being obtuse, ignorant or purposely deflecting of the effort needed to solve these problems, to fix them,” Underwood said.
The 2028 petition effort is Underwood’s own statutory audit, a multistep approach because of the Nebraska Constitution’s “single subject” requirement. 
“It can’t just throw everything into one petition and say, ‘let’s audit everything,’” Underwood said.
How many signatures needed?
Most of the 2028 efforts seek to amend or create new laws. The petitions would need valid signatures from at least 7% of registered voters at the time petitions are due in July 2028. Some are constitutional amendments, which would require signatures from at least 10% of voters.
In both cases, the signatures must include a geographic distribution of at least 5% of voters in at least 38 of Nebraska’s 93 counties. The 2028 due date would be the first week of July.



Quotation







You can’t have the conversation if it’s not on paper, and if it’s not going to be willed into paper form at the Legislature, now it is.


– Eric Underwood, leader of Advocates for All Nebraskans


Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
A new Nebraska-based signature-gathering firm with only Nebraska circulators will assist the effort, Underwood said, and his team will use a prioritized list of voters — Republicans, Democrats, nonpartisans and otherwise — to pursue the ballot. The list includes more than 200,000 voters across 150 cities statewide. Underwood said the two-year window gives room to prioritize petitions and go door to door.
As Underwood eyes 2028, he expects more advocates nationwide to also lean into petitions.
“Whether it’s good, bad or ugly, the part that I believe the most in is that if it gets on the ballot, at least the people have a choice,” Underwood said.
The exact wording of Underwood’s petitions is subject to change as they work through the Nebraska Revisor of Statutes. The launch of petitions and the release of the exact wording of each effort are expected after the Nov. 3 election.
The people and the lawmakers
Though a public vote is more than two years away, Underwood said an initial goal is conversation.
Ideally, all of the changes could come at the 49-person statehouse, which isn’t necessarily a bad process, Underwood said. But he said the legislative process adds other variables.
State lawmakers gather on the final day of Nebraska’s 2026 legislative session. Not pictured: State Sens. Jana Hughes of Seward and Dan Quick of Grand Island. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“If I truly believe in these, why wouldn’t I go through a path that is constitutionally aligned, that’s a right to the people, and it would allow me to present to the ultimate voice of the outcome of Nebraska’s future: the people?” Underwood said.
State lawmakers would also be free to take up any of the ideas Underwood is pursuing, as state Sens. Loren Lippincott of Central City, Dan Lonowski of Hastings and Barry DeKay of Niobrara did in the 2026 legislative session with previous Underwood-offered petitions. Doing so also helped get fiscal estimates for Underwood’s efforts.
“From that moment forth, I realized that there is just as much an opportunity that these can become state statutes that they (senators) amend,” Underwood said. “And I don’t care who gets the credit. The people in Nebraska need this, and let’s make that our focus.”
‘Antithesis to that chaos’
Underwood doesn’t expect much progress in the 2027 or 2028 legislative sessions, in part because of likely changing margins between Republicans — who have a 33-vote supermajority now — and Democrats. He said Republicans might lose one to three seats. Democrats and Democratic-endorsed registered nonpartisans are aiming to pick up even more.
A woman signs a Support Our Schools petition in Omaha. July 8, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)
It takes 33 votes to overcome a filibuster. Overriding a governor’s veto requires 30 votes.
“I’m not predicting outcomes, I have no say on it,” Underwood said. “These are variables we have never seen before and so, if anything, maybe petitions become the antithesis to that chaos. Maybe petitions cut through all the noise, all the winter of discontent, as I called it, and get to a level of, ‘Is this what people want?’”
Nebraska’s one-house Legislature is, by design, officially nonpartisan, so a legislative candidate’s party doesn’t appear on the ballots and lawmakers don’t officially organize by party.
Underwood said if it’s supposed to be a nonpartisan group, and if a petition starts to gain support, that could lead to action at the statehouse.
Working toward solutions
Since 2008, Republicans have won every single statewide election in Nebraska, and for years, Republicans had been gaining on solidifying a 33-vote supermajority in the Legislature. In that time, some lawmakers worked to incrementally impose change, but Underwood said incrementalism risks nothing happening.
A sign encouraging Nebraskans to register and get out to vote sits at the Harvest Moon Festival in Lincoln outside a booth for multiple civic advocacy organizations on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Democratic Party Jane Kleeb and others have argued that Nebraskans should try something different because of the repeated GOP control. But Underwood, while he was an envied party chairman nationally in keeping dozens of Nebraska’s top elected positions in GOP hands, said Democrats do control more than 1,000 local positions, including seats dealing with property taxes.
“If we’re fighting more in the conversation as to whose fault it is, we’re not even looking at solutions,” Underwood said.
Underwood said he has heard from voters in the past year frustrated with legislative changes to ballot measures, some they supported and others they didn’t but didn’t like the changes. He worries this reflects the state is being “very obtuse” and, at times, “oblivious” to its electorate.
“Maybe this actually helps with that as well, because if the people start to sign on to something and they start to make their voice louder and louder through one singular paper on a certain principle, you can’t be ignored at some point,” Underwood said.
‘A potential bookend’
On the fuel tax holiday idea, Underwood said, Pillen’s proposal left other Nebraska drivers wondering, “What about us?” Underwood pointed to concerns expressed by state Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, a Democrat, who told KETV Newswatch 7 that Nebraska is either in a budget crisis or it’s not. 
If the state executive order doesn’t have a huge impact on the state budget, Conrad asked, what impact will it have on farmers?
“Let’s move away from reactionary,” Underwood said. “Let’s become proactive.”
Whatever happens in the 2027 and 2028 legislative sessions, Underwood said, people could have a different choice come November 2028.
Said Underwood: “I believe that this provides a potential bookend to what needs to happen in this next legislative cycle.”

title: Stockard on the Stump: Tennessee governor shuts down questions
text:
Let them eat cake! Or at least, let them drink Champagne on Air France's direct flight from Nashville to Paris. State and local officials, including Economic Development Commissioner Stuart McWhorter, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Metro Nashville Airport Authority Board Chair Jimmy Granbery and Gov. Bill Lee hoisted a glass on Wednesday at the formal announcement. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville airport folks moved “faster than grease through a goose” this week to stop media questions that dared stray from their Air France announcement. 
Blame Davy Crockett for that time-tested idiom.
When a Lookout reporter tried to go “off topic” during a press gaggle after Wednesday’s main press conference, an airport authority flack and Lee quickly shut it down and referred questions to the governor’s office spokesperson, who hasn’t responded to emails since Moby Dick was a minnow. Technically, whales were never minnows because they’re mammals, but you get the gist.
For the most part, the term-limited Lee, who leaves office in mid-January, has been in hiding all summer.
But considering we were less than a week from a failed execution that displayed an embarrassing lack of preparation on the part of state prison personnel and, clearly, the medical team tasked with putting convicted murderer Christa Pike to death, Lee should be ready to field more queries about something other than Air France.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
After all, this botched execution, which led to the sudden resignation of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, could wind up being his legacy. People won’t remember the Paris junkets that led to the new French flight and other business investments in Tennessee. They might not even remember his preferred legacy: establishment of private-school vouchers for all students, regardless of income.
But people on every side of the death penalty issue will recall the failures of the Lee administration to carry out the punishment effectively — right or wrong. They also could remember that he refused to take responsibility for the disaster the day after it happened, instead blaming the protocol developed by Strada’s Department of Correction and “vetted and approved” by Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti. (We will give him partial credit for holding a press conference last week.)
Lee says he doesn’t want the U.S. Senate seat that could be vacated by Sen. Marsha Blackburn, if she wins the gubernatorial race as expected. Maybe he’d prefer to count cattle or make sure crap runs downhill. But he sure is doing a great job of avoiding the Capitol press corps, though he does appear more willing to take press questions than Blackburn.
Departing: U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn on her way to leave a press conference at Nashville International Airport on Wednesday, with no questions taken or answered. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Incidentally, Wednesday’s event would have been a great opportunity for Blackburn to do what she says she’s been doing: “talk to Tennesseans every day.”
Instead, after a short greeting and photo op, Blackburn vanished like the ghost of Hamlet’s father. Of course, he ratted out his murderer, and they all died eventually.
This is not a prediction.
It is fitting, though, that Lee and Blackburn gathered with airport officials to celebrate the Air France deal with, what else, French champagne. (One waiter dropped a couple of glasses.)
As for the unwashed masses who can barely buy groceries these days, much less a plane ticket to France and wouldn’t take one if they could: Let them eat cake.
Another big deal
A consortium led by the same group set to build Nashville’s first toll lane landed another major contract, this time with the Georgia Department of Transportation, for nearly 38 miles of work on I-285 around Atlanta.
Top End Mobility Group, headed up by Spain-based Ferrovial, agreed to make nearly $24 billion in “concessions,” or payments to Georgia to win the $8.9 billion project, a similar amount it offered to Tennessee to land the deal here. The contract will last 50 years, but the consortium will make payments to Georgia in six installments up front and reimburse the state for $515 million it’s already spent on the project.
Ferrovial, which is leading the Tennessee effort on a southeast Nashville corridor toll-road project, saw its stock value dip because of concerns about the project here. It took another tumble this week because investors are concerned about its ability to take on debt to pay $50 billion to Tennessee and Georgia before it ever collects in toll fees from motorists.
Losing bidder in I-24 toll lane project files suit seeking contract records

Public records tiff
Another road-building consortium, 24 Choice Lanes Partners, that failed to win the Tennessee bid after offering only $7 billion in “concessions” filed a public records lawsuit Oct. 5 through former Metro Nashville Legal Director and now private lawyer Jon Cooper against the state, claiming it was blocked from obtaining documents connected to the project. 
The Attorney General’s Office responded this week with a Davidson County Chancery Court filing that says the public records request was made too soon, before Sept. 30 when the state reached a point in the deal with DriveTN called “commercial close,” enabling them to finalize the contract. Until that point, it said, the documents were confidential.
The AG’s Office said in its filing that the Department of Transportation wasn’t concealing information or documentation and that it “remains fully prepared to produce responsive records and comply with the Tennessee Public Records Act.”
As usual, the AG’s Office said the plaintiff lacked standing to sue, this time under the public records act, and called for the complaint to be dismissed.
Take that
The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance levied a $300 civil penalty against the Sumner County Constitutional Republicans in September for failing to file reports on time. 
This sort of penalty is common, especially for neophytes unaccustomed to dealing with campaign finance reports. But it came two years after the Registry board forced the Tennessee Constitutional Republicans and its operation group in Sumner County to register as political action committees.
Tennessee election finance board to subpoena members of Constitutional Republicans

In 2024, the group said it was nothing but a coffee klatch intent on spreading “conservatism.” During a hearing two years ago, Registry members noted Tennessee Constitutional Republicans brought in about $18,000 last year and spent about $12,000, according to information the group provided.
Granted, they didn’t spend millions of dollars. But they had a modicum of influence on local politics.
The group hired private investigators to vet candidates, rented space at community events, held breakfasts, brought stickers, sold T-shirts, and endorsed and disavowed candidates on their website, which also had donation links to bring in — you guessed it — money. 
They “started full tilt” but found themselves in “pretty considerable of a snarl.” Now they’re just about “cooked up to a cracklin’.” Give credit to Davy Crockett.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Poll shows Democrat Beau Bayh with advantages in final weeks of Indiana campaign
text:
Secretary of state candidates, from left: Independent Greg Ballard, Democrat Beau Bayh, Republican Max Engling and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. (Photos provided by campaigns)New poll results show Democrat Beau Bayh with advantages in name identification and voter support over Republican Max Engling going into the final weeks of the race for Indiana secretary of state.
The poll, commissioned by the Free Press Indiana news organization, found 43% were likely to vote for Bayh and 35% likely to cast their ballot for Engling. Libertarian Lauri Shillings had 6% support, with Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard at 5% and 11% undecided.
Bayh — the son of former Gov. and U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh — also had much better name recognition and favorability ratings than Engling.
The poll results showed Bayh with a favorability mark of 35% to 18% unfavorable. Engling had 12% with a favorable opinion and 17% unfavorable.
But the biggest factor could be that 48% of those polled said they had never heard of Engling, with 27% saying they didn’t know of Bayh.
“Not only does he have a name ID advantage, he’s got almost a two-to-one favorable unfavorable rating, which is almost unheard of,” pollster Christine Matthews told the Capital Chronicle. “The fact that Beau Bayh has driven up his favorable rating, not just his name ID, is, I think, a real testament to why he is positioned the way he is on the ballot.”
(Courtesy of Free Press Indiana)
Matthews is the president of Virginia-based Bellwether Research, which conducted the poll. Matthews has overseen extensive polling in Indiana, including for former Republican Gov. Mitch Daniels.
The poll found 85% of Democrats saying they supported Bayh, whose strong fundraising allowed him to start statewide television advertising in August — a month before Engling. Independent voters were giving Bayh 39% support — more than double any other candidate.
Engling had more tepid backing among Republican voters at 68% support. Engling only started his campaign in May as a little-known staffer to U.S. Sen. Jim Banks before defeating current GOP Secretary of State Diego Morales at the state Republican convention.
Other poll results found government corruption as the top voter concern and that 69% oppose the construction of new data centers in the state.
Bayh has pushed both topics in his campaign advertising and denounced what he calls corrupt spending by Morales.
“Corruption has been a big part of his paid media message, so that’s really I think resonating,” Matthews said.
Bayh appears able to continue his advertising push as campaign finance reports filed Thursday show him maintaining sizable fundraising and spending advantages over Engling.
The Free Press Indiana poll surveyed 839 likely voters during Oct. 8-11. It oversampled Republicans, in line with the state’s GOP lean, and has a margin of error of 3.4 percentage points.
The findings showing Bayh and Engling far ahead of Ballard and Shillings follows a poll from Hoosier Leadership for America, a political group associated with Banks, with a similar result.
The Hoosier Leadership for America poll, taken Sept. 27-30, showed Engling with 38% support to Bayh’s 37%. Shillings had 6% support and Ballard 5% with 14% undecided.

name: WyoFile
title: A lightless stasis
text:
Opinion

There is a point when crossing the Garfield Street pedestrian bridge in Laramie where the overhead lights stop working. In daylight, this sidewalk suspended above the Union Pacific Railroad is quite magnificent. You can see in all directions across the highway to the mountains and watch the trains pass below.
At night, on the side where the lights don’t work, you can’t see anything; not even what’s a few yards ahead. It has been this way since I moved to Laramie’s West Side Neighborhood six years ago, working only sporadically before returning to its lightless stasis. 
In late September, after a survivor filed a civil lawsuit, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul reopened a closed 2024 investigation of the alleged gang rape of Jane Doe at Cornell University. National news outlets were ablaze with a slew of previously unreleased information regarding the case from past records, the accused fraternity members and the Cornell campus. 
Survivors and allies across the nation began declaring themselves “Jane Doe” in solidarity with Cornell’s Doe-of-note. Meanwhile, speculation about her recollection of the attack became fodder for comment sections and talk show commentary. We’re met with the all-too-familiar questioning of the attacked woman’s responsibility in “inviting” the young men to her body. 
This Jane Doe’s story is not new. There is no novelty in the discourse around the alleged perpetrators’ responsibility to the survivor, to one another, to those they see as objects of sexual desire. To women, this is a familiar walk down an uncomfortable path — as familiar as the dark stretch on my commute home across the railroad.Stories of assault and half-hearted institutional attempts to reconcile are not unique to a private college fraternity across the country. Our neighbors cautiously move through our towns, aware of the darkness that surrounds them, regardless of where we live. Wyoming’s small towns hold stories of atrocious crimes, too. 
Even cowboys are perpetrators. 
Even cowboys are survivors. 
Women swap horror stories in private conversations about where to be extra cautious, share recommendations of purse-sized protection devices and walk each other to their cars just in case. They don’t make these choices because of young men’s poor choices in Ithaca, New York. These choices come from experience — local and relatable. 
According to a statewide assessment from the Wyoming Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault/Colorado Futures Center, 25% of adult women in Wyoming have experienced sexual assault. Statistically, it would be unusual for you to not know someone who has experienced assault. And chances are, you know someone who has committed assault. 
In a Wyoming Crime Statistics report from the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation, only 80 of the 434 sexual assault crimes reported in 2025 were reported as perpetrated by a stranger or unknown individual. More than 8 in 10 were perpetrated by family, acquaintances and intimate partners. The dark truth isn’t a stranger in the shadows. It’s someone we know.
Cornell’s survivor reported the intimate details of her attack, left school and exchanged her planned future and her name for a pseudonym no woman wants. Jane Does across the country could line up to stretch from Laramie to Ithaca. Yet somehow they go unseen, as if the light can’t quite reach.
The pedestrian bridge in downtown Laramie is simply an unlit sidewalk. Its care is held somewhere between a national railroad corporation and a well-meaning small-town government. A lit path would be appreciated, but I’m not asking someone to change a light bulb for me. 
I want to know that you see the same dark I see. 
The Wyoming Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault is a tenant of the Laramie Plains Civic Center, where the author serves as executive director.

title: University of Wyoming student finds elusive insect in Yellowstone alpine
text:
University of Wyoming junior Will Anderson spent the 2025 field season picking through debris-covered glaciers in Yellowstone National Park in a hunt for a tiny and elusive insect that prefers cold temperatures. 
Will Anderson takes a break from looking for ice crawlers in Yellowstone National Park. Anderson and other University of Wyoming students were returning from surveying a rock glacier near Mount Holmes. (James Sims)
For all the rocks he turned over, he found not a single Grylloblattodea, or ice crawler. One of the rarest orders of insects in the world, ice crawlers only have 35 described species.
Anderson, a biology major from Casper, ventured out again this summer with Audrey Lindsteadt, a third-year doctoral student researching rock glaciers. And on his first outing, while flipping over rocks near Antler Peak, he discovered two ice crawlers. A couple weeks later, he found a third near Grey Peak. That’s where he and Lindsteadt detoured to after a sow grizzly bear blocked their originally planned route. 
Ice crawlers are extremophiles, meaning they prefer cold habitats. The insect is only found in small pockets of northeastern Asia, Siberia and the western U.S. and Canada, Anderson said. Populations are usually restricted to small, disconnected areas in mountains and caves. 

While flipping rocks on top of a large rock glacier near Antler Peak in northwest Yellowstone National Park, Will Anderson discovered two ice crawlers. (Audrey Lindsteadt)

Anderson identified the specimens he collected as Grylloblatta campodeiformis, which is the most widespread North American species, he said. He believes ice crawlers can help scientists better understand alpine ecosystems, he said in a University of Wyoming press release. 
“I am interested in this insect because there is so much not known about them, with their life history, habitat and distribution all not being fully understood,” he said. “I also am passionate about and interested in their alpine habitats, which are understudied.”
Anderson will present his results at the Entomological Society of America’s 74th annual meeting in November.

name: WyoFile
title: Spreading fear about wolves never goes out of style
authors: Story Warren, Writers on the Range
text:
In early September, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that continued to rely on big-bad-wolf myths. He claimed that living in wolf country is “very dangerous.”

Opinion

He then directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican wolves should lose federal protection under the Endangered Species Act. Without waiting for an answer, he also directed Burgum to support Congressional removal of gray wolves from the endangered species list.
Wildlife defenders noted that Trump’s directives were in part meant to distract the public from the impact of the president’s decision to ease tariffs on imported beef, making life harder for American ranchers. The truth is that killing wolves won’t do a thing to lower meat prices or help the industry, as according to USDA data, just 1% of cattle and sheep losses are attributed to wolves in states with wolf populations. 
Research also shows that killing wolves doesn’t prevent conflict. When conflicts do occur, there are tools like range riding, carcass removal, scare devices and other deterrents. Sens. Adam Schiff, D-California, and Steve Daines, R-Montana, recently introduced the Human-Wildlife Conflict Reduction Act, which would help ranchers by assisting with such livestock protection strategies.
Beyond dramatically overstating wolves’ impact on the cattle industry, it was particularly troubling to see an American president repeat the absurd claim that federal protections for wolves should be eliminated because they put people’s lives at risk — that “innocent people can get in bad shape.”
Such misleading statements not only have serious consequences for wolf conservation and recovery, they also do a disservice to those living in wolf country by stoking unnecessary fear. It is already legal to kill a wolf, even a federally endangered one, in defense of human life.
More importantly, wolves want little to do with people and generally avoid us. Like bears and cougars, they share spaces with us in rural communities and areas in which human development and wild spaces overlap, where they can be curious. They can also be territorial toward domestic dogs and can sometimes follow us at a distance until we’re away from their pups. Wolves can sometimes approach hunters imitating animal calls, too, not realizing what’s making the noise.
But wolves are simply not out to get us.
I began tracking wolves — following their tracks through the woods — in my teens, sometimes with friends and family, sometimes solo, sometimes for fun, sometimes for work (always carrying bear spray). I’ve been close to a lot of wolves. If humans were on their menu, a short woman hiking alone should be like a free hot dog. But I’ve never once felt threatened.
One encounter now on video, where a wolf walked in my direction (not knowing I was there) and then retreated, was published by the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife to educate people about wolf behavior. It has amassed over 23 million views: “What to Expect if You Encounter a Wolf” on YouTube. It’s worth watching.
Every year, millions of people live, hike, and hunt in wolf territory without incident. Since their populations began to recover in the 1980s, wolves have caused just one human injury in the Lower 48 states. In Canada and Alaska, where more wolves roam, only about 10 incidents — two fatal —  have occurred since 2000. Almost all of these involved wolves conditioned to human food or garbage. Lightning killed more than 40 Canadians in that timespan. Mexican wolves, a smaller subspecies in the Southwest, have never attacked a human.
In a recent review of wolf-human conflicts, researchers stated that “the risks associated with a wolf attack are above zero, but far too low to calculate.”
Millions flock to Yellowstone National Park for the opportunity to see wolves. Sometimes hazing is required when wolves become too comfortable with people — for their safety more than ours. Yellowstone wolves are targeted by trophy hunters and recreational trappers when they cross the invisible park boundary. In Montana, Wyoming and Idaho, wolves are killed by the hundreds, demonstrating the deadly consequences for wolves when protection is removed.
The return of wolves is an opportunity for curiosity, wonder and respect, not scapegoating. Wolves deserve better than to be used as a distraction by the Trump administration, and those living alongside wolves deserve better than fearmongering.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: In race for Idaho attorney general, a Democrat is trying to unseat a long-time Republican official
text:
Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman says she has a long track record of being a straightforward attorney who is running to keep politicization out of the office — something she says her opponent hasn’t done. 
But Raúl Labrador, the Republican incumbent running for a second term, says he transformed the office for the better — pointing to his legal victories defending state laws in court — in part because he followed through on a promise he made when he first campaigned: being an aggressive attorney general. 
The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. 
The attorney general is an elected office that serves as the state’s top attorney, which includes defending the state and its laws in court, and serves on the Idaho Land Board, which manages state endowment lands. The attorney general serves a four-year term and receives an annual salary of $146,730.
In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic attorney general more than 30 years ago.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Who is Lori Hickman, Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general?

Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman speaks at a press conference announcing her endorsements on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
Hickman, 61, is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron and as a clerk in Idaho’s federal courthouse, the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho. She hasn’t run for public office before.
She spent her childhood moving around the country as part of a military family. She said she has lived for 30 years in Idaho, where she said her family has deep roots. In 2013, she joined the Boise-based law firm McFarland Ritter as an attorney focusing on business negotiation and litigation.
She served as board chair for Mormon Women for Ethical Government, a nonpartisan and 501(c)(4) faith-based nonprofit organization that joined a lawsuit unsuccessfully challenging an Idaho law that established tax credits for students to attend private, religious schools. Hickman said the people she encountered in her involvement in that group encouraged her to run for the attorney general’s office. 
Though she’s running as a Democrat, she says she wishes the race was nonpartisan, like elections for judges in Idaho. 
“A good attorney just follows the law, wherever it goes,” Hickman said in a recent interview. 
Before filing to run, she said she was a registered Republican so she could vote in the state’s closed GOP primary elections. But Hickman said she joined the race as a Democrat because she felt she didn’t have enough time to gather 1,000 signatures to run as an independent, or to mount a competitive campaign for the Republican primary election in May, where Labrador ran unopposed. 
Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman stands in front of more than a dozen deputy attorneys general, and two former Republican AGs, who endorsed her in the 2026 election. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
Earlier this month, Hickman announced a slate of endorsements from dozens of former deputy attorneys general, including a handful who left the office around the start of Labrador’s first term. Those endorsements also include two former Republican Idaho attorneys general: Lawrence Wasden, the state’s longest serving attorney general, and Jim Jones, who also served on the Idaho Supreme Court and is a frequent critic of Labrador. 
On Thursday, she announced endorsements from more Republicans in Idaho, including former Republican state Rep. Julie Yamamoto, former Republican Idaho Secretary of State Ben Ysursa, and former Sergeant at Arms of the U.S. Senate Gregory Casey, who served as chief of staff to former U.S. Sen. Larry Craig, R-Idaho. 
If elected, Hickman would be the state’s first female attorney general. She is a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. 
At a news conference announcing her endorsements, she talked about her vision for the office.
“Idaho deserves an attorney general who practices law, not politics,” Hickman said. 
“I have over 20 years of legal experience as an attorney, seeking results, not headlines. I never planned on running for office. But as anyone here standing beside me can tell you, the attorney general’s office has lost its way and lost focus on serving the people of Idaho. Under my leadership, the office of Idaho’s attorney general will once again be a zealous advocate for the state of Idaho and for all of its citizens.”
 Who is Raúl Labrador, the Republican candidate for Idaho attorney general?

Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 24, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Labrador, 58, is an attorney and has held elected offices as a Republican in Idaho for nearly two decades. 
Between 2006 and 2010, he served two terms in the Idaho House of Representatives, before running for the U.S. Congress.
In 2010, he defeated the last Democratic congressman elected in Idaho, Walt Minnick, in the general election. Labrador went on to serve four terms in Congress, and was a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, a group of conservative lawmakers. Born in Puerto Rico, Labrador was the first Hispanic person to represent Idaho in Congress.
In 2018, instead of seeking re-election to Congress, he ran unsuccessfully for governor, losing out to now-Gov. Brad Little in the GOP primary election.
“I thought I was done with politics,” Labrador recalled in an interview this week at his office in the Idaho State Capitol. 
But soon, Labrador said attorneys general in other states encouraged him to run for the office in Idaho. So he did, saying he believed the incumbent, 20-year GOP attorney general Wasden, wouldn’t seek re-election. They both ran, and Labrador defeated Wasden in the 2022 Republican primary election, and won in the November general election.
Labrador said he set out to transform the Office of the Attorney General by being an aggressive attorney for the state. And nearly four years later, he said he’s proud of what he’s accomplished — pointing to his work to address a backlog of tips for child sex abuse material cases, and to improve legal strategies in court cases.
“I made a bunch of promises to the people of Idaho of what I was going to do in the Office of Attorney General,” Labrador said. “I told them that I was going to be more aggressive. I thought that we were going to be more successful. I told them that we were going to create an office of solicitor general, and that I was going to leave the office better than I found it. And I think in every single way, the office has improved from the prior administration. (It) has been more successful. We’ve won more cases. We have helped not just the state debate but the national debate on some of the most important issues of the day.”
He is also a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador poses in his office near a golden fiddle he received as a gift after legal victories that his office described as defeating Satan on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
On a bookshelf lined with books of state laws in Labrador’s office, a golden fiddle sits as a reminder of legal victories his office portrayed as defeating Satan. The fiddle, which Labrador said was a gift, is a nod to the song “The Devil Went Down to Georgia.”
He dismissed criticisms of his actions as, in part, fear of change. He cited a quote by former Alabama football coach Nick Saban.
“He said something that I think applies to this situation, many situations in life. ‘Mediocre people do not like high achievers,’” Labrador said. “And I came in. I started doing things better than were being done before. And they’re mad that things are actually going pretty well in this office.”
 Candidates clash over legal opinions to lawmakers

In his first term in office, Labrador has faced criticism about his actions as attorney general — including investigating a state agency he legally represents, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. 
Hickman’s campaign touches on many of those developments and has criticized Labrador’s office for not providing written legal opinions to lawmakers, which state law outlines as a duty of the attorney general. She said those opinions, which can assess the enforceability or constitutionality of a proposed bill in the Idaho Legislature before it passes, are “the way a good government runs.”
“Do your job at the front end, and provide that legal guidance and analysis that they need — (which) is required by statute — because that’s the way a good government runs,” Hickman said. “… The Legislature’s doing its job, and because they’re passing laws that affect every single Idahoan, then make sure those laws are legally sound and they’re not running afoul of Idaho’s Constitution or the federal Constitution, or other laws or statutes.” 
Labrador said he is still providing those opinions to legislative sponsors of bills — not to critics in the Legislature who want to “attack” a bill.
Back when he was in the Legislature, he said he remembered seeing dueling opinions from different attorneys in the attorney general’s office. 
“To me, that was almost close to malpractice to use this office to go attack somebody’s bill that you were then going to have to defend in the courts later,” Labrador said.
Now, when Labrador says he has bad news for a lawmaker who asked for legal advice, he said he verbally relays the bad news — and asks if they want it put in writing.
“Because the law also says that if I put it in writing, it has to be then published — it’s a public record,” he said. “So I said, ‘Do you want me to tell them that your bill sucks?’ And most of them say, ‘No, it’s OK. Thanks for letting me know.’ And they either go change it or just scrap it or something like that.’”
He says he’s fulfilling his legal duties, and that it is better for the state because he has an improved relationship with the Legislature.
“Some people are mad. …  Because this office was being allowed to be used as a political weapon, (bill critics) don’t like it. But most of the legislators are thanking me,” he said. “They’re like, ‘Great, this is the way I wanted to have a relationship with the office of attorney general.’ Because then I’m actually an assistance to the Legislature, not a weapon to be used against the Legislature.”
That shift has also, Labrador says, helped the state in court. He said a critical legal opinion issued under his predecessor on Idaho’s first-in-the-nation ban on transgender athletes was cited by the groups suing over the law in 2020. Years later, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld Idaho’s law.  
Labrador said he doesn’t agree with every law he defends. But if it passes, he said, “I’m going to defend it.” 
Hickman has her own story about the importance of legal opinions from the attorney general’s office.
More than a decade ago, her daughter, Ilah Hickman, spent years advocating in the Legislature to name the Idaho giant salamander as the state’s official amphibian. 
At the time, some lawmakers had worried that the symbolic declaration could invoke environmental protection laws. A legal opinion by the office of Wasden, Labrador’s predecessor, helped clear the air, the Spokesman-Review reported. 
Back then, Hickman remembers other lawmakers scoffing at the concerns.
But the experience proved a quirky reminder of the attorney general’s role.
“That was how she learned about it and how I realized: Oh yeah, the lawyer’s giving out good advice, and it doesn’t mean they have to take it. But at least it’s written, and it’s in the record,” Hickman said. 
“Hopefully, it is a behind-the-scenes role too — not making headlines, not having sound bites on any news shows or anything like that,” she continued. “If lawyers are doing their job, they’re kind of in the back room, boring, like accountants, like just like doing the good job of protecting and representing Idahoans to the best of the lawyer’s ability, without having it be some big flashy, headline-making part of running our good government here in Idaho.”
Hickman also cited a legal opinion Labrador wrote on Idaho’s abortion laws to a state lawmaker — which sparked a lawsuit that ended with the state paying nearly $400,000 in legal fees. The lawsuit was brought by a Planned Parenthood affiliate.
Labrador pushed back on the characterization. 
He said his office told the court his office withdrew that opinion because it was incomplete. The opinion said medical professionals who refer or prescribe abortion pills to pregnant patients across state lines are subject to criminal penalties under Idaho’s strict abortion ban. And Labrador said the fines his office paid in the case — which ended in a legal agreement last year — pale in comparison to the $300 million his office recouped in his term, and to the millions of dollars in legal fees that he said his predecessor’s office paid in litigation in his last term.
That opinion, Labrador said, was part of what inspired his shift in providing written opinions to lawmakers.
“It’s one of the reasons, actually, I don’t write letters, because I noticed that the courts were going to treat everything that came from this office differently than my predecessor,” he said. “Because my predecessor … one thing that has changed dramatically, is he loved to acquiesce to the other side. We lost a lot of cases in Idaho because he would concede the point that the other side was making.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Senior adviser from Idaho Gov. Little’s campaign reportedly advised pro-Russian government
text:
FBI Director Kash Patel, right, takes a picture next to Chris LaCivita ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)One of the political consultants who the New York Times recently reported received hundreds of thousands of dollars to advise the Russia-aligned government of Republika Srpska was previously named a senior adviser to Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s campaign in February. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Oct. 6, the New York Times reported LaCivita and another adviser traveled to Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina to advise the country’s government before its recent election. 
The Times and other national reports identified LaCivita as the co-manager of President Donald Trump’s 2024 election campaign and a senior adviser to the MAGA Inc. super PAC.
While LaCivita is more well-known for his work for Trump and MAGA Inc., he has also worked in Idaho. 
In February, Little announced that LaCivita joined the Brad Little for Governor campaign as a senior adviser.
Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Chris’ immense experience and understanding of political campaigns and strategy in races all across the country will be a huge asset to our campaign operation,” Little said in a written statement issued Feb. 26. “His insight and ability to deliver winning messages and tactics are unparalleled. I am glad to have him on the team.”
Efforts to reach LaCivita this week were unsuccessful. 
Little’s campaign manager, Joan Vargas, did not respond to multiple requests from the Idaho Capital Sun asking if LaCivita still serves as a senior adviser to Little, and whether Little knew about the trip.
Back when he joined Little’s campaign in February, LaCivita issued a written statement saying he was excited to help Little get re-elected in Idaho.
“Joining the Brad Little for Governor campaign is a great honor and opportunity,” LaCivita said. “Gov. Little has been delivering results for Idahoans, and he is just getting started. I look forward to working with his team to keep Idaho one of the best states in the country.”
It was not immediately clear what work LaCivita did for Little’s campaign or if LaCivita still serves as a senior adviser on Little’s campaign.
In its story, the New York Times said it is common for political consultants to also work with foreign candidates and governments. However, the New York Times said LaCivita’s trip to Republika Srpska was notable because it occurred while LaCivita is working to help Trump-aligned candidates in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
