name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Finance reports: Tennessee Democrats boost funding for key races in final push to election day
text:
Tennessee Democrats are pouring money into a handful of target state House races in an effort to flip seats from Republicans. (Photo illustration: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Campaign finance reports released Wednesday show Tennessee’s Democratic party and legislators pouring tens of thousands of dollars into select campaigns in an effort to flip Republican house seats.
Here’s a run-down of the most competitive races.
House District 97: John Gillespie (R) vs. Jesse Huseth (D)
Republican incumbent John Gillespie is once again facing Democratic businessman Jesse Huseth in the race to represent central Shelby County, parts of East Memphis and part of Cordova.
Tennessee’s House Democratic Caucus has made flipping this seat a priority in the 2026 election cycle, funneling $27,000 into Huseth’s campaign. Gillespie is the only House Republican to hold a seat in a district won by then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
The pair are evenly matched in terms of cash on hand leading up to Nov. 3: Gillespie has just over $84,000 left in his coffers and Huseth has a slight funding edge with nearly $88,700. Gillespie has an outstanding $25,000 self-endorsed loan, and Huseth has a $3,600 loan.
Huseth first challenged Gillespie in 2024, but Gillespie held onto the seat with 51.7% of the vote to Huseth’s 48.3%.
Reboot: Memphis businessman Jesse Huseth is making his second bid to unseat Republican incumbent state Rep. John Gillespie. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)Heading into the November 3 midterm election, Rep. John Gillespie, a Memphis Republican, is evenly matched with his Democratic challenger. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Gillespie brought in $50,800 in the third quarter of 2026, including a $5,000 contribution from Tennessee House Majority Leader William Lamberth’s political action committee. Other notable donations include $2,500 each from the Memphis Police Association PAC and the Memphis Fire Fighters Association PAC and a $1,500 contribution from the TIM PAC, associated with State Rep. Tim Hicks.
Huseth brought in $98,072 in the same fundraising period, with contributions coming from multiple states. This includes the $27,000 contribution from the state House Democratic Caucus, $15,400 from the Tennessee Education Association Fund for Children and Public Education PAC, $5,000 from The Progress Fund (a PAC funded by Knoxville developer Phil Lawson), $1,900 from the Ready PAC (tied to Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell), and other contributions from labor union PACs.
Huseth also received individual contributions from some notable Memphis and Nashville officials, including state House Minority Leader Karen Camper, Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy, former Shelby County Mayor Lee Harris, District 8 Congressional candidate Heidi Kuhn and former Metro Nashville Law Director Wally Dietz.
Huseth reported more than $29,640 in in-kind contributions, including $22,000 of research and polling from the House Democratic Caucus and roughly $7,500 in voter mail from the Tennessee Democratic Party. Huseth’s largest expenditure this quarter was a $41,000 contribution to the Tennessee Democratic Party.
House District 80: Andrea Bond Johnson (D) vs. Julian McTizic (R)
Democrat Andrea Bond Johnson is vying against Republican Bolivar Mayor Julian McTizic for the District 80 seat being vacated by Democratic Rep. Johnny Shaw, who announced his retirement this year after serving since 2000.
The district includes portions of Hardeman, Haywood and Madison counties.
Bond Johnson raised nearly $28,000 in the third quarter, going into the Nov. 3 election with nearly $22,200 on hand. McTizic raised nearly $23,500, bolstered by thousands of dollars in contributions from Republican legislators hoping to flip the seat.
Democrat Andrea Bond Johnson, photographed in downtown Brownsville, Tennessee, in 2020, is running for the District 80 House seat vacated by retiring state Rep. Johnny Shaw. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)
Bond Johnson reported receiving $1,000 from House Minority Leader Karen Camper and $2,500 from Madison United, a political action committee linked to a group of Jackson business owners.
Other contributions include $1,000 from O’Connell’s Ready PAC, $1,000 from former Tennessee State University President Glenda Glover, and $750 from the Davidson County Democratic Women Gwen McFarland fund. Beverly Shaw of Stephenson-Shaw Funeral Home donated $200, and former Madison County Sheriff David Woolfork donated $200.
Tennessee Sen. Page Walley, a Bolivar Republican, personally contributed $1,000 to McTizic’s campaign in addition to funneling $7,500 through his PBW PAC. A PAC connected to Rep. Clark Boyd, a Wilson County Republican, gave $1,500. McTizic also received contributions from local officials: $500 from former Madison County Mayor Jimmy Harris, $500 from Atoka Mayor Brett Giannini, and $300 from Richard Holland, vice mayor of Sardis.
Both candidates received $250 contributions from the Tennessee Forestry Association PAC.
House District 75: Michael Lankford (R) vs. Allie Phillips (D)
Republican incumbent Michael Lankford is running against Democrat Allie Phillips to keep the seat he was appointed to after the November 2025 death of Rep. Jeff Burkhart.
The district covers Western Montgomery County, including parts of Clarksville and Ft. Campbell.
Phillips, who is running for the seat a second time, goes into the election with more than $66,600 on hand after raising nearly $113,000 during the third quarter. Lankford raised about $40,500 and reported nearly $64,800 remaining.
Phillips’ contributions come from multiple states and include $15,000 from the House Democratic Caucus and thousands of dollars from various union-affiliated PACs. Phillips also received $1,000 from O’Connell’s Ready PAC, contributions from current Democratic legislators and donations from philanthropists Frank and Amy Garrison, Ripley Mayor Craig Fitzhugh, former Metro Nashville law director Wally Dietz and Nashville Council members Mike Cortese and Brenda Gadd.
She also received $1,900 from actress Amanda Seyfried, who produced a documentary about Phillips’ campaign. Phillips entered politics after losing her unborn daughter and being forced to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy due to Tennessee’s near-total abortion ban.
Phillips spent $135,900 in the third quarter, including $30,000 for video ads, about $30,000 for digital fundraising and a $38,000 donation to the Tennessee Democratic Party.
Lankford’s funding includes thousands of dollars in contributions from Republican legislators, including $5,000 from Lamberth’s PAC. Other contributions include $1,000 from Amazon.com Services LLC, $1,000 from the Excellence in Public Education PAC, $500 from ATT Services INC, $100 from Circuit Court Judge Robert Bateman, and donations from trade association PACs and government relations firms.
Lankford spent around $39,800, including more than $11,500 on advertising and roughly $18,500 in contributions to the Montgomery County Republican Party.
House District 67: Ronnie Glynn (D) vs. Chris Lanier (R)
Democratic incumbent Ronnie Glynn is defending his seat against business owner and Clarksville-Montgomery County School Board member Chris Lanier. The district covers Clarksville and Austin Peay State University in Montgomery County’s core.
The House Democratic Caucus and Tennessee Democratic Party bolstered Glynn’s campaign with around $58,000 in advertising and mail in the third quarter, according to Glynn’s report.
Glynn has just over $34,600 on hand going into the election and reported raising nearly $42,000 this quarter. Lanier has $30,700 and raised $14,600.
Glynn received a $5,000 contribution from The Progress Fund, $1,900 from O’Connell’s Ready PAC, $1,000 from Amazon.com Services LLC and contributions from Camper, Rep. Bob Freeman, Rep. Jesse Chism and union PACs.
Glynn also recorded donations from Dietz, Fitzhugh, Glover, Clarksville Mayor Joe Pitts and Nashville Council member Burkley Allen.
He spent nearly $43,500, including a $20,000 contribution to the Tennessee Democratic Party.
Contributions to Lanier’s campaign include $5,000 from Lamberth’s PAC, $1,500 from Rep. Clark Boyd’s PAC and $1,500 from Rep. Tim Hicks’ PAC. Another $5,000 came from Republican Women’s groups and $500 came from the National Federation of Independent Business Tennessee PAC.
Lanier spent about $7,000, mostly on advertising.
House District 60: Shaundelle Brooks (D) vs. Eva Romero (R)
Democratic incumbent Shaundelle Brooks is facing Republican real estate broker and businesswoman Eva Romero for the District 60 seat, which represents eastern Davidson County.
Brooks, who entered politics after her son, Akilah DaSilva, was killed in a mass shooting at a South Nashville Waffle House in 2018, has held the seat since 2024.
Brooks has roughly $15,800 on hand compared to Romero’s $61,800, though Romero also has $40,100 in self-endorsed outstanding loans.
Brooks raised around $22,000 this quarter, including $1,250 from Davidson County Democratic Women, $1,000 from Camper, $1,000 from O’Connell’s Ready PAC, and several contributions from union and trade association PACs.
The Democrat also gained support from Davidson County Clerk and former Metro Nashville Council member Sharon Hurt, Nashville Council member Zulfat Suara, Metro Nashville Public Schools Board member Zach Young and gun safety advocates. She spent just under $8,000 this quarter, mostly on campaign work, travel and constituent meetings.
Romero was appointed to the Tennessee Housing Development Agency by Gov. Bill Lee, and her third quarter report shows contributions from real estate developers and builders. She also received $2,500 from Lamberth’s PAC, $500 from Rep. Aron Maberry, $500 from Latinos for Tennessee and $250 from conservative social media activist Robby Starbuck.
Romero spent around $23,600, including $8,500 on direct mail and $5,000 on consultants.
House District 59: Bill Hancock (R) vs. Mark Proctor (D)
Republican Bill Hancock and Democrat Mark Proctor launched their first campaigns to vie for Rep. Caleb Hemmer’s seat representing southern and western Davidson County. Hemmer announced he would not run for reelection after representing the district since 2020.
The House Democratic Caucus gave Proctor’s campaign a $65,000 infusion this quarter, bringing the caucus’ total contributions to Proctor to $81,200 this election cycle.
Retired Tennessee state trooper Mark Proctor, Democratic candidate for state House District 59. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Proctor has more than $126,700 on hand going into the election compared to Hancock’s $157,300 war chest.
Hancock’s donors include Former CoreCivic CEO Damon Hininger and Carrie Hininger, several owners of real estate and development companies, the Davidson County Republican Party and Republican legislators. He also received $1,000 from Thomas Lehrman, a member of the Tennessee Public Charter School Commission and co-founder of investment firm Teamworth Ventures. Lehrman previously served as director of the Office of Weapons of Mass Destruction Terrorism in the U.S. Department of State.
Hancock spent nearly $106,300 this quarter, mostly on direct mail, digital advertising, canvassing and consulting.
Proctor’s contributions include $1,900 from Hemmer, $15,400 from the Tennessee Education Association Fund for Children and Public Education, $1,900 from Dietz, $1,900 from Ingram Industries Chairman John Ingram and multiple contributions from Democratic legislators or their affiliated PACs.
He also earned support from Metro Nashville Vice Mayor Angie Henderson, Metro Council member Burkley Allen, Fitzhugh, Metro Nashville Clerk Howard Gentry, Metro Judge Lynda Jones, Metro Council member Sheri Weiner and multiple union and trade PACs.
Proctor spent $92,000 this quarter, including a $40,000 contribution to the Tennessee Democratic Party, direct mail, databases and campaign workers. In-kind contributions include $16,200 in research from the House Democratic Caucus and $10,200 in mail from the Tennessee Democratic Party.
House District 18: Elaine Davis (R) vs. Bryan Goldberg (D)
Republican incumbent Elaine Davis faces another challenge from Democrat Bryan Goldberg for House District 18, which represents part of Knox County.
Davis was elected to the seat in 2022 as a Republican after switching party affiliations; she ran for Knox County Commission as a Democrat in 2006. Davis has about $64,300 on hand going into the election compared to Goldberg’s $79,800.
Rep. Elaine Davis, a Knoxville Republican, faces a challenge from Democrat Bryan Goldberg in a rematch of 2024’s race. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Goldberg’s total $75,500 third-quarter contributions include a $25,000 boost from the House Democratic Caucus, $5,000 from The Progress Fund and $1,900 from O’Connell’s Ready PAC. His donors also include former Knoxville Mayor Victor Ashe, philanthropists Stephen and Ann Bailey, Dietz, and H.M. Hashemian, president and CEO at nuclear engineering firm AMS Corporation.
Goldberg spent $88,000 this quarter, $40,000 of which went to the Tennessee Democratic Party. The party also provided Goldberg’s campaign with roughly $8,150 in in-kind contributions.
Davis’ $60,700 in third-quarter contributions includes $10,000 from Tennesseans for Student Success Action, $5,000 from Lamberth’s PAC, $2,000 from the Knox County Republican Party, and thousands of dollars from Republican legislators or their affiliated PACs.
Davis also received $1,900 from Knox County Chief Operating Officer and Harris Restaurant Group President Doug Harris, and $1,900 from hospitality business owner David Colquitt.
Davis spent $63,700 and has $20,000 in outstanding self-endorsed loans.
Senate District 13: Dawn White (R) vs. Angela Wynn (D)
Republican incumbent Dawn White brings a considerable war chest of more than $260,400 into the final pre-election push against Democrat Angela Wynn.
Wynn, a nonprofit executive and director of stewardship and donor relations for Tennessee State University, has roughly $3,600 on hand, and $3,000 in outstanding self-endorsed loans.
State Sen. Dawn White, a Murfreesboro Republican, has a large cash advantage heading into the November 2026 election. (Photo: Tennessee General Assembly)
White’s $20,000 in third-quarter contributions include $3,000 from Middle Tennessee Business Leaders for Common Sense, $2,500 from the HCA Tristar Fund, $2,000 from a PAC funded by Texas-based short-term lender Community Choice Financial, and a combined $2,200 from John and Laura Arnold, co-founders of Arnold Ventures LLC.
White spent more than $86,000, including a $50,000 contribution to DawnPAC, her political action committee, and a $15,000 contribution to the Senate Republican Caucus.
Wynn recorded roughly $8,400 in contributions in quarter three, with around $1,500 coming from the Senate Democratic Caucus and $1,112 from Marlayna Trego, who ran for the House District 37 seat but lost in the Aug. 6 primary.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In Public Service Commission race, reorganization bill looms over candidates
text:
(Left to right) Republican nominee Matt Gentry faces Democratic nominee James Gordon for Alabama Public Service Commission Place 1; Democratic nominee Sheila McNeil faces Republican nominee Jim Zeigler for Alabama Public Service Commission Place 2. (Photos of Gentry, Gordon and McNeil courtesy of candidates; photo of Jim Zeigler: Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector; photo illustration by Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Legislature’s decision to expand the Alabama Public Service Commission forced those running to sit on the utility regulator to make some campaign adjustments.
Gov. Kay Ivey this spring signed HB 475, which expanded the PSC from three members to seven; put the PSC under the supervision of a secretary of energy to be appointed next year, and banned formal rate hearings on the state’s high residential energy prices until 2029. The move to a larger board made it significantly less likely that the PSC would get a majority calling for formal hearings on Alabama’s high residential energy prices.
James Gordon and Sheila McNeil, the Democratic nominees for Place 1 and Place 2 on the PSC, said in separate interviews that they plan to work for competitive rates and greater accountability through negotiations with their colleagues and utility companies.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It is going to take one hell of a negotiation to get that ball across the line,” Gordon said. “But that would be my goal, to get us some relief.”
McNeil filed a federal lawsuit in May to void the law. The case remains pending.
“I am absolutely not happy with the way they changed the rules,” she said. “The way they changed the rules, I think, violates our constitutional rights, our voting rights, my due process rights, equal protection rights and separation of powers.”
Messages seeking comment were sent to Place 1 Republican nominee Matt Gentry and Place 2 nominee Jim Zeigler on Thursday. Neither of their campaign websites made specific statements about HB 475. Both candidates have said in public statements that the PSC needs to conduct oversight of public utilities.
Alabama has some of the highest residential electricity rates in the Southeast. Residents pay about 16.4 cents per kilowatt-hour for July, according to the Energy Information Administration. That is higher than the 14.61 cents on average that comparable states like Kentucky and Mississippi pay.
As originally filed by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, HB 475 would have required a formal rate hearing on utility prices at least once every three years. The rate case would require sworn testimony, the disclosure of finances and public input.
Alabama since 1982 has mostly used a process known as rate stabilization and equalization instead of formal rate hearings. Under RSE, utilities are effectively guaranteed a certain profit. Critics say the process makes the reasons for rate increases opaque.
Senators rewrote HB 475 to expand the number of commissioners serving on the PSC from three to seven. Gov. Kay Ivey earlier this year appointed four of the new members, who will face elections in staggered terms.
“At least immediately, because of the change from elected to at least partly appointed, there is reduction in the amount of power that the individual voter has in order to control the makeup of the Public Service Commission,” said Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, an organization that advocates for more renewable energy.
The secretary of energy, created by the bill, will control the PSC agenda and after 2029 will have the authority to convene a rate case. A vote of five commissioners could also lead to a rate case.
“It doesn’t require regular rate cases,” said Jaclyn Brass, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, a nonprofit environmental legal advocacy organization with an office in Birmingham. “It doesn’t require you to be let into the room, into the process.”
Candidates interviewed by the Alabama Reflector said they would need to negotiate with not only their colleagues on the commission but also with utility companies to convene a rate case and to reduce utility rates, particularly for electricity.
Gordon wants to reduce the rates to 12 cents per kilowatt-hour. However, he also wants to extend the rate freeze, currently in place until 2029, to 2030.
McNeil said that discussing rates with investor-owned utilities, like Alabama Power, and reasoning with them to reduce their rates would be difficult, but that the PSC can appeal to the utility’s reasonable side.
“We can push for Alabama Power to submit to a rate case review out of good faith,” she said. “If what you are charging the citizens of Alabama is legitimate, then you should not have a problem opening up the books. And it is our job to regulate.”
McNeil also wants to review and reform the Rate Stabilization Equalization formula to ensure fairness.
“It is an opportunity for us to maybe have some way to lower utility bills through that process,” she said.
McNeil also wants to establish an advisory council to give rate payers a voice on the PSC.
Data centers have also come up in the race.
“I would like to leave it up to the vote of the citizens of a community whether or not to have a data center in a community, but that is up to the mayor and county commissions whether it is allowed,” Gordon said. “It is not the Public Service Commission’s scope to say that a data center is allowed here or there.”
Gordon also said that data centers need to provide for their own electricity to power the operations at the site. One way is to install a solar farm to feed electricity to the facility so it is not taking power from the grid.
McNeil said she wants to study the issue and take a regional approach to approve the development of data centers. She proposed creating an organization similar to that of a Metropolitan Planning Organization for data centers. An MPO brings together multiple leaders, from local elected officials and state agencies, to decide on road projects.
The organization would consider a data center’s impact on the electricity demand and water use for the site. It would also consider the demand for fire protection and the need for first responders.
Gentry’s campaign website called for transparency and community engagement on data centers but did not outline any specific policies. Ziegler said on his campaign website that he will protect ratepayers from the potential added cost of data centers and will thoroughly review rate requests.
“I will bring my experience to thoroughly review rate requests, ask detailed questions, and ensure transparency in how costs are recovered from ratepayers,” Ziegler’s site says.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Groups propose legislation allowing West Virginia dentists, hygienists to administer HPV vaccine
text:
Dentist checking patient's teeth. (Photo by Tunvarat Pruksachat/Getty Images)West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates lag below the national average. The state has some of the highest rates for cancers associated with the virus. 
Some oral health care providers in the state say there’s a promising way for West Virginia to address both problems, but it’s going to require lawmakers to approve changes to state code.
The West Virginia Oral Health Coalition and other organizations want the state Legislature to pass legislation allowing dentists and dental hygienists to administer the HPV vaccine. 
“(Dental providers are a) ready, educated workforce that can increase access to care around cancer prevention,” said Gina Sharps, executive director of the West Virginia Oral Health Coalition. “By recognizing and authorizing dentists and dental hygienists with local anesthetic permits to administer that, then we’re just casting a wider net when we look at cancer prevention.”
Dental hygienist talks to patients about HPV in pilot project
Lauren French
The push follows a pilot project by Community Care of West Virginia and Mountains of Hope, the state cancer coalition. The project enlisted dental hygienist Lauren French to talk to her patients in a rural West Virginia county about HPV and the HPV vaccination. HPV can cause oral cancers, among others. 
French is the only dental hygienist at Community Dental Care of Green Bank, the only dental clinic in Pocahontas County. The clinic sits directly across from the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and near the Monongahela National Forest, so there’s no cell service for miles. 
“It’s a pretty cool place to be, but dental care is sparse here… We stay pretty busy. We stay booked out,” she said. 
In the first six months of the project, 34 age-eligible unvaccinated patients were educated about the HPV vaccine. Of them, 10 patients agreed to be vaccinated. But notably, none of those people actually went and got the vaccine, French said. 
Referring patients even to a nearby medical clinic presented a hurdle for parents, even though they said they were willing to have their children be vaccinated, she said. 
“(The medical clinic) is just right down the road, but it’s one of those things where some people come over for their cleaning. It’s scheduled for an hour. They’re just taking their lunch break to come do this,” French said. “Or they’re the last patient of the day, so they’re coming after work. They don’t have the availability to go right over to the health clinic at that moment.”
One conclusion from the pilot project was that more kids could be vaccinated for HPV if dental hygienists and dentists were able to administer the HPV vaccine themselves instead of referring people to a medical provider, French said. 
French said talking about the HPV vaccine fits in nicely with the oral cancer screening they already do with patients. Oral cancer is one of the biggest concerns patients ask about, she said. 
“It actually is a lot easier to bring up with patients than you might think,” French said. “During every routine cleaning, there’s an exam… And we’re telling the patient, ‘We’re doing an oral cancer screening just to make sure there’s no lumps, bumps, or anything that’s suspicious in your mouth.’”
And especially with children, there’s no need to mention that HPV is a sexually transmitted infection, she said. 
“The way that I go about it is I don’t have to bring up sex at all.” she said. “It’s just, ‘This is a virus that most people come into contact with.’ We want them to get vaccinated before they come into contact with this virus. That’s why we suggest age 9 to 16 max, getting them fully vaccinated, and that potentially prevents them from getting oropharyngeal cancer or vaginal and penile cancers.”
French said that about half of her patients were hesitant to get any vaccines, HPV or otherwise. 
Education important to improving West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates 
HPV is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in the United States. Nearly all people are infected with the virus within months or years of becoming sexually active, according to the state Department of Health. 
In most cases, there are no symptoms and the body clears itself of the infection. In some cases, though, high-risk cases can lead to cervical, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar and penile cancers. 
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends HPV vaccination for pre-teens ages 11 and 12 — before they come in contact with the virus. The vaccine is not part of those required for school attendance in West Virginia. Some people can also catch up on the vaccine later in life if they haven’t completed the series at the recommended age. 
According to the CDC, only about 57% of 13 to 16 year olds in West Virginia were up to date on their HPV vaccine in 2025, compared to 63% in the United States a whole. A CDC report last month found HPV vaccination coverage in rural areas is lower than that of urban areas. West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates have increased in recent years. 
Lindsay Barr, program manager for the West Virginia Immunization Network, said the difference between the state and national vaccination coverage emphasizes the importance of educating parents and caregivers about the role of the vaccine in preventing cancer. 
“HPV vaccination is cancer prevention,” Barr said. “It not only prevents cervical cancer, but other HPV-associated cancers like oropharyngeal cancer, anal cancer, vaginal, vulva and penile cancers as well. So we think that that lack of knowledge and the confusion among parents plays a big factor in it. So we do a lot to overcome those gaps.”
Barr said the Immunization Network’s survey of parents and caregivers showed that West Virginia parents have a vague understanding of what the HPV vaccine does and little understanding of the negative health outcomes associated with HPV.  Most parents were only aware that the virus leads to cervical cancer, leading them to believe the vaccine is only recommended for girls, she said. The HPV vaccination recommendation was expanded to include boys in 2009. 
In West Virginia between 2015 and 2019, HPV accounted for the majority of cervical, vulvar, anal, oropharynx and vaginal cancers in women and the majority of oropharynx cancers in men, according to the West Virginia Department of Health. 
The vaccine prevents new infections of HPV but does not treat existing ones, Barr said, which is why it’s important for people to get vaccinated at young ages and why some medical associations recommend vaccination start at age 9, she said. 
Dental professionals in other states administer vaccine  
The HPV Dental Integration Pilot Project has expanded to include Bridge Valley Community and Technical College and the Monongalia County Health Department in Morgantown.
West Virginia would not be the first to allow dental professionals to administer the HPV vaccine. Kentucky, Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New Jersey and Oregon have all passed legislation allowing dental providers to administer the vaccine, according to the Oral Health Coalition.
Sharps, with the Oral Health Coalition, said she’s drafted bills based on laws in other states. She’s not yet approached state lawmakers or gotten sponsors for the bill. The 2027 legislative session begins in January. 
In order for dental workers to administer the vaccine, state code would have to change and the state Board of Dentistry would have to incorporate the new law into its rules. The board supports allowing dentists to administer the vaccine, according to a position statement on its website.
French said dentists and dental hygienists are poised to educate their patients on what HPV causes. They see patients every six months and in some cases every three months, which fits in with the recommended timeline for HPV vaccination doses, she said. 
Dental hygienists can get certified to administer local anesthesia, a procedure that’s more complicated than administering a vaccine, she said. 
“It’s a lot more intricate to anesthetize someone for a tooth or for periodontal procedure or something like that than it is to get an intramuscular vaccination,” French said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Pentagon searching medical records to identify transgender troops
text:
An aerial of the Pentagon, May 12, 2021. (Photo by Staff Sgt. Brittany A. Chase/U.S. Air Force)By Rachel S. Cohen
The military is searching protected medical records to find transgender troops who have tried to continue serving amid the Trump administration’s ban on transgender Americans in uniform, multiple sources tell Federal News Network.
Commanders around the world have started receiving notices that members of their units are violating Pentagon policy, and are being instructed to begin the separation process. The sweep is believed to have outed several hundred active-duty and Reserve troops, including service academy and Reserve Officer Training Corps cadets, over the past two months, according to the trans advocacy nonprofit SPARTA Pride and Priya Rashid, an attorney with the National Institute of Military Justice.
The Pentagon is moving to separate troops as multiple lawsuits challenging the ban move through the federal court system. In August, the administration petitioned the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the policy is unconstitutional before a key case goes to trial in January.
The situation has spurred a military-wide scramble to cover the work of troops placed on leave, connect them with legal help and, in some cases, find money and lodging for those facing homelessness.
“The military was my life; it was my everything. I gave my entire self to my job and to my country, and I was serious about my career,” said one sailor, who was granted anonymity because they fear retaliation. “They’re about to completely upend my life and my career, and I’m not prepared for that.”
Finding trans troops
The Trump administration argues that any history of gender dysphoria, the medical condition where a person’s gender identity doesn’t match their biological sex, is incompatible with “high standards for troop readiness, lethality, cohesion, honesty, humility, uniformity and integrity.”
After President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the Pentagon issued directives that formed the basis of the ban. It initially allowed troops to leave during a grace period that ended in July 2025, then began removing them itself.
Pentagon to screen older troops for low testosterone

Now SPARTA officials say dozens of people have reached out to report “unprecedented use of military medical systems to identify individuals.”
Five sources, including two transgender service members facing separation after their gender dysphoria-related diagnoses were flagged to their commands, described what they called a “witch hunt” for honorably serving troops.
Documents obtained by Federal News Network indicate that, in some cases, the information is coming from the Pentagon’s highest echelon.
The Office of the Secretary of Defense has identified service members “who may have a current diagnosis or history of or exhibit symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria in their electronic healthcare record,” according to an internal Air Force email sent July 31 and viewed by Federal News Network.
Spokespeople for the Defense Department, the Defense Health Agency and each of the military services declined to answer emailed questions, citing ongoing litigation.
MHS Genesis, DoD’s electronic health records system, and other databases contain medical histories, prescriptions, mental health notes, TRICARE-covered civilian care documentation and even records from before members joined the military. Personnel databases can also reveal changes in a person’s listed gender over time.
Some, but not all, transgender people experience gender dysphoria; it can be resolved through treatment. Kara Corcoran, SPARTA’s executive director, who is an active-duty Army infantry officer facing separation, said people are being punished for successfully addressing a past medical issue.
“A new line has just shifted and said that these people are inadequate for being able to serve,” she said.
Those details are being shared with unit leaders across the force in conversations and memos from local medical and legal offices, alarming some who argue it violates troops’ privacy and doctor-patient confidentiality.
One separation referral sent to an airman’s commander quoted directly from the service member’s health history, including when they sought treatment for gender dysphoria, their number of counseling sessions and prescribed medication.
The airman said they were never evaluated in order to receive the separation referral, do not currently experience dysphoria and had not shared details of their past treatment with their colleagues.
A widening sweep
SPARTA estimates thousands of trans troops have been kicked out or are in the process of separating, including those placed on leave until their discharge.

Still, it’s difficult to pinpoint the number of service members who identify as transgender. DoD estimated around 4,200 troops with gender dysphoria were in uniform when the ban began. That’s about four times higher than in 2019, when the department told a congressional defense committee that about 1,000 currently serving troops were diagnosed with at least one of seven medical codes related to the condition — a figure pulled from Military Health System data. Other outside estimates have ranged from about 6,000 to as many as 25,000 people.
Out transgender members who publicly transitioned were among the first to go when the policy changes began. But that’s no longer the case in the ban’s second year, sources said.
Rashid, who represents many of the trans troops in their separation cases, said her calls have exploded in recent months, with about 25 people reaching out each week for advice on involuntary separation procedures.
She said she’s heard from many troops younger than 21 who transitioned before joining the military and served in accordance with regulations for their preferred gender from the start.
The latest phase is also flagging older people who transitioned years ago, when they could do so without penalties, and whose current colleagues may not know. The Pentagon is identifying people whose medical notes reference a current or previous transition but who haven’t changed their names or gender markers, as well as those who continue to meet the appearance and fitness requirements of their biological sex.
They are also identifying troops diagnosed with gender dysphoria who didn’t transition, those who sought treatment outside the military but used TRICARE, and those who detransitioned to save their jobs.
“They didn’t do anything wrong,” Rashid said. “They followed the rules and policies and procedures of the year that they were in. We were the ones who changed the rules on them.”
The search is also catching people who aren’t transgender, she said, including members who underwent procedures such as mastectomies or hysterectomies or sought a gender dysphoria diagnosis to obtain treatment for other conditions.
What the military can see
MHS Genesis hosts the patient data of more than 9.5 million troops, spouses and children. Authorized users can search military health databases by diagnosis code to identify people with a certain condition and create registries of patients with particular ailments.
For instance, Military Health System software has been used to track outbreaks of communicable diseases, and identify people at high risk for bone marrow abnormalities.
MHS records have also been used to research service members with gender dysphoria-related diagnoses before. The 2019 report to the House Armed Services Committee lists the specific codes used to identify troops in the MHS Data Repository, including five that fall under gender dysphoria, one for cross-dressing fetishes and one for a history of sex reassignment.



Quotation







They didn’t do anything wrong. They followed the rules and policies and procedures of the year that they were in. We were the ones who changed the rules on them.


– Priya Rashid, an attorney with the National Institute of Military Justice, on Pentagon push to separate transgender service members


Military medical providers have also relied on that data for studies on issues like inequities in hormone prescriptions for active-duty troops with a gender dysphoria-related diagnosis.
Health privacy laws are more complicated inside the U.S. military. To ensure enough troops are fit for duty at any given moment, HIPAA allows military treatment facilities to disclose protected health information to a service member’s command.
But the Military Health System says that information remains protected under the Privacy Act of 1974, which generally bars disclosure without written consent except in certain circumstances. Those exceptions include cases where an agency’s employees “have a need for the record in the performance of their duties,” according to statute.
The administration appears to be relying on a provision of the 2023 National Defense Authorization Act designed to reduce the stigma around mental health treatment, Rashid said. Congress directed the Defense Department to protect the confidentiality of mental health services except in exigent circumstances. That can allow disclosure when national security, safety or good order and discipline are at stake.
Rashid argues those exceptions don’t apply to transgender troops being removed from the military, including F-35 avionics technicians, pilots, air defenders and surgeons.
“These are zero-fail tasks that would require a high level of occupational finesse, a high level of technical proficiency,” she said. “Mentally unwell people would have a very difficult time.”
The separation process
The Pentagon’s initial guidance on identifying trans troops explicitly said it would do so using medical records. That’s evolved over time.
A March 2025 DoD memo noted that reviewing medical records would be the “primary means” of identifying troops with a history of gender dysphoria. Two months later, another memo clarified that the services should look to troops’ annual checkups and bloodwork to find instances of dysphoria.
That process looks slightly different in each branch of the armed forces. An internal Army order, which was issued in August but was not made public, formalizes a monthslong blueprint for ousting soldiers.
The order, obtained by Federal News Network, explicitly bars commanders from broadly searching health and personnel records to find soldiers with gender dysphoria, or from asking providers for a batch of information about the people in their unit.
It also stops leaders from ordering a behavioral health consult to confirm whether a person has gender dysphoria unless they have personal knowledge of the diagnosis. That could stem from past conversations with the soldier, their request to follow different grooming standards, social media posts, or “reports from higher headquarters to commanders indicating an individual’s medical records reflect a past diagnostic code consistent with gender dysphoria.”
In the Air Force and Space Force, medical readiness boards will determine whether airmen qualify for separation before sending cases to unit commanders, according to the internal email. Commanders then have three business days to send paperwork to a centralized legal team in Washington.
The Navy and Marine Corps have similar processes, with Navy Installations Command handling involuntary separations. Sailors have 10 days to request a separation board or waive that right.
The boards are directed to decide only whether someone was diagnosed with or has symptoms of gender dysphoria, regardless of their character or their job performance. Each service secretary makes the final call on whether to remove them.
What happens next
Separation measures have continued as trans troops await a federal district court’s decision on who will be covered by a class-action lawsuit.
Lawyers representing more than two dozen service members warned in an August filing with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit that the Pentagon is expediting removals while a key lawsuit is tied up in appeals. In June, a federal judge allowed Talbott v. USA to become a class action but has not yet said who qualifies to join. The judge’s March 2025 order pausing separations has not taken effect amid administration pushback.
Corcoran said junior enlisted troops are among the most at risk. Those who have served less than six years are ineligible for separation pay, may have to repay part of their enlistment bonus, are last in line for veterans benefits and could become homeless.
SPARTA has provided more than $36,000 in financial support to 29 recipients so far this year, including four who used the money to leave states with anti-trans laws.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Clearing of Durham’s homeless encampments tests NC community’s resolve
text:
A biker on the American Tobacco Trail near Fayetteville and Pilot streets this week, in the area where police recently cleared a homeless encampment. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)Tito Husband began his first week as store manager of the Food Lion on the corner of Fayetteville and Pilot streets about a week after Durham police launched “Operation Safe Passage” to remove a nearby homeless encampment, which allegedly doubled as an open-air drug market. 
Husband told NC Newsline that he was already aware of the encampment and its resulting chaos before his arrival. Residents who live near the store had begun to shop at the Lakewood Shopping Center Food Lion, where he worked before his new assignment, to avoid aggressive panhandling at the Fayetteville Street store, he said.
Since Husband has become store manager at the Fayetteville Street store, customers have told him that the panhandling has eased since police cleared the encampment that was along the city’s popular American Tobacco Trail.
“There’s still a little bit of panhandling in the area, but I’m trying to deal with it as best as I can,” Husband told NC Newsline last week. “As soon as customers let me know that panhandlers are in the area, we try to get police involved so we can make a better experience for our customers.
The former encampment — and others still intact across Durham — have tested a city long known as a welcoming haven for people struggling with homelessness, addiction, or other social challenges.
Chelsea Cook (Photo: City of Durham)
“We’ve been hearing a lot from people who are unhappy about the way we’ve approached encampments — both directions, right?” Durham City Councilwoman Chelsea Cook said during a recent work session. “Some folks are unhappy that we have cleared encampments and not others. They feel that because there is no policy that we’re sort of applying things and they don’t see the reason behind them.”
Even socially conscious residents who live in neighborhoods where encampments have sprung up have grown weary of the criminal activity, debasement of property and life and violence they say sometimes accompany such encampments.
“I can speak for thousands and thousands of African Americans who live in this city — we are tired of the crap,” Victoria Petersen, a longtime Durham activist, said during the  work session. “We’re tired of these tents all over the place and talk about we’ve got to find someplace for all of these homeless people.”
Petersen said the encampment near Fayetteville and Pilot streets was rife with drugs, prostitution and gang activity. Its location near Fayetteville Street Elementary School, “where children can see,” made its presence in the neighborhood worse, she said.
Police made several arrests and confiscated drugs and weapons during Operation Safe Passage. It cleared the homeless encampment and erected a chain link fence to prevent people from returning to the area. City officials have told area media that police have responded to more than 700 calls for service in the area. Those calls included two for homicides and one for a sexual assault. 
Former Durham city councilwoman Jackie Wagstaff told NC Newsline that the encampment was “truly out of control.” 
“The bus shelter became an extension of their tents. They would go sit in there all day,” Wagstaff said. “You could drive by anytime and see somebody sitting in there with no shirt on, high as a kite. That is what we had to deal with.”
Wagstaff said the encampment also created a harrowing experience for residents who used the trail for biking or walking.
“The people who bike on that trail, when they got to the encampment, they literally had to part the Red Sea to get through there,” Wagstaff said.
At the work session, Wagstaff complained that it took multiple calls to the city to get police to address the encampment problem. Similar calls from more affluent areas are addressed more quickly, she said.
“This is bigger than one block,” Wagstaff said. “It is about whether Durham will treat residents fairly no matter their zip code, income level or political influence, and whether unhoused people will be met with real solutions instead of inconsistent crisis management.”
Others who spoke at the council work session were critical of the police clearing the encampment.
“It was a reprehensible targeting and vilification of the most vulnerable people in our city, and also cruelly orchestrated to dehumanize its victims and be celebrated as if it were a victory,” said Rayna Rusenko, a sociologist of homelessness and public policy. “These actions do not bring safety.” 
Ellie Nobblitt, a member of the National Union of the Homeless in Durham, said sweeps of homeless encampments are violence against poor and homeless people who have nowhere else to go.
“There is no alternative shelter right now for folks,” said Nobblitt. “The shelter is not safe.”
Shanetta Burris (Photo: City of Durham)
But Councilwoman Shanetta Burris said critics who insist homeless encampments are being targeted by police are displaying a “level of irresponsibility.”
“To my knowledge, that’s not what’s happening in the city or the community,” Burris said. 
She said the encampments police raided were drug hubs where she saw “able-bodied people posted in the tent selling poison to their own people.”
“I want to know what’s dignified about people who look like me who are sleeping in tents on the ground, who have nowhere to bathe, who have nowhere to use a restroom,” Burris said.
Nate Baker (Photo: City of Durham)
City Councilman Nate Baker has proposed a new encampment policy that would, among other things, prohibit clearing encampments unless a shelter alternative  is available for residents. The policy would also require the city to protect unhoused residents’ personal belongings by storing them for a “period of time.” 
“There are also some detailed and stringent provisions, in cases of emergency, where the city does need to move quickly to protect health and safety,” Baker said. “And of course, none of this impacts the other  laws that we implement. If there’s a fire, you put out the fire. If there’s lawbreaking, you can address that.”
Baker also noted House Bill 437, which bans unauthorized public camping, establishes penalties for drug offenses near homeless shelters and allows local governments to designate temporary public locations for people experiencing homelessness. HB 437 has been vetoed by Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, but the Republican-led General Assembly is expected to pursue a veto override after the November election.
“If the veto is overridden, I don’t think that would render this null and void,” Baker said. “We would have to change some of the language in order to be more in compliance with that.”
North Carolina advocacy groups speak out against homeless ban bill

Ryan Smith, director of the Durham Community Safety Department, said that there are approximately 1,000 people in Durham experiencing unsheltered homelessness and another 1,000 experiencing other forms of homelessness.
“We currently have a waitlist of nearly 200 people to get into our main shelter for single adults, and another 50 families on a waitlist for our family shelter,” Smith said in an email response to questions.
He pointed to the city’s new “Strategic Framework to Make Homelessness Rare and Brief” by quickly moving more people into housing through a process known as Housing Sprints. 
“Through this process, Durham has housed 104 people, including 50 children,” Smith said. “Thirty-eight people were housed through two August sprints alone, including 25 members of nine families.” 
The city’s goal is to “build a system that is both robust enough and nimble enough to house anybody experiencing homelessness in Durham within 30 days,” Smith said. 
“That goal is still at least five years away, but successes over these past six months give us confidence that it is a horizon we can reach,” he said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Marylanders can’t afford the cost of a climate superfund
text:
Efforts to make fossil fuel companies pay for the effects to climate change have not fared well in courts, writes Mary D. Kane, and Maryland should think twice if it's thinking of enacting such a law. (Photo by Airman 1st Class Colin Perkins/U.S. Air Force)Marylanders are already feeling the strain of rising costs in their utility bills, at the gas pump and in the everyday expenses of running a household or a business. Those pressures do more than squeeze budgets. They shape where people can afford to live, whether employers can hire and grow, and where businesses choose to make their next investment.
That reality should be front and center as Maryland considers the findings of its “Cost of Climate Change Study” and any renewed effort to enact a climate superfund law.
During the 2025 legislative session, lawmakers considered but did not pass the RENEW Act, which would have imposed billions of dollars in retroactive assessments on certain oil and gas companies for activity that occurred decades ago. Instead, Maryland authorized a study examining the costs associated with climate change.
That study, due Dec. 1, should give policymakers an objective assessment of the costs, consequences and tradeoffs of any policy that follows.
Importantly, Maryland’s own agreement establishing the study recognizes one of the questions that deserves serious scrutiny: Whether requiring fossil fuel companies to compensate the state could result in costs being passed on to taxpayers.
That question cannot be an afterthought.
Maryland families and businesses do not operate separately from the energy system on which our economy depends. We rely on affordable, reliable energy to heat and cool homes, commute to work, manufacture products, operate hospitals, move goods through the Port of Baltimore, and keep stores and restaurants open.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




When government imposes billions of dollars in new costs within that system, policymakers should not simply assume those costs disappear. They can affect investment, infrastructure, supply and, ultimately, the prices families and employers pay.
There is another reason for caution.
Before Maryland follows other states down this path, lawmakers should look carefully at what is happening beyond our borders.
New York enacted a climate superfund law requiring fossil fuel companies to pay $75 billion toward climate-related infrastructure. In the span of less than a month, two federal courts struck it down. Both concluded that the law was preempted by federal law, including the Clean Air Act.
At the same time, the U.S. Supreme Court this week heard arguments in Suncor Energy v. Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County, a case involving whether federal law prevents state-law claims seeking damages for harms attributed to interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions.
The cases are not identical, and the Supreme Court case is not a direct challenge to a climate superfund statute. But together they raise an important question for Maryland: Why rush toward a new state liability regime when the legal boundaries surrounding state efforts to assign financial responsibility for global emissions are being actively contested?
Federal climate policy itself is also shifting. The Environmental Protection Agency has recently changed significant portions of the federal greenhouse-gas regulatory framework, including vehicle and power plant rules.
Whatever one thinks of those changes, they reinforce a basic reality: greenhouse-gas policy operates in a complicated national legal and regulatory system. Maryland should understand how a new state program fits within that system before asking families and employers to bear the consequences if it does not.
Maryland must confront the costs of climate change and prepare for future resilience needs. But we should not address one set of costs without understanding whether the proposed solution creates another.
That makes it especially important that the final analysis examine the full picture, including potential impacts on taxpayers, consumers, energy prices, businesses, investment, jobs, competitiveness and energy reliability.
When the study is complete, lawmakers should use it to weigh both the benefits and the risks of what comes next.
Before Maryland moves toward a climate superfund policy, policymakers should be able to answer three questions with confidence: Do we understand the legal and economic consequences well enough to move forward? Will it make Maryland less affordable? And who will ultimately bear the cost?

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Think balancing Colorado’s budget is easy? Try it.
text:
Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters face some big decisions about taxes and spending this election. A new digital tool lets them see how three big ballot measures would affect the state budget — and whether they can close the state’s $1.6 billion budget gap. 
The online tool, called Colorado Tradeoffs, focuses on two ballot measures that would potentially increase the state budget and one that wouldn’t:

Amendment 87 would replace Colorado’s 4.4% income tax with graduated rates, raising taxes on incomes above $500,000 and lowering them below that level. The change would be enshrined in the state Constitution.
Proposition 136 would lock in the 4.4% flat income tax rate.
Proposition NN would eliminate tax refunds in order to provide billions more dollars for K-12 public schools over 10 years.

The tool also asks users to consider how to balance the budget when it comes to K-12, higher education, early childhood education, health care, prisons, affordable housing and rainy day reserves.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado Newsline is among the Colorado news outlets hosting the simulation developed by the Colorado News Collaborative, University of Colorado Denver’s School of Public Affairs and Weigh In, a Colorado-based public benefit corporation focused on community engagement.


More than 6,000 people have used Colorado Tradeoffs already, with about 6% reaching a balanced budget. Completion typically takes about 7 minutes.
About 14% of those who completed the exercise have changed their minds on the ballot measures, said Chris Adams, founder and CEO of Weigh In and a senior fellow at the CU School of Public Affairs, who designed Colorado Tradeoffs. Most of those said they’d vote for Proposition NN and Amendment 87, after previously being opposed.
Adams acknowledged the completion rate looks low, but said it’s comparable to websites that ask people for their email addresses or other simple tasks. Adams said he was pleased with the number of people who get to a balanced budget because “It’s a really hard exercise.”
Adams noted that Colorado’s Taxpayers Bill of Rights, approved by voters in 1992, gives those voters the responsibility to approve any tax increases at the state or local levels. That’s even though the state’s 100 lawmakers must make decisions on how that tax revenue is spent, and what is cut when there isn’t enough money to go around.
“It kind of gives Colorado residents sort of an awesome power,” he said. “The ultimate deciders of tax rates are not the ones under the dome. It’s the rest of us.”
Joint Budget Committee member Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, a Republican from Brighton, tried the simulation and noted that it doesn’t take into consideration all of the complexities of balancing the state budget. The six-member JBC works full-time for nearly seven months to create the annual budget, which must pass both the House and the Senate before it goes to the governor, who has the power to veto specific line items.
“I don’t think it necessarily captures the nuances of what goes on in our budget or how things actually work within the budget,” Kirkmeyer said. “It doesn’t really give the full picture.”
Kirkmeyer opposes Amendment 87 and Proposition NN. The only JBC member who has endorsed 87 is outgoing Sen. Jeff Bridges, a Democrat running for state treasurer. All four Democratic JBC members voted to place Proposition NN on the ballot.
Adams noted that JBC members “have a full range of resources but also responsibility for making decisions. The part (they) can’t make decisions on is the tax rate.”
He said the goal of the simulation is to help Coloradans decide a basic question: “Do I want less government, do I want more taxes? … We want people to really wrestle with the tradeoffs, because that’s what policy makers do.”
About one-third of those who completed the Tradeoff thus far said they’d cut the state’s reserve fund, while 44% said they’d increase funding for early childhood education.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: We never imagined abortion would become part of our Idaho family’s story
text:
While doctors were discussing risks, lawyers were discussing statutes. At one point, LifeFlight was standing by in case we needed to leave Idaho to save my life, writes guest columnist Sadie Gorr. (Photo illustration by Sadie Gorr)When people talk about abortion, they often imagine a choice. A political issue. A debate.
What they rarely imagine is a married couple preparing a nursery, a little girl excited to become a big sister, and parents eagerly waiting to welcome a wanted baby.
That was our family.
We were excited to grow our family. We were planning baby showers, maternity photo shoots, and getting ready to welcome our son. We knew Idaho’s abortion laws had changed, but we never imagined those laws would have anything to do with us.
Then, last September, my water broke. I was halfway through my pregnancy.
Doctors confirmed that our son would not survive. I had no amniotic fluid left, which meant his lungs could not develop. There was no treatment that could change the outcome.
As we tried to process the loss of our baby, another reality emerged. Doctors explained that every day the pregnancy continued increased my risk of developing a life-threatening infection, hemorrhaging or going septic.
I didn’t fully understand the severity of the situation until I looked at my husband’s face. He looked terrified that he was going to lose his wife. That’s when it hit me: I could die from this.
What happened next was one of the most agonizing experiences of our lives.
We spent days waiting. Waiting to see if labor would begin naturally. Waiting to see if my condition would worsen. Waiting while doctors consulted with specialists and lawyers to determine what care was legally allowed under Idaho’s abortion ban.
We knew our son could not survive. We knew the risks to my health were increasing. Yet we were frozen, unable to move forward.
There is something difficult to explain about losing control over your own medical crisis. You lose your sense of autonomy. Your life and decisions are suddenly in someone else’s hands. While doctors were discussing risks, lawyers were discussing statutes. At one point, LifeFlight was standing by in case we needed to leave Idaho to save my life.
Thankfully, I received the care I needed. I am alive. I can be with my husband. I can raise my daughter. But that isn’t true for every Idaho family.
We share our story because many people don’t understand why a pregnant woman might need abortion care. They consider abortion as morality or as a choice. Sometimes it is neither.
Sometimes abortion becomes necessary during a wanted pregnancy and a medical emergency. Sometimes it’s the one lifeline that allows a husband to save his wife, or a mother to return home to her child.
Our son was deeply loved. If there had been a way to save him, we would have done it. Instead, we faced an impossible situation that required us to navigate grief, fear, and uncertainty all at the same time.
We share our story because families like ours exist. Behind every statistic, every headline, and every political debate are real parents, real children, and real medical emergencies.
We hope our family’s loss helps others better understand the reality that some Idaho families face.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Educational Television Commission member resigns
text:
Tijuanna Adetunji (seated a long table, fifth from the left) and other members of the Alabama Education Television Commission listen to speakers during a meeting in Montgomery, Alabama on April 21, 2026. Adetunji has resigned from the commission, leaving just one of the members who served on the body last month. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Tijuanna Adetunji has resigned from the Alabama Educational Television Commission, leaving just one of the seven commission members who served on the board last month.
Gina Maiola, communications director for Gov. Kay Ivey confirmed Adetunji’s resignation Thursday afternoon but did not provide a reason. A request for further comment was left with Maiola Thursday afternoon.
Alabama Public Television Executive Director Wayne Reid said in a statement early Thursday evening Adetunji submitted her resignation letter last Thursday without explanation.
“With Tijuanna Adetunji’s resignation, the commission has experienced a complete turnover over the past twelve months,” Reid said. I have confidence that the Governor’s replacement appointment will bring another strong representative to the commission. APT will make an announcement once the appointment has been made. I look forward to working with the new commission and building on the exciting future ahead for Alabama Public Television.”
A message seeking comment was left with Adetunji  Thursday afternoon. According to the Alabama Public Television website, Ivey has not yet made a new appointment. Reid said APT is “hoping to hear something very soon (from Ivey) on the appointment.”
Adetunji served as the AETC’s Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District representative. She ran for the Alabama House of Representatives as a Republican in 2014 and as an independent candidate in 2018. Adetunji also ran for Montgomery City Council in 2015; she was not successful in the campaigns. 
Adetunji’s decision comes after Ivey removed five members from the commission earlier this month and after nearly a year of sometimes heated arguments among commissioners about maintaining affiliation with the Public Broadcasting Service.
Last October, then-commissioners Ferris Stephens and Les Barnett brought the idea to disaffilitate from PBS prompting public backlash from donors. In November, the commission voted to maintain PBS programming. Adetunji was not present for the November vote.
In September, the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority voted to fund a survey conducted by Cygnal, a polling firm that mainly works with Republican candidates, on Alabamians attitudes towards PBS. Adetunji voted against doing the survey.
The survey’s results showed 54% of viewers support APT continuing its PBS affiliation and 62% said they wanted public officials to stay out of programming decisions.
Adetunji leaves commissioner Logan Glass as the only member of the board to not be dismissed or removed over the last month.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: When it comes to Medicaid cuts in Kentucky, it’s always Groundhog Day
text:
Hundreds of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers. July 17, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Over the next few years, Kentucky is facing the largest Medicaid cuts in the program’s history. Starting in January, the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act will take Medicaid coverage away from many thousands of Kentuckians. Separately, state Medicaid cuts will go into effect in July unless the 2027 General Assembly restores funding to the program. And in January 2028, the OBBBA will begin lowering Medicaid payments to providers with reductions that will deepen over the following decade.
If allowed to occur, these perilous cuts will worsen Kentuckians’ health and well-being, increase burdensome medical debt, and cost providers and jobs including by putting 35 rural hospitals at risk of closure.
The cuts are the latest in a long series of threats. Medicaid has faced danger ever since the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded the program in 2010 and became a political punching bag. But here’s the thing: time after time, in the face of organized public opposition, decision makers have halted major Medicaid rollbacks before the pain to communities began.
That tells us a lot about what’s at stake. And it shows why Kentuckians should urge federal and state lawmakers to stop harmful cuts yet again.
The push to cut Medicaid and repeal the ACA began as soon as the law passed. Republicans were unified in their opposition and rode the Tea Party wave in the 2010 midterms catalyzed in part by opposition to so-called Obamacare. Opponents demonized the ACA and capitalized on all it didn’t do to fix an ailing American health care system, while obscuring the good it did.
However, then-Governor Steve Beshear expanded Medicaid under the ACA in 2013, citing an obscure state law and acting right after the General Assembly had adjourned for the year. By the time the legislature reconvened, thousands of people were already gaining coverage and getting healthcare. Republicans controlled the state Senate and could have picked a fight over blocking Medicaid expansion and refusing the federal funds. But knowing that would be devastating to constituents and providers, they stood aside.
Nevertheless, rhetorical opposition to Obamacare continued throughout the 2010s — with the U.S. House voting over 50 times to overturn it — until Republicans took control of the Congress and the presidency with Donald Trump’s election in 2016. But even with a unified government, their effort to repeal the ACA failed with then-dying Senator John McCain’s famous “thumbs down” vote on the floor of the Senate. Though Republican leaders expressed disappointment at the loss, some no doubt felt relieved when tens of millions of Americans did not lose their health care.
Back in Kentucky, the legislature kept Medicaid expansion even after Republicans took full control of the legislature in 2016. Then-governor Matt Bevin attempted to establish paperwork requirements like are now in law from the OBBBA but lost in court and then in his re-election bid, in part due to his unpopular positions on health care, education and public employees. 
The legislature also tried to put in place similar barriers to Medicaid enrollment through four different bills in 2019, 2020, 2022, and 2025. All of them failed to pass or were largely stripped of their harmful measures after concerted opposition campaigns led by health advocates.
But after Trump was elected a second time with Republican majorities in Congress, lawmakers passed the OBBBA and its major cuts to Medicaid in 2025. Yet fearing backlash, the law was designed so the pain didn’t go into effect immediately. It pushed the paperwork barriers until after this year’s midterm elections and set the payment cuts to start a year later and grow gradually over time.
Most recently, the Kentucky General Assembly passed a budget in April that underfunded Medicaid by hundreds of millions of dollars compared to the executive branch forecast of costs. That forced Governor Beshear to put in place Medicaid payment cuts this summer. After an outcry from constituents and providers, he reversed course and made extraordinary appropriations to Medicaid that are likely outside his legal authority. Legislators chose not to sue, standing aside yet again and averting the pain that would result. 
It’s always Groundhog Day when it comes to Medicaid. We see repeated efforts to cut the program and create barriers to care. But after patients, providers and communities organize, lawmakers pull back from the brink.
Will this time be different? If so, we’ll finally witness the harm long feared by so many.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Data center moratorium bills stack up ahead of Virginia legislative session in January
text:
A data center in Prince William County, Va., one of over 680 of the facilities that are operational or planned in the commonwealth. State lawmakers have filed a slate of bills that would temporarily pause all data center development in the state. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Come January, state lawmakers will debate a slate of bills that would halt data center development, including one by Sen. Russett Perry, D-Loudoun, which recommends a three -year moratorium on building the high-powered digital warehouses.
Perry has filed Senate Bill 843 alongside Sen. Danica Roem, D-Prince William. It would block localities, the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and the State Corporation Commission (SCC) from approving any data center building permits statewide from July 2027 until July 2030. 
The bill would also prevent the advance of distribution lines, on-site power, or related projects that  solely serve data centers during the same timeframe. 
“The people of Virginia just continue to be saturated, and it’s not just with data centers,” Perry said Thursday. “In my district in particular, it’s these 765 kilovolt transmission lines. People forget it’s not just the data center that might move next door to you. But it’s all the other things that come out from that.”
Virginia is home to nearly 400 data centers in operation,with over 280 planned and more proposed each year, according to Pew Research Center. 
The growing industry is tied to exploding energy demand as well as rising tensions in communities across all of the state over water use, noise levels and concerns about siting and loss of character in rural areas. 
Roem is also filing a separate moratorium bill that is more closely tied to the interconnection queue – the list of large-load customers, namely data centers, that have requested power from Dominion Energy, which the utility is obligated to serve. 
Currently, Dominion has about 25,000 megawatts of power assigned to projects with an energized date, and an additional 75,000 MW will go to projects that don’t yet have power up dates. The utility says it will take about seven years for the customers in the queue to get power, a wait that starts when the facilities are added to the queue.
Roem’s bill would block new data centers from being approved statewide until that queue is energized and the necessary infrastructure is built to do so.
“Until the industry and Dominion Energy deal with the hundreds of data centers already awaiting power, they shouldn’t be siting more data centers or building more transmission lines that wouldn’t exist if not but for the data centers,” Roem said this week.
In the House, Del. Irene Shin, D-Fairfax, proposed a bill that was continued from the 2026 session that would block localities from approving zoning and permitting requests until “the fulfillment of all pending requests for interconnection to distribution service by an electric utility customer that is a data center” or July 2028, whichever comes first.
Across the aisle, Sen. Glen Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, has been calling for a data center moratorium for months. He plans to file his own version to be debated during the session.
“I’m hearing it more and more from my constituency that they’ve checked their electric bill and their energy usage from last month versus the same month last year, and they are shocked at how much their electric bills have gone up,” Sturtevant said Thursday.
Virginia senators request special session to act on ’deeply alarming’ groundwater report

“One of the major driving factors is the proliferation of the data centers, and the costs of their power generation in transmission being subsidized by Virginia ratepayers in their electric bills,” he added.
Lawmakers that represent areas of the state east of Interstate 95 — where a recent groundwater report showed that water availability would start to decline in the near future if the state doesn’t change course — have criticized how much water data centers’ non-closed loop cooling systems use.
The evaporative cooling systems can use hundreds of millions of gallons of water annually. 
The groundwater report led to Perry and Sen. Richard Stuart, R-King George, to call on Gov. Abigail Spanberger to initiate a special session to pass policies that address the water concerns before the January regular session. 
Spanberger denied their request.
Language in the budget lawmakers adopted earlier this year also directed DEQ to conduct a study and identify groundwater scarcity areas, especially in the eastern coastal regions of the commonwealth. The report, due this month, will also detail how non-closed loop systems can be retrofitted to be more water efficient.
However, the closed-loop systems still take an initial large batch of water and use more energy  than the evaporative systems. 
The bills represent a possible shift in the legislature, which rejected most bills that would have taken major action on data centers, including a proposal by Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Newport News, to end sales and use tax exemption for the industry. 
Debates over the measure delayed the budget for months, with lawmakers opting to preserve data centers’ tax break and add a new tax for the facilities that is expected to generate $1.2 billion over the biennium.
Sturtevant signaled that he hopes to reopen the debate about the sales and use tax exemption in the coming session.
 Workers, data centers oppose moratorium bills

The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), a prominent workers union that has staunchly advocated against legislation that would restrict data center growth, are already pushing back against the new bills.
Jobs in manufacturing, electrical and construction have expanded in Virginia due to the data center industry, they said, and protecting them should take priority over shutting down data center development .
“I don’t think a moratorium is gonna pass because you’re taking out your tax base, you’re taking out your jobs,” said Don Slaiman, director of communications for IBEW Local 26. “(Lawmakers are) so proud of being number three in the CNBC poll. That would be eviscerated.”
The Data Center Coalition, a national group focused on advocating for policies on behalf of the industry, said data centers have invested $80.56 billion in Virginia and generated$5.34 billion in state and local taxes.
“Local or state moratoriums could deprive communities of the opportunity to compete for investment and jobs, jeopardize multibillion projects that are in development, and force jurisdictions to relinquish significant long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring states,” said Nicole Riley with the Data Center Coalition.
Spanberger presents slate of data center regulation proposals, puts first directives in motion

The plans for these bills come weeks after Spanberger revealed her data center policy framework. 
Much of her plan focuses on transparency in the permitting process by limiting nondisclosure agreements, assigning more transmission costs onto data centers, limiting on-site gas generation and other objectives. To be enacted, most of the measures must be translated into legislation that the General Assembly will have to pass. 
“I think the vast majority of people here in Virginia want a comprehensive framework and guardrails put around data centers before we continue to just keep approving more of them,” Perry said. “We already have more data centers than anywhere else in the world. I don’t know how we can responsibly continue to just keep approving more.”
Like all legislation, lawmakers’ data center moratorium bills must win approval from both chambers and the governor to be made law.
The General Assembly’s regular session begins on Jan. 13.
