name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley says he would repeal data center tax subsidies, regulate AI and social media
text:
Crowley at a press conference in Madison in August 2026. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Democratic gubernatorial candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley said he would sign a bill to repeal tax incentives for data centers if he’s elected, marking a change in his position on the issue.
Gov. Tony Evers and Wisconsin Republicans approved a provision during the 2023 state budget that exempts data center developers from paying sales and use taxes for the “sale of property and equipment to construct, renovate or operate data centers.” The policy is estimated to have already saved data center developers $1.5 billion. 
However, as data centers have become increasingly unpopular, Democrats and Republicans alike have changed their minds on providing these subsidies. 
A group of Republican lawmakers, some of whom voted for the budget that created the tax subsidies in 2023, introduced a bill earlier this month that would repeal the tax breaks, though the bill won’t go anywhere as the Legislature is out of session.
Crowley said he would “absolutely” sign that bill to repeal the tax subsidies if it were sent to him as governor during an event at the Overture Center on Wednesday evening.
“The fact that these tech companies are getting a billion dollars in tax breaks — it’s being delivered on the backs of hard-working families,” Crowley said. “I want to be very clear about my position. We’re going to be aggressive when it comes down to holding data centers to account, making sure that we protect our land, protect our water, have strict environmental standards, but also communities need to have a seat at the table.”
Crowley had previously been noncommittal when it came to repealing the tax benefit for data centers. He told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that he did not “believe Wisconsin should automatically roll back all data center tax incentives” but that he believed that the state needed “a more rigorous review of whether taxpayers are receiving sufficient value for the incentives being provided.” 
Republican candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany had previously criticized Crowley’s position on the tax incentives, saying that he wanted to give “a blank check to data centers” and that data centers “do not need to be subsidized by us, the taxpayers.” Tiffany has not always been a champion of tough regulation on data centers, either. He previously voted for legislation in Congress that would have banned state and local governments across the country from being able to enforce laws or regulations on AI models, systems, and related digital infrastructure, including data centers, for 10 years. 
Crowley’s changing position comes with less than three weeks left until Election Day and as data centers and AI continue to be unpopular across the political spectrum. A September Marquette Law School poll found that 74% of Wisconsinites say the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits.
This week Crowley laid out an 11-point policy plan for restricting and regulating AI and social media companies. The policies include:

Requiring platforms to set kids’ accounts and new accounts to the highest privacy setting and cut off unsolicited messages. Users over 18 would have the option to turn the restrictions off. 
Prohibiting infinite scroll, autoplay and other addictive features for minors’ accounts as well as a ban on push notification for the users overnight and during the school day. 
Banning surveillance advertising. 
Allowing parents the option to sue platforms over design choices that harm a child including content promoting suicide, eating disorders and drug sales 
Regulating AI chatbots by restricting them for users under 13, prohibiting chatbots from posing as doctors and therapists and requiring disclosures on AI chatbots designed to form emotional bonds with individuals
Increasing the penalties for online predators and sextortion and implementing those same penalties for creating or sharing AI-generated sexual images of children
Penalizing companies that knowingly make money from scam ads
Requiring identification verification for advertisers before they can place ads
Requiring platforms to implement a scam reporting tool that’s easy to use and requiring that they confirm the reports and report the action that they took within a set timeframe
Funding the state Department of Justice and the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection to support their work to combat online fraud and enforce anti-trust law
Investing in county and tribal adult protective services and aging and disability resource centers, so victims of scams have support to recover

Crowley said during the Wednesday evening event that the state needs to do something in the absence of the Trump administration and Congress taking action. 
“It’s unfortunate that the federal government has actually not put in these guardrails to protect our young people, protect our families, but also to protect our seniors,” Crowley said. “Look, I’m a father, I have three daughters and I want to make sure I can protect my girls from these chatbots. You have, you know, social media platforms that allow them to chat about sexuality. That’s not what I want my 9 and 7-year-old to be introduced to. My oldest right now is a freshman at Whitewater. I don’t want her having pictures out there, and all of a sudden, she can’t be protected.” 
Crowley said the policies are aimed at putting the burdens on the tech, social media and AI companies, rather than on individuals. 
Tiffany also supports some guardrails for these companies. He said in a statement to the Examiner that the state needs “common sense guardrails that protect children and seniors, safeguard personal privacy, and prevent sensitive data from falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” His campaign noted that in Congress Tiffany cosponsored a law aimed at strengthening law enforcement’s ability to investigate financial fraud targeting seniors. The legislation covered scams involving AI.
“We cannot allow artificial intelligence to become another tool for harvesting Americans’ personal information or exploiting vulnerable individuals. We must hold Big Tech accountable when its platforms enable the creation of sexually explicit AI-generated images of children or expose minors to sexually inappropriate chatbot conversations,” Tiffany said. 
Tiffany said he would support imposing age verification requirements for app providers, strengthening parental consent protections and “give parents greater control over their children’s online activity.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel joins lawsuit seeking consumer protections as chatbot service declares bankruptcy
text:
A bipartisan U.S. Senate bill would create a panel to advise Congress on artificial intelligence policy. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined 38 other states and the District of Columbia in a lawsuit focused on privacy and safety concerns after a chatbot service that allows users to converse and roleplay with AI characters filed for bankruptcy. 
The platform, Character.AI, announced its bankruptcy filing on Monday, stating that it would sell $20 million in assets to Disney.
Founded in 2021, the company has faced legal scrutiny over its chatbots, including a 2024 wrongful death lawsuit filed after a 14-year-old died after a chatbot allegedly encouraged him to take his own life. The case was settled in January.
Several states, including Michigan, have launched investigations into Character.AI. According to the lawsuit, filed Wednesday, those investigations identified several potential legal concerns, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, minors being exposed to explicit sexual content, self-harm, violence and other harms through chatbot conversations; insufficient age assurance practices; misrepresentations around the product’s safety; and a failure to comply with state privacy laws.
Although Character.AI has taken steps to restrict minors’ access to chatbot features, the attorneys general note that these features can be circumvented. They also contend they do not address concerns around characters representing themselves as licensed individuals, provide safeguards for users discussing self-harm, suicidal ideation or violence, or bring the platform into compliance with state consumer protection laws.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nessel and her fellow attorneys general also raised concerns about the sensitive nature of the conversation many users have with the platform’s chatbot characters and the large number of minors using Character.AI. 
“As the Debtor collects and maintains a large volume and variety of consumer personal data, including sensitive data and children’s data, and has demonstrated safety risks to both minor and adult users, the States need to be assured that sufficient safety and privacy programs are in place with any purchaser of any or all of the Debtor’s business,” the lawsuit states.
Any company purchasing Character.AI or its assets should be prepared to comply with regulatory requirements, the attorneys general state. 
This would include age-verification measures beyond users simply providing their birthdates, removing characters that portray themselves as licensed professionals such as therapists or lawyers, implementing a privacy program and ensuring consumers have the opportunity to access their data and delete it prior to any sale.
“Character.AI’s financial troubles should not leave consumers to deal with the privacy fallout the company leaves in the wake of its bankruptcy,” Nessel said in a statement. “Voluntary safety measures are not enough if they can be reversed by a business’ next owner. I’m joining my fellow attorneys general to push for safeguards that will remain in place no matter who takes control of this company.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: A look at who could be SC’s next agriculture chief
text:
Democrat DeShawn Blanding (right) and Republican Cody Simpson (left) are each running to be the next South Carolina agriculture committee. (Photos courtesy of the Blanding and Simpson campaigns)COLUMBIA — The race to be South Carolina’s next agriculture commissioner features a Republican with a background in state government who’s backed by President Donald Trump and a Democrat with federal government experience who touts a willingness to buck the administration.
Both nominees hail from rural Clarendon County. But their paths diverge.
Republican Cody Simpson is a fifth-generation farmer who left the fields to become Gov. Henry McMaster’s agriculture adviser until his May 2025 appointment as the U.S. Department of Agriculture Farm Service Agency’s executive director for South Carolina. It’s a long title he shortened to “Trump’s farmer in South Carolina.”
Democrat DeShawn Blanding, a former staffer for agriculture committees in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate, is working to restart his family farm that skipped a generation.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


Whoever wins Nov. 3 will be the first new commissioner in 22 years, replacing Republican Hugh Weathers of Orangeburg County, who said four years ago he’d retire at the end of this term.
The commissioner is chief advocate for the more than 22,600 farms statewide. While South Carolina lost its status as primarily agrarian decades ago, agribusiness — a combination of agriculture and forestry — remains South Carolina’s No. 1 industry, accounting for nearly 260,000 jobs, according to the state Department of Agriculture the commissioner oversees.
The agency’s duties include promoting the state’s various agribusiness sectors, keeping the food supply safe, and — since 2024 — handling all inspections of places that sell food, such as restaurants and cafeterias.
The job entails more than people realize, Blanding said.
“Farmer advocacy is a key part of it, but this entire food system is the commissioner of agriculture,” he said. “This is about a food supply chain — about the food, fiber and fuel that we need to sustain ourselves.”
Both Simpson, 35, and Blanding, 29, say a top priority will be protecting South Carolina’s farmland from encroaching development.
“We’ve got to have a farm to come back to,” Simpson said. “We have to protect our farms, our families, and our future.”
The state has lost about 1,900 farms in the last two decades, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. And a 2022 report by American Farmland Trust, titled “Farms Under Threat,” gave South Carolina the nation’s eighth-worst threat ranking.
Both nominees’ proposals to reverse that trend in the nation’s fastest-growing state include preserving more land through the state’s Working Farmland Protection Fund, created by state law in 2024. This year’s state budget puts $10 million toward that effort, following $12 million last year, and $3 million in the launch year.
Here’s a look at differences in the nominees’ backgrounds and platforms:
Blanding
Blanding, who became the nominee without a primary opponent, is the president and founding partner of the consulting firm AgQuity Solutions. 
The Manning native left South Carolina after high school, first to get his bachelor’s at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, then to Washington, D.C., to earn a master’s degree from George Washington University. He stayed in the nation’s capital to work for congressional agriculture committees, as well as stints with two nonprofits: the Union of Concerned Scientists and the Rural Coalition.
He moved back home in 2024 to care for family and restart his family’s former farm. 
Blanding said his grandfather, a fourth-generation farmer, discouraged his children from continuing the family tradition due to discrimination he faced as a Black farmer, including struggling to get loans and being offered lower prices for his products than white farmers. When he died in the 1990s, the family sold their livestock and farming equipment.
But Blanding and his father have worked over the last year to farm again on 5 acres. He’s working to clear the land to plant specialty crops and raise cattle.  
His personal experience is why he wants the Department of Agriculture to be of more help to historically disadvantaged farmers, including small farms and Black farmers.
His “Growing Together” policy proposal includes putting a so-called “navigator” in each county to help farmers cut through bureaucracy, keeping food processing and packaging in South Carolina, and hiring more food inspectors.
Programs Weathers started that he wants to build on include the Growing Agribusiness Fund, launched in 2023 with a $40 million allocation in the state budget. This year, legislators put an additional $20 million into the initiative. And he has a specific goal for farmland preservation: 40% more land protected by 2040.
“Where our campaign is really trying to focus on is smoothing out processes, filling in a lot of those gaps, and then more importantly, making the South Carolina Department of Agriculture a primary resource for our farmers and our agricultural system, and not a secondary resource to the U.S. Department of Agriculture,” Blanding said. 
Unlike his opponent, he said, he’s willing to publicly criticize the Trump administration when policies harm farmers, such as rising diesel costs due to the war with Iran.
And he touts his experience in both writing and advising agriculture policy. 
Simpson
Simpson, who won a four-way GOP primary, contends he can better help farmers by working with the Trump administration and ensuring the federal government understands their needs.
He left his appointed federal job and jumped into the race in February after both McMaster and Trump gave a preliminary endorsement.
A social media post from Trump encouraging him to run concluded with “RUN, CODY, RUN!” Two weeks later, he announced his bid. He then quickly broke fundraising records for the unusually competitive down-ballot race.
That fundraising has enabled him to get his message on TV.
“We’ll encourage South Carolina-grown in every grocery store,” he says in an ad titled “From the Pump to the Plate,” released last week.
“And I’m going to make sure every gallon you pump is accurate,” he says, referring to the agency’s job to inspect and certify gas pumps.
Simpson, who has bachelor’s and master’s degrees from Francis Marion University, joined McMaster’s office in 2018 after volunteering for his gubernatorial campaigns since 2010.
Though he lives in Columbia, he still helps out at his family farm during harvests in the unincorporated Home Branch community in Clarendon County.  
His plans for modernizing the agency include putting licensing and permitting systems online, auditing all existing programs, and adding an office focused on disaster preparedness and recovery.
He also wants to assist farmers in getting USDA certifications that enable them to sell their products in more markets and host roundtable discussions with chefs and waiters about their needs.
“We want to return their voice,” Simpson said. “Cutting this red tape and bureaucracy, in order to do that, you’ve got to talk to people. You got to talk to the people that are doing it every day, and I’m not talking just about the business owners.” 
He also supports legislation that would ban citizens from China or any other country the U.S. labels a “foreign adversary” (also Russia, North Korea, Iran and Cuba) from buying farmland in South Carolina.
A proposal not specific to farmland passed the state Senate in 2023, but that bill died in 2024 without the House taking it up. Similar legislation passed the House earlier this year but died with the end of session without a vote in the Senate.
The election
The Nov. 3 ballot includes two minor-party candidates: Libertarian Michael Sullens of Anderson and Chris Nelums of Columbia for the United Citizens Party. 
A Democrat hasn’t won the seat since Leslie Tindal, who switched his party affiliation during his third term to Republican. He was first elected in 1982 and served until 2002.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: If Wisconsin is in great financial shape, why can’t we afford to fund our schools?
text:
A hallway in La Follette High School in Madison. (Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)It was a dreary, rainy Thursday morning when the state education department announced some depressing news: According to the final, official numbers, 62% of Wisconsin school districts will receive less money in state general aid this year than they did last year. 
Schools are struggling because, for the third year in a row, the state budget put no new money into general school aid, the Department of Public Instruction pointed out in an Oct. 15 press release. That’s after more than 15 years during which per-pupil spending in Wisconsin schools has failed to keep pace with inflation. The latest school funding data arrived from DPI under the header: “Nearly two-thirds of districts will receive less aid due to flat state funding, antiquated funding formula,” 
About an hour later, a press release from Gov. Tony Evers’ office cheerfully announced that Wisconsin has ended the fiscal year with a $3.3 billion budget balance and a record  $2.1 billion in the state’s “rainy day” fund. The top line from the governor’s office message was upbeat: “Despite continued national economic turbulence, Wisconsin maintains strong fiscal position, reaching seven consecutive years of record-high General Fund balances during Gov. Evers’ tenure.”
These two announcements, although dramatically different in mood, are directly connected. The reason Wisconsin has a big budget surplus is largely because the state has abandoned its commitment to fund its public schools. 
A slide presentation by Anne Chapman, research director for the Wisconsin Association of School Business Officials graphically illustrates the decline in per-pupil spending on Wisconsin public school students since the 2008-2009 school year. Using Legislative Fiscal Bureau data, Chapman shows the steadily widening gap between the money schools would have had each year if revenue had kept pace with inflation and what they actually had. This year the shortfall reached $3,571 per kid. 
At the same time, schools have been carrying about $1.29 billion in special education costs that used to be paid for by the state. 
Schools have never bounced back from the drastic cuts to education spending during the administration of former Gov. Scott Walker. But the current budget situation is unprecedented, Chapman says. 
“The 2025-27 state budget provided no increase to general school aids. This was an extremely unusual policy choice, especially in light of the fact that the state had a $4.3 billion surplus going into the budget process,” she says. “The last instance of flat or negative general aids across both years of a biennial budget was the 2009-11 budget, at which time the state was facing a deficit.”
In other words, in a historic act of stinginess, the Legislature, while staring at a sizeable budget surplus, chose not to put a dime of it into public schools. That was a deliberate policy choice, not some sort of emergency measure taken under duress. 
Wisconsin’s school funding formula is complicated —  a mix of state and local funds divvied up based on school districts’ property wealth, enrollment numbers and spending patterns. Enrollment is figured out on a three-year rolling average, and different districts get different amounts of funding from the state — and some get none at all. When funding is flat, statewide, some districts get more and some get less. This is the “antiquated” system DPI referred to in its press release. It uses outdated metrics, and doesn’t account for the effects of high poverty or large numbers of English language learners. 
State schools superintendent Jill Underly expanded on this in her State of Education speech in September: “The formula places value on the wrong things. It values enrollment, district spending, and property value, rather than student needs. It fails to ask the most essential question: how much does it actually cost to educate the students who live in a district so that they have an equal opportunity to succeed? A student’s opportunity for success should not depend on their zip code. If we are going to improve the academic outcomes for ALL students, then the funding formula must prioritize student need.”
Because of the complexity of school finance, and the patchwork of have and have-not districts, it’s hard to figure the exact amount Wisconsin has underfunded its schools since 2009, when overall per-pupil spending stopped keeping pace with inflation. But you can get a rough, back of the envelope estimate by taking DPI’s total enrollment number from 2025-26  — 781,367 students — and multiplying it by the Legislative Fiscal Bureau’s estimate of the shortfall in per-pupil spending that year compared with inflation, which was $3,468.60. The number you get is $2.7 billion in combined state aid and property tax levies. If the state returned to its much-discussed commitment to fund two-thirds of the cost of public schools, that would mean we’d have to allocate $1.8 billion of the current $3.3 billion surplus to make schools whole. Add to that the $1.29 billion in special ed costs the state has sloughed off on the schools, and it reaches $3 billion.
One of the main effects of the state deciding not to fund schools is that the burden has fallen instead on local property taxpayers, who are confronting another surge in referendum requests from their local school districts in the voting booth this fall.   
Gov. Evers has proposed, by his own estimate in an address to the Wisconsin Public Education Network, $7 billion in new funding for schools that was rejected by the state Legislature over his two terms. He was bitterly disappointed when the state Senate rejected a $1.8 billion deal he struck with Republican legislative leaders that included some money for increased special education funding and property tax relief along with income tax cuts. 
But in his latest message, the governor embraces the unspent money sitting in state coffers as “damn good news.” 
“We’ve ended every fiscal year I’ve been governor with a positive balance,” he says. “We’ve shown that state government can work, and work better for the people we serve, and I’m incredibly proud of our efforts.”
Along with the surplus, the governor’s office celebrates the “largest balance in the ‘rainy day’ fund in state history” — at $2.1 billion, it’s  six times larger than when Evers took office.
Meanwhile, schools are in worse and worse shape, and all over the state, people are struggling to keep up with the cost of housing as property taxes rise. 
Whatever feeling of satisfaction there is in knowing the state has squirreled away a fat rainy day fund, when you look outside, it’s raining.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Will Trump’s Georgia rally be a lifeline or an anchor for the GOP candidates he seeks to boost?
authors: Ross Williams, Ignacio Perez, Alander Rocha
text:
President Donald Trump touts his economic record in a February speech in Rome, Georgia. The president is scheduled to return to north Georgia Friday for a Dalton rally ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderPresident Donald Trump is set to visit Dalton in northwest Georgia Friday to stump for Republican candidates as early voting is underway for the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Members of the crowd cheer at a 2021 Dalton Trump rally. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Trump visited Dalton in early 2021 at the end of his first term to drum up support for then-Sens. David Perdue and Kelly Loeffler in a runoff following the 2020 election that Trump lost. Perdue and Loeffler went on to lose the runoff to Democrats Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff after Trump claimed without evidence that the election system was rigged. Some Georgia Republicans at the time blamed those claims for driving down Republican turnout and helping Warnock and Ossoff clinch victory.
Trump’s next visit to Dalton is expected to include appearances from U.S. Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson. Whether it will help or hurt them in November remains an open question.
Friendly turf
Dalton is the county seat of Whitfield County, where Trump won nearly 72% of the vote in 2024 compared with just under 51% statewide.
Many voters there expressed excitement over the president’s visit.
“I think it’s cool that he values the opinion of people from small towns,” Dalton resident Sally Knox said in an interview. “We live in Nowhere, Northwest Georgia.”
Knox said regardless of what side of the aisle Trump is on, it is nice that a president thinks it’s worth visiting them and hearing them out.
President Donald Trump points into the crowd after headlining a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The president has been barnstorming the country ahead of the pivotal election, calling on GOP voters to pretend he’s on the ballot.
Republicans say Trump has had a knack for bringing out conservative voters who would otherwise stay home on Election Day, but those low propensity voters are less enthusiastic about voting when his name is not on the ballot.
“I don’t think it’s going to hurt the Republican party’s chances. If anything it does good,” Tanner Maynor, chairman of the Northwest Georgia Young Republicans, said about Trump telling people to vote as if he was on the ticket. “A lot of people look to Trump and to his endorsement.”
Self-identified Republicans in Dalton said they would vote Republican regardless of Trump’s involvement.
“I would vote that way anyway. I’ve voted that way so far,” Dalton local Terry Ingle said in an interview.
Other Republicans on the statewide ballot expressed confidence in Trump’s ability to get conservatives to the polls.
Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King answers reporter questions after the Atlanta Press Club debate on Oct. 13, 2026. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“President Trump has an incredible ability to energize the base, and I think as Republicans, we need to make sure that the base shows up, and I can’t see anybody else who is more passionate about energizing the base than President Trump,” said Georgia Insurance and Fire Safety Commissioner John King, who is up for re-election this year.
State Sen. Brian Strickland, the Republican candidate for attorney general, who Trump endorsed in July, told reporters in Atlanta he thinks messaging will be more important than the messenger and said Republicans should stay focused on communicating how they plan to improve Georgians’ lives.
“Whether it be President Trump, Brian Kemp, whoever it is, or Brian Strickland talking to voters, we need to talk about the issues that matter to them,” he said.
State School Superintendent Richard Woods, a Republican up for re-election this year, struck a similar tone.
“Would I appreciate the president’s support? Sure. Anything that we’re doing to advance our kids,” he said. “But like I said, we have 1.8 million students in the state of Georgia. That has to remain our focus, and that means we have to bring everybody together. And I think that we’ve done a good job working across the aisle with all aspects of the political spectrum.”
‘A double-edged sword’
University of Georgia political communications professor David Clementson said a lot of people look to Trump’s endorsement as a red flag.
“Having these rallies and telling his supporters ‘Vote for Republicans as though I’m still on the ballot, imagine that I’m going to be on the ballot,’ that’s a double-edged sword,” he said. “It’s a double-edged sword because there’s no bigger motivator for Democrats to go vote for the Democrat than to imagine that Trump is on the ballot.”
A Civiqs poll finds Trump at 33% approval in Georgia, the lowest since his second term began.
Clementson said campaign staff for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms will likely be eagerly watching the rally for soundbites to clip.
Democratic nominee for governot Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks at a press conference with U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock in DeKalb County on the first day of early voting on Oct. 13, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
At a press conference in DeKalb County on the first day of early voting Tuesday, Bottoms and Warnock repeated Trump’s plea to Republican voters to vote as if he was on the ballot. Bottoms urged voters to “think about the policies that have come from the Trump White House and the man who didn’t even have the courage yesterday to stand on a podium and face the voters of this state and answer for those policies,” referring to Jackson’s absence from a debate organized by the Atlanta Press Club.
“People are intent on disrupting our democracy, but they have gone too far. So when Donald Trump says he wants people to imagine that he is on the ballot, I am asking the people of Georgia to do just that. Imagine that he is on the ballot,” Bottoms said.
Warnock pointed to tariffs the Trump administration pushed and high gas and diesel prices as a result of the war with Iran.
“Georgians should vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot. He is. His name is Rick Jackson. Rick Jackson is Donald Trump, and Donald Trump is Rick Jackson. And so, if you like these tariffs, which are really a tax on everyday items, then vote for Rick Jackson,” Warnock added.
DeKalb residents voting that day said they were voting accordingly.
“He is on the ballot through Rick Jackson. He is on the ballot,” said 79-year-old retiree Antoinette Bradley, who said that she is concerned that people with life-threatening conditions are not getting the healthcare they need because of Trump’s crackdown on Medicaid spending.
“I believe that’s wrong,” Bradley said. “Everyone should have healthcare, affordable healthcare, especially the poor.”
Deborah Martin, a DeKalb resident, poses for a picture after voting on the first day of early voting on Oct. 13, 2026, in DeKalb County. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Deborah Martin, a 60-year-old who works in local government, said she was motivated to come out to vote on the first day of early voting because she’s tired of “the way this country is being run” by the Trump administration, saying that she is tired of today’s “divisiveness.”
“I felt like it was really important to come out on the first day in hopes that we have record turnout on the first day of early voting,” Martin said.
Melanie Taylor, a 72-year-old retiree, said that she’s tired of how Republicans on a local, state and federal level have been running government and wanted to vote early because this was her “chance to let them know that in a meaningful way.” When asked if she was voting as if Trump was on the ballot, it was an unequivocal yes.
“I’m definitely voting against his policies. I am tired of being embarrassed by the president of the United States, and I just don’t like the shift the United States has taken in terms of policies for immigration, to war, to the economy,” she said.
Georgia Recorder Editor-in-Chief Jill Nolin and reporter Maya Homan contributed to this report.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio saw the biggest decline in homeownership affordability, new report shows
text:
A For Sale sign on a home. (Photo by Grace Cary/Getty Images)Ohio had the steepest decline in homeownership affordability between 2020 to 2025, according to new reporting from the National Housing Conference. 
The number of occupations able to afford a typically priced home with a 10% down payment fell nearly 41% across Ohio’s metropolitan areas from 2020 to 2025, according to the second annual Priced Out: When a Good Job Isn’t Enough report.
“This report shows that home ownership is becoming a luxury in Ohio, and that jobs that used to be considered solidly middle class — like being a firefighter or mail carrier — are getting shut out of the American dream,” said Marcus Roth, spokesperson for the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mansfield, Cleveland, Springfield, Toledo and Akron ranked among the 25 largest affordability declines in the country, according to the report. 
“Ohio’s numbers show just how quickly the path to homeownership can disappear for working families,” National Housing Conference President and CEO David M. Dworkin said in a statement. 
In Ohio, 67% of occupations could purchase a home with 10% down in 2020, but that dropped down to 26% in 2025, according to the report. 
When it came to renting a two-bedroom apartment, 77% of occupations in Ohio could afford to do so in 2020. That number dropped to 69% in 2025, according to the report. 
Mansfield experienced the biggest loss in homeownership affordability in Ohio. A typically priced home was $115,041 and the annual income needed to qualify for that home was $28,483 in 2020. 
In 2025, a typically priced home in Mansfield rose to $188,863, which requires an income of $62,931 — a 121% increase, according to the report. 
Elementary and special education teachers, emergency medical technicians and paramedics, firefighters, and postal service mail carriers could afford a typical Mansfield home in 2020. But by 2025, firefighters, postal service mail carriers, executive secretaries, and loan officers could no longer afford a typically priced Mansfield home. 
“In Mansfield, more than four out of five occupations could afford a typical home just five years ago,” Dworkin said. 
“Today, fewer than one in three can. When teachers, firefighters, EMTs, postal workers and other essential workers are increasingly priced out of the communities they serve, it is not just a housing problem—it is a workforce and economic problem.”
The average annual salary among occupations that lost the ability to purchase a home with a 10% downpayment between 2020 and 2025 was $70,283. 
“Ohio needs more homes at prices its workforce can afford,” Dworkin said. 
“That means building and preserving housing near jobs, reducing unnecessary costs and delays, and aligning federal, state and local policies around increasing supply. A good job should still provide a realistic path to a stable, affordable home.”
People remain renters longer when they are unable to afford to buy a home, so that means more demand for rental housing, Roth said. 
“There’s a huge (rental housing) shortage, so with so many more people that used to be in that category of homeowners or future homeowners now are solidly renters,” Roth said. 
“That increased demand has driven up the cost of rents, so we’re seeing the impact in the rental market too.” 
A full-time Ohio worker needs to be making at least $23.82 an hour to be able to afford a “modest” two-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO’s annual Out of Reach report.
Ohio also has a shortage of 266,000 affordable and available rental units, according to to the 2026 Gap Report by the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: As efforts to intimidate and confuse Ohio voters grow, voters can protect themselves, and volunteer
text:
Voting location. (States Newsroom file photo)With every day that passes, we’ve seen the President of the United States and others double down on efforts with debunked conspiracy theories and misinformation to get everyday voters to think twice about their trip to the ballot box. 
As the 2026 midterms come into view, it’s clear that efforts to prop up long-debunked claims about the 2020 elections and lay the groundwork to undermine the 2026 election results will only grow louder. 
Here’s what we know: this deluge of misinformation will not end on Election Day. But we also know that we won’t let cynicism silence any voter. Our freedom to vote is fundamental, and we will not let anyone convince us otherwise. 
For many of us, these lies and election denialism have become white noise in the background of our everyday lives. 
What was once shocking has become normalized in large part because of the willingness of our legislators and elected officials to use these debunked conspiracy theories and false narratives to impose barriers to voting. 
That willingness to embrace these false narratives has had consequences for everyday Ohioans trying to cast their votes. 
We have lived through the enactment of one of the country’s most restrictive voter ID laws, the implementation of unnecessarily aggressive voter list maintenance processes, and, most recently, the elimination of the four-day acceptance period for absentee ballots. 
At its core, this security theater does little to improve election safeguards and administration, but it is very effective at keeping eligible voters from voting, especially those who have historically faced barriers. 
Take Ohio’s voter ID law, for example. 
The law, which was so restrictive that Gov. DeWine claimed further election statutory changes would not be necessary, has had predictably bad outcomes. 
In 2024 alone, 34,000 provisional ballots were rejected, and over 7,000 of those can be directly attributed to these new, strict voter ID requirements. 
That is thousands of Ohioans who showed up to vote and had their voices silenced at the ballot box by strict photo ID laws. 
But evidence that these policies do more harm than good hasn’t stopped the Ohio legislature from passing, and Gov. DeWine from signing into law, the elimination of the state’s four-day grace period for absentee ballots, reducing access to a tried-and-tested voting method ahead of the 2026 primaries. 
In June, the legislature tried to deceptively upend Ohio’s vote-by-mail system by attaching requirements to submit a photocopy of your state ID with your ballot to an unrelated bill. 
Gov. DeWine did the right thing here and vetoed that legislation after outcry from election officials and advocates for older adults who saw the enormous potential for abuse if the state started requiring older adults to send copies of their ID in the mail. 
Despite this, Ohio’s election administrators continue to work under unnecessary strain and rapidly shifting legal and cultural environments to ensure that Ohioans like you and me can exercise our freedom to vote. 
This commitment to running our democracy is just as important as our commitment to participating in it. In this way, we’re all election defenders.
If you’re feeling motivated and inspired to get involved and protect free and accessible elections in Ohio, but don’t know where to start, first, I recommend checking that your voter registration is up to date and that you have the documentation needed to cast your vote this fall. 
While our processes are imperfect, the very fact that legislators rely on policies that try to keep eligible voters from voting demonstrates just how powerful your vote is. 
If you’re looking to take your involvement one step further and learn how elections work in our state, you can attend public logic and accuracy testing for voting machines or apply to become a nonpartisan poll worker to help ensure your community can vote safely, easily, and free from intimidation. 
What happens next is up to us. Our country is strongest when we all show up, speak out, and refuse to be intimidated. 
From now to Election Day and beyond, we will continue to ensure every voter has the freedom to vote, every vote is counted, and that the will of the people is upheld.
Steve David is the Ohio state director for All Voting Is Local, a nonpartisan organization that works for free and democratic elections at the state and local level.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Catching Our Eye News Roundup, Oct. 16, 2026
text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• Publicly funded stadiums. Cleveland Scene’s Mark Oprea reports, “Publicly Funded Stadiums Are Bad Business. Sports Economist J.C. Bradbury Says the Browns’ Brook Park Dome Won’t Be Any Different.”
A professor at Kennesaw State University, Bradbury is one of the nation’s leading researchers on publicly financed stadium and arena projects. And he’s just released his latest book, This One Will Be Different: False Promises and Fiscal Realities of Publicly Funded Stadiums, a 440-page dive into how sports teams time and again attract taxpayers dollars to pay for new stadiums that, decades later, never turn a profit or deliver on economic impact pledges.
We recently asked Bradbury, who visited Cleveland this summer to research the city’s stadiums, his thoughts on our own controversies in the world of sports infrastructure—from repair woes in the Gateway District, to the Haslams’ $800 million state subsidy for their Brook Park dome and mixed-use development project, to how Downtown Cleveland may fare when Huntington Bank Field is a mound of rubble in 2029. His take was pretty cynical: the Browns flight to the suburbs will pad their pockets and no one else’s.
• Ohio congressional races. Ideastream’s Ella Abbott reports, “What effect could Ohio’s midcycle redistricting have on congressional races?”
Ohio underwent a midcycle redistricting last year that reshaped several of the state’s congressional districts.
While several states used their midcycle redistricting to draw stronger lines for Republicans across their states, David Cohen, a professor of political science at the Bliss Institute of Applied Politics at the University of Akron, said Ohio took a much more balanced approach.
• No press allowed? WOSU’s George Shillcock reports, “Amy Acton campaigns at closed-door rally while Vivek Ramaswamy criticizes her at Columbus forum.”
While Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Dr. Amy Acton campaigned Wednesday at a closed door rally near Ohio State University’s campus in Columbus, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, her opponent, criticized her at a community forum across town.
Acton paid to rent WOSU Public Media’s Sandy and Andy Ross Community Studio for a campaign rally with Ohio State student supporters. Despite this, the campaign didn’t allow WOSU reporters or other media outlets to cover the rally or ask Acton questions after it concluded.
• Ohio working class voters. Reuters’ reports, “Ohio’s working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party.”
A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.
Now midway through his second term, the president’s magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support.
• Trump’s ballroom. The Washington Post reports, “Secret documents reveal donors behind $330 million for Trump’s ballroom.”
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member…
The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls.
Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving.
The Post’s reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government.
