name: Florida Phoenix
title: In the Dark?  2026 ‘Government in the Sunshine’ manual seemingly shelved
text:
The Government in the Sunshine manual has not been updated by Attorney General James Uthmeier. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has not published the Government in the Sunshine Manual this year, seemingly breaking an annual effort by attorneys general in the state for decades.
The book is typically published in partnership with the Florida First Amendment Foundation and explains Florida’s public records and public meeting laws plus any changes made via case law or the Legislature since the last edition.
The Phoenix verified that the manual has been published every year since 1994, identifying earlier versions, too.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, via Department of Legal Affairs
A representative from Uthmeier’s office in Tallahassee confirmed to the Phoenix the 2025 edition is the most recently published edition. Uthmeier’s office did not, however, respond to Phoenix questions as to why his office has not published the 2026 manual. 
First Amendment Foundation Director Bobby Block said the absence of the manual has resulted in requests “pretty much every day from record custodians, whether they’re from sheriff’s offices or county departments asking, ‘When is the 2026 manual coming out?’” Block doesn’t have an answer.
“If you really look who is suffering from the fact that there is no manual, it’s the clerks of courts, it’s the records’ custodians through agencies around the state, whether it’s municipalities or county government or soil and water boards or school boards, whatever the case may be,” Block told the Phoenix. “… Without this, it becomes more difficult for them to do their job.”
The guides typically appears in the spring of each year.
 Block said his organization has not received a clear answer as to why the guide has not been published. He speculated it could be because the foundation has opposed Gov. Ron DeSantis’ attempt to rewrite the state’s defamation law or supported legislation to impose stronger penalties on agencies that don’t comply with public records requests.
“Maybe it has nothing to do with FAF’s positions; maybe it has to do with there’s a desire to just kind of sink Florida’s open government laws. I don’t know, because that’s the direct impact,” Block said. 
No response
Block said his organization made a records request four weeks ago for a draft of the manual but has not received a responsive record. There is no statutory requirement to publish the manual, although Block said he’d be “encouraging sponsors to make sure publishing the manual becomes a statutory requirement. It’s that important.”
“It has been published out of the sense of pride and obligation since its inception,” Block said. 
“I find it deeply disturbing,” Block said. “And I find what’s disturbing about it is, Florida has a commitment to its citizens, and when you don’t honor your commitment, and yet you hide behind slogans like ‘the free state of Florida,’ you have to wonder, do those slogans actually mean anything when you’re not honoring the contract that you have with the public?” Block said.
He pointed out that access to public records is a constitutional right in Florida, not a privilege. 
Uthmeier, appointed AG by Gov. Ron DeSantis in February 2025, is campaigning to keep the position in his own right. The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Former Miami Democratic state Sen. José Javier Rodriguez (via Twitter).
His opponent, Democrat José Javier Rodríguez, said the guide is too important to go unpublished.
“For more than 20 years, I have represented individuals taking on powerful corporations and institutions that have taken advantage of them. I know firsthand how critical our public records and public meetings laws are to holding government accountable,” Rodríguez said in a written statement to the Phoenix.
“The Government in the Sunshine Manual is an essential resource for Floridians to understand their rights and hold public officials accountable. As Attorney General, I will ensure this important resource continues to be published and remains accessible to the public. Floridians deserve an Attorney General who believes in transparency, not one who keeps them in the dark.”
Moody made it an event
Uthmeier’s predecessor, Ashley Moody, is running for election to keep the Senate seat DeSantis appointed her to fill. (It was vacated by Marco Rubio.)
Moody’s office published the Government in the Sunshine Manual 2025 edition, the 47th.
It actually was published under then-acting AG John Guard, who served in the position until DeSantis appointed Uthmeier to the post. Guard was Moody’s chief deputy attorney general.
“Our system of open government is a valued and intrinsic part of the heritage of our state. Each day, Floridians use these laws to inform themselves as citizens, to attend government meetings and to review government records. As a result of these efforts, government leaders can be held accountable for their actions,” Guard, now a  judge on the state’s Second District Court of Appeal, wrote in the introduction of the 2025 edition.
Moody at times made a ceremony of publication, as she did in 2022, releasing it in recognition of National Sunshine Week.
“In recognition of National Sunshine Week, I am proud to release Florida’s 2022 Government-in-the-Sunshine Manual on our website free of charge,” she said in a press release. Our office works hard every year to produce and publish this important guide that helps citizens navigate Florida’s public records laws and access government meetings,” Moody continued.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s small wildlife sanctuaries deserve a bigger place in conservation
text:
When we think about conservation in Connecticut, our minds often turn to sprawling state parks, protected forests and scenic stretches of coastline. These landscapes are unquestionably important, but some of our state’s most valuable wildlife habitats are far less conspicuous.
Tucked among residential neighborhoods, agricultural fields and suburban development are smaller parcels of protected land that provide essential refuge for birds and other wildlife. They may not attract thousands of visitors or generate headlines, but their ecological significance extends well beyond their boundaries.
As a member of the board of directors of the Hartford Audubon Society, I’ve gained a deeper appreciation for the role local conservation organizations play in protecting these often-overlooked places.
Founded in 1909, Hartford Audubon is one of the nation’s oldest birding organizations. While many people associate the society with birdwatching excursions and educational programs, an equally important part of its mission involves protecting and maintaining wildlife sanctuaries.
The organization has long been associated with four sanctuaries: Station 43 Wildlife Sanctuary in South Windsor, Tobacco Valley Wildlife Refuge, Lewis Farm Bird Sanctuary in Suffield and Greenstone Hollow Nature Preserve in East Granby.
Each illustrates why conservation cannot rely on a one-size-fits-all approach.
Station 43, situated in the Connecticut River floodplain in South Windsor, is particularly remarkable. The sanctuary encompasses approximately nine acres of shallow pond and marsh, surrounded by a much larger landscape of wetlands, meadows, farmland and woodland.
Approximately 240 bird species have been documented in the area, including species classified as endangered, threatened or of special concern. Station 43 is also recognized as an Important Bird Area, underscoring its ecological significance beyond the boundaries of the sanctuary itself.
In Suffield, the nearly 90-acre Lewis Farm Bird Sanctuary tells a different conservation story. Once agricultural land, much of the property has gradually returned to woodland. Its combination of forest, wetlands, a stream and a small pond provides habitat for a variety of wildlife.
Greenstone Hollow Nature Preserve encompasses approximately 38 acres in East Granby. With more than two miles of trails, it offers visitors an opportunity to experience the natural world firsthand while preserving valuable habitat.
Tobacco Valley Wildlife Refuge is another property associated with Hartford Audubon’s conservation history, reflecting the organization’s longstanding commitment to protecting open space.
These landscapes are not interchangeable. Wetlands support different species than mature forests. Former farmland provides different ecological opportunities than wooded uplands. Together, they demonstrate why protecting a diversity of habitats is essential in an increasingly developed state.
Conservation is not simply about how much land we protect. It is about what kinds of habitat we preserve, where those habitats are located and how they connect to the surrounding environment.
For migratory birds, these connections are especially important.
Each spring and fall, millions of birds travel through Connecticut along migration routes that can extend thousands of miles. Along the way, they depend on suitable places to rest, forage and replenish the energy needed to continue their journeys.
A seemingly insignificant wetland or wooded parcel may provide precisely the refuge a migrating bird needs.
For resident species, these protected spaces offer nesting habitat, food sources and shelter throughout the changing seasons. They also support countless other organisms, from pollinating insects and amphibians to the native plants that sustain entire ecological communities.
Yet protecting land is only the beginning.
Wildlife sanctuaries require ongoing stewardship. Invasive plants can displace native vegetation, trails need maintenance and changing habitat conditions sometimes require active management. Without continued attention, the ecological qualities that make these properties valuable can gradually deteriorate.
Much of this work happens quietly, often through the dedication of volunteers who understand that conservation is not a single accomplishment but a continuing responsibility.
At Station 43, for example, volunteers have worked to remove invasive plants, including multiflora rose, Oriental bittersweet and privet, helping protect the habitat that makes the sanctuary so valuable.
It is easy to celebrate the acquisition of protected land. Far less attention is given to the years, and sometimes decades, of work required to care for it.
This is why local conservation organizations deserve greater recognition and support.
Connecticut’s land trusts, birding organizations and conservation volunteers contribute to environmental protection in ways that may never attract widespread public attention. Yet their collective efforts help preserve the ecological character of communities throughout the state.
These smaller sanctuaries also serve an important purpose beyond wildlife protection: They connect people to the natural world.
Not everyone has the time, resources or ability to travel to distant parks or expansive wilderness areas. Accessible natural spaces close to home provide opportunities to observe wildlife, appreciate biodiversity and develop a personal connection to the environment.
For children especially, these encounters can leave a lasting impression.
A child who hears a wood thrush singing in the forest, watches a great blue heron hunting along a wetland or discovers the brilliant colors of a migrating warbler may begin to understand that conservation is not an abstract concept debated in legislative chambers.
It is about protecting living things and the places they depend upon.
That understanding matters because the future of conservation depends not only on policies and funding, but also on cultivating generations of people who recognize the value of the natural world.
Still, appreciation alone is not enough.
As Connecticut continues to balance housing, infrastructure, economic development and environmental protection, conservation must remain an integral part of land-use decisions.
Municipalities should prioritize the preservation of ecologically significant parcels, encourage connections between existing habitats and recognize the contributions of nonprofit organizations that protect and maintain open space.
State and local leaders should also consider how conservation funding can support not only the acquisition of land, but its long-term stewardship. Protecting a property on paper means little if the resources necessary to maintain its ecological health are overlooked.
Residents have a role to play as well. Volunteering for habitat restoration projects, supporting local conservation organizations, participating in municipal land-use discussions and becoming familiar with nearby natural areas are all meaningful ways to contribute.
The responsibility for protecting Connecticut’s biodiversity cannot rest solely with state agencies or large environmental organizations.
It must also involve the smaller organizations and dedicated individuals who recognize the importance of a marsh, meadow or patch of woodland that others might overlook.
More than a century after its founding, the Hartford Audubon Society continues to demonstrate the lasting impact of conservation at the local level.
Its sanctuaries may occupy only a modest portion of Connecticut’s landscape, but their ecological importance cannot be measured by acreage alone.
Every protected wetland, woodland and meadow represents an investment in the future of our state’s biodiversity.
And as development pressures continue to reshape Connecticut’s landscape, we must recognize that the places most worth protecting are not always the largest, most scenic or most celebrated.
Sometimes, they are the quiet places we barely notice — until they are gone.
Erin Mahoney lives in Avon.

name: Michigan Advance
title: In Detroit debate, Benson and James each blame the other’s party leadership for today’s problems
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, appears with Republican gubernatorial candidate, U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), at a televised debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at WDIV-TV, in Detroit, Mich.Jocelyn Benson and John James could agree on one thing at a Thursday debate hosted by WDIV in Detroit — something needs to change in Michigan. But they disagreed on who was to blame.
James, a U.S. representative from Shelby Township and the Republican nominee, said it’s Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and the last eight years of Democratic executive power in Lansing. Benson, the secretary of state and Democratic nominee, pointed the finger at President Donald Trump and the Republican leadership in Washington.
“Who do you want Michigan’s next governor to work for? I will work for you, not the highest bidder, not Donald Trump,” Benson said in her closing remarks. “He’s done everything Donald Trump asked. Every lie that Donald Trump tells, he repeats. Every bad economic policy Donald Trump promotes, he promotes. I defend our elections. He denies their results.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson talks to reporters after at a televised debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at WDIV-TV, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
James shot back, saying, “My opponent wants you to believe that she hasn’t been in Lansing for the past eight years in power, and has done nothing to change the way you’ve been living for the past eight years. I want you to believe your own eyes. I want you to believe what we can do to increase cost of living and affordability for all of us to make it better. I want you to believe that we can come together and make excellent schools. I want you to believe that we can fix our infrastructure when her party promised to fix the roads that are still not fixed.”
Speaking to reporters after the debate, James also criticized the focus on Trump in midterm races nationwide, calling him “some dude in Washington, D.C., who’s going to be gone in two years.” James was not present at a rally featuring Vice President J.D. Vance earlier in the day.
Benson repeatedly criticized James’ congressional voting record, condemning his votes on legislation that cut SNAP benefits, increase healthcare premiums and continue the war in Iran.
While James disputed each of those attacks from Benson, he did not levy similar ones during the debate on her tenure as secretary of state — though he was widely critical of Democratic leadership in Lansing, he did not actively target any of her specific actions in the Michigan Department of State, focusing instead on the growth of state budget spending and on a lack of transparency in agencies like the Michigan Economic Development Corporation.
He did express skepticism to reporters afterwards about the department’s recommendation not to certify for the ballot a citizens-only voting ballot measure. The measure narrowly failed to meet the required number of valid petition signatures before the bipartisan Board of State Canvassers.
Both candidates centered much of their messaging on affordability and economic growth in Michigan, though their plans to do so differed. 
Asked what one state-level change they would each make in order to make life in Michigan more affordable, James responded that energy prices need to go down and blamed clean energy policies for higher energy costs, while Benson focused her response on healthcare costs and blamed federal cuts to programs such as Medicaid coming from Republicans. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate, U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), talks to reporters after a televised debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at WDIV-TV, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Much of Thursday’s debate echoed the first debate of the general election cycle, held Oct. 6 in Grand Rapids — for example, both candidates suggested an openness to suspending the federal and state gas taxes in order to lower prices at the pump.
Tariffs were also a recurring topic of conversation. James highlighted federal legislation that he introduced to use tariff revenues to offset costs on manufacturers, while Benson spotlighted a plan to develop subnational agreements between Canada and Michigan in order to lower tariff impacts.
Each had new responses to each other’s plans, however — Benson said that James “says he has a plan to do something about, but he waited until Congress was out of session to actually do everything he just talked about,” while James questioned the legality of Benson’s plans and called them “basically tantamount to smuggling.”
The U.S. Constitution and federal law grant control over international trade, including tariffs, to the federal government, raising questions about how enforceable Benson’s plan would be.
Benson defended her plan to reporters after the debate, saying, “I hope to be able to work with the federal government to drive down those costs, but I’m also willing to negotiate agreements with our neighbors to the north that are legally enforceable, so that we can find ways to drive down costs and ensure if goods or services are going just between Michigan and Canada or Canada to Michigan, that we’re able to negotiate carve-outs of existing federal policy that can hold up in court and protect our jobs and protect our costs.”
Benson tied together issues of property tax reform and improving educational outcomes, both of which are also central to James’ plans. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“One of the ways we can truly reform property tax in the state, and I agree we need to reduce it, is a better revenue sharing model between the state and our local communities, so that our local communities aren’t forced to find ways to make ends meet without the support of the state,” she said, reiterating her plan to scrap the longtime school funding model in the state budget of a per-pupil allowance. “Replace it, as my plan will, with a weighted, equitable funding model that will meet the unique needs of every school district and every community. That’s how we actually can put districts and local communities in a place where they can reduce the cost of property tax.”
James, on the other hand, focused messaging on lowering property taxes as well as income taxes by cutting spending on the state level, and noted in response to Benson that the per-pupil allowance in the state budget has increased over recent years — though that increase is smaller than it appears or even a decrease in actual year-to-year spending power when inflation is considered.
As in the first debate, attacks on the issue of data centers got personal, with Benson targeting James for owning stocks in companies developing data centers and James targeting Benson for her husband’s employment at the company developing the large-scale data center in Saline. 
Both candidates have proposed a moratorium on data center development in Michigan if elected, but when asked what happens when that moratorium ends, the candidates seemed to have differing approaches. 
Benson said that, during the moratorium, guardrails on issues like water and energy usage and noise abatement would need to be developed before turning the choice to communities, while James has said that his “moratorium is the locals come before Lansing,” and that he wants to leave decisions up to local control.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: More donor disclosure is always in the public interest
text:
RECENTLY IN CommonWealth Beacon, Jim Stergios of Pioneer Institute and Paul Craney of the Fiscal Alliance Foundation took issue with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance over disclosure of donors in ballot campaigns. They wrote, “This isn’t about whether donor disclosure has a role in elections; it’s about whether the government can expand those rules through vague interpretations.” This issue, in fact, is entirely about donor disclosure in elections.  
Stergios and Craney couched their argument on the narrow grounds of OCPF’s “new interpretation” of a specific law governing donor disclosure requirements for spending within 90 days of the general election. I did not think the “new interpretation” case was clear, so I emailed OCPF about it. The office replied, “we’re not aware of a ‘new interpretation.’”  
This disagreement leaves us with a more vital question: Should the Office of Campaign and Political Finance be enforcing the law to require entities spending money on “communications purchased to influence or affect the vote on a question submitted to the voters” within 90 days of the general election to disclose their donors? The answer to that question is a resounding yes. 
Richard Hasen, a leading scholar of campaign finance, reminds us in Plutocrats United: Campaign Money, the Supreme Court, and the Distortion of American Elections that the Supreme Court enabled unlimited spending on ballot questions in in First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti (1978). The Bellotti decision served as a precursor to Citizens United v. FEC in 2010, which opened the floodgates of “independent expenditures” in candidate elections.  
The result, Prof. Hasen writes, has been that “the collapse of campaign finance regulation in the United States has facilitated a path toward oligarchic power redistribution.” The very least we should expect is that the oligarchic powers be identified to the voters.  
That is what the Citizens United majority expected, and what Justice Antonin Scalia envisioned. As he wrote in a concurrence in Doe v. Reed a few months after Citizens United: 
Requiring people to stand up in public for their political acts fosters civic courage, without which democracy is doomed. For my part, I do not look forward to a society which, thanks to the Supreme Court, campaigns anonymously … and even exercises the direct democracy of initiative and referendum hidden from public scrutiny and protected from the accountability of criticism. This does not resemble the Home of the Brave. 
Wealthy donors such as the ones being hidden by Fiscal Alliance Foundation have been fleeing the Home of the Brave ever since.  
The term “nonprofit” repeated by Stergios and Craney has no magical properties. It simply identifies the sections of the Internal Revenue Service code under which these entities are organized. In practice Pioneer Institute and Fiscal Alliance Foundation serve as conservative advocacy groups.  
Fiscal Alliance Foundation and Pioneer Institute are both affiliates of the State Policy Network (SPN), a coordinating hub of state-level right-wing policy shops. Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance is an SPN partner. Prof. Elena Aydarova and her colleagues place SPN at the center of “the Conservative Industrial Complex’s war on education.” Prof. Alex Hertel-Fernandez finds SPN part of an effective 50-state “right-wing troika” with the American Legislative Exchange Council and the Koch Brothers’ Americans for Prosperity. (The late David Koch contributed a million dollars to Pioneer.) The left-leaning Center for Media and Democracy and right-leaning Influencewatch agree: SPN is a conservative policy advocacy operation.  
Fiscal Alliance Foundation and Pioneer are organized under IRS section 501(c)(3). Such organizations are tax-exempt and tax-deductible to donors. A 501(c)(3) cannot donate to candidates but may donate to ballot committees.  
Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance is a 501(c)(4). It is tax-exempt but not tax-deductible to the donor. As a “social welfare” organization it can donate money directly to a ballot committee and make independent expenditures supporting a candidate. Another Fiscal Alliance Foundation-related entity is Fiscal Partners, organized as a business association under section 501(c)(6), which is tax-exempt but not deductible to the donor. As The Boston Globe explained in 2019, Fiscal Partners exists to take in money and pass the cash to Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance without revealing donors’ identities.  
Fiscal Partners has done its job well. From 2017-2024, the last year for which records are publicly available, Fiscal Partners sent $1,756,000 to Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance and $50,000 to Fiscal Alliance Foundation. The true sources of those funds remain dark.  
The most recently available IRS Form 990 tax returns from 2024 show all three “Fiscal” organizations at the same address. Craney is listed as principal officer of Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance and Fiscal Partners. Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance’s current webpage lists Craney as executive director. Fiscal Alliance Foundation’s current webpage lists him as executive director and a board member. The secretary of state’s Corporations Division lists Craney as president of Fiscal Partners. Fiscal Alliance Foundation and Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance explicitly promise to protect their donors’ names from disclosure.  
It is ironic that Stergios and Craney specified August 3 as the dread date when donors would face disclosure. August 3 is the tenth anniversary of OCPF’s determination that the Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance should disclose the identity of a dark money donor in two legislative special elections held that year. The organization has ignored that finding and never disclosed the donor.  
Stergios and Craney argue that their polls and studies are merely efforts to “educate” the public. In 2019 CommonWealth Beacon fact-checked a Fiscal Alliance Foundation poll that was “worded in a way that seemed designed to influence the response.”  
In 2018, Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance founder Rick Green was running for Congress as a Republican. The Alliance issued a report showing what it claimed were irregular voter registrations in four municipalities in Green’s district. Each of the localities had large Latino populations. Heavily Democratic Lawrence, 74 percent Latino, was singled out by Mass Fiscal. The secretary of state rightly ignored the study. 
It seems plain that Pioneer and Fiscal Alliance run “communications purchased to influence or affect the vote.” They are not arguing that they do not, just that they think the obvious interpretation of the statute caught them by surprise.  
Avoiding the substance make sense since Americans overwhelming favor disclosure. A 2025 YouGov poll for the non-partisan group Issue One asked Americans whether they would support a ballot question in their own state to eliminate corporate money, anonymous donors, and dark money spending in elections. After being informed of arguments for and against such a measure, including the “free speech” argument offered by Stergios and Craney, 72 percent of Americans said they would support such a ballot question, with only 12 percent opposed. Republicans, Democrats, and Independents all favor disclosure of dark money donors.  
A June 2014 Suffolk University poll asked Massachusetts likely voters if they support stricter regulations of super PACs, including “making them disclose the names of their donors?” Disclosure was supported by 67 percent with 13 percent opposed and 20 percent undecided. In 2018 by 71 percent to 29 percent Massachusetts voters supported the creation of a commission to study a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United. Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance was opposed.  
The Brennan Center for Justice’s Secret Spending in the States details how dark money affects elections. Unidentified funders often hold direct economic interests in election outcomes, especially in ballot questions.  
Dark money spending can dominate local elections (such as the local measure used as an example in Stergios and Craney’s commentary). And dark money may mislead voters, malign or intimidate candidates, or even discourage good people from running at all. 
In 1825, the British philosopher Jeremy Bentham wrote, “In the darkness of secrecy, sinister interest and evil in every shape, have full swing. …  Where there is no publicity there is no justice.” 
The American campaign finance system provides a perfect example. We deserve to know who is spending vast sums of money to choose our candidates and overwhelm our ballot questions. The Office of Campaign and Political Finance’s interpretation of the statutory language is correct. The public would be well-served to see it aggressively enforced. 
Maurice Cunningham is a retired professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Boston and author of Dark Money and the Politics of School Privatization. His Substack is Sinister Interest & Evil in Every Shape: A Dark Money Reader.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Dunlap and LePage continue campaign quarrels in final debate
text:
U.S. House candidates Democrat Matt Dunlap (left) and Republican Paul LePage (right) met for the second time on the debate stage on Oct. 15. (Photos by Jim Neuger and Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)During their second and final debate appearance Thursday evening, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage resurrected many of the same disagreements from their initial debate, digging further into each other’s record in state government. 
The forum, hosted by WABI and WAGM, gave the candidates vying to replace outgoing Democrat U.S. Rep. Jared Golden in Maine’s 2nd District one last opportunity to make their pitch to voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.
Much of the debate, and subsequent barbs, focused on healthcare. 
On Thursday, LePage defended his record as governor, when he vetoed five bills that would have expanded MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program. He argued that his issue with expansion was that the reimbursement rates to healthcare providers are too low and it endangers services. 
“And I never said to get rid of Medicaid,” LePage said. “I said Medicaid, folks, Medicaid would work if you reimburse the hospitals and the medical profession at cost, but below cost, everybody loses.”
On the campaign trail, LePage has repeatedly touted how the state government paid off $750 million in debt to hospitals when he was governor, and brought it up again at the debate. 
But Democrats at the time criticized LePage for stalling the payments, and Dunlap noted that LePage vetoed an earlier bill that would have made the payments and expanded Medicaid.
“If you don’t believe people should have healthcare, then you follow Paul LePage, which is getting rid of Medicaid,” Dunlap said. “I don’t see how you actually improve healthcare by taking healthcare away from people.”
As before, LePage pivoted to the issue of fraud. 
“The first thing that we should do, and this gentleman has been in the power to do it, is to fight fraud in Maine,” LePage said, referring to Dunlap’s position as state auditor. 
Fate of Medicare, Medicaid emerge as key issue in 2nd District race

State and national Republicans have alleged widespread fraud in Maine’s healthcare programs and have tried to make it a key issue throughout the midterm campaign. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has found five providers guilty of fraudulent billing and suspended their contracts, but Republicans claim the problem is much more rampant. 
In the most recent federal review, Maine’s Medicaid payment error rate was 2.4%, lower than the national average of 3.2%. And only about 0.1% of total program spending was confirmed by federal reviewers to be definitively incorrect. 
Dunlap said his office is not in charge of pursuing criminal charges, only identifying issues — which it has done. 
“I would have assumed, with the experience that Paul LePage touts as governor, that he’d actually understand what my job actually is and what it is not,” Dunlap said. 
Social Security
Dunlap also returned to an issue he brought up in the previous debate: a 2014 press release from LePage’s office, which Dunlap argued quotes LePage calling Social Security “welfare.”
“I think that’s something that gives an indicator of how he would feel about this,” Dunlap said. “And I would not trust him to be a champion for Social Security.”
The release discusses how the federal government calculates personal earnings growth and the inclusion of certain benefits, such as Social Security benefits and Medicare payments. 
“It doesn’t matter what liberals call these payments, it is welfare, pure and simple,” LePage is quoted as saying in the release. 
During the debate, LePage said he “can see” where Dunlap comes from with the accusation, but argued he was talking broadly about transfer receipts, not about Social Security. 
“We can read the whole press release, but you said that Social Security was welfare,” Dunlap said. 
Medicare for All
LePage also criticized Dunlap’s support for Medicare for All, and said it was too expensive. 
“Believe me, if you want somebody that’s going to be a spender, he’s your guy,” LePage said of Dunlap. “If you want somebody that’s going to lower costs, go after fraud. I’m your guy.”
Dunlap defended his support of universal coverage by saying he would reprioritize spending to pay for such a program, which would save money for private businesses and individuals who no longer would have to pay for private insurance. 
“We can do these things if we prioritize our neighbors instead of simply prioritizing the desires of the corporate class who just want to bring in more of the pie for themselves,” Dunlap said. 
LePage said that he has lived in a “socialized medicine scenario,” although he did not specify where or when that was.  
“You get rationing, you lose your doctors because if you go to a hospital, you don’t go to a doctor, you don’t have a private doctor, unless you’re very very wealthy, and so and the cost is astronomical,” LePage said. 
Dunlap said that scenario is “not what we’re seeing.”
“I don’t think people should be scared of the idea of having access to healthcare, and scaring them with ideas of rationing and long lines,” Dunlap said. 
The conversation turned to whether Dunlap has lived in a place with such a policy, and he reiterated that he’s lived in Maine his whole life.
“Oh, is that right? Well, I’ve lived in Maine longer than you’ve been alive,” LePage said.
Dunlap and LePage try to outgun each other over support for Second Amendment

“Except for the time that you spend in Florida,” Dunlap interjected, returning to a long-time criticism of LePage’s residency. 
LePage acknowledged, “Yes, I’m a snowbird.” 
“At my age, I don’t like snow anymore,” he said. “I’ve got knee problems, so I don’t ski and I don’t play hockey anymore. So yes, in the winter months we go to Florida. I have never been in Florida a whole year.”
Iran War and affordability
The pair were also asked about heating costs, which Dunlap was quick to point to as the source of the challenge. 
“I do think that one of the things that is critical here is the war in Iran, because these prices haven’t sloped up over the years — they’ve spiked since the attacks began at the end of February, and it’s only gotten worse as this war has dragged on,” Dunlap said. 
And while LePage agreed it was a factor, he said it wasn’t entirely to blame. 
“The Iran War is adding to it, but the bigger problem started under Joe Biden,” LePage said. 
Dunlap took the opportunity to criticize LePage for not having a clear stance on the war, and going “back and forth” on the issue. 
“I want the war to end as quickly as possible,” LePage said. “However, I do not want Iran to get a nuclear weapon. I do not support having any boots on the ground.” 
LePage said the current regime in Iran is not trustworthy, and the United States must force a change. 
“Paul LePage is talking about regime change, and yet not putting any boots on the ground,” Dunlap said. “I’m not sure how that happens without having American troops committed in a combat situation, which I don’t think anybody really wants to see happen.”
Throughout the conversation, LePage frequently touted his relationship with President Donald Trump, and his access to the White House — an approach that Dunlap criticized. 
“And I want to be very clear here that we don’t elect representatives to Congress to talk to the White House,” Dunlap said. “We elect them to provide oversight of the executive branch.”
But LePage countered that his focus will be on Maine people, not the president. 
“Your job may be to have oversight over the president, the White House,” LePage said. “My job is to do the best I can for the people of Maine.”
Dunlap responded, “I think doing the best job that we can for the people of Maine means standing up for the people of the state of Maine in the chamber that you’re elected to, and that’s what I will do in Washington.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: In final debate, Collins and Jackson share different outlooks on future of democracy
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenge, Troy Jackson, met in Bangor for their fourth and final debate on Oct. 15. (Screenshot courtesy of Maine Public/ News Center Maine) Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson offered new insight on how they view the state of American democracy, gun rights, campaign finance and more during their final debate on Thursday. 
The debate, hosted jointly by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine at Gracie Theatre in Bangor, was the fourth in two weeks and the only that included questions submitted directly from voters, in addition to moderator questions. 
While the debate had a live audience, attendees were invited by the campaigns, not members of the general public. The format of debates had been a point of disagreement, as Jackson’s campaign had requested town hall-style forums, where voters could ask questions on the spot. 
Jackson continued to try to tie Collins to President Donald Trump on Thursday, while the five-term senator again pitched her seniority as most beneficial to Mainers, something that has been a thorough line in earlier debates and the campaign season. 
Tensions were high both on and off stage Thursday. In addition to the candidates continuing to take jabs at one anothers’ records, fifteen minutes into the debate a member of the audience interrupted, yelling to Collins, “AI data centers are destroying our climate,” before being escorted out. 
Collins turned the blame on Jackson, saying, “so this is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded, “Oh shut up, I don’t even know that kid.” The audience member had a press badge on but it was unclear who he was. 
Collins says democracy ‘will be just fine.’ Jackson disagrees. 
One of the voter questions came from Bridget O’Brian of Harpswell, who asked what they thought of the state of democracy in America today. 
Collins called the U.S. “the greatest nation on earth,” before saying presidents from both parties have tried to expand their power historically. 
“I think that Congress does need to keep reasserting itself,” she said. “But I think our democracy will be just fine.”
Jackson responded that it would not be fine if the administration takes away people’s voting rights. Trump has attempted to restrict voting by mail, purge voter rolls and send sensitive personal information to the Department of Homeland Security, among other efforts. 
The Democrat pinned the future of democracy on his party taking control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate to be able to hold Trump accountable. 
“The Republicans have totally given up their willingness to do that,” he said. 
Gun rights 
Both candidates were asked if they would support an assault weapons ban, like the one that had been in place nationally from 1994 to 2004. These assault weapons have been used in many mass shootings, including the one in Lewiston in 2023.
Collins said she has voted to ban bump stocks and supports a “reasonable limit” on magazine capacity. She also pointed to her support of the 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act.
Meanwhile, Jackson said outright he would support an assault weapons ban, though with the caveat that he wouldn’t take firearms from people who already own them. “I don’t see a good reason for assault weapons,” Jackson said. “You can’t use them for hunting or anything like that.”
The candidates were also asked if they would raise the age to buy a gun from 18 to 21. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jackson said no. Collins said she’d be open to raising it, but didn’t specify an age. 
Jackson’s views on gun rights have shifted. He initially voted against proposals to expand background checks and implement a 72-hour waiting period for firearm purchases, but after the Lewiston mass shooting, came out in favor of such proposals. 
National debt 
The national debt is roughly $40 trillion and Trump’s signature spending law, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” adds another $4 trillion to that total. That debt impacts everyday Americans through higher borrowing costs, stagnant wages, and higher prices, according to the Government Accountability Office. 
Collins said the government should focus on growing the economy and “not pursue policies as Troy would and as he has here in Maine that impose enormous tax burdens on the people of Maine.”
Jackson criticized tax cuts for wealthy people in the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which Collins helped advance but ultimately voted against. He also pointed out that the national debt has grown nearly eight-fold during her tenure, which began in 1997. “And somehow it’s my fault?” Jackson said. “I mean, in Maine, we have a balanced budget. Has it grown? Yes, but it’s still balanced.”
Collins pointed to the state’s projected $1 billion structural gap saying, “That happened under Troy’s watch.” (Such gaps are not novel and revenue projections due in December could also alter the estimate.)
Jackson, who served as president of the Maine Senate from 2018 to 2024, responded, “I don’t think I’ve been in the Legislature for the last two, three years.” That response was met with laughs from the audience.  
Campaign finances 
During the third debate on Tuesday, Jackson said he would release his financial disclosure the next morning, which he did not do. Collins brought that up Thursday night.
Both Jackson and Collins submitted their reports to the Federal Elections Commission on Thursday, the deadline to do so. Overall, they show Jackson, who became his party’s nominee in late July, outraised Collins from July through September. 
Jackson admitted to not meeting his self-imposed deadline. “We had over 200,000 people that gave to our campaign,” he said. “I had to make sure this report was done right. It was my first one. I had to make sure it was right because I don’t have Donald Trump getting me out of investigations like you do.” 
He was referring to reporting from ProPublica last month that found the FBI had been looking into Collins’ alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme in recent years until Trump’s purge of the bureau ended the inquiry. Collins has denied any wrongdoing.  
Jackson has pledged to refuse corporate PAC money. On Thursday, Collins painted the ads he has done with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as breaking that pledge. 
“Those ads obviously are done without my approval,” Jackson said, later adding, “that would be illegal for me to make those decisions.” 
But ads between a national party and candidate are legal. And over the summer, the U.S. Supreme Court removed limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates. 
Both Jackson and Collins have ads with the DSCC and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, respectively. 
Ad spending by outside groups for this race has reached $200 million, $75 million of which is from essentially untraceable sources, known as dark money. Both candidates were asked if they think it is important for the public to know who is trying to influence their vote. 
Both said they did. 
Collins pointed to her co-sponsorship of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, which largely has not stood constitutional muster. She said she supports full disclosure of donors. 
Jackson said he supports overturning the Supreme Court’s landmark Citizens United v. FEC decision in 2010, which allowed for unlimited election spending by corporations and labor unions. He also said he’d be open to exploring if Maine’s Clean Elections program could work on the national level.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Citizen panel rejects pay hike for WA governor
text:
Gov. Bob Ferguson, seen here during an event in June, will not receive a raise in the next two years under a recommendation adopted Thursday by the Washington Citizens Commission on Salaries for Elected Officials.(Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, who did not offer raises to thousands of state workers in recent contract talks, will not get one himself for the next two years, under a recommendation adopted by a citizen salary-setting panel on Thursday. 
Salaries for the attorney general and lieutenant governor will be frozen too with the proposed schedule drawn up by the Washington Citizens Commission on Salaries for Elected Officials at a daylong meeting in an Olympia hotel.
Commissioners did agree, however, to give state lawmakers, along with the superintendent of public instruction, treasurer, and commissioner of public lands increases of 2% on July 1, 2027 and another 2% on July 1, 2028. Judges, including state Supreme Court justices, would also receive 2% hikes next July and 2% a year later.
And, in one of their final votes, they agreed to boost the salaries of the offices of the secretary of state, insurance commissioner, and state auditor by 5% in each of the next two years.
“We have salaries that will not attract the best candidates available in our state,” said Commissioner Steve Smith in explaining why these state executives should receive a greater bump in their annual earnings.
Thursday’s action stood in stark contrast to the last round of salary setting, in 2024, when the commission raised pay for the jobs of governor and attorney general by 14% over two years. Cost of living adjustments made up a third of the total with the rest intended to account for growing duties of the elected positions and rising costs of living. 
On Thursday, commissioners balked at boosting their salaries in light of the state’s strained fiscal condition and the belief that their job responsibilities haven’t noticeably changed from that last round. Ferguson earns $234,275 a year while Brown hauls in $221,614, making him one of the nation’s highest paid attorney generals.
Commissioner Melody Adams-Forsstrom made the motion to freeze the salary for the governor’s job.
“He got a huge increase last time,” she said. “Though I am speaking for myself, I think we really represent the taxpayers of the state and what they’re facing and their circumstances.”
Throughout the day’s discussions, members made references to new two-year contracts Ferguson’s staff negotiated with state workers unions that contain no across-the-board wage increase or cost of living adjustment.
“In my view if public workers don’t get that I’m not comfortable giving it to elected officials,” said commissioner Sarah Tucker.
One of the day’s closest votes was on a motion to not give a raise to legislators, who earn $72,494. The motion garnered seven votes of support but needed 9 of the 15 present.
The commission will spend the next four months gathering comments on the recommendations. Virtual public hearings are planned Nov. 12, Dec. 10 and Jan. 7. A final hearing is set for Feb. 10 in Olympia, at which commissioners could revise the schedule before taking final action.
Voters established the salary commission in 1987 to end the practice of politicians deciding their own pay. Though funded by the state, it operates independent of the legislative, executive and judicial branches.
Its 17 unpaid members include residents from each of the state’s 10 congressional districts plus representatives of business, organized labor and higher education. Also represented are the legal and human resources professions.
Every two years this panel comes together to consider salary changes. Commissioners are supposed to base decisions on the duties of the job — not the man or woman doing it at the time. They don’t have to give any raises, but they cannot lower the salary of anyone in office.
Elected officials and judges cannot alter what the commission approves.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

title: President Trump to rally in Clemson next week
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham introduces President Donald Trump at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)It’s official: President Donald Trump is returning to South Carolina next week to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham and other Republicans ahead of the midterms.
The rally will be Wednesday in Clemson. The scheduled start time is 7 p.m., the Republican National Committee announced Thursday evening.
The announcement did not say where in Clemson.
But the Upstate college town is only a few miles from Central, the hometown of Graham and her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
Darline Graham, his younger sister, was appointed in July to fulfill his fourth term, which ends in January. She then won a 10-way special GOP primary to replace her brother on the Nov. 3 ballot for the next six-year term — a race she entered at Trump’s encouragement.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


Polls show her in a tighter-than-expected contest with Democrat Annie Andrews in a state Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points two years ago.
In a call-in rally Thursday night, Trump called Graham “one of the greats,” adding that she has “great genetics,” referring to her brother.
The tele-rally was held with Graham, as well as Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, and Jenny Costa Honeycutt, the GOP nominee for the coastal 1st District.
The call was intended to ramp up enthusiasm ahead of early voting, which starts Monday in South Carolina.
He told callers to pretend he’s on the ballot when they vote, whether that’s during the two-week early voting window or on Election Day.
“Essentially, I am on the ballot,” Trump said.
Trump last rallied in South Carolina in August ahead of Graham’s GOP runoff against U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman.
The Myrtle Beach rally seemed to help with turnout. Her biggest win came in ruby red Horry County, where she won 73% of the vote.
But Norman won the Upstate.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: In Alaska campaign rally, Trump and Sullivan say Iran war is worth the cost to Americans
text:
A U.S. Air Force E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft refuels from a KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft during Operation Epic Fury, March 31, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo)At a rally in Wasilla on Tuesday, President Donald Trump and Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan said America’s war with Iran is worth the resulting increased cost of fuel and food for Americans.
“No matter what it is, it’s a small price to pay for stopping them from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump said of Iran.
Fuel prices have risen in Alaska and the United States at large since Trump began the Iran war alongside Israel on Feb. 28. According to the latest available state report, heating fuel prices in rural Alaska climbed to an average of $8 per gallon by August, up from $6.49 per gallon in January.
Sullivan has voted 14 times against War Powers Act resolutions that could limit or end American involvement in it.
Before the current war, Sullivan supported the Trump-ordered bombing of Iran last year and has advocated military action against the country.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Speaking on Tuesday in Wasilla, Sullivan said the best way to reduce fuel costs in Alaska is to produce more oil and gas locally, and he said Alaskans should re-elect him because national Democrats oppose oil and gas development. 
“It’s important to remember this: the best way to address Alaska’s energy challenges is to produce more Alaskan energy by and for Alaskans,” Sullivan said. 
“Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs. That’s the forever war,” he said. 




 Trump and Sullivan on Russia and Putin
While Sullivan and Trump are aligned on Iran, they differ in their opinions on Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin.
Sullivan has called Russian President Vladimir Putin a dictator, the leader of a mafia regime, and an authoritarian. Trump has called Putin a friend.
In a TV interview before Tuesday’s rally, the President was asked about their difference of opinion.
“Well, look, I have to make deals with people, so I don’t go around calling them names. I’m a dealmaker; I’ve always been a very good dealmaker. I became very rich because of deals, so I don’t go around mocking people,” he said. 
Trump has issued orders that allow Russia to export diesel fuel, possibly lowering global prices but contributing to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Members of Congress, including Sullivan and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, have criticized Trump’s decision, but the President defended his choice in the interview.
“It’s not oil coming to us, and it’s diesel, which you need. I feel that it’s great because it’s released to the world,” Trump said.




Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, is in a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, who has criticized Trump for starting the war and Sullivan for supporting it.
“We should be standing up to the president, and there have been many times where the Senate and the House have said no to the administration on wars. Where is our backbone?” Peltola said during an Anchorage forum on Oct. 8.
Peltola and Sullivan are in a four-person general election that also includes Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg and Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer.
Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said, “We’re very close to winning — I mean, we’ve — I think we’ve won the war because they will — Iran will not have a nuclear weapon, let me put it that way. That war is going to end very soon and when it does, your prices are going to come tumbling down. They already are.”
National and state data has not shown a significant decline in fuel prices over the past month, and consumer price inflation in September was 3.7%, up from August.
In a visit to Fairbanks earlier this month, Vice President J.D. Vance offered comments similar to the ones that Trump made this week, including statements to the effect that Democrats are the enemy.
Peltolta said it’s outrageous to call half of Americans an enemy.
“No American is my enemy. … No Republican is my enemy. No Democrat is my enemy. No Alaskan who is independent, nonpartisan, undeclared is my enemy,” Peltola said. 
She seemed to also rebut a New York Times article stating that she once wished a local Planned Parenthood board member would die of a botched abortion: “I have not one person I wish ill will or malice or injustice to in all of Alaska and all of America. We are all in this together. There is no reason to create division amongst ourselves.”
With Sullivan remaining behind in Alaska, Trump repeated his Wasilla message at rallies in Arizona and Montana the following day. 
The President has been campaigning nationwide in an effort to boost Republican candidates in the November general election.
“That’s going to end very soon,” Trump said on Wednesday morning in Bullhead City, Arizona, of the Iran war. “And when that ends, your gasoline is going to go down to even lower than it was before it started.”
“If they had a nuclear weapon, within 24 hours they would use it. They’ll knock out the Middle East. Then they’ll start hitting us on the West Coast. They’ll hit Europe because they’re crazy. They’re crazy people. So, this is a very small price people pay. And I thought it would go up much higher,” Trump said of fuel prices.
Later that day, in Kalispell, Montana, Trump gave similar remarks.
“We had the greatest economy in the history of our country in my first administration. We are going to blow it away in this administration, as soon as — as soon as Iran — Iran is going to be over very quickly,” he said.
Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, south of Iran, have risen in recent months but have not yet returned to pre-war levels.
On the same day as Trump’s remarks in Arizona and Montana, two commercial ships sank in the Strait of Hormuz south of Iran, and CNN reported that the United States is considering whether to attack Iran with the largest non-nuclear bomb in its arsenal. 
Yereth Rosen contributed reporting from Anchorage.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Trump to hold two Iowa campaign events ahead of Election Day
text:
President Donald Trump greeted supporters who attended his speech at the Horizon Events Center in Clive Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)President Donald Trump will make two trips to Iowa ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026 general election.
Iowa Republican Party Chairman Jeff Kaufmann said in a statement Thursday the president plans to be in Iowa Thursday, Oct. 22, and Sunday, Nov. 1. Information on where Trump will be and which candidates he will campaign with has not yet been released.
“I just got off the phone with President Trump. He told me that he will be in Iowa on October 22 and November 1,” Kaufmann said. “He is anxious for Iowans to hear his message before they vote. Stay tuned for further details.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The president’s visit comes as many Iowa races are considered hotly contested in the upcoming midterms. Iowa’s race for U.S. Senate between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, is rated as a “toss-up” by political forecasters. Three of the state’s four GOP-held House races are also considered potential Democratic pickups. Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts are rated as “leans Democrat” by Cook Political Report, favoring Democratic challengers against incumbent Republicans, and the 2nd District is rated as a “toss-up.”
The Iowa races could play key roles in determining which party controls the U.S. House and Senate.
Though Iowa is expected to see tight elections in November, it is not the only state where Republicans are seen as endangered in comparison to the 2024 general election. Trump, alongside other national Republican leaders, have been on the campaign trail in recent weeks across states including Alaska, Arizona, Georgia and Michigan supporting Republican candidates in the final stretch before Election Day.
The president and other GOP leaders are emphasizing Republicans’ efforts to lower federal spending through measures like the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act, decreasing taxes on tips and overtime, as well as the administration’s work to heighten immigration law enforcement as they aim to persuade voters to keep GOP majorities in Congress.
But as many voters in recent polls cite high costs, rising inflation and healthcare as top concerns, Democrats say Republicans’ agenda has hurt Americans. Top points of contention are the continued U.S. war with Iran, which has contributed to high fuel and fertilizer costs, and cuts to Medicaid made in the OBBB Act.
Though forecasters and polls show tight races in Iowa, Republicans retain a state lead in registered voters. GOP candidates and leaders have urged Republicans to mobilize and participate in the Nov. 3, 2026 election, rallying with national figures at campaign stops in the weeks ahead of voting. Prior to Trump’s visit, House Speaker Mike Johnson rallied with U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, running for reelection in Iowa’s 1st District against Democrat Christina Bohannan, and Vice President JD Vance held a campaign event with Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn in September.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Another lawsuit filed over 2025 property tax legislation
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Three current and former legislators have filed another lawsuit over Senate Bill 542, a property tax bill signed last year.
State Sen. Greg Hertz, Senate Majority Leader Tom McGillvray and former legislator Keith Regier, all Republicans, jointly filed the lawsuit this week saying SB 542 violates the constitution’s equal protection clause. 
Under SB 542, residential property tax rates differ depending on their market value. The lawsuit, which was filed in Gallatin County, says setting different rates within the same property class violates the constitution.
“Tax relief for one group of Montanans should not come at the expense of unfairly taxing their neighbors. The Montana Constitution protects equal treatment, and we are asking the courts to enforce those protections,” McGillvray said in a press release. “This lawsuit is not about opposing property tax relief. It is about ensuring that tax relief is provided in a manner that respects the constitutional rights of every Montana property owner.”
The lawsuit says equal protection clauses protect individuals from “state action which selects him or her out for discriminatory treatment by subjecting him or her to taxes not imposed on others of the same class.”
Hertz, McGillvray and Regier previously filed a suit over the bill, saying it violated the constitution’s single-subject rule, which says a bill must address just one topic, and it must be clear. That suit, which the state GOP joined on the side of the plaintiffs, is still pending and was also filed in Gallatin County District Court.
“Montanans deserve a property tax system that is fair, transparent, and constitutional,” Hertz said in a press release. “The Legislature has the authority to establish property classifications, but once property is placed within the same class, the constitution requires that taxpayers be treated equally.”
SB 542 was passed during the 2025 session and signed into law by Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte. Some legislators referred to it as a “Frankstein” bill during the sessions, as it drew heavily from other legislation that didn’t pass.
The Governor’s Office did not immediately comment on the suit, but has expressed support for the legislation, saying 80% of Montanans got property tax relief.

name: Daily Montanan
title: 17 groups sue Montana Public Service Commission to require considering climate change
text:
The Missoula County Court House  pictured on December 20, 2020. (Provided by Tommy Martino for the Daily Montanan)A coalition of 17 groups that want the Montana Public Service Commission to consider the effects of climate change in its decisions is taking its case to court.
Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center filed a complaint Thursday against the Public Service Commission.
It asks the Missoula County District Court to find the PSC has a constitutional obligation to account for climate risks in its decisions.
“Climate change poses an urgent threat to Montana and its people,” the complaint said.
It said the Public Service Commission can allow utilities to keep investing in fossil fuels or encourage them to pursue “cleaner and ultimately less costly alternatives.”
But it said the PSC has “refused to recognize and regularly disregards” the costs of climate, such as smoke that hurts asthmatic children, floods that destroy homes, and anglers who can’t fish.
The groups include healthcare providers, youth organizations and clean energy and climate advocates.
Amy Cilimburg, with lead plaintiff Climate Smart Missoula, said the PSC’s failure to regulate with climate in mind affects the health of Montanans and their ability to afford power.
“When the PSC fails to consider climate change in its decisions, Montanans bear the high costs and risks that come with fossil-fuel electricity, as well as the unaffordable and unconstitutional effects of a changing climate,” Cilimburg said in a statement.
In February 2024, more than 40 organizations and businesses asked the PSC to address its “obligations to consider climate impacts,” but the PSC denied the request in September 2025 and again last month.
The PSC regulates monopoly utilities and is made up of five elected commissioners, all of whom are currently Republican.
The complaint asks the court to vacate the PSC’s decisions and find the commission has a constitutional responsibility to consider climate as part of the state’s obligation to “maintain and improve a clean and healthful environment.”
The PSC could not be reached for comment Thursday afternoon.
When the commission voted to deny the petition by the groups in 2025, its legal counsel said the PSC is an administrative agency, so it didn’t have the authority to do what the groups wanted — to declare the constitution requires the PSC to consider the adverse impacts of climate change.
Then-chief-legal-counsel Lucas Hamilton also said the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment appears along other rights the PSC must consider, such as to pursue life’s basic necessities — including water service.
In a news release about the lawsuit, the groups said the PSC took nearly two-and-a-half years to make a decision on their petition but never addressed its substance.
In the meantime, the PSC was making “consequential decisions,” they said.
They pointed to the PSC’s decision to approve “NorthWestern Energy’s request to charge customers for the high construction and operation costs for the Yellowstone County Generating Station.”
In December 2024, the Montana Supreme Court affirmed the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment includes “a stable climate system” in the historic Held vs. State of Montana decision.
In a statement, Sarah Lundquist, executive director of Families for a Livable Climate, said youth fought for their constitutional rights in the Held case and have been advocating “for climate justice” ever since.
Families for a Livable Climate is part of the lawsuit.
“Now it’s our turn,” Lundquist said. “The Public Service Commission has enormous influence over Montana’s energy future, and we must ensure climate change is at the center of its decisions. It is our responsibility as adults to protect the future our kids deserve.”



Groups filing lawsuit
Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center represent Climate Smart Missoula, Citizens for Clean Energy, Earthworks, Families for a Livable Climate, Forward Montana, Helena Hunters and Anglers, Helena Interfaith Climate Advocates, Montana Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Montana Environmental Information Center, Montana Health and Climate, Montana Public Interest Research Group, Montana Renewable Energy Association, NW Energy Coalition, Park County Environmental Council, Renewable Northwest, Sierra Club Montana Chapter, and 350 Montana in the lawsuit.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New polling site puts NC State students farther from the ballot box
text:
The entrance to the new polling location on N.C. State's campus. It was moved a mile from its original location at the Talley Student Union. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)For N.C. State senior Joshua Ni, voting early meant fitting a ballot into the rhythm of campus life.  
But earlier this year, the polling place he used in 2024 was moved from the Talley Student Union, making the trip less convenient for Ni and other students who might otherwise walk to the polls.  
Talley Student Union sits at the center of campus and is a short walk for many students. The center houses restaurants, apparel shops and several student organizations. 
“Clearly, moving it away from central campus to me seems like they wanted fewer students to vote,” he said after voting Thursday. 
The new location at the N.C. State Western Boulevard Services building is about a mile away from Talley Student Union.  To get there, students must cross either a two-lane road or the heavily trafficked four lanes on Western Boulevard.  
The move followed a 3-2 vote by the Wake County Board of Elections in June. Republican board members rejected a proposal to keep Talley, which had hosted early voting during previous election cycles, including the 2024 general election. 
Republicans axe NC State student center as an early voting site

Republican board members argued the Business Services building would be easier for voters arriving by car because it had more parking space. Opponents of the move said the Talley location was a familiar, accessible site for students. 
N.C. State’s Pack the Polls voter engagement program is offering a free shuttle service between Talley and the new polling location from Oct. 21 through Oct. 31, the final day of early voting. The service was not running on the first day of voting, Thursday. 
“Even then, it won’t compare to just being in the student union,” Ni said. 
Wally Robertson, the chief judge at the new site, said it’s too early to determine whether the move affected turnout. He said voter totals and age ranges will be available through the Wake County Board of Elections website. 
Karen St. Clair, who plans to greet voters next week and offer rides to those who need transportation, visited the new polling place Thursday to vote early and familiarize herself with the location. 
“If I’m going to help people where I live, because I’m going to offer rides and bring them here, I need to see it,” she said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nunn, Trone Garriott agree to 3rd District debate on Oct. 27
text:
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott and U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, a Republican are competing to represent Iowa's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)The candidates for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, Republican Zach Nunn and Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, agreed  Thursday to participate in their only televised debate of the campaign.
After weeks of impasse on scheduling the event, the candidates agreed to debate at 9 p.m. Oct. 27 on KCCI. But the candidates continued to argue about why a debate wasn’t scheduled before now.
The race for Iowa’s 3rd District is among the most competitive in the country, according to political forecasters, and could play a key role in determining which party wins control of the U.S. House in 2026. KCCI confirmed the debate, which will take place one week before Election Day.
Trone Garriott, a state senator from West Des Moines, said in a statement, “I’ve been looking forward to this debate from the beginning, and I’m glad it’s happening.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’ve held town halls in every county in this district, and I’ve heard the same things everywhere I go,” she said in a statement. “Families are paying too much for groceries, health care, and child care, and people are tired of politicians in Washington who look out for themselves. I’m excited to share my vision for change and how I’ll work hard for every Iowan, whether they agree with me or not. I’ll see you on October 27.”
Nunn, the incumbent Republican, said the debate will be a chance to show 3rd District voters the “clear choice between my record of delivering bipartisan results for all Iowans and my opponent’s radical record of wanting the largest tax increase in Iowa history and driving up costs for families and farmers.”
“Sarah Trone Garriott knows that record is hard to defend in front of Iowans, which is why she hid from this debate for more than a month, until nearly a third of voters in our district will have already cast their ballot,” Nunn said. “Iowans expect better. I said yes to this debate in September because Iowans deserve to hear from both candidates, and I stand ready to make my case on October 27.”
Prior to Thursday’s announcement, Iowa’s 3rd District was set to be the only congressional race in Iowa where candidates had not agreed to participate in a debate ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
On Wednesday, Nunn held a news conference after casting his ballot in early voting, where he told reporters his campaign “just said yes again to KCCI to do this on the 27th of October.”
“I wish we would have done this before early voting started, but as we turn out here today as one of the first candidates to vote, it’s important Iowans of all stripes get to hear from their candidates,” he said.
But Trone Garriott argued she had agreed to debate on Oct. 27 “weeks ago.”
Iowa Field Report, a conservative-aligned news organization, published an audio recording of staff members for the two campaigns on a call with KCCI staff, who failed to reach an agreement on when to debate. In the call, Nunn’s campaign advocated for debating on dates before or shortly after the start of early voting in Iowa on Oct. 14. Trone Garriott’s campaign pushed for dates in late October because of scheduling conflicts in early and mid-October.
In a news release Thursday, Trone Garriott’s staff wrote, “it’s clear that Nunn was lying about his availability during negotiations and playing political games in an attempt to distract from his flailing campaign.” Nunn’s campaign has argued they accepted every debate date offered before or during the first week of early voting, and said in a news release the 3rd District debate will be “the latest first debate of any race for governor, U.S. Senate or Congress in Iowa this cycle,” at a point after many Iowans have already voted.
