Duane Roger Wohlbrandt
Goodbye for Now
Duane Roger Wohlbrandt, a lifelong resident of Buffalo, Wyoming, passed away on October 2, 2026, at the age of 68. He was born on June 2, 1958, in Mammoth Hot Springs, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, to Leroy “Wally” and Shirley Kumor Wohlbrandt.
Duane faced challenges throughout his life that might have defeated many people, but he met them with incredible courage and quiet perseverance. When he fell or was knocked down, he got up again—and again—without complaint or self-pity. He wanted to do things that might have seemed out of reach, and he did not give up. His own struggles gave him great empathy for others facing difficulties. He loved children and was kind and patient with animals.
Duane attended school in Buffalo, graduating from Buffalo High School with the class of 1977. He was a member of the school’s FFA chapter and showed a steer from the family ranch at the Johnson County Fair. He also competed with other projects, one of which went on to the State Fair.
In his teenage years, Duane, a leftie, loved practicing his baseball pitching. He rode his gasoline-powered minibike with joy and abandon and enjoyed working in the ranch shop, welding and helping repair equipment. He was always game for gathering and splitting firewood and enjoyed target shooting with both pistol and rifle.
After high school, Duane attended vocational school in Cheyenne. He held various jobs around Buffalo and worked on the family ranch. He had a talent for small-engine repair and operated his own lawnmower repair business.
Duane loved hunting and fishing in the Bighorn Mountains and visiting Yellowstone National Park with his family. He enjoyed family gatherings and the feasts and festivities that came with those good times. Comedy movies and television delighted him, and he had a quick sense of humor and a joyous laugh.
The greatest strength in Duane’s life came through his genuine faith in Jesus. He enjoyed volunteering at Bighorn Baptist Church. His greatest joy and blessing on Earth was his beloved wife, Barb, who brought him true happiness and endless love and meant all the world to him. God truly brought them together. Duane and Barb were married on January 4, 2004, in Buffalo, Wyoming.
On November 8, 2013, Duane was admitted to Amie Holt Care Center where he lived for the remainder of his life.
Duane was preceded in death by his parents; his maternal grandparents, John and Amy Kumor; his paternal grandparents, Philip Henry and Irma Wohlbrandt; many aunts and uncles; and several cousins on both sides of the family.
He is survived by his wife, Barb; his brothers, John (Chris) and Phil (Tani); his sister, Lorena; and four nieces and their spouses and children.
Visitation will be held on Thursday, October 8, 2026, from 1 to 9 p.m. at Harness Funeral Home. A service will take place on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 10 a.m. followed by a graveside service at Willow Grove Cemetery, where Duane will be laid to rest in the family plot. A meal will follow at Calvary Chapel. Mike Leibee of Calvary Chapel will lead the service.
Memorial contributions may be made to Calvary Chapel in remembrance of Duane, a kind and courageous man whose faith, laughter, and love will remain with the family he leaves behind for a while.
Goodbye for now, Duane.

Farren Jame Zabriskie, known to everyone simply as F’kin Farren, passed away on October 5, 2026, in Buffalo, Wyoming, one day shy of his 79th birthday, after health-related complications. He was born on October 6, 1947, in Berkeley, California, and spent a life that was equal parts hard work, good humor, and the kind of stubborn decency that makes a person unforgettable. He was a Christian, a proud veteran, a devoted family man, and a man who seemed to understand that if life was going to be complicated, it might as well be handled with a grin and a strong cup of coffee.
Farren grew up with a work ethic that could outlast a Wyoming winter and a practical streak that made him useful in just about any situation. He graduated from Hillcrest High School in Midvale, Utah, and later earned an Associate of Adolescent Psychology from Central Wyoming College. That combination of education and common sense suited him well, because Farren had a way of understanding people that did not require a degree, although he had one anyway. He spent his life learning, observing, and figuring out how to get things done, which was handy considering he never seemed to meet a job he could not improve with grit, patience, and a little bit of sarcasm.
His work history read like the greatest hits of American labor. Farren worked as a carpenter, in concrete, in coal mines, in construction, at the Wyoming State Training School in Lander, Wyoming, and in various odd jobs that probably could have filled an entire second obituary by themselves. He was also a Union Ironworker with Local 229 and Local 27, and he took that role seriously. He knew what it meant to show up, to sweat, to build, and to keep going when the day got long. If there was a heavy object that needed moving or a problem that needed solving, Farren was the kind of man you wanted nearby, preferably before the situation got worse.
He served his country honorably in the United States Marine Corps during the Vietnam era from 1966 to 1969, including AutoMech-CamPen-6weeks, and he carried those years with the quiet pride of someone who had done his duty and then some. His military honors included the National Defense Service Medal, the Vietnam Campaign Medal with device, the Vietnam Service Medal with 6, the Republic of Vietnam Cross of Gallantry with Palm, the Good Conduct Medal, 1st Award, and the Presidential Unit Citation. Those medals told part of the story, but anyone who knew Farren would say his real decoration was the way he lived afterward, with loyalty, resilience, and an ability to keep his sense of humor even when life was clearly trying to be difficult.
Farren was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Angie Rosalez Zabriskie, and he carried her memory with him always. He is survived by his brothers, Lee (Linda) Zabriskie, Paul (Wendy) Zabriskie, and Carl Zabriskie; his sons, Chance (Teri Ann) Zabriskie, Dylan Zabriskie, and Waylon (Alli) Zabriskie; his sons by marriage, Paul Luthi and Tyson Mcdougall; his daughters by marriage, Lindsay Avila and Shannon Nesheim; 12 grandchildren; and 14 great-grandchildren. His family was a source of pride and joy to him, and he loved them in the straightforward, no-nonsense way that meant he showed up, helped out, and made sure everyone knew where they stood. He was loving, selfless, and generous, which is a fine way to be remembered and, frankly, a rare enough combination to deserve its own medal.
Farren also knew how to enjoy life, which he did without apology. He loved his local watering hole, the Century Club, where the atmosphere undoubtedly benefited from his presence and where he probably left more memorable stories than anyone could reasonably count. He took pride in helping others who needed help unconditionally, which was one of those traits that made people trust him immediately. He loved the wind blowing through his hair on his motorcycle, and he had a special appreciation for his Harley Davidsons and old hot rod vehicles, because subtlety was never the point and neither was Farren. He enjoyed listening to music of all kinds and singing along, whether the song needed help or not. He also took great joy in the outdoors, whether he was fishing, camping with family and friends, or watching the sun rise and set as if he had someplace important to be, which he usually did not. He loved to sightsee and travel, and one suspects he did so with the confidence of a man who believed every road had a story and most of them were worth hearing twice.
In the spirit of Farren’s humor and larger-than-life personality, one fitting line comes from the beloved comedian George Carlin, who said, “Don’t sweat the petty things and don’t pet the sweaty things.” Farren would have appreciated that kind of wisdom, because he understood that life was serious enough on its own and did not need any extra nonsense added for free. He had a comedian’s timing without trying to be one, and a straight man’s delivery that made his dry wit even funnier. He could make people laugh simply by telling the truth in a way that was too honest to ignore and too funny to forget.
Farren’s life was built on service, work, loyalty, and love. He leaves behind a legacy that is as solid as the things he built and as warm as the stories he told. He will be remembered for his big heart, his steady hands, his generous spirit, and his ability to find the good in people, even when they had not fully earned it yet. He was the sort of man who made a place better just by being in it, and now that he has gone, the world feels a little quieter, a little rougher around the edges, and a lot less interesting.

Norma was born on September 7, 1935, in St. Louis, Michigan, to Clarence and Clara (Meyer) Feltman. On July 4, 1953, at seventeen, she married FD Allen. A meal will follow at Calvary Chapel. Mike Leibee of Calvary Chapel will lead the service.
Memorial contributions may be made to Calvary Chapel in remembrance of Duane, a kind and courageous man whose faith, laughter, and love will remain with the family he leaves behind for a while.
Goodbye for now, Duane.



Alice WoodwardSeptember 22, 1949 – October 14, 2026Cody, WyomingShared by: Ballard Funeral HomeAlice Woodward, 77, of Cody WY passed away at Casper Mountain Rehab Center on Wednesday, October 14 2026. A full obituary will follow.







Farren James Zabriskie06 Oct 1947 – 05 Oct 2026Buffalo, WyomingShared by: Harness Funeral HomeFuneral services for Farren James Zabriskie, a 78-year-old Buffalo resident who passed away on Monday, October 5, 2026, will be held Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. at the Harness Funeral Home Chapel in Buffalo. Family and friends are invited to gather in remembrance of Farren’s life and share in the comfort of being together. Interment will take place at a later date at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia.
Memorial donations in Farren’s memory may be made to the Tunnel to Towers Foundation at www.T2T.org. Online condolences may be shared at www.harnessfuneralhome.com.
Farren Jame Zabriskie, known to everyone simply as F’kin Farren, passed away on October 5, 2026, in Buffalo, Wyoming, one day shy of his 79th birthday, after health-related complications. He was born on October 6, 1947, in Berkeley, California, and spent a life that was equal parts hard work, good humor, and the kind of stubborn decency that makes a person unforgettable. He was a Christian, a proud veteran, a devoted family man, and a man who seemed to understand that if life was going to be complicated, it might as well be handled with a grin and a strong cup of coffee.
Farren grew up with a work ethic that could outlast a Wyoming winter and a practical streak that made him useful in just about any situation. He graduated from Hillcrest High School in Midvale, Utah, and later earned an Associate of Adolescent Psychology from Central Wyoming College. That combination of education and common sense suited him well, because Farren had a way of understanding people that did not require a degree, although he had one anyway. He spent his life learning, observing, and figuring out how to get things done, which was handy considering he never seemed to meet a job he could not improve with grit, patience, and a little bit of sarcasm.
His work history read like the greatest hits of American labor. Farren worked as a carpenter, in concrete, in coal mines, in construction, at the Wyoming State Training School in Lander, Wyoming, and in various odd jobs that probably could have filled an entire second obituary by themselves. He was also a Union Ironworker with Local 229 and Local 27, and he took that role seriously. He knew what it meant to show up, to sweat, to build, and to keep going when the day got long. If there was a heavy object that needed moving or a problem that needed solving, Farren was the kind of man you wanted nearby, preferably before the situation got worse.
He served his country honorably in the United States Marine Corps during the Vietnam era from 1966 to 1969, including AutoMech-CamPen-6weeks, and he carried those years with the quiet pride of someone who had done his duty and then some. His military honors included the National Defense Service Medal, the Vietnam Campaign Medal with device, the Vietnam Service Medal with 6, the Republic of Vietnam Cross of Gallantry with Palm, the Good Conduct Medal, 1st Award, and the Presidential Unit Citation. Those medals told part of the story, but anyone who knew Farren would say his real decoration was the way he lived afterward, with loyalty, resilience, and an ability to keep his sense of humor even when life was clearly trying to be difficult.
Farren was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Angie Rosalez Zabriskie, and he carried her memory with him always. He is survived by his brothers, Lee (Linda) Zabriskie, Paul (Wendy) Zabriskie, and Carl Zabriskie; his sons, Chance (Teri Ann) Zabriskie, Dylan Zabriskie, and Waylon (Alli) Zabriskie; his sons by marriage, Paul Luthi and Tyson Mcdougall; his daughters by marriage, Lindsay Avila and Shannon Nesheim; 12 grandchildren; and 14 great-grandchildren. His family was a source of pride and joy to him, and he loved them in the straightforward, no-nonsense way that meant he showed up, helped out, and made sure everyone knew where they stood. He was loving, selfless, and generous, which is a fine way to be remembered and, frankly, a rare enough combination to deserve its own medal.
Farren also knew how to enjoy life, which he did without apology. He loved his local watering hole, the Century Club, where the atmosphere undoubtedly benefited from his presence and where he probably left more memorable stories than anyone could reasonably count. He took pride in helping others who needed help unconditionally, which was one of those traits that made people trust him immediately. He loved the wind blowing through his hair on his motorcycle, and he had a special appreciation for his Harley Davidsons and old hot rod vehicles, because subtlety was never the point and neither was Farren. He enjoyed listening to music of all kinds and singing along, whether the song needed help or not. He also took great joy in the outdoors, whether he was fishing, camping with family and friends, or watching the sun rise and set as if he had someplace important to be, which he usually did not. He loved to sightsee and travel, and one suspects he did so with the confidence of a man who believed every road had a story and most of them were worth hearing twice.
In the spirit of Farren’s humor and larger-than-life personality, one fitting line comes from the beloved comedian George Carlin, who said, “Don’t sweat the petty things and don’t pet the sweaty things.” Farren would have appreciated that kind of wisdom, because he understood that life was serious enough on its own and did not need any extra nonsense added for free. He had a comedian’s timing without trying to be one, and a straight man’s delivery that made his dry wit even funnier. He could make people laugh simply by telling the truth in a way that was too honest to ignore and too funny to forget.
Farren’s life was built on service, work, loyalty, and love. He leaves behind a legacy that is as solid as the things he built and as warm as the stories he told. He will be remembered for his big heart, his steady hands, his generous spirit, and his ability to find the good in people, even when they had not fully earned it yet. He was the sort of man who made a place better just by being in it, and now that he has gone, the world feels a little quieter, a little rougher around the edges, and a lot less interesting.








Judy E. ZwiegAugust 9, 1947 – October 12, 2026Laramie, WyomingShared by: Montgomery-Stryker Funeral HomeJudy E. Zwieg, 79, of Laramie, passed away October 12th at Ivinson Memorial Hospital.
She was born on August 9, 1947, to Phyllis and Marion Towns.  She was raised on her family’s farm in Hillsdale and graduated from Hillsdale High School in 1965. 
After graduation, she married William K. Zwieg on February 20, 1966.  Their story began in Cheyenne, Wyoming.  Judy and Bill had two kids: William Glen Zwieg, born in 1967, and Brenda (Zwieg) Benson, born 1969.  They later moved to Hanna, Wyoming, where her husband worked in the mines until 1984.  They then moved to Laramie.
She worked a number of different positions during her time in Laramie, including Godfather’s Pizza, Advanced Auto Parts, Laramie Ford, and finally the University of Wyoming as an Office Associate Senior, where she retired.
 She enjoyed sewing, crafting, making floral arrangements, and cake decorating.  Later on, she was an active volunteer for the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation.  She enjoyed attending Wyoming Cowgirls basketball games and spending time with her family.
Cremation has taken place, and a graveside service will be held in Wheatland, Wyoming, at a later date.
Judy is preceded in death by her husband, her parents, and her daughter, Brenda. 
She is survived by her son and daughter-in-law, William and Mindy Zwieg; her brother, Don Towns; her grandsons and granddaughters-in-law, Drew and Rebecca Zwieg and Forrest and Krista Zwieg; her granddaughters and grandson-in-law, Ashley and Brendon Ayers and Shanda Benson; her aunt Nancy Lloyd; and numerous great-grandchildren.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Lieutenant governor’s race heats up as candidates spar over public safety, healthcare, Trump
text:
Candidates for lieutenant governor, Greg Dolezal (left) and Josh McLaurin, participate in the Atlanta Press Club debate at Georgia Public Broadcasting’s studios. Pool photo via J Glenn PhotographyWith early voting already underway across the state, the race to be Georgia’s next lieutenant governor is becoming increasingly contentious as the two candidates strive to appeal to undecided voters — and explain why their opponent is the wrong choice.
Both men are members of the state Senate with reputations for being outspoken and unafraid to advocate for their beliefs on the Senate floor. But that’s where the similarities end. 
Georgia voters kick off early voting with nearly 189,000 ballots cast

The Democratic candidate, Sen. Josh McLaurin of Sandy Springs, is running as a consensus candidate, and has touted his ability to work alongside Republicans in the state Legislature even he advocates for policies like expanding Medicaid, repealing the state’s six-week abortion ban and raising the state’s minimum wage.
The Republican, Sen. Greg Dolezal of Cumming, has centered his campaign around more traditional conservative goals like cutting state income and property taxes and expanding Georgia’s school voucher program. He has also incorporated culture war issues into his campaign, such as pledging to oppose sharia law, religious rules for how Muslims live and worship. (The Congressional Research Service reported back in 2012 that “religious laws have no legally binding effect on U.S. citizens because religious laws cannot be adopted by federal, state or local governments under the First Amendment.”) 
During a pair of debates this week hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and 11Alive, the two candidates sharpened their attacks and spent much of their time pushing each other to defend their political records.
Sen. Greg Dolezal, a Cumming Republican and 2026 candidate for Georgia lieutenant governor speaks at a Trump rally near Marietta. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
In both instances, Dolezal sought to cast McLaurin as being out of step with members of the Democratic party on issues like public safety and criminal justice reform.
“I respect that he firmly believes what he believes, but what he believes belongs in California,” Dolezal said. “It doesn’t belong here in Georgia.”
McLaurin, in turn, has repeatedly questioned Dolezal about his ties to President Donald Trump, accusing him of revamping his website after the primary runoff election to make references to Trump less prominent. He also criticized an AI-generated ad Dolezal published during the Republican primary that depicted Muslims terrorizing white Georgia residents, characterizing him as “the Mike Collins of this race.”
“He may be a state-level politician, but he is bringing MAGA and Trumpism to Georgia,” McLaurin said.
On healthcare, the two candidates again took opposing positions. McLaurin pledged to fully expand Medicaid, arguing that Georgia’s current policies leave too many people uninsured and struggling with healthcare costs.
“There are hundreds of thousands of people in Georgia who do not have coverage and have to make decisions about fixing a car [or] getting something checked out at the doctor,” he said, adding that rural Georgia has been hit particularly hard by declining healthcare coverage rates. He also criticized Gov. Brian Kemp’s signature Pathways to Coverage program, arguing that it “gave more money to Deloitte consultants than it did for care.”
Rick Jackson pledges ‘intelligent’ Medicaid expansion, but offers few specifics

Dolezal, on the other hand, said he backs an “intelligent” Medicaid expansion plan introduced by Republican nominee for governor Rick Jackson, arguing that fully expanding Medicaid would result in some Georgians being forced off their private insurance and onto a state-run insurance plan.
“What we do not need to do is move people from private plans that they have through their employer or through the exchange onto the government plan,” he said.
Dolezal also criticized McLaurin’s record on public safety as being “soft on crime,” questioning his opposition to a 2020 proposal that would have required registered sex offenders to post warning signs on their house during Halloween.
“Josh McLaurin, alongside Keisha Lance Bottoms, when it comes to public safety, will be like pouring gasoline on a Wendy’s fire,” Dolezal said, referencing a period of unrest in Atlanta during 2020.
State Sen. Josh McLaurin. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
McLaurin pushed back, arguing that he declined to support the measure because it would have violated the Constitution and likely lead to costly litigation.
“We know when federal courts have already ruled against some of these laws, and we know when we’re walking into lawsuits where we’re going to have to spend taxpayer money,” he said. “At the end of the day, taxpayers have to pay the bill when we do unconstitutional things.”
McLaurin added that he supported what he calls common sense criminal justice reforms like those implemented by former Gov. Nathan Deal, a Republican.
“I’m in line with the moderate Republican take on criminal legal reform, which is it needs to be smart, it needs to be thoughtful, it needs to actually protect us, invest in public safety, invest in police officers and their pensions, but not engage in this crazy politics that’s just fearmongering,” he said.
While the national political landscape appears to be tilting towards Democrats, Georgia’s statewide races remain more difficult to gauge, experts say. Recent polls show Jackson with a slight edge over Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms. 
No major polls have been conducted for the lieutenant governor’s race, but Emory University political science professor Andra Gillespie said that unlike the top of the ticket, where independent or split-ticket voters may be the deciding factor in the race, the success of down-ballot candidates will likely depend on which party can more successfully motivate their voters to turn out and vote all the way down the ticket.
Early voting is underway in Georgia. Here’s where you can cast a ballot in your county.

“I don’t expect that split-ticket voting is going to be so much the factor in [the lieutenant governor’s] race so much as it is attrition,” she said. Although Republican voters still outnumber Democrats across the state, Democrats may have the advantage this year when it comes to voter enthusiasm, Gillespie added.
“I think the closeness of those contests is going to reveal how well Democrats, in particular, were at being able to mobilize voters to participate in all of the elections and not just the top two,” she said.
Early voting for the midterm elections in Georgia has already begun, and runs until Oct. 30. Voters can locate their polling place at the secretary of state’s My Voter Page or by using the Georgia Recorder’s early voting map.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Ex-Biden appointee faces attorney general in US House race with differences on tariffs, immigration
text:
Democratic U.S. House of Representatives candidate Nikki Gronli, left, and Republican candidate Marty Jackley participate in a debate at the Sioux Falls studios of South Dakota Public Broadcasting on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Nikki Gronli would love to have her old job back.
During a debate earlier this month with Attorney General Marty Jackley, her Republican opponent in the race for the state’s lone seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, the Democratic former South Dakota director of rural development for the U.S. Department of Agriculture said she’d have “happily” continued doing that job under Republican President Donald Trump.
“It was the best job I ever had,” Gronli told South Dakota Searchlight the following week.
She was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden, and lost her job early on in Trump’s second term, as did some of her staff amid Trump’s widespread reduction of the federal workforce.
“In South Dakota, a quarter of my staff lost their jobs,” said Gronli, who’d supervised 38 staff members at USDA after spending most of her career in marketing.

 Hear Democratic U.S. House nominee Nikki Gronli’s views on immigration, artificial intelligence, social media, agriculture and more in this episode of the Searchlight Report podcast.


It wasn’t long before Gronli was traveling the state, talking to people at town halls about the impact those federal job cuts were having and could have in the future for South Dakota. By the end of 2025, the Aurora native and Dell Rapids resident — who’d been vice-chairwoman of the South Dakota Democratic Party prior to her Biden administration appointment — was a candidate for the seat Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson was vacating for what would ultimately be a failed attempt to secure his party’s nomination for governor.
The election for the open U.S. House seat is Nov. 3, advance voting is underway, and the voter registration deadline is Monday.
As with her past roles as a hockey parent-advocate for the construction of the Scheels IcePlex in Sioux Falls, a member of the Siouxland Historical Society Board and member of the Minnehaha County Housing and Redevelopment Commission, Gronli said running for office is about “stepping up where I was needed.”
Jackley: From private sector to public service and back again
Jackley’s path to a congressional run was also paved in part by a political appointment.
The Sturgis-born lawyer, who also has a degree in electrical engineering and has a farm in Butte County and a ranch near Pierre, served as South Dakota’s U.S. attorney under Republican President George W. Bush. It was his first full-time public service job, taken after working part-time prosecuting drug cases for former South Dakota Attorney General Larry Long.
“That appointment was a career shift for me,” Jackley told South Dakota Searchlight.

 Hear Republican U.S. House nominee Marty Jackley’s views on immigration, artificial intelligence, social media, agriculture and more in this episode of the Searchlight Report podcast.

When President Barack Obama took office, Jackley was replaced as U.S. attorney. A year later, Long became a circuit judge in Minnehaha County. Jackley was appointed to replace him as South Dakota attorney general. Jackley’s father, Mike, the longtime Meade County state’s attorney and unsuccessful 1986 candidate for attorney general, swore him in.
His dad never ran again for statewide office, but was elected multiple times to the county post. There’s more money for lawyers in the private sector, but “our family’s always believed in public service,” Jackley said.
He was elected as attorney general in 2010 and reelected in 2014.
He stepped away from public life in 2019 after losing the Republican primary race for governor to Kristi Noem, and went to work at the same Rapid City law firm he’d started at in the late 1990s.
He returned to the attorney general job in 2022 after running unopposed.
Jackley was elected president of the National Association of Attorneys General from 2015 to 2016, and was chosen as president-elect in December of 2025. As a part of that group, he worked with his Democratic and Republican counterparts on multi-state law enforcement initiatives, including as one of the lead plaintiffs in a recent multi-state lawsuit in California that led to a settlement with Meta, the parent company of Facebook, over its products’ alleged damage to children’s mental health.
“I look at this as that opportunity to use what I’ve learned as attorney general, the relationships I’ve developed with Republicans and Democrats, to go to Washington and address the important issues for South Dakota,” Jackley said.
Challenges for both candidates
Mike Card, a retired political science professor for the University of South Dakota, said Gronli’s party is her biggest challenge in the race. Registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats in South Dakota, but Democrat registrations also run behind the combined number of people registered as independent or with no party affiliation.
To become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. House from South Dakota since 2008, Card said, Gronli “has to find a way to take positions that stand out from her opponent and resonate with voters.”
“It does seem that she’s got to find a way to give voice to her perspective, being different and better than what Marty Jackley has for issue positions,” Card said.
Jackley has name recognition and the advantage of being the Republican in the race, Card said, but the professor also sees the attorney general as a lackluster political communicator, perhaps a reflection of Jackley’s engineering background and years spent in the weeds of lawyerly rhetoric.
“He’s certainly got the credentials. He’s got lots of evidence he could be using. He just doesn’t seem to be using it to his advantage,” Card said.
Tariff issue divides, but both candidates say Congress should be involved
Gronli said during an Oct. 1 debate that Trump’s “blanket tariffs” and tariff threats have hit South Dakotans in the pocketbook, contributing to high prices for goods and services. Tariffs are taxes paid by those who import goods from other countries.
Outside the debate, Gronli has said the tariffs cost South Dakotans $1,300 a year, citing a figure from the nonprofit Tax Foundation used in a February Newsweek article.
Gronli didn’t use the $1,300 figure in the debate, but Jackley brought it up.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
After the U.S. Supreme Court struck down some of Trump’s tariffs, the foundation’s current figure for how much more the average household will pay because of tariffs is $820. Jackley said that $820 was “still too high” a burden on South Dakota families, but said the number is coming down. He later told South Dakota Searchlight that his opponent was either using the larger, earlier estimate for political effect or that “she doesn’t understand the issue.”
He also criticized Gronli’s use of the term “blanket tariffs”
“We don’t have blanket tariffs,” that cover all goods from all countries, Jackley said in a follow-up interview with Searchlight, “so she’s wrong on that.”
“We have had an impact in South Dakota, but she inflated it,” Jackley said, referencing the $1,300 figure from February, “which is wrong.”
Free trade deals with targeted tariffs, ideally built with input from Congress, could ultimately benefit the U.S. economy, Jackley told Searchlight.
“My position has always been that it has to be targeted,” said Jackley.
Gronli said Jackley used the $820 figure as a “gotcha,” but “$820 is too much for families to take on when grocery prices are high, gas is high, and everybody’s concerned.”
Gronli said Congress needs to be a check on the president on trade.
“We should have trade experts that are negotiating in good faith, getting us good deals, but also considering our American economy has a lot of reliance on those neighbors,” she said.
Immigration differences
During the debate and in a later interview with Searchlight, Jackley said Gronli “wants to get rid of” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“I’m a former U.S. attorney and an attorney general, and the relationship we have with ICE is essential,” said Jackley, citing the immigration agency’s contributions to the state’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force.
Jackley pointed to the state Division of Criminal Investigation’s enforcement agreement with ICE, which allows agents to question people about their immigration status and detain them for the federal agency. Jackley said he’s limited that authority to cases involving violent crime, and said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement actions and moves to secure the border between the U.S. and Mexico have improved public safety.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Border security is important, Gronli said, but she sees the administration’s deportation efforts as counterproductive to discussions on comprehensive immigration reform.
“I want Congress to take up looking at the visa programs that we have for workers, because going out and talking to those in poultry and egg-laying operations and dairies, those visas are not working for them,” Gronli said. “They can’t fill roles without having immigrant labor.”
Gronli said she doesn’t support ICE’s immigration enforcement efforts in South Dakota, but she’s not interested in dismantling the agency or ending its partnerships on crimes against children.
She wants “new leadership” and “a well-run department,” as well as a shift in priorities for federal spending away from deportations. ICE is targeting too many immigrants who don’t have a violent criminal record, she said, and its tactics have been too aggressive.
“We’ve spent just an exorbitant amount of money on that department, and it has shifted away from the American people,” Gronli said. “I feel like we have a misalignment with the way we’re using our dollars, and it’s been shifted towards an organization that’s brutalizing and has even killed American citizens.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Civil rights leader William Barber stops at NCCU to encourage early voters
text:
Marchers arrive at NC Central University's School of Law on the first day of early voting.  (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)Civil rights leader and Repairers of the Breach President Bishop William Barber led multiple marches to the polls across North Carolina on Thursday to mark the first day of early voting, which ends Oct. 31 at 3 p.m.
At North Carolina Central University (NCCU) in Durham, Barber said the march was meant to inspire students and other voters and to remind them that the right to vote was not won by “staying quiet.”
Bishop William Barber was in Durham to talk to college students on the first day of early voting at N.C. Central University. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
“We marched for it. We fought for it, mobilized,” Barber said in an interview with reporters in front of the NCCU Law School where early voting was taking place.
In North Carolina, voters fought to hold on to same day voter registration and early voting, Barber said.
“Now that we’ve held onto the power, it’s no good if we don’t use it,” Barber said. “One of our mantras is, it’s time to get our power out of our pocket. Don’t hold on to it. Get it out of your pocket.”
Barber’s appearance in Durham was part of his national Love Forward Together voter mobilization initiative that’s designed to mobilize five million low-wage infrequent voters, particularly in the South and battleground states. He held a press conference in Raleigh before traveling to Durham. Stops in Wilson, Charlotte, Greenville and Winston Salem were also planned for Thursday. 
The campaign has organized 652 marches in 428 locations across the United States, according to Repairers of the Breach. It is expected to hold 1,000 such marches before the Nov. 3 election.
Barber arrived at NCCU ahead of dozens of marchers who rallied at St. Joseph AME Church. The marchers carried signs and chanted before gathering in front of the law school where Barber spoke with some of them individually but did not give a speech.  
Political candidates must tell voters what they are for and not just what they’re against, Barber said to reporters.
“Don’t just name the problem,” Barber said. “What are you for?” If people don’t have healthcare in the wealthiest country in the world, what are you for?”
Barber said “everything is on the ballot” including healthcare, fair funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities and whether the parents of NCCU students and others will earn a living wage.
“Politicians who get elected determine all of those matters,” Barber said. “Politics is not benign. It affects your life. Your vote is not benign, because it determines who gets to affect your life.”
Barber noted that 90 million people didn’t vote in the 2024 presidential election, including five million African Americans.   
“You cannot have a democracy unless you have participation,” he said. 
Alana Byrd (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Alana Byrd, a third year law student at NCCU, was on her way to class and to vote. Byrd said students must bring the same energy to voting that they brought to celebrate last week’s homecoming.
“We need all those people who were out here celebrating to come out and vote,” Byrd said. “If you come out and have a good time, you can come out and make a difference. Your voice matters now more than ever.”
Byrd said she is concerned about the economy and the current leadership in Washington.
“Everything is at stake,” Byrd said.
Ashley Marshall (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Ashley Marshall, co-founder of Forward Justice, a Durham-based organization that focuses on racial, social and economic justice, said it’s important for voters to push back against efforts to roll back voting rights by showing up at the polls.
Marshall said presidential elections get most of the attention, but the midterms and local elections often impact voters more. She said it’s important that people understand their right to vote and advocate for that right.
“These elections can completely change the tide and people’s living experiences and what they feel at the bottom line in their pockets,” Marshall said. “So, it’s really, really important for folks to turn out in the local elections and midterms just as they would in the presidential election.”
Raymond Smith said he hasn’t missed an opportunity to vote since 1969 out of respect for the people who “bled and died” for Black people’s right to vote.
“It’s important,” Smith said. “I have two kids. I make sure they go vote and my grandson [votes]. It makes a difference in your life. It may not make a difference today but it could tomorrow.”
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) made an appearance at the Durham County Library on Thursday as part of a “barnstorming” tour across the South to rally voters.
“The path to a Senate majority runs right through the South,” Warnock said. “I’m the embodiment of that. I don’t think people saw Georgia coming a few years ago.”
In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, is facing Republican Michael Whatley in a Senate race that could help change the balance of power in the Senate.
Warnock said stopping the bleeding will be the first order of business if Democrats gain control of the House and Senate.  
“People are being crushed by these prices, which are connected directly to these tariff taxes that Donald Trump has placed on everything.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: The Blueprint board makes legislative recommendation, more could be coming
text:
Joy Schaefer, government relations director for the Accountability and Implementation Board sitting at table, summarizes a legislative recommendation Thursday during a Blueprint for Maryland's Future AIB meeting. It was the first in-person meeting held inside the board's new office in downtown Annapolis. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The board overseeing the state’s Blueprint education reform plan wants to pause expert review teams visiting schools through fiscal year 2029, and instead allocate funding toward coaching teachers.
That decision was the only recommendation that came out of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board meeting Thursday. It was the seven-member board’s first in-person meeting in their new 3,000-square-foot office in downtown Annapolis. Only board vice chair William “Brit” Kirwan participated virtually because he was at a conference in Ocean City.
The visits are mainly done to observe math and literacy practices as implementation of the Blueprint plan is halfway through. They were already paused this fiscal year, but were scheduled to resume in fiscal 2028 based on a legislative proposal from the state Department of Education. Although review teams visited nearly 300 schools since the 2021-22 school year, “the snapshot visits only allow for a limited understanding of the school’s strengths and areas needing additional support and have had a limited impact on improving student outcomes,” according to the department.
Joy Schaefer, who handles government relations for the board, said work would be done to assess and redesign the expert review team program. It would resume in fiscal year 2030 which includes funding for it.
The board also said the legislature should allocate fund the existing statewide teacher development program.
The General Assembly approved $14.2 million during this year’s 90-day legislative session toward the program to hire more than five dozen literacy and math teachers for this school year.
Although there’s support for the training, a few board members asked why not keep both programs running.
“I recognize that this is a better spend of the money. I’m always for instructional coaching,” said board member Justin Robinson, a middle school math teacher in Prince George’s County. “But I think the ERT (expert review team) program also provides a school level lens, and I think that’s missing often — the opportunity for schools to learn from each other, the opportunity for us to learn from those schools that are doing things well, and schools that might need to partner with schools with a similar demographic.”
Board chair Isiah “Ike” Leggett said the pause would allow for additional time to assess how to make the expert review team program better.
Last month, the board reviewed 15-pages of legislative recommendations that included funding for more college and career readiness classes; conducting a study to assess how much to increase the base level of per pupil funding; and easing certification requirements for private providers who employ educators who teach prekindergarten students.
Any legislative changes must receive approval by the General Assembly when it convenes for the 2027 session that begins Jan. 13.
But how extensively any changes would be made remain unknown as the state faces a projected $3 billion budget gap for the upcoming fiscal year, about $1.8 billion of which is tied to education under the Blueprint, according to the Maryland Associations of Counties (MACo).
The projected budget shortfall for fiscal 2028 also comes in the first year in which Blueprint costs will exceed dedicated revenues.
Leggett said Thursday the board may present more legislative recommendations based on at least three reports due later this year: special education funding study from the Department of Education by Dec. 15; increasing teacher diversity from the Accountability and Implementation Board  by Dec. 31; and another report due by that same day on compensatory education from both the department and the board.
The board’s next meeting is scheduled for Nov. 19, but this time strictly virtual.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi college board approves contracts, potential million-dollar payments for Ole Miss and MSU leaders
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
University of Mississippi Chancellor Glenn Boyce and Mississippi State University President Mark Keenum will continue leading the state’s largest public institutions for another four years under new contracts approved by the state’s college board. 
The Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning Board of Trustees in September unanimously approved Boyce’s and Keenum’s annual salaries, including potential retention payments exceeding $1 million each. 
The contracts keep Boyce and Keenum as Mississippi’s highest-paid public university leaders. 
Both contracts took effect Oct. 1 and end Sept. 30, 2030. Trustees did not publicly discuss the matter. 
Both leaders previously earned $950,000 a year, with taxpayers supporting $500,000 of their salaries and their respective university’s foundations making up the rest. 
Under their new contracts, Boyce and Keenum will each earn $1,012,500 million in the first year, including $562,500 in state-funded salaries and $450,000 from their university foundations. Their annual compensation will slightly decrease to $1 million for each of the remaining three years, with a state-funded salary of $550,000 annually. 
Both presidents are eligible for additional retention payments if they remain in their jobs through June 2027 and June 2023. Boyce could receive up to $1.15 million in retention payments over four years, while Keenum could receive up to $1.35 million. The university foundations will determine the payment amounts. 
IHL Board President Steve Cunningham said Thursday that the raises reflected Boyce’s and Keenum’s job performance and their universities’ growth in recent years. Trustees considered several factors when evaluating the presidents, including enrollment, university rankings and research grants, he said. 
Trustees also wanted to keep both presidents in their roles, Cunningham said. Their university foundations agreed to fund the potential retention payments because state funding for salaries is limited. 
“It’s just great to have leaders that are still willing to serve because the average time span for (university presidents) is maybe four or five years,” Cunningham said. “Both leaders have exceeded that average time span.” 
Keenum declined to comment. Boyce said that he appreciates the board’s confidence in his university leadership and the direction that Ole Miss is heading. 
IHL policy requires trustees to review university presidents’ pay annually, considering state funding, university resources and contributions from university foundations and alumni associations. The board also reviews regional and national information about executives’ compensation when determining salary decisions. 
By comparison, University of Southern Mississippi President Joe Paul earns $700,000 annually, while Jackson State University President Denise Jones Gregory earns $465,000, according to the college board’s May meeting minutes. 
Delta State University President Dan Ennis earns $355,000, and Mississippi Valley State University President Jerryl Briggs earns $315,000. 
Alcorn State University President Tracy Cook earns $305,000, and Mississippi University for Women interim president, Scott Tollison earns $300,000 annually. 
Keenum has served as Mississippi State’s president since January 2009, while Boyce has led Ole Miss since 2019. Both institutions have experienced record enrollment growth under their tenures. 
The board also approved changes to National Collegiate Athletic Association compliance provisions in university presidents’ contracts, requiring them to cooperate with investigations and disciplinary proceedings. Executives found to have violated NCAA regulations could face disciplinary action, including suspension without pay or termination.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Drummond drops lawsuit over Jewish charter school vote
text:
Attorney General Gentner Drummond speaks at a press conference Feb. 25, 2025, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Attorney General Gentner Drummond has dropped a lawsuit against a state board after it rejected a proposed Jewish charter school for the second time.
Drummond dismissed his case Thursday in Oklahoma County District Court without prejudice, meaning it could be filed again.
The lawsuit accused the Statewide Charter School Board of deliberately rigging its March 9 vote to reject the Jewish charter school solely because of its religious character. 
Drummond alleged there were other material reasons besides the religious element to deny the school, like a lack of community support and wild swings in projected enrollment, but the board intentionally left those issues out of its vote, which strengthened the school’s case in court.
Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School proposed an online, faith-based education that would teach both Judaism and secular subjects. 
The board’s legal counsel has received Drummond’s dismissal letter and has begun to read it, said A.J. Ferate, an attorney representing the board.
“Given that the board is trying to determine its next steps, (it) will decline to comment at this time,” he said.
The board on Monday voted again on Ben Gamla after an Oklahoma City federal court judge granted a preliminary injunction in the school’s favor. The judge decided a charter school can’t be denied solely for being religious. 
But, the school’s application fell one vote short of receiving board approval in the Monday meeting.
The Statewide Charter School Board meets Monday at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Ben Gamla has faced vocal opposition from Oklahoma’s Jewish community, raising concerns about the school’s ability to recruit students. 
Board member William Pearson said that was “what played mostly in my mind” when he voted against the school on Monday. Two other dissenting board members declined to comment on the reasoning for their votes.
The school’s leading founder, former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, of Florida, told a Tulsa rabbi on Sept. 30 the Ben Gamla school expected only 10 students to enroll in its first year.
The board’s vote, combined with the low enrollment expectations, confirm Ben Gamla’s application “fails on grounds having nothing to do with religion,” Drummond contended in his dismissal motion.
The attorney general expects the school’s federal lawsuit to be dismissed as a result of the rejection, his motion states. After that, the federal preliminary injunction would “carry no continuing legal force,” and a previous Oklahoma Supreme Court decision against religious charter schools “remains the law of this state,” he wrote.
State law allows no further board action on Ben Gamla unless its founders file a new application, the attorney general said.
“From day one, this case was about making a state agency tell the whole truth about why it rejected a deeply flawed application,” Drummond said in a statement Thursday. “My office warned this Board in March that the school had no community support and no realistic path to the enrollment it promised. The founder’s own words have now proved that right, so the court no longer needs to step in.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore orders review of campus sexual assault policies following Cornell case
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) during an August 2026 meeting with reporters in the Maryland State House. (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) is asking an independent state agency to take a closer look at sexual assault policies on college campuses in Maryland amid a national reckoning caused by allegations of a gang rape at Cornell University.
In a directive on Thursday, the governor asked the Maryland Higher Education Commission to make recommendations for improving campus sexual assault policies within 90 days, meaning the recommendations could arrive just as Maryland’s next General Assembly session is beginning in mid-January.
Moore’s order comes in the wake of an accusation of sexual assault that has stirred the nation. Last month, a former Cornell University student, identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit accusing seven male students at the university of raping her over a period of seven hours while she was under the influence of ketamine at an October 2024 fraternity party.
At the time, local law enforcement officials in New York declined to pursue charges in response to her report, although several of the young men faced sanctions from the university, including suspension and expulsion.
“Deeply troubling accounts have emerged in recent days of how students outside of Maryland have bravely come forward to report sexual assault and have been failed by the institutions that are supposed to ensure their safety,” Moore wrote in his directive.
In addition, the Trump administration last month rescinded a set of Biden-era Title IX rules, which sought to extend protections to LGBTQ+ students, but had faced significant legal headwinds.
“This is a call to action,” Moore wrote. “In Maryland, we will continue to identify opportunities to enhance the safety of our college campuses and to ensure accountability when these efforts fail.”
The formal rescission may not change much for schools, since Trump’s Department of Education had already been enforcing a prior set of guidelines from the first Trump administration, which set a stricter definition of sexual harassment and gave more due process rights to the accused.
Though the federal higher education landscape is “currently evolving,” Moore’s order is “designed to provide stability,” said the commission’s interim secretary Elena Quiroz-Livanis in a statement on Thursday.
“Our approach is not about waiting for Washington to finalize every rule; it is about establishing a gold standard right here at home,” Quiroz-Livanis said. “By partnering with the Office of the Attorney General, MHEC is ensuring that regardless of how federal regulations shift, Maryland institutions will have a solid, statewide framework that holds offenders accountable, protects survivor rights, and provides our campus leaders with the clear, consistent guidance they need.”
In a statement, a spokesperson for the University System of Maryland, which includes the University of Maryland, Towson University, Bowie State University and a number of other public campuses, said its institutions “routinely evaluate these policies and programs.”
“The USM is committed to creating safe environments on our campuses where all students can learn and thrive. This includes having strong sexual misconduct policies, educational programs and resources for students, faculty and staff,” read the statement from Michael Sandler, a spokesperson for the university system.
Maryland’s Higher Education Commission — which is responsible for setting statewide policies for Maryland’s 14 public four-year institutions, 16 community colleges, 32 private institutions, and more than 140 private career schools — already studies campus sexual assault on a biennial basis.
Campuses in Maryland are required to adopt written sexual misconduct policies, keep track of misconduct cases and conduct a student survey focused on the subject.
In a report released in August 2026, which aggregated data from 49 different Maryland colleges and universities, the commission found 3,435 incidents of sexual misconduct dating back to 2024. Of those, 92% were reported at the state’s four-year colleges.
Some 476 incidents during the two-year period were considered sexual assault I, the most serious type of incident. But in many instances, the colleges either didn’t have any authority over the suspected perpetrator, or the victim declined to move forward with an investigation.
Those sexual assaults resulted in 53 formal investigations, 20 of which were still underway at the time the report was issued.
But campuses did offer a wide array of accommodations for victims, including alternative housing, academic aid such as test rescheduling and referrals to counseling and other services.

name: California
title: California files its 100th lawsuit against Trump, this time over ICE at courthouses
text:
In summary
California leaders want immigration agents to stay away from courthouses. They worry enforcement will prevent people from testifying in criminal trials.


California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed the state’s 100th lawsuit against the federal government since President Trump took office for a second time in 2025. 
Bonta reached that milestone in 21 months. During the first Trump administration, California officials sued the federal government a total of 123 times in four years. 
The lawsuit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California alleges that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement overstepped its Constitutional limits by taking people into custody at state courthouses, a practice forbidden by a U.S. District Court judge that the lawsuit alleges ICE nevertheless continues to employ. 
For instance, the California Justice Department found that ICE detained 34 people at state courthouses in June 2026. In July 2026, the month after the judicial order to stop making arrests at courthouses, ICE detained 28 people at courthouses. 
“ICE’s directive on courthouse enforcement and the resulting enforcement activities have had a profound chilling effect that has hindered California’s ability to enforce the law and protect public safety,” the state Justice Department said in a news release.
Picking people up at a courthouse can have a chilling effect on witnesses, victims and even suspects who are afraid to show up for court, California Supreme Court Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero said last year. 
“Making courthouses a focus of immigration enforcement hinders, rather than helps, the administration of justice by deterring witnesses and victims from coming forward and discouraging individuals from asserting their rights,” Guerrero said. 
In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law a measure that requires federal immigration agents to present a judicial warrant and identify themselves before making arrests within 1,000 feet of a state courthouse.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After death and injuries, two Iowa nursing homes added to federal watchlist
text:
The Northbrook Healthcare and Rehabilitation Center, formerly known as Northbrook Manor, in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)The federal government has added two Iowa nursing homes to its list of the worst care facilities in the nation.
Adel Acres and Northbrook Healthcare and Rehabilitation Center in Cedar Rapids have been added to the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ nationwide list of care facilities that are eligible for special-focus status, indicating a history of serious, recurring resident-care issues.
At any given time, two to five nursing homes per state appear on the list of federally designated “special-focus facilities,” while 10 others in each state are typically designated as eligible for such a designation due to recurring resident-care issues.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 100 facilities that are designated special-focus facilities are subject to a comprehensive, on-site inspection at least once every six months, with the expectation that they will eventually take substantive action to address any ongoing issues.
The two Iowa nursing homes that are currently enrolled in the special-focus program are Garden View Care Center in Shenandoah, and Pine Acres Rehabilitation and Care Center in West Des Moines. Garden View has been in the program for 14 months and Pine Acre for 16 months.
Adel Acres cited for resident death
Adel Acres’ addition to the list of eligible facilities appears to be tied to the 24 state and federal violations cited at the facility during the past 12 months.
In October 2025, the state proposed, but held in suspension, $14,500 in fines against Adel Acres. Inspectors alleged a resident of the home fell and subsequently died of blunt force head trauma after the staff failed to promptly intervene and assess the resident’s condition. In a separate incident, the home allegedly failed to follow a physician’s order to administer antibiotics for a resident with an infection. The resident was re-hospitalized for sepsis, a potentially life-threatening condition that stems from an infection.
In response to that situation, the federal government imposed a $16,544 fine against Adel Acres.
In March 2026, the state proposed, but held in suspension a $15,000 for medication errors at Adel Acres. A resident who was mistakenly given an overdose of Oxycodone later “appeared pale, with garbled speech and not making sense,” inspectors reported. Two employees had each mistakenly given the resident three times the prescribed amount of the drug, inspectors concluded.
In response to the March 2026 findings, the federal government imposed a $41,470 fine against Adel Acres.
In June 2026, the state proposed, but held in suspension, a fine of $5,250 against Adel Acres, alleging the staff failed to provide adequate nursing supervision for a female resident who fell from the bed to the floor, causing “significant pain and injuries.”
A worker at the home had allegedly attempted to change the sheets on the resident’s bed, with the resident still in the bed. According to inspectors, the worker stated he stood on one side of the bed and pulled the sheet toward him, causing the resident to slip off the opposite side of the bed and onto the floor. One employee told inspectors the woman was “in true pain and was screaming out in pain — a blood-curdling scream.”
CMS has yet to publicly report any federal fines associated with the June 2026 findings at Adel Acres.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach the home’s administrator for comment.
Northbrook fined by federal agency
The addition of Northbrook Healthcare and Rehabilitation Center to the list of eligible facilities appears be tied to the July 2026 findings of state inspectors who proposed, but held in suspension, a $10,000 fine against the home. Inspectors alleged the staff failed to monitor the urinary output of four residents with catheters, three of whom were then diagnosed with a urinary tract infection.
One of the residents allegedly showed “no urinary output for 32 hours” and on Jan. 12, 2026, was taken to a hospital where his catheter was removed, resulting in “a large gush of blood from the patient’s urethra.” According to inspectors, the man was then transferred to an intensive care unit for treatment of acute kidney injury and a life-threatening case of sepsis. The resident was then placed in hospice care and died on Feb. 5, 2026, according to inspectors.
In response to the July 2026 findings, the federal government imposed a $16,435 fine against Northbrook Healthcare and Rehabilitation Center.
Earlier this year, the home’s administrator declined to comment on the situation but said the home had procedures in place to ensure residents were properly cared for.
Other Iowa homes on federal list
The eight other Iowa nursing homes currently deemed eligible for special-focus status, and the number of months they have been on that list, are:
Azria Health Park Place, Des Moines: Nine months.
Bishop Drumm Retirement Center, Johnston: 10 months.
Caring Acres Nursing and Rehab Center, Anita: Eight months.
Chapters Living, Council Bluffs: Five months.
Greater Southside Health and Rehabilitation, Des Moines: 46 months.
The Ivy, Davenport: Eleven months.
Northgate Care Center, Waukon: Four months.
Royal Oaks Nursing and Rehabilitation Center, Urbandale: Four months.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska tax revenues hold steady ahead of new economic forecasts
text:
The top of the Nebraska Capitol Mar. 19, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — With a crucial economic forecasting meeting just weeks away, the last round of monthly revenue reports available to forecasters held mostly level with their previous predictions.
The Nebraska Department of Revenue’s report on September’s tax receipts showed a net gain of 0.2% compared to what Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board had predicted in late February. That difference equates to about $1.2 million in extra revenue headed to the state’s coffers.
Though $1.2 million is meager compared with Nebraska’s multibillion-dollar annual budget, it was an encouraging sign to state Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, the term-limited chair of the Nebraska Legislature’s Appropriations Committee. Prior to August’s tax report — which broke the pattern — the state’s monthly tax receipts had fallen below forecasts for five months in a row.
“I’m glad to see that we’re stabilizing with our revenues and our receipts,” Clements said.
For legislative fiscal analyst Keisha Patent, September’s tax report showed a continuation of many trends seen throughout 2026. Sales and use tax revenues have consistently risen above predictions — in September they were 13.9% above forecast at $28.3 million. However, those gains were offset by individual income tax revenues, which have regularly fallen below forecast, this time by 16.4% for a $54.9 million loss.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
September also continued the trend of Nebraska tax refunds steadily waning, yet still coming in above projections. The latest report shows that refunds were 1.8% — $2.4 million — above forecast, while August’s report had refunds 2% above forecast.
Lawmakers divided on influence of newest Nebraska Economic Forecasting Board Pillen appointees

One notable difference in September’s report were corporate income taxes, which came in 6% — $7.3 million — above forecast after consistently falling below projections through most of 2026. Patent noted that September is typically a big month for corporate income tax revenues, as it’s when businesses submit their estimated tax payments for the third quarter.
The forecasting board will meet Oct. 30 to make new predictions, which will determine the size of the projected budget deficit state lawmakers will be tasked with filling when they convene in January. The 2027 session is expected to be the third consecutive session the Legislature will deal with a projected deficit.
Clements said he anticipates that the board’s new projections will increase the deficit somewhat, but not by a large margin.
Nebraska’s projected deficit currently stands at $208 million by the end of the current budget period ending June 30, 2027. An $846 million deficit is also projected for the next biennium ending June 30, 2029.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG, Dem lawmaker announce legislative proposals to empower human trafficking survivors
text:
From left to right, New Mexico Dream Center Executive Director Shelley Repp, state Rep. Meredith Dixon (D-Albuquerque), New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, Unica Behavioral Health interim CEO Tracy Townsend and Unica Behavioral Health Forensic Interviewer Supervisor Camille Bowens, on Oct. 15, 2026, announced two legislative proposals to increase criminal penalties for sex traffickers and to empower survivors. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and state Rep. Meredith Dixon (D-Albuquerque) stood alongside advocates for human trafficking survivors Thursday morning to announce a pair of legislative proposals they say will be a key step toward fixing the state’s outdated victim protections.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dixon said she plans to carry two measures in the upcoming legislative session — one bill and one proposed constitutional amendment — to increase penalties for human trafficking; close the loophole that allowed Jeffrey Epstein to avoid registering as a sex offender in New Mexico; and shield survivors from being retraumatized during their traffickers’ criminal trials.
The Trafficking Investigation and Meaningful Enforcement Act would place no statute of limitations on prosecuting sex trafficking, would raise the age of protection to 18 and would update criminal penalties, particularly in cases where the victim is a child. It would also treat forcing someone to work off a debt as trafficking and expand the list of offenses that require someone to register as a sex offender.
Despite pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, Epstein was never required to register as a sex offender in New Mexico, where he owned property, largely because New Mexico law set a lower age limit for victims than Florida. In addition to raising the age of protection to 18 and expanding the offenses that require sex offender registration, Dixon said the law would require lifelong sex offender registration for people convicted of child prostitution crimes.
Her other measure, the Victims’ Rights Amendment, would go to voters in the next general election as a proposed constitutional amendment if it passes out of both chambers of the state Legislature.
The proposed amendment to the state Constitution’s victims’ rights section would give survivors greater privacy protections, expand the state’s definition of who counts as a survivor and give survivors the right to refuse being interviewed by the suspect’s attorneys. Under the amendment, if a survivor agreed to participate in such an interview, they would have the power to end it at any time and could have a support person in the room with them.
Both measures will “close gaps that leave our survivors of human trafficking and child sexual exploitation without the protection and voice they deserve,” Dixon said at a news conference in the New Mexico Department of Justice’s Albuquerque headquarters. 
Torrez, who began his career by trying child abuse cases, said he has long believed New Mexico’s protections for survivors of sex crimes stand among the weakest in the nation.
As an investigatory subcommittee at the state Legislature and Torrez’s NMDOJ investigate Epstein’s time and potential crimes in New Mexico, he said it’s particularly important for state leaders to make good on their promises of delivering justice for survivors and their families.
“There are literally hundreds, if not thousands, of survivors in this state that are victims of horrific crimes year in and year out,” Torrez said. “Their perpetrator is not internationally known, politically connected or otherwise prominently featured in national news stories…these are the victims that go unseen all too often in our criminal justice system.”
Advocates for human trafficking survivors backed the proposals at a news conference with Dixon and Torrez Thursday morning. 
Shelley Repp, executive director of the Albuquerque nonprofit New Mexico Dream Center, which advocates for trafficking survivors, said the provision to let survivors opt out of repeatedly recounting the abuses they endured before a criminal trial will make it easier for them to navigate the criminal justice system.
“It is important to me and it is important to the clients I represent to be able to say, ‘You can be protected,’” she said. “You, as a victim, can have the time that you need to recover. You, as a victim, can have the protections that you deserve. We, as the legal system, do not want to retraumatize and revictimize you.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s top election official forwards suspicious mail to FBI
text:
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen speaks at an election security summit with his counterparts from Iowa, Missouri and South Dakota as well as the director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Also joining the news conference was the director of the National Counterterrorism Innovation, Technology and Education Center at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Oct. 9, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office is among election and congressional offices nationwide that received suspicious envelopes this week.
Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office said the envelope wasn’t opened and was quickly isolated once detected, “in accordance with established protocols. The mail was turned over to the FBI for further analysis.
The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of mailings, some of which contained a powdery white substance, according to Thursday reporting from NPR, NBC News and others.
Evnen’s office did not give further details on the envelope.
Election officials in Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma, as well as some congressional offices, received similar mailings, according to NPR. The Louisiana Secretary of State’s Office said an employee who opened a letter sent to the office on Tuesday wasn’t injured but was taken to the emergency room as a precaution. 
Nebraska was among election offices that received suspicious packages in September 2024, too.
“This is the second time we have had a situation like this occur during my time as Nebraska’s secretary of state and, in both instances, swift action was taken to isolate and then investigate the suspicious mailing,” Evnen said in a statement. “I’d like to thank both my staff at the Secretary of State’s office for their diligence and law enforcement for their assistance.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Matt Gaetz and two others named as defendants in sex trafficking civil lawsuit
text:
Matt Gaetz via U.S. HouseTwo women have filed a federal civil lawsuit accusing former Florida U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz and two others of participating in an sex trafficking scheme involving young women, drugs, and travel across state lines.
It came nearly two years after a House Ethics Committee report said Gaetz made payments totaling tens of thousands of dollars to women for sex, including a 17-year-old girl. Gaetz denied the allegations at the time, but it led to his withdrawal from his nomination by President Trump to serve as U.S. attorney general.
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida in Orlando. It alleges Gaetz and former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg, from 2017 through January 2019, coordinated recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts from young women.
It further alleges that former Florida House Republican member Chris Dorworth “knowingly” participated in such events and Greenberg Dental and AWG Inc. supplied the money that funded these illicit acts.” Those businesses are owned by Greenbergs father.
The two women are listed in the lawsuit as “Jane Doe 1” and “Jane Doe 2.” Jane Doe 1 was 20 years old when she met Gaetz and Jane Doe was 22. They are demanding judgement against Greenberg Dental and AWG for compensatory damages and attorney fees and seek a jury trial.
Gaetz is denying the allegations and says he intends to fight the claims in court.
“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” he said in a written statement published in The Guardian. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee Report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”
Gaetz served in the Florida House from 2010 to 2016. He was elected to represent Florida’s 1st Congressional District from 2016 until Trump nominated him for attorney general in November 2024.
But he stepped down soon afterwards because of growing doubts he could be confirmed due to the Ethics Committee report.
Gaetz said at that time that he had “NEVER had sexual contact with someone under 18. Any claim that I have would be destroyed in court — which is why no claim was ever made in court.”
Greenberg was a close associate of Gaetz who pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal offenses: sex trafficking of a child, illegally producing a false identification document, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud, stalking, and conspiracy. He is serving an 11-year federal prison sentence.
Cash and travel
The lawsuit closely follows the allegations included in the 2024 House Ethics Committee report. It alleges that between July 2017 and January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg paid Jane Doe 1 on at least 19 occasions, ranging from $150 to $1,000.
The suit alleges that in place of cash payments, “the venture also paid with travel,” flying Jane Doe 1 to Venice Beach, Calif.; Las Vegas; the Florida Keys; the Bahamas; and New York City in exchange for sexual activity.
The woman listed as Jane Doe 1 alleges that she saw Gaetz “having sex with Victim A” who was “only 17 years old” at the time, and that Gaetz “gave Victim A $400 in cash that night, which Victim A understood to be payment for sex.”
The lawsuit says the defendants’ actions caused the two women severe emotional and psychological trauma and that they continue to suffer emotional distress, humiliation, and loss of employment as a result.
Greenberg Dental and AWG Inc. were businesses associated with Greenberg’s family. Seth Greenberg’s father, Andrew W. Greenberg, is the principal of AWG, Inc. and serves as president of Greenberg Dental. The lawsuit alleges he controlled the disbursements AWG made to his son.

Rex James ClothierJanuary 7, 1943 – September 28, 2026Thermopolis, WyomingShared by: Mortimore Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesRex James Clothier was born in a suburb of Los Angeles, CA, on January 7th, 1943.  He attended public schools in Pawnee Park Kansas, Sidney Nebraska, and Torrington Wyoming, graduating from Torrington High School in 1960.
Rex started a lifelong love of coaching with a little league team in Torrington in 1961 while attending Eastern Wyoming College.  He married his high school sweetheart in November 1961.  That relationship produced three daughters; Susan Elaine and twins Cathy Lynn and Cindy Lee.  The marriage ended in 1977.  Barbara Lee Brekke became his bride in 1978, and Rex adopted her son Ted.
Rex’s education included an Associate of Business at EWC, Bachelor’s Degree at Oregon State, Master’s Degree at Northern Arizona University, and graduate stints at O.U. and NMSU.  His vocational activities included coaching in various sports from the age of 18 through 74, majoring in wrestling for more than 35 years, including his last 10 years of coaching in Thermopolis. 
Rex’s love of competition led him to the game of Bridge, where, with excellent partners, he achieved the rank of Silver Life Master. 
Rex was preceded in death by his parents Jim and Dorothy Clothier, beloved wife Barbara, his brother Harvey (Myrna) Clothier, and sister Dorothy Ehrman.  He is survived by his brother Gary (Ruth) Clothier, his son Ted Clothier, his daughters Susan (Frank) Martinez, Cathy (Greg) Bryant, Cindy (Keith) Baker, six grandchildren, 14 great grandchildren, and several nieces and nephews.
