Rex James ClothierJanuary 7, 1943 – September 28, 2026Thermopolis, WyomingShared by: Mortimore Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesRex James Clothier was born in a suburb of Los Angeles, CA, on January 7th, 1943.  He attended public schools in Pawnee Park Kansas, Sidney Nebraska, and Torrington Wyoming, graduating from Torrington High School in 1960.
Rex started a lifelong love of coaching with a little league team in Torrington in 1961 while attending Eastern Wyoming College.  He married his high school sweetheart in November 1961.  That relationship produced three daughters; Susan Elaine and twins Cathy Lynn and Cindy Lee.  The marriage ended in 1977.  Barbara Lee Brekke became his bride in 1978, and Rex adopted her son Ted.
Rex’s education included an Associate of Business at EWC, Bachelor’s Degree at Oregon State, Master’s Degree at Northern Arizona University, and graduate stints at O.U. and NMSU.  His vocational activities included coaching in various sports from the age of 18 through 74, majoring in wrestling for more than 35 years, including his last 10 years of coaching in Thermopolis. 
Rex’s love of competition led him to the game of Bridge, where, with excellent partners, he achieved the rank of Silver Life Master. 
Rex was preceded in death by his parents Jim and Dorothy Clothier, beloved wife Barbara, his brother Harvey (Myrna) Clothier, and sister Dorothy Ehrman.  He is survived by his brother Gary (Ruth) Clothier, his son Ted Clothier, his daughters Susan (Frank) Martinez, Cathy (Greg) Bryant, Cindy (Keith) Baker, six grandchildren, 14 great grandchildren, and several nieces and nephews.
Rex wrote:
“I have valued my time on earth through loving parents, my precious Barbara, son Ted, daughters Susan, Cathy, and Cindy, and dear friends and students who encouraged me and brought joy and fulfillment to me.  I look forward to a heavenly reunion.”

title: Trump sues California over allegations of noncitizens registering to vote
authors: Jeanne Kuang and Ana B. Ibarra
text:
In summary
The Trump administration is demanding records from Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties as it looks for instances of noncitizens voting. 


The Trump administration on Thursday sued California and Los Angeles County to try to force elections officials not to count potentially 20,000 registered voters’ ballots, in an extraordinary intervention 19 days before a consequential national election. 
Federal prosecutors from the U.S. Justice Department this week wrote to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and LA County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan demanding that they verify the citizenship status of a specific list of registered voters, or set aside their ballots without counting them in November. 
It’s part of a national push by the Trump administration to find instances of non-U.S. citizens voting illegally in elections. The Department of Homeland Security recently claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls; they sent the state the names of only 185 voters, who Nevada officials confirmed were all U.S. citizens.
California sends all registered voters a ballot in the mail; county registrars across the state have already done so ahead of the Nov. 3 election in which Californians will decide on a new governor, 14 statewide ballot measures and several competitive races that will be key to which party controls Congress. 
The Justice Department letters, sent to Los Angeles County and Weber by Acting Deputy U.S. Attorney General R. Trent McCotter, gave officials 48 hours to comply with its request to review a thumb drive containing a list of registered voters that federal prosecutors allege aren’t citizens. 
On Wednesday, Logan said he hasn’t reviewed the drive because it’s an unsecure format. Weber wrote McCotter saying she had requested data and methodology after federal officials claimed without evidence in July that 190,000 California voters “may be” noncitizens, but that the officials never provided it.
Gov. Gavin Newsom scoffed at the lawsuit on Thursday as “a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day” and said the prosecutors’ request to throw out ballots “should scare the hell out of every American.”
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook,” Newsom said in a statement.
He pointed out the request asks local elections officials to violate federal law: The National Voter Registration Act prohibits purging voter rolls within 90 days before an election.
Both federal and California law require residents to be U.S. citizens to register to vote. Voter fraud is extremely rare, numerous studies have found. 
California Democrats urge people to vote
The Trump administration’s actions have alarmed state leaders who say they amount to voter intimidation.
“I think that this is very concerning …because it is perceived by so many in California and across this country as a way to deter people from voting,” said Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limon at a rally in Los Angeles for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra Thursday morning. 
“We will continue to defend, to protect the integrity of our elections. California has a robust system of protecting our elections. We check, we verify, and we follow up,” she said. 
Becerra did not directly address the federal action in his remarks at his rally but promised to put up a fight against the Trump administration. 
“Whether it is voting, whether it is going to work, whether it’s having good schools, or whether it’s protecting our families against ICE mercenaries, we are here, estamos presentes, and we will fight,” Becerra said from El Pueblo de Los Angeles Historical Monument. 
But right now our fight is to get the vote out, to make sure everyone understands that our power lies in our vote,” he said. 
More subpoenas to Orange and San Diego counties
The lawsuit and Justice Department’s demands come weeks after federal investigators issued grand jury subpoenas to Los Angeles elections officials seeking information on registered voters.
Federal prosecutors also sought information on registered voters in San Diego County, the news outlet inewsource reported, as well as Orange County, according to previously unreported records obtained this week by CalMatters. 
Orange County’s registrar of voters received three subpoenas for records about individual registered voters on Sept. 10. Subpoenas for both LA and Orange counties were sent at the request of Southern California’s acting U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli and Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Wheat. They asked local officials to deliver the information to a Department of Homeland Security investigator.
One subpoena sought the full voter file for a redacted list of what appears to be 18 registered Orange County voters including any “attestations regarding citizenship status;” two others sought more detailed records on two separate voters including information about whether they had changed their addresses or party affiliation and “correspondence related to voter registration.” 
Orange County Registrar of Voters Bob Page said his office produced the records and hasn’t gotten any further requests or demands from the Trump administration. 
“We do not know why the grand jury requested registration records for these individuals,” Page wrote in an emailed statement. “The request for this registration information has had no impact on the administration of the 2026 General Election.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota keeps teaching scholarship open to all, but special education gets priority
text:
A Sioux Falls School District educator teaches students reading at Lowell Elementary during the 2024-2025 school year. (Courtesy of the Sioux Falls School District)A South Dakota board voted Thursday to keep a critical needs scholarship open to all prospective K-12 teachers while prioritizing special education and language arts.
Demand for special education teachers is expected to grow over the next decade, creating a need that outpaces other teaching positions in the state, according to data presented Thursday by state Education Secretary Joseph Graves during a teleconference meeting of the Critical Teaching Needs Scholarship Board.
Graves pointed out that special education has been consistently near the top of the list in turnover and need. Turnover is likely attributable to burnout, Graves said, due to the profession’s more demanding nature.
“If these numbers are correct — and they are projections, you never know — in special education, we’re seeing a lot of openings in those areas compared to the number of positions there are. That’s going to remain a hot field,” Graves said.
‘I plant seeds’: Harrisburg teacher named South Dakota teacher of the year

Graves said programs including the state’s Teaching Apprenticeship Program — which allows full-time teacher’s aides to earn their teaching degree while continuing to work — and the critical needs scholarship are designed to address the shortage.
Language arts was the second priority, the board deemed. The profession had lower turnover and vacancy numbers than special education, though still higher than other specialized teaching positions. 
State lawmakers created the scholarship program in 2013 to encourage South Dakota high school graduates to earn their teaching degrees in South Dakota and remain in the state after graduation. The board expanded the scholarship from targeted subjects to all teaching positions last year in response to teacher shortages.
Awardees sign an agreement to stay and work in a high-need teaching position in South Dakota for five years after graduation. If they do not complete the requirement, the scholarship is converted into a low-interest loan, with repayments going back into the scholarship fund.
Anna Schwan, vice president for academic affairs at Northern State University in Aberdeen, told board members the scholarship motivates college students “to keep going.”
“It’s the tie at the end that really helps push them, especially during their student teaching semester where they virtually have no income to pay for tuition,” Schwan said.
State officials presented data showing persistent turnover and vacancies across nearly all teaching disciplines. At the end of the 2024-25 school year, public school districts reported 1,178 full-time teachers no longer employed, and at the start of the current school year, 137 full-time teaching positions were unfilled statewide.
Teaching vacancy rates have fallen in the years since South Dakota’s peak teacher shortage after the COVID-19 pandemic, Graves said.
“The crisis is not over. We still have a problem, but it is not the severity we saw three years ago,” Graves said.

A map shows where Critical Teaching Needs Scholarship recipients are working in South Dakota. Many work in Minnehaha and Lincoln counties, which include the Sioux Falls metro area. (Courtesy of the South Dakota Board of Regents)

After the board opened the scholarship to all teaching positions in the state, there were 86 applications, South Dakota Board of Regents System Academic Program Manager Molly Weisgram said. It was a “significant increase” in applications over previous years, but board members said they wish there were more. Schwan told board members some students might be afraid of committing to working in the state for five years.
“That’s something we’re struggling with,” Schwan said. “They stay — traditionally speaking, they don’t leave South Dakota — but it’s a shame. There are a lot of supports available, but they’re very intimidated by that expectation.”
Nineteen students were awarded and accepted a combined total of $101,946 in scholarships for the 2023-24 school year, averaging about $5,300 per student. The program has awarded 148 scholarships worth about $1.4 million since 2014, funded by interest earned on the state’s Education Enhancement Trust Fund — a dedicated state account for education spending.
Thirty-one awardees so far did not complete the program requirements, resulting in $291,663 converted to loans repaid into the fund.
The Critical Teaching Needs Scholarship application window opens Nov. 1 and closes Dec. 15.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Dr. LouAnn Woodward, first woman to lead UMMC, announces she will retire next year
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
University of Mississippi Medical Center’s Dr. LouAnn Woodward announced Thursday she will retire in June after more than a decade at the helm of the state’s only academic medical center. 
Woodward, 62, serves as the medical center’s vice chancellor for health affairs and dean of the UMMC School of Medicine. She became the first woman to lead the medical center and school when she was appointed in 2015.
Woodward’s current four-year contract will expire June 30.
University of Mississippi Chancellor Glenn Boyce recommended Dr. Alan Jones, vice chancellor for health affairs at UMMC, as the medical center’s next leader, Woodward wrote in a Thursday email to staff. 
Woodward said that the Institutions of Higher Learning’s Board of Trustees accepted Boyce’s recommendation Thursday.
“I have absolute confidence in Dr. Jones and our leadership team,” Woodward said. “He has played an integral role in our shared successes over the years and has advanced many of our strategic priorities. UMMC’s future is bright, and it will be in excellent hands with Dr. Jones at the helm.”
Dr. Alan Jones, associate vice chancellor for clinical affairs at UMMC, answers questions during a Health Affairs Committee meeting at the Universities Center in Ridgeland, Miss., Wednesday, January 18, 2023. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Woodward, a Carroll County native, was trained as an emergency room physician at UMMC after graduating from Mississippi State University. She is also a tenured professor in the academic center’s Department of Emergency Medicine, according to UMMC’s website. 
She joined the medical center’s administration in 2003, and previously served as associate vice chancellor for health affairs and vice dean of the UMMC School of Medicine before accepting her current role. 
Woodward has led the health system, which includes six health science schools and the state’s only Level 1 trauma center, through the COVID-19 pandemic, a major dispute with the state’s largest private insurer and a cyberattack that forced the medical center to close clinics across the state and cancel elective procedures for nine days.
Under her leadership, the medical center completed a major children’s hospital expansion, adding a seven-story tower adjacent to Children’s of Mississippi designed to expand neonatal and pediatric intensive care, surgery and imaging services.
She has also led the medical center’s charge to construct a new cancer center, which is expected to break ground this month. Officials consider this an important step in Mississippi’s quest to gain a national designation that could improve outcomes for patients in the state with one of the nation’s highest cancer mortality rates, according to hospital leaders.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Immigrant Coalition supports resolution pressing Congress to tackle immigration policy
text:
Florida Immigrant Coalition photoThe Florida Immigrant Coalition on Thursday joined Illinois U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez and other advocates calling on Congress to tackle immigration policy and provide a pathway to citizenship for millions of undocumented people. 
Support for change, fueled by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and deportations, has never been greater, Ramirez said as she announced the resolution. It is being co-sponsored by 19 other House members.
The resolution calls on the House of Representatives to pass legislation providing pathways to citizenship for undocumented long-term residents of the United States and provide “humanitarian protection pathways” including providing “broad and meaningful access” to asylum.
U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Illinois, via U.S. House
Ramirez’s parents emigrated from Guatemala. Her husband is a former Dreamer (he obtained a green card in 2024). And she’s the niece of an uncle who worked and put his children through college but, she says, lives in the shadows out of fear of being deported.
“Now is the time to build a system that recognizes the contributions of our immigrant neighbors. No more excuses. No more fibs. It’s important to do it,” Ramirez said, noting that it had been 40 years since the U.S. House of Representatives last passed immigration legislation.
Gov. Ron DeSantis has aggressively enforced federal immigration policy and called the Legislature into a special session to pass a state law aimed at carrying out the policy. The law includes directives for Florida counties to enter into 287(g) agreements, which allow state and local authorities to work with federal immigration authorities. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Florida Immigrant Coalition Executive Director Tessa Petit said the resolution recognizes the urgency of the moment for immigrants across the United States who are afraid to live, work, and send their children to school. The coalition, Petit said, works with 80 organizations. The goal, according to the group’s website, is  to “strengthen pro-immigrant power.”
“As a Haitian immigrant experiencing the agonizing pain and fear of the Haitian community in Florida every day, who have lost TPS in looking at detention and deportation in their near future,” she said, “I particularly welcome the resolution because it brings to light all the changes needed in our immigration system to ensure the safety of our immigrant friends and family members who are here and deserve justice and dignity.”
She added: “It is time for immigrants to be fairly recognized as part of this country, and this resolution will set the path to a promising future for immigrants.”
Specifically, Ramirez’s resolution calls on Congress to eliminate arbitrary caps on visas, including country-based limits, ban use of temporary visas that bar immigrants from changing employers, and ban limits on access to services and benefits, such as Medicaid.
Ramirez’s resolution came days after she filed a bill to abolish the Department of Homeland Security Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and ICE.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota health dept. urges people to get measles vaccine amid outbreaks
text:
A 3-year-old girl gets an MMR vaccine at a clinic in Texas in March 2025. (Photo by Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)The Minnesota Department of Health is urging people to get vaccinated for measles if they haven’t already.
The guidance comes amid two unrelated outbreaks of measles since mid-September in rural Fillmore and Todd counties. Minnesota has had 42 recorded cases of measles in 2026, already exceeding the total of 26 cases in 2025. The year prior saw 70 measles cases, largely affecting unvaccinated Somali American kids in the Twin Cities.
All of the people who have contracted measles in recent outbreaks were unvaccinated, the health department said.
Kids in Minnesota are required to get two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine — known as the MMR vaccine — before kindergarten, unless their families submit an exemption.
The number of kindergartners with a non-medical exemption has risen sharply since 2020, reflecting growing vaccine skepticism. In the 2025-2026 school year, 6.8% of kindergartners had a non-medical exemption in Minnesota compared with the national rate of 4%, according to data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Around 86% of Minnesota kindergartners have received the MMR vaccine, according to health department data — the third lowest rate in the nation, MPR News reported.


Vaccine skepticism has become federal policy under President Trump’s Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long promoted unsubstantiated claims about vaccines. Under Kennedy’s leadership, the federal government cut the childhood vaccination schedule (later blocked by a judge), cut funding to vaccine development projects and started a program to study vaccine injury.
Kennedy has encouraged the measles vaccine but has stopped short of supporting a mandate for it.
“The most effective way to prevent the spread of measles is the MMR vaccine,” Kennedy wrote on X in 2025, following a visit to families of children who died in a Texas measles outbreak. He also previously said that he’d “probably” vaccinate his own child for measles.
Minnesota adds two cases to measles surge amid decline in routine vaccinations

Measles is a highly contagious illness that, before the 1960s, nearly all children contracted and from which tens of thousands were hospitalized every year. Thanks to decades of widespread vaccination, it was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, though the number of measles cases in 2026 — the highest in three decades — is now threatening that status. The U.S. now has had more than 4,000 cases in 2026, far exceeding the 2,289 total confirmed cases in 2025.
Symptoms start with a fever, cough and runny nose, and progress to include a characteristic, blotchy head-to-toe rash. Around 1 in 5 unvaccinated Americans who get measles are hospitalized, according to the CDC.
People can get the MMR vaccine at any age. Generally, one dose of the vaccine is sufficient for adults.
In light of recent measles outbreaks, NPR published a guide for those who don’t know their measles immunity status. In short: People born before 1957 are presumed immune because measles used to be very common; people born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 might need an additional dose; those at high risk and in areas with high measles activity might want to get a second dose; and there’s no harm in getting an additional measles dose if you really don’t know if you are vaccinated.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Landowner group says property rights is still a major election issue
text:
Iowans opposed to carbon dioxide pipelines asked candidates on the upcoming ballot how they felt about the pipeline and private property rights. Pictured are buttons the group handed out at the Iowa State Capitol March 18, 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)A group of Iowa landowners opposed to a carbon sequestration pipeline say the issue of property rights is still “one of the biggest issues in the state of Iowa” though fewer than 70 candidates on the upcoming ballot responded to a questionnaire about eminent domain. 
Kathy Stockdale, a landowner affected by the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline and vocal opponent of the project, said the leaders of the state “must stand up in opposition to this risky land grab.” 
“It’s time for individual landowners to stop bearing the burden of keeping this multibillion-dollar company accountable,” Stockdale said in a news conference Thursday. “Our elected leaders need to do their jobs and stand up for the constitutional rights of the people they represent.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Stockdale is among a group of landowners who have been fighting against the carbon sequestration pipeline and more specifically Summit’s right to eminent domain, or the ability to force private landowners to allow use of their property for infrastructure projects deemed in the public interest.
Landowners sent a five-question survey to candidates for governor, U.S. Senate, U.S. House, state Legislature and several county level races, asking if the candidates believed eminent domain should be used for carbon capture pipelines, what they have done, and what they would be willing to do, to protect private property rights in Iowa. 
Both gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn, responded to the questions, but other races were less balanced in garnering responses. Only the Democratic and independent candidates for U.S. Senate submitted responses to the questionnaire. Libertarian and independent candidates in the U.S. House races responded to questions, but most major party candidates did not.
Overall, 28 Democratic candidates and 30 Republican candidates responded to the survey. Six “no party” or independent candidates and two Libertarian candidates responded to the questions. 
Emma Schmit, an organizer with Bold Alliance, said that if the names and party affiliations of the candidates were hidden from the responses, readers “wouldn’t really be able to tell what party they were from.” 
“Everybody that answered gave very similar responses of ‘No, this is unconstitutional; No, I don’t think this pipeline should go through,’ and so it just goes to show that there was really, I think, bipartisan support, and it’s really just a matter of right versus wrong,” Schmit said. 
Aside from Lahn and several folks running for county supervisor positions, the majority of Republican respondents were candidates running for Iowa House or Iowa Senate. 
Eminent domain has been a prominent issue at the Iowa Statehouse during the past several legislative sessions as lawmakers have worked to push legislation that would restrict or ban the use of eminent domain for carbon sequestration pipelines. In 2025, the issue led to a split among Iowa Senate Republicans, who traded jabs at one another on the Senate floor.  
Sand and Lahn both said they oppose the use of eminent domain for carbon capture pipelines and said the state privilege to take land should not be used for “private gain.” Both candidates said they would sign legislation that would ban the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines. 
Gov. Kim Reynolds, who is not running for reelection, vetoed legislation passed in 2025 to restrict carbon capture pipelines in Iowa. A bill banning the use of eminent domain for the projects did not make it to her desk this year. Lahn or Sand, depending on who wins the Nov. 3 election, would be responsible for approving or denying future legislative efforts on this front, and on appointing commissioners to the Iowa Utilities Commission, which approved a permit for Summit Carbon Solutions’ project in 2024. 
State Rep. Josh Turek, who is running as a Democrat for U.S. Senate against U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, responded to the survey and said he was against the Summit pipeline and the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines. 
Thomas Laehn, a Libertarian running for the Senate seat, said he also opposed the projects and, if elected, he would work to eliminate 45Q and 45Z tax credits which incentivize carbon capture and sequestration and biofuel that is produced with a small carbon footprint. 
Deb Main, a Woodbury County landowner, said Iowa representatives in Washington, D.C., need to have the “courage to end the 45Q tax credit for carbon pipelines.” 
Michael Bridgford, running as an independent in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, responded to the questionnaire, as did no-party candidate Dave Bushaw and Libertarian Rick Stewart running in the 2nd District. All three candidates said they opposed the use of eminent domain for private projects. 
Dave Dawson, the Democratic candidate running against Republican Chris McGowan in the 4th Congressional District, opposed the use of eminent domain and said he would push for private property rights protections at the federal level, if elected. 
Greene County landowner Mike Henning said the website with candidates’ responses will help voters as they head to the polls, but he said he encourages Iowans who care about the issue to question the candidates who didn’t respond to the questionnaire. 
“Call them, go to their forums, write, ask the candidates to talk about property rights and stuff as part of their stump speeches and public interactions between now and the election,” Henning said. “Make property rights an issue for your candidate now, so they will prioritize it again in the Legislature.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Report: Work requirements could threaten progress against overdose deaths
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
text:
LOOMING MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY CHANGES could unravel the state’s recent progress in reducing the number of opioid-related overdose fatalities, according to a new Boston Indicators report released Thursday.
Roughly 55 percent of Massachusetts adults who have opioid use disorder and are enrolled in MassHealth will need to satisfy new federal work requirements outlined in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That translates into 33,647 residents who could be at risk of losing MassHealth coverage, the report estimates.
“People with OUD often face barriers to work, including symptoms of the disorder itself,” the report says. “Importantly, OBBBA carves out mandatory exemptions for ‘medical frailty,’ which includes individuals with a substance use disorder (SUD) and individuals in an active treatment program.”
The number of overdose fatalities in 2025 fell below 1,000 for the first time in more than a decade. Deaths have declined for three consecutive years, after Massachusetts hit a record-high volume of 2,364 in 2022, according to state data.
Bureaucratic hurdles could hamper people with opioid use disorder from successfully seeking an exemption and providing evidence that their condition “significantly impairs” their ability to fulfill the work requirements, according to Boston Indicators. States can rely on self-attestation to verify exemptions and work requirements in 2027, but that dynamic will change in 2028. Despite MassHealth’s efforts to keep people enrolled and automatically verify their eligibility, the report says “many people with OUD will likely fall through the cracks.”
“And without MassHealth, many people won’t be able to afford MOUD and will likely be forced to pause or drop treatment altogether, creating a window where these individuals will be at much higher risk of overdose death,” the report says, referring to medications for opioid use disorder. “Since the change doesn’t take effect until January 2027 and people may lose coverage over time as verification falls through, we may not see the impact in overdose data until 2028 and beyond.”
Federal funding cuts and uncertainty, plus agency layoffs, could also undermine harm reduction efforts and national overdose surveillance programs, according to Boston Indicators.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Flock camera opponents say they were left out of state-led policy review
text:
A Flock automated license plate reader records data on Main Road in Tiverton on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s two-month pause on new automated license plate reader installations is set to expire Monday, the same day State Police may be ready to announce new policies governing the surveillance technology.
Lt. Col. Erik Yanyar, a State Police spokesperson, said officials were making final edits to the policy as of Thursday. But advocacy groups and the Office of the Public Defender say they have been left out of the review process entirely.
Gov. Dan McKee on Aug. 18 directed Rhode Island’s Department of Public Safety to conduct a 60-day “comprehensive review” of automated license plate reader systems amid growing resistance to Flock Safety cameras over concerns about privacy and how police are using the surveillance technology.
Before McKee ordered the pause, four Rhode Island communities — South Kingstown, Narragansett, Glocester, North Kingstown — voted to cancel their Flock contracts. The Tiverton Town Council, by contrast, voted in July to approve four cameras that have not yet been installed.
The Woonsocket City Council on Sept. 17 gave first passage to an amended ordinance regulating its 15 Flock cameras, with a second vote required. 
As municipalities across Rhode Island resist Flock cameras, McKee orders review

In Providence, three City Council members were scheduled to introduce an ordinance Thursday to ban the technology and require its deactivation. The city’s police chief, Col. Oscar Perez, said in a statement Thursday he respects elected officials’ authority to set policy but would have welcomed the opportunity to weigh in before the legislation was drafted, citing the potential consequences for police operations and criminal investigations.
McKee’s order called for the Department of Public Safety, overseen by State Police Col. Darnell Weaver, to work with stakeholders including the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association and the Rhode Island League of Cities and Towns.
“We’re probably close on the main issues,” Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association Executive Director Sidney Wordell said in an interview Thursday.
In an Oct. 9 letter to Weaver, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island and three other organizations — the Alliance to Mobilize Our Resistance, the state’s Office of the Public Defender and Planned Parenthood of Southern New England — wrote that the public safety working group made no effort to solicit public feedback.
In the letter, the four organizations offered their own recommendations, calling for stricter limits on how police use the cameras, retain and share data, and ensure public oversight.
“With less than two weeks left of this study period, we are concerned that there does not appear to have been any attempt to seek out any meaningful incorporation of public input in the process,” they wrote.“We hope that you consider these critical safeguards when studying the policy recommendations for these cameras in Rhode Island.” 
Steven Brown, executive director of the ACLU of Rhode Island, said the group had not heard back from State Police about the letter as of Thursday afternoon. The letter was also shared with the police chiefs association and the League of Cities and Towns.
Wordell said he had reviewed the letter and found the four organizations repeated concerns of which the working group is already aware. 
“There’s nothing new there,” he said. 
The groups called for limits on how long police can retain license plate data and share it with other law enforcement agencies, including prohibitions on using the technology to monitor constitutionally protected activities or assist federal immigration enforcement.
Concerns about privacy and potential misuse are largely a matter of trust, Wordell said, arguing that officers who misuse the technology should be held accountable. He pointed to Flock’s own policies on data retention and sharing as safeguards against misuse.
Police departments must also closely monitor which officers have access to the cameras’ data and how they use it, he said. “We would suggest, expect and support that there’s tight reins on making sure that that’s happening,” he said.
But Wordell took issue with the recommendation to limit the cameras’ use to specific serious offenses. The groups urged police to use the technology to identify stolen vehicles, locate missing or wanted people, and assist investigations into violent felonies and domestic violence.
He argued that restricting the cameras to certain offenses could rule out their use in other cases, including property crimes.
“The average citizen is more likely to be affected by someone stealing property from them, which causes a hell of a lot more financial issues,” Wordell said.
A spokesperson for the Rhode Island League of Cities and Towns did not immediately respond to request for comment.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Arts Commission’s interim director steps down, following 2 board members’ resignations
text:
The South Carolina Arts Commission meets Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, after two board members resigned and the interim director stepped down. (Screenshot of Arts Commission livestream)COLUMBIA — The interim director of the state Arts Commission stepped down Thursday, following the resignations of two board members in the weeks after a controversial decision not to fund two LGBTQ+ organizations.
Ashley Brown, who has been interim director since August, will stay with the commission, returning to her role as a deputy director, commissioners said Thursday. Board chair Flavia Harton and commissioner Rip Parks resigned effective Friday, according to letters they sent to the governor, who appoints the entire board.
None of the three mentioned the recent funding vote as the reason for their decision.
SC Arts Commission refuses grant funding to 2 LGBTQ+ organizations

Harton, who joined the board in 2022, told the commission she needed more time to focus on her full-time job. Parks, who was among those opposing the grants, wrote in his letter to the governor he didn’t feel he could meet the “all-consuming time demands that I anticipate in the foreseeable future.”
Brown did not give a reason for her decision to step down, which commissioners announced during a Thursday, all-virtual meeting. The commission unanimously chose Ce Scott-Fitts, the agency’s interim senior deputy director, to take her place.
Brown “has done a great job,” Harton said. “She and I have gone through a lot of challenges during this time and a lot of learning experiences, and I have truly enjoyed working with Ashley.”
Harton, of Greenville, did not vote on the grants for the Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus and Spartanburg’s Proud Mary Theatre Company. As board chair, she votes only in the event of a tie, which was not the case in the 5-3 vote taken Oct. 1 to reject their applications.
Parks, who is from Easley, was one of two commissioners to write emails to commission leadership opposing funding for the organizations. He was among the five voting not to give the Gay Men’s Chorus $13,000 and the theater company nearly $4,000.
“While these organizations have every right to promote their agendas privately, it is not the role of a state funded agency to promote them,” Parks wrote in a June 12 email made public in an open records request.
The commission’s funding for LGBTQ+ artists and groups has become a target for the Legislature’s most conservative members in recent years. During budget debates, members of the House’s ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus often ask to slice the commission’s funding, describing some of its grant-funded projects as inappropriate or overly political.
What the governor said
Gov. Henry McMaster likely won’t have time to appoint replacements on the board before he leaves office at the end of the year, he told reporters earlier this week. A new governor, elected in November, will take over in January, potentially shaking up any of McMaster’s appointees.
Although McMaster could select interim members, permanent appointments require a vote in the Senate, and senators aren’t expected to return to the Statehouse until the next legislative session begins in January.
Members on the state’s dozens of citizen governing boards are often tough to keep because the work takes so much time, McMaster said. The Arts Commission’s board is unpaid.
“It’s very hard to get people to serve for free and give all their time to these various commissions, but we have to have them because we just can’t hire that many people,” McMaster said.
That’s especially true when decisions become controversial, he added. The risk of potential lawsuits or bad publicity for the members or their businesses might turn people away from wanting to serve on boards, he said.
In this case, the decision not to fund the two LGBTQ+ organizations drew pushback from the state’s American Civil Liberties Union, which sent a letter to the board saying the decision might violate the First Amendment and open the commission up to lawsuits.
McMaster said he didn’t know whether that directly led board members to resign, adding he hadn’t spoken with either of the resigning commissioners as of Tuesday.
“I wish they’d stayed, because they were good people,” McMaster said.
Funding for ‘ideology’
Questions over what the board should or shouldn’t put money toward arose again Thursday as commissioners talked about grants for artists early in their careers.
This time, concern came not from artists’ sexual identity but whether their work might violate a resolution the board passed in August banning grant funding for work promoting any sort of ideology.
When awarding funds, the resolution requires evaluators to “disfavor any projects that promote any ideology without distinction as to the content or nature of the promoted ideology,” without defining what that might look like.
Board members did not give a reason for the resolution before passing it, though it states that “in recent years controversies have arisen across the United States regarding public funding of endeavors that promote ideologies.”
Some lawmakers call SC Arts Commission funding a ‘waste.’ Supporters say it’s essential.

Jace Woodrum, director of the state ACLU, called the resolution vague and a way of “attempting to silence ideas” board members disagree with.
“All art conveys ideas — and if an arts commission doesn’t support art about ideas, it doesn’t support art at all,” Woodrum said in a statement soon after the resolution passed.
Parks called one artist’s work up for consideration Thursday “pure political ideology,” without elaborating on what part of it he felt was too political.
“I don’t see the artistic merit,” Parks said of the work.
The artist, Shakira Olivera-Bautista, graduated from Furman University in 2025 and specializes in oil painting, though she also dabbles in mixed media, photography and other forms of illustration, according to her website.
“My artistic practice is rooted in the identity, heritage, and emotional landscape of the Latinx community,” Olivera-Bautista’s website reads. She did not respond to a call requesting comment.
The Arts Commission declined to release the samples of her work the board saw before voting. Spokesperson Jason Rapp said the commission doesn’t make applications public unless the artist has been awarded and accepted a grant.
The commission unanimously declined to award Olivera-Bautista the $1,800 grant.

name: VTDigger
title: Barre wins flood recovery funds for long-awaited North End housing
text:
The playground at Wobby Park in Barre City’s North End will be redeveloped into 17 townhomes. Photo by David Littlefield / Vermont Public 
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
A few months after flooding devastated Barre City in 2023, Gov. Phil Scott unveiled a bold vision for redeveloping his hometown. Buildings near the river in the city’s hard-hit North End neighborhood would be demolished and converted back to a floodplain, and hundreds of new homes would be built on higher ground.
But recovery efforts in the neighborhood stalled as the Republican governor’s plan sat on ice for years – even as another flood inundated the area. 
Three years onward, Scott returned to Barre on Thursday to announce that a scaled-down version of North End redevelopment is now moving forward. City leaders say it’s just a first step. 
“It isn’t as grand as I had originally hoped, but it’s still going to be impactful to this region and this part of the city, in particular,” Scott said at a press conference marking the occasion. 

Gov. Phil Scott speaks at a press conference in Barre on Thursday to announce the award of funding for a flood recovery project in the city’s North End. Photo by Carly Berlin / Vermont Public

State officials have awarded the city $4.2 million for a housing development on city-owned land just outside the flood zone, combined with several flood buyouts of properties nearby. The funding represents the last allotment of Vermont’s nearly $68 million tranche of federal disaster recovery money approved by Congress in late 2024.  
The city-owned land is currently a playground and park located next to Barre’s public safety complex. The city plans to sell the land, known as Wobby Park, to housing developers for one dollar, according to Barre City Mayor Thom Lauzon. The developers, local contractors Trym Chouinard and Eric Lajeunesse, plan to build 17 townhomes there. 
Two commercial and one residential property across the street will be bought out and torn down, restoring the area to green space, according to the state’s funding award. The city will then create a new park at that site to replace the one where the future homes will go, Lauzon said.  
The 17 homes will be sold at subsidized prices, a requirement of this type of long-range federal disaster recovery funding. The target for-sale price is $270,000, according to Chouinard. Qualified buyers will also receive down payment assistance, he said, though details on the amount of aid are still being finalized.
The two-bedroom homes will be constructed in an East Montpelier factory by modular homebuilder Huntington Homes. Chouinard expects to break ground in May 2027 and wrap up construction next summer. 

Two properties on North Main Street in Barre that are slated for buyouts with federal flood recovery funding. Photo by David Littlefield / Vermont Public

The city has been trying to court a housing development on the relatively high ground of Wobby Park for years. The nonprofit developer Downstreet eyed building three or four homes there in 2024 but ultimately didn’t move forward. 
The city applied for the federal disaster funds twice previously for the area, with a focus on paying for buyouts and increased flood storage, Lauzon said. Once they added more housing to their application, they were approved on their third try.
Vermont’s $68 million in federal recovery funds have offered a rare opportunity to help build new housing outside of the state’s most flood-prone areas. While the Federal EmergencyManagement Agency’s aid programs generally require a homeowner to repair their damaged home, for instance, or buy them out with no guarantee of an available home to move into, these more flexible funds can allow a community to create homes where they didn’t exist before. 
The state has allocated the funding toward building out infrastructure to support new homes on higher ground in Plainfield and Montpelier, renovating a vacant Vermont State University building in Johnson into housing, and replacing a bridge in Cabot to better accommodate rising waters, among other projects. Two other housing projects in Barre also received funds.
One of the epicenters of flood damage in recent years, Barre has struggled with how to bolster its tax base as flooded properties get torn down. Twenty-eight Barre City properties have already gone through the buyout process and more are underway, said Central Vermont Recovery Officer Patricia Moulton at Thursday’s press conference. 

Second Street in Barre’s North End after flooding in July 2024, one year after historic floods hit the area. Photo by Peter Hirschfeld / Vermont Public 

The federal recovery funding is expected to support the construction of about 139 new homes in the city overall, Scott said. The new homes won’t specifically be earmarked for people displaced by the floods, though disaster case managers will help connect flood survivors to the new options, said Chief Recovery Officer Douglas Farnham.
Lauzon, the mayor, emphasized that the new townhomes in the old park are only the first phase of redeveloping the area.
“We probably need to replicate this project four or five more times in order to bring meaningful recovery to the North End,” he said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Hospital’s lawsuit alleges patient-poaching by doctor, rival health system
text:
RWJBarnabas Health, which owns Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital in New Brunswick, is accused in a new lawsuit of colluding with a doctor and using confidential information to lure patients away from Saint Peter’s University Hospital. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Saint Peter’s Healthcare System is suing a doctor and a competing health system alleging they conspired to divert patients and lucrative medical procedures away from the New Brunswick hospital, endangering its financial future.
In a lawsuit filed in Superior Court in Middlesex County on Wednesday, Saint Peter’s claims that Dr. Maureen Cernadas illegally used her power as the head of a busy regional OBGYN practice and information she obtained as a Saint Peter’s board member to plot with RWJBarnabas Health, one of the state’s largest hospital systems, to lure patients away from Saint Peter’s to a Barnabas hospital nearby.
Saint Peter’s alleges that Cernadas and Barnabas had access to critical information about the financial importance that referrals from Cernadas’ practice had on the Saint Peter’s bottom line. This information, collected as a result of discussions about a potential merger between the two systems that was blocked by the Federal Trade Commission in 2022, was supposed to remain confidential, the suit claims.
According to the lawsuit, Barnabas sought to “target” the most “economically important area of care” at Saint Peter’s to jeopardize its future. Referrals and hospital-based care associated with Cernadas and her associates generated roughly $28 million for Saint Peter’s in 2025, it says.
“As part of this scheme, the health care giant set out to acquire Saint Peters’ surgical and delivery practices by poaching the Brunswick Hills practice headed by Dr. Cernadas, and exploiting Dr. Cernadas’ position on Saint Peters’ Board to steer Saint Peters’ patients to Barnabas Health,” the lawsuit says.
Barnabas operates a slew of hospitals in central and northern New Jersey, including Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital, a teaching hub for Rutgers University’s clinical programs that sits just a mile from Saint Peter’s University Hospital. Saint Peter’s has just one hospital, the one in New Brunswick, that is respected for its maternal healthcare.
George Helmy, executive vice president for RWJBarnabas Health, said the company has not sought or used any confidential Saint Peter’s information and said the allegations in the lawsuit are meritless.
“Where a mother chooses to deliver her baby is a deeply personal decision, made in consultation with the physician she trusts. Physicians are free to choose where they practice, and patients are free to seek care where they choose. We are proud that more families and providers entrust their care to RWJBarnabas Health, New Jersey’s academic health system, every day,” Helmy said in a statement.
A call and email to attorneys representing Cernadas in a separate matter were not returned Thursday.
Cernadas led a practice called Brunswick Hills OB/GYN that referred patients to Saint Peter’s to deliver babies, for surgeries, or for other hospital treatments, according to the lawsuit. She was also on staff at Saint Peter’s for three decades, it says, and held leadership positions there since 2019. In 2023, she became a member of the health system’s board.
The Saint Peter’s merger negotiations with Barnabas began in 2019, according to the lawsuit, and both sides exchanged detailed financial and operational information and signed a mutual confidentiality agreement that is still binding.
Starting in 2024, Cernadas began “covert discussions” with Barnabas about redirecting her referrals from Saint Peter’s to Robert Wood Johnson hospital, the suit claims.
The following year she sent a letter to a handful of patients suggesting she would be transitioning to the Barnabas system, a letter the lawsuit alleges was “intended to sow doubt and confusion” about the quality of care at Saint Peter’s.
While Cernadas continued to tell Saint Peter’s leaders she was not leaving, she took additional steps to align with Barnabas, the suit claims.
In the spring of 2026 she visited staff at Saint Peter’s with bagels, doughnuts, and flyers to advertise a new practice she was forming with eight other doctors from Brunswick Hills, a group that said it planned to refer patients to Barnabas starting next year, according to the suit.
Saint Peter’s is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, attorney fees, and more.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Superintendent candidates debate teacher bonuses, classroom tech, funding public schools
text:
North Dakota Superintendent Levi Bachmeier, left, and superintendent candidate Tracy Foss, right, check the camera locations next to Plain Talk Podcast hosts Rob Port, center-left and Chad Oban, center-right, at Bismarck State College on Oct. 13, 2026, before beginning their debate for superintendent for the Department of Public Instruction. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Candidates for superintendent of the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction discussed teacher bonuses, tech in the classroom and funding public schools during a debate this week.
The debate hosted by Plain Talk Podcast co-hosts Rob Port and Chad Oban featured Superintendent Levi Bachmeier, a former business manager for West Fargo Public Schools who is running in his first statewide election, and Tracy Foss, a teacher with more than two decades of classroom experience from middle school to college students.
Teacher bonuses
Bachmeier said a proposal to provide teachers annual bonuses spearheaded by himself and Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, is a step to addressing the state’s teacher shortage.
“I’ll be the first to say that money does not solve every problem,” Bachmeier said. 



He said high schoolers have told him during his school district trips across the state that teacher pay is one of the biggest barriers for them in choosing a career in education. Bachmeier said teachers make about 20% less in North Dakota than other careers that require bachelor’s degrees.
“I think we have an obligation to do something,” Bachmeier said. “This isn’t a silver bullet, but I think it’s a meaningful step to solve, what I think is probably one of the biggest issues facing education in North Dakota, and that is ensuring that every kid in our state has a quality teacher standing in the front of the classroom.”
The bonus program would require approval from the 2027 Legislature.
Annual bonuses proposed for North Dakota teachers to improve recruitment, retention

Foss said the bonus proposal is “a start” to stem the outflow of teachers from the career field, but she said pay isn’t the only reason educators are leaving.
She cited a 2023 North Dakota United survey that listed burnout and heavy workloads as major contributors to teachers leaving the profession.
“Teachers’ plates aren’t overflowing; they are breaking,” Foss said. 
Foss added the bonus program wouldn’t guarantee financial stability. She said a North Dakota teacher’s average wage is about $60,000 while minimum living wage is $65,000. She added a teacher’s starting pay in North Dakota is about $45,000.
“We also need to focus on, not just giving them a bonus for a little while, but really working on getting them the salaries that will get them up to being financially stable,” Foss said.
State funding
Both candidates agreed that state funding for school districts has lagged in recent years. 
Bachmeier, appointed to the job in October 2025, said the percentage of the state budget going to K-12 education has decreased over the last several years. He said state support for schools has not kept up with inflation, in part because schools received one-time federal funding during the COVID-19 pandemic that has since dried up.
“Now our schools are hurting,” Bachmeier said.
Foss said the state should have planned better for the expiration of federal funding.
Superintendent candidate Tracy Foss speaks during a Oct. 13, 2026 debate at Bismarck State College. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“We should have known that that money was going to dry up, and we probably should have had a backup plan by this time to figure out how were we going to make up that money,” she said.
Bachmeier said he didn’t disagree.
The state constitution requires the state to provide free public education, Foss said. Without adequate support, schools don’t have enough paraprofessionals or bus drivers and teachers spend $1,000 a year on supplies. It also shows up in local discussions about keeping music and art programs in the district.
She advocates for providing state funding to K-12 schools at a level that does not require school boards and administrators to make tough decisions every year.
Superintendent candidate Foss supports teacher bonuses as temporary fix, not long-term solution

“We should be giving them enough money to fund the services of what it means to be a school,” Foss said.
Tech in schools
During the 2025 legislative session, lawmakers banned the use of cellphones in schools during the school day. Lawmakers are expected to debate the use of other technology, such as laptops and tablets in the classroom, during the legislative session that begins in January.
Foss said she supports locking up cellphones during the school day, but she has noticed some students appearing to have withdrawal from their personal devices.
“We need to do a better job of educating parents and guardians about how these devices are actually affecting the way students think,” she said. 
Any new policy on laptop use in the classroom should find a balance between what is educationally beneficial and what feeds into the addictive nature of technology, Foss said. She added limiting or prohibiting use for younger students should be considered.
Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier speaks during a Oct. 13, 2026, debate at Bismarck State College. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Bachmeier said technology is “creating an addiction” with many young people. A positive impact of the cellphone ban is that lunch rooms are loud again across North Dakota.
“Students are asking to learn how to play card games from teachers,” he said. 
An outright ban of technology in the classroom would be a disservice to students, Bachmeier said, because they will be using technology in college, the military and in the workforce.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
“I think we certainly need to be more skeptical of it,” he said. Lawmakers should consider some reasonable guardrails when they discuss the issue, Bachmeier added.
Any technology policy would need to balance letting school districts control their curriculum locally while addressing student health as a statewide wellness issue, he said.
Bachmeier identifies as a Republican, but did not seek a letter of support from the North Dakota Republican Party during the primary. Foss received a letter of support from the Democratic-NPL Party during its state convention in March and is running in her first statewide election.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CSCU launches a way to track reforms after harassment scandal
text:
The Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system announced it will undertake a series of reforms following the resignation of former interim Chancellor John Maduko in April over sexual harassment allegations.
Those reforms are free to view on the system’s new accountability dashboard, CSCU in Focus, which CSCU spokesperson Sam Norton presented at the Board of Regents meeting on Thursday. So far, there are nine reforms listed, most of which deal with updating various CSCU policies and trainings regarding sexual harassment.
Norton said in a text that the office of interim chancellor Natalie Braswell and the Board of Regents developed the reforms.
The proposed changes are a direct response to a September report from Grand River Solutions, which reviewed CSCU’s handling of the allegations against Maduko. The review found CSCU had systematically failed to support individuals affected by Maduko’s behavior, lacked clear processes for addressing sexual harassment complaints and allowed private information to leak, enabling instances of possible retaliation.
As of Thursday afternoon, the system had already completed one of the nine reforms: adoption of discriminatory harassment, nondiscrimination and Title IX policy. That step was completed at the Board of Regents meeting itself.
The reforms yet to be completed include:

Amending the Title IX policy to provide greater clarity to CSCU members
New and amended executive appointment policies
Reporting obligations training
Sexual harassment prevention training
Personnel actions in response to the Grand River Solutions report
Developing onboarding and ongoing training for Board of Regents members
Recurring system-wide communications on employee rights and responsibilities
Governance and organizational reform to strengthen accountability and oversight

In a press release, Norton wrote CSCU expects to present a “formal policy codifying the enhanced vetting process” for leadership roles “by the end of the fall 2026 semester.”
CSCU faculty members in attendance at Thursday’s board meeting expressed deep dissatisfaction with how the system has been operating. Kari Swanson, an associate librarian at Southern CT State and the president of that school’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, expressed shock at the findings in the Grand River Solutions report.
“I and many other faculty members expect that those who were derelict in their responsibilities will be held accountable,” Swanson said, noting that, while the allegations against Maduko prompted some resignations, many others who held leadership roles at the time remain. That includes now-interim chair Ari Santiago, who first joined the Board of Regents in 2020.
At one point in the meeting, Colena Sesanker, a philosophy professor at Gateway Community College and chair of the board’s Faculty Advisory Committee, interrupted proceedings to read a faculty resolution calling on the system to halt its search for a new chancellor “until we have a better understanding of how the system works.”
Sesanker said she had to interrupt because the Faculty Advisory Committee does not have an agenda item for regular Board of Regents meetings. Santiago acknowledged her concerns but said they would still have to table the resolution because there was no agenda item.
During public comment, David Blitz, professor emeritus at Central Connecticut State University, reiterated Sesanker’s frustration and called for sweeping changes to CSCU.
“Major structural reforms are needed, perhaps including splitting the system into separate university and college systems,” Blitz said. Alternatively, he said, a “bottom-up approach based on the constituent universities and colleges” would be better than the system’s current top-down model.
Republican Sens. Stephen Harding, Henri Martin and Jeff Gordon released a brief statement following Thursday’s board meeting. The senators did not address the nine reforms listed but called on Braswell to appoint an independent party to investigate allegations against former Central Connecticut State University president Zulma Toro, who recently resigned.
Rep. Greg Haddad, D-Mansfield, who co-chairs the General Assembly Higher Education and Employment Committee, said the reforms were “a good first step” but said the legislature needs to reevaluate whether the leadership structure of CSCU, first created in 2011, is working.
“I am deeply skeptical that the changes that were adopted in 2011 have worked,” Haddad said. “I’m just not sure that that system has achieved any of its desired outcomes.”
He added, “I think that we should look very closely at what is going wrong there and come up with an alternative structure if we think that more modest reforms aren’t going to be effective.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Mixed reception in Trenton for union-backed bill to revamp school health benefits
text:
Teachers union officials have a plan to help fix the state-run health benefits plan for school workers. Critics say it needs more work. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)hA proposal to shift public health plans for school workers to a new trust where state officials play a lesser role in governance received a mixed reception during discussion before a Senate panel Thursday.
Though union officials who back the bill said its changes are needed to maintain health coverage, groups representing school boards and school administrators, among others, warned that the proposal would do too little to rein in rising health insurance costs.
“You can put a new name on the box. You can give it a gold-plated guarantee, but you don’t fix what’s inside the box, you’ve just made a prettier box. The bill as proposed right now is a prettier box,” said Patrick Duncan, legislative co-chair for New Jersey Statewide Recruitment of Visionary Educators. “There’s really not the material, significant changes that are needed to control the costs going forward.”
The bill discussed before the Senate’s state government committee would sunset plans under the School Employees Health Benefits Program and require all school districts to join new plans run by a trust the bill would create.
It comes as public plans for school and local government workers swirl in a death spiral, riven by years of departures prompted by steep premium hikes that have left their risk pools increasingly smaller and sicker, driving up costs for units that remain and pushing more to seek cheaper options in the private market.
The bill’s supporters said mandating membership in the trust plan would stabilize risk pools and bring down rates for school districts facing the worst of the increases while boosting purchasing power across the board, potentially enough to bring down healthcare costs for units that already moved away from the public option.
“You’re probably going to hear people say there’ll be winners and losers in this pool. There’ll be winners, but I’m not too sure there’s going to be a loser in this pool because when you have a pool, it doesn’t mean you have to pay the same amount,” said Kevin Kelleher, executive director of teachers union the New Jersey Education Association. “I’m in a car insurance pool. My car insurance is different than my neighbor’s, but we both have the same insurance company.”
But forcing school districts to join the proposed new plan is opposed by some districts whose premiums would likely rise if they joined a risk pool formed of all public education workers across the state.
Elizabeth Ginsburg, executive director of the Garden State Coalition of Schools, which represents close to 100 New Jersey school districts, said the bill relies on the provision too heavily and would be better served by limiting districts’ ability to freely move in and out of state plans.
The new plan would effectively be the current plan “cloaked in a shiny new outfit that is secured by only one giant safety pin: the compulsory district participation,” Ginsburg said.
“It is imperative districts be able to leave the state plan if they can find more cost-effective coverage elsewhere,” she said.
The bill’s extension of salary-based premiums for school workers also poses a problem, detractors said.
They warned that a 2020 law, known as chapter 44, that set school workers’ health premiums to a percentage of their salaries eliminated incentives for unions to negotiate to reduce costs, at least until districts’ healthcare burdens became dire enough to prompt layoffs.
“While chapter 44 has indeed delivered a tremendous amount of financial relief for employees, it did nothing to produce long-term savings for boards of education and taxpayers, which have been forced to absorb nearly all of the increase in premiums,” said Jonathan Pushman, senior director of advocacy at the New Jersey School Boards Association.
Union officials indicated they were willing to cede some ground and insisted they already had in some cases.
The premium levels set by chapter 44 were a starting point for negotiations, unions said, and the bill discussed Thursday would allow the 10-member board overseeing the trust to alter the percentage of a worker’s salary that went to health premiums. Still, unions said the bill should be amended to make that flexibility more apparent.
“We’ve been asked: Can they negotiate the plan value? Well, yes, they can. Can they negotiate the percentage of salary? Well, yes, they can, but it’s not said explicitly,” said Deb Cornavaca, director of government relations for the New Jersey Education Association. “So for some of our partners who seem unsure of what the scope is, we feel that being a little more explicit would be helpful.”
Other changes to the bill should ensure the trust’s fiduciary duty is applied to the plan’s health as well as to its beneficiaries, witnesses on both sides said.
Cornavaca added the board’s makeup, which would be split evenly between labor and management, should change somewhat to reflect school supervisors’ and principals’ labor status. They’re currently counted among the board’s management members.
The bill isn’t the only plan percolating to rework health benefits for public workers. Gov. Mikie Sherrill has convened a working group to weigh changes to the State Health Benefits Program. That group’s first meeting is Friday.

name: VTDigger
title: Expenses for EB-5 mop up total $14 million as judge OKs $1 million more in fees
text:
Michael Goldberg, the court-appointed receiver in the EB-5 fraud case, speaks at a Statehouse news conference in 2017. File photo by Michael Dougherty/VTDigger

More than $14 million in legal and financial expenses have been rung up over 10 years since the largest investor fraud scandal in Vermont’s history, according to an Oct. 9 court filing by the receiver overseeing properties in the Northeast Kingdom that were engulfed in the scheme.
Michael Goldberg, the court-appointed receiver, submitted a new request seeking $1,017,849 to help with the latest costs and expenses, including help from accounting and immigration experts.  
The new request covers the fees and expenses from May 1, 2025, to Aug. 31 of this year.  
Federal Judge Darrin P. Gayles, who has presided over the receivership since it began in April 2016, this week approved Goldberg’s latest expense and fee request. 
Goldberg wrote in his filing that along with other financial and legal professionals, he has been working on “winding down” the receivership with the goal of closing it out as soon as the end of the year.
He could not be reached Thursday for comment.
Goldberg was named the receiver in April 2016 when state and federal regulators leveled civil investor fraud enforcement actions against Ariel Quiros, then Jay Peak’s owner, and Bill Stenger, the resort’s former CEO and president.
Quiros and Stenger, as well as Bill Kelly, a key adviser to Quiros, all later reached plea deals with federal prosecutors on criminal charges and served jail time in connection with one of the EB-5 projects, a more than $100 million biomedical research facility proposed for Newport, known as AnC Bio Vermont.
According to filings from the state and federal regulators, the developers misused hundreds of millions of investor dollars raised through the EB-5 visa program, which was designed to reward foreign investors with green cards or permanent U.S. residency in exchange for putting money into qualified projects in the country.
The investments were to pay for massive upgrades at Jay Peak and Burke Mountain ski areas and additional projects in other communities in northern Vermont, including the proposed biomedical facility in Newport.
Some of the projects materialized, but later ones ran into financial trouble when authorities said the “Ponzi-like” scheme began to fall apart. 
The receivership case was brought in federal court in Florida because that was where Quiros was living at the time the civil enforcement actions were filed.
Money to pay for Goldberg’s requested fees and expenses comes from previous sales of properties, including the resorts, as well as legal monetary settlements reached over the years.
Last year, the receiver oversaw the $11.5 million sale of Burke Mountain Resort to Bear Den Partners LLC, a group of people with longtime ties to the ski area. 

READ MORE

That transaction followed the sale of Jay Peak Resort in 2022 to Pacific Group Resorts Inc., based in Park City, Utah, for $76 million.
In 2017, Goldberg reached a nearly $150 million settlement with Raymond James & Associates Inc., a financial institution that federal regulators said Quiros had used to carry out fraudulent transactions.
This summer, Goldberg agreed to sell off the last receivership property, land in downtown Newport known as “the pit,” for $1.1 million.
According to Goldberg’s latest court filing, the receivership in the past few months has been working on that Newport sale. In addition, Goldberg wrote, he has been assisting foreign investors whose green cards were put in jeopardy by the fraud.
A breakdown of Goldberg’s latest billing request shows $996,370 to cover professional fees and $21,478 for expenses, bringing the total to $1,017,849.
