name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Eversource files appeal of PURA’s storm costs decision
text:
Eversource filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging state regulators’ decision to cut more than $500 million from the company’s reimbursement for responding to a series of powerful storms in Connecticut. 
The lawsuit, which was filed in Superior Court in New Britain, claims that the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority ignored state law and its own precedent by rejecting the company’s request to be paid interest on the costs it incurred responding to storms, while waiting several years for regulators to determine whether those expenses were necessary.
Because Eversource had to finance the cost of its storm-related expenditures, the lawsuit argued the company is now entitled to recoup that interest.
“The ramifications of this appeal are significant and will help to provide clarity regarding the legal principles which dictate our ability to finance storm cost recovery for customers who demand that their power be restored as fast as possible with minimal interruption,” Eversource spokeswoman Jamie Ratliff said in a statement Thursday. 
The lawsuit also challenged PURA’s decision to cut roughly $7.7 million in crew costs from Eversource’s reimbursement, which the company said was based on faulty methodology.
A spokesperson for PURA declined to comment on Thursday.
PURA reached its decision in the storm costs case in July, approving more than 90% of Eversource’s request to be reimbursed for nearly $1 billion worth of expenses that the company said it incurred while responding to dozens of “catastrophic” storms between 2018 and 2023. Those storms, which each cost the company more than $4 million, are treated differently than smaller, more routine storms, which Eversource is expected to respond to using money from its base rates.
While PURA sided with Eversource in allowing most of those expenses to be reimbursed, regulators denied the company’s request to be paid an additional $400 million in interest while the case was adjudicated. (PURA also cut about $100 million in actual expenditures from Eversource’s reimbursement, though some of those costs may be recovered in the future if the company provides additional supporting evidence.)
The decision further said that Eversource is only entitled to earn interest on storm costs once those expenses have been reviewed and deemed prudent — meaning from the date of the final agency’s final decision until the costs are actually repaid.
In a statement on Thursday, Attorney General William Tong said that Eversource itself was to blame for the long wait in getting paid for its storm costs. 
Eversource filed its initial request for reimbursement in 2023, several years after the earliest expenses in the case were incurred. Tong said the company then dragged its feet responding to questions about those costs from his office and the Office of Consumer Counsel, filing motions for extensions that resulted in more than 1,000 additional days of delay. 
“The workers who restore our power following catastrophic storms deserve compensation and gratitude — that is without doubt,” Tong said in a statement. “PURA was right to approve those costs. But that wasn’t enough for Eversource. This fight is about hundreds of millions of dollars in unjustified interest payments for years where they had never even asked for recovery. In the real world, when kids hand in late homework, they don’t get bonus points. We’re going to fight this appeal with everything we’ve got to ensure Connecticut families aren’t stuck paying this outrageous, unaffordable and unjustified demand.”
Claire Coleman, who heads the OCC, also criticized Eversource’s decision to file an appeal of PURA’s final decision despite receiving the majority of its request. Her office, she noted, sought an additional $171 million in cuts based on its review of Eversource’s expenses.
“At a time when families are struggling to pay their monthly electric bills and make ends meet, Eversource seems more interested in bleeding customers dry and draining state resources than accepting the outcome of a three-year regulatory review,” Coleman said in a statement. “Instead of moving forward and focusing on serving customers, Eversource is choosing to bankroll costly, meritless appeals, diverting time and attention from the critical work of addressing Connecticut’s energy affordability challenges.” 
During a call with investors last month, Eversource chief executive Joe Nolan said he was “very, very pleased” with PURA’s decision to approve the vast majority of the company’s expenditures in the storm costs case. He also signaled that the company would continue its fight over interest payments, or “carrying charges.”
“Listen, we asked for these carrying charges, carrying charges are important,” Nolan said. “We feel they owe us the money, and that’s not over yet.”
The storm costs case is separate from Eversource’s request for a double-digit rate increase, which remains pending before PURA.
However, Eversource has sought to finalize its storm costs in time to allow those charges to enter customers’ bills around the same time that new rates go into effect next July. As a result of a new law passed by the Connecticut legislature in 2025, utility companies are allowed to “securitize” their storm costs, essentially borrowing money at low interest rates in order to lessen the impact on customers.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma CareerTech system requests budget increase of $73.37 million
text:
State CareerTech Director Brent Haken, center, leads a meeting of the state CareerTech board on Thursday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s system for vocational education has asked for $255 million in state funding for the next fiscal year to add support for career training and adult learning programs.
The governing board for the Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education approved the request Thursday for the 2028 fiscal year.
If granted in full, it would represent a $73.37 million budget increase for the state CareerTech system, shrinking waitlists for job training programs, supporting middle and high school courses, and adding funds for adult education.
The request now goes to the Oklahoma Legislature. Lawmakers will consider it along with other state agencies’ needs as they craft a state budget during the 2027 legislative session, which begins in February.
The CareerTech board similarly asked for a major funding hike last year, but its request was largely discarded.
State CareerTech Director Brent Haken said he’s more optimistic this year. The two leading candidates for governor, Republican Mike Mazzei and Democrat Cyndi Munson, have given vocal support for CareerTech programs, generating the “most positive discussion I’ve heard since I’ve been here,” said Haken, who took office in 2023.
“The reason why is because (the candidates) always couple that with their discussions of, ‘We have to support business and industry,’” Haken said. “If we’re going to support business and industry, they have to have a workforce, and so, they’ve been very positive in linking those two things together.”
The largest piece of the $73.37 million increase is a proposal for $27.65 million in additional funds for postsecondary workforce training. Haken said this would whittle down an 11,000-student waitlist for job training programs and would support apprenticeships.
The smallest ask for an increase is $3.72 million and a $750,000 supplemental appropriation to cover the rising cost of CareerTech employees’ insurance benefits.
Another $16 million in added funds would expand CareerTech courses at the K-12 level, particularly in middle schools. While about half of all Oklahoma high school juniors and seniors have participated in a CareerTech class, only 34% of middle school students take a vocational course, Haken said.
Early exposure to career opportunities is critical in preventing high school dropouts, he said.
“We need to make them aware of what it looks like to be in a path that is trades-focused, that has direct career ties, that has great income, that is attainable pretty easily,” Haken said. “We are a high-dropout state, and a lot of that is because they don’t understand why I would stay in school. What’s it going to do for me? And so, we need to get them to understand you could go to a trades-based education, and you could be very successful without any debt, without any cost.”
State CareerTech Director Brent Haken speaks at a state CareerTech board meeting Thursday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Another $10.5 million would add more vocational classes, student organizations and certificate-granting programs in high schools, like agricultural education, family and consumer sciences, engineering, and trade and industrial courses.
There’s a waitlist of 76 such programs in K-12 districts that don’t yet have state funding, Haken said.
The $10.5 million fund also would add “more salary support” for CareerTech teachers working with K-12 students. These teachers are required to file more reports and complete more tasks than other K-12 educators.
“Those things that we require take more work on their behalf, and we need to probably give them more than $2,000 for doing that,” Haken said.
A one-time $10 million appropriation would create an incentive fund to open new CareerTech centers in parts of the state that don’t yet have one.
An additional $5.5 million in recurring funds would support adult education and family literacy programs for people age 16 or older without a high school diploma. 
These programs, which currently rely on federal funds, help students complete a high-school equivalency program, like the General Education Development test and teach, reading, math and career-readiness skills as an “on ramp” to job training or higher education, agency staff told the board before the budget vote.
The federal government withheld funds for adult education nationwide this year. That uncertainty caused some adult programs in Oklahoma to close, Haken said. Fulfilling the $5.5 million request “would be a way that Oklahoma could at least get in the game and try to participate in some way,” he said.
An initial version of the CareerTech budget plan included the $5.5 million for adult education within the $27.65 million request for postsecondary workforce training. It has since been split out as a separate budget item, raising the overall budget request.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Poll: CT voters sour on Trump and economy, an anchor on Fazio
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat with a positive job approval and a double-digit lead over Republican Ryan Fazio, appears immune to concerns over the high cost of living in Connecticut as voters direct their ire at a Republican president whose brand has become toxic in the midterm election. 
A new Wesleyan SurveyLab CT poll finds Lamont leading Fazio by 57% to 34% among likely voters, fresh evidence of the inability of the Republican challenger to exploit pocketbook concerns that typically would land at the feet of an incumbent seeking a third term. 
Instead, voters’ focus is on the Republican who has become an asset to the Democrats and a liability for the GOP: President Donald Trump, who insisted on live television Thursday outside the White House, “Our economy is, literally, we’ve never had anything like it, it’s so good.”
Trump’s job approval sank to 36% in a Fox News poll this week, a new low in the national survey. In Connecticut, it’s worse: Only 27% of those surveyed by Wesleyan approved of Trump’s performance and 70% disapproved, an anchor on Fazio and other blue-state Republicans.
“Voter pessimism about the economy seems to be driving down Trump’s approval rating in the state, which matches a nationwide trend,” said Logan Dancey, associate professor of government at Wesleyan. “Although voters are also concerned about the economy in Connecticut, it doesn’t appear to be dragging down Lamont’s approval ratings to the same extent.”
Lamont’s job performance was approved by 56% and disapproved by 37%.
The poll was designed by Wesleyan with input from The Connecticut Mirror and The Connecticut Project. It was conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 7 by YouGov and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.54 percentage points in the full sample and 4.84 points in the likely voter analysis.
The Lamont campaign moved Thursday to link Fazio to Trump in the eyes of voters as early voting opens Monday, the start of a two-week countdown to the Nov. 3 election. It released a 30-second commercial tightly reviewing Trump’s performance and a clip of Fazio saying, “I think he’s doing a good job.”
A narrator makes three statements: “Trump’s war in Iran is making gas prices skyrocket; the federal deficit is now $2 trillion; and Trump’s reckless tariffs are jacking up the price of everything.” After each statement, the spot jumps to same cut of Fazio saying, “I think he’s doing a good job.”
The Wesleyan poll found nothing matched pocketbook issues for commanding the attention of voters. Forty percent named inflation and the cost of living as the most important issue facing Connecticut, with taxes a distant second at 17%. Nothing else broke double digits.
The dominant mood on the U.S. economy is pessimism, with 70% seeing deterioration over the past year, albeit to varying degrees: 33% saw it as “somewhat worse;” 37.4% called it “much worse.”  The view of Connecticut was better, yet still concerning — about 55% saw its economy as worsening.
“Cost of living issues and expenses are top of mind for Connecticut voters,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a government professor at Wesleyan. “Affordability is far and away the top issue voters see facing the state as over 8 in every 10 think it is at least somewhat hard to earn a living wage and afford basic goods in our state.”
Only 16.6% viewed earning “a living wage” and affording “basic goods and services” as somewhat easy (14%) or very easy (2.6%.) And more than 70% say that task has gotten harder.
Not quite half of voters said that their financial situation had gotten somewhat or much worse over the last year, but the Wesleyan analysts said that masked significant variation across groups: Sixty percent of working class respondents said their situation had gotten worse, compared to 43% of middle-class respondents and 30% of upper-class respondents. 
“More strikingly,” the analysts said, “25% of working-class respondents said their personal financial situation had gotten ‘much worse,’ compared to 7% of middle class respondents and 1% upper class respondents.”
Fazio, 36, a state senator from Greenwich elected five years ago, has campaigned heavily on those issues, promising to cut electric rates by eliminating most programs currently financed by the public benefits charge on electric bills. The Wesleyan poll is the fifth public survey of the governor’s race in recent weeks, all showing Lamont with comfortable leads.
Fazio proposes tax cuts that he says would return $2,000 to $2,500 annually to middle-class families by 2031. To finance that relief, Fazio says he would cut annual spending by more than $1.2 billion and borrowing by another $500 million, steps Democrats say would force cuts in vital services.
“We are running on specific plans that will provide thousands of dollars of economic relief for the average middle-class family in my first term and build on that work in a second term,” Fazio said at a campaign stop Wednesday. “We can make the state affordable. We can create opportunity. That’s my message to voters.” 
The governor has countered with a campaign noting that Connecticut has achieved fiscal stability since he took office with a string of budget surpluses that have filled the state’s budget reserve to its statutory maximum and paid down an funded pension liability.
Fazio was asked at Wednesday how he can compete with the president for the attention of voters and counter a string of polls indicating the public blames Trump for the economy, not the governor.
“We have a unique cost of living crisis in Connecticut that requires a change in state policy in order to make Connecticut affordable,” Fazio replied. “You can’t blame it on anyone else that the governor raised taxes on food, that the governor raised taxes on online purchases, that the governor raised payroll taxes, that the governor raised hidden taxes and fees in the electric bill.”
Less than two hours later, Quinnipiac University released a poll showing Lamont leading, 58% to 38%, with 29% disapproving of Trump’s performance. It also found that Lamont scored best among voters who identified the economy and cost of living as their most important issues.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Elections Commission to send clerk guidance on law enforcement at polls
text:
The polling site at Madison's Wil-Mar community center during Wisconsin's 2026 spring election. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin ExaminerThe Wisconsin Elections Commission voted Thursday to send a memo to clerks across the state with guidance for what they should do if local, state or federal law enforcement shows up at polling places. 
WEC discussed the guidance as fears have risen across the country that President Donald Trump could send armed federal agents to polling places in an effort to intimidate voters. 
The agency’s administrator, Meagan Wolfe, said at the commission’s Thursday morning meeting that “we don’t expect anything unusual at the polls on Election Day.” 
“We expect voters to have the same experience that they’ve had at previous elections, and so by no means are we looking to make anybody feel panicked or anything about this,” Wolfe said. “But clerks are asking very directly for this type of information because they are getting hundreds of emails from voters and from groups asking, ‘Do you have a plan if these sorts of things were to happen?’ And so I see this just like any other contingency planning that we do to assist our clerks.” 
The memo to be sent to clerks notes that unless law enforcement officials are conducting a legitimate law enforcement activity or casting their own ballots, they generally shouldn’t be at the polls. If they are, the memo states, officers are subject to the same rules as any other election observer. Armed federal agents and the military are not allowed at polling places. 
The guidance says that if agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security or the FBI show up at the polls, poll workers should immediately notify the municipal and county clerks and WEC staff. 
The commissioners noted that in many communities across the state, local law enforcement regularly checks in with election staff to make sure there aren’t any problems. Commissioner Ann Jacobs said it’s preferable if that’s done by plainclothes officers, because that’s less intimidating than a uniformed officer with a gun and bulletproof vest on. 
Republican Commissioner Robert Spindell said he was worried the guidance would depress turnout. 
“It seems to me that the Democrats are worried about federal agents showing up at some of these polling places, and you know, obviously, to instruct the clerks what to do if they do,” he said. “But I think this guidance is only going to scare away some people from the polls when they, when this law enforcement guidance hits the news. I think it will, and I personally think this guidance is unnecessary, as we have not seemed to have needed this for the last 201 years.”

name: VTDigger
title: Don’t pour more money into a broken healthcare system
text:
Dear Editor,
Every attempt at public involvement in healthcare in Vermont in the last 25 years has not only failed, but left Vermont with some of the highest-cost healthcare and insurance in the world — though not the best outcomes.
The public explanations for this situation appear to be tired bull: We are older and sicker and get less money from the government. Until we can publicly explain this train wreck and get some accountability, I would be extraordinarily reluctant to shovel more money into a clearly broken system. What would happen here? I hate to say it, but it wouldn’t be rainbows and unicorns and lollipops — the Vermont hospital monopoly would problem-solve how to maintain a death grip on the market, spend millions of our dollars to maintain it, and deliver inaccessible care while charging higher prices than nearly anywhere in the country.  

READ MORE

The universal care folks need to explain what the hell happened in the last two decades and why it won’t happen again.  And no, so-called administrative savings don’t cut it. I just don’t trust the system not to return to its default setting: “Those with the money make the rules.”
Roger BrownRichmond, Vt.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hospital’s pediatric-unit ambulance driver faces child pornography charges
text:
(Photo via Getty Images, logo courtesy of the State of Iowa)An Iowa City paramedic who allegedly drove an ambulance for the pediatric unit of the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics is now facing child pornography charges.
Kanrry Kang, 24, of Iowa City, is charged with five counts of felony possession of items depicting sex acts with a minor. Kang has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Police allege two different devices and two Gmail accounts belonging to Kang contained 50 images and 10 videos depicting minors. In describing the images and videos, the police report states that “some were toddlers, and some were bondage.”
In an application for a search warrant, an Iowa City police officer told the court that in November 2025, he was assigned to investigate a tip that was received through the Iowa Internet Crimes Against Children online portal. The tip was “from the software/social media company Google,” the application stated.
“Google advised the user (of an account) had uploaded four images between May 30, 2025, and November 6, 2025,” the application stated, adding Google also provided the “actual files containing the offending media.”
In a separate warrant application, Detective Tiffany Lord of the Iowa City Police Department told the court the images appeared to have been uploaded by Kang, who worked for Midwest Medical Transport, company that has a contract with the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics for ambulance service.
Lord told the court she then spoke to a UIHC employee who said Kang drove an ambulance for the hospital’s pediatric unit at one time. Lord said she later received data from Kang’s Google account that included images of Kang’s driver’s license, Social Security card, job applications and the images that were part of the original tip investigated by police.
In the warrant application, Lord said she then interviewed Kang and that he acknowledged possessing the images of children while stating that “he seldom looked at adult porn.”
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services’ Bureau of Emergency Medical and Trauma Services has issued an emergency suspension of Kang’s paramedic license, citing his arrest.
A case management conference in the criminal case is now scheduled for Oct. 19, 2026.

name: California
title: This landmark California brewery was slated for closure: Instead it’s returning to its roots
text:
In summary
Stone Brewing’s Escondido site was one of many California breweries scheduled to close. Now, its original owners will revive it under a new name.


A month before its scheduled closure, Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens in Escondido got a last minute reprieve, when its original owners Greg Koch and Steve Wagner announced plans to resume operations of the landmark brewery.
“The legacy will continue,” Koch announced on Instagram. “Steve Wagner and I are taking over the restaurant and gardens at 1999 Citracado Parkway in Escondido and carrying them forward as an independent restaurant under a new name.”
The news allayed the worries of beer fans who mourned the loss of the site, with its walled gardens and extensive tap menu.
“I’m literally CRYING TEARS OF JOY” one instagram user posted.
Koch said the site will close as planned on Nov. 13, then reopen at a later date, once the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control approves the required license change. He said he and Wagner are exploring possibilities for the adjacent brewery.
“To everyone who has shared a meal, celebrated a milestone or spent an evening with friends in these gardens: we look forward to welcoming you back,” Koch wrote.
Stone Brewing, which helped popularize IPA-style beers and the craft brew movement, launched in San Diego County in 1996, and then opened its flagship location in Escondido a decade later in 2006.
The unique site served as a taproom for Stone’s signature brews, such as its Ruination IPA and Arrogant Bastard Ale: bold, higher alcohol beers that contrasted with milder, mass-produced American lagers and pilseners.
It includes a full service restaurant and sprawling grounds hidden behind a walled exterior, with tiered gardens and patios clustered around a granite koi pond and waterfall. The unique site serves as a gathering place for locals, who toast births, marriages and anniversaries there, and also draws global tourists.
“We did a pilgrimage to Escondido and Liberty Gardens a number of years back all the way from Scotland and we’d never experienced anything like it,” one person posted.
In 2022, Japanese beer-maker Sapporo bought the Stone Brand, including its production and distribution facilities, restaurants in Escondido and Liberty Station, and taprooms throughout Southern California. In April the company announced it was selling the brand to Firestone Walker, based in Paso Robles, California, and its Belgian parent company Duvel Moortgat.
But the San Diego taproom wasn’t part of the sale. In the summer, Sapporo stated it would close the site in November, filing WARN notices with the California Employment Development Department stating that it expected to lay off 272 employees, starting next week.
It was among numerous breweries throughout San Diego and California that are closing or downsizing, as the craft brew industry faces cultural changes and economic pressures.
Then on Wednesday, Francisco Vargas, economic development management analyst for the city, announced that Koch and Wagner would buy it back, preserve most of the hospitality jobs and open under a new name and brand.
The plan reflects collaboration with local economic development officials and “strong community support for preserving the Bistro & Gardens and its role in the Escondido community,” Vargas wrote in an email to CalMatters.
On social media, Stone fans peppered Koch with questions about the revamped site and offered name suggestions, such as “Hop Rocks,” “Chisel” and “Granite.” In response, Koch teased an upcoming poll of possible names.
“Will death metal still be played in the men’s room???” the very first commenter asked.
“The answer is somewhere between Yes and Hell Yes!” Koch answered, promising that “It WILL return. Louder.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Republican’s push for initiative restrictions criticized in Arkansas secretary of state debate
text:
Arkansas Secretary of State candidates Kelly Grappe (D), Sen. Kim Hammer (R), and Michael Pakko (L), meet on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 to debate at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Republican Sen. Kim Hammer defended his stances on noncitizen voting and restrictions on the state’s ballot initiative process during a televised debate against his two opponents for secretary of state Thursday.
Democrat Kelly Grappe and Libertarian Michael Pakko said during the debate on Arkansas TV that they agreed with a federal judge’s ruling that several 2025 laws restricting the initiative process Hammer sponsored are unconstitutional. 


 

 
The laws declared unconstitutional imposed requirements including that canvassers request photo ID from signers and that paid signature-gatherers’ home addresses be provided to the state. The case is under appeal.
Hammer said the ruling was “one judge’s opinion” and the purpose of the laws was to protect the state’s constitution. Grappe and Pakko disagreed.
“You don’t do that by passing laws that are unconstitutional in and of themselves,” Pakko said.
Federal judge rules Arkansas initiative restrictions unconstitutional

Arkansas is one of two dozen states that allow the public to propose and vote on their own laws and constitutional amendments. Grappe called this “a sacred right” that aligns with the state motto, Regnat Populus, Latin for “the people rule.”
“As secretary of state, I believe my job is to hold the hands of the organizations who are walking through that process,” Grappe said.
The secretary of state’s duties include overseeing elections, vetting proposed citizen-led ballot measures and keeping a database of licensed businesses. Republican Secretary of State Cole Jester is ineligible to defend the seat because he was appointed, not elected, and is running for land commissioner.
 The voter rolls

Hammer also said he plans to vote for Issue 1, or the Citizens Only Voting Amendment, which the Legislature referred to the November ballot last year.
The amendment would affirm that only U.S. citizens can vote in Arkansas. A proposed law with the same affirmation failed in the Legislature last year.
Noncitizen voting is already illegal in federal elections. It has been legalized for local elections in a few cities, but none in Arkansas.
Jester reviewed voter rolls last year and found that 0.013% of all registered voters, or 240 people, were likely noncitizens.
Hammer lost his first run for the Legislature in 2006 by more than 300 votes, and he won this year’s Republican secretary of state primary runoff by 913 votes. He said Thursday that every illegal vote disenfranchises a legally registered voter and that he would work with “everyone that has a seat at the table” to ensure only citizens are registered.

Federal appeals court upholds injunction of ‘wet signature’ rule for Arkansas voter registration

 

“Every vote matters, and if you don’t think it matters, then you’re okay with some people who are registered to vote who are not legal citizens,” Hammer said.
Pakko noted that Jester’s office did not publicly confirm how many of the 240 potential noncitizens were actually noncitizens or whether they actually voted. He and Grappe both said they oppose Issue 1.
Grappe and Pakko also said Arkansas is behind the times as one of eight states that does not allow online voter registration. Both said they would support a legislative effort in this area.
Grappe said she trusts county clerks to verify that registered voters are who they say they are. Hammer said he believes a “wet signature” — a physical signature written by hand on a paper document — is necessary for voter registration.
In March, a federal appeals court upheld an injunction prohibiting Arkansas from enforcing a 2024 rule that all voter registrations be signed in ink.

(Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Kelly Grappe (D), candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State, answers questions at the press conference following the debate at Arkansas TV studios on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Michael Pakko (L), candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State, answers questions at the press conference following the debate at Arkansas TV studios on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Sen. Kim Hammer (R), candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State, answers questions at the press conference following the debate at Arkansas TV studios on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
 Voter engagement and trust in the process

All three candidates agreed that Arkansas’ consistently low voter turnout is a problem the secretary of state must address.
Grappe said she hopes to use the secretary of state’s voter education arm to the best of its ability. She said she is already working to form a bipartisan election advisory commission made of experts who can answer questions from the public.
“We are going to get under the covers on every single piece of our electoral process to make sure that the people can trust [it] every time they go to the polls,” Grappe said.
The three candidates also discussed hand-counted paper ballots, a method of voting some conservatives have favored since the 2020 presidential election. Arkansas counties have the authority to choose their method of voting: Searcy County’s quorum court voted in 2023 to swap voting machines for paper ballots, and Independence County voters approved the same initiative in 2024.
Pakko said he does not discourage hand-counted paper ballots even though “it’s not a perfect system.”
“I’m not saying the touch-screen vote-marking devices are a problem, but some people don’t trust them, and I think it’s important that we give people the opportunity to vote in a way that they clearly know their vote is going to be counted the way they intended,” Pakko said.
Arkansas election officials debate voting machines vs. hand-counted paper ballots

A 2024 audit from Jester’s predecessor, John Thurston, revealed errors in Searcy County’s hand-counting process.
Grappe said that as secretary of state she would ensure counties are fully equipped to manage hand-counted paper ballots if they employ this method.
Hammer says the state has “an excellent paper ballot system” that includes voting machines, and he praised the state’s auditing and recount processes. A recount in several counties confirmed Hammer’s primary victory.
“That’s why we’re number one in election integrity and security,” Hammer said.

title: After a stormy week, cold arrives and much of Vermont passes peak foliage
text:
Fallen leaves cover a picnic table in Jericho Center on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This year, VTDigger is teaming up with Henry’s Weather Channel to help answer the annual question of when and where peak foliage will make its appearance across the state.
Each week, we’ll bring you an updated look at how foliage is unfolding statewide, paired with a weekend forecast, so you can plan your drive, hike or porch-sitting accordingly. Henry brings meteorological experience and on-the-ground reporting with photos and videos from across the region.

After a stormy week, trees have shed their leaves and peak foliage is in the rearview for much of Vermont. But as cold weather arrives this weekend, there are still opportunities to find color. Here’s what to know before you head out this weekend. 
Foliage forecast data courtesy of Explore Fall – https://www.explorefall.com
Waning color
Much of the state is now past peak foliage, but you just need to know where to look. Current foliage across Vermont shows past-peak color across the Green Mountains with high to peak color across the lower elevations. 
By next week, much of the state will lose its fall luster, with any high color that remains being confined to the lower valleys. Bundle up on Saturday, as winter temperatures make an appearance before we warm back up Sunday into next week.
Foliage forecast data courtesy of Explore Fall – https://www.explorefall.com

The temperatures Saturday will be around 20 degrees below average for this time of year. Low temperatures Saturday night are expected to be in the 20s. name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Pipeline spill contaminates dry creek bed in northwest North Dakota
text:
The Department of Environmental Quality does not expect there to be any downstream impacts from a produced water spill that affected a tributary of Cherry Creek in McKenzie County. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)A pipeline spill released thousands of barrels of an oilfield byproduct in McKenzie County, state regulators said Thursday. 
The pipeline operated by Tallgrass Water spilled an estimated 3,402 barrels, or 142,884 gallons, of produced water on Wednesday. Produced water is a byproduct of oil production, sometimes called saltwater or brine, that can cause significant environmental damage. 
Bill Suess, manager of the Department of Environmental Quality’s spill investigation program, said the incident is “larger than a typical spill” but far from the biggest spills in the state’s history. 
“We’re treating it as a larger spill, but I don’t anticipate this one to be a long-term cleanup,” Suess said. “It seems to be fairly isolated.”
Some of the spill flowed into the creek bed of a tributary of Cherry Creek about 10 miles southwest of Watford City, according to a press release from the Department of Environmental Quality. 
The tributary was not flowing at the time, and the agency does not anticipate any downstream impacts on Cherry Creek, Suess said. 
“This tributary is isolated right now, so they’re working to get everything pumped out of there before we get precipitation and it starts flowing,” Suess said Thursday. 
The spill has been contained and cleanup is underway. The company constructed a berm across the tributary and is pumping out the produced water. Suess said the company will move on to addressing the contamination of soil in the area next. 
An estimated 1,200 barrels, or 50,400 gallons, of produced water had been recovered as of the spill report filed Wednesday afternoon. 
The cause of the pipeline leak is unknown. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Murphy’s office among those targeted by ‘suspicious substances’
text:
Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide — including U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy’s office — and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”
The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.”
In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly.
The letter targeted Murphy’s office in Hartford, and it was intercepted by law enforcement, according to the senator’s spokesperson Josh Sorbe.
“Sen. Murphy’s office was sent a letter with a suspicious substance. Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement,” Sorbe said in a statement.
“Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger,” he continued. “Our office is grateful for the investigators involved in this incident, and we intend to continue close coordination as the investigation continues.”
Murphy is currently traveling around the country to help boost Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections. He campaigned with Angie Nixon, who’s running for the Senate in Florida, a day earlier. On Thursday, Murphy traveled next to Tennessee to campaign with Justin Pearson, who’s seeking a U.S. House seat.
An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement read. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Maryland, Mississippi and South Dakota officials on Thursday said their election offices also were targeted by separate mailings but that the letters were intercepted by the Postal Service.
News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections.
Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff.
“Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” they said in their statement.
Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that “any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable” and that “we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia; and Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Ossoff reports raising another $33 million for homestretch of U.S. Senate reelection bid
text:
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks with reporters after casting his ballot at the Bessie Branham Recreation Center on the first day of early voting. Ossoff reported a $33 million fundraising haul in campaign filings as the Nov. 3 election approaches. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderDemocratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff’s campaign reported raising $33 million from July through September, entering the final stretch of his re-election campaign against Republican Congressman Mike Collins with $26 million on hand.
“Senator Ossoff is known for building juggernaut political operations and his re-election campaign continues to build unstoppable momentum, including boosting Democrats up and down the ballot in Georgia, heading into Election Day,” said campaign manager Ellen Foster in a statement Thursday.
The campaign has reported transferring more than $3.6 million to other Democratic candidates, including former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor. Ossoff is set to share a campaign stage with Bottoms Saturday and has shouted her out on each of his debate appearances.
Collins’ third quarter haul has not yet been posted to the Federal Election Commission’s website, and the campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. The filing deadline was Oct. 15, but the commission says newly filed reports may take up to 48 hours to appear.
Ossoff has been the consistent leader in the money race, with the Federal Election Commission listing him as the top-raising Senate candidate in the nation ahead of the latest filings. In the previous set of required financial disclosures released in July, Ossoff reported bringing in $42 million for the quarter compared with $2.1 million for Collins
Ossoff’s campaign said nearly 97% of the 760,000 donations received during the third quarter were less than $100, with the average contribution coming in at $46.
Campaign staff say the senator plans to spend the remaining $26 million cash on hand on getting out the vote through TV ads and voter contact operations in the final three weeks of the election.
The Democratic Party-aligned Senate Majority PAC also announced plans this week to pull ad spending in Georgia citing confidence in Ossoff’s polling.
“Senate Majority PAC will continue to monitor this race closely but has made the decision to remove its week 3 ad spending,” said PAC spokesperson Lauren French in a statement: “Sen. Ossoff continues to have a competitive lead in the polls, bolstered by his broad appeal to independent and swing voters who want a senator who will fight to lower costs.”
Republicans say they are continuing to invest in the state, pointing to a recent visit from U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the Collins campaign is continuing to fight to get out the vote with Georgia conservatives, including via a rally with President Donald Trump in Dalton scheduled for Friday.
Early voting is underway and will end on Oct. 30. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Puget Sound Energy announces development of new solar project
text:
Cranes and construction crews setting up part of the Beaver Creek Wind Farm in Stillwater County, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).Puget Sound Energy announced a groundbreaking for a 130-megawatt solar array near Rapelje in southcentral Montana.
Called the “Battle Butte Solar Project,” it’s expected to provide enough energy for 20,000 homes as the company looks to comply with Washington state law, which reduces the amount of power generated from fossil fuels and increases renewables. Puget Sound Energy provides electricity and energy services for a broad swath of northwestern Washington. The company has worked in Montana since the 1970s and this project is expected to add about 250 construction jobs.
PSE also has another facility nearby, the recently completed 248 MW Beaver Creek Wind Project.
“Battle Butte solar represents a critical component of our clean energy strategy,” Craig Pospisil, Senior Vice President and Chief Development Officer for PSE said in a press release. “This project will give us the opportunity to build upon the positive relationships we’ve forged with our neighbors in Stillwater County through the development of the Beaver Creek Wind facility and it positions PSE to meet our customers’ growing clean energy needs.”
PSE said that since 2019 they’ve added 22 long-term clean energy projects totalling about 4,000MW.
Local leaders also hailed the project.
“We look forward to Battle Butte bringing construction jobs, tax revenue and new economic activity to Stillwater County while adding another important piece to Montana’s all-of-the-above energy portfolio,” said Roger Webb, Stillwater County Commissioner. “Throughout the process of developing both Beaver Creek and Battle Butte, PSE has shown a commitment to working with our county and investing in Montana while being a good neighbor – we look forward to the ongoing partnership.”
The project will sit in the high plains near Rapelje on 1,400 acres of flat, open ranch land with full site control. PSE hosted an open house sharing information and answering questions about the Battle Butte Solar Project in Rapelje at the end of January. Construction is expected to start this fall with an anticipated completion date in mid-2028.
As part of Montana’s “all-of-the-above” energy economy, PSE continues to build energy projects and partner with energy producers throughout the state. PSE has power purchase agreements with Energy Keepers, Inc., the tribally owned corporation of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes for hydroelectric power, and an agreement with NextEra for power from Montana’s largest wind farm, Clearwater Wind, based in Rosebud, Custer and Garfield Counties as well as a long-term contract with Clearway Energy Group for wind from Haymaker Wind Farm in Wheatland and Meagher counties.
PSE has already eliminated coal from its energy portfolio at the end of 2025 and added 22 long-term clean energy resources totaling more than 4,000 MW since 2019, when the Clean Energy Transformation Act was passed.

name: WyoFile
title: Four takeaways from the Wyoming governor’s debate
text:
Republican Eric Barlow, Democrat Kenneth Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel squared off Wednesday in the one televised debate scheduled ahead of November’s general election, when Wyoming voters will select their next governor. 
In August, Barlow, a state senator from Gillette, won the Republican nomination against two other candidates, while Casner, a small business owner in Elk Mountain, and Bextel, a Teton County conservative activist, sought and secured their respective parties’ nominations unopposed. 
The debate, hosted by Wyoming PBS, Wyoming Public Media and Cowboy State Daily, was held at Riverton High School auditorium. Candidates fielded a variety of topics including energy, education and the executive branch. 
Here are four takeaways from the 50 minute debate. 
Bextel went on the attack and stayed there.
While voters will have three candidates to choose from on the ballot, Bextel, a Teton County conservative activist, promptly told debate viewers she only considers one as her opponent. 
“When I refer to my opponent, it is not the precious Mr. Casner. He is as cute as he can be,” Bextel said. “I’m talking about somebody else.”
When Bextel announced her run in May, she said she would only stay in the race if Republican voters nominated Barlow over Trump-backed Megan Degenfelder, or GOP-endorsed Brent Bien. Members of Wyoming’s far right have criticized Barlow for not being conservative enough.
Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel laughs after taking a jab at Eric Barlow during the Wyoming PBS gubernatorial debate on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Bextel began and ended the night in attack mode, mentioning Barlow in nearly every one of her responses. She also took aim at several people separate from the governor’s race including Robert Short, the Republican nominee for secretary of state, Jackson Democratic Rep. Liz Storer, and a man she identified as both a University of Wyoming trustee and a Wyoming Business Council board member named “Bruce.” Bruce Pivic sits on the business council board, but there is no one named Bruce on UW’s board. 
Bextel used the word “scam” no fewer than a dozen times, and told voters four times the state is at risk of “becoming Colorado” — echoing a recent warning from the Wyoming Freedom Caucus. 
“I might do nothing but veto legislation for the next two years to stop us from being Colorado,” Bextel said when candidates were asked whether the Freedom Caucus losing its statehouse grip in August’s primary election would make the governor’s job easier or more difficult.  
Barlow didn’t take the bait — mostly.
Overall, Barlow kept things positive on the debate stage. Only once Wednesday evening did he directly address Bextel’s blitz. 
“Like a lot of times, everything you believe, just because you say it louder or faster, doesn’t make it any more true,” Barlow said.
“I am faster,” Bextel said. 
Republican candidate for governor Eric Barlow listens to a question from the panel on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, during the Wyoming PBS debate in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
At another point, Barlow pointed to legislation Bextel mentioned when the candidates were asked to weigh in on recruiting health insurance companies to Wyoming. 
“My husband and I actually get our health insurance through a co-op. It’s called Medi-Share,” she said. “There are certain conditions like you can’t abuse alcohol, you can’t take illegal drugs, and you can’t use tobacco. But it has saved our family a lot of money. I want to look at options like that.” 
Medi-Share is a Christian-based healthcare sharing ministry where paying members share each other’s medical expenses. In 2015, Barlow was the lead sponsor of a bill that exempted the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate for those who share medical expenses through a faith-based healthcare sharing ministry. 
“Healthcare is a challenge,” Barlow said in response to the prompt. “And I’m pleased that the Medi-Share is working out because that’s actually legislation that I sponsored to provide to Wyoming families.”
Half the debate was spent on a ‘lightning round’ of prompts.
Steve Peck of Wyoming PBS, Clair McFarland of Cowboy State Daily, and Jordan Uplinger of Wyoming Public Media made up the panel for the Wyoming governor and secretary of state debates on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Instead of questions, candidates at one point were given about two dozen broad subjects to quickly weigh in on, including “gun rights,” “grizzly bears,” “traditional energy,” and “crypto and blockchain technologies” — a format that frequently led to short answers lacking substance. 
At one point, the panelists appeared to run out of prompts with time left on the clock.
The day before the debate, candidates were given a ‘preview’ question” regarding the property tax ballot measure.
In November, Wyoming voters will decide whether to create an additional tax exemption for certain residential properties. If passed, the exemption is officially estimated to result in a roughly $188 million revenue loss for local governments in its first two fiscal years. 
The candidates were asked to prepare a 60-second answer to: “Do you support Proposition 1, both from the perspective of the office you seek and as an individual voter? Why or why not?” 
All three candidates diverged. 
Barlow said he does not support the measure, pointing to the local services funded by property taxes, and the work the Wyoming Legislature has already done to decrease the cost of property taxes for homeowners. 
Democrat Kenneth Casner answers a question from the panel on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton during the Wyoming PBS gubernatorial debate. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Casner did not specify whether he opposed or supported the proposition. 
“You have a bigger problem than referendum number one,” Casner said, appearing to point to a data center under construction near Fremont County’s unincorporated community of Lost Cabin. 
Bextel said she opposes property taxes altogether and cast doubt on the revenue loss the ballot measure would create. 
“I never trust official estimates, they’re always wrong,” she said. “Property tax is a scam. You’re renting your house.”
The general election is Nov. 3, and early voting is underway.
The post Four takeaways from the Wyoming governor’s debate appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Department of Justice hasn’t requested late removal of suspected noncitizens from Alaska voter rolls
text:
The Alaska Division of Elections director's office in Downtown Juneau is seen on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)One day after the U.S. Department of Justice requested the state of California remove suspected noncitizens from that state’s voter list, a spokesman for the Alaska Division of Elections said the DOJ has not made a similar request here. 
“We can confirm that to date the DOE has not received any requests from the DOJ to remove names from voter rolls,” said Steve Kirch, a spokesman for the Alaska Division of Elections, by email on Wednesday.
In December, Alaska Division of Elections director Carol Beecher turned a copy of the state’s voter rolls over to the federal government and signed a memo stating that Alaska would remove suspected noncitizens identified by the DOJ from the state’s active voter list. 
On Sept. 16, in courtroom arguments over a lawsuit challenging that memo and the decision to turn over the voter list, an attorney representing the state said that it had not been contacted by the DOJ to remove any voters. 
Under federal law, there is a 90-day “freeze period” preceding elections. During that period, systematic removals from the state voter list are banned. 
It isn’t yet clear whether the Department of Justice’s request of California would violate that freeze period or whether it would be covered under exceptions to the rule. 
On Thursday, the DOJ sued the state of California for failing to remove the suspected noncitizens that it had identified, and for not stating that it will void absentee ballots cast by those voters.
Earlier this year, the Alaska Division of Elections removed thousands of voters from the state’s active voter roll, citing data from the Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles that indicated they may have registered to vote despite not being citizens.
Since then, many of those voters have contacted the division to say they are citizens and were removed erroneously because the DMV data was old and they have become citizens since obtaining driver’s licenses as noncitizens.
Corinne Smith contributed reporting from Juneau.

name: Mississippi Today
title: What will the next era of apprenticeships look like? Mississippi Marketplace
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Over the past 10 years, there’s been a growing number of job apprenticeships in Mississippi and nationally. 
With the high cost of a four-year college degree, difficulty for recent grads to find jobs and uncertainty over artificial intelligence’s impact on work, there’s increasing interest in apprenticeships. 
Gov. Tate Reeves has said the state’s goal is to have 7,000 active apprentices, almost double the current number. It’s seen as a way to grow the state’s skilled workforce and stop population loss. Mississippi’s labor force participation rate has improved but still swings back and forth with West Virginia as the lowest in the country. 
Katherine Lin
During the last legislative session, the governor signed a bill creating a state-run Office of Apprenticeships. Responsibility for certifying apprenticeships in the state would shift from the federal Department of Labor to the new state office. Proponents say that this will mean programs will be more engaged with and responsive to the state’s workforce needs. 
Last week, I hosted a panel on apprenticeships for Mississippi Today’s second annual “All in on Mississippi” summit. Some key takeaways from my conversation with experts from across the state:

Apprenticeships are expanding beyond the trades into fields such as healthcare and IT. Singing River Health System on the Gulf Coast offers apprenticeships for students to become nurses, pharmacy techs, phlebotomists and other in-demand health professions. 
Community colleges play a key role. They are the most front-facing entities and offer the apprenticeship programs, work directly with students and partner with employers. 
Experts said that in order to grow the pipeline and give more students the opportunity to “learn while they earn,” there will need to be close collaboration between the state, community colleges and industry partners. 

Lawmakers seek to increase cybersecurity
The Senate Cybersecurity Committee met Tuesday to hear recommendations from state, national and corporate experts on how to improve the state’s defenses. Artificial Intelligence and the February ransomware attack on University of Mississippi Medical Center have brought cybersecurity to the forefront. The committee is supposed to develop policy recommendations for the upcoming legislative session.
Most of the recommendations focused on ways to protect local and state governments. There was a proposal for a state law to incentivize private businesses to be proactive about cybersecurity. The law would limit damages and/liability against a private company after a cyberattack. This voluntary program would require the company to maintain certain security requirements and framework. 
The Mississippi Business Alliance also highlighted the importance of cybersecurity liability protections in its 2026 Legislative Report.
The group, one of the leading business organizations in the state, wrote that it was “encouraged to see the House advance practical measures in both of these areas. However, we were disappointed that cybersecurity liability protections and procurement reform ultimately failed to pass the Senate. These issues may not always attract the same public attention as larger economic development or tax proposals, but they matter to the day-to-day competitiveness of our state.”
Other news:

Bill Cork, who recently stepped down as the head of Mississippi’s economic development agency, announced he has taken a job with the Texas Economic Development Council as its president and CEO. Cork served as executive director of the Mississippi Development Authority for almost three years. “I couldn’t be more proud of the work did for the Reeves administration and the 10.5 years he served Mississippi,” Gov. Reeves said on social media. 
ALO, a Los Angeles-based clothing company, will establish a new fulfillment center in Southaven. The brand, which is popular with celebrities and influencers, will spend $176 million and create 400 new jobs.
Huntington Bank, which acquired Mississippi-based Cadence Bank last year, is spending more than $40 million to renovate its campus in Tupelo. 
Westwin Elements is investing over half a million dollars to set up a nickel refinery in Natchez. 
A plastics manufacturer is investing $7.7 million in Sunflower County. The startup called Koinonia said it will make products for the packaging industry and create 18 jobs. 
There are still no structures at the location of a Brandon data center according to the Clarion Ledger. The company behind the project originally said the data center would be up and running in the first half of 2027.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Gwen Graham spends a ‘workday’ helping to install solar panels
text:
Democratic lieutenant governor candidate Gwen Graham helps to install solar panels in northern Hillsborough County on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
LUTZ — Democratic lieutenant governor candidate Gwen Graham spent part of her Thursday helping to install solar panels on a roof of a firefighter’s home in northern Hillsborough County.
It was the 63rd such “workday” of her career, when she does the jobs of everyday Floridians firsthand. It’s a tradition she inherited from her late father, Bob Graham, the former Florida governor and U.S. senator who performed similar events throughout his political career.
The former North Florida U.S. House member, now running mate to Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly, said that doing such events helps her understand specific industries in the state and the challenges everyday Floridians face.



See the Phoenix 2026 Voter Guide 


“I do this for many, many reasons,” she said. “To learn. To build relationships. And to be better informed on decisions I make in the future.”
The occasion also allowed her to put a focus on solar power, which generates approximately 8% of the energy powering homes in Florida, according to a 2026 report from the Florida Public Service Commission (PSC). Nearly 75% of the energy generated in Florida comes from natural gas. Another 11% comes from nuclear power, 3% from coal, 2% from purchases, and less than 1% from oil.
“Energy is a significant cost in people’s lives,” she said. “Using solar is a way to drive it down. Common sense. And it’s what we should be doing in the state of Florida significantly more than we are doing now.”
Graham said she was unaware of the recent comments by Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, who derided solar power as “a fad.”
“We’ve seen these solar arrays all over the state of Florida,” Donalds said during a campaign event in Daytona Beach Shores. “They’re taking land out of production and taking land off the interstate. We’ve seen how this has worked time and again. What happens very clearly is you have some power in the day, no power at night, when most people are using electricity anyway. And so it’s not consistent power.”
Graham said that response reminded her of Donalds’ comments at the Economic Club of Miami last year when said, “We have actual land in our state that is still pristine, available to use,” in regard to data centers. (He now says it should be up to every local community in Florida to decide for itself whether such centers should be built).
The use of solar energy has increased in the United States in recent years due to the dramatic reduction in its costs. Solar panels that sold for $5 to $6 per watt around 2000 now cost about 12 cents per watt, according to Dave Ember, chief analyst and co-founder of a global energy think tank.
The rooftop solar industry in Florida and across the country received a body blow at the beginning of this year when language in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated a 30% federal solar tax credit that had been in place for nearly two decades.
Gwen Graham with Steve Rutherford, president of Tampa Bay Solar, on the rooftop of a home in northern Hillsborough County on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/ Florida Phoenix)
Steve Rutherford, president and founder of Tampa Bay Solar, said the immediate elimination of the federal tax subsidy has significantly damaged the rooftop solar panel industry.
“We’ve seen at least a 30% to 40% drop in business from last year and prior years,” he said ahead of leading Graham onto the roof of Hillsborough County resident Jason Turk’s home. Last year, approximately 400 rooftop solar companies were based in the state, he said, and that could be reduced to around 200 by the end of this year.
“It’s almost 40,000 people in the industry. Those jobs are not coming back,” he said.
Under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, the 30% tax credit rate was scheduled to remain in place until 2032, with a step-down schedule before expiring completely after 2034.
“We would have appreciated if they had phased it out,” Rutherford says of the legislation.
Tampa Bay Solar first installed solar panels on Turk’s house in the northern Hillsborough County town of Lutz eight years ago. Turk is now building a 1,000 square foot addition to his home for his mother to move in and getting new solar panels installed. After the upfront costs (aided by that 30% subsidy), the solar panels have reduced his monthly electricity bills in the summer from around $650 to $700 to $40, he said.
“It was the cost savings,” he said of why he was able to install the panels initially. “The 30% tax credit helped a ton.”
Graham said Thursday’s “workday” was unique for her in that it was the first time she had repeated an event, but that it was appropriate because she wanted to emphasize the importance of renewable energy sources.
Byron Donalds’ running mate, former GOP state Sen. Bryan Ávila, returned to the campaign trail this week. He was activated last week ahead of Hurricane Isaias as a captain in the Florida Army National Guard.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Amendment 7 would let New Orleans use federal money for private lead-pipe removal
text:
The Sewerage and Water Board plant in New Orleans, pictured Aug. 18, 2022. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana voters will decide Nov. 3 whether public money can be used to remove potentially harmful lead pipes from private property. Its approval would immediately give New Orleans access to more than $150 million to tackle a small portion of the city’s outdated drinking water system. 
The proposed change to the Louisiana Constitution, Amendment 7, would free up a $152 million loan the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has approved for the New Orleans Sewerage and Water Board to address lead pipes. Voters are being asked to create an exemption to a general provision in state law that prohibits public money from being spent on or given to an individual or other private entities, such as a business.
Although Amendment 7 would provide immediate access to federal money in New Orleans, the change would apply statewide. 
The Sewerage and Water Board can freely change out lead pipes in the public right-of-way with public dollars, but private property owners have been asked to swap out any lead lines that connect their structures to water mains when feasible. 
Long-term exposure to lead in drinking water systems has been linked to neurological issues and development delays in children as well as high blood pressure and seizures. 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency banned the use of lead in drinking water infrastructure in 1986 — eight years after it was required to be removed from paint. According to federal figures, roughly 90% of New Orleans’ housing stock was built prior to these lead prohibitions being put in place.  
“Lead is a pervasive issue,” said Jessica Dandridge-Smith, executive director for The Water Collaborative, a New Orleans group focused on access to safe water. “It’s not a matter of public money or private money, but it’s an understanding that when you invest in your ecosystem, particularly water systems, you invest in public health.”
Verite News reported earlier this year that previously unpublished city data revealed there was lead-contaminated drinking water in 70% of homes tested between 2022-25
The $152 million available for New Orleans will address just a fraction of the city’s lead-pipe abatement needs, which the Sewerage and Water Board has estimated exceed $1 billion. But for those who can’t afford to take on the expense, the federal money can make a difference, said Hannah Levi, a spokeswoman for The Water Collaborative. 
“It’s a really large amount of money that we’re talking about that is not feasible for most people in those small businesses to do it on their own,” Levi said. “This funding is really necessary to get lead lines replaced on a large scale.”
An overarching project to replace lead water lines in New Orleans is expected to take until 2037 to complete. 
A state attorney general’s opinion has concluded New Orleans could legally use the federal money to remove lead pipes from private property, but the amendment’s author, state Sen. Royce Duplessis, D-New Orleans, and its proponents insist a constitutional change would solidify the exemption.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. PAC supporting nurse practitioner independence releases candidate surveys
text:
Janice Miller, the president of the Pennsylvania Coalition of Nurse Practitioners, pushes for independence from physician oversight at an Erie press conference on Oct. 15, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)In a continued push to practice to the full extent of their licensing and training, the lobbying group for nurse practitioners is pressuring state legislative candidates to commit to change ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. 
Healthcare costs and accessibility both loom large in the minds of voters this election cycle, and nurse practitioners pitch themselves as a solution — if only lawmakers would grant them full practice authority. 
“The people who are elected to Pennsylvania’s General Assembly in November will have significant ability to enact policies that can make healthcare cheaper and easier to get,” said Janice Miller, the president of the Pennsylvania Coalition of Nurse Practitioners. “Who can argue with that?”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Current Pennsylvania law requires Certified Registered Nurse Practitioners (CRNPs) to have a written collaborative agreement with a licensed physician, but Miller’s organization claims getting a doctor’s approval slows down the process. 
More than half of states fall under the “full practice” designation. But the effort is routinely opposed in the commonwealth by the Pennsylvania Medical Society, which generally resists any expansion of duties for non-physicians, including pharmacists and says nurse practitioners add to the bottom line.
But the number of doctors across the nation is declining — potentially exacerbated, in part, by the federal immigration crackdown.
“In many communities like mine, it’s becoming harder and harder for rural Pennsylvanians to access and afford the healthcare they need. Family practice physicians are retiring with no replacements lined up,” said Tammy Huey, a former CRNP in Venango County. 
Nurse practitioners renew push for independence from physician oversight in Pa.

Of the 382 General Assembly candidates running for election — including 25 senators and all 203 House members — 82 submitted their responses to the coalition’s political action committee. 
The first three questions ask about prioritizing healthcare, concerns about the healthcare workforce shortage and specialties for nurse practitioners — to which all candidates responded in the affirmative. 
Just one candidate indicated that he didn’t support full practice across the last three questions: James Edwards, a Republican challenging incumbent Rep. Dan Goughnour (D-Allegheny). All others said that they supported expanding independence for nurse practitioners. 
In this 2026 cycle, the PAC gave money to two candidates — Rep. Peter Schweyer (D-Lehigh) and Sen. President Pro Tem Kim Ward (R-Westmoreland) — according to the state’s campaign finance reporting. 
Elections are Nov. 3 and the last day to register to vote is Oct. 19.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Democrat keeps up fundraising advantage in secrtary of state’s race
text:
Democrat Beau Bayh, right, speaks during a secretary of state candidate debate alongside, from left, Libertarian Lauri Shillings, Republican Max Engling and Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)Beau Bayh is pulling off that rarest of feats for statewide Democratic candidates in Indiana — outraise and outspend the Republicans.
Campaign finance reports filed Thursday by the secretary of state candidates show that Bayh spent $3.9 million during the July-September period.
That’s more than double the $1.6 million spent by Republican candidate Max Engling’s campaign.
Bayh, the son of former U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh, put that money to use by starting widespread television advertising in August, a full month ahead of Republicans ads for Engling.
The campaign reports show Beau Bayh spent $3.3 million with an advertising firm in August and September for TV and digital ads. Republicans countered with $1.3 million for Engling, with most of that paid for by the state GOP organization.
The Bayh and Engling campaigns did not immediately reply to questions from the Indiana Capital Chronicle about the fundraising and spending reports.
The reports show that during the three-month span ending Sept. 30:

Beau Bayh raised $2 million and ended with about $394,000 in cash. His campaign has since reported raising $1.95 in contributions topping $1,000, including $1.95 million from the state Democratic Party.
Engling collected $1.85 million and ended with about $422,000 in the bank. His campaign has since added about $700,000 in large contributions, including nearly $600,000 from the state GOP.
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard raised $435,000, spent $182,000 and ended with $278,000 in cash. He’s since reported $11,000 in large contributions.
Libertarian Lauri Shillings raised about $30,000, spent $21,000 and had $16,000 in cash.

Federal Election Commission reports show that Evan Bayh’s dormant U.S. Senate campaign fund transferred $700,000 to a federal campaign committee operated by state Democrats called the Indiana Democratic Congressional Victory Committee.
That left the Evan Bayh Committee with about $1.5 million as of Sept. 30.
The Engling campaign claimed Thursday that state Democrats took that money and “then passed it to Beau’s campaign. The campaign expects that number to rise to about $2.3 million after further public disclosures.”
Ballard, the former Republican mayor of Indianapolis, lamented Thursday that collecting some 70,000 petition signatures to put his name on the statewide ballot cost his campaign more than $800,000 last spring — money that Republicans and Democrats didn’t have to spend.
“We’re on TV statewide right now,” Ballard said. “We’d like to have more ad buys, obviously, throughout the rest of the state. But they’ve been on TV for a while now because they’ve got a foundation behind it. The law is on their side. The history is on their side.”
