name: Washington State Standard
title: Workers and communities shouldn’t foot the bill for Big Oil’s mess
text:
Climate change is driving expensive disasters such as flooding and the recent Spokane fires. Washington lawmakers can bring in new progressive revenue by holding climate polluters accountable, two activists argue. (Photo via InciWeb)More than 70,000 people were evacuated as wildfires engulfed Spokane, reducing entire neighborhoods to ash. Hundreds lost their homes. Damage is expected to exceed $1 billion, the most expensive wildfires in Washington’s history.
And while some point out that arson started the fire, it’s clear that the damage wouldn’t be nearly as destructive without the dry, hot conditions fueled by climate change.
When fires, floods, and heatwaves strike, the costs fall disproportionately on taxpayers, workers, small businesses, and vulnerable communities. Meanwhile the major fossil fuel corporations most responsible for the emissions warming our planet get off scot-free.
Workers bear the impacts in ways that don’t often make the headlines. Firefighters, heavy equipment operators, and foresters risk their lives, with long-term health consequences from exposure to carcinogens. Outdoor workers — construction crews, farmworkers, delivery drivers —  face direct exposure to dangerous wildfire smoke and extreme heat. Others face lost shifts and lost paychecks, or have to work through unsafe conditions to pay the bills.
As farmworkers, our livelihoods depend on working, even through wildfires or floods. In Skagit County, we’ve experienced two 100 year floods in five years. While the governor issued emergency orders for people to seek refuge, farmworkers kept working, choosing between safety and making rent.
After a long slog, climate change lawsuits will finally put Big Oil on trial

And as climate disasters strain state and municipal budgets, public sector workers — teachers, transit operators, service workers — face wage suppression, shrinking benefits, and hiring freezes. We are in the era of climate change where unions and communities alike are being forced to absorb the costs of a crisis they didn’t create.
The Pacific Northwest wildfires were unprecedented, supercharged by a climate crisis that Big Oil’s own scientists predicted with incredible accuracy as early as the 1970s. They waged massive deception campaigns to sow doubt, denial, and delay. Now, workers and communities are paying the price.
Extreme weather disasters in Washington are growing in scale and frequency, causing billions of dollars in damage. The 2025 atmospheric river, for instance, caused the Green River levee breach, bringing life-threatening flash floods in Tukwila, and cost over $180 million – excluding damage to homes, businesses, and livelihoods.
We pay to recover and rebuild, then we pay again for the resilience measures needed to weather future climate storms. The climate crisis is also exacerbating the affordability crisis. Groceries, gas, energy, healthcare, and home insurance costs are all climbing. Washington home insurance rates have risen 51% in six years, driven in no small part by rising flood and wildfire risk.
Meanwhile, the fossil fuel industry is reaping another windfall. Fueled by higher oil prices from the war on Iran, eight of the largest oil and gas companies made over $93 billion during the second quarter of 2026.
 Why should we keep paying for a crisis fueled by Big Oil’s pollution?

Fortunately, there is one common sense step we can take — Make Polluters Pay for the costs of climate harms. Washington is building a movement to pass Climate “Superfund”  legislation, to be introduced in the 2027 session, that would require the largest fossil fuel corporations to pay their fair share for climate damages caused by their historical greenhouse gas emissions.
The idea is rooted in a simple principle we learned as kids: you make a mess, you clean it up. New York and Vermont already passed these laws, and bills are now moving in over a dozen states around the country.
Climate Superfunds apply the “polluter pays” principle from toxic-waste cleanup to the climate crisis. Using climate attribution science, states can identify major contributors – think BP, Exxon, Chevron, Shell – then assess fees to recoup part of the climate costs resulting from their pollution.
Coal gets a boost as renewables are gutted

That revenue would fund resilient infrastructure, protect overburdened communities, and create thousands of good jobs. Rebuilding Spokane, retrofitting homes, schools and community centers for clean air and cooling, hardening the grid, and other resilience measures will all require skilled labor. The sooner polluters pay, the sooner local workers can get to work protecting communities.
This kind of dedicated funding will also help protect farmworkers and other vulnerable populations who are often overlooked. In the long-run, these investments will help build a more resilient and affordable Washington.
Someone has to pay for disaster recovery, and for future climate harms. That burden should not fall on workers, families, and overburdened communities. It should fall on the Big Oil corporations that knowingly created this mess and continue to profit from pollution and war.
Washington lawmakers can bring in new progressive revenue by holding polluters accountable.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s land laws should incentivize people who heal the land
text:
This commentary is by Ben Falk, a land planner and the founder of Whole Systems Design. He lives in Moretown.
“A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community,” the conservationist Aldo Leopold wrote in “A Sand County Almanac,” his classic account of restoring a worn-out Wisconsin farm. 
For 25 years, I’ve tried to put Leopold’s “land ethic” into practice at my beat-up, abandoned sheep pasture. Here’s what I’ve learned.
First, “sustainable” was always the wrong word. Doing less bad was never doing good. Second, when you aim for revitalization instead, things start to make sense. You see that you were meant to be here. You’re not the one creature that only destroys and never heals. You belong to a place. Not just to a human community, but to the whole land community, and to the watershed. Land health is integral to thriving human habitat.
I started with the water and let its dynamics organize everything else. In ecological design we say, “You can’t get anything right if you get the water wrong.”
So first I dug swales and some shallow ponds. Then I planted fruit trees, nut trees and berry bushes on contour, along with herbaceous perennials. Everything was built to slow, spread and sink water, and to encourage biodiversity, food, beauty and medicine.
Then came Aug. 28, 2011: Tropical Storm Irene. Over 12 hours, more than half a foot of rain came down.
By that night, my village, Moretown, was under 8 feet of water. Our fire department was one of the first buildings to flood — in the same flood plains where Act 181’s Tier 1 maps actively encourage development under local flood rules.
I woke up that Monday to a changed Vermont, almost all of it for the worse. But before I knew that, I walked the land. Every pond had filled with crystal-clear water. The swales were brimming, trickling slowly over their sills, totally clear. Not a speck of ancient soil or newer hard-earned soil was moving.
Six inches of rain on 25 acres — our 10, plus 15 above us that flow onto our land — is about 4 million gallons. We banked it in the groundwater, filled our storages, fed our soil. In one event, we kept the runoff from more than twice the land we manage out of the flood.
Here’s the irony: Vermont’s Acts 59 and 181 were meant to deliver three things: more carbon stored, more biodiversity, less flood damage. My hillside does all three faster than a so-called nature preserve devoid of humans, while generating economic yield, improving local food security and being prime human habitat: my family’s home.
Soil organic matter has risen from 2% or 3% over most of our ground to between 4% and 12%. Each percentage point is about 16 tons of carbon dioxide per acre in the top 6 inches. Across our 10 acres, that adds up to hundreds of tons held in the ground, which fuels better plant yields and stormwater absorption.
The place is now prime bear and turkey habitat. The bears have been climbing my fruit and chestnut trees and have become almost pests. When people ask what we plant for wildlife, I just laugh. What don’t we plant for them? A graduate student in entomology at the University of Vermont visited a few years ago and said, “I’m seeing insects I haven’t seen on one site in Vermont before. Do you have an unusual amount of plant diversity here?” The birds arrive earlier and stay later.
If we did this on a small fraction of our landscape, our rivers would be noticeably less flood-prone. Keeping water in the hills is a no-brainer. We’ve seen multiple new springs form. And drought resilience matters as much as flood resilience, as dry spells grow more frequent.
This is nothing more than a land ethic applied to one’s home, but it takes time, energy and funding. And nobody digs swales or plants white oaks for their grandkids when they’re drowning in regulatory hurdles. They need the creative space that livability enables.

READ MORE

Vermont’s Current Use program ties its tax relief to acreage and sales income; permit costs and regulatory hurdles favor scale. Go big or get out.
Laws that view people as the problem throw away the maximum leverage for reaching their own stated goals. Vermont became a place worth protecting because of the relationship between people and land: a working landscape, not a wilderness preserve. The mutual flourishing of people and the more-than-human world has married Vermonters to this land for generations. No one is regulated into good husbandry. Vermont can become a shining example of thriving human habitat if our Legislature supports rather than hinders long-term land tenure.
We might ask those seeking to represent us: What are you doing to help Vermont be an example of “small is beautiful,” not competing at the bigger, faster, more efficient corporate industrial model, but doing it with more care, craft, resilience and beauty?
How are you supporting diverse land uses through tax policy that values subsistence homesteads, not just commercial farms?
What are you doing to encourage cottage industry and enterprise, and zoning for rural production and processing?
And most of all, what are you doing to harness the landscape, legacy and brand that have made Vermont unique in all 50 states, and play our own game rather than compete with outside forces at a game out of scale with the reality of this place?
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s land laws should incentivize people who heal the land.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Of 5K Utah voters needing to prove citizenship under new law, fewer than 2K have responded
text:
A voter drops off a ballot on primary Election Day at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)Of about 5,000 Utah voters who state election officials notified earlier this year needed to provide proof of their U.S. citizenship before this year’s November election, only 1,827 have responded and confirmed their citizenship, according to Utah’s lieutenant governor’s office. 
Those voters received a ballot with state and federal races — but those who didn’t respond, 4,307, were sent a ballot in the mail this week with only federal congressional races printed on them. 
A fraction — 57 — requested to be removed from Utah’s voter rolls because “either they could not confirm citizenship or otherwise asked to be removed,” the lieutenant governor’s office told Utah News Dispatch in a statement Wednesday. 
More than 5,000 Utah voters need to provide proof of citizenship under new state law

“Voter rolls are always changing and we are continually working with county clerks to keep them updated — including verifying citizenship,” the office said. 
The new proof of citizenship requirements were enacted earlier this year after the Republican-controlled Utah Legislature passed a new state law, HB209. It requires voters to provide “documentary proof” of their U.S. citizenship before the Nov. 3 election — or else they would be provided a federal-only ballot with no state or local elections. 
Under that new law, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s office earlier this spring sent letters to 5,007 Utahns who had a citizenship status that her office was unable to confirm using existing documentation on file. The letters notified those voters of the state’s new proof of citizenship requirements.
Many of those were “legacy” voters, or registered to vote years before driver license or Social Security numbers were required to register under state law, Henderson said at the time.
With HB209, Utah lawmakers created a “bifurcated ballot system” for elections starting in November 2026. Federal law does not require proof of citizenship to vote for members of Congress or the president, though it maintains that only U.S. citizens can legally cast a ballot.
‘Not a widespread problem’: Lt. gov. releases early findings from voter citizenship review 

“Federal law says that you only have to say you’re a citizen and attest to being a citizen under penalty of perjury,” Henderson said in May, when she issued a report on a state review that found 27 “noncitizen” registered voters in the state, a tiny fraction of the state’s 2 million.
“Our state law used to mirror that. And now this year it changed, so we can’t just tell (people who don’t provide proof of citizenship) they can’t vote. We would get sued and it would be unconstitutional,” Hendersaid said at the time. “So they would get a federal only ballot because now our state law has changed.” 
Critics of the new law argued it would create unnecessary barriers for Utah voters and potentially disenfranchise them even if they’re eligible — especially elderly voters who have stayed on Utah’s voter rolls for decades but now may not have the documentation on hand to continue voting in all elections. They have also argued it would pile greater administrative burdens on election officials, while federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting. 
Proponents, including the law’s sponsor, Rep. Cory Maloy, R-Lehi, have argued it’s an added layer of security to ensure no one who isn’t a U.S. citizen casts a vote — and that if even a few noncitizens were on Utah’s voter rolls, “that’s a few too many.” 
Utah bill requiring proof of citizenship to vote advances 

During a news conference on that report at the time it was issued, Henderson told reporters she’s “always concerned” about the potential for unintentional eligible voter disenfranchisement. 
“It keeps me up at night,” she said in May. “Honestly, I’ve had a lot of angst about this.”
However, she also said that HB209 “serves a really valuable purpose.” 
“I think it’s good to have a place to kind of sequester folks who don’t have that documentation in a way that doesn’t completely disenfranchise them,” she said. “I think the way we’ve done it is responsible and tries to balance the idea of preserving rights for people while also making sure that, you know, ineligible people aren’t registering (to vote).” 
For those roughly 4,300 Utah voters who were only given by-mail ballots with the option to vote in their district’s congressional race and not any state legislative or local races, it isn’t too late. 
“Voters can still provide proof of citizenship and receive a full ballot,” Henderson’s office said Wednesday. “The last day to mail ballots is Oct. 28, but voters are also able to show proof of citizenship to their county clerk on Election Day.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Views on abortion, AI set Oklahoma attorney general candidates apart
text:
Democrat Nick Coffey, left, and Republican Jon Echols, right, are both on the Nov. 3 ballot to be Oklahoma's next attorney general. (Photos provided)OKLAHOMA CITY — While they share similar views on a controversial aluminum smelter, two candidates for Oklahoma attorney general vary in how they’d handle an abortion lawsuit and artificial intelligence. 
Democrat Nick Coffey and Republican Jon Echols, both from Oklahoma City, are competing to be the state’s next attorney general. Gentner Drummond, the current attorney general, made an unsuccessful bid for governor instead of running for another term. 
A former federal prosecutor with the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Coffey said his experience in a courtroom working with jury trials, law enforcement and major drug and money laundering cases make him the most qualified candidate. Coffey, 35, is a graduate of the University of Oklahoma College of Law. 
“I guess what sets me apart from my opponent is experience in the courtroom,” he said. “The best I can tell, I’m the only one that has overseen the extradition of a Mexican cartel leader. I did it twice at the U.S. Attorney’s office. The AG should be a prosecutor, not a politician.”
Echols, 46, served in the Oklahoma House for 12 years and was the majority floor leader for eight of them. He holds a law degree from Oklahoma City University.  
“The major difference in this race just comes down to political philosophy,” he said. “I have the legislative experience, the legal experience and the small business experience to go in from day one and to run the Attorney General’s Office.”
Inola aluminum smelter
Drummond has sued to prevent the construction of what would be the country’s largest aluminum smelter from being built in Inola over environmental and foreign ownership concerns. The project has the support of President Donald Trump, Gov. Kevin Stitt and other elected state leaders, while many residents of the community located about 25 miles east of Tulsa oppose it. Residents have implemented a moratorium until April to block the $4 billion project, which is expected to produce about 600,000 tons of aluminum each year and create over 1,000 jobs.
Oklahoma AG sues to stop construction of Trump-endorsed aluminum smelter in Inola

Both Coffey and Echols said they plan to continue the lawsuit and have concerns about it being 60% foreign-owned. The smelter is part of a $200 billion deal Trump made with the United Arab Emirates.
“You know, we love in Oklahoma to talk about how we value property rights for an agricultural state. But hey, you wouldn’t know it if you looked at the way this thing had played out,” Coffey said.
Coffey said while he understands the state needs the jobs, he thinks the smelter ownership group should take a more active role in listening to the concerns of residents. 
Echols said he’s concerned about the foreign ownership and high fluoride emissions from the potential smelter. 
“I’m still open to learning more about the project, and I’m not against economic growth and job creation,” he said. “It just has to be done in a way that is safe for the citizens of Inola and northeast Oklahoma.”
The ownership group needs to prove the safety of the project to the attorney general and the residents of Inola, Echols said. 
Holding other elected officials accountable 
The office has faced criticism in recent years for how it prosecuted unrelated cases against two lawmakers. In both cases, the Attorney General’s Office allowed the legislators to enter into plea agreements on the same day the charges were first publicly unveiled. 
In one case, Rep. Ajay Pittman, D-Oklahoma City, pleaded guilty to fraud-related felony charges and received a deferred sentence. In the other, Rep. Ty Burns, R-Pawnee, pleaded guilty to three domestic-violence related crimes and received a suspended sentence. 
Nick Coffey, a Democrat, files to run as a Democratic candidate for attorney general at the Oklahoma State Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 1, 2026. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)
Coffey said this “double standard” and “negotiating behind the scenes” needs to end.  
“Oklahomans, I think, have lost a lot of trust and faith in their elected officials,” he said. “And I don’t think we’re going to get it back until we have until we see an AG actually hold state officials accountable when they break the law.”
Publicly holding officials accountable will have a “trickle down effect” that will force other officials to “cut the nonsense” and address the real issues facing Oklahomans, Coffey said. 
Echols said elected officials need to be held accountable, no matter their party affiliation, and he has a track record of doing this in the Legislature when he worked on a special committee that recommended the expulsion of a fellow Republican lawmaker. 
“If anything, elected officials need to be held to a higher standard, not a lower standard,” he said. “… It’s not just elected officials. We have a problem in the state of Oklahoma with the rich and powerful getting away with things that the rest of us don’t get away with.”
No political corruption will be “swept under the rug” if elected attorney general, Echols said. 
Abortion lawsuit
A group of Oklahoma mothers and physicians sued state officials last month, including the attorney general, alleging the state’s abortion ban forced them to leave Oklahoma to access abortion care when they had been given fatal fetal diagnoses by medical professionals. 
The lawsuit is very concerning because these are mothers who were given medical diagnoses that their wanted children would not survive, Coffey said. 
He said the attorney general’s role is to defend the laws passed by the Legislature rather than to draft policy. 
“I’m gonna be in a better position to evaluate the legal defense of a law if I have all the facts (as attorney general),” Coffey said. “But right now, with what they’re describing, it is inhumane. And I would have a very hard time figuring out morally and legally how to defend this law and make these women suffer in the manner that they are describing.”
Echols said the attorney general needs to defend the law, and he would defend the state’s law as written. 
“As somebody who’s 100% pro-life, I would follow the law,” he said. “And I think that’s the job of the attorney general. The job of the attorney general is not to say what they wish the law would be, the job is to follow the law.”
Echols said during his time as a lawmaker, he filed a bill attempting to clarify the definition of “terminal” in state law and allow for early inducement of labor in terminal cases. 
Artificial intelligence in the courtroom
Use of artificial intelligence in the courtroom has garnered more attention this year. The Oklahoma Supreme Court in June issued a warning against the use of artificial intelligence by attorneys in court filings. An Oklahoma judge in September admitted he used AI in a filing that cited cases that do not exist.
Jon Echols speaks to news reporters after filing to run as a Republican candidate for attorney general on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Artificial intelligence has been used in the legal profession for years for things like researching legal briefs, but there should be serious sanctions for those who use AI to draft filings without checking the final product for accuracy, he said.
He said banning the technology altogether may not be possible. 
“That would seem to be unfeasible and not seem to be where the economy is headed,” he said. “But look, I’m a big believer in respect for the legal profession, and attorneys that dilute the legal profession by telling ChatGPT or Claude to draft court filings and then don’t check it, yeah, they absolutely should be heavily sanctioned.”
Echols said the next attorney general will be dealing with AI issues, from its use in the courtroom to clearing up laws on how it relates to child pornography. 
“Lawyers are responsible for candor with the judiciary,” he said. “And there will need to be more regulations put on (AI) just like there needs to be additional updating of the criminal code.” 
But Echols said he can also see a use for the technology in the attorney general’s office as a supplemental tool for efficiency, not to replace hard work.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Rep. Pearson sues Memphis alleging First Amendment violation
text:
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, who is also the Democratic nominee for Tennessee's 9th Congressional District, is suing the city of Memphis over his two-meeting ban from Memphis City Council. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)After being banned from Memphis City Council meetings, state Rep. Justin J. Pearson filed suit Tuesday against the city alleging the action violates the First Amendment. 
In the suit, which was filed in the U.S. District Court of West Tennessee, Pearson and six other plaintiffs, including his brother, Keshaun Pearson and mother, Kimberly Owens-Pearson, allege Memphis City Council’s public comment policies unconstitutionally restrict free speech. 
“Every person, whether you disagree with them or not, is entitled to speak their opinion and give their ideas in public forms,” Pearson said. “There is no right that gives a City Council chairwoman or anyone else the ability to go beyond the bounds of Tennessee law and the United States Constitution to discriminate or retaliate against those who do not agree with their actions.”
Pearson, the Democratic nominee for the 9th Congressional District seat being vacated by retiring U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen, is running against Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor. 
An Oct. 8 letter signed by Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington and other city council officials notified the Pearsons and community activists Amber Sherman, LaJuana Abraham and Jasmine Bernard they were banned from the Oct. 10 and Nov. 10 council meetings. 
The action came after a contentious Oct. 6 meeting in which community members packed the council chambers and vocally protested after the body deferred a vote to issue a moratorium on approval of data centers. 
The suit alleges Taylor posted a copy of Justin Pearson’s ban letter to social media before Pearson received a copy. 
The Memphis City Council’s Rules of Procedure include a section on “decorum,” which says speakers participating in public comment “shall not make personal, impertinent, slanderous or profane remarks to any member of the Council, staff or general public.” Enforcement of the policy can result in the speaker being barred from further participation in the relevant meeting, but lays out no guidelines for banning a member of the public from future meetings. 
Requests for comment from Swearengen-Washington were not returned by publication time.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC officials express confidence in election integrity as early voting begins
text:
NC Board of Elections Executive Director Sam Hayes, at podium, said on Sept. 3, 2026 that counties are prepared to begin mailing absentee ballots to voters on Sept. 4 as scheduled. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Early voting is off to a strong start for the 2026 midterms with more than 27,000 ballots cast before noon Thursday, the first day of early in-person voting, according to North Carolina State Board of Elections Executive Director Sam Hayes.
Seventy-four percent of North Carolina voters cast their ballots early in the 2024 general election, and Hayes anticipates similar participation this year across the state’s 370 early voting sites.


Key election dates:
Oct. 15: In-person early voting begins; same-day registration available. Vote Early in Person.
Oct. 20: Absentee ballot request deadline
Oct. 31: In-person early voting ends (3 p.m.).
Nov. 3: Election Day.  Absentee ballots due by 7:30 p.m.
Source: NC State Board of Elections


For months leading up to the early voting period, county elections directors and thousands of poll workers have been training election volunteers, preparing and testing voting equipment, and securing voting locations.
“Our responsibility is to ensure that elections are administered fairly, accurately, securely,” Hayes said during a Thursday press availability. “That means maintaining accurate voter registration records, enforcing election laws, and protecting the integrity of the entire voting process.”
 Targeting noncitizens 
Earlier this week, the State Board of Elections began sending out letters to nearly 1,400 registered voters flagged by the federal SAVE database as potential noncitizens.
The letter asks people who are not U.S. citizens to complete an enclosed form to cancel their voter registration. Those who are citizens are asked to contact the board by phone or email and provide proof of citizenship so officials can update their records.
Hayes stressed that those voters will be allowed to cast a regular ballot in this election.
“No one is being removed automatically because of anything we find on the SAVE database because they received this letter,” Hayes said.
He said those receiving the letter who may have a question about their status should contact the state board.
“If you cast a vote illegally and there are severe criminal penalties for doing that,” Hayes warned. “But at the same time, if you are sure that you are a citizen of the United States and duly registered to vote, then we encourage you to vote.”
Hayes said the letters were “a service” to let them know in advance that state elections officials and federal prosecutors were looking into their eligibility to cast a ballot.
“We’re going to need to communicate with all of these folks at some point to try to verify their citizenship,” said Hayes.
NC elections board to notify 1,392 voters flagged as potential noncitizens

The Southern Coalition for Social Justice says the federal SAVE system is an incredibly unreliable source of citizenship information with the potential to flag naturalized, eligible voters.
SCSJ attorneys stress that eligible citizens can cast a ballot in the Nov. 3 election regardless of whether they respond to the State Board of Elections about the letter.
Hayes also spoke briefly about Wednesday’s announcement that 10 noncitizens have been indicted on federal charges of unlawfully voting in the 2024 election.
“Everyone is aware that the state board has run our voter rolls through the SAVE database, and we did share information with federal authorities, with the FBI,” said Hayes. “I think a lot of that formed the basis of these investigations. We’re always going to do that.”
 No grace period 
Hayes also reminded eligible voters who requested an absentee ballot to be certain the completed ballot is received by their county board of elections no later than 7:30 p.m. on Election Day.
“There is no longer a grace period,” said Hayes.”Voters should not assume that mailing their ballot on election day will be sufficient.”
Voters who requested an absentee ballot but have not returned it and are worried about that deadline may still choose to vote in person.
More than 33,400 absentee ballots had been cast as of Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Voters with additional questions can contact their county board of elections.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Delta school districts’ successes not reflected in new state rankings
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Districts across the Delta region saw the largest academic gains in the state in the past year, according to new district rankings released Thursday. 
Because the state implemented higher cut-off scores this year, however, the accountability scores didn’t always reflect that progress. 
Some of last year’s lowest performing districts saw large improvements. Clarksdale’s city school district jumped a whopping 102 points since last year, moving from an F to a C. Greenwood-Leflore moved 98 points from a D to a C. Both made some of the largest single year gains out of any other district in the state.
Clarksdale schools were in bad shape last year. A big factor was record teacher vacancies in state tested subjects. The district had the second highest number of teacher vacancies in July 2025. Over a third of students were chronically absent. 


Superintendent Toya Harrell-Matthews took a chance on a new school leader to change the culture in a school plagued by dysfunction and low academic outcomes for students. It paid off.
“I knew what her abilities were, and how well she worked with students,” Harrell-Matthews said of Denise Calhoun, the new principal at W.A. Higgins Middle School. “And that’s the thing, you have to be able to build relationships before you can do any type of instruction, before anything else can happen in the classroom.”
Calhoun, a Webb native, helped to move the school over 186 points on the state accountability score. The rate of students proficient in math nearly tripled from the previous year.
“I felt that that was going to be a cornerstone in turning this building around to have someone who could build relationships and build trust with students and understand that even if a student has behavioral issues, that you have to champion them, and not just give up on them,” Harrell-Matthews said.
Through social media and her network, Calhoun was able to hire 15 teachers to ensure the school was fully staffed. She brought back choir and art as electives to give students something to look forward to in the day. She also worked with teachers on new strategies to incentivize better behavior, instead of relying solely on removing disruptive students from classrooms. She also restarted after-school detention.
Calhoun celebrated days without student fights, which were frequent in years past. She started a countdown tracker she called “days of peace.” After 50 days of peace, she held a citywide parade and celebrated the students. Students later made it 85 days without any fights.
“And so every time that our students reached another milestone, we would celebrate them even bigger. And so it got to the point where students were so appreciative of everything that was going on that they would report when issues were arising,” she said.
She instituted a bootcamp in the eight weeks leading up to state testing, where students practiced math, science and reading skills. Teachers provided additional support and remediation for special education students. She called it Success Academy.
Also, Harrell-Matthews was adamant that schools in the district have a clean clothes closet for low-income students, who might stay home to avoid ridicule for wearing old or dirty clothes. 
“You have to address student needs first before you can educate them,” Harrell-Matthews said. “So we take the child where they are, and we try to work with them as best we can.”
Superintendent Kenneth Pulley also credits professional development and support for principals with Greenwood-Leflore’s gains. He met with school leaders weekly to review student data to determine which students required additional support.
“We have to hold people accountable, and have high expectations for all students, and maintain a positive atmosphere,” he said. “As long as we know that what we’re doing was right for children, then we know we’ve made the right decision.”
He said a collaborative and receptive board helped implement policies as problems arose. He also put into place professional development sessions that were geared towards curriculum planning.
“As superintendent, yes, we wear a lot of hats, but as superintendent, we must first be instructional leaders,” he said. “That’s where my focus is. And I think when people know where the leader’s focus is, then they will keep their focus there, too.”
Amanda-Elzy High School in Greenwood, Miss., Wednesday, July 2, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
He decided to shutter Amanda Elzy Junior High School last October after a failing grade on the state accountability system and low enrollment. Now, all district middle schoolers attend the same school, which allowed the district to pool resources. He said school culture improved, too. Greenwood Middle jumped 100 points in the accountability scale.
“I have to have the hard conversations when they need to be had. My staff members know when we do that, it’s coming from a good place. It’s coming from a place of wanting the best for our children.”
Nearly a third of Leflore County residents live below the poverty line. The fact is not lost on Pulley, who grew up in the community he now serves.
“Our attitude is that, in spite of where you come from or what situation you find yourself in, it is our job to still provide quality instruction,” he said.
Western Line School District, which is based outside Greenville, and West Tallahatchie School District, which is based in Sumner, also made sizable academic gains. Both districts would’ve been a B under last year’s cut-off scores.
Lawrence Hudson, Western Line’s superintendent, said his district’s improvements were a result of “a little bit more fussing” and personnel shakeups at different schools. 
Western Line School District Superintendent Lawrence Hudson, wishes second grader Dalary Salazar, center, a happy birthday, during a visit at Riverside Elementary School, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“We had a few teacher areas that were not producing, and they brought the whole district down,” he said. “Our biggest focus is not on strategies but making sure we’ve got the right people.”
Nearly all of the district’s schools posted improvements across the board, he said. 
That’s why Hudson was disappointed when he received his district’s letter grade this year. 
“To be at a point where you’ve gotten every school up and not get the recognition, it’s a little discouraging, but we know what we’ve got to do,” he said. “We’ve got to buckle down and do what it takes to be recognized as a high-performing district.”
When reached by phone on Wednesday, House Education Chairman Rob Roberson, a Republican from Starkville, commended Delta schools on their progress. 
However, he admitted it may not be enough to ward off consolidation talks swirling at the state Capitol. State lawmakers are eyeing both Western Line and West Tallahatchie schools for mergers next year. 
“We obviously don’t want to mess up good things, but here’s the problem I see,” he said. “When you are constantly losing students, it’s just a matter of time when you’re eventually going to have no money to keep the school afloat.”
Mississippi has lost nearly 70,000 public school students since 2013, taking funding with them. Delta schools, in particular, are shrinking.
“Educators for years have said we need more money, and sometimes they’re not wrong, they do need more money,” Roberson said. “But do we put more money from the state side or start trying to look at this differently?”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Report card: Most Michigan school districts failing to meet safe firearm storage law requirements
text:
Getty ImagesAccording to data compiled and released by End Gun Violence Michigan, only seven public school districts received an “A” grade for meeting the requirements under Michigan’s Safe Homes, Safe Schools law, which requires districts to publicly notify parents and guardians of the state’s safe firearm storage laws. 
Lauren Jasinski, a trustee at Royal Oak Schools, noted that a recent poll from End Gun Violence Michigan showed only 30% of Michiganders were aware of the state’s safe storage law, which led to the need for the Safe Home, Safe Schools law. 
“We created a really easy-to-use rubric where we were looking for whether or not the correct link was posted, whether or not they had some additional information, and what they’re messaging to their community surrounding this important issue,” Jasinski said. “Schools are trusted messengers about how to keep kids safe, and we need to make sure that every school is doing their part.”
More than 58% of the 593 public school districts included in the report card received an “F”, meaning that the district is not in compliance with the law that requires schools to link directly to the Michigan Department of Education’s Safe Homes, Safe Schools page on the district website.
Schools are required by law to notify parents by Oct. 1 of that school year. 2026 marks the second of those deadlines, with the law first going into effect in 2025. At a previous press conference, End Gun Violence Michigan noted the importance of meeting that deadline and sharing the information as close to the start of the school year as possible. 
The data analyzed in the report card is accurate, according to Jasinski and the group’s website, as of Sept. 1, 2026, so it does not necessarily show a completely accurate portrayal of compliance with this year’s mandate. However, Jasinski said that it can be seen as a reflection of which districts were compliant after the 2025 deadline had passed.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dr. Brenda Goss Andrews, a retired deputy chief with the Detroit Police Department and the former national president of the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement, emphasized that the report card is not intended to be overly critical of any of the school districts. 
“We recognize, and it’s been stated before, the tremendous workload, and we know they’re doing their best,” she said. “Many districts, like Garden City Public Schools, mentioned safety, but did not include the correct links or shared outdated resources. Other districts, like Clio Area Schools, sent letters to the community. However, there was no safe firearm storage information nor resource links on their website.”
Around 18% of the districts received “D” grades, 14% received “C” grades, and 8% received “B” grades — districts that Jasinski said were more complicated than just those strictly out of compliance with the law. 
“The only districts that are outright not following the law are the true zeros. That means that we could not find the link anywhere on the whole website,” she said. “Anything that did receive some credit means that mention of safe storage was found somewhere on the website, but it was either super hard to find, not up to date, or not the direct MDE link.”
The research was done by volunteers — something that Ryan Bates, the executive director of End Gun Violence Michigan, said he believed should not be the case going forward when examining compliance with the law. 
“This should not be up to volunteers,” he said. “The government should be doing this, so we really want to encourage the Department of Education to take this on and make sure that they’re holding school districts accountable to state law. So we hope next year that the Department of Education does a much better job reminding school districts to do their homework.”
Sherri Masson, a retired teacher and a member of Indivisible Michigan, described how the report card was put together, saying, “Our members graded every single school district website in the state on how compliant they were with the law, over 500 school districts. We weren’t able to track who sent flyers home because that information isn’t public, but the website is the easiest thing for schools to do, and it’s a good proxy for compliance.”

name: Delaware
title: Coons, Katz to Meet at Oct. 22 Senate Candidate Forum in Wilmington
text:
Scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons and Republican challenger Dr. Mike Katz appear together at a public forum hosted by the Rotary Club of Wilmington.
One of the most anticipated candidate forums of Delaware’s 2026 election season will bring the U.S. Senate candidates together at the Hotel du Pont as early voting begins.
WILMINGTON, Del. — One of the most anticipated candidate forums of Delaware’s 2026 election season is now scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, when Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons and Republican challenger Dr. Mike Katz appear together at a public forum hosted by the Rotary Club of Wilmington.
Both candidates have agreed to participate in the noon event at the Hotel du Pont, giving Delaware voters an opportunity to hear directly from the two candidates seeking to represent the state in the U.S. Senate.
The forum will be moderated by Jake Owens, editor-in-chief of Spotlight Delaware, and will feature questions submitted by members of the Rotary Club of Wilmington.
The event comes at a particularly important moment in the election calendar. Oct. 22 marks the beginning of early voting in Delaware, with Election Day scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3.
For voters who have followed the Senate campaign, the forum provides an opportunity to compare the candidates’ perspectives on issues facing Delaware and the nation.
A chance to hear both candidates
The forum follows earlier discussions about whether Coons and Katz would appear together during the campaign, including an unsuccessful effort by University of Delaware student political organizations to arrange a bipartisan debate.
With both candidates now committed to the Rotary event, attention shifts to the issues voters want addressed and the differences in how the candidates would approach the next six years in Washington.
Coons, who has represented Delaware in the Senate since 2010, is seeking another term. Katz, a physician and former state Senate candidate, is challenging the incumbent.
The Oct. 22 appearance will allow voters to hear their responses to questions in the same setting, offering a direct comparison of their priorities, experience and views.
Rotary builds on successful candidate forum format
The Rotary Club of Wilmington will use the same basic format it employed last week for its candidate forum featuring Democratic state treasurer candidate Ted Lauzen and Republican candidate Mike Ramone.
Club members will submit questions, which will be presented by the moderator.
Although the event will be structured as a candidate forum rather than a traditional debate, it will bring the two Senate candidates before the same audience and provide an opportunity for each to address issues important to Delaware voters.
The Rotary Club has a long history of civic engagement and community leadership in Wilmington, making the gathering a fitting setting for a discussion about Delaware’s representation in Washington.
Public invited to attend or watch online
The Rotary Club of Wilmington is inviting the public to participate in the event, either in person or through an online livestream.
In-person attendance at the Hotel du Pont will be limited by available seating, and advance registration is encouraged.
Those interested in attending should contact Rotary Club of Wilmington Executive Director Ashly Cloud at 302-388-7176 or office@rotarywilmington.org.
For voters unable to attend in person, the forum will be livestreamed on the Rotary Club of Wilmington’s Facebook page.
With early voting beginning the same day, the Oct. 22 forum offers voters a timely opportunity to hear from both candidates before making their decisions in one of Delaware’s highest-profile races.

Election dates: Early voting begins Oct. 22. General election is Nov. 3.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Republicans Tillis, Moore prepare for GOP losses in upcoming election
text:
U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis speaking at an energy conference in Cary on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)Two sitting GOP members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation say they’re bracing for Republicans to lose seats in November. 
Speaking at an energy conference in Cary on Thursday, retiring U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis said the Republican party has changed over the 20 years he’s spent in public office.
“The election’s in 19 days,” Tillis said. “Twenty days from now, I’ll be reaching out to Republicans who aren’t crazy and try to figure out how we can recover from what I think are almost certain losses this election cycle.”
Recent polls have shown a tough political climate for the GOP. President Donald Trump’s approval rating hovers in the upper thirties in the Tar Heel State. That’s been a problem for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who’s tied himself closely to the president ever since entering the race with Trump’s endorsement.
In the contest to succeed Tillis, Whatley, a former Republican National Committee and North Carolina GOP chair, has consistently trailed his Democratic rival, former Gov. Roy Cooper. With little movement in the polls, national groups on both sides have pulled funding from the race, choosing to focus on other states instead.
NC elections board to notify 1,392 voters flagged as potential noncitizens

The seat could play a pivotal role in control over the Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber. In the House, the GOP has a 218-212 majority, with four vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. 
“I’m happy to help any candidate, and that includes Whatley and anybody else,” Tillis told reporters. “What we have to do in the state is resonate with unaffiliated voters and have some separation from the president when you legitimately have a difference in opinion.”
Towards the end of his two terms in the U.S. Senate, Tillis has become known for straying from the party line and going against Trump. Rather than face a Trump-backed candidate in the primaries, Tillis decided not to run for reelection in 2026. 
Tillis delves further into his quarrels with Trump in his memoir, How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents: The Trouble with Sycophants, Courage Outsourcing, and Partisan Groupthink. The book was released last week.
“I still have a good relationship with the president, and I will as long as he wants to have it,” Tillis said. “Then I’ll have whatever relationship, if it’s other than that, that he chooses to have.”
Last year, Tillis voted against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” due to its language regarding Medicaid. The measure cut about $800 million from Medicaid funding in North Carolina.
The senator said he opposed the bill because it hurt North Carolinians, and advised Trump against the Medicaid provisions.
“I’m here to try and make policy better and get Republicans elected every election cycle,” Tillis said. “I was just saying, ‘This is not going to work, and it’s not going to help your legacy. It’s certainly not going to help our chances in the election cycle.’ And I think both are proving to be true right now.”
U.S. Rep. Tim Moore speaking at an energy conference in Cary on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
U.S. Rep. Tim Moore, who represents the state’s 14th Congressional District, served as the Speaker of the North Carolina House before his election to Congress. He succeeded Tillis in the state House leadership role. 
Moore said he thinks Republicans will retain their majority in the U.S. Senate, but is unsure about the U.S. House. He’s more confident in his party’s performance at the state level, where Republicans have drawn legislative districts to maximize their partisan advantage.
Republicans hold a 30-20 majority in the North Carolina Senate and a 71-47-2 majority in the House. After the 2024 election, they fell one seat short of a veto-proof supermajority in the lower chamber. 
“Absolutely, Republicans will maintain a majority in the state legislature,” Moore said. “I’m very familiar with those legislative districts, and I see the quality of the candidates who are working. I do think that the Republicans may lose about three seats.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators say Laurel could be breaking federal law
text:
Signs line the lawn of the Laurel Public Library as community resident gather before a listening session on a proposed state psychiatric facility. The meeting happened on April 22, 2026 (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). Montana legislators accused the City of Laurel of potentially breaking federal law in a fight over a mental health facility outside of the city in a meeting and a letter to the local government earlier this month.
Legislators in the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee also threatened to withhold municipal funding following a moratorium Laurel unanimously passed last month that halted annexing any land so it can study the city’s water system. Those issues also include aging infrastructure, fire protection problems and areas of low water pressure. There’s also been problems with the city’s water intake from the Yellowstone River.
State plans call for building a 32-bed mental health facility at the edge of Laurel city limits in Yellowstone County. Laurel residents have pushed back on the proposal citing problems they say could arise when the facility is built, including concerns the city’s utilities won’t be able to keep up.
City officials say they pressed pause on annexation applications so Laurel can study its water system. Some legislators, meanwhile, say the city is discriminating against those with mental illnesses and could be breaking federal law.  
A letter sent from the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee to Laurel and Montana’s congressional delegation says the city’s decision “essentially means the city will not provide water service to the proposed new mental health facility for forensic patients” and goes on to say the ordinance was “discriminatory.” 
State officials decided during the summer to place the facility outside Laurel. Onsite work at the facility has been paused while a lawsuit over the construction proceeds.
The letter from legislators to the City of Laurel says the action “may subject” the city to a lawsuit for violating federal law. Legislators unanimously approved the letter during an Oct. 8 committee meeting. 
Additionally, during that meeting, legislators by a 4-3 vote approved a “global motion” to direct the legislature to consider not directing any funding to any municipality under investigation for violations to the Americans with Disability Act, the Fair Housing Act or the Montana Human Rights Act.
The vote does not immediately strip any municipalities of any funding but means the issue of whether cities under federal investigation are eligible for state money will be taken up by the Legislative Finance Committee when it resumes during the 2027 session. Laurel was the only city discussed during the meeting.
“The legislature is not going to investigate the city of Laurel,” said John Esp, a Big Timber Republican and chairperson of the committee. “Somebody’s going to file a complaint on fair housing grounds, or on Americans with Disabilities grounds, or with the Montana Human Rights Commission, and while they’re under investigation by the Human Rights Commission or some federal agency, that’s when the prohibition on getting state money kicks in.”
Any sort of penalties wouldn’t begin unless the Legislature passes a bill to that effect next session.
When asked if any complaints have been filed against the City of Laurel, a Department of Labor and Industries employee within the Montana Human Rights Bureau directed the Daily Montanan to file a records request, which it has done. Federal Fair Housing Act violations would fall within the  U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, while Americans with Disabilities Act violations are investigated by a variety of federal entities.
In a five-page response to the lawmaker’s letter, Laurel Mayor Kris Vogele said he disagrees with the legislators, and expressed concern about any potential loss of funding. Some legislators worried the motion could negatively impact cities that are under investigation but end up not having broken federal law. Laurel receives millions of dollars in state funding per year, though city officials said they weren’t sure how much. 
For example, per the Montana League of Cities and Towns documentation, cities are projected to receive about $26 million in roads funding from the state, which is protected by statute. Laurel is projected to receive about $300,000 from that funding stream.
The legislative motion made by Sen. Ellie Boldman, a Missoula Democrat, said “that the legislature not consider or fund any local government request while under investigation for discriminating against a state facility.”
“Our intent right here on this call is to encourage the City of Laurel to take a look at this on their own,” Boldman said during the meeting, “so that nobody has to withhold anything.”
In a separate email to media members, Vogele said the committee was advancing a “deeply troubling allegation.”
“These are extraordinarily serious accusations, made with potentially far-reaching consequences not only for Laurel, but for communities across Montana,” Vogele wrote in a statement. “An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing. An allegation is not proof of discrimination. And a Montana community should not risk losing state funding simply because its elected officials raise legitimate questions about whether its infrastructure can safely support a major state project.”
The Laurel response also references a 95-page document the city sent the state regarding its environmental assessment of the mental health facility property. That document, sent to the state in September, asks for more assessment of the site “to establish a complete and supportable record.” 
The mental health facility has been an issue in Laurel for more than a year, and some residents have also expressed worry about the impacts to the city’s sewer and water systems, while others have been concerned about its location within a mile of an elementary school.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Business Council CEO resigns amid agency reform efforts
text:
Wyoming Business Council CEO Josh Dorrell resigned Wednesday after the agency’s board of directors met in executive session. His departure, which comes months after a failed legislative push to defund the agency, is effective at the close of business on Friday, according to the board. 
The council did not offer an explanation for Dorrell’s sudden departure.
“The Wyoming Business Council is very proud of the work Josh has done for the agency, and the board is focused on continuity and on the council’s future,” Wyoming Business Council Board of Directors Co-Chair Derek Smith said via email. “Out of respect for Josh and for the council, I won’t discuss private personnel matters or the details of the transition.”
The agency’s work will continue “uninterrupted” as the board seeks an interim CEO and while it searches for a permanent replacement, leaders said. 
“I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve built over these past few years, and proud that Wyoming has a solid foundation to build on,” Dorrell, who grew up in Rawlins, said in a statement Wednesday afternoon. “But what I’m most proud of is the strength, resilience and devotion of the team at the Business Council, and the committed coalition of thousands of people across Wyoming who have partnered with us in making real progress toward a bright future.”
Participants meet in Riverton for the Wyoming Business Council’s Assessment to Action program. (Wyoming Business Council)
Dorrell’s six-year tenure saw Wyoming’s top economic development shop navigate through a wildly shifting economic landscape, from managing federal emergency relief measures during the COVID-19 pandemic to new initiatives aimed at retaining and attracting new businesses, as well as fortifying communities both on the upswing and those that face growing budget constraints — all in the midst of a national shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
The agency is a regular target of scrutiny, and a Wyoming Freedom Caucus-led effort during the past legislative session sought to defund and dismantle the business council. Despite criticism of the agency and Dorrell’s leadership, the council dodged its demise in exchange for an ongoing effort to reform and more narrowly focus its work — an endeavor Dorrell has said he enthusiastically embraced.
“We are very willing to not defend our programs, or to defend the efforts that we’ve taken so far, but rather to seek out the problem and address it with the right statutes and the right investment mechanisms,” Dorrell told a legislative panel in January.
The political firestorm around the council followed declarations by Dorrell in the summer of 2025 that both the council and state leaders need to radically change course due to a “long-term economic decline in Wyoming,” and a lingering, painful youth exodus that exacerbates workforce limitations to grow the economy.
“Over nearly seven years, Josh has demonstrated a genuine passion for Wyoming and a steadfast commitment to the businesses and communities that make our state special,” Smith said in a prepared statement. “His leadership has made a meaningful and lasting impact, and we are grateful for the energy, dedication and heart Josh has brought to the Wyoming Business Council and its mission.”

name: VTDigger
title: English programs face rising anxiety amid fears of immigration enforcement
text:
Helene Rassias-Miles, Executive Director of the Rassias Center for World Languages and Cultures, leads a training session with her team while refining future lesson plans in Hanover, Nh., on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Photo by Sophia Sahni/Valley News

This story by Sophia Sahni first appeared in the Valley News on Oct. 12, 2026.
Across the Upper Valley, a network of free English language learning programs serves immigrants at every level.
In Hanover, New Hampshire, the Supporting Refugees Club, created by Hanover High School students and the Rassias Center, trains students in the Rassias Method, a high-energy teaching style that replicates life-like situations, to provide weekly English lessons to immigrants working at a local hospital. This year, the club has reached record involvement, with up to 50 students attending club meetings each week.
Just across the river, in White River Junction, Vermont Adult Learning offers a range of in-person and online services to help Vermont residents improve their English language skills, encourage conversation and support professional development.
Recently, some managers of the English language learning programs say fear of immigration enforcement is making it harder to bring students together.
“There is so much fear. People are way more cautious,” said Helene Rassias-Miles, executive director of the Rassias Center for World Languages and Cultures in Hanover. “There is just so much anxiety.”
In August, a local volunteer group, Upper Valley Immigration Solidarity, reported that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained three people in West Lebanon, New Hampshire, on the morning of Aug. 7, the Valley News reported. Hartford police said at the time they were unaware of any ICE arrests.
Despite rising fears, these programs continue to meet weekly. What keeps them running is not just the students’ commitment to learn English, but the personal relationships and community found in the classroom.
‘A bunch of different cultures’
The Upper Valley is home to a diverse demographic of immigrants, with people from Afghanistan to Haiti to Ukraine. “We don’t have a giant population of one ethnic group. Rather, we have a few people from here and there, and as a result, a lot of our classes are a mix of a bunch of different cultures,” Rassias-Miles explained.
While having a diverse classroom can make creating an English curriculum that accommodates various native languages challenging, Rassias-Miles emphasized that in her experience, it also creates a unique community where people are united by their desire to learn English. As students progress through weekly sessions, English soon becomes a common medium where communication and collaboration can thrive.
Nate McFetridge, a senior at Hanover High School and a leader of the school’s Supporting Refugees Club, said that a strong community comes from years of repeated connection between the teachers and students.
“The other teachers and I feel more like their friends than ever, mostly because of how well we know them now,” McFetridge explained.
The classroom environment is friendly and lighthearted. According to Amanda Gillen, the programs and finance coordinator at the Rassias Center, the Rassias Method emphasizes “creating a safe environment where people can mess up and feel the support of the people around them.”
McFetridge emphasized, “I definitely think the students look forward to class time. We’ve really created a community where learning for them is super enjoyable.”
‘What’s new?’
At the English language learning program at Vermont Adult Learning, students come weekly to improve their language skills for a variety of reasons.

Joy Gaine, center, English teacher at Vermont Adult Learning, explains common idioms to students Fernando Arias Otero, right, Cici Zhang, and Nataliya Ruml during an ELL class in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Photo by Sophia Sahni/Valley News

Some focus on career advancement, hoping to one day start their own business or apply to a Ph.D. program. Others want to improve their day-to-day interactions, eager to better understand their doctor’s appointments or find friendship with those in their community.
Joy Gaine, an English language teacher at Vermont Adult Learning, fosters an environment where students can connect through shared experiences. Students come to the course with distinct languages, cultures and reasons for learning English, but the classroom can reveal they have more in common than they think.
At the beginning of each lesson, Gaine asks, “What’s new?” This simple question invites students to share what preoccupies their minds.
Conversations are not always easy. Students discuss hurdles in their lives, from the challenges of living in a rural environment to feelings of isolation, difficult family situations and the sadness of not knowing how loved ones are doing in another country.
Students take turns sharing their personal experiences as Gaine helps them articulate their thoughts. They are honest and vulnerable, revealing their struggles to an audience of open ears. Mutual understanding underpins each discussion, and students often reassure each other that they share the same experience, Gaine said.
While the conversations can be heavy, they also bring plenty of joy and laughter. Students celebrate each other’s accomplishments, discuss their favorite hobbies and plan future visits to each other’s gardens. The conversation flows seamlessly between sharing moments of hardship and stories of contentment, interrupted only by Gaine’s intermittent grammatical corrections.

Students Fernando Arias Otero, left, and Cici Zhang, right, fill in a worksheet about seasonal vocabulary and fall traditions at Vermont Adult Learning in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Sophia Sahni/Valley News

According to Gaine, “It’s important to give everyone a chance to chat. Grammar, vocabulary, fluency — they are all important skills, but I always make sure to have time for conversation.” This atmosphere encourages students to put themselves out there and make mistakes, supporting vulnerability beyond language skills.
“This community would not exist if it were just a club for immigrants,” emphasized Cici Zhang, a visiting student at Vermont Adult Learning. “Even though we have the same problems and the same challenges, we don’t know how to express our feelings. The teacher is like a light.”
The teachers themselves don’t always recognize the impact they have on their students.
“If we are afraid to do anything, the teachers give us confidence to speak out, speak up, and to push to keep on going. She opens her heart so we can open ours,” Zhang said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI Health and Human Services head to replace Roger Williams, Fatima hospitals CEO
text:
Rhode Island Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest is leaving state government to take a job as CEO of CharterCARE Health of Rhode Island, the local owners of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)In November, Rhode Island Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest’s covert courtship of another hospital buyer for Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital drew a strong rebuke from the head of the nonprofit already approved to buy the hospitals.
Eleven months later, with the sale to The Centurion Foundation complete, Charest has been tapped to lead its Rhode Island hospitals operations.
CharterCARE Health of Rhode Island, Centurion’s local subsidiary, announced Wednesday that Charest will replace retiring CEO Jeffrey Liebman on Nov. 1. Charest submitted his resignation letter to Gov. Dan McKee the same day, according to the letter shared with Rhode Island Current.
Charest, 74, has worked for McKee’s administration since 2021, leading the Executive Office of Health and Human Services since 2023. He was appointed by CharterCARE’s 13-member board of directors, Ben Mingle, Centurion CEO and CharterCARE board president, said.
“Our Board felt that Rick’s experience and skill set made him uniquely qualified over other candidates to step right in and begin executing on our comprehensive strategic turnaround plan,” Mingle said in a statement.
Liebman has led CharterCARE since 2018, including through the sale to Centurion. The CharterCARE website lists him as a member of the board of directors, and it was unclear if he intends to remain on the board after he retires.
Otis Brown, a spokesperson for CharterCARE, did not respond to questions regarding the search process, including how many other candidates were considered by the board, or requests for a copy of Liebman’s resignation letter.
“I look forward to tackling the challenge of leading CharterCARE Health of Rhode Island,” Charest said in a statement. “We must deliver on the strategic turnaround plan to stabilize finances and strengthen operations of these essential safety-net hospitals. I commit my best efforts to CharterCARE’s board, providers, and employees to make this happen.”
Charest initially sought to retire from state government in July but then reversed course, agreeing to McKee’s request to stay in the $238,597 cabinet role and guide the massive state health and human service organization through massive federal policy and funding changes to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
In his Oct. 14 resignation letter to McKee, Charest indicated he had previously planned to leave state office on Nov. 28. Now, his last day will be Oct. 31, Charest wrote.
McKee, who leaves office in January after losing his primary reelection bid to Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Charest’s departure.
Strained relations 
Charest’s 26-year career includes nine years as president and CEO of Landmark Medical Center in Woonsocket, including through its receivership and sale to Prime Healthcare in 2013.
Charest reached out to his former employer last year, with the blessing of McKee’s office, to see if they were interested in buying Roger Williams and Fatima hospitals. At the time, Centurion had already received conditional approval from state regulators to buy the facilities, but had not closed the deal, struggling to secure the investor-backed financing amid poor credit ratings. Meanwhile, then-owner Prospect Medical Holdings, in the midst of Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings, threatened to close the hospitals if the sale didn’t go through.
McKee’s office defended the secret outreach to Prime as a necessary backup plan if the sale to Centurion failed. But Mingle blasted state officials for undermining the deal already in place, while unionized healthcare workers at the hospitals staged a public press conference accusing the state of breaching contract and business law by reaching out to Prime.
In the end, Prime wasn’t interested, and with an $18 million boost of state reserve funds, Centurion closed the sale in March.
Yet the initial work to resuscitate the hospitals has not gone smoothly. Contract disputes with 1,200 unionized hospital workers are entering a seventh month, with the United Nurses and Allied Professionals set to issue a strike notice Friday if they can’t reach a deal, said Chris Callaci, general counsel.
Meanwhile, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha rejected the new owners’ turnaround plan — one of 85 conditions imposed by state regulators in their June 2024 approval — deeming it insufficient to keep the facilities operating beyond a few months. A revised plan submitted by the Sept. 15 deadline remains under review, said Tim Rondeau, a spokesperson for Neronha’s office.
And now, a leadership change might necessitate review by the state ethics panel, according to Neronha.
“We hope the Board has undertaken a diligent and thorough vetting process in selecting their next leader,” Neronha said in a statement. “We do note that given his current position at EOHHS there may be some ethical considerations that would be most appropriate for the ethics commission to address.” 
Neronha did not specify what part of the state ethics code may be in question in Charest’s move from state government to private sector work. 
Back through the revolving door 
A potential problem for Charest’s hire: the revolving-door clause, which limits state officials and administrators from representing themselves before state agencies where they worked for at least one year after leaving the position. 
“He pretty clearly would be prohibited from interaction with EOHHS for a period of one year,” said John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island.
Separate provisions of the ethics code would ban Charest from using confidential information obtained in his government role to help his new employer financially.
In 2017, when former Senate President Teresa Paiva Weed stepped down from her paid, elected position in the General Assembly to take a job leading the Hospital Association of Rhode Island, she sought an ethics recommendation regarding the revolving door provision of state law.
The commission advised that Paiva Weed could not lobby on behalf of or otherwise represent the hospital trade group before the legislature for one year, though the ban did not apply to other branches of government.
Marion thought Charest should also seek an advisory opinion from the Ethics Commission for his pending job move.
“It always makes sense when somebody moves from government to an industry that they regulated while in government to seek an advisory opinion so they know the boundaries under the code of ethics,” Marion said.
The Ethics Commission has not received any requests for advisory opinions about Charest’s new job as of Thursday afternoon, Teodora Papa, a staff attorney, confirmed via email.
Brown, of CharterCARE, did not respond to requests for comment on concerns over ethical conflicts with Charest’s hire. 
Callaci, who blasted Charest for interfering in the Centurion deal last year, was indifferent to the leadership change. He remained focused on the contract battle between union workers and CharterCARE executives — a negotiation that Charest will not be part of, Callaci confirmed.
In a separate email sent to CharterCARE employees and shared with Rhode Island Current, Mingle also specified that Charest’s appointment was not tied to his past relationship with Prime.
“I thought that was weird,” Callaci said.“But, as long as he’s not carrying Prime’s water, look, Rick has a long resume, I can’t challenge his qualifications.”
Callaci continued, “He’s going to be tested, just like Jeff was. Let’s see what the outcome is. We wish him well, we want the hospitals to succeed.”
Mingle acknowledged the “short-term cash flow pressures” facing the hospitals in the wake of the sale while noting that there has been “positive progress,” including in the contract negotiations.
“Volume has since been trending up, we have recruited several new physicians and specialists, implemented new programs and services, invested in equipment and our physical plants, all contributing to improved financial performance,” Mingle said in a statement. “Again, our Board is acutely aware of the critical role our hospitals play in our state’s health care system, and we are laser-focused on doing what is needed to preserve our mission and our community’s access to quality health care.”
