title: 2026 gov race: Hatley puts in another $5M, Blackburn raises $2.1M, Green $1M
text:
With early voting underway and 19 days till the general election, state campaign finance reports show how much money gubernatorial candidates have raised to date. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) 
Independent candidate David Hatley loaned his gubernatorial bid another $5 million in September, bringing his total self-funding to $12 million less than three weeks before the November election.
Hatley’s campaign holds a significant cash advantage over his rivals, as the latest state campaign finance reports due Tuesday showed he entered the final stretch of the campaign with over $6.8 million available to spend. 
Despite Hatley’s cash advantage, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee, is the favorite to win the race, as Tennessee hasn’t elected a Democrat to a statewide office in two decades, and never has elected an independent candidate. 
Blackburn’s campaign raised $2.1 million in the reporting period spanning from the end of the August primary election to Sept. 30. She has $3.1 million heading into the race’s final weeks. 
Jerri Green, the Democratic Party candidate, raised nearly $1 million this quarter, her largest cash haul in a single reporting period this election. Independent Lauren Pinkston raised around $150,000.





 

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Republican gubernatorial candiate, photographed on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)







 

Democratic nominee for governor,Jerri Green at a Memphis forum at Teamsters Local 667 October 09, 2026 in Memphis, Tennessee. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)







 

David Hatley, independent candidate for governor, photographed on Oct. 1 at Elliston Place Soda Shop in Nashville. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)







 

Lauren Pinkston, photographed in Brentwood, Tennessee on Sept. 3, 2026, independent gubernatorial candidate. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






Independent candidate David Hatley loaned his gubernatorial bid another $5 million in September, bringing his total self-funding to $12 million less than three weeks before the November election.
The latest campaign finance reports shed light on funding for the Choose Freedom PAC and its TV ads attacking Hatley over the past month.
The Choose Freedom PAC is registered in Alabama and disclosed that it received $4.2 million from Choose Freedom Inc., a Massachusetts-based dark-money group. Choose Freedom Inc. formed earlier this year and has spent $22 million in U.S. House and U.S. Senate races, according to The New York Times.
The associated phone number couldn’t receive calls. Choose Freedom’s ads follow a pattern similar to Blackburn’s own attacks on Hatley after she won her primary, as she apparently tries to keep the conservative independent from gaining traction. 
President Donald Trump, at a rally Saturday for Blackburn and other GOP candidates in Tennessee, made an explicit plea telling his supporters, “you have to vote Republican.”
At the same rally, Blackburn said she was the “only conservative” in the governor’s race. 
Outside help for Blackburn
Blackburn is also being boosted by two PACs formed during the primary campaign. Team Tennessee and the Tennessee Freedom Fund spent millions on advertisements boosting her and attacking her main rival in that race, and they continue to raise money.
Marsha Blackburn, the $100M woman

Team Tennessee took a $50,000 donation from prediction market Kalshi in September. Kalshi is currently involved in a legal battle in Tennessee over its right to offer sports prediction markets.
The Tennessee Freedom Fund raised roughly $670,000 during the reporting period, taking $100,000 each from Smith Douglas Homes founder Tom Bradbury, entrepreneur Richard Spanton, Jr. from Franklin and Holly Jacobson-Peterson from Nashville. 
Those two PACs previously raised money from a pro-private school voucher group funded by billionaire Jeff Yass, payday lender Advance Financial, Artificial Intelligence company Anthropic, tobacco giant Reynolds America, private prison operator CoreCivic and its former CEO Damon Hiniger, Tamara Stephens, logistics entrepreneur Spencer Patton, Dr. Ralph Korpman, Copart founder Willis Johnson and Franklin Home Mortgage CEO Daniel Crockett.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Lowndes commission approves $1.15 billion tax break for a data center despite pushback
text:
Residents of Lowndes County holding up signs that read "No Data Center" at a County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in Hayneville, Alabama, in the Lowndes County Courthouse. The commission approved a project proposal and 20-year, $1.15 billion tax break for Alabama's largest planned data center on Tuesday amid pushback from residents. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Lowndes County Commission unexpectedly approved a 20-year, $1.15 billion tax break for Alabama’s largest planned data center development Tuesday morning amid concerns and pushback from residents. 
The vote came after what residents and environmental advocates describe as a “tense” question-and-answer session with the project’s developers on Friday. They’ve demanded transparency from the developer, Texas-based Cloverleaf Infrastructure, and from the commission but have been unsatisfied with the communication so far.
Commissioners did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment sent Tuesday and Wednesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The agenda for Tuesday morning’s meeting said that the commission would consider the adoption of Cloverleaf’s development and tax abatement agreement in a week on Oct. 20. Instead it approved both Tuesday morning.
Ryan Anderson, a staff attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center, expected the commission to put the vote on its next meeting’s agenda. 
“My perspective is that tax revenue is one of, if not the only, benefit that comes to communities from data center development. So we know that there’s not really any job creation associated with data centers, and we know that they place a strain on local infrastructure like power and water and roads,” she said in a phone interview on the way to the meeting.
Lowndes County residents demand transparency in hyperscale data center development

Residents have attended commission meetings to protest the development in recent months, forcing the commission to change locations to accommodate the audience size. Lowndes County District Judge and future neighbor of the data center Adrian Johnson attended Tuesday’s meeting and said in a phone interview that there were only about 40 people there. 
“There were probably 150 people here on Friday for the public hearing. This morning there were probably only 40 people here for the regular scheduled county commission meeting because no one anticipated, based on the resolution that was on the table, that there would be any vote on this today,” Johnson said. “It’s continued to be this lack of transparency. None of those agreements were provided to the public.”
Thomas Ellis, chair of the Lowndes County Economic Development Commission, said in a statement that the data center is an “incredible opportunity” for the county. 
“Through the revenue generated and jobs created, we’ll be able to support our schools, fund essential services, and improve the quality of life for our residents here,” he said after the tax break was approved. 
The data center should bring about 225 permanent jobs, according to the project proposal, and at least 1,000 temporary construction jobs over a three-year period.
Johnson and other residents have asked for months who will run the data center after it’s built. He said they were met mostly with non-answers on Friday. 
Dave Berry, co-founder and CEO of Cloverleaf Infrastructure, said in a phone interview Tuesday that transparency is important to him too, but there is only so much he can share, and he can’t share who will operate the data center right now.
He said Cloverleaf is close to finalizing the end user, and construction will not begin until then. Both should happen “soon,” he said.
“We still have some details to finalize, but once we have those details finalized, we’ll absolutely be able to share the identity of the end user. They’ll be involved in the community before we go start construction,” Berry said. “They’re not going to show up and just be a surprise.”
Despite the tax breaks, Berry said the project will generate $124 million in local tax revenue and $25 million in state revenue per year. The abatement — a 50% reduction in the non-educational county taxes that Cloverleaf is responsible for as a business — is about $57.5 million per year. 
According to the agreement, Cloverleaf will be relieved from some county sales and use, property and other taxes. Under Alabama law, education taxes are not eligible for tax breaks. 
According to the proposal, the project will be Alabama’s largest planned data center, operate 24/7, and it’s requested 1,500 megawatts of energy capacity from Alabama Power — enough to power roughly 1 million homes. The entire state of Alabama has about 2 million households and about 2.4 million housing units.
Its planned location is along U.S. Hwy 80 and Alabama Hwy 21 in unincorporated Lowndes County, which runs along the historic Selma to Montgomery trail. 
Data centers emerge as top Alabama election issue as community concerns grow

Lowndes County, like many counties in the Black Belt, has seen a population decrease between 2010 and 2020. But the census tract at the proposed location of Project Red Clay via the U.S. Census Bureau shows that it is the most densely populated part of the county at 21.7 people per square mile. Other tracts in the county are 14.8, 12.3 and 9.7 people per square mile. 
“It’s extremely frustrating for those of us who live in the area because we know what the impact is going to be, and it’s going to continue to exacerbate population loss. It’s going to continue to cause people to move outside the county and not drive people into the community,” Johnson said. 
Because the location is unincorporated, the county does not have planning and zoning authority like cities do. 
Berry said that because of the location of the development, Cloverleaf wanted to ensure that there were more regulations and restrictions for the facility than its other developments. That is why the company agreed to a 55 decibel cap and restrictions on vegetation destruction. The company also agreed to low water usage and to pay for water infrastructure improvements.
“We learn as we go, but we’ve learned a lot about how to do these projects in a way that they’re good neighbors and good citizens,” Berry said. 
A spokesperson for Cloverleaf said Wednesday that the company has ongoing developments in Wisconsin and Oklahoma.
Lowndes County has struggled with wastewater issues for decades due to a combination of low population density and a heavy, clay soil that makes many septic tank systems ineffective.
The facilities, which store digital data in servers, are not new to Alabama. There are dozens across the state, according to Data Center Map, a website that tracks the facilities across the country. Berry said that the facilities have gotten more responsible, not less.
“I think good regulation has a place. Infrastructure projects need to build trust, and part of the way you do that is by having some restrictions,” Berry said. “I’m not expecting a pat on the back here, but we actually agreed on some restrictions and guidelines and limitations that legally we didn’t have to because it was the right thing to do.”
Anderson said that the regulations and restrictions that Berry and Cloverleaf have entered into with Project Red Clay are voluntary, and she wants to see a law on the books.
“I think we need some commonsense regulations about how much water they can use, what their wastewater discharges can look like, where they’re sited, and the public notice and  opportunity to be heard around those citing decisions,” she said. “Those are all things that I think can and should be taken care of through state legislation.”
John Urquhart, a Lowndes County resident, speaking to the Lowndes County Commission on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
John Urquhart, another Lowndes County resident that neighbors the proposed data center site, said in a phone interview Tuesday afternoon that the commissioners approving these tax breaks “takes your breath away.”
He bought 230 acres of land in the county after retiring a few years ago and said it’s peaceful now. 
“I grew up in Montgomery, and you just don’t have all that background noise. I’ve traveled all over the country with work, and it’s just so peaceful,” Urquhart said. “Certainly we didn’t put everything we’ve got into buying that to be parked beside a 3 million-square-foot data center. It certainly wasn’t in our plans for the future.”
Cloverleaf expects construction to begin within the first quarter of 2027, according to the project proposal.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A former school finds new life as affordable housing for NC seniors
text:
The front of the Dillard School Apartments, where former students once entered for classes. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)YANCEYVILLE — When Cassandra Henderson returned to Dillard Junior High School, memories from her time there decades ago came roaring back. 
She remembers the school bus dropping her off at the front steps, the hallways with metal lockers lining the walls and the auditorium where students gathered. Even the small church across the street is still there. 
Cassandra Henderson moved into the Dillard School Apartments in August. She now stands at the same entryway where a bus let her out for school. (Photo: Tre Spencer/ NC Newsline)
Nearly 60 years after graduating in 1968, Henderson is back—this time as a resident of the former school, which has been transformed into dozens of affordable apartments for seniors. 
“Some of my happiest years were here, and I can remember them like they happened yesterday,” she said. “I am so glad that the school is still standing, and they found such a great reason for keeping it standing.”
After years living in Richmond, Virginia, Henderson wanted to return to Yanceyville, where she had family and friends. But finding a place to live made that difficult. 
“My sister said, ‘Why don’t you move back home?’ I said, ‘There’s nowhere for me to move,’” Henderson said. 
The redevelopment gave her a path to come home. 
For other older North Carolinians, developments like Dillard are addressing the growing challenge of finding housing that fits a limited budget as rising rents and other expenses compete with fixed retirement income and Social Security benefits. 
Few options for seniors 
In Caswell County, the need for affordable housing is significant. About 42% of renters and 20% of homeowners are cost-burdened, meaning households spend more than 30% of their gross monthly income on housing costs. 
Dillard School Property Manager Charity James said the community has few affordable housing complexes, and even fewer for seniors.  She said when the property started leasing last year, more applicants than units were available, leading to long waitlists. 
“I’ve been in Yanceyville all of my life,” she said. “For seniors here, the housing market isn’t where it should be. We have very few housing options in the community.” 
The shortage goes beyond Caswell County. North Carolina has an estimated shortage of 215,000 affordable rental homes for extremely low-income residents. Of the state’s 348,000 renter households in that income category, 29% are headed by seniors. 
The state’s median monthly rent is about $1,338, according to the North Carolina Housing Finance Agency. It’s been rising for years, making it difficult for older adults living on fixed incomes to find affordable housing. 
For some, the lack of available options can determine whether they can stay in their communities or have to move away from family and friends. 
Cassandra Henderson’s one-bedroom apartment. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
Dillard School was designed to address at least part of that need. Its 53 apartments include studios and one-bedroom units, with rent based on residents’ incomes. Residents pay up to 30% of their income toward rent, with the remaining cost covered by federal housing funding. 
The development is not assisted living. Residents must be able to live independently, but the property includes elevators, accessible features, and community spaces. 
A second life for a vacant school 
Originally known as the Caswell County Training School, the school was the first in the county to offer 11  grades for Black students when it opened in the early 1950s.  After desegregation, it then took the name of longtime principal Nicholas Longworth Dillard. 
When it closed in 2002,  it was placed on the National Register of Historic Places. It sat vacant for over 20 years until its conversion. 
The building’s windows were broken, parts of the gym roof were gone, and the interior was exposed to the elements, said Alex Walker, a representative of DreamKey Partners, the project’s developers. 
He said transforming the property into affordable housing offered a chance to preserve local history while putting the property back in use. 
The project, designed specifically for seniors,  was financed through the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development’s Section 202 program as well as state and federal historic tax credits.
“Through layering all those financing pieces, we were able to, especially with the significant grant from HUD, put this project together to restore the building and make it possible for residents to live here,” Walker said. 
Rows of seats in the former Dillard School auditorium. The wooden seats were restored to their original condition. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
Earlier this year, the project received national recognition from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, which honored Dillard in its 2026 rural housing category. 
Emily Cadik, the coalition’s CEO, said federal tax credits like the low-income housing tax credit have become more important as families struggle with the rising cost of living. 
“Each winner… has made a lasting impact in the communities they serve and for the families who now have an affordable place to call home,” Cadik said. 
But the project’s significance extends beyond the award, offering one example of how communities can both preserve historic buildings and create housing for seniors on limited incomes. 
For former students like Henderson, the impact is already tangible. She can live in the community where she grew up, surrounded by memories of a place that has remained part of her life, even as its purpose has changed. 
“Being back is like a shot of adrenaline or a vitamin,” she said. “This is where I am meant to be.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado food banks strapped for resources to meet growing demand amid inflation, SNAP cuts
text:
Erin Pulling, right, CEO of Food Bank of the Rockies, talks to U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, middle, and Ron Meehan, government relations manager for Feeding Colorado, on a tour of the food pantry's Aurora facility on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline) Fueled by the rising cost of living and cuts to federal benefits, food assistance programs from around the Denver metro area have seen growing demand and an influx of new, first-time families in need of support this year.
Leaders with local food pantries and other nutritional aid groups highlighted the need for expanded funding for federal benefits like the Emergency Food Assistance Program and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, as well as broader reforms to make it more effective for the people it benefits, at a roundtable Wednesday hosted by U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet at the Food Bank of the Rockies. 
In the last year, about 40,000 Coloradans have lost access to SNAP benefits amid changes to program requirements, according to Ron Meehan, government relations manager for Feeding Colorado. Food pantries have seen growing demand as costs for regular families tightened, increasing the number of people who need their services on top of the low-income families who already relied on them.

“This has been a dark moment for our network in terms of need and in terms of significant cuts to a lot of these federal programs,” Meehan said. “At the same time, I think we have a real opportunity moving forward to not just undo damage, but really work together to improve programs and strengthen them more than where they were.”
The Adams County Emergency Food Bank has seen 3,400 new people come through its doors since January, executive director Steph Wayne said. People have started to treat food banks, which are meant to be supplemental, as their primary grocery stores, asking for personal and healthcare products they don’t have the capacity to provide, she said. 
Recent changes to SNAP have disrupted the kinds of food families are able to purchase, as well as how much they can afford each month. Wayne said food banks cannot personalize their offerings to the individual needs of each family, and that’s the gap SNAP served.
“Their monthly amount changed so heavily that it really takes away a piece of dignity when you can’t go to the store and get what you want,” Wayne said. “Feeling like that is taken away from you I think is huge, and maybe sometimes overlooked, because we’re so worried about the financial implication and not the implication of people as a human.”
Food assistance programs for seniors could also be improved to better serve their needs, Wayne said. For example, seniors need transportation support, because while volunteers and workers at the food bank can load food into their cars, they can’t help them get it into their houses. KaCy Fowles, CEO of HALO Community Outreach, said SNAP benefits paying for grocery store delivery fees would make a huge difference for seniors.



Quotation







The idea that we're living in a nation right now where our school teachers cannot afford to feed their families without going to the food bank to supplement their income says something really terrible about our priorities.


– Sen. Michael Bennet


Simret Kahsai, director of programs at Project Worthmore, which offers various services to immigrant and refugee families, including a food market, said the organization distributed 400,000 pounds of food between January and September this year, compared to 183,000 pounds last year. They’ve seen a 90% increase in the number of families the organization has served.  
When SNAP benefits froze during the government shut down last year, organizations like Food for Hope, an organization that supports nutrition for kids, were suddenly asked to triple or quadruple their output within a week, Executive Director Emily Stromquist said. Families who had never needed food support suddenly found themselves relying on food banks, she said.
“The conversation was, ‘Well, these families are losing their SNAP support. Everyone just go to your local food pantry,’” Stromquist said. “And local food pantries were left with very few resources to handle that.” 
One mother helped by Food for Hope is unable to work consistent hours because she supports four children with disabilities, Stromquist said. While her kids are fed lunch at school, she relied on food pantries for dinners. That meant better nutrition for the mother, too, because while kids are fed at school, parents aren’t, so she sometimes skipped meals.
Food stamp changes will cost states billions, raising fears about SNAP’s future

Bennet said he’s seen the increased demand across the state affect all kinds of families, and blasted the Trump administration for decisions he said have actively made it worse. 
“The idea that we’re living in a nation right now where our school teachers cannot afford to feed their families without going to the food bank to supplement their income says something really terrible about our priorities,” Bennet said. 
Renewed support for SNAP is a key priority Bennet said must be included in the next Farm Bill, a federal funding bill that supports agriculture and nutrition initiatives. But he acknowledged that there’s a small chance of a new Farm Bill passing through the current Congress. Bennet is a member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture.
The 2025 Republican tax cut and spending bill known as H.R. 1, which President Donald Trump signed into law last year, cut funding and added new work requirements for anyone who receives food stamp benefits through SNAP. To remain eligible for SNAP, an able-bodied adult without children must “participate in a work activity” for 20 hours a week. SNAP enrollment has dropped nationwide after Trump signed H.R. 1.
Other recent changes to SNAP requirements for states could result in billions of dollars in additional costs for states to administer the program.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s botched execution of Christa Pike raises tough questions
text:
Death row offender Christa Pike was taken taken by ambulance to a hospital for treatment after two failed lethal injections on Sept. 30. Hers is one in a series of failed executions in America over decades. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Editor’s note: This commentary includes descriptions of botched executions. 
Tennessee’s botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike has left behind some lingering and disturbing questions. 
As for Pike, she was hospitalized with serious injuries, now is in a prison rehabilitation center and as she heals, the state has not indicated if Tennessee will take another shot at killing her. Gov. Bill Lee faces awkward questions about former Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. Yes, Lee has dumped him, but why was he hired in the first place? CNN is among the outlets that has documented that he “reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.”
Veteran journalist John North of WBIR in Knoxville was a witness to Tennessee’s attempt to kill Pike. He detailed the irregularities that erupted, Pike’s snoring sounds, the frequent closing of blinds so the witnesses could not see certain things. “Prison officials led us into a staff room to give us a few minutes to gather our thoughts,” he wrote. “We needed it. We all looked at our notes. We came to the same conclusion — this hadn’t gone according to plan, and she was still alive.”        
Botched U.S. executions are not as rare as one might think. One researcher tallied the 8,776 executions between 1890 and 2010. In 276 of them (3.15%) something went wrong.
Attorney Louis Nizer years ago wrote The Implosion Conspiracy about the espionage trial and execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Both were executed by electrocution on June 19, 1953. The death of Ethel was particularly gruesome. Nizer wrote, “There was a strong smell of burning flesh as her body reached 140 degrees. Thin smoke rose from her scalp and turned blue in the overhead light, as it flattened out in an ugly cake against the skylight overhead.”
One doctor stepped forward and listened to her heart, saying in a hollow voice “This woman is still alive.” After some whispered conversations, she was strapped in again for two more jolts of 57 seconds each. The second jolt “made sputtering noises and sent a plume of smoke out of her head. Then silence and collapse.” The doctor applied his stethoscope to the smoldering chest and pronounced her dead.
A survived execution in Tennessee exposes the grim science of lethal injection

The newspaper columnist Russell Baker once wrote about his experience in the early 1950s as a reporter called upon to witness a hanging. “The hangman, of course, was an amateur,” declared Baker. “Even at the rate Maryland was then working its gallows, it was hard to get enough practice to do the job professionally. Consequently, a certain percentage of his ministrants failed to receive professional neck fractures when they dropped. These failed works hung there — before the mantlepiece, as it were — gurgling and choking for 15 or 20 minutes. On occasion, prison guards might seize them by the knees and pull down forcefully to speed the evening along.” These events routinely left observers shocked and sickened.
Future Texas Gov. Ann Richards survived a three-way 1990 Democratic Party primary in which all three candidates vied to be the most pro-death-penalty. Bill Clinton when he was governor of Arkansas and running for president let an execution go forward of a man with seriously degraded mental capacity, all so Clinton could burnish his “tough on crime” credentials. Lee has responded to the botched execution of Christa Pike by delaying the one execution left during his term, but he has not wavered in his overall support for the death penalty.
Politicians of all stripes across the South routinely support death sentences, knowing that people overwhelmingly support executions, at least in the abstract. Executions, of course, do not happen in the abstract. They occur in prison chambers with the sounds of Christa Pike snoring as she survived a megadose of the same chemical we use to put down animals.
Tennessee politicians are unmoved to reconsider the moral dimension of executions, and seem to restrict their analysis to tinkering with the methods used. Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, a Franklin Republican and candidate for Senate Speaker, suggested the electric chair or firing squads as alternatives. 
Republican gubernatorial nominee, U.S. Sen.Marsha Blackburn, has said she favors reinstating the electric chair. House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, is open to several alternatives including the electric chair, firing squad or hanging, which Tennessee used as its primary method of execution until 1913. Johnson and Sexton both insist Tennessee’s Republican supermajority has no intention of moving away from capital punishment.
If we ever are to restrict or rescind the death penalty, it will be a case of the people getting ahead of the politicians. For that to happen, we never can forget the horrors guilty murderers have inflicted on innocent people and their surviving family members. We also must ask ourselves: Do we want the state to commit vengeful horrors in our name? Should we join the 113 countries and 23 states that have abandoned the death penalty? How long can the Supreme Court maintain the pretense that executions are not the cruel and unusual punishment prohibited by the Eighth Amendment?
We must allow ourselves to consider the notion that we need to curtail, if not eliminate, death penalty executions.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Data centers can’t be stopped, but good policy is needed, NDSU researcher says
text:
Tony Clark, executive director of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, right, speaks Oct. 14, 2026, in Fargo on a panel discussing data centers. Also pictured are, from left, Robert Mayo, research specialist at North Dakota State University, Paul Matthys, president and CEO of Cass County Electric, and agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)FARGO — There’s no way of stopping the development of data centers and artificial intelligence, a North Dakota State University researcher said Wednesday, adding that attempts to slow development would only push it to other areas.
“It’s important to understand that AI is coming. These data centers will be built. There is nothing that can be done to stop it,” Robert Mayo, a research specialist at NDSU’s Challey Institute of Global Innovation and Growth. “All we can do is, through good public policy, choose how it develops and where it develops.” 
Mayo noted that local governments and large governments, like the state of New York, have implemented moratoriums as people question the impact of data centers.  
“All that does is move it to another county, another state, or another country,” Mayo said. 
2nd Fargo-area data center would use double the power of Harwood site

Mayo was part of a panel discussion of data centers organized by the Challey Institute, titled “Powering the AI Economy: Data Centers and North Dakota’s Future.”
Paul Matthys, president and CEO of Cass County Electric Cooperative, said there are many investors eager to put money into data center projects. 
“There’s a tremendous amount of venture capital that’s available,” Matthys said. But those investors are also eager for a return on that investment. 
“It’s partially what’s pushing the speed in the market,” Matthys said. 
He said Cass County Electric, which will supply power to the Applied Digital data center at Harwood, is content to take its time to ensure its existing customers don’t face higher utility bills or diminished service because of data centers. 
“The cooperatives are going to move at our speed, and we’re going to be slow and methodical and do this right,” Matthys said. 
The data center at Harwood, north of Fargo, will use as much power as all of the co-op’s other customers combined, he said. But with Applied Digital paying for a new substation and power line upgrades, that benefits existing customers, he said. 
He said bringing new power generation to eastern North Dakota is important for serving existing customers, and that new power is not just for data centers. 
Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

Minnkota Power Cooperative, which supplies power to Cass County Electric and 10 other co-ops, plans to add a power plant north of Mapleton, using natural gas from the planned Bakken East Pipeline. The pipeline will send natural gas from McKenzie County in the northwest to eastern North Dakota. 
Tony Clark, executive director of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissions and a former member of the North Dakota Public Service Commission, commented on data center  public policy in North Dakota. 
He said North Dakota and other Midwest states typically regulate utilities that generate power, transmit the power and bill customers. He said in the northeast United States and in Texas, those different functions have been broken up among multiple companies, making it harder to regulate. He said that has led to data centers driving up utility bills for some customers in those areas. 
Clark said governments typically have authority over data center zoning, such as setting acceptable noise levels and setback distances from buildings and homes. The state has the ability to regulate utility rates from for-profit power providers, while the reliability of the electrical grid falls to regional or national entities. 
Doug Goehring, North Dakota agriculture commissioner, noted that the state’s Department of Environmental Quality and Department of Water Resources play a part in regulating industry and power generation. 
Moderator Rob Port of Forum Communications asked Goehring if North Dakota had the right policy tools in place for data centers. 
“I think there’s always an opportunity to tweak things, and when it comes to water management in the state, I think we could definitely, probably do more,” Goehring said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Judge disciplined for speaking about harmful CPS staffing shortage takes case to WV Supreme Court
text:
Third Judiciary Circuit Court Judge Tim Sweeney asked the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals to throw out his admonishment after raising issues about Child Protective Services shortages in his judicial district. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals)West Virginia Supreme Court justices heard arguments Wednesday about a judge who pushed back on his discipline for speaking out about critical Child Protective Services shortages in his judicial district.
Third Circuit Judge Tim Sweeney was admonished by the West Virginia Judicial Investigation Commission in June 2025 after drawing attention in the media to CPS shortages impacting children’s care. 
Last February, Sweeney learned through cases on his docket that local CPS workers were overworked and understaffed, leading to missed deadlines and treatment for children. In response, the judge ordered state health officials, including the former Human Services secretary, to report to the Ritchie County Courthouse and receive assignments as CPS workers. 
“Judges have to make difficult decisions on the bench, the ends do justify the means,” J.H. Mahaney, an attorney representing Sweeney, said in court. “Sometimes when it comes to the welfare and safety of children, the ends are what really matters.”
Sweeney contacted Ogden Newspapers reporter Steven Allen Adams about the issue, and Adams was the first to report on the order. 
“I think the bus stops with me. I think somebody needs to stand up for the public, particularly the most vulnerable members of our community — the children,” Sweeney told Adams in an interview in February 2025. “From a legal point of view, abuse and neglect cases are of the highest priority, and they should be, in my opinion, for the department and the government in Charleston as well.”
Human Services officials contacted Sweeney within hours of receiving the order and addressed staffing issues, according to a filing from Sweeney. 
“Staffing was increased within a matter of days. Before the Feb. 20 hearing ever got here … their safety was being improved. The caseworkers were improved. That has to count for something,” Mahaney said, adding that the department didn’t object to Sweeney’s order. 
The Judicial Investigation Commission said Sweeney violated five rules of the Code of Judicial Conduct including releasing judicial statements on pending and impending cases. 
“All of this arose from a confidential abuse neglect proceeding, we have to remember, where the information contained in that hearing is confidential,” said Teresa Tarr, attorney for the Judicial Disciplinary Council. “My reading of the rule is: if you’re going to release confidential information from an abuse neglect hearing, a judge has to do it, and it has to be done with findings of fact and conclusions of law, and that was not done in this case.”
Mahaney noted that Sweeney had talked about systemic issues, not a pending child welfare case.
No formal disciplinary action was taken due to Sweeney’s reputation as a good judge, according to the WV Record. 
Sweeney objected to the commission’s admonishment. He asked the state Supreme Court to toss the disciplinary admonishment, arguing that he had an ethical duty to bring attention to the state’s CPS staffing crisis. 
Justice C. Haley Bunn
Supreme Court Chief Justice Haley Bunn questioned Mahaney on whether a lack of discipline in Sweeney’s case would result in other judges contacting the media about systemic issues. 
“What’s to stop any judicial officer from seeing a systematic problem, which there are systematic problems, and using his or her position to step outside the role of the judiciary’s branch and wielding the media and wielding the robe to improperly force an adversary proceed one side or the other in an adversary proceeding?” Bunn asked. 
Mahaney said that’s “the tough call” in this case. 
“Sweeney acted for the sole purpose of helping children, and that he did help children, and that at some point in time, that that has to be enough,” he said. 
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals recently dismissed ethics charges against Kanawha County Circuit Court Judge Maryclaire Akers stemming from a radio interview where she spoke about the state’s foster care system and children living in hotels.
Like Sweeney, Akers had asked the Supreme Court to intervene and force the dismissal of judicial ethics charges. Akers contended that she tried to stay within what she understood were her ethical limits while commenting on the hotel monitoring arrangement. She has faced no prior discipline as a lawyer or judge.

Sweeney was also admonished by the Judicial Investigation Commission for participation in charitable, fraternal or civic activities regarding some social posts that were unrelated to the CPS staffing issue. One of the social media posts shared by Sweeney was about a local volunteer fire department’s ice cream social and $10 raffle for a bike. The commission said this violated solicitation rules for judges.

“I think the fact that he posted, and the public can construe those as solicitations, indicate that he violated the code of judicial conduct with respect to solicitations,”  Tarr said. 
The West Virginia Supreme Court will issue a decision in the case at a later date.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana doesn’t see safety improve when 17-year-olds are jailed far from home
text:
Stock photo by Motortion/Getty ImagesImagine a 17-year-old boy on a prison bus being taken nearly 200 miles from his home  in East Baton Rouge Parish because its jail cannot house him separately from adults as required under federal law. He is innocent until proven guilty but still sent away to a jail in Jackson Parish, far from his family, lawyer, school and community. 
Louisiana spends public money to move 17-year-olds from parishes without separate facilities for adults and minors because a state law change in 2024 treats them, regardless of the offense, as adults and no longer allows them to go to juvenile detention. But parish jails still must house them separately under the Prison Rape Elimination Act, a federal law approved in 2003. To prevent sexual abuse behind bars, its prohibits housing anyone under age 18 within the sight or sound of adult inmates.
Louisiana approved a Raise the Age law in 2016 to include 17-year-olds in its juvenile justice system. Its reversal two years ago moved them back to adult courts and detention, regardless of the offense. It also forces parishes to pay high rates to confine them far from home, and critics say the policy produces outcomes that weaken rather than strengthen public safety.
For example, St. Landry Parish now pays $325 per day to house each 17-year-old at the Jackson Parish Correctional Center, up from $250 in 2024, according to parish President Jessie Bellard. 
As reported by The Advocate, East Baton Rouge Parish spends $100 each day to secure a bed and an extra $175 daily for each teenager it sends to jails in Jackson and Catahoula parishes. Records show East Baton Rouge pays about $1.17 million more each year than before the Raise the Age law was changed. 
The state broke ground last year on an 80-bed Concordia Parish facility that will house only 17-year-olds from nine parishes. Without ensuring local jails had capacity for keeping the affected teens separate from adults, repealing the Raise the Age law shifted unavoidable costs onto parish budgets and the public’s pocketbooks.
Let us put logistics aside and concentrate on young people for a minute. 
Washington Parish Sheriff Jason Smith told The Advocate that sending a teen to Jackson Parish “deprives the 17-year-old who, again, is presumed innocent, from visiting with his family.” 
An American Bar Association assessment found that distant detention facilities can make it difficult for lawyers to meet with young clients. 
State inspectors found the Jackson Parish jail fell short of required school-day minutes, The Appeal reported last year. David Utter, an attorney representing youth in state custody, said two state agencies found the jail lacking basic treatment and educational programs. 
In a 2011 academic study, psychologists found incarcerated teens who received visits from parents experienced a faster decline in depression symptoms than those who did not. The longer a child is held in far-flung jurisdiction, the less families can provide the support their child needs while detained, a federal review determined.
Holding 17-year-olds responsible is crucial, especially after they’ve inflicted serious harm. But experts have found treating them as adults does not guarantee public safety.
An independent study published by the U.S. Department of Justice showed that transferring adolescents into adult systems contributed to a median 33.7% increase in violent rearrest compared with youth kept in the juvenile system. 
Those in power in Louisiana cannot deny that, at 17, adolescents still depend on family, school routines and supportive relationships. Confinement can interrupt education and compound existing mental health vulnerabilities. In some cases, detention might be necessary. but Louisiana should not mistake confinement for rehabilitation or distance for accountability.
The $325 a day St. Landry Parish spends should be reserved for young people who genuinely require secure confinement, not as a substitute for intensive, family-centered intervention for 17-year-olds who can be safely supervised at home. 
One example is multisystemic therapy, an intensive family- and community-based program for teens who have committed serious offenses. The Washington State Institute for Public Policy estimates the program cost $9,486 per adolescent in 2022, or about 29 days of St. Landry pays to jail its youth in Jackson Parish. 
The Washington program returns $3.01 for every dollar spent, according the the institute’s analysis 
“Kids do better when they’re home,” Utter, the attorney representing imprisoned juveniles, told The Appeal. “… Kids do better when we wrap services around them in their community. But Louisiana keeps on sending children to these punitive environments in the face of proven justice policy.”
Our state pays to ship 17-year-olds away without making their communities safer. It is buying distance from parents, schools, lawyers and the very conditions that could help a teenager come home and stay home.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Enrollment in Alabama’s public community colleges surpasses 100,000 students
text:
The Alabama Community College System Board of Trustees meets on Aug. 12, 2026. This week, Neil Scott, vice chancellor of student success for ACCS, told the board enrollment reached 100,000 students for fall 2026. (Photo by Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Enrollment in Alabama Community College System schools hit the highest number of students for the fall semester in over a decade.
Neil Scott, vice chancellor of student success for ACCS, told the Board of Trustees that the combined student headcount across the system is over 100,000 students — a 3.5% increase over the final enrollment count for fall 2025.
“That’s an increase of 3,421 students,” Scott said. “Sixteen of our colleges are ahead in headcount, and these students are enrolled in over 836,000 credit hours. That’s a 3% increase over the final fall 2025 number. Over 24,000 more credit hours being produced by our students or taken by our students.”
Higher Ed Dive reported in June that students are still enrolling in community colleges more than public or private four-year institutions, but the rate is slowing down. Community college enrollment nationwide saw an increase of 4.6% from Spring 2023 to 2024; a 5.2% increase from Spring 2024 to 2025 and a 3.1% increase from Spring 2025 to 2026.
Scott told board members that the overall headcount includes duplicate students, or students who take classes at more than one community college. The unduplicated number also reached 100,000 students.
“Our total unduplicated headcount across the community college system is 100,262 as of yesterday (Tuesday). That is the highest unduplicated fall headcount that we have had since 2010,” Scott told board members.
Final enrollment numbers for the system will be available in November. During fall 2025, the system had over 98,000 students, a 9.6% increase over the final fall 2024 headcount.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Hemp can be a winner for KY. But it needs legislative stability.
text:
Kentucky was a top producer of hemp before World War II. (Photo by Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)Farmers are reeling from tariffs, rising fuel and fertilizer costs, soaring insurance premiums, and the increasing cost of debt. Now, more than ever, America’s agricultural community needs diversification. Agricultural hemp is part of that solution.
“We farm 25,000 acres of soybeans, wheat and corn, and to be an enduring enterprise we, like most farmers, need meaningful diversification,” says Alice Peterson, president of Kentucky Heritage Hemp and whose family owns Peterson Farms. “We made significant investments in hemp after the 2014 pilot program was introduced. We learned a lot about growing hemp, added processing capabilities, and built a strong hemp business. With legislative stability, we know that hemp can be a winner for the American farmer.”
That need for legislative stability is now urgent.
According to a September 2026 report by Whitney Economics, “data from hemp operators in 35 states indicates a profitable, growing industry that is adapting to expanding state regulations. The report estimates a $38.7 billion total addressable market, approximately 350,000 jobs, and $13.9 billion in wages. Hemp cannabinoids and the growing hemp beverage sector are significant contributors to the U.S. and state economies.”
But an unexpected federal ban, put in place by Sen. Mitch McConnell, who had championed the 2018 farm bill, has put all that in jeopardy.
According to Whitney, the ban, which would take place in December, “threatens to eliminate the majority of the nation’s 50,000 hemp operators, displace an estimated 225,000 jobs, reduce potential state sales tax revenue by $2.1 billion, and effectively shut down the cannabinoid industry.”
For farmers and businesses that have invested years and significant capital, the consequences would be devastating.
Kentucky’s model for research and regulation
Kentucky has already demonstrated what responsible hemp policy can look like.
The state’s 2014 Hemp Pilot Program, under the direction of then-Kentucky Agriculture Commissioner James Comer, was a four-year research program that allowed farmers, businesses, and regulators to better understand production methods, market dynamics, and consumer demand. Lessons learned during those years helped pave the way for the Hemp Farming Act of 2018, removing hemp and its derivatives from the federal Controlled Substances Act.
Since legalization, Kentucky farmers, businesses, and industry organizations have worked with regulatory bodies, including the Kentucky Department of Agriculture, USDA, and Kentucky Department for Public Health to develop responsible standards for safety, licensing, manufacturing, product testing, packaging, distribution, and retail sales. The result is an agricultural industry that has demonstrated the potential for sustainable production, positive income per acre, entrepreneurial opportunity, and growing consumer demand alongside public safety.
Kentucky offers an important lesson for policymakers: regulation can evolve as an industry evolves.
There are encouraging signs that some policymakers in Washington understand the need for a regulatory solution rather than prohibition.
U.S. Representatives Andy Barr (R-KY) and Angie Craig’s (D-MN) have co-sponsored the Lawful Hemp Protection Act, which establishes similar taxation and consumer protection mechanisms for the entire market as opposed to a single product category.
The choice before us should not be framed as hemp versus public safety because regulation will provide more public safety than prohibition. The real choice is whether we will establish a thoughtful regulatory system or leave consumers, farmers, businesses, and states to deal with the consequences of an abrupt and sweeping prohibition.
Rather than discard the lessons learned through more than a decade of hemp research, production and regulation, federal policy makers should work with states like Kentucky, Minnesota and Tennessee that have already developed regulatory and taxation mechanisms. Once a tax measure is established, a portion of that revenue should be reinvested to support harm reduction and future industrial hemp market opportunities.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. lawmakers, Spanberger grapple with loss of federal healthcare funds for trans youth
text:
A crowd gathers outside of Virginia's Capitol on Feb. 10, 2025 to call on legislators to protect transgender people. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Federal Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program money can no longer be used for certain gender-affirming care to young people in Virginia and other states, after a new U.S. Department of Health and Human Services rule took effect on Oct. 13. 
This means that people under 18 on Medicaid and under 19 on CHIP would lose that financial assistance, but Virginia’s chapter of the American Civil Liberty Union argues Virginia’s state government could fund state-level coverage to replace it. 
While patients with private insurance can still seek care where it is offered, the new HHS rule specifically prohibits young people using Medicaid or CHIP from having services like puberty blockers, hormone therapy or surgery covered. 
Though about half of U.S. states restrict gender affirming care for minors, there are about 133,000 transgender youth in states without bans, including Virginia, that use Medicaid or CHIP coverage for their care, according to KFF Health News. 
“Decisions about healthcare, including for transgender youth, should be made by families and their doctors — not the government,” ACLU attorney Wyatt Rolla said in a phone call Wednesday. “It’s important that every parent is able to get the healthcare that their child needs, no matter what kind of health insurance they have.” 
Rolla noted how Virginia took a similar step by setting aside millions to help low-income citizens maintain healthcare  after Congress let Affordable Care Act subsidies expire last year. Leaders could use the same strategy to support Virginia’s transgender youth, Rolla said.  
Virginia’s most recent state budget earmarked $150 million to target assistance to households with incomes between 138% and 250% of the federal poverty level. 
As of July, that range represents about 45% of people who had already dropped their ACA health insurance due to rising premiums and eligible households can tap into the state funding beginning next month. 
Del. Rodney Willett, D-Henrico noted that the state “shouldn’t have had to” “plug the (ACA) subsidy gap,” but federal actions prompted lawmakers to do what they could. He supports the ACLU’s call for the state to take the same tack concerning trans youth care. 
Willett chairs the House Health and Human Services Committee and co-chairs a subcommittee in the House Appropriations Committee. His insights can help shape which bills advance and which budget items get funded. 
Whether or not the money will be able to be there, however, is the question. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration estimates the state could face a $2 billion to $6 billion revenue loss starting in 2028 due to the federal changes to Medicaid and other social services that levy more costs and administrative burdens onto states. 
State agencies are already coordinating efforts to comply with H.R. 1, the reconciliation bill Congress passed last year that triggered the major shifts, and prevent eligible Virginians from losing their benefits.
“How do we keep filling all of these holes?” Willett asked. 
Transgender minors have been a point of focus for President Donald Trump’s administration. Days after assuming office in January 2025, an executive order prompted three Virginia hospitals to pause offering gender-affirming care to patients under 19. 
The order said the U.S. will “not fund, sponsor, promote, assist or support” what Trump labeled “destructive” procedures.
Now, with the modified rule, more youth stand to miss out on care, advocates say.
“These are low-income families that are in these programs, and the thought of them losing access to this healthcare is really devastating,” Rolla said. 
ACLU and representatives from LGBTQ+ advocacy group Equality Virginia had met with DMAS director Steven Ford in August in advance of the changes to relay their concerns. 
By late-September, a bulletin post from Virginia’s Department of Medical Assistance Services, noted that Virginia would no longer administer funds starting Oct. 13 when the HHS rule took effect. 
In an Oct. 9 joint letter, the groups alleged Virginia violated its own procedural rules by complying with the HHS rule without proper process and emphasized that the rule doesn’t prohibit states from adopting their own substitutes for the lost federal funding. 
“This is not a question of whether or not our administration is making a choice to pull back funds,” Spanberger told reporters at The Advocate last week when asked why Virginia was ending coverage. “This is a question of an example once more of a federal government and a Trump administration that is changing access to health care.”
On Wednesday, Spanberger’s office offered no new statement and said potential funding could stem from the legislature. 
Meanwhile, Virginia is part of a 22-state lawsuit challenging  the HHS rule and a court could potentially block or affirm it. 
Willett said he hopes state lawmakers may be able to allocate some funding during its 2027 legislative session to aid affected families, but preliminary conversations have not yet started. 
“It’s like everyday you wake up and before you read the news of the day, you think ‘what else could the Trump administration do?” he said. “Everyday there is something else that goes from bad to worse, and we’re constantly reacting to that.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia sees gains in kindergarten readiness, but gaps persist for underserved students
text:
Children playing at Peake Childhood Center in Newport News in October 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A new report shows Virginia students’ kindergarten readiness rose six percentage points to 57% over the past year, with underserved students making notable gains, according to the Department of Education.
Last year, state lawmakers directed VDOE and the University of Virginia’s Center for Advanced Study of Teaching and Learning to use Virginia Kindergarten Readiness Program assessment results to determine how the state’s preschool initiative promotes school readiness.
The Oct. 1 report recommends targeted teacher training, continued assessments, expanded data reporting, and individualized student supports.
“If we can get everybody coming in more ready, then it dramatically increases the likelihood they’ll be on level for reading or math by the end of third grade,” said Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway to the Mercury on Wednesday.
In 2020, state lawmakers found that 44% of Virginia’s children enter kindergarten without literacy, math and social-emotional skills. Lawmakers argued those skills are necessary for children’s success, especially for at-risk children. 
 Findings

The study found that kindergarten readiness is improving, rising from 51% in 2025 to 57% in 2026, with improvements among Latino children (+7%), Black children (+6%), low-income children (+6%), English learners (+5%), and children with disabilities (+4%). 
Literacy readiness increased by six percentage points, while math readiness rose by two.
However, about 43% of children did not meet the overall readiness benchmark last fall. 
Math and literacy skills also improved. Still, social and emotional skills remain a concern, with some children struggling to self-regulate, manage emotions and interact with others.
The data also shows that readiness gaps persist between children from low-income families, children with disabilities, multilingual learners, Black and Hispanic children and boys, who were more likely to fall below the overall readiness benchmark.
 Recommendations

To improve how the commonwealth supports young children, the report recommends identifying children who are struggling earlier and paying more attention to social-emotional development.
One method to achieve this is to use assessments throughout the school year to monitor progress, identify gaps and provide additional instruction or individualized help when needed.
On social-emotional development, the agency said schools could support children’s self-regulation, social skills and well-being alongside literacy and mathematics. It also said teacher concerns should help prompt closer attention and appropriate support.
The agency also recommended that families and schools work together to improve understanding of school readiness and strengthen home-school connections. It suggested improving assessments in grades 1-3 to track children’s progress beyond kindergarten and strengthening data and reporting systems.
Other recommendations focus on better training and support for teachers so they can adapt instruction to children’s needs. Preschool programs should be strengthened, the report stated, so educators can better understand and support children’s development. 
State lawmakers will discuss new legislation to implement these goals when they return to Richmond in January.



 VQB5 Update

On Wednesday, the Virginia Department of Education announced that the 2026 Virginia Quality Birth-to-Five (VQB5) Quality Profiles show continued improvement in early childhood education quality and kindergarten readiness. 
Lawmakers created VQB5 to improve children’s school readiness and expand access to parents and support providers. Advocates say the new system is a critical tool for the state, providers and families to gauge the effectiveness of Virginia’s early childhood education programs.
Across 3,220 early learning sites serving more than 125,000 children, the average quality score increased to 594 out of 800, while sites requiring state intervention dropped to a record-low 10.
VDOE and its partners credited these gains to investments, educator dedication and collaboration across the state. 
However, affordability and access to quality child care remain major challenges. State leaders are continuing efforts to develop sustainable funding strategies to make early childhood education accessible and affordable for all families.

name: National
title: 2 states, 2 abortion ballot measures, and the effort to win over Gen Z voters
text:
A volunteer helps a young person fill out a form on National Voter Registration Day in 2025. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue, but for many others it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. (Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action)Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th.
Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. 
But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on.
“It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said.
In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns.
Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago.
People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using  social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention.
“I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. 
Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them

In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million.
But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge.
The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal.
The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men.
But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation.  The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried.



Quotation







We want abortion and reproductive rights to stop being presented as this women-only issue and more so as an economic issue that affects everyone and is a family issue.


– Selasi Tagbor Morales, 25, Alliance for Youth Action


Sandra Kelly, volunteer and leadership program coordinator at the University of Idaho, runs the campus food pantry and has seen the signs of economic stress in students.
“A lot of people use it daily. I’ve seen it increase now that people know about it – a big day used to be like 18 (people) three years ago. That’s a slow day now,” Kelly said.
Selasi Tagbor Morales, communications manager at the national progressive grassroots organizing group Alliance for Youth Action, said reproductive rights should be and often are viewed in the same category as economic issues. Financial difficulties are cited as one of the reasons people terminate a pregnancy, and in that way, she said it is an issue that affects everyone.
“We want abortion and reproductive rights to stop being presented as this women-only issue and more so as an economic issue that affects everyone and is a family issue,” said Tagbor Morales, 25. 
Chris Melody Fields, executive director of the national progressive group Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, said that while reproductive rights is an issue that only physically affects a certain population, people of all genders and ages have seen the effects of abortion bans on those they love. 
“When we center it on the people that they care about, I think we have a real opportunity to bridge gaps and divides,” Melody Fields said. 
Campus outreach and social media campaigns
Missouri and Idaho are among four states that will have reproductive rights on the November ballot. Voters in Nevada and Virginia, which have few abortion restrictions, will consider codifying abortion rights in their state constitutions.
Although the national fervor over abortion access has waned since 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade with the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision, abortion remains a highly debated issue in Idaho and Missouri.
Missouri was the first state to ban abortion following the court’s decision, and two years later, it became the first state to overturn an abortion ban at the ballot box. 
Many young Missourians who collected signatures for the 2024 reproductive rights ballot measure are back canvassing to keep abortion legal in 2026, but the motivation runs deeper, said Tori Schafer, a spokesperson with the Stop the Ban campaign. They’re offended that lawmakers rejected the will of the people by putting an abortion ban back on the ballot.
“To feel so much autonomy in moving that campaign forward, and then to have it go directly back to the ballot, we’ve seen those volunteers come back and also bring their friends with them,” said Schafer, who, at 30, is a millennial slightly older than Gen Z. 
Tori Schafer, a spokesperson with the Stop the Ban campaign, addresses abortion rights advocates gather for a canvassing kick-off event on Aug. 29 in St. Louis County. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent)
The campaign supporting the ban also has eager volunteers. Students for Life members organized four canvassing events across the state to talk to potential voters, while others are on campus. Those who prefer not to be out front take up prayer.  
Hazel Myles, the 20-year-old president of the University of Missouri chapter of Students for Life, saw “how emotionally charged the issue really is.” 
In 2024, weeks before Missourians narrowly overturned the state’s near-total abortion ban, Myles said she was met with hostility talking to students about abortion. But it changed her approach two years later. She takes as much emotion out of the conversation as possible, trying to convince students that the abortion rights amendment was “too radical” rather than trying to convince them to become anti-abortion.
Not long after the August primary, most students she asked about the abortion ban amendment hadn’t heard of it. 
“Most college students seem pretty ambivalent about a lot of political issues,” she said. “ … If they’re not a (political science) major, their interest in sitting down to do more homework about what they should vote about is pretty limited.”
For some groups, social media plays a significant role in Gen Z outreach.
Monica Snyder, executive director of Secular Pro-Life, a national atheist-led anti-abortion advocacy group based in the St. Louis suburbs, said her organization relies on short-form videos on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram to reach young voters. 
“We fill a unique role in anti-abortion advocacy because we’re led by atheists,” Snyder said. “This approach can be particularly effective with younger audiences. Gen Z tends to be highly interested in questions of social justice and human rights. We find that when we emphasize that abortion is a human rights violation, and not primarily a religious or partisan issue, Gen Z is much more willing to consider the pro-life position.”
Here’s what’s driving the Gen Z gender gap

Alyssa Smith, of St. Louis, was 18 in June 2022 when Roe was overturned. Now 22, Smith is volunteering with Stop the Ban to defeat the proposed abortion ban, called Amendment 3, and keep the reproductive rights amendment in place. 
“Though there’s a lot of performative posting on social media, people are willing to have these discussions and open up in these more difficult conversations about what the reality of Amendment 3 and abortion bans actually holds for us,” she said.
Melody Fields, who leads the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, said the Missouri Legislature’s action on the amendment is one of many attempts to overturn the will of voters. The Legislature repealed a mandated sick leave policy in July 2025 after voters approved it in 2024. 
Missouri voters will be asked to reinstate the prior abortion ban, and at the same time prohibit gender-affirming care for minors. State law already prohibits gender-transition surgery for minors. Missouri law also bars minors from beginning hormones or puberty blockers, though this law is set to expire in August 2027, at which point lawmakers have said they intend to consider a ban without an expiration date.
Those now championing Amendment 3 point to the August 2027 sunset of the restrictions on cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers as a reason for asking voters to prohibit something that’s already banned. The ban on gender-affirming surgeries for minors has no expiration.
“This is the first time we’re seeing a near-total abortion ban and a ban on gender-affirming care for minors on the ballot,” Melody Fields said. “What happens in Missouri is critically important, because if the opposition is successful, they will use this to undo every single gain we’ve had at the ballot box since the Dobbs decision.”
Reaching a ‘jaded’ and transient population
Idaho has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. It applies to all stages of pregnancy, with narrow exceptions for rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report, and only an exception to prevent a pregnant person’s death, not to preserve their health. State Attorney General Raúl Labrador, a Republican, is fighting a recent federal court ruling that would allow abortions in cases in which the patient’s physical or mental health is threatened by staying pregnant.
Idaho’s Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act would restore access to abortion and protect access to other forms of reproductive healthcare, including contraception and certain fertility treatments such as in vitro fertilization. It qualified for the ballot in July.
The number of registered Gen Z voters who signed the petition for the initiative in Idaho was low overall, partly because it can be a challenging cohort of voters to reach under the best of circumstances, said the campaign’s lead organizer, Melanie Folwell. 
“They’re quite cynical, they’re quite jaded, they are not necessarily taken in by easy promises from a broken political system,” said Folwell, who has two Gen Z-aged children. 
But Idaho’s political environment added another layer of complexity to signature gathering, Folwell said. 
Gen Z women want politicians who can make the ‘American dream’ feel attainable

“We did not do a lot of campus gathering, given the current posture of Idaho’s Legislature and animosity towards any discussion of anything related to reproductive rights (and) birth control,” Folwell said. “We did not want there to be additional scrutiny or focus on our institutions.”
Lawmakers have repeatedly singled out the University of Idaho and Boise State University, including a proposed $2 million cut for each school that was pitched in 2025 by a Republican representative who said he was frustrated by diversity, equity and inclusion programs and the classes that were being taught.
The cut did not become law, but the proposal followed a few months after the Idaho State Board of Education passed a ban on DEI at college campuses, prompting the closure of the University of Idaho’s Women’s Center, which had been a staple on campus since 1972. Other campuses followed suit.
All of that came four years after the University of Idaho changed its policy to no longer allow student health facilities to dispense birth control or distribute condoms for pregnancy prevention, citing the state’s 2021 No Public Funds for Abortion Act, which also prohibited any university employees from counseling or referring someone for an abortion.
Despite those challenges, Folwell remains optimistic about young voters supporting the measure at the ballot box. The campaign, led by nonprofit Idahoans United for Women and Families, is active on social media, with messages about how politicians have let people down and how the initiative represents an opportunity to take back some power. Folwell said the campaign receives a lot of engagement on TikTok and Reddit. 
“This is not an age group that’s hanging out on Facebook or even really Instagram, and I think that’s always one of the unique challenges about engaging this generation,” Folwell said. “I think it’s important to reckon with the fact that this is a group that is not taking in information from traditional news sources.”  
But there aren’t that many other ways to easily engage with young voters, either, she said. About 4% of homebuyers in 2025 were between the ages 18 and 26, meaning the vast majority are renters who can be difficult to track down for door-to-door canvassing. And others may leave the state before the election is held. 
Folwell said young men the campaign has contacted for signature gathering tended to think it wasn’t an issue that affected them, but she watched many volunteers convince them otherwise, especially if they had a partner. 



Quotation







As with all Idaho voters, there is a strong culture of protecting life among young Idahoans.


– Mary Strow, Stop Prop 1


Stateline asked representatives with the campaign against Idaho’s initiative how they were engaging with young voters, including specific means of connecting with them and any unique challenges.  
“Our campaign is eager to share the truth about Prop 1 with voters of all ages,” Mary Strow, communications director for Stop Prop 1, wrote in an emailed statement. “As with all Idaho voters, there is a strong culture of protecting life among young Idahoans. Our campaign resonates with Idaho values that cross all generational lines. We are urging voters of all ages to vote No on Proposition 1.”
Adam Pendergrass, a senior majoring in political science at Boise State University, said the women he talks to support reproductive rights and the ballot initiative, and they are the ones who bring it up in his classes. While there are more young men who support reproductive rights than he thinks people give them credit for, he does think that on the whole, young men are more conservative on the issue.
“It’s kind of tough to say what the general consensus is, because I do think many men kind of stay away from the issue and don’t want to be pressed on it,” said Pendergrass, who favors the initiative. 
But for one Gen Z woman, the salience of the issue is increasing. Cynita Peña, 25, also attends Boise State and said a relative had an ectopic pregnancy in 2021 that turned into a medical emergency. She thinks about how much worse it might have been if that emergency had happened after Idaho passed its ban. 
After the ban, she said she’s watched people she knows who are in their early 20s have to commit to unwanted pregnancies without abortion access. 
“Just being able to have that choice has been completely taken away from them,” Peña said. “It was hard to see the people around me have to go through that.”  
Said Folwell: “Most people are one bad day away from having their feelings about (the abortion ban’s) relevancy changed forever. When you’re 18 to 25, you haven’t lived a lot of life yet, and you don’t know the ways that this could impact you at some point.”
