name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Positions on election hand-counting split candidates in South Dakota’s secretary of state race
text:
A vote tabulation machine scans ballots during the 2026 Sioux Falls mayoral recount on July 8 in downtown Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota voters are selecting a new person to oversee elections in the state, with a choice between a candidate who has supported hand-counting and the elimination of vote tabulation machines, or candidates who say they want to support an election system that’s working well.
Republican Heather Baxter, Democrat Terrence Davis and Libertarian Tamara Lesnar are the nominees for secretary of state, an office that not only oversees elections but also manages campaign finance reporting, business filings, lobbyist registrations and other administrative functions. 
The current officeholder, Monae Johnson, was elected in 2022 and sought another term but lost her bid for the Republican nomination at the party’s state convention during the summer. Baxter defeated Johnson with 59% of the party delegates’ votes, and Johnson has since endorsed Davis.
The election is Nov. 3, advance voting is underway, and the voter registration deadline is Monday.
Heather Baxter
Baxter, of Rapid City, has been serving as a state representative for the past two years but lost a primary race on June 2 and has since focused on the secretary of state race. 
She is a small-business owner from a well-known family in the Black Hills, where her late grandfather Korczak Ziolkowski started the Crazy Horse mountain carving. Her business experience has included running a tanning facility, women’s day spa and fitness center. She currently works as a strength and flexibility coach for elderly people, offering services at home or in assisted living centers. 
Baxter’s campaign website says she supports “improved hand-counting” methods. She co-sponsored state legislation to prohibit the use of automatic tabulating machines to count votes. 

Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City, speaks in the South Dakota House of Representatives on Feb. 10, 2026. Baxter is this year’s Republican nominee for secretary of state. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Baxter told South Dakota Searchlight she supported that bill because some counties use outdated software and laptops that don’t meet federal election standards; therefore, “we shouldn’t be using these tabulators.” 
“And that’s why I was willing to support that,” she said. “If we’re not compliant, let’s get rid of them.”
But if elected, Baxter said she would take a different approach. She said that if she found county auditors using outdated software, for example, she would have “a sit-down conversation” with them. 
Baxter said she likes hand-counting because “you can see the voter intent.” She gave an example of a voter scribbling out a first choice and circling an intended one, and a hand-counter spotting the issue “where a machine didn’t read that.”
Those sorts of positions helped Baxter defeat Johnson at the Republican convention. Activists who had previously supported Johnson had become frustrated that Johnson did not implement some of their preferred changes, including a move away from electronic tabulation. Some of those same people testified in favor of the 2025 bill to ban tabulation machines. 
Baxter told Searchlight she would focus on ensuring counties comply with state and federal requirements while giving county auditors greater local control over their elections.
“The biggest misconception is that I’m going to go in and just completely get rid of these machines when I don’t even have that in my wheelhouse of what I’m allowed to do,” Baxter said. 
She said the Legislature, rather than the secretary of state alone, would have to implement such a change.
Baxter said she wants to meet with auditors to identify inconsistencies in how counties are instructed to administer elections, and to hear from business owners about how the secretary of state’s office could work better.
“Transparency and accountability are not a burden. They’re the job,” Baxter said.
Terrence Davis
Davis, of Sioux Falls, is a former South Dakota and Tennessee state trooper who is pursuing a doctoral degree in law and policy. He worked as an intake specialist with East River Legal Services prior to the campaign. He was born in Peoria, Illinois, and said he experienced homelessness and grew up in a low-income environment. 
Davis is a Democrat arguing that the secretary of state should be treated as an administrative job, not a vehicle for partisan politics. He said that’s what Baxter is doing. 
“South Dakotans like boring politics,” he said. “They just want the system to work the way it’s designed to work and to find solutions if there’s an issue.” 

Terrence Davis is the 2026 Democratic nominee for South Dakota secretary of state. (Photo courtesy of Terrence Davis campaign)

Davis said his first priority would be rebuilding trust in the office through more timely responses to county auditors, members of the public and the media. He also wants to improve the secretary of state’s website and strengthen relationships with county auditors.
Davis said his clearest policy disagreement with Baxter is over her support for hand-counting and her criticism of electronic tabulation. He favors using technology alongside human oversight. 
“With that being said, it doesn’t mean we cannot improve, but I think it should be a very gradual, measured approach,” Davis said. 
Davis said Baxter has been pivoting away from her anti-election-machine stance, which he said is ultimately motivated by “the whole situation surrounding the 2020 election,” referring to President Donald Trump’s false claim that the election was fraudulent. 
Davis is pitching himself to voters who might normally vote Republican. He pointed to his past as a registered Republican and described himself as someone who sits in the middle on many issues. 
“Look beyond ‘Democrat,’ and look at a person for the skill set, for what they want to offer all South Dakotans,” Davis said.
Tamara Lesnar
Lesnar, of Grenville, is a former compliance officer at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, where she was responsible for holding traders accountable for violations. She now runs a small business selling collectibles.
Lesnar is running on the Libertarian ticket, rejecting what she called a power struggle between the state’s two major parties that leaves voters behind. 

Tamara Lesnar is the 2026 Libertarian nominee for South Dakota secretary of state. (Photo courtesy of Tamara Lesnar campaign)

She is not new to South Dakota politics. Lesnar ran unsuccessfully for the U.S. Senate as the Libertarian candidate in 2022 and for the South Dakota House in 2024. 
Lesnar’s campaign website highlights priorities including protecting voting rights, reducing government burdens on businesses and making state government more responsive.
Lesnar also said she supports continuing to use voting tabulation machines. She sees no compelling reason to eliminate them, she said, and widespread hand-counting would require more labor than local election offices can provide. 
Lesnar has ideas to use technology in new ways. She proposed databases that would allow residents to anonymously indicate their preferences on issues before state lawmakers vote.
“I’m more about direct democracy,” she said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota US House candidates discuss debt, healthcare, farmers during podcast debate
text:
Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer, right, speaks to moderators Rob Port, center-left, and Chad Oban, center-right, during a U.S. House debate with Republican incumbent Rep. Julie Fedorchak at Bismarck State College on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s Republican and Democratic-NPL candidates for U.S. House debated the national debt, surging healthcare costs and farming concerns during their first – and probably only – debate of the 2026 election.
Republican incumbent Rep. Julie Fedorchak and Democrat Trygve Hammer also clashed over the Iran war during a recorded episode of Plain Talk, hosted by Forum Communications columnist Rob Port and Chad Oban, at Bismarck State College on Tuesday.
Fedorchak said she’s received classified briefings on the Iran war and saw “some pretty compelling evidence” that the actions taken by President Donald Trump were justified.
Hammer said he does not believe Trump’s claims that Iran was two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon and thinks Congress could have kept the U.S. out of the war if members had been holding the president accountable.



$40 trillion national debt
Fedorchak, who is seeking a second term, said her concern about the federal debt was one issue that drove her to run for Congress. She said that there is “no silver bullet” to solve the country’s debt problems.
“It’s taken a long time to get here, and it’s going to take a long time to get back,” she said. Fedorchak said three major initiatives can help: growing the economy, reducing spending and eliminating fraud, waste and abuse.
Provisions in the 2025 budget reconciliation package stimulated the growth, she said, by giving North Dakota households about $2,000 on average back to them through provisions that don’t tax tips or overtime, among others. 
“Most North Dakotans do not think we have a revenue problem,” she said. “We have a spending problem. We cannot tax our way out of this.”
Republican incumbent U.S. House Rep. Julie Fedorchak speaks during a U.S. House debate hosted by the Plain Talk Podcast at Bismarck State College on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Fedorchak said reforming mandatory spending programs, like Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid, will allow the next Congress to “get a lot more serious” about controlling federal spending. She said Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid are “unsustainable in their current forms.”
Hammer said the country needs to stop operating under a budget deficit in order to begin bringing down the national debt. 
“I don’t think we’re going to find enough fraud, waste and abuse out there to do it,” Hammer said. “We are going to have to tax these billionaires, and some of them are asking for it.”
He said reducing the national debt will take an all-of-the-above approach, including increasing revenue through taxes and cutting spending.
“If we’re making cuts, let’s make them meaningful and well thought out,” he said. “Not like what we saw with DOGE that ended up just being destructive.”
Medicaid, healthcare and the Affordable Care Act
Fedorchak and Hammer differed on new requirements for Medicaid recipients that were part of the 2025 budget reconciliation.
Fedorchak said the new eligibility checks beginning next year will ensure those receiving Medicaid benefits are supposed to receive them. She said that type of oversight will ensure Congress is “being responsible with taxpayer dollars.”
Issue spotlight: North Dakota US House candidates differ on solutions to affordability

She also spoke in favor of work requirements for Medicaid recipients that begin next year, which are projected to cut about $1 trillion in government spending over a decade. People who receive Medicaid under expansion provisions will be required to meet work, school or community service requirements unless they qualify for an exemption.
“I have yet to find a North Dakotan who doesn’t agree with me that able-bodied, working-age people who can work, should work,” Fedorchak said.
Hammer cited statistics that show 44% of North Dakota Medicaid recipients work full time and 43% who benefit from Medicaid are children.
He said the Medicaid work requirements create more red tape for people to access healthcare. 
“They’re going to have to do more paperwork. We’re not going to have more staff to help them do that paperwork, and some of them are going to drop their insurance,” Hammer said.
Hammer added it was “kinda rich” that Congress passed the work requirements during a session that has had several recesses. House lawmakers have been in session a total of 72 days in 2026 with an additional 20 days scheduled before the end of the year.
Fedorchak said the Affordable Care Act isn’t operating as planned and said the cost of healthcare “has gone through the roof” since the program began.
Issue spotlight: North Dakota US House candidates discuss AI regulation, data centers

“It’s going to take some time to unwind the ACA,” she said.
Fedorchak reiterated her support for expanding health savings accounts to help people take control of their own healthcare decisions.
Farmers and Canada
The candidates also disagreed on tariffs and federal policy decisions affecting farmers.
Hammer said it’s Congress’ job to control tariffs, which have strained North Dakota agriculture markets.
“The tariffs have been this tax that made our ag markets go away, and now they try to buy back votes with bailouts,” he said. “We don’t want a bailout economy.”
Ending the Iran war would allow fertilizer costs to come down, he said, which farmers desperately need. 
“We have plenty of natural gas here in North Dakota that we could use to make nitrogen fertilizer,” he said. “We have to start doing some of those things at home as well.”
Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer speaks during a U.S. House debate hosted by the Plain Talk Podcast at Bismarck State College on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Fedorchak said increasing crop reference prices and improving crop insurance were included in the 2025 budget reconciliation. She added she supports the Farm Bill passed by the U.S. House that is under consideration by the Senate and another bill to provide E15 fuel year-round.
“That creates a lot of domestic markets for those products,” she said. 
Fedorchak said Canadians are friends of North Dakota and she wants the trade dispute addressed quickly by the Trump administration.
However, she also pointed out that Canada has implemented non-tariff trade barriers for some U.S. products.
“This approach that the president is taking to renegotiate some of these trade agreements … was an effort to address some of those issues,” she said. “And Canada walked away from the negotiations. They need to come back and we need to get that done as soon as possible.”
Hammer said the Trump administration and a Republican-controlled Congress have created the impression that the U.S. is an unreliable trading partner.
“We are an unreliable ally because everything is just up to this capricious leader who might decide something one day and then that night, in a Tweet, reverse it,” he said. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Hammer added that Canada is moving on by building pipelines to their west coast and making deals on their potash fertilizer that don’t involve the U.S.
“If you are a farmer or rancher in North Dakota, if you run a small business in North Dakota, you need some predictability because you need to plan ahead,” he said. “We need Congress to be that guard rail and be the adults in the room so we can reestablish a stable economy that people can count on.”
Independent candidates Helene Neville and Charles Tuttle are also running for North Dakota’s U.S. House seat.
Fedorchak declined to participate in a debate hosted by Prairie Public last week, which featured the two independent candidates in addition to Hammer. No other debates between the candidates have been scheduled.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: ‘God’s work will go on’: Sister Carolyn Brockland upholds Ursuline legacy in New Orleans
text:
Sister Carolyn Brockland, originally from St. Louis, has spent the majority of her time as a member of the Ursuline order in New Orleans, where she was a teacher and principal at Ursuline Academy. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)NEW ORLEANS — Inside the National Shrine to Our Lady of Prompt Succor on the Ursuline Academy campus, Sister Carolyn Marie Brockland points out stained glass, jewel-encrusted crowns and items that are hundreds of years old, explaining each story. These objects are the heritage of the Ursuline Sisters, a religious order that has helped heal, teach and shape the Crescent City since 1727. 
Brockland, 85, is the only Ursuline sister left in New Orleans, potentially the last one to carry on the legacy and tell their stories. 
“I don’t know what the future is going to hold,” Brockland said. “Maybe there’ll be another resurgence of people who want to live a religious life, but if not, God’s work will go on in another way.”
Overall, there are only about 100 Ursulines of the Roman Union remaining in the United States. With a sharply-declining population, the sisters have been preparing Ursuline schools for their absence, training laypeople to become spiritual leaders and carry on traditions.
A statue of the Virgin Mary holding a young Jesus sits on a coffee table at the Ursuline sisters’ residence in New Orleans, where Sister Carolyn Brockland is the lone remaining member of the order in New Orleans. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)
Sitting in the sisters’ residence adjacent to the shrine and the academy’s Uptown campus, Brockland talked about the first sisters, who came in 1727 at the encouragement of French colonial governor Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville. The Ursulines were asked to provide a stabilizing moral influence for an already chaotic young port colony and educate the young women of New Orleans. 
The idea proved successful. Ursuline Academy is the oldest continuously operating school for girls and the oldest Catholic school in the U.S. The order still oversees more than a dozen secondary schools around the country.
The Ursulines have marked New Orleans history at every turn, from tending wounded soldiers after the Battle of New Orleans to helping in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. Mayor Helena Moreno presented Brockland with a key to the city at a September ceremony to recognize the Ursulines’ legacy. 
“I knew I was doing it in honor of all the sisters, and there’s so many sisters who’ve gone before me,” Brockland said about accepting the key on behalf of the Ursuline order. 
Sister Carolyn Brockland holds a key to the city of New Orleans that Mayor Helena Moreno presented to her commemorating the 300th anniversary of the Ursuline order in New Orleans (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)
New Orleans Archbishop James Checchio described the sisters as the city’s first teachers, nurses and pharmacists. The sisters’ legacy of education and service formed the root of the city’s foundation, he said. 
“Three hundred years ago the Ursuline sisters left everything behind in France to answer God’s call in service to the people of New Orleans,” Checchio said in a statement. “Immediately upon their arrival, they began their mission of ministering to the colonists with little more than faith and hope in God’s providence … The Ursulines’ history here and the history of the city and our region are intertwined in such a way that they are truly inseparable.”
Brockland recalled one of the first Ursuline sisters in New Orleans who detailed her voyage from France to New Orleans in her diary. A journey that was supposed to take three months took five months due to bad weather. Other mishaps along the way included encounters with pirates, getting stuck on a sandbar and having to find ways to protect themselves from alligators, snakes and mosquitoes. 
“She writes all this down, and she says, ‘But now that I look back, it just seems like a wonderful adventure,’” Brockland said. “I thought, what a spirit. To have that wonderful spirit to start out. It’s something that we’re doing for God, and we’re going to help other people.”
Brockland, who grew up south of St. Louis, joined the Ursuline order at age 16 right after graduating high school.
Sister Carolyn Brockland, second from left, stands for a photo with her parents, Sylvia and Gus Brockland, and Sister Damian Aycock after professing her final vows to the Ursuline order on Jan. 6, 1965. (Photo courtesy of Sister Carolyn Brockland)
“We had spiritual programs that taught us how to pray, not just to say prayers, but to actually talk to God and listen,” Brockland said. “And so one of those times when I was trying to listen, I thought I heard God say that I was called. Of course you never know for sure. You have to test it.”
After a year of prayer and reflection, Brockland said she was sure of her decision, embarking on what’s now an almost seven-decade journey.  
She joined the order in the 1960s as its sisters began transitioning from wearing a traditional floor-length habit, wimple and veil. For her recent interview, Brockland wore a long skirt and cardigan over a light-blue pullover, with a simple crucifix on a necklace to mark her faith. She remains quick on her feet, navigating through the shrine and academy grounds with ease. 
Brockland has moved to and from New Orleans over the years, including a stint as a teacher and then principal of the Uptown academy, among other roles.
When Hurricane Katrina hit in 2005, Brockland was in charge of the sisters’ community. At the time, nine sisters lived in the residence, with two others hospitalized. More than 40 people would take shelter in the house, from kids to people over age 90. 
“People came and stayed with us because they knew we’d be here, and we just knew we’d be here,” Brockland said. “The sisters never left. You know, we just believed that we would always be here for the people.”
Looking ahead to the tricentennial of the Ursuline’s presence in New Orleans, Brockland said he plans to stay as long as possible in the city. 
“I’m not going to go around moping,” Brockland said. “We’ve done all we could, it’s just that today’s world is different. God will take care of it.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: State grants schools $1.75M to teach healthy social media use
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
text:
WHILE SOCIAL MEDIA legislation remains stagnant in closed-door legislative negotiations, the state is using $1.75 million in an attempt to help schools address the technology’s use and effects on young people. 
Through the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education’s Safe, Healthy and Responsible Digital Life Grant program, schools can apply for funding and then use it for “age-appropriate” classroom instruction, materials, educator training and resources to help families support healthy social media use, according to the Healey administration.
“Our kids are growing up in a world that looks very different from the one we experienced, and schools and families need to work together to help students make healthy choices,” Education Secretary Steve Zrike said, invoking his experience as a parent of two teenagers. “These grants will give educators more tools to have those important conversations and help students develop the skills to stay safe online.”
Gov. Maura Healey announced the funding at Peabody Veterans Memorial High School on Wednesday, telling reporters, “This is about setting kids up for success. It’s a fast-paced world. Technology is evolving quickly, and we have to evolve with it.”
Social media legislation is at a standstill on Beacon Hill and it’s unclear how or if lawmakers will move forward with a slate of varying proposals. Educators and advocates continue to warn about the harmful impacts of social media on kids; a $17.1 billion settlement with Meta in August resolved claims that the company created and ran its platforms in a way that harmed young people and violated state consumer protection laws.  
The House in April passed a bill (H 5366) banning kids under 14 from using social media platforms and requiring that platforms obtain parental consent for users aged 14 and 15. The proposal is embedded in a bill that would also ban student cellphone use in schools, which the Senate took up in a standalone bill. The Senate in July passed different social media regulations (S 3175) requiring all social media platforms to adopt “default” settings for minors that disable things including addictive feeds, “autoplay” and “infinite scroll” capabilities, and that turn off notifications during a period at night.
Healey proposed language in April that would require social media companies to deactivate certain addictive features and notifications and to limit platform use for users under the age of 18. She tucked it into a supplemental spending bill focused mostly on snow and ice removal costs.
The grant program is funded through a $2 million fiscal 2027 budget item meant for online safety and education, the administration said. The additional $250,000 will be used for reviewing instruction materials and developing educational videos and resources to help schools teach students about social media use and digital literacy.
Through the program announced Wednesday, public school districts, charter public schools, and educational collaboratives can apply for approximately 25 to 30 grants of up to $60,000 each, per the administration, which said the grants aim to teach students how to “recognize false or misleading information, including AI-generated content, protect their personal information, understand the risks of social media and cyberbullying, and make responsible decisions online.”
Asked if there’s a balance between cellphone use in schools and parents wanting to have access to their kids during the day, Healey said, “I think that’s part of this discussion today. Figuring out, you know, is it bell-to-bell? Should there be a cellphone ban all day, or is it something modified where when you’re in the classroom you have to put your cellphone away and you can use it at different times in the day, maybe to have that contact with your parents?”
“These are really important things we’ve got to think through,” she continued.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Fuck the Flock cameras’: On big tech, Vermont’s candidates for governor differ on style and substance
text:
A license plate reader camera on VT Route 7A in Manchester seen on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
“Fuck the Flock cameras, dude. Let’s ban ‘em.”
Amanda Janoo, the Democratic nominee for governor of Vermont in this fall’s election, left no room for doubt about her feelings on the controversial license plate readers used by police in Vermont and around the country in a social media video last week. 
In the same post, Janoo also said Vermont needs to pass legislation telling the companies that run large data centers that “you are not welcome here,” at least for the time being. On that front, she drew a distinction between herself and her Republican opponent, five-term incumbent Gov. Phil Scott.
Scott vetoed a bill earlier this year, Janoo noted, that would have put new regulations on where large data centers could be built and how they could operate, though would not have banned their construction outright. Passing the bill was the right decision, she said — and “let’s do it again.”
There are a host of differences between Vermont’s leading candidates for governor this year in a race that polls and campaign spending suggest could be the closest in a decade. And the style and substance of Scott and Janoo’s comments on data centers and artificial intelligence technology make those differences especially clear. 
Janoo says new regulations on AI and the data centers that power it are needed to reign in what she called, at a recent campaign event in Marlboro, the rise of “techno-authoritarianism” in the U.S. That trend, she said, threatens people’s civil liberties and access to the resources they rely on. Scott has taken a softer tack, saying the potential impacts of AI worry him but he thinks it should be the federal government — working alongside tech companies — that regulates it.
Scott’s distaste for new state regulations mirrors how he has approached other issues, such as housing and data privacy, said Matthew Dickinson, a professor of political science at Middlebury College. Meanwhile, Janoo’s support for more locally-tailored standards has echoes of how she talks about local schools in the face of Scott’s attempts to force some schools to close or merge, he said.
“I think what you’re seeing here is an issue that really gets to the heart of the different governing philosophies between the two,” Dickinson said in an interview Tuesday.
Across the country, Democrats like Janoo are betting that the broad unpopularity of data centers will be a winning issue for them in next month’s election, Dickinson noted — particularly as President Donald Trump, a Republican, has become a strong supporter of building more of the facilities, which he says are vital to growing the U.S. economy.
 “Janoo is playing off that a little bit,” Dickinson said.
In response to what her campaign website calls “one of the greatest threats of our time,” Janoo wants Vermont to enact “the nation’s strongest public standards for AI,” including independent testing, human oversight and ongoing audits. The site also calls for banning “AI systems designed for mass political or immigration surveillance.”
Scott’s campaign has shared few, if any, public proposals about AI. Asked about the technology at a recent press conference, he said he sees a difference between “good AI and evil AI.” The former could be used to cure cancer, Scott said, while the latter could “take power away from humans and go rampant.” Because the technology has upsides, he said, it’s important to take a balanced and measured approach when regulating it. 
“We don’t need a patchwork quilt of state regulations. We need the federal government to take control of this,” he told reporters, adding that the feds “should be working with the private sector to determine what is needed to make sure this is safe as we move forward.”
In a statement Tuesday, Dustin Degree, a spokesperson for the governor’s campaign, said Scott has been collaborating with other governors around the country, of both parties, “to coordinate action in Washington and ensure the voices of states and state governments are at the table” about their concerns over AI. Degree also pointed to how Scott signed an executive order in May creating a task force to study how the state could use AI to better serve the public and educate state leaders how to do so.
More recently, the governor’s administration has started to embrace the technology itself. Vermont Public reported last month that state officials have been using AI created by Anthropic to probe their IT systems for security vulnerabilities.

READ MORE

Janoo’s AI platform also includes banning license plate readers manufactured by the Atlanta-based company Flock Safety. According to the company, more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies around the country use its AI-powered cameras to track vehicles. VTDigger reported in June that some police departments in Vermont are among the users.
Janoo would not be alone in her opposition. The Republican governors of Florida and Texas, for instance, took steps to curtail the use of license-plate readers in their states last month, and lawmakers in other states are now considering similar measures. 
While Flock cameras have been used in Vermont, the state does not have any large data centers like the ones that would have been subject to the regulatory framework Scott vetoed. The governor has said repeatedly that he doesn’t think one would be built in the state regardless of the regulations lawmakers put on the books. 
“Vermont’s current regulatory system virtually guarantees that no large-scale data center will ever be (sited) within Vermont’s borders,” Degree said, pointing to how it took decades for a Walmart store to get built in St. Albans Town.
He added that Scott would support a moratorium on large data center construction while the state monitors what steps the federal government takes, but remains opposed to the broad slate of regulatory changes in the bill he vetoed. Lawmakers also considered a moratorium proposal during this year’s legislative session but did not advance it.
Janoo also supports a moratorium on data center construction, though couches it in very different terms. “We will oppose the development of energy-intensive AI data centers,” her campaign site states — “not subsidize the growing concentration of wealth and power in a handful of global technology corporations.”
In addition, Janoo has proposed enacting new taxes on revenue that many of those companies generate from digital advertising on Vermonters’ screens. She says the plan would help Vermont extract revenue for public services from companies that, in her view, should be contributing more to Vermonters’ wellbeing. 
And while Scott has made a case for letting the federal government regulate AI, Janoo thinks regulating the technology at the state level could, instead, be a way to push back against a federal government she views as harmful and aligned with the interests of those very same companies.
At the national level, Democrats have criticized President Trump for having close ties to AI executives and tech investors, making the case those relationships have led to weak federal oversight. Trump and the leaders of the country’s largest AI companies announced last month they had signed a “self-policing” agreement governing future development of the technology.
Janoo’s platform calls for reviewing Vermont’s public pension investments for stock “in companies that enable mass surveillance, political repression, algorithmic discrimination, or other practices that undermine democratic rights.” 
The state should also be ready, it says, to “pursue coordinated divestment” from harmful companies though does not specify any in particular.
“We have more economic power than we recognize right now, and it’s a moment where we really need to be thinking strategically on, like, how are we using this?” Janoo said at the Marlboro forum. “I do think there are ways in which we can use strategic, nonviolent political resistance in this moment to stop this (Trump) administration.” 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Fuck the Flock cameras’: On big tech, Vermont’s candidates for governor differ on style and substance.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: More than 250 Mainers request attorney general investigate Collins corruption allegations
text:
Sen. Susan Collins' campaign staff and supporters greet her at P&K Sand and Gravel in Naples on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)More than 250 people sent a letter to Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey Wednesday requesting that his office investigate corruption allegations against U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. 
The group argues that a state statute would permit such an investigation because it governs state election laws and does not distinguish between state officials or federal officials. Title 17-A M.R.S.A. Section 33 states that the Maine Attorney General “shall” designate the deputy attorney general or an assistant attorney general to investigate alleged violations of election law.
Among the signees is the state’s former Public Advocate Bill Harwood, who told press during a virtual meeting that he is not aware of a precedent for evoking a state law to conduct such an investigation.
“But I think we live in unprecedented times,” Harwood said. “We’re seeing a level of corruption we have never seen before, so it’s one of those situations where if the federal government isn’t going to do its job, then we need somebody to do it.” 
Danna Hayes, director of public affairs for the Maine Attorney General’s Office, confirmed they received the letter and are reviewing it.
Collins has continued to deny her alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme, new details of which were revealed by ProPublica last month. The senator’s campaign staff did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Collins’ staff has said the FBI has not contacted them since 2021, when it was investigating her donor, Martin Kao, the former CEO of defense contractor Navatek, who pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions involving a pro-Collins super PAC. No one in Collins’ orbit was charged as a result of the investigation then.
But ProPublica reported that the FBI was looking into the senator again in recent years — that was until Donald Trump returned to office for a second term and the probe died as part of his purge of the bureau. 
“With all due respect to Senator Collins, I just don’t think her denial can be the end of this,” Harwood said. “I think we need to have an independent investigation, and if it turns out that she’s done nothing wrong that should be the result of the investigation. But simply denying it, I don’t think is going to satisfy the people in Maine, especially the 250 people who have signed this letter.”
Several signees on the press call said they would not expect such an investigation to be completed before the election on Nov. 3. 
“So, in terms of consequences on the election, I don’t think we see that as an issue,” said Jamie Kilbreth, an attorney with Drummond Woodsum who was the lead lawyer in the State of Maine’s litigation against the tobacco industry in which it secured a landmark $1.5 billion settlement.
Janis Cohen, a retired attorney, added, “I would think that the senator’s office would welcome an investigation, and if there was no foul deed, terrific, and then everybody will know that.” 
This letter comes after attorney Valerie Adams, who unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic nomination for Cumberland County district attorney, filed a formal ethics complaint against Collins with the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics earlier this month.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas State University president accepts appointment as Virginia Tech president
text:
Kansas State University President Richard Linton, and colleague Valentina Trinetta, share signs of Wildcat loyalty while visiting the campus ice cream store on Feb. 23, 2023. Linton will leave K-State in December to serve as president of his alma mater Virginia Tech University. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas State University president Richard Linton agreed Tuesday to take his academic career full circle by accepting an appointment to lead his alma mater, Virginia Tech University.
“My 40-year journey in the land-grant system began at Virginia Tech,” said Linton, who served as K-State’s president since 2022. “Having earned three degrees here, the opportunity to return home and serve as president of my alma mater is a true honor.”
Linton said he would complete the fall semester at K-State in Manhattan before assuming duties at Virginia Tech at start of the spring semester in Blacksburg, Virginia.
He earned a bachelor’s degree in biology, master’s degree in food science and a doctorate in food science at Virginia Tech.
“Although my professional responsibilities will take me elsewhere, my appreciation for Kansas State University and the people of Kansas will endure for a lifetime,” Linton said.
He said he was leaving K-State after launching a strategic plan to make the university a “next-generation” land-grant institution. He said K-State achieved two consecutive years of enrollment growth, increased research expenditures, generated $1.2 billion in philanthropic support and secured more than $400 million in state and federal funding.
Previously, he was agriculture dean at North Carolina State University, food science department chairman at Ohio State University and a food science faculty member at Purdue University.
“Virginia Tech is poised to make a generational leap as a public research university, and Richard Linton is the right leader to guide us forward,” said Jim Miller, director of Virginia Tech’s Board of Visitors. “As a Hokie, Richard has a deep appreciation for what makes this university and its community so special. His extensive leadership experience, a career dedicated to land-grant institutions and a strong commitment to fostering a culture of service uniquely position him to lead Virginia Tech into its next chapter.”
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, a Kansas Republican, said Linton worked diligently to bring educational and research opportunities to K-State.
“Upon becoming president, he set an ambitious goal to expand K-State’s agriculture footprint,” Moran said. “Dr. Linton’s vision for K-State has helped drive enrollment and led to record-breaking investments for the university.”
He said Linton’s time at Kansas State wasn’t easy, given a cancer diagnosis he received in 2023.
“While supported by the Manhattan community, Dr. Linton continued serving the university while undergoing treatment, showing tremendous strength and commitment,” Moran said. “I’ve appreciated working alongside Dr. Linton and enjoyed our sunrise walks around campus as we discussed our shared goal of making certain Kansas is a place where students can get a quality education and build a meaningful career.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State study aims to identify retired power plant sites that can be reactivated
text:
A map from the Pennsylvania Accelerated Transmission and Energy Redevelopment Study report shows sites that could be chosen for redevelopment. (Screenshot/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Nearly two dozen former power plant sites across Pennsylvania are part of a study to identify potential locations for new generating facilities that could help ease the region’s power crunch.
The study is being carried out with a $2 million U.S. Department of Energy grant awarded to the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC). It’s being conducted by consulting firm KeyLogic Systems and the Electric Power Research Institute in a partnership between the PUC and the economic development nonprofit Team Pennsylvania.
The goal  is to narrow the list to five to seven sites with the best opportunities to quickly deploy new power generation and optimize investments to get the most out of existing infrastructure. That will help ensure the reliability of the region’s power grid as unprecedented demand from data centers and other large electricity users mounts, according to those carrying out the process.
Named the Pennsylvania Accelerated Transmission and Energy Redevelopment (PATER) Study, it also aims to revitalize communities with industrial legacies to create long-term economic growth.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Tom Murphy, managing director for energy at Team Pennsylvania, said PATER is a way to look at Pennsylvania’s power generation and transmission system as a whole, while energy regulators and state leaders across the country look to spur new investments in the electricity grid.
“Is it possible to bring some of those brownfield sites back into the grid and restore power back?” he said, adding that the site assessments look at the potential for any new power technology such as battery storage, renewables or new nuclear technology, such as small modular reactors.
Team Pennsylvania, funded by philanthropic foundations, federal grants, public-private partnerships and industry contributions, is co-chaired by Gov. Josh Shapiro and McNees Wallace & Nurick law firm chair Brian Jackson. 
The PUC held a nearly-three-hour hearing on the initial part of the study Oct. 5. The second part will run from November through March, with a public meeting set Feb. 10. That will be followed by an opportunity for public comment, PUC spokesman Niks Hagen-Frederiksen said.
Pennsylvania, the study notes, is the nation’s leading energy exporter, sending nearly 89 million megawatt-hours of electricity to other states in the PJM Interconnection grid and beyond.
PJM, based near Philadelphia in Montgomery County, is a nonprofit company tasked with managing the electricity supply and distribution for 67 million electric customers in 13 states including Pennsylvania.
In the last two years, PJM has faced pressure from regulators and elected officials, including Shapiro, as electricity prices soared, driven by forecasts showing the demand for power will increase to unprecedented levels in coming decades. 
At the same time, electricity industry leaders and public officials have criticized PJM for delaying approvals for new generation to connect to the grid.
While PJM halted the queue from 2022 until this spring, it has since cleared a backlog of projects and reformed its review process to prioritize proposals with significant financial commitments.
But another report from the PUC released in September warns that the PJM region could experience rolling blackouts even if new power generation resources are built over the next 15 years, as data centers come online.
The PATER study will provide guidance for future investors on where new power plants can be added to the grid to power homes, businesses and industry, Murphy said.
“How much can we squeeze out of the grid that we have? How much can we squeeze out of the power gen that’s out there, and where do we need to upgrade both of them?” he said.
“We’re also agnostic on what the end use of the power could be. We’re not suggesting this power needs to go to this manufacturing plant or to a data center or to an EV plant or whatever,” he noted “We’re saying, ‘Where can you bring more power into the grid in a place that the grid can accept it?’”
A screenshot from the Pennsylvania Accelerated Transmission and Energy Redevelopment Study report shows locations that could be chosen for redevelopment. (Screenshot/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The study began with 76 power generation sites that have been decommissioned since 1971. Those locations were filtered by the size of the former power plant, whether the site is fully retired and whether the circumstances make redevelopment feasible to narrow the list to 21. 
Those sites identified in the first phase of the study include retired coal-, natural gas- and oil-fired power plants in 16 counties. 
The analysis found most of the sites are physically ready for redevelopment with transmission lines and substations within a mile. About half are less than 1.5 miles from natural gas pipelines and many are within a few miles of major fiber networks. The average size of decommissioned coal-fired power plant sites is about 200 acres, while former natural gas and oil-fired sites were much smaller, with nine at less than 100 acres. 
Transmission capacity for those sites is significant but limited at 9 gigawatts statewide, the study found, indicating the commonwealth’s grid “retains meaningful capability to support both new generation and new load development at the candidate deactivated sites.”
It also analyzed risks present at the site, identifying groundwater contamination, flooding and geological issues at potential liability. Available transmission capacity is site-specific and could be taken up as PJM approves more new power generation. 
The Shippingport Bridge is located adjacent to the Beaver Valley Power Station in Beaver County. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
It also notes that any new development would be subject to complex regulation for air, water and land use permits and that local opposition could present challenges. It cited the redevelopment of the former coal-fired Homer City power plant as a massive natural gas plant and data center campus as an example.
Energy and tech industry leaders appear bullish on investment in new power generation, which would benefit the grid as a whole. Earlier in October, Baltimore-based Constellation Energy and Google announced a $4.3 billion commitment to upgrade 11 of its nuclear power plants, including three in Pennsylvania, to generate an additional 890 megawatts of power. 
In addition, the companies inked a 15-year agreement to add another 2,700 megawatts of generating capacity to Constellation’s fleet. 
And PJM is planning to conduct an auction, known as a Reliability Backstop Procurement, intended to match data center companies with investors willing to build new generating capacity in a process designed to put more power on the grid while insulating residential and business ratepayers from additional costs. 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission last month accepted PJM’s proposal but delayed the process by five months to work out details of the plan.
“At the end of the day … it’s a story about economic development in Pennsylvania,” Murphy said, noting the PATER Study is intended to fill a need driven by increased electrification. 
“If we don’t have the power, or if we have the power and we don’t have the transmission capacity to move it from point A to point B, then it’s going to stifle economic development someplace within the state, if not multiple locations,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Probe of DOC doctor finds issues with credentials, patient care
text:
A Connecticut Department of Correction doctor repeatedly engaged in behavior that compromised patient care, according to an investigation released on Wednesday by the Correction Ombuds’ office.
The report concludes that DOC failed to adequately carry out and follow up on internal investigations regarding the doctor, Francesco Lupis, since his hiring in 2020. And it states that DOC officials could not provide any documentation to show that Lupis, who was not board certified, was in compliance with the state’s required qualifications for the role.
The findings come amidst widespread reports from people incarcerated about lacking medical care within DOC facilities. A March 2026 report catalogued “systemic deficiencies” in access to medical and mental healthcare, particularly outpatient specialty services.  
Correction Ombuds DeVaughn Ward said in an interview that the findings regarding Lupis continue to raise questions about the quality of healthcare DOC provides.
“All of this information puts into question whether or not the agency is meeting its obligation to provide care at the community level standard,” Ward said. “Certainly someone like this would have trouble being employed in a community healthcare setting.”
Over his six years with DOC, Lupis was named as a defendant in 27 federal lawsuits filed in U.S. District Court in Connecticut by people who had resided in DOC facilities. Allegations included delayed specialty care, medication management and medical accommodations. One of those cases resulted in a $50,000 settlement.
Lupis earned a projected annual salary of roughly $260,000 as of 2026, according to figures published by the Office of the State Comptroller. 
DOC spokesperson Andrius Benevicius confirmed Lupis has been placed on paid administrative leave pending further review.
“The Connecticut Department of Correction takes its responsibility to provide quality health care to individuals in our custody seriously,” Banevicius said. “We will continue to review our policies, practices, and oversight mechanisms to ensure the delivery of safe, effective, and accountable health care throughout the correctional system.”
Lupis could not be reached for comment. 
The report found that the department could not confirm whether Lupis was compliant with board certification requirements.
Lupis did not have current board certification, but DOC policy does not require that doctors have board certification when they are hired. However, they must obtain it within five years, and Lupis was hired in 2020. 
Doctors who do not obtain board certification can fulfill the requirement by successfully completing an “established agency competency program.” DOC did not have documentation of Lupis’ completion of the program, leading investigators to conclude that “compliance with the staff physician qualification requirements therefore remains unresolved.”
The report outlined problematic behavior towards both patients and colleagues, including allegations that Lupis yelled at patients, disregarded medical histories and inappropriately discontinued or reduced medication. 
Ward said one of the findings that most alarmed him was an incident in Lupis’s personal life. In November 2022, Lupis was arrested for yelling and cursing at his son, retrieving an axe and threatening him, according to the report. At the time, Lupis stated he did not intend to injure his son or break down a door. DOC investigated the incident and Lupis received formal counseling in February 2023, the report said.
DOC launched six internal investigations related to complaints about Lupis’ conduct. The ombuds report found that some of these investigations suffered significant delays and the agency was not able to provide records establishing that recommended corrective measures were actually taken. 
Lupis’ alleged problematic behavior was well documented before DOC hired him in 2020. Massachusetts denied Lupis a medical license in 2013, citing his prior professional conduct. In 2017, Florida allowed him to relinquish his license provided he agreed “never again to apply for licensure as a physician in the State of Florida,” the report said.
Lead investigator for the Ombuds office Amy Zipf said she could not confirm whether DOC officials were aware of the Massachusetts denial when they hired Lupis, but said she was able to obtain the information by sending an email.
DOC officials have in the past blamed delays in care to staffing shortages, as well as issues with recruitment and retention. Zipf acknowledged the difficulty of recruiting physicians but noted that shortages shouldn’t result in hiring of physicians with patterns of problematic behavior.
“It’s probably hard to hire and keep other healthcare professionals who are expected to work alongside someone whose behavior is like this,” Zipf said.
Ward gave DOC credit for placing Lupis on leave following the report.
“That is the highest hope when we issue these reports. It really is to try to spur action on the part of the department. And to their credit, they did take the substance of the report seriously and take immediate action,” Ward said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SLED arrests 3 SC men US Rep. Nancy Mace accused of sex crimes
text:
Three men U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace accused of sexual crimes during a House floor speech were arrested Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Screenshot from C-SPAN)COLUMBIA — Three of the men U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace accused on the House floor of sexual crimes were arrested Wednesday.
The arrests of Mace’s ex-fiancé, Patrick Bryant, as well as John Osborne and Eric Bowman come 20 months after Mace’s shocking, hourlong public speech, when she accused them of being sexual predators, with a posterboard of their photos as background. All immediately and have since repeatedly denied the allegations.
The three men were booked in the Charleston County jail Wednesday, the State Law Enforcement Division said.
A fourth man she accused in her speech was not charged.
Osborne, of Charleston, faces charges of assault and battery, as well as two counts of criminal sexual conduct. Bryant, of Mount Pleasant, and Bowman, of Sullivans Island, were both charged with voyeurism, and Bowman had additional charges of obstruction of justice and publishing the name of a victim of criminal sexual conduct.
All of the allegations in their arrest warrants are from October 2018, four years before Mace’s engagement to Bryant.
Bowman and Bryant received cash bonds of $50,000, according to court records. Osborne’s bond was set at $75,000.
Osborne’s attorney, Ryan Schwartz, said his client is innocent and “intends to defend himself vigorously.” He did not give details on Osborne’s side of the story, saying those will come out in court.
“An arrest is an accusation, not a conviction,” Schwartz said in a statement.
Bowman and Bryant, along with attorneys who have represented them previously, did not respond Wednesday to calls from the SC Daily Gazette requesting comment.
Not charged with a crime was Brian Musgrave of Fort Mill, who Mace included in her public accusations. Musgrave sued Mace over the claims, but a judge later dismissed the lawsuit, pointing to the “speech or debate” clause that protects members of Congress from being sued over what they say on the floor.
“Obviously, Brian is happy not to have been criminally charged and not to be grouped with the others recently charged, but it has opened up some pretty deep wounds,” Musgrave’s attorneys, Eric Bland and Ronald Richter, said in a statement Wednesday. “To this day, Ms. Mace has never apologized to Brian and his family for what she falsely said about him.”
During her bombshell speech, Mace accused the men of sexual misconduct against herself and other women, saying she found videos and photographs of herself and other women on Bryant’s phone that appeared to mostly have been taken without the women knowing. The posterboard behind her as she spoke included their names and addresses with the heading, “PREDATORS. STAY AWAY FROM.”
In a statement Wednesday, the 1st District congresswoman did not directly address the charges but pointed to bills she supported to increase penalties for sexual crimes, strengthen protections for survivors of sexual assault and fight voyeurism.
“Every survivor deserves to be heard,” Mace said in the statement. “Every victim deserves justice. Every predator deserves accountability. We will not stop fighting until our laws put victims first and predators behind bars.”
The investigation focused on a then-23-year-old woman, according to the arrest warrants, which do not name her.
The woman, who is also suing the three men over the incident, came back to Bowman’s home in Sullivan’s Island after drinking on Oct. 26, 2018. She was so intoxicated, she fell in the pool while wearing her clothes, according to arrest warrants for the three men, which all lay out the same events. She is identified in the lawsuit, filed in May 2025, as Jane Doe.
After undressing, she passed out on the couch, where she covered herself with a pillow, according to the warrants.
The arrest warrants accuse Bowman, Bryant and Osborne of discussing “sexual exploits” while she was unconscious, then agreeing that Bowman and Bryant would watch while Osborne had sex with her.
Osborne assaulted the woman, “who was mentally incapacitated and physically helpless due to her extreme intoxication,” an investigating officer said in the warrants.
According to the warrant, an unnamed witness heard the conversation and watched what happened through the home’s security cameras. She saved photos from the video feed and wrote down what she saw in a journal entry, investigators said.
The woman didn’t know what had happened that night until Mace told her more than five years later, in April 2024, according to her lawsuit, which recounts the same events.
According to Mace, she learned about the incident after checking her then-fiancé’s phone and finding the photos and videos.
During her speech, Mace mentioned telling a woman she’d been assaulted by the three men. In her lawsuit, Joe Doe says she is the victim Mace referenced.
Bowman faces an additional charge of posting the woman’s name on social media and sharing a video of her despite knowing SLED was investigating, according to the warrant for his arrest. He is also accused of wiping his phone when SLED investigators attempted to seize it under a search warrant, the SLED documents read.
Mace sued Bowman for defamation, saying he posted false statements about her on social media last year. Bowman denied the claims, and the lawsuit has been on pause since June.
Bowman was arrested in August 2025 on unrelated charges of harassment and domestic violence. Those charges remain pending.
The latest charges Wednesday come four months after Mace lost her bid for governor.
Mace, first elected in 2020, will leave office in January. She launched a podcast called “Get Maced” in August.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ board approves $498 million Newark school lease
text:
A rendering of the proposed Riverfront Elementary School in Newark. (Courtesy of Newark Public Schools)The New Jersey Local Finance Board approved a $498 million lease for a Newark school building that local officials said is needed to alleviate overcrowding, a vote taken after complaints from Republicans who alleged corruption and mismanagement.
The board’s vote will permit the Newark School District to lease the property for 30 years, and the district’s agreement allows it to purchase the building for $1,000 at the close of the lease term. The proposed Riverfront Elementary School is set to open in the fall of 2028 on the site of a closed Catholic school.
What on Earth is going on in Newark schools?

Robert Jackson is one of the finance board’s members who voted to allow the lease.
“No one is debating the fact of the need, and I think there is a tremendous need for our school space in the East Ward,” Jackson said. “I also believe, as I said previously, that the costs — I believe something could be built a lot cheaper and done a different way.”
District officials said Newark’s East Ward needs more and newer classroom space, and that other potential locations were inappropriate.
The ward’s eight school buildings are overcrowded, and five date back to the 1800s, said Newark Schools Superintendent Roger León, and the district is leasing other buildings and busing East Ward students to other parts of the city to make up for the lack of space.
Paul Kanitra, a Republican assemblyman who represents portions of Ocean and Monmouth counties, argued the lease is irresponsible, noting it costs more than new school buildings being constructed in Elizabeth, another district like Newark where the Schools Development Authority funds and manages school construction, and in Pleasantville.
“I want people across the whole state of New Jersey, when they read about what you guys are doing here today, to understand how much money we’re talking about. New Jersey has 9.5 million residents,” he said. “This one school alone represents more than 52 bucks in proposed payments for every man, woman, and child in the entire state over the 30-year period.”
Lease payments for the school begin at about $11.3 million and are indexed by 2.25% each year, said José Fuentes, the school district’s business administrator.
Ryan Cooper, another member of the Local Finance Board, said he found many of the meeting’s critical comments unhelpful. Speakers, he said, raised matters related to the state’s annual budget, which is approved by the Legislature and which the board has no say over.
The detractors, he said, had brought denigrating comments instead of solutions of their own.
“Perhaps there are better solutions, but no one’s proposing them,” he said. “I’m not going to hold these children hostage.”
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex), a charter school administrator who has been critical of León’s tenure as superintendent and the Riverfront deal specifically, noted to the board that the developer of the proposed school has given “large donations to political campaigns in Newark.” NJ Spotlight News has reported the developer is Scott Fields, who last year backed Newark Mayor Ras Baraka’s unsuccessful bid for governor.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Dem governor nominee Haaland’s fundraising advantage grows heading into Election Day
text:
New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland raised roughly $1.9 million in recent weeks, according to new filings she provided to the Secretary of State’s Office on Oct. 13, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland continued her fundraising dominance over Republican opponent Gregg Hull with fewer than three weeks until the Nov. 3 general election, new campaign reports show.
In the most recent campaign finance period, which captures fundraising activity between Sept. 8 and Oct. 5, Haaland received roughly $1.9 million from a little more than 34,000 donations, according to New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office records candidates were required to submit Tuesday. That amounts to an average donation of roughly $55. 
Hull received about $634,000 from 1,400 donations — averaging to roughly $450 per donation.
The Democrat, a former U.S. congresswoman and the nation’s first-ever Indigenous cabinet secretary during Joe Biden’s presidency, has drawn on her national profile to outraise both her primary and general election opponents by large margins. 
In total, Haaland has raised nearly $20 million across the primary and general elections, including more than $6.4 million during the general election, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
Hull, a former Rio Rancho mayor, has raised approximately $1.5 million this general election, though his campaign has stressed that the vast majority of his donors come from New Mexico, unlike the donors to Haaland’s campaign. 
Ryan Saylor, Hull’s campaign manager, stressed that difference Wednesday in an interview with Source NM. 
“We’re happy with where we are,” Saylor said. “We’re getting a ton of grassroots support from people all across New Mexico.”
The new campaign filings show that 99% of Hull’s donors come from New Mexico. In contrast, just 17% of Haaland’s donors are state residents. A little more than 6,000 donations came from donors with California addresses, according to a Source NM review, compared with fewer than 5,900 donations from New Mexico residents. 
Hannah Menchoff, a spokesperson for Haaland’s campaign, noted in an emailed statement to Source NM that Haaland’s average contribution is far lower than Hull’s, which she said is an indication of her widespread support from typical voters, not corporations or wealthy interests.
“I know firsthand how hard people work to earn every paycheck, and I am deeply grateful for everyone that shares my vision for New Mexico,” Haaland said in a statement. 
The filings show that both candidates are spending their donations about as quickly as they are receiving them, with expenditures going primarily to digital and television advertisements.
Haaland has spent more than $2.5 million over the most-recent reporting period, leaving her with a little over $2.8 million in cash on hand heading into the election. Haaland’s newly reported campaign expenditures included multiple purchases of more than $300,000 to Sage Media, a Washington, D.C.-based firm that specializes in progressive campaign advertising. 
Hull spent all but about $13,000 of the roughly $634,000 he raised this period. Most of that money has gone to Red Surge Strategies, an advertising firm that boasts “demonstrated adeptness in navigating the intricate terrain of right-wing politics.” Hull has about $520,000 remaining, records show. 
The public will have one more glimpse into fundraising activity before the Nov. 3 general election with another round of filings on Oct. 29.

name: Mississippi Today
title: AccelerateMS seeks $2.5M budget increase to expand staff and workforce programs
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s workforce development agency is seeking more state money to add staff as it launches and expands job training programs. The request comes as the state prepares for thousands of jobs to open in the next decade. 
AccelerateMS is requesting a $7.1 million operating budget for fiscal year 2028, which begins July 1. That is about $2.5 million more than its current appropriation, according to information that agency officials recently presented to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee. The increase would go toward hiring staff to help manage new programs, including UPSKILL (Upgrading Priority Skills for Key Industry Learning and Labor), which launched this summer, and the new Workforce Pell Grant program, said Courtney Taylor, executive director of AccelerateMS. 
The State Workforce Investment Board estimated in 2025 that Mississippi will face a shortage of 19,000 workers in priority fields such as manufacturing, construction and healthcare through 2035. Taylor said closing the gap will require the state to train more workers and students and to connect them to high-demand jobs. 
“The investment is crucial for our state and to meet the economy where it’s going,” Taylor said. 
AccelerateMS currently has 28 employees, Taylor said, and wants to hire an additional eight. 
One of those positions is a full-time Workforce Pell manager, Taylor said. The  Workforce Pell Grant program launched in July will allow eligible students to use federal Pell Grants for certain short-term job training programs. 
The expansion of the Pell Grant program, which traditionally helped low-income students pay for college, will allow students to pay for workforce programs lasting as little as eight to 15 weeks. 
Having a dedicated employee to review applications from the state’s universities, community and technical colleges seeking approval for eligible programs to qualify for Workforce Pell would help, she said. For now, an employee who oversees other federal initiatives, including the opioid-settlement workforce training program, reviews Workforce Pell applications. 
In September, Mississippi secured $8.5 million in federal funding to help launch Workforce Pell across all 15 community colleges.
Northwest Mississippi Community College will lead the effort, but AccelerateMS will help to coordinate and set up the program statewide, Taylor said. 
Workforce Pell requires a lot of management, including tracking data required by the federal government for students’ graduation rates, job placement and wage outcomes, said Iris Palmer, director of community college initiatives at New America, a national public policy think tank. 
The requirements for Workforce Pell “are very complicated,” and the process of getting these types of programs set up at colleges can be difficult, she said.  
Lawmakers will consider AccelerateMS’s request during their three-month session that begins in January, as they finalize the state budget for the next fiscal year. 
State Sen. Briggs Hopson III, R-Vicksburg, answers questions from fellow senators during a special session at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Wednesday, May 28, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Senate Appropriations Chairman Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg, said it is too early to know whether AccelerateMS will receive its full request. Lawmakers are reviewing agencies’ budget requests and the state’s major spending needs, including Medicaid, he said. Hopson said lawmakers will consider how much money the state has available and determine where it can be spent when developing the final budget.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: East Arkansas congressional race debate highlights divide over Iran war
text:
U.S. Congressional District 1 candidates for Arkansas including Rep. Rick Crawford (R), Dr. Terri Yarbrough Green (D), and Steve Parsons (L) participate in a debate at the Arkansas TV studios on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)The war in Iran was a contentious topic for candidates vying for Arkansas’ 1st Congressional District seat during an Arkansas TV debate Wednesday that also included discussions of tariffs and rural healthcare. 
Democrat Terri Yarbrough Green and Libertarian Steve Parsons are challenging U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford, who’s seeking a ninth term representing a district spanning 31 counties in eastern Arkansas. 
Crawford, who was first elected in 2010 and chairs the House Intelligence Committee, said he believed Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon and supported President Donald Trump taking action, even though the war has led to higher fuel prices. 
“Nobody wants to pay this price, but we also don’t want a nuclear-armed Iran,” Crawford said. 



 
Parsons said the United States needs “to stop being the puppet of Israel” and end the Iran war to get fuel and fertilizer back to the country. Parsons also noted Israel was the United States’ primary ally in the conflict.
“That’s a terrible sign, and a part I don’t like that because Israel is the one that in Gaza killed 20,000 children,” he said, citing a number from a United Nations panel. 
Crawford questioned the number of deaths and noted more than 1,000 Israelis were killed in an unprovoked attack in October 2023 that led to the Israel-Hamas war. 
“I’m not antisemitic like the gentleman on the end here,” Crawford said.
Parsons argued complaining about those deaths “is absolutely not an antisemitic statement, but it is a statement about Israel.”
Green agreed Iran has been a threat, mainly to Israel, and noted other countries have chosen diplomacy because they knew Iran would close the Strait of Hormuz. The move has restricted the flow of oil, increasing gas prices worldwide. 
“I think this war was started on a whim and it was not initiated, like the Constitution insists, agreed upon by Congress,” she said. “And I think Congress needs to take its power back and say, ‘no.’”
Green also criticized Congress for not pushing back against Trump’s tariffs, like those imposed on Canada. While tariffs applied meaningfully can be useful, most of the president’s tariffs have been imposed “willy nilly,” Green said.
“His decisions on who to impose a tariff on has more to do with ego, whims, who he can extort for something he wants,” she said. 
Parsons, a retired economist and consultant, said tariffs are inherently bad if they’re generically applied. 
Tariffs are a tax on American businesses, Parsons said. Oftentimes businesses have to obtain components for their products outside the U.S., and majority of those costs are passed on to consumers, he said.

Mississippi County, located in Arkansas’ 1st Congressional District, is the largest steel-producing county in the country. Industry leaders have said the industry surged after Trump imposed tariffs on China in his first term.
One industry that has struggled throughout the district and Arkansas is healthcare. Access to healthcare in rural areas has decreased as facilities close or cut back services due to increasing costs and low reimbursement rates. 
Green, a retired pathologist, said rural hospitals are closing because of Medicaid cuts. She noted Crawford supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax and spending cut legislation Trump signed last year that’s expected to reduce federal spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion during the next decade to help pay for tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the wealthy. 
If elected, Green said she would reverse the cuts, expand Medicare and Medicaid, and have a commission study ways to decrease the bureaucracy involved with the programs so hospitals wouldn’t need a separate department to fight denials. 
“That’s a waste of patients’ money,” Green said.
