Crawford rejected the assertion that he supported Medicaid cuts.
“What we’ve been trying to do is prevent spending a trillion dollars a year and lower the trajectory on Medicaid spending so we can reduce costs and deliver better value to Arkansans who need help,” he said. 
Crawford also blamed the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, for problems with Medicaid and Medicare. Under the policy, Crawford said private insurers won’t reimburse higher than the rate prescribed by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. 
“That’s what’s killed private insurance, and that’s why those hospitals are suffering,” he said. 
Parsons said he would like to study how the reimbursement rate formula allows states to receive different amounts for the same procedure.
Parsons recommended Medicaid block grants — a fixed sum of money from the federal government — instead of matching grants. He said a variety of regulations, such as certificate of need requirements, should be cut. Parsons also called for limits on lawsuits against medical providers.
“A lot of medical procedures are done because the medical professional is concerned about lawsuits,” he said. “And this is, let’s be clear, the United States is the lawsuit capital of the world.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration from moving Forest Service headquarters to Utah
text:
A sign for a camp site managed by the U.S. Forest Service in the Ashley National Forest is pictured on July 19, 2026. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)A federal judge has issued a preliminary ruling blocking the Trump administration from moving the U.S. Forest Service’s headquarters from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City while the rest of the lawsuit over the relocation plays out in court. 
In the order signed Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria, in California’s northern district, granted a stay on the move, writing in the order that Congress has put restrictions on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s “ability to reorganize without congressional buy-in.” 
The USDA — which oversees the Forest Service — “has almost certainly been violating those restrictions,” the judge wrote, adding that “preliminary relief is necessary to protect the congressional prerogative, prevent irreparable harm to federal employees, and vindicate the public interest.” 
Idaho Forest Service employees told their positions may be affected by federal agency restructure

In March, when the USDA announced in a news release it would be moving its headquarters to Utah as part of a “sweeping restructuring” of the Forest Service, Secretary Brook Rollins called it a “common sense” way to position the agency “closer to the landscapes we manage and the people who depend on them.” 
The restructuring would also close and consolidate nearly two dozen research facilities and open new, smaller state-based offices. Affected employees, including in Idaho, were told they may have to move, find another position, or resign, the Idaho Capital Sun reported in April. 
At the time, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox called the agency’s move a “big win for Utah and the West” in a statement included in that USDA news release. 
“Moving away from a regional model to a more state-focused approach strengthens federalism and helps the Forest Service do its job more effectively,” Cox said. 
In response to the ruling, the governor and Utah’s top Republican legislative leaders — House Speaker Mike Schultz and Senate President Stuart Adams — issued a joint statement Wednesday calling the decision a “setback for common sense and responsible management of our public lands.” 
“Decisions affecting Western forests and communities should be made closer to the people who know these lands best, not by bureaucrats and special interests thousands of miles away in Washington, D.C.,” Cox, Schultz and Adams said. “We hope this decision is quickly reversed so Forest Service leadership can better serve the West.”
Forest Service headquarters to relocate to Salt Lake City in major restructuring plan

Last month, a group of nonprofits, local governments and labor union organizations filed a lawsuit to block the plan as unlawful, calling it an “unprecedented reorganization” that would close offices across the country and force thousands of USDA employees to “choose between their families, communities, churches, and lives they have built, and their careers.” 
In a response to the lawsuit, USDA officials said they estimated about 250 employees would be relocated, not thousands. However, the judge determined that regardless of that number, the proposed reorganization would “certainly affect more than 10 staff members and therefore fall within the definition of reprogramming” that would require congressional approval. 
In the lawsuit, the groups said USDA leaders — after they first announced the reorganization plan in July of last year — failed to get congressional approval for the plan. Congress not only rejected it, the plaintiffs wrote in the lawsuit, but it “went beyond rejecting the Administration’s budget proposal that reflected the reorganized and downsized USDA, and expressly prohibited the reorganization of the agency without further congressional approval.” 
In the ruling issued Tuesday, the federal district court judge agreed.

“Congress did not contemplate USDA using its appropriated funds to shut down offices or relocate employees,” Chhabria wrote. “To the contrary, Congress was actively working to restrict the agency’s ability to do so.”
While the rest of the lawsuit plays out in court, the order blocks Rollins and other USDA leaders from closing offices or reassigning employees to new locations outside of their areas. The judge noted the order doesn’t prevent the department from relocating or reassigning employees from within the National Capital Region in Washington, D.C., but it does prevent moving positions outside of the area. 
However, the judge also noted in his ruling that the “temporal scope of this relief could end up being quite short.” 
“The relevant appropriations statutes are set to expire in less than two months. If the agency wishes to move forward with its plans to close offices and relocate employees, it will soon have the opportunity to convince Congress of the merits of those plans,” the order says. “Congress, if it agrees, can choose not to extend the restrictions at issue in this case.” 
“But until then,” the judge wrote, “USDA is preliminarily enjoined from spending appropriated funds on the challenged office closures and employee relocations.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont’s lead over Fazio reaches 20 points in Quinnipiac poll
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat seeking a third term as Connecticut’s governor, had a commanding lead of 58% to 38% over Republican Ryan Fazio in a Quinnipiac University poll released Wednesday.
Despite Fazio’s campaign spending $7.2 million for ads on broadcast, cable or streaming television since July, 30% of those polled said they hadn’t heard enough to express an opinion about the 36-year-old state senator from Greenwich.
“This is the biggest lead a candidate for governor in Connecticut has had in two decades since Jodi Rell led John DeStefano by 24 points in Quinnipiac University’s Nov. 1, 2006 poll,” said Doug Schwartz, the poll’s director.
Rell was a Republican still riding a wave of goodwill 18 months after a corruption scandal forced the resignation of Gov. John G. Rowland and she succeeded him. She was reelected with 63% of the vote.
Lamont is a hardly a fresh face. The new poll found the prospect of a third term for the 72-year-old Lamont is generating relatively little passion: Only 30% of his supporters described themselves as “very enthusiastic,” while 54% were “somewhat enthusiastic.”
Fazio did better on the enthusiasm measure: 46% of his supporters were “very enthusiastic” about their choice and 42% “somewhat enthusiastic.” 
But Lamont has the numbers, a favorable tail wind and a string of positive polls.
Lamont has not trailed in any public poll, with an average lead of about 15 percentage points in the four surveys released over the past four weeks.
President Donald Trump remains a drag on the GOP, with a job approval rating nearly 40 points under water: Only 29% of voters approve of the president’s performance, while 67% disapprove.
Connecticut Republicans remain loyal to the president, with 78% approving of his performance and 17% disapproving. 
Lamont’s job approval was comfortably above water, 53% to 40%.
The economy and cost of living were the most important issues identified by voters, and Lamont was deemed more capable in those areas. Among likely voters who say the economy was most important, Lamont was favored, 73% to 25%; on cost of living, Lamont was favored, 67% to 30%.
To those who see taxes as most important, Fazio was favored, 77% to 23%.
The poll of 1,225 likely voters was conducted from Oct. 8-12 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. Quinnipiac polls using live interviews, reaching voters by random digit dialing to a mix of landlines and cell phones.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: New resiliency center offers free trauma support for those affected by Brown and Pawtucket shootings
text:
A sign hangs in the window of the Ever Hope Center, a federally funded resiliency center for people affected by the mass shootings in Pawtucket and at Brown University. The center run by Family Service of Rhode Island officially opened Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) Healing takes time.
For Chris Librizzi, the process remains ongoing nearly eight months after a gunman opened fire during a high school hockey game he was coaching at a Pawtucket rink, killing three people, including the shooter.
Even after his Blackstone Valley Co-op hockey team won the state championship in March, Librizzi struggled with sleep disturbances, nightmares and reliving the shooting. Loud noises also triggered intense reactions that he mistook for gunshots, he said.
“I know I will never fully heal, and I believe my players and their families are experiencing the same struggles,” he recounted to reporters and advocates gathered Wednesday at the Rhode Island Foundation’s One Union Station headquarters in downtown Providence.
With help from Family Service of Rhode Island, Librizzi and his team began working through their trauma almost immediately after the shooting occurred on Feb. 16. Counselors arrived at the Pawtucket police station within an hour of the shooting and continued meeting with the players and coaches over the next 10 days.
In the months that followed, the organization continued connecting players, coaches and their families with support, including group therapy to help them cope with the shooting’s lasting effects.
That work helped inform the need for longer-term support, leading to the creation of the Ever Hope Center, a federally funded resiliency center run by Family Service of Rhode Island. 
The center officially opened Wednesday at the Rhode Island Foundation’s headquarters in Providence, offering free, ongoing support services to people affected by the Pawtucket shooting and the December mass shooting at Brown University that killed two students and injured nine others.
“We cannot undo the events that happened on December 13th or on February 16th, but we can decide what happens next,” said Rachel Caruso, the executive director of the new Ever Hope Center. “We can be a community that responds in the moment, and we can be a community that stays.”
Chris Librizzi, head coach of the Blackstone Valley Co-op hockey team, speaks about the long road to recovery after a Feb. 16, 2026, shooting during a game he was coaching in Pawtucket at the opening of the Ever Hope Center in Providence on Wednesday. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Caruso said the center grew out of months of work after the two shootings, as Family Service of Rhode Island, where she worked on its victims service team, considered what resources would be needed in the months and years ahead.
“Too often support is strongest at the beginning, and it fades over time,” she said.
The Ever Hope Center is funded primarily through a $2 million grant from the U.S. Justice Department’s Antiterrorism and Emergency Assistance Program, with an additional $200,000 allocation through the federal Victims of Crime Act.
Located on the main floor of Providence’s historic Union Station building, the center occupies space formerly used by Rhode Island KIDS COUNT, which moved out at the end of 2025 after more than three decades.
The center offers trauma-informed support groups and activities, including plans for art therapy and trauma-informed yoga — all for free, Caruso told reporters after the press conference. Other resources include games, fidget toys, books about grief and meditation, and journals with colored pencils and markers for what staff call “doodle meditation.”
A “quiet room,” still in development, will give visitors a place to decompress, with couches, pillows, blankets and noise-canceling headphones.
“We want to make sure that we’re a safe space,” Caruso said.
The Ever Hope Center in Providence includes a warmly lit space with seating, games, fidget toys, books and art supplies for visitors seeking support after the mass shootings in Pawtucket and at Brown University. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Trauma-trained staff
For now, the federal funding can only be used for people impacted by either the Brown or Pawtucket shootings, though Caruso said she and her team would be available in case of another large-scale tragedy.
Caruso said the center currently has three trauma-trained social service professionals, including herself, as well as a victim navigator and a training and outreach specialist. The center plans to hire an additional victim navigator and a clinician.


The center expects to be open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For now, people seeking support can contact staff at hello@everhopecenter.org. 


Pawtucket Police Chief Tina Goncalves said the February shooting underscored the importance of having support available beyond the immediate aftermath of a tragedy.
“While being on the ground is an important aspect while an event is occurring, we will know the impact of these events extends beyond the physical space where they have occurred and also beyond initial moments,” Goncalves said. “And this center helps with that.”
Hugh Clements, a former Providence police chief who now oversees Brown University’s Department of Public Safety and Emergency Management, also sees the center as a way to address the lasting effects of mass violence.
“When the sirens fade, the long work of healing begins for survivors, families, first responders, and the wider community,” Clements said.

name: Delaware
title: Breast Cancer Awareness Month highlights early detection and access to care in Delaware
text:
State officials, healthcare providers and advocates gathered Wednesday at ChristianaCare’s Wilmington Hospital to encourage women to stay current with recommended screenings, understand their family medical histories and seek help when cost, transportation or access to care becomes a barrier. Photo Courtesy of the State of Delaware. 
With nearly 5,000 women diagnosed over five years, Delaware health leaders emphasize the importance of screening, affordable treatment and addressing disparities in breast cancer outcomes.
WILMINGTON, Del. — With nearly 5,000 Delaware women diagnosed with breast cancer over a recent five-year period, health leaders are using Breast Cancer Awareness Month to reinforce a message that could save lives: Early detection and timely access to treatment can dramatically improve the chances of survival.
State officials, healthcare providers and advocates gathered Wednesday at ChristianaCare’s Wilmington Hospital to encourage women to stay current with recommended screenings, understand their family medical histories and seek help when cost, transportation or access to care becomes a barrier.
The event brought together Gov. Matt Meyer, former first lady Dr. Jill Biden, Lt. Gov. Kyle Evans Gay, Delaware Department of Health and Social Services Secretary Christen Linke Young, Delaware Surgeon General Dr. Neil Hockstein and ChristianaCare President and CEO Jenn Schwartz.
Meyer signed a proclamation recognizing October as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, honoring survivors, remembering those who have died from the disease and recognizing the healthcare professionals, caregivers and advocates who support patients and families.
Delaware faces significant breast cancer challenges
Breast cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer among Delaware women from 2018 through 2022, with nearly 5,000 diagnoses during that period.
Delaware’s breast cancer incidence rate ranks second nationally, according to state officials, and disparities remain significant. Black women in Delaware experience higher breast cancer mortality rates than white women.
The difference between detecting cancer early and discovering it after it has spread can be substantial.
According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate exceeds 99% when breast cancer is detected before it spreads beyond the breast. That rate falls to approximately 32% when the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.
“Early detection saves lives, and access to timely diagnosis and effective treatment gives patients the best chance for a successful outcome,” Hockstein said.
“Breast cancer touches nearly every family in Delaware and while we’ve made tremendous progress in screening and treatment, significant disparities remain, particularly among Black women, who continue to experience higher mortality rates,” he said.
Screening is important, but access remains a concern
Health officials emphasized that knowing when to get screened is only part of the challenge. Some Delawareans delay mammograms or follow-up care because of cost, transportation problems, difficulty finding an appointment or lack of insurance.
Delaware’s Screening for Life program helps eligible residents obtain cancer screenings and related services, reducing some of the financial barriers that can prevent early detection.
“No one should have to put off a potentially lifesaving screening because of cost, transportation or difficulty finding an appointment,” Linke Young said.
“Through programs like Screening for Life and partnerships with health care providers across Delaware, we’re working to make breast cancer screening and treatment more accessible so more Delawareans can get the care they need, when they need it.”
The broader challenge is not simply encouraging more screenings but ensuring patients can move promptly from an abnormal mammogram to additional testing, diagnosis, treatment and follow-up care.
“Every woman deserves high-quality, accessible care regardless of her ZIP code, income or insurance status,” Meyer said. “Early detection is critical, but so is ensuring that once Delawareans are diagnosed, they can afford the appointments and care that follow.”
ChristianaCare’s Schwartz emphasized the role of healthcare providers in supporting patients throughout the screening and treatment process.
“We are here for our neighbors when they need an annual mammogram, when they have a question, when they’re waiting for results,” Schwartz said. “And, if you receive a breast cancer diagnosis, we’re here for that too, with extraordinary physicians.”
A personal reminder to prioritize screening
For some participants, the message was personal.
Gay, who turned 40 this year, shared that she had scheduled her own mammogram and encouraged others to make time for preventive care.
“This year I turned 40 and I got my mammogram. I encourage others to take time to take care of themselves,” Gay said.
She also recognized the caregivers and advocates who support patients through diagnosis, treatment and recovery.
Biden, who founded the Biden Breast Health Initiative in Delaware before serving as first lady, has been a longtime advocate for breast cancer education and women’s health.
“Early detection could save your life,” Biden said. “There’s nothing on your to-do list more important than that.”
Biden’s work has included encouraging young women to learn about breast health and advocating for greater attention to women’s health research and cancer treatment.
Understanding family history and genetic risks
Breast Cancer Awareness Month also provides an opportunity for Delawareans to learn more about inherited risks.
Certain genetic changes can increase the likelihood of developing breast and ovarian cancers. Genetic counseling can help patients understand their family histories, assess inherited risks and determine whether genetic testing may be appropriate.
A Delaware law signed in August 2025 is intended to make that process easier.
Senate Bill 70, sponsored by Sen. Nicole Poore and Rep. Krista Griffith, allows licensed genetic counselors to order genetic tests directly, eliminating an additional step for some patients seeking information about inherited health risks.
The law maintains requirements for physician referrals when medical assessments are necessary.
By improving access to genetic information, healthcare providers and patients can make more informed decisions about additional screening, preventive care and treatment options.
Turning awareness into action
While Breast Cancer Awareness Month brings additional attention to the disease, health leaders emphasized that its value ultimately depends on people taking action.
That includes discussing screening recommendations with a healthcare provider, knowing family medical history and following up promptly when additional testing is recommended.
For women facing financial or logistical barriers, state programs and healthcare organizations can provide assistance in accessing screenings and care.
The Wilmington gathering underscored a shared message from medical professionals, advocates and public officials: Early detection can save lives, but those benefits must be accessible to every Delawarean, regardless of income, insurance status or where they live.
TO GO: Breast Cancer Awareness Month

What: October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, encouraging early detection, screening and support for patients and survivors.
Who should consider screening: Women should discuss mammogram recommendations with their healthcare providers based on age, individual risk factors and family medical history. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends mammograms every two years for women ages 40 to 74 at average risk.
Need help paying for screening? Delaware’s Screening for Life program provides assistance with cancer screenings for eligible residents.
Concerned about family history? Ask a healthcare provider whether genetic counseling or additional screening may be appropriate.
Where to learn more:

Delaware Screening for Life: https://www.dhss.delaware.gov/dph/dpc/sfl.html
Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition: https://www.debreastcancer.org
American Cancer Society: https://www.cancer.org


Important reminder: An abnormal mammogram does not necessarily mean cancer, but prompt follow-up is essential. Anyone experiencing a new breast lump or other concerning breast change should consult a healthcare provider rather than wait for a routine screening.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds says states must work with ICE, but a dozen of them aren’t
text:
An airplane sits on the tarmac at Mesa Gateway Airport on the evening of April 9, 2026, outside of the Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center, an ICE facility where detainees are temporarily housed before they are put on a plane to either be deported or moved to a different ICE facility. (Photo by Jerod MacDonald-Evoy/Arizona Mirror)Florida Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says that under the U.S. Constitution, states “have” to work with the federal government in enforcing immigration laws.
However, nine states have adopted laws forbidding compliance with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainers and 12 states overall haven’t reached enforcement agreements with the agency.
Donalds made those remarks Tuesday during a roundtable discussion with members of the business community in Jacksonville. A local homebuilder asked about a scarcity of construction workers able to build affordable housing in Florida “because of the methods of ICE enforcement raiding our job sites.”
“We cannot continue to build houses, and we cannot continue to build houses affordably, if we can’t find the workers to do the work,” said Mathew Meskimen, first vice president of the Northeast Florida Building Association. “So, as governor, how would you protect our workforce and draw workers to the state of Florida so I have enough people to build my houses for our great people in Florida?”
Donalds wasn’t sympathetic, saying that, if elected governor, he would “have to comply with federal law.”
“That’s actually our constitutional requirement,” he said. “In politics, people are saying, ‘Well, governors can pick and choose how that’s going to be implemented.’ That’s actually not true. ICE is federal law enforcement. Not state law enforcement. Under the Constitution, every state has the responsibility to comply with federal law enforcement, because the states gave authority to the federal government for immigration and naturalization, deportation.”
He went on to say, “States don’t set immigration policy. The federal government does.”
A legal analyst counters that what Donalds said is inaccurate.
“There is no federal law that requires states and localities to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement, whether statutorily or constitutional,” said Kathrina Szymborski Wolfkot, senior counsel and manager in the Judiciary Program at the Brennan Center for Justice at the NYU School of Law. Whether local law enforcement agencies are going to cooperate with federal immigration laws is a question of state law, she added.
Florida’s on board
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a sweeping package of immigration laws aimed at carrying out President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda just weeks after Trump was inaugurated as president for a second time in January 2025.
It includes directives for Florida counties — but not municipalities — to enter into 287(g) agreements, which allow state and local authorities to work with federal immigration authorities. Before the legislation, 47 counties and the Department of Corrections had already executed agreements with ICE. The mandate expanded those agreements to all 67 Florida counties.
According to ICE, the agency has signed 2,660 memoranda of agreement for 287(g) programs covering 38 states and two territories.
The Trump administration has initiated an effort to crack down on local governments and states that don’t participate in its mass deportation campaign but has little to show for it. Since Trump returned to the White House last year, the Justice Department has filed lawsuits against more than a dozen Democratic-led states, counties, and cities, according to a CBS News review of court filings.
States like Oregon and Illinois adopted laws preventing law enforcement agencies from asking about or collecting information about immigration status.
“We have states that have passed state laws that forbid state and local officials from entering into 287(g) agreements or honoring immigration detainers, and everywhere that those have been challenged by the federal government the judges — including judges appointed by Donald Trump — have said, ‘No.’ States are completely within their rights under the federal Constitution to pass these laws,” Wolfko saidt.
Florida has the highest rate of requests for local jails to hold people for ICE after they’ve been picked up for another arrest this year, according to a study by the Prison Policy Initiative. It has the second-most detainer-related arrests in the country this year, behind only Texas.
Donalds’ Democratic opponent, David Jolly, has said if elected he would end the state mandate for counties to participate in 287(g) agreements.
What about cities?
There has been some dispute over whether the 2025 Florida legislation requires municipalities to enter into 287(g) agreements. The law says they do not. However, locally elected officials have been threatened by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier when they’ve considered rescinding agreements with ICE.
The city of South Miami filed suit against the DeSantis administration last year to determine whether municipal governments must participate. In oral arguments, the state’s attorneys argued cities aren’t explicitly required to enter agreement but can’t cancel them once in force.
Mathew Meskimen did not respond to the Phoenix’s request for comment but he’d prefaced his question by saying he is a lifelong Republican, “as conservative as it gets and a capitalist by nature.”
The National Association of Home Builders say the housing industry faces a severe labor shortage, with members reporting increased immigration enforcement and that work site raids are heightening worker fears. They cites government data indicating construction is by short about 300,000 workers.
Donalds acknowledged other states don’t look at immigration enforcement in the same way Florida or Texas does.
“We have leadership in other states that I quite frankly disagree with,” he said. “They’re not doing what their duty is under the Constitution.”

name: VTDigger
title: Turn Trump’s $90 payment into a campaign check
text:
Dear Editor,
Several acquaintances have told me they recently received $90 deposits in their checking accounts. They determined the money was sent under the authority of the president. 
Whether this was or is an attempt by President Donald Trump to buy people’s votes in the Nov. 3 election is something I don’t know. I do know I think it is a good idea that these acquaintances said they were donating their $90 to candidates of their choice.
I will check with my bank this week to see if I also received $90 from the president. I understand the payments are one-time Medicare premium rebates for eligible traditional Medicare enrollees. If the money is there, I believe it is legally my money, and I am free to use it as I wish. I am going to write a check in that amount and send it to a candidate of my choice. I encourage others to do the same.
Ross Connelly,Hardwick, Vt.

title: Michigan election officials say there is room for improvement in signature petition review process
text:
Members of the the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections hear testimony from Canvassers Chair Richard Houskamp, middle left, and Mary Ellen Gurewitz, the board’s vice-chair, center left, on the morning of Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan election officials defended the state’s previous review of ballot petitions and its decision-making processes during a special House committee meeting held Wednesday, but they also agreed with the committee’s Republican majority that some changes needed to be made to give petitioners more time in collecting and reviewing valid signature counts.
The conversation before the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections focused mostly on the board’s rules and rule-making process, which is handled by the Michigan Bureau of Elections, and how the body handles a random sampling process to check the validity of petition signatures collected by circulators — a process that has been in place since the 1970s.
But there was some discussion on the potential for the state to adopt and use advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, to do that work in the future, drawing some concerns from lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle.
Appearing before the committee were Richard Houskamp, the Republican chair of the Board of State Canvassers, Mary Ellen Gurewitz, the board’s Democratic vice-chair, and Jonathan Brater, the executive director of the Bureau of Elections.
The committee was formed after the American for Citizens Voting ballot measure, which would have required proof of citizenship before a person could cast a ballot, failed before the Board of State Canvassers earlier this year.
Mary Ellen Gurewitz, the vice chair of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers, gives testimony to the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections on the morning of Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
The Bureau of Elections had determined that its random sample showed the measure did not turn in a sufficient number of valid signatures to make the ballot, and the board deadlocked 2-2 on a decision to move it forward. The deadlocked vote meant that the petition could not be placed on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.
The move was controversial in part because of the partisan interests involved. Support for the proof-of-citizenship measure came mostly from the state’s Republicans, who felt slighted when an issue they cared deeply about in the 2026 cycle was rejected. Compounding the controversy was an earlier approval by the board of a ballot measure that seeks to eliminate the state’s regulated utilities from making political donations, a so-called progressive “money out of politics” initiative.
Organizers have said that they are now eyeing the 2028 cycle to revive the proof-of-citizenship measure.
Houskamp, Gurewitz and Brater each said that the processes they have in place work, and that sometimes popular petitions fail even though it appears that they have momentum from their respective political bases. 
In the case of the Americans for Citizens Voting, Houskamp said that the board “didn’t just do a block” of the measure that was highly coveted by the GOP; rather, the board listened to the attorneys involved with the petition and made a decision based in part on the bureau’s recommendations.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gurewitz noted, too, that the mechanism the canvassers use to determine whether a petition has valid signatures is guided by past judicial decision. She brought up the 2012 “Stand Up For Democracy” decision from the Michigan Supreme Court, which called for strict compliance of the rules set out in statute on everything from the typeface of the petition to its heading, down to the sufficiency of valid signature questions the canvassers and the bureau examine each election cycle.
Gurewitz said the strict compliance standard leads to decisions on petitions “which seem kind of harsh, possibly even irrational,” but the courts have ruled. While there have been attempts to switch to a substantial compliance standard, allowing more wiggle room on the rules in statute, Gurewitz said that law, which was passed during the 2024 lame duck session, was ultimately vetoed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. 
Officials acknowledge room for improvement
Fallout from another decision, Neilson v. Board of State Canvassers, a decision from 2024, further limited the number of days a person or a group has to issue affidavits or evidence that would help them keep signatures deemed invalid. The board, in the wake of the decision, adopted a rule that only gives those individuals or groups 48 hours before a hearing to submit evidence, and not after.
That said, each of the officials noted areas where there was room to improve.
Gurewitz noted the sampling procedure has been in effect for decades, and it’s the only way they have to evaluate signatures that come before the board. That procedure was changed recently to draw 1,000 signatures and evaluate a certain threshold of that separate universe of signatures. Gurewitz said she and Houskamp hope, as they are term limited, that the next group of leaders on the canvassers takes a look at that procedure and makes changes.
She also said that the strict compliance of the timelines and rules has given the canvassers a time-consuming and difficult task when it makes these decisions.
“Had substantial rather than strict compliance been in effect, I’m quite confident that this petition would be on the ballot, and we wouldn’t have had so much difficulty with MIMOP either,” Gurewitz said.
Brater also said there were changes to be made — including going back to a two-stage signature validation process, which Brater said would have been advantageous for Americans for Citizens Voting. The issue is, state law would need to be changed to give petitioners more time.
State Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township), the committee’s chair, agreed that those trying to change state law or the constitution through the ballot initiative process needed more time, whether that was in terms of deadlines or the 48-hour rule, out of fairness.
“I’m not blaming you, but I think there’s a problem when we disenfranchise 700-plus to 1,000 signatures over an argument over a handful, and it very easily could have been that way with MIMOP, too,” Harris said.
State Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township), chair of the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, speaks during a meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
AI proposal raises concerns about accuracy and oversight
Another solution that Houskamp and Gurewitz floated — letting AI do the verification and sampling work for the board — was met with some pushback from both a Democratic and a Republican member of the select committee, the latter a top member of the GOP caucus.
Gurewitz said the canvassers had talked “extensively” about the future intention to “use AI more effectively to review signatures and to further examine, as we have done in the past, what other states are doing with regard to ballot questions.”
She also noted that Houskamp has been urging, ever since he was placed on the board, to incorporate AI into the evaluation process for petitions. In response to a question from state Rep. Jason Woolford (R-Howell), Houskamp said an AI program could be devised to scan submitted petition sheets and evaluate them for validity and form.
There are no states currently using AI in this fashion, Houskamp said, and if Michigan considers it, the Great Lakes state would be there first.
“It would also look at every signature on that page, and it would have a backdoor to the state Qualified Voter File,” Houskamp said. “The application, the software I’m describing, would be an employee of the bureau to protect the QVF, and it would look at the QVF file, and it would evaluate that signature, and it would evaluate the address and the voter, and it would have all that information.”
When asked if it would eliminate the human in the equation, Houskamp said no.
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) listens to testimony during a House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
“We still have a thing that we have to work on there,” he said. “What it would get to is … that run could be done in literally a day, it could process massive, massive petitions in less than a week.”
The job of making a decision on whether those signatures pass muster would still be the job of the canvassers, he said.
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) had some immediate concerns over AI being involved.
“I don’t think it’s 100% accurate,” Xiong said. “Even technology requires humans to be properly trained to utilize it.”
State Rep. Ann Bollin (R-Brighton Township), a former township clerk and the chair of the House Appropriations Committee, echoed Xiong’s concern.
“AI is only as good as, really, the human confirmation of that information,” Bollin said.

title: Democrats aiming for control of Congress vow action on healthcare, cost of living, Iran war
authors: Shauneen Miranda, Ariana Figueroa, Ashley Murray, Jonathan Shorman
text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats are touting an ambitious legislative agenda centered on affordability and accountability if they take back the U.S. House or Senate — or both — in November. A slew of pressing policy debates are on tap for Democrats, including healthcare, immigration, voting rights, the war in Iran, oversight, education and beyond, as they aim to reverse many of President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans’ actions since January 2025. Some issues, while surging to the forefront, likely will provoke internal divisions, such as “Medicare for All,” a movement popular among progressives to extend single-payer national health care to all Americans. “Healthcare costs have consistently been at or above other concerns on the public's affordability worries,” said Liz Hamel, a senior vice president and director of public opinion and survey research at KFF who oversees the nonpartisan health organization’s polling program.Democrats also are poised to conduct tougher oversight of the Trump administration.

 






(Photo by Getty Images)

Any legislation from Democrats faces the threat of Trump’s veto, making any legislation without broad bipartisan support almost certain to fail. In addition, Democrats would need a filibuster-proof majority of 60 votes to advance most measures in the Senate.Democrats remain heavily favored to regain the majority in the House, while Senate races continue to move in the party’s favor, amid Trump’s plummeting popularity, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, an elections forecaster. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who generally vote with the party.“House Democrats are committed to fighting for an affordable America, lowering the high cost of living, lowering the cost of groceries, lowering the cost of gas, lowering the cost of housing and fighting to make healthcare affordable for every single American,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in September. The New York Democrat is in line to become the next speaker — the first Black person to hold that office — if the party clinches control of the lower chamber. Jeffries announced five working groups on affordability — housing, healthcare, gas and utilities, groceries and goods, and caregiving — which House Democrats will concentrate on at the beginning of the new Congress. The Democratic Party’s campaign apparatus for House races echoed an agenda centered on affordability. “House Democrats are going to win the majority because voters know we’re focused on lowering costs, and that’s exactly what we’re going to do when we’re in charge,” Nebeyatt Betre, a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson, said in a statement shared with States Newsroom.“From ending the war in Iran to lower gas prices, restoring (Affordable Care Act) tax credits to lower health care prices, to rolling back reckless tariffs to lower prices on everything in between, House Democrats’ number one priority will be making life more affordable for working families,” Betre said. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the corresponding campaign arm for Senate races, cited healthcare access and affordability as a top priority in a Democratic-led upper chamber. “I think the most important issues that I’ve heard from voters is restoring their healthcare, making sure that those cuts to Medicaid get restored, making sure that people can afford healthcare and get access to good, high-quality healthcare,” Gillibrand said in a September interview with States Newsroom and other members of the Regional Reporters Association. 

 







Dozens of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers, on July 17, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)

The New York Democrat, who leads the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said other major priorities include “trying to fix the problems Trump has created, end the war in Iran” as well as getting “costs of groceries, housing, and healthcare and other everyday costs down.” While not a major part of the party’s messaging in the general election, House Democrats are poised to take a harder line with Israel amid the country’s war in Gaza. Jeffries said a measure meant to discourage violence in the West Bank, where Israeli settlements have inflamed tensions, “should be considered” next year, according to The Hill. With less than three weeks to go until Election Day on Nov. 3, here’s a closer look at what Democrats want to accomplish in both chambers: Anti-corruption, impeachments Democrats are all but certain to open investigations into the Trump administration if they gain power over congressional subpoena decisions.“Our promise to the country in the new Congress is that beginning on Day One, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” Jeffries vowed at an Oct. 8 press conference. High-ranking Democratic House members say multiple probes are on the table, including Trump’s IRS settlement, brokered by his administration’s Justice Department, which delivered retroactive tax audit immunity for him and two of his sons as well as the creation of an “anti-weaponization” fund.A federal judge slammed the settlement in a July order prohibiting Trump, his sons Eric and Donald Trump Jr., and the Trump Organization from claiming they reached a “settlement,” and referred Trump’s personal attorneys to the bar for investigations. Democrats are also weighing whether the party would attempt to impeach Trump if they take back control of the House. The president was impeached twice in the House and acquitted twice in the Senate during prior sessions of Congress. Jeffries told PBS Newshour in September “we certainly haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out,” when asked about any impeachment proceedings against the president if Democrats regain the majority in the lower chamber. 

 







President Donald Trump headlines a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)

Democrats could also try to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if they clinch control of the House. Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September for the secretary’s handling of the war in Iran.But House GOP leadership sent the lower chamber home early for its weeks-long campaign break, punting any vote until after the midterms. House Democrats will also likely dog the administration’s legally mandated release of files related to the 2019 federal sex trafficking investigation of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, who kept the company of powerful and wealthy individuals, including Trump.Trump denies any knowledge of Epstein’s involvement in trafficking girls and young women for sex.Democrats and Republicans on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform opened a months-long probe, subpoenaing documents from the Epstein estate and compelling closed-door testimony from Epstein associates and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. Healthcare On the healthcare front, House Democrats want to undo the healthcare provisions tucked into a mega tax and spending cut law signed by Trump in July 2025, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”  “Undoing (that law) is the floor, but not the ceiling,” according to a September memo obtained by Politico from Democrats’ affordability working group on healthcare. The 84-page memo proposes myriad healthcare policy priorities in the first 100 hours, first 100 days and first year of the next session of Congress, broken down into eight wide-ranging categories. “There is broad consensus in the Democratic caucus that the Democratic agenda must both reverse the immediate harms of the administration while also taking bold action to rein in corporate monopolies, invest in a durable healthcare system, and pursue an ambitious path towards universal coverage,” per the memo.  

 







Hundreds of public workers rallied outside the Statehouse in Trenton, New Jersey, on June 18, 2026, to demand lawmakers rein in rising healthcare costs. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)

Part of Democrats’ healthcare agenda includes reversing the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law’s sweeping Medicaid cuts, which axe roughly $1 trillion in program spending over 10 years and impose new work requirements.The party is also looking to “permanently restore” the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, which expired in December 2025 and were used by individuals who buy their own health insurance through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace. The expiration of those credits has “sharply increased” individuals’ out-of-pocket costs toward premiums, according to KFF. The memo also underscores a commitment to “achieving universal coverage” in the first year of the next session of Congress, and mentions the “Medicare for All Act” as one avenue to examine in achieving this ambition. The bill would establish a national health insurance program administered under the Department of Health and Human Services. Iran warThe costly war in Iran that has caused prices at the gas pump to soar for Americans is a major reason for Trump’s sagging poll numbers, and Democrats, if the House and Senate flip, would likely pass a measure to try to end any further conflict without congressional approval.The war has cost $40 billion and counting, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, and will continue to cost American taxpayers $2 billion to $3 billion per month as the conflict drags on.The national average price of diesel remains above $6 per gallon in the U.S., according to AAA, as Iranian officials continue to block petroleum products from reaching the global market. The national motor club, which monitors daily fuel prices, reported that Americans were paying a national average of $4.33 for a gallon of gasoline as of Oct. 14.

 






Gas and diesel prices at a station in Silver Spring, Maryland, on Oct. 12, 2026. (States Newsroom photo)

Meanwhile, Democrats’ attempts to rein in Trump’s military campaign in Iran have slowly picked up some Republican support over multiple votes in both chambers.Senate Democrats have forced 14 War Powers Resolution votes to curb Trump’s unilateral military decisions without input from Congress. The votes are privileged, meaning they can be brought to the floor without the blessing of majority leadership.The measure has advanced twice in the upper chamber, but the latest attempt to advance a House-passed War Powers Resolution narrowly failed, 49-50. House Democrats picked up seven Republicans on Sept. 15 to approve the War Powers Resolution. Administration officials contend the War Powers Resolution, established by Congress during the Vietnam War era, is unconstitutional, so it’s unclear what might happen if a resolution were approved. Immigration To help the president carry out his mass deportation campaign, congressional Republicans used a legislative tool to skirt Democratic support and allocate more than $200 billion for immigration enforcement through two measures. With the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” more than $170 billion was given to the Department of Homeland Security to hire more immigration agents, expand detention centers and carry out deportations. The “Secure America Act” funded Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement until late September 2029, at nearly $70 billion, after Democrats refused to approve funding for DHS following two deadly shootings of American citizens by immigration officials in Minneapolis. Though it’s unlikely Democrats will be able to claw any of that funding back even if they take both chambers, there are several avenues they are likely to pursue amid the president’s immigration crackdown. The first avenue is oversight and the ability to subpoena Trump officials. Democrats are likely to hold oversight hearings into the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed by federal immigration officials in Minneapolis in January. Members of both parties on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee reached rare bipartisan agreement at a grilling of top Trump immigration officials after the killings. Democrats will also likely hold hearings on the scores of U.S. citizens detained by ICE and also shot by federal immigration officers, such as Marimar Martinez, who has already appeared several times before lawmakers as the minority witness for Democrats. She was shot in her car five times by Border Patrol agents during the aggressive immigration deportation campaign in Chicago in October 2025 and was labeled a domestic terrorist by DHS. The DOJ dropped charges against Martinez after the Trump administration accused her of using her car as a weapon.

 







Bypassers stop by a memorial to Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the Biddeford, Maine resident and father who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)

Democrats are also likely to continue with oversight at federal facilities that detain immigrants, including the high death toll of immigrants at those detention centers. So far, 61 immigrants have died in ICE detention, which has doubled under the second Trump administration. Democrats have demanded answers from the administration about the deaths, along with concerns about medical neglect at the facilities. And even though former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem stepped down earlier this year, Democrats still plan to question some of her decisions while leading DHS, such as a $220 million ad campaign that prominently featured her and the practice of no-bid contracts awarded to her close allies. Apart from oversight, Democrats are likely to introduce and pass legislation related to immigration reform, such as creating a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who were stripped of their Temporary Protected Status and for children brought into the country without legal authorization under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA. The Trump administration has stripped more than 1 million immigrants of their legal status, and House Democrats, with a handful of Republicans, in April moved to extend TPS for more than 500,000 immigrants hailing from Haiti. TPS is granted to nationals who hail from a country deemed too dangerous to return to due to violence, disasters or other destabilizing forces.In the Senate, Democrats have tried to pass legislation through unanimous consent to grant a pathway to citizenship for TPS recipients, but were blocked by Republicans. If Democrats regain the Senate, they will need a 60-vote majority for that legislation to move ahead. Some Democrats in Congress also likely will advocate an end to funding for ICE, but it’s unclear whether that would have enough support to advance.Voting rights and democracyVoting rights and democracy are likely to be high priorities for Democrats if they retake one or both chambers of Congress. A gerrymandering war egged on by Trump and a U.S. Supreme Court decision this spring that severely weakened the federal Voting Rights Act left Democrats and their base deeply angry and eager for action.Democrats are likely to again turn to the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, named after the late civil rights activist and Georgia Democratic Rep. John Lewis. Though the U.S. House last passed the measure in 2021, the bill did not advance through the Senate. The legislation would seek to restore preclearance, a major provision of the Voting Rights Act that was previously blocked by the Supreme Court in 2013. Preclearance required states and local governments with a history of discrimination to obtain federal permission before making voting changes, and it applied to most Southern states and a handful of others.

 







A woman raises a fist as protesters march on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama as part of the All Roads Lead to the South rally on May 16, 2026. The two rallies, protests against redistricting efforts by southern Republicans, drew over 5,000 people. (Photo by Andi Rice/Alabama Reflector)

“We fight to pass the John Robert Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act so we can end the era of voter suppression in the United States of America once and for all,” Jeffries said in an August speech.The renewed focus on the voting rights legislation comes after the Supreme Court in a 6-3 decision in April sharply weakened Section 2 of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. The section prohibits voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race and other characteristics. In 1982, Congress expanded Section 2 to ban voting practices that have a discriminatory effect, whether or not the law was intended to discriminate.Louisiana had redrawn its congressional map in response to a court order to include a second majority-minority district where a majority of residents are Black. The Supreme Court ruled the new map was an unconstitutional gerrymander.In response, several Southern states quickly redrew their congressional maps to eliminate majority-minority districts — part of a larger wave of gerrymandering that swept the country over the past two years after Trump initially urged Texas to enact a more GOP-friendly map.In response, some Democrats are also pushing for gerrymandering reform. At a minimum, some lawmakers want to require states to return to a once-a-decade redrawing process. That was the norm before 2025, and followed the census every 10 years.Over the summer, the bipartisan House Problem Solvers Caucus unveiled a framework for changes to the redistricting process. The proposal calls for restricting new maps to once a decade, requiring “clear, objective” criteria to draw lines and supporting steps to reduce partisan influence, such as turning to independent commissions to develop district lines.Education Congressional Democrats also want to halt and undo the administration’s ongoing efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education and repeal major education provisions in the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law.The department has entered into a series of interagency agreements with other departments that transfer several of its responsibilities to those agencies, including Health and Human Services, Labor, Interior, State, Justice and Treasury. If Democrats take back the Senate, Virginia Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine told States Newsroom his first goal in education is to “stop the handoff of critical components of (the Education Department) to other agencies that don’t want them.”In the most-far reaching of the interagency agreements yet, the department said in June that HHS would administer programs under Education’s Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, while civil rights enforcement under Education’s Office for Civil Rights would be transferred to the DOJ. 

 







From left, Olivia Sawyer and Jeremy Bauer-Wolf protest the U.S. Education Department’s mass layoffs during a "honk-a-thon" and rally March 14, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)

Kaine sponsored a bill, with GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska as original co-sponsors, that would block interagency agreements that transfer programs regarding special education, elementary and secondary education, postsecondary education and Native American education. That measure advanced out of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions in July. Sen. Mazie Hirono told States Newsroom “we need to restore federal support for education and how it’s going to look, I mean, clearly we need to support IDEA and support it to a greater extent than we have normally,” pointing to the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which guarantees a free public education for students with disabilities.The Hawaii Democrat is also looking to repeal a national school voucher program baked into the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law that’s set to launch in early 2027. The program allocates up to $1,700 in federal tax credits for people donating to organizations that provide K-12 scholarships, with 31 states having opted in so far. Hirono and Arizona Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, joined by more than two dozen of their colleagues, introduced legislation in April to repeal the program. Wisconsin Democratic Rep. Gwen Moore introduced a companion bill in June with Reps. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, Maxwell Frost of Florida, Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin and dozens more original cosponsors.

title: Trump’s DOJ demands California halt ballots to suspected noncitizens
text: The U.S. Department of Justice is demanding California not count ballots from voters it says are suspected noncitizens, a move by the Trump administration to apply last-minute pressure as voting begins in the midterm elections.The Justice Department on Tuesday gave California election officials 48 hours to remove voters on a list contained on a thumb drive provided to Los Angeles County, the most populous county in the country. The DOJ also wants election officials to withhold mail ballots from these voters. The demand appeared in letters to the California Secretary of State’s Office and the Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk. The DOJ gave the state until noon Eastern on Thursday to comply, threatening legal action if that deadline is not met.The letters set the stage for a courtroom confrontation between the Trump administration and the largest state in the country ahead of Election Day. The Justice Department’s demand marks an extraordinary effort to dictate to state officials who will be allowed to cast a ballot even as voting is underway.“The United States hopes that you share our commitment to ensure that only American citizens participate in our federal elections. Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” R. Trent McCotter, an acting deputy U.S. attorney general, wrote in a letter to California Democratic Secretary of State Shirley Weber.Questions lingerIt’s not clear whether the Justice Department plans to send letters to additional states. The Justice Department provided copies of the letters to States Newsroom on Wednesday but didn’t answer a question about whether other states would receive them.In the letters, McCotter asked California election officials to segregate the mail ballots of the suspected noncitizens until their citizenship status is determined. The individuals shouldn’t be sent mail ballots if they haven’t already been sent one, McCotter added, and any returned ballots should not be tabulated until citizenship can be determined.McCotter did not say how many individuals are on the DOJ’s list or how the federal government came to believe they aren’t citizens. He wrote that the Justice Department would “seek emergency relief” if California didn’t comply. Requests for comment to Weber’s office and the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk weren’t immediately returned. A request for comment to California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office was referred to the California secretary of state’s office.Voter roll changes prohibited during election seasonFederal law prohibits most states from conducting systematic purges of voters less than 90 days before an election. If the Justice Department sues to force California to remove the suspected noncitizen voters, a judge would likely grapple with whether the DOJ-provided list represents the kind of mass removal that’s not currently allowed.Voting rights groups and Democratic election officials, as well as some Republicans, have warned that Trump may try to interfere in the midterm elections. If Republicans retake control of the U.S. House or Senate, the final two years of the president’s term could be mired in investigations and legislative gridlock.Federal courts have uniformly blocked the department’s efforts to force states to turn over their voter rolls, including sensitive personal information such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. And a federal judge last week ruled against the DOJ’s use of voter data even from states that voluntarily provided the information.The U.S. Supreme Court also blocked Trump’s attempt to restrict voting by mail through the U.S. Postal Service, leaving the president with few remaining avenues to assert authority over elections, which are administered by the states under the U.S. Constitution.“Donald Trump’s attempt to invalidate votes in California is an attack on every voter across the country. The president is abusing his position in a callous attempt to take away the power of everyday people, but here in California we’re not going to let him,” Jonathan Paik, a leader with Can’t Stop California, a nonpartisan voter mobilization group, said in a statement.Trump has long complained about California elections, especially the speed of ballot counting in the state. California’s long count is a well-known feature of its elections, with election officials given about a month to process and tally all ballots and doesn’t indicate fraud.The Justice Department has followed Trump’s lead in scrutinizing California’s elections. The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles has linked suspicions about California’s elections to the state’s refusal to turn over its unredacted voter roll.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State office building to reopen after multi-year, $70M renovation
text:
The Jim Thorpe Building is pictured on the Oklahoma Capitol Complex on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — After three years and $70 million of renovations, state leaders announced Wednesday that the Jim Thorpe Office Building on the Oklahoma State Capitol Complex is reopening. 
The Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state Election Board, the Oklahoma Arts Council and the Oklahoma Water Resources Board will occupy the building and lease space from the Office of Management and Enterprise Services. 
The building, located southeast of the Capitol at 2101 N. Lincoln Blvd., was renovated with funds appropriated in 2023. 
Mark Wood, director of OMES, said the project was focused on preserving what makes the Jim Thorpe building special while creating an accessible and functional government workplace.  
Mark Wood, director of the Office of Management and Enterprise Services, speaks about the reopening of the Jim Thorpe Office Building on the Oklahoma Capitol Complex on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
“Jim Thorpe’s name carries a remarkable legacy in Oklahoma,” he said. “… We hope this building continues to be a place worthy of his name and the example he left for future generations of Oklahomans and Americans.”
Thorpe, a Native American of Sac and Fox and Potawatomi descent, was a highly successful Oklahoma athlete who competed in the Olympics and played both professional baseball and football. 
Thorpe died in 1953, but some of his descendants were in attendance at Wednesday’s ribbon cutting ceremony. 
Budget chair Sen. Chuck Hall, R-Perry, said while it’s easy to focus on new ideas and projects in government, it’s also important to preserve what’s already been built. 
“We must balance investing in Oklahoma’s essential infrastructure with being responsible stewards of taxpayer dollars,” he said. “We also have a responsibility to preserve the places that tell Oklahoma’s storied history and pay tribute to Oklahoma legends, while ensuring our residents continue to benefit from the state assets that they paid for.”
Hall said the tenants of the building will use it to serve Oklahomans every day which makes it a worthwhile investment. 
“This building is going back to work,” he said. 
Bonnie Campo, director of outreach for OMES, said some finishing touches need to be completed, such as furnishing offices, before the building’s tenants move in. Agencies are expected to move in this winter, she said. 
Paul Ziriax, election board secretary, said their agency will maintain its public-facing offices at the Capitol and use space at Jim Thorpe for some administrative functions. 
New artwork was commissioned by the Oklahoma Arts Council through the state’s public art program, according to a news release.
