name: Kansas Reflector
title: Hays foundation pledges $1 million in matching funds to help save Sternberg museum
text:
A foundation is pledging $1 million to match donations for preservation of Fort Hays State University's Sternberg Museum of Natural History. FHSU president Tisa Mason says the museum may close in wake of a $2.4 million state budget cut. In this image from Oct. 29, 2024, Mason is interviewed by Kansas Reflector in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A private foundation offered to match contributions dollar-for-dollar up to $1 million for benefit of the financially struggling Sternberg Museum of Natural History at Fort Hays State University.
In September, FHSU said the museum and its three million geology, zoology and paleontology specimens would close to the public in December. Officials said the decision was tied to the 2026 Kansas Legislature’s $2.4 million reduction in state appropriations to the university in western Kansas. Closure of the museum would save FHSU an estimated $850,000 annually.
FHSU president Tisa Mason didn’t sugarcoat what it would take to save the museum. She said the university required infusion of $1 million in new revenue each year.
“Not once, but annually, in perpetuity,” she said. “This is a recurring cost, and it will not be solved by a one-time gift, a single fundraiser or any single event.”
On Tuesday, trustees of the Bob and Pat Schmidt Foundation committed a maximum of $1 million to incentivize contributions to the FHSU Foundation’s Save Sternberg campaign. The Hays foundation was created by the family of Bob Schmidt, who was in the radio business. He was owner of what became Eagle Communications, which operates in Kansas, Nebraska and Minnesota. Eventually, the company was purchased by its employees.
“The Sternberg Museum is vital to Fort Hays State University, our community, our state and anyone seeking to understand our region’s remarkable history,” said Gary Shorman, president of the Bob and Pat Schmidt Foundation. “This gift is intended to bridge short-term funding needs while a sustainable, long-term operating plan is developed for the Sternberg Museum.”
The Schmidts, who shared an appreciation for FHSU, believed the foundation should invest in community-building projects.
Mason proposed the FHSU Foundation set a goal of securing $1 million in private gifts by Dec. 31 through the Save Sternberg campaign. So far, $237,000 has been contributed to the museum campaign.
“We are humbled by the outpouring of generosity from those who believe in the Sternberg Museum and are stepping forward to help secure its future,” said Jason Williby, president and CEO of the FHSU Foundation.
Individual and business donations to the museum fund would qualify for the match, but gifts from other foundations wouldn’t be eligible for the incentive.
The Sternberg Museum, which documents life in the Great Plains region, began taking shape in the early 1900s.
FHSU said the museum wasn’t financially sustainable with average annual expenditures of $1.3 million and annual revenue of $470,000.
FHSU’s president said the university couldn’t “absorb repeated, deep legislative reductions and simultaneously preserve everything our community values.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: How to talk about AIPAC without fueling antisemitism
text:
A visitor holds an AIPAC folder in an elevator in Rayburn House Office Building on March 12, 2024 on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Nothing is more important for Jewish safety here in Michigan and across the United States than a robust, healthy democracy. Yet, we have unlimited dark money flooding the airwaves with political ads, thanks to a Supreme Court that prioritizes corporations over people.
As the leader of a national American Jewish organization with many members in the State of Michigan, fighting for free, fair, and just elections is my top priority this year. It is critical that the public knows who is spending millions of dollars to elect and curry favor with our future elected officials, and focusing on those big spenders is fair game, especially during the hotly contested primary and general election cycles for the open Senate seat.
Recent polling reveals that more than half of Michiganders have an unfavorable view of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), and rightfully so. As folks across the state continue to engage in these conversations, I’m hoping to offer advice on how to talk about AIPAC in meaningful and thoughtful ways, without inadvertently fueling antisemitism.
One of the biggest of those spenders is the AIPAC, a lobbying group and political action committee that works to strengthen the U.S.–Israel relationship. For decades, they never endorsed candidates—until 2022, when AIPAC launched a PAC, coming out of the gate by endorsing 109 January 6th insurrectionists. Since then, their strategy has been to funnel Republican dark money into Democratic primaries, using shell PACs, SuperPACs, and bundled donations, often without mentioning Israel or Palestine at all.
That strategy has defined this year’s primary season, with AIPAC’s main super PAC United Democracy Project spending record-breaking sums trying to defeat progressives, and it will continue to be a point of contention heading into the midterms.
But the way we talk about a big spender like AIPAC can have a meaningful impact on the safety of American Jews. It is critical to get this right, and to support our movement in keeping our focus and our rhetoric on the right track, I want to offer a few guidelines I urge progressives to adhere to.
Which brings me to my first recommendation: Do not talk about AIPAC like it is a Jewish organization because it is not. AIPAC does not represent the majority of American Jews, and in fact, most American Jews oppose its core priority: advocating for unconditional support, partnership and aid to Israel. AIPAC doesn’t even claim to be a Jewish organization—because they’re not. It is critical to never conflate AIPAC with Jews.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Like lots of unpopular organizations, from the gun lobby to crypto and AI, AIPAC can’t win on its own issue. AIPAC’s actual policy positions are deeply unpopular, especially among Democrats and Jewish voters. Over 90% of American Jews believe you can criticize the Israeli government and still be “pro-Israel,” and 70% of American Jews believe “criticizing Israel for any reason” is not a form of antisemitism. AIPAC’s strategy relies on obfuscation because it can’t win on the merits. Acknowledge this when you talk about AIPAC and your policy positions.
Second, avoid fueling antisemitic tropes when talking about AIPAC. Criticism of AIPAC can be weaponized as antisemitism. Be vigilant against framing that mirrors antisemitic tropes about Jewish “outside influence,” wealth, “puppet-mastery” or “dual loyalty.” Even though AIPAC is not a Jewish organization, attacks on it are too often extrapolated into attacks on all Jews.
Third, and because of number two above, precision in your language matters. Always specify when you’re talking about the “Israeli government,” the “State of Israel,” or the “Israeli military,” and never use “Israel” as shorthand. Avoid undefined terms like “pro-Israel,” “Zionist,” or “anti-Zionist,” and never use “Zionists” or “Zios” as a stand-in for “Jews.” These terms mean lots of different things to different people, and clarity and specificity is key.
Relatedly, fourth, use facts—not euphemisms—when talking about AIPAC’s involvement in campaigns. Frame them alongside other dark money (e.g. oil, crypto, AI) and call for campaign finance reform. Exaggerating AIPAC’s influence to make it appear more powerful than any comparable dark money group, or using terms like the “Israel lobby,” “Zionist lobby,” or “Jewish lobby,” can fall into some of the antisemitic tropes I mentioned above.
Fifth: resist the urge to ally or find common cause with the MAGA anti-AIPAC Right. There are some MAGA figures like Tucker Carlson or Marjorie Taylor Green who regularly criticize AIPAC and others with Israeli government ties, but the distinction is that their critique is rooted in xenophobia and Christian Nationalism, not solidarity. There is sometimes an urge when looking at unlikely bedfellows in politics to say “well, you gotta give it to them.” Under no circumstances do you have to give it to them. Don’t give credit to or ally with Christian nationalists and fascists.
Finally, it is critical that progressive leaders and movements make space for Jews and build fluency in fighting antisemitism. Build authentic relationships with your Jewish neighbors and include Jewish organizations in your coalitions. Use resources like those found at DismantlingAntisemitism.org. Including Jewish people in your vision for the future is an important step toward building the multiracial, multiethnic democratic society of our dreams and to thwarting the aims of groups like AIPAC and undermining the right’s intentional strategy of division.
We the people have a right to know—and raise concern about—who is funding our elected officials’ campaigns. But the way we do it matters. Progressives should be able to challenge powerful political organizations, debate U.S. policy toward the State of Israel without fear, and make space in our coalitions for Michigan Jews. Together, we can build a true multiracial democracy where all can thrive.

name: Nevada Current
title: Trump administration blocks maintenance funding for Nevada national parks
text:
The Desert Research Institute faced the largest single-project financial loss in the state and across the country, losing around $3.4 million for mapping of unapproved roads in the Lake Mead National Recreation Area and the survey of nearby buried cultural resources exposed by falling lake levels. (Photo: NPS/Lake Mead National Recreation Area/Andrew Cattoir)The Trump administration has blocked millions of dollars in federal funding for numerous projects in Nevada’s national parks which would have supported everything from long-term weather stations and road mapping to wildlife monitoring and cultural resource preservation. 
In August, the U.S. Department of the Interior canceled eight contracts for projects in Nevada and downgraded four additional projects across the state to “low priority status,” putting at least $4.4 million in previously secured funding on hold, according to the nonpartisan conservation group Center for Western Priorities.
The blocked agreements would have paid outside organizations for specialized environmental and cultural resource work in Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument, the Lake Mead National Recreation Area, and the Mojave Desert. 
The conservation group pulled records from an internal National Park Service database and published them in an interactive map that contains details for each of the canceled or downgraded projects. 
Nationally, the Trump administration blocked more than 130 agreements and downgraded roughly 1,500 projects across the country, pulling nearly $26 million in funding. The blocked projects had already obtained funding, largely through congressional appropriations and existing federal programs.
Neither the Department of the Interior nor the National Park Service immediately responded to Nevada Current’s requests for comment.
The Great Basin Institute, a Reno-based conservation nonprofit, accounted for more than 70 of the blocked agreements nationally, amounting to $12.7 million in funding. In Nevada, the nonprofit accounted for all but two of the canceled contracts.  
The Desert Research Institute faced the largest single-project financial loss in the state and across the country, losing around $3.4 million in federal funds. Those funds would have supported the mapping of unapproved roads in the Lake Mead National Recreation Area and the survey of nearby buried cultural resources exposed by falling lake levels. 
The survey would have helped determine the damage to buried cultural resources by unapproved roads and identified potential areas where new approved roads could be developed without further damaging significant cultural resources. 
Funding for the operation and maintenance of long-term weather stations that provide essential, real-time climate data for Mojave Desert parks was also blocked. The Desert Research Institute said that without the funding “real-time updates would be less accurate, putting staff, visitors, and surrounding communities at greater risk during extreme weather events.”
The next largest loss of funding for Nevada’s state parks was a roughly $345,000 project headed by the Great Basin Institute that would have collected long-term ecological data on wildlife, vegetation, and hydrology in the Mojave Desert.
Funding would have paid for a bat specialist to conduct surveys and manage data, and two ecological technicians to monitor vegetation and desert springs. Project managers noted that without the funding vital conservation efforts would halt and jeopardize the health of desert ecosystems. 
Several projects at the Lake Mead National Recreation Area were downgraded to “low priority” status, including a flash flood warning system, safety lights, and restroom maintenance. 
Flash floods during monsoon season remain a critical issue at the Lake Mead National Recreation Area. Funding for the project would have provided for annual maintenance on the alarm system at Cottonwood Cove and Willow Beach that detects incoming floods and plays a recorded warning telling people to leave.
Great Basin National Park also saw funding blocked for a project to restore native trout habitat, ranger fishing programs, backcountry patrol, and thinning to reduce wildfire risks.

name: California
title: Dozens of California dams need repair as El Niño winter draws closer
text:
With an El Niño winter threatening heavy rain, the State Auditor warns that California’s aging dams “continue to pose a risk to public safety,” especially in the Bay Area, San Diego, and Los Angeles areas. 
Lawmakers gave the state the power to penalize dam owners that violate safety requirements  in 2017, after the Oroville spillway failure forced the evacuation of nearly 200,000 people. Water managers have yet to use that power, the audit found.
Even if state water managers had wielded their enforcement powers, dam owners likely couldn’t have afforded the fixes. 
An audit released Monday found 57 dams in poor or unsatisfactory condition as of May, up from previous counts. That number is likely to keep rising, as state water officials reevaluate aging dams. 
The 40 riskiest dams — rated high or extremely high hazard — are located throughout the state, but cluster near densely populated coastal cities. 
Should these dams fail, the auditor reported, “they could collectively endanger as many as 1.5 million people and cause more than $265 billion in economic damage.” 
Almost a decade ago, lawmakers strengthened the California Department of Water Resources’ authority to impose penalties such as reservoir restrictions, property liens, and fines when dam owners violate state safety laws and other requirements. 
State engineers have referred owners of 44 dams for enforcement as of April. But, the auditor wrote, the water resources department “has never taken punitive enforcement actions against dam owners that fail to remedy their violations.” 
Aging dams, limited funds
The problem is that dams are getting older. Many were built when safety standards were softer. State laws never required dam owners to set aside funds to keep them safe, so when concrete crumbles, sediment accumulates and spillways threaten to erode under floodwaters, most dam owners lack the money for repairs. 
The state’s water resources department oversees the safety of more than 1,220 dams, most of them in satisfactory condition. Responsibility for maintaining the dams falls to the local governments, utilities, water agencies, and the private landowners and companies that own them. Some of the dams rated in poor condition are owned by state agencies. 
Disasters are extremely rare. But when they do occur, like in Oroville, or the 1928 collapse of nearly-new St. Francis dam northwest of Los Angeles — they can be catastrophic. 
San Diego’s Lake Hodges Dam under repair in fall of 2022.  The dam is expected to be replaced in the next decade. The dam, built as a multiple arch design, was completed in 1918, and purchased by the City of San Diego in 1925. Photo courtesy of John Gastaldo
The auditor applauded the water resources department’s inspection program but blasted its failure to enforce against dam owners who fail to meet state planning, safety or other requirements, “thereby allowing serious deficiencies to persist.” 
One of the cases involved a dam with a 47-foot-wide hole in its spillway that has gone unrepaired for more than 30 years, which the audit said could cause flooding affecting nearly 300 people and more than $88 million in damage. 
The audit doesn’t name the dam. State water managers said more specifics could pose security concerns, though the department makes each dam’s hazard potential and condition public in an annual report. 
State water managers finalized the enforcement regulations in 2022. But they told the auditor they haven’t been able to adequately staff an enforcement branch and aren’t confident they could afford to defend their actions in a hearing. 
Even with staff and money, the auditor concludes, if a dam owner remained noncompliant, the state “cannot act before the dam poses emergency-level danger. This leaves a gap in state law that puts public safety at risk.” 
Drop in the bucket
Gov. Gavin Newsom touted dam repairs in his drought-era water supply strategy four years ago, as a way to shore up water supplies. Two years later, in 2024, Newsom and lawmakers slashed funding for a dam repair grant program.  
Since then, a 2024 ballot proposition delivered a $464 million infusion for the program. A Federal Emergency Management Agency grant also awarded California $629,198 this September, according to Jason Ince, a spokesperson for the Department of Water Resources 
But the audit cited estimates that repairing the state’s less-than-satisfactory dams could cost around $28 billion, making the funding a drop in the bucket. 
The report urged state lawmakers to set deadlines and require dam owners with high and extremely high hazard dams — meaning ones that could kill people if they fail — to submit maintenance and repair plans to state agencies. 
It also called for lawmakers to expand state water managers’ enforcement authority, and for the agency to use the full force of its powers.
“To ensure that the safety of the public is addressed before a dam’s condition results in an emergency,” the audit said, “the Legislature should amend state law to allow Water Resources to order the condemnation and decommissioning of a dam when Water Resources’ other means of enforcement are unsuccessful.” 
Laura Hollender, deputy director of flood management and safety with the Department of Water Resources said that the department worked closely with the State Auditor but disagrees with some of the report’s findings and recommendations. 
Still, she said in a statement, they are carefully reviewing the recommendations and preparing for whatever El Niño brings. “Protecting public safety is DWR’s highest priority, and we recognize the critical role that dam safety and levee maintenance play in reducing flood risk for California communities.” 
As the wet season approaches, the auditor also highlighted that dam safety planning statewide is incomplete. 
The Governor’s Office of Emergency Service has not yet approved emergency plans for 245 dams describing what their owners would do to protect people and property should the dam fail. Officials told the auditor’s office that dam owners haven’t completed required revisions, and state law doesn’t require deadlines.

name: California
title: Prop 38 asks: Should California take on more debt to fund a single field of medical research?
text:
Three decades ago, as the 20th century was winding down, a culture war erupted over the use of human embryos in researching stem cell cures for dreaded diseases.
It was a subset of the nation’s never-ending conflict over abortion. After Republican George W. Bush won the presidency in 2020 his administration barred the use of embryos in genetic research, a policy President Barack Obama later revoked.
In 2004, Robert Klein, a wealthy Bay Area real estate developer whose son suffered from Type 1 diabetes, launched a campaign to stimulate genetic research in California that didn’t rely on federal funds.
Actors Michael J. Fox and Christopher Reeve, who were dealing with their own chronic medical conditions, starred in ads promoting Proposition 71, a 2004 ballot measure creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine. The measure also authorized $3 billion in bonds that the new state agency would distribute to research projects.
Klein contributed heavily to the Prop. 71 campaign, raised money from others and served as the first chairman of the agency’s board. The campaign’s pitch to voters was not only that dread diseases would be cured but that California would reap the economic benefits of taking the lead.
Voters endorsed the measure over the opposition of religious anti-abortion groups, and the agency began awarding grants to researchers, many of whom had ties to members of the new agency’s board of directors.
Over the ensuing years it has touted several successes, but there has been no independent analysis of results. As the initial $3 billion was running out, advocates wrote a 2020 ballot measure, Proposition 14, that authorized another $5.5 billion in bonds. It won voter approval.
Now the willingness of California voters to again float bonds for medical research underlies Proposition 38 on the Nov. 3 ballot. And it raises questions about whether its sponsors would have the inside track for its $8.4 billion in proposed bond money.
CalMatters delved into the very specific language of the measure and determined that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, founded and headed by billionaire Gary Michelson, would be the only organization that would qualify for half of the money. Michelson is one of the major backers of Prop. 38.
The other half of the bond issue would be distributed as grants to research applicants by a new council selected by representatives of seven University of California campuses, and each grant recipient will be linked to a member of the council. 
At this juncture, it’s important voters understand something about state general obligation bonds: They are not free money, even if sponsors often imply that they are. Bonds are loans from banks and other investors and, like all loans, must be repaid with interest.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office has estimated the state budget would have to appropriate about $500 million a year for 25 years to service Prop. 38’s bonds, or about $12.5 billion total. Bond repayments have the highest legal priority in the budget, so they displace funds that could otherwise be spent on education, healthcare or other services.
Issuing bonds to support one avenue of medical research is a questionable activity regardless of cost. If the state has a legitimate role to play in such research, all potential fields should be explored, not merely pet projects and organizations that some billionaire patrons have chosen to the exclusion of others.
Nevertheless, immunology is not the last field that voters will be asked to support.
Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed new legislation, Senate Bill 895, that creates another new agency to award scientific research grants, the California Foundation for Science and Health Research. The measure places a $7.5 billion bond issue on the 2028 ballot to provide the new foundation with funds to distribute.

name: California
title: As beloved craft breweries close around the state, beer lovers wonder what’s next
text:
In summary
Changing consumer tastes, market saturation and rising costs from tariffs has forced the closure of some of the most beloved craft breweries in California. 


To the dozen regular customers sipping the final ales and lagers at Prohibition Brewing Company in Vista on a recent Friday night, it not only marks the end of an era, but also raises questions about the future of craft beer.
“There’s a sense of loss. It’s like when ‘Cheers’ closed in the last episode,” said Vista resident Greg Johnson, in a nod to the 1980s sitcom about a neighborhood bar, “where everybody knows your name.” 
Prohibition will shut its doors this month after the last kegs are drained, making it one of several high-profile brewery closures in San Diego, a region that pioneered the craft brew industry.
Japanese beer-maker Sapporo is selling Stone Brewing, which it acquired in 2022. To the dismay of North County beer lovers, it’s closing the brand’s flagship site in Escondido, Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens, with its sprawling complex of terraces and gardens.
“That place was so unique,” one Stone fan wrote on Facebook. “A place to take out of town guests. A place of Escondido pride.”
“We are devastated by losing this part of our community,” another wrote. 
In August, the 19-year-old Mission Brewing in East Village shuttered its tasting room at the historic, brick Wonder Bread building near Petco Park. At the end of last year Ballast Point Brewing closed its 600-seat bar and restaurant in San Diego’s Miramar district.
Brewers and customers are divided on whether the changes represent the leveling of a mature industry, or a bad omen for San Diego’s beer scene.
“Any explosion we’ve seen is going to flatten out, and that’s what we’re doing now,” said Erik Fowler, a local brewer and former executive director of the San Diego Brewers Guild. “San Diego takes such pride in its brewing industry that when Stone shifts its operations, there’s a very visceral reaction.”
Other landmark California breweries are also closing up shop; Triple Rock Brewery in Berkeley is shutting its doors after 40 years of making beer, the award-winning Lost Coast Brewery in Eureka is auctioning off its equipment as its founder retires after 36 years. And the towering Angel City Brewery near downtown Los Angeles closed in April.
Declines in craft beer
The suite of closures is part of a downward trend for breweries across the state and nation, driven by market saturation, changing consumer tastes and rising costs. 
Nationwide, the number of craft breweries fell 3.5% between 2024 and 2025, craft beer production dropped 3.8%, and production of all beers declined 5.7%, according to the Brewers Association, a national trade organization. In California, the number of craft breweries fell 5% between 2023 and 2025, from 987 to 939. 
But that’s not the most alarming news, said Matt Gacioch, economist for the Brewers Association.
“The big change from a few years ago is not a huge jump in breweries closing,” he said. “What’s changed is the number of breweries opening is going way, way down.”
From left, Kyle Adams, general manager of Prohibition Brewing Company, serves a beer to longtime customer Jodi Spears at Prohibition Brewing Company in Vista on Sept. 30, 2026. The brewery will soon close its doors after 15 years in business. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters 
That dropoff reflects the economics of craft beer production. Steep U.S. tariffs have raised the price of imported aluminum and steel, which American breweries need for cans and equipment. In response, most Canadian provinces have banned or restricted American alcohol, so beer imports to Canada have plunged 90%, Gacioch said.
Mercurial trade war politics make it hard for brewers to know whether tariffs are on or off, and what current tariff rates are, said Kelsey McQuaid-Craig, executive director of the California Craft Brewers Association: “There’s just so much volatility that people can’t plan ahead.”
Changes to the beer industry also mirror shifts in drinking habits. Younger Americans, particularly Gen Z, drink less alcohol than previous generations, or prefer beverages such as canned cocktails or hard seltzers.
Most poignantly, declines in craft brewing reflects Californians’ conflicted impulses toward community gatherings versus screen-focused solitude.
“People are looking for that option to actually see other human beings, talk and get to know your neighborhood and people in your community,” McQuaid-Craig said, pointing out that “public houses” or alehouses have filled that role for centuries.
Some local brewpubs offer food, game nights and trivia contests with themes such as sports or science fiction. A few have putting greens or volleyball courts. Most importantly they provide a comfortable space to meet friends, neighbors and maybe even future spouses. That’s a source of hope for the faltering craft brew business.
“It’s interesting that the breweries that are focused on onsite sales, that are focused on developing these innovative, welcoming, hospitality models, tend to be doing better than the ones focused on large distributions,” Gacioch said.
The end of Prohibition
Prohibition Brewing was born from the 2008 recession and a knack for home brewing. The owners worked in construction, so when home-building slowed down after the mortgage crisis, they tried their hand at making beer, General Manager Kyle Adams said.
They made the site cozy, with wood tables and warm lighting. Wall displays showcase the brewery’s awards along with mementos from the Prohibition Era. The brewpub has hosted car shows, clothing sales and puppy adoption drives.
In contrast to the dark, decidedly adult ambience of a bar, Prohibition Brewing offered a space where locals could gather for a family birthday or after a Little League game.
“You’re not going into a dark room with dingy walls,” said Kurt Grover, from neighboring Fallbrook. “It was a social activity. It was a scene.”
The dining area of Prohibition Brewing Company in Vista on Sept. 30, 2026. The brewery will soon close its doors after 15 years in business. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters 



First: Prohibition-era decorations and photos hang from the walls of Prohibition Brewing Company. Last: Draft beer handles in the bar area of the brewery in Vista on Sept. 30, 2026. Photos by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters
Prohibition is on a commercial street in Vista, with an unassuming storefront and little foot traffic. You don’t stumble on it. You have to know it’s there. 
“This has become our third place from a friends perspective,” Johnson said, pointing to his drinking companions and referencing the concept of a ‘third place’ for socializing, apart from work or home. “Kurt and I met here. Kathy and I met here. We’re taking active steps toward where our next third place will be.”
Some couples fell in love with their husband or wife at Prohibition Brewing, invited Adams to their weddings, then came back to celebrate anniversaries. 
To keep up with evolving tastes, the brewery added lighter lagers, pilseners and fruit-flavored hard seltzers to its tap menu of red ales and IPAs.
They offered “glitter beer,” with shiny glitter particles that “make it look like a unicorn, I guess,” Adams said. Vista resident Jennifer Johnson celebrated her daughter’s 21st birthday at Prohibition, where staff created a custom apple seltzer for the occasion.
Unlike other breweries that found the business doesn’t pencil out anymore, Prohibition is closing because Adams’ parents, who own the building, plan to retire. Adams hopes to sell the business and property to a new owner who can revamp the brewery, but said there are no plans yet.
Stone-cold truth about craft brew
By contrast, Sapporo’s sale of the Stone Brewing brand was a financial calculation. A 2025 corporate disclosure document detailing Sapporo’s business results from the previous year revealed that its U.S. operations “faced unexpected challenges and profitability declined significantly.” Sales of the Stone brand dropped 16 percent between 2022, when it bought the brand, and 2024, it stated.
In April of this year, Sapporo announced it was selling Stone Brewing to the craft beer company Firestone Walker, based in Paso Robles, California, and its Belgian parent company Duvel Moortgat. The new owners will brew Stone beer at their facilities n Paso Robles and Kansas City, Missouri, said Zach Keeling, CEO for Stone USA. They’ll keep the Stone restaurant at San Diego’s Liberty Station and other Southern California taprooms.
But Sapporo is closing Stone’s flagship site in Escondido, a walled garden where guests can stroll around a pond or view enormous beer vats through soaring glass walls in the rustic-industrial interior.   
In August Sapporo filed a WARN notice with the California Employment Development Department stating that it expected to lay off 220 employees from its Escondido operations. In September, it revised that upward to 272.
“It’s really sad that consolidation of the brewing industry has led to the closure of Stone in Escondido,” said Francisco Vargas, economic development management analyst for the city. 
Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens in Escondido on Sept. 30, 2026. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters 
Social media posts about the closure reveal the way that Stone Escondido has been woven into customers’ lives.
“So many memories including our daughter’s rehearsal dinner,” a Facebook user wrote, adding that she now enjoys “hiking” with her grandson through the brewery’s valley and water features.
A new dad who grew up with Stone Brewing “snuck out” of nearby Palomar Hospital after the birth of his child to toast the milestone at Stone. 
“My engagement pictures were taken there,” a woman stated. “The brewery lasted a lot longer than the marriage did.”
But Stone, known for its intense, hoppy IPAs, left some beer fans flat. A detractor posted on Nextdoor that Stone products were too expensive “for a beer that tastes like potpourri.”
As local beer fans brace for the closure, officials are trying to ease the transition. Escondido is working with the San Diego North Economic Development Council and Sapporo to find a new tenant for the site, possibly another brewery, Vargas said. Sapporo is offering job training and hosting a career fair to help laid off employees land on their feet.
“It’s important to highlight the transferability of skills,” Vargas said. “We want to give the Sapporo employees the best chance they can to find a job in Escondido or the broader region, and to make sure they feel supported during this very difficult time.”
Fowler cautioned that while brewing skills are transferable, it might be harder to duplicate the spirit of the craft brew business in another position.
“People who are into brewing tend to be in it for the passion,” he said. “While on its face value it’s a manufacturing job, a lot of those people might not find the same fulfillment making another product.”
Hope for hops
There are some bright spots amid the bad news about craft brewing. 
The Roadies Brewing Co., a Vista brewpub featuring a live music stage, shut down in August, only to reopen a month later with new catering and business partners, following public outcry over its closure.
“Roadies is back, baby,” the owners announced triumphantly on Instagram, listing a lineup of punk, ska and alternative music and a tap list of beers with names such as Helles Bells, Deep Cuts and Future Jams.
Kyle Adams, general manager of Prohibition Brewing Company, pours the brewery’s on tap Hoppy Lager beer into a glass in Vista on Sept. 30, 2026. The brewery will soon close its doors after 15 years in business. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters 
Despite his inside knowledge of craft brewing’s failures, or perhaps because of that insight, Fowler opened his own brewery last year. He launched Good Pressure Brewing with his wife on Mission Gorge Road in San Diego about five miles north of San Diego State University. They reasoned that suburban communities to the east of the area lacked amenities.
“We were able to find a neighborhood that was thirsty for a brewery and a space that they can claim as their own, that has a local connection,” he said.
Rather than adopt the surf and sea motif of many San Diego breweries, Fowler said they chose a theme reflecting the color palette and botanical features of San Diego’s backcountry, where the couple grew up.
They open their doors to local organizations and nonprofits for meetings and fundraisers, brewed a brown ale to benefit the Center for Plant Conservation, and offer wines and seasonal seltzers to complement their beers.
“For a long time craft beer was almost too cool for itself, dictating the trends for its customers,” he said. “Now it’s moving with our guests and crafting these last few years together.”

name: California
title: Democrats’ identity crisis takes center stage in California insurance commissioner race
text:
California got rid of the traditional party primary system years ago. Now, instead of November elections automatically pitting a Democrat against a Republican, they match up the two highest vote-getters, no matter what political party they belong to.
That may be common knowledge, but it bears repeating because a quick look at ballots now arriving in mailboxes could leave you thinking that it’s still the old days. 
In seven of the eight statewide races there is one Democrat and one Republican. Governor, attorney general, treasurer, controller and on and on: one candidate from column A and one from column B. Even in the one supposedly nonpartisan race — superintendent of public instruction — it’s a Democrat versus a Republican. 
So what was all the panic this year over the top-two primary really about? Everything somehow seems just as it was before.
But then there’s the race for state insurance commissioner. 
Ben Allen, the Democrat, is running against Jane Kim. The Democrat.
This is what the architects of the so-called jungle primary system had in mind all along. No knock on Republicans, who by registration make up about a quarter of California’s voters, but in this bluest of states the real contest is between left-leaning Democrats and — well, what do we call them? Lefter-leaning Democrats?
Allen is what formerly would have been labelled a progressive Democrat, with strong environmentalist and campaign finance reform credentials. A member of the state Senate since 2014, he is known for authoring the bill that requires deep reductions in single-use plastics by 2030. Matcha-latte enthusiasts, take note. His district includes Pacific Palisades, much of which was destroyed by the January 2025 fire.
As insurance commissioner, he claims he’ll use his regulatory power to “lower costs, bring insurers back to the market, and make sure Californians are paid what they are owed in a time of crisis.”
In other words, he will work miracles.
Kim is a product of San Francisco politics. As a member of the Board of Supervisors, she led efforts to eliminate tuition for community colleges, raise the minimum wage and require affordable units in new developments.
She was the first California state director of the Working Families Party, a political organization that generally supports Democrats on the left side of the spectrum. Particular policy planks may differ, but in elections, the WFP plays a generally similar role as the Democratic Socialists of America.
Insurance commissioner candidate Ben Allen speaks during the “Can California Fix Its Insurance Crisis? The Candidates Weigh In” event co-hosted by CalMatters and UC Student and Policy Center in Sacramento on Oct. 8, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Kim says that if she is elected, she would create a public single-payer disaster insurance system that would charge affordable premiums — including in high-risk areas — invest in prevention and resilience and still ensure there is plenty of money to pay all legitimate claims.
In other words, she will work miracles.
The California Democratic Party is endorsing Allen, making him the establishment candidate, at least in comparison. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who does not belong to the Democratic Party but caucuses with Democrats in the Senate, is endorsing Kim.
It should also be noted that Sanders describes himself as a democratic socialist, but not as a Democratic Socialist.
Ever since Sanders sought the Democratic nomination for president in 2016, Democratic candidates have gradually backed away from the term “progressive.” There was never any clear consensus on what it meant in the modern context, except that it signalled something to the left of merely liberal. But in Sanders’ wake, merely “progressive” started to sound downright centrist in comparison with “socialist.”
That works out nicely for out-of-state Republicans, who did not bother with a lot of self-reflection or analysis paralysis when they staged their version of populist revolution the same year. They elected Donald Trump president, MAGA became the new order of the day and traditional Republican values fled into political exile alongside traditional Republicans. Now Trump brands all Democrats as socialists — and indeed, more Democratic candidates are describing themselves that way — but also, by extension, communists, Marxists, enemies of the people, traitors and vermin.
California Democrats meanwhile seem engaged less in populist revolution than a comparatively slow-burning family feud. Voters in progressive (can we still use that word?) San Francisco and San Jose have in recent years elected corporate-backed Democratic mayors who call themselves moderate, pragmatic or “normie.” In Los Angeles, progressive (perhaps now meaning “normie”?) incumbent Mayor Karen Bass is being challenged for reelection by a former supporter, Democratic Socialist-backed City Councilmember Nithya Raman. But those campaigns are city-specific.
Perhaps it’s fitting that the insurance commissioner race is the one statewide campaign in which Democrats are working through their political identity issues. Much of the progressive-normie-socialist-establishment debate boils down to the degree to which a candidate rejects or embraces the support of large corporate interests — like the insurance industry.
Termed-out incumbent Ricardo Lara called himself a progressive when he first ran in 2018 and promised not to accept donations from insurers whom he would regulate. He disappointed backers when he took money from some of the companies anyway.  
Allen also promised not to take any such donations. A couple donations were made anyway, but unlike Lara, Allen returned the money, which he said had been accepted in error.
Still, Kim’s website states that she is the only candidate who hasn’t accepted industry donations.
This is the kind of conversation that takes center stage, in part because many Californians seem uncertain of exactly what the insurance commissioner does, other than try to keep insurers in California while also compelling them to pay more of what policyholders believe they are owed.
Confidence in the system, never particularly high, has nearly vanished in the wake of the Southern California fires and the difficulty survivors have in getting their insurers to pay.
Kim’s single-payer idea may remind voters of health insurance reform, but at least for now, it’s just an idea, without a firm plan for implementation or a consensus that it’s workable. Electing her would be a strong signal of voter support for the idea, but it won’t by itself bring the program to fruition. 
Allen’s more traditional regulatory approach could keep insurers, and their capital and risk-management focus, in play. But California can expect more fires, earthquakes, landslides and other costly natural disasters. Balancing the need to fairly compensate policyholders while keeping insurers solvent and in the California market will be no easy task.
So voters with no expertise in the insurance industry are left to make their choice based on which approach sounds more plausible, which candidate inspires more confidence, and which political quasi-philosophy — Normie? Working Families? Democratic establishment? Democratic socialist? — seems the right direction for now, and perhaps for the long haul as well.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: More sex abuse allegations filed against former Mercer County doctor
text:
Thirteen more women claim in a lawsuit filed in Superior Court in Mercer County on Tuesday that they were sexually assaulted by a former OBGYN. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Thirteen more women allege in a new lawsuit filed Tuesday that they were sexually assaulted by a former OBGYN who lost his license in 2024 and faces similar charges from dozens of other one-time patients.
New York-based law firm Levy Konigsberg filed a civil complaint in state Superior Court in Mercer County on behalf of the women, New Jersey residents who allege former Dr. Bruce Pierce assaulted them during routine office visits dating back to 2003.
Jerome “Jerry” Block, a partner at Levy Konigsberg, told the New Jersey Monitor he expects more women will continue to come forward since Pierce had practiced for decades under a license granted in 1996. Block said Pierce’s employers ignored evidence that he was a “serial sexual predator.”
“We’ve seen in these cases that women complained about Dr. Pierce for years and that these corporate defendants failed to act. Companies operating health systems cannot ignore red flags and put profits over patient safety,” Block said.
At least 45 women have accused Pierce of sexual abuse through a handful of civil lawsuits filed in the past year alone, several of which also blamed the clinic where he worked and entities that oversaw its operations.
The claim filed Tuesday also alleges Pierce’s employer, Delaware Valley OB-GYN and Infertility Group; national provider network Lifeline Medical Associates; and Unified Women’s Healthcare, a regional network that oversaw the clinic’s business operations, were negligent in their training and oversight of his work, oblivious to an obvious pattern of abuse, and failed to contact law enforcement or protect patients.
As medical providers, these entities and their representatives were “outrageous in their disregard for Plaintiff’s rights and safety,” the complaint reads.
The plaintiffs include first and longtime patients, pregnant women, and one who had invited Pierce to her children’s wedding and considered him “family.”
“Provider Defendants gave Pierce authority, space, power, and control over Plaintiffs with no reasonable oversight. It was that authority, space, power, access, and control that allowed Pierce to commit the wrongful conduct and sexual abuse against Plaintiffs,” the complaint says.
According to the claim, the women faced psychological trauma, depression, anxiety, humiliation, and more, and continue to be impacted by the abuse. They have also lost trust in medical professionals, particularly men, have avoided medical care and intimate exams, and have a diminished quality of life as a result, it says.
An attorney who represented Pierce in an earlier civil suit declined to comment on the latest complaint, which they had not seen. Calls to Delaware Valley, Lifeline, and Unified were not returned.
The new case comes just weeks after two other women filed separate lawsuits in Mercer County that allege similar abuse by Pierce and blame Delaware Valley, Lifeline, and Unified for not doing more to protect patients, court records show.
“Plaintiff was entitled to competent, ethical, and safe medical care. Instead, she was subjected to sexual assault in a clinical setting, facilitated by the failures of Defendants to supervise, control, and protect her,” wrote attorneys from a Piscataway firm representing one victim in papers filed Oct. 6.
In late July, a Philadelphia firm filed a lawsuit on behalf of 31 New Jersey women who claim they faced similar assaults by Pierce and blame his employer for failing to address the problem. At least eight of them reported the behavior to other employees at the Delaware Valley clinic, and several times there were chaperones in the room when the alleged abuse occurred, according to the lawsuit.
In October 2024, the state Office of the Attorney General called for the New Jersey Board of Medical Examiners to investigate Pierce and, after a hearing that involved testimony from two witnesses who said they had also been sexually abused by the doctor under the guise of medical care, the board revoked his license two months later. One of the witnesses also reported the incident to local police.
Block said Lawrenceville Police have received at least 15 complaints of sexual abuse involving Pierce, and his clients want to know why the former physician has not been charged. The Mercer County Prosecutor’s Office said they do not comment on investigations or their existence, but confirmed Tuesday there were currently no charges pending against Pierce.
Some medical providers have opted to notify patients when a doctor in their network is charged with abuse, Block said, like Columbia University did when former OBGYN Robert Haddon was convicted of sexual assault in 2023 and sentenced to two decades in prison. But Block said Delaware Valley and its co-defendants have not conducted an internal investigation or contacted patients.
“These hospital systems should want to know for themselves fully what happened, so they could avoid having anything like this happen in the future. They should not just be interested in defending these cases and limiting their liability. They should be interested in knowing how their systems failed and how their systems permitted a doctor to sexually abuse patients for so many years,” he said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Rep. Moore says he puts policy over ‘toxic’ politics; Crosby calls himself a chance for change
text:
Candidates for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Peter Crosby, left, and Republican Blake Moore shake hands following a debate at Utah State University, Tuesday, Oct.13, 2026, in Logan, Utah. (Pool photo by Eli Lucero/The Herald Journal)In the race for Utah’s newly-drawn 2nd Congressional District, Republican incumbent Rep. Blake Moore squared off with one of his challengers, Democrat Peter Crosby, on the debate stage at Utah State University on Tuesday, three weeks before the Nov. 3 election. 
The debate — hosted by the Utah Debate Commission, moderated by KUTV news anchor Heidi Hatch and broadcast live by PBS Utah — put Moore and Crosby through their paces on a wide range of issues, including data centers, water, energy, the shrinking Great Salt Lake, the national debt, tariffs, the Iran War and more. 
Moore defended his record and painted himself as a “productive” member of Congress that’s focused on solutions rather than “toxic” politics. 



“I’ve been able to pass more legislation than anybody else in my cohort, from Great Salt Lake to Hill Air Force Base, to pro-growth and family policy with regards to tax, and it’s something that I’m going to continue to do,” Moore said.
Crosby, an adjunct professor for the Center for Anticipatory Intelligence at USU, argued he’s the right candidate to fix a “broken system” and “build a future for every generation to come.” 
“The distinct difference between (Moore) and myself really is down to Blake Moore is fine with the path that we’re on. I’m not,” Crosby said. “And if we’re going to have something different happen, we need different representation.” 
The debate
The two candidates shared common ground on several topics. They both expressed support for local control over data center development, both called for the creation of a fiscal commission to tackle the national debt, and both credited Utah state leaders for the way they’ve tried to handle artificial intelligence regulation. 
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

During the debate, Moore and Crosby stayed focused on policy and there were no fiery back-and-forths between the two. 
However, Crosby took some shots at Moore when discussing tariffs, fuel prices and the Iran War, arguing Moore has stood by while his own party, as President Donald Trump’s administration, has enacted policies that have hurt Utahns, especially farmers. 
“You have to end a broad tariff regime. Tariffs are fine when they’re used for strategic purposes, but this isn’t strategic. This is now an effective tax on the American people that disproportionately hurts our agricultural community,” Crosby said. 
He then pointed to the U.S.-Israel war in Iran, saying “when the executive decides to attack the two of the largest oil producers in the world, close a strait that’s necessary for the transportation of goods and energy, and then we buy more diesel from the country that’s funding the country that we’re being attacked by? Like, all of that is going to directly contribute to challenges in the ag sector.” 
Candidates for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Peter Crosby, left, and Republican Blake Moore participate in a debate at Utah State University, Tuesday, Oct.13, 2026, in Logan, Utah. (Pool photo by Eli Lucero/The Herald Journal)
Moore said he “did not expect” fuel prices to rise like they have while Republicans have been in power, and he acknowledged that the war in Iran is “becoming a major, major problem.” 
“I’ve encouraged a ceasefire. I was hopeful for the MOU to be able to play out, and simply … fell to the wayside, unfortunately. And there is a strong motivation to be able to get this figured out, so we can move past this. This is way too difficult, particularly on those important industries.” 
On gas prices, Moore said there’s a permitting bill “that is likely going to pass here in the coming months” with a goal of increasing “our domestic supply so we don’t have to rely so much on foreign sources.” 
“If we can accomplish that, you could see some relief that’s actually substantive,” Moore said. 
Crosby said “we don’t need hope” to fix gas prices and inflation. “We need votes.” He also argued it would only take a few Republican votes in the House to end the war in Iran. 
“It only takes one or two Republicans to cross the aisle and say, ‘I’m going to put the needs of my district before my political party or loyalty to an executive that seems to be maybe a little bit strategically challenged when it comes to putting the needs of Americans first,” Crosby said. “That doesn’t require committee work; it just requires courage.”
Candidates for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Peter Crosby, left, and Republican Blake Moore participate in a debate at Utah State University, Tuesday, Oct.13, 2026, in Logan, Utah. (Pool photo by Eli Lucero/The Herald Journal)
Crosby also attacked Moore over energy development, saying Congress and the Trump administration through the “big, beautiful” budget and tax bill passed year, “stripped subsidies for residential solar,” which he said “deliberately and directly targeted the northern Utah solar industry” and is going result in a loss of up to $1.8 billion in economic revenue. 
“So not only do we have a failure to invest in a green energy solution that’s proven to be viable, but we are destroying Utah jobs and Utah economic outcomes. I’m against that,” Crosby said. He added: “That was a bill that was co-authored by my challenger.” 
Moore pushed back, saying a bipartisan group in Congress is working on energy permitting reform that’s aimed at an “all-of-the-above energy approach.” He also argued “you can talk to every solar company in the entire state (about) how I went to bat for them.” 
“What we’re trying to do is get an all-of-the-above energy approach where there’s a level playing field,” Moore said. “You go talk to every single solar company in Utah, they’ll know that I was somebody that was willing to go and create tough conversations and push back heavily in support of those organizations.” 
Candidates for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Peter Crosby, left, and Republican Blake Moore participate in a debate at Utah State University, Tuesday, Oct.13, 2026, in Logan, Utah. (Pool photo by Eli Lucero/The Herald Journal)
Could the race for CD2 be closer than expected?
Utah’s new court-ordered map has widely been expected to have created a single Democratic-leaning district concentrated around northern Salt Lake County and three other sprawling, heavily Republican districts. 
However, some recent polling suggests that Moore in the new 2nd Congressional District could be in a tighter race than expected. And he’s facing not just one challenger, but four. 
Three other candidates are also competing in the general election — Libertarian Daniel Cottam, Independent American Carlton Bowen and unaffiliated candidate Robert Moesinger — but they didn’t qualify for the debate based on polling commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission, which hosted the debate. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In that poll conducted Sept. 10-24 of 515 registered voters, Moore got 39% and Crosby got 34%. Moesinger and Cottam each got 4.9%, and Bowen received 4.1%. The poll’s margin of error was plus or minus 4.32%. About 10.7% of voters were undecided at the time the poll was conducted. 
Earlier this month, the Utah Democratic Party said those poll results showed Crosby “within striking distance” of Moore “in a competitive race with weeks to go before Election Day.” 
Asked about those poll results during a scrum with reporters after the debate, Moore said he’s confident in his campaign, though he acknowledged third-party candidates and undecided voters can create some wild cards in polling. 
“Some elements of that could definitely play out in this election,” Moore said. “But we’re confident where we are. We’re going to continue to drive the message home, and I look forward to an opportunity to kind of continue on a lot of the things that I’ve been working on.” 
Crosby said his message to undecided voters is they have a choice between a change with him or the status quo with Moore. 
“The conversation (with voters) really boils down to, ‘What do you need help with, and how can we fix that?’” Crosby said. 
Tuesday’s debate took place the same day clerks began mailing ballots to eligible registered voters across the state. Once they have their ballots in hand, Utahns don’t need to wait until Election Day. They can cast their votes and send their ballots back through the mail, drop boxes at their convenience, or vote early at a polling place. 
For those who want to wait until Election Day, polls close on Nov. 3 at 8 p.m.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: At Alaska rally, Trump endorses Wilson and seeks to boost Sullivan and Begich
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)In a surprise announcement Tuesday, President Donald Trump said he is endorsing Republican Alaska gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson in the four-way race to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
Polls indicate Wilson and two other Republicans — Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — are trailing the lone Democratic candidate, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
In a rally at Wasilla’s Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center, Trump offered his support for Wilson, urged Alaskans to vote for a ballot measure repealing Alaska’s current elections system and encouraged votes for incumbent Republicans U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan and U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III.
Tuesday’s rally made Trump just the third American president to visit the Matanuska-Susitna region and was part of a nationwide campaign by the President, who was in Ohio on Monday. He’s expected to be in Nevada and Arizona on Wednesday, with other stops in Montana and Georgia this week. 
In 90 minutes of rambling remarks, the President made his goal clear: He wants to motivate Republicans to turn out at the midterms and vote.
“Pretend that I’m on the ballot because here’s what happens. Every time I’ve been on the ballot, we win,” he said.
Attendees of President Donald Trump’s rally on Tuesday, Oct. 16, 2026, fill the stands of the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
Nationally, polling indicates that Republicans are trailing in key elections that may determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the U.S. House and U.S. Senate. 
Polls indicate Begich is ahead of Democratic Party-backed independent Bill Hill in a four-way race that also includes imprisoned Democrat Eric Hafner and Libertarian Jim McDermott.
Sullivan, meanwhile, is in a tight race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola in a four-way election that also includes Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes. Polling indicates Peltola holds a small lead.
It isn’t clear how much Trump’s visit will affect those races. 
In a representative statewide survey of registered voters conducted Oct. 1-3, Alaska Survey Research found 58% of respondents had a negative view of Trump.
“We’ve asked this exact question maybe 50 times on surveys dating back to 2015. This is the worst rating we’ve ever recorded,” said company director Ivan Moore on social media. “58% is an all-time high negative.”    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

But among voters in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, the site of Tuesday’s rally, Trump had a positive rating, with 44% of voters approving and 43% disapproving. 
“You are here in the heart of Republican Alaska,” Sullivan told the President. 
Trump landed at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson Tuesday afternoon before taking a helicopter to Wasilla’s airport and a car to the nearby Menard Center. He was met by a cheering crowd that filled the Menard Center’s seats before returning to his helicopter and an eventual flight to Las Vegas. 
The Menard Center has a capacity of about 3,500 people, and the Mat-Su Sentinel reported that some potential attendees were turned away at the door for lack of space.
Trump was interrupted about 10 minutes into his remarks by a protester who was rapidly rushed out of the rally by security.
Away from the Menard Center, Trump opponents held protests and Democrats organized counterprogramming away from the Republican-focused event inside. Other events took place Tuesday morning in Anchorage.
Alaska Republican governor candidate Treg Taylor talks with reporters on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
Trump backs Wilson in crowded gubernatorial race
Of Alaska’s four candidates for governor, three were present in Wasilla on Tuesday. 
Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins was in Fairbanks, attending a forum hosted by the local chamber of commerce. 
Before the rally, Republican gubernatorial candidates Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor each said they didn’t expect Trump to make an endorsement.
But about one hour before he took the stage, Trump took to social media and endorsed the leading Republican in the primary election, Bernadette Wilson.
Trump called Bronson and Taylor “lesser candidates” and said Bronson begged Trump for an endorsement. 
“I wouldn’t do it because he didn’t win the Primary and, therefore, wasn’t deserving of it. I then asked him to get out of the Race, and he agreed! … He agreed to get out, but three days later, without notification, quickly jumped back in, along with a third ‘Republican’ Candidate, who I never heard of, named Treg Taylor,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
Afterward, Bronson said, “My recollection is different than the president’s of that meeting.”
Bronson said that when he spoke to Trump, he agreed to leave the governor race if Treg Taylor did so but warned Trump that if both left the race, they would simply be replaced by other Republicans.
Taylor never withdrew, “so there was no deal,” Bronson said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
On stage in Wasilla, Trump said that “now is the time for all Republicans to unite behind Bernadette” and wished her luck.
“It ain’t gonna be easy, Bernadette,” he said. 
Trump’s endorsement came hours after the Cook Political Report, one of the nation’s top election prognosticators, said Alaska’s race for governor now leans Democratic, in large part because the Republican vote is being split among three candidates.
Alaska uses ranked choice voting in general elections, which could eliminate vote-splitting, but election results since 2022 have shown that Republican voters are much less likely to rank multiple candidates than independents and Democrats are.
Incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who is term-limited and cannot run again this year, spoke at the rally about three hours before Trump took the stage.
“The only way we’re going to win is if we all vote for the Republican candidates for governor, and that’s very important,” Dunleavy said. 
Bronson and Taylor have urged Republicans to rank all three candidates, but Trump spoke against that appeal, calling ranked choice voting a “scam.”
In a text message, Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign said the President is in Alaska “because national Republicans know that we’re neck-and-neck in this race, and electing a Democratic governor for the first time in a generation would send shockwaves across the country.”
Alaska hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since Tony Knowles, in 1994 and 1998.
As she left the Menard Center, Wilson said she was thrilled by the endorsement. 
“I think it signals, you know, a lot of excitement on our side, a lot of momentum on our side. You’re seeing everyone come together. They’re unifying behind us. We could not be more excited,” she said.
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan talks with reporters on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
Trump offers warnings about a Democratic Congress
Speaking in support of Sullivan and Begich, Trump insulted their leading opponents and the Democratic Party, and he predicted dire consequences for Alaska if Democrats win control of the U.S. House and U.S. Senate.
“Alaska is a special place to be, a very important place to be. And nobody’s done more for Alaska than Donald J. Trump,” he said. “With your support, just 21 days from now, Alaska is going to defeat the radical left Democrats.”
Later in his remarks, Trump said, “If the Democrats win, we will have a 1929-style economic depression. And I don’t like saying it, but they don’t know what the hell they’re doing.”
A relative handful of the seats in the U.S. House and Senate are considered competitive, and Alaska’s two federal races fall into that category, even though Republican presidents have won Alaska each election since 1964. 
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, recruited Peltola to run against Sullivan and has said that her victory would be a step toward becoming Majority Leader and thus in control of the Senate agenda.
At Tuesday’s rally, Sullivan said he thinks that would be a disaster for the state because a Democratic Senate would seek to block oil and gas drilling.
“This would be horrible for Alaska,” Sullivan said of Schumer becoming Majority Leader. “The D.C. Democrats don’t have a positive agenda for Alaska. They have a target on Alaska. But this would also be horrible for the country we love, for the great United States of America. So, ladies and gentlemen, especially here in the Mat-Su Valley, you need to understand Alaska is the firewall for freedom for the entire country.”
An attendee of President Donald Trump’s rally on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla, holds up a sign urging a yes vote on Ballot Measure 2. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
President urges Alaska to repeal top-four primary, ranked choice general
In addition to boosting Republican candidates, Trump urged attendees of the rally to vote yes on this year’s Ballot Measure 2 and eliminate the state’s top-four primary election system and ranked choice general election.
That system was installed in a 2020 ballot measure and retained after a 2022 repeal effort narrowly failed.
Trump has repeatedly called ranked choice voting a “scam” and has urged states to not adopt it.
Under Alaska’s system, all candidates for an office run together, and the top four vote-getters, regardless of party, advance to the general election.
In the general election, voters rank the four remaining candidates in order of preference. If one candidate gets the majority of the first-choice votes, they win.
If no candidate has a majority, the candidate with the fewest first choices is eliminated and that candidate’s votes are redistributed to the voters’ second choice candidates. 
The process continues until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
“Vote against the ranked choice. Vote yes for the elimination of ranked choice,” Trump said.
Pardons signed for two diesel mechanics
During the rally, Trump signed presidential pardons for two local diesel mechanics who pleaded guilty to Clean Air Act violations during the Biden administration. 
Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming were convicted in 2022 of removing anti-pollution equipment from dozens of vehicles.
Sullivan had championed the pardons, saying the removals were justified because the anti-pollution equipment can cause poor performance at low temperatures.
Trump previously pardoned Mackenzie Spurlock, co-owner of Matanuska Diesel, in a related case.
Trump repeats ‘$5,000 dividend’ promise, but with new conditions
Speaking in Wasilla, Trump repeated a pledge he first made in September in Texas — a $5,000 payment to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the House and Senate during the midterms.
“The Trump dividend that you get, you’ll get it very quickly after the election,” he said.
That payment would cost $1.2 trillion, significantly increase the national debt and likely would increase the national rate of inflation, an independent analysis concluded last month.
At the Menard Center, Trump said he would restrict the dividend so that it could only be spent in the United States. He did not say how he would track Americans’ use of the money.
“I don’t want you to go to Japan. I don’t want you to go to China. You’ve got to spend it in the United States of America,” he said.
Visit makes local history
Trump became just the third President to visit the Matanuska-Susitna region. The first, Warren Harding, died on his return home after ceremonially opening the Alaska Railroad in 1923. The second was Jimmy Carter, who restricted his visit to a remote mountain lake for fishing.
Trump has repeatedly visited Alaska aboard Air Force One, which frequently stops in Anchorage to refuel during trans-Pacific flights.
His last notable venture away from Air Force One was one year ago, when he met Russian President Vladimir Putin briefly at JBER. 
Trump visited Alaska for a campaign rally in 2022 to endorse Dunleavy, U.S. Senate candidate Kelly Tshibaka and U.S. House candidate Sarah Palin. Of the three candidates, only Dunleavy won that year’s election.
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
