name: Washington State Standard
title: Voting underway in Washington in the midterm election
text:
Washington state election officials encourage voters to return ballots via designated drop boxes to ensure they arrive in time to be counted. In the primary, the state tallied a higher number of ballots with late postmarks than prior years. (Photo by Donna Gordon Blankinship)The wait is over in Washington.
Washington’s 5.1 million registered voters are starting to cast ballots for the Nov. 3 general election, which could see Democrats strengthen their grip on power in the state Legislature and retake the majority from Republicans in Congress.
In theLegislature, where Democrats hold majorities in both chambers, all 98 seats in the state House and 24 of 49 in the state Senate are up for election. 
Five of the nine state Supreme Court seats will be filled, giving voters a rare opportunity to pick a majority of the bench.
And all 10 congressional seats are on ballots. The race for the 3rd District in southwest Washington is drawing national attention because the outcome could help decide which political party controls the chamber in 2027. And the winner of the 4th District will succeed Republican U.S. Rep. Dan Newhouse, who is retiring.
Today, the Washington State Standard is publishing its voter guide for the unusually active off-year election.
There are responses to our surveys from all candidates for the Supreme Court as well as for 34 of the most competitive legislative contests and those two races for U.S. House seats.
Readers will find short explainers of the three statewide initiatives dealing with Washington’s new income tax on high earners, parental rights of public school students and transgender students’ participation in school sports.
Several counties began mailing ballots last week, well ahead of the Oct. 16 deadline to do so. People have until Oct. 26 to register or update their address online. After that you can register at a county election office or voting center, including on Election Day.
State and county election officers are hoping voters will return their ballots, preferably by depositing them in one of Washington’s 594 designated drop boxes or casting them at one of 61 voting centers. 
They’re cautioning about relying on the U.S. Postal Service. A recent rule change by the postal service does not guarantee ballots sent through the mail will be postmarked on the day they are put in the mail box.
Ballots should be mailed at least a week before election day to ensure they’ll be counted. If mailing within a week of Nov. 3, go in-person and request a manual postmark at the counter.
If ballots are not postmarked on or before Election Day, they will not count. More than 20,000 cast in the August primary were rejected because they came in too late.
Voters can sign up at VoteWA.gov to track their ballot and confirm it is received and counted.
Meanwhile, in Snohomish County, where ballots went out Oct. 9, election officials are alerting voters that the word “General” is misspelled on the return envelope, and assuring them it is not a problem.
“This is a printing error only. Your ballot is still valid, and this typo does not affect how your ballot is processed or how your signature is verified,” reads a statement from the Snohomish County auditor. “You can complete and return your ballot as usual.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar, Demuth have school plans, but neither addresses funding challenges
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Minnesota State Fair. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota’s next governor will face multiple education challenges when they take office, and few aspects of the job are more important. Funding for public schools comprises nearly 40% of the state budget and is the single biggest line item. That funding accounts for about two-thirds of all spending on public schools in Minnesota. 
Under Gov. Tim Walz, Minnesota’s students’ academic assessments declined significantly following the pandemic, with the number of students meeting grade-level expectations in reading and math down about 10 percentage points. Unlike students in some states, Minnesota students have shown no sign of academic recovery. Minnesota has long suffered one of the nation’s worst opportunity gaps between white and Black and Native children, which has continued during the Walz years. 
Neither Republican nominee Lisa Demuth nor Democratic-Farmer-Labor nominee Amy Klobuchar responded to Reformer requests for interviews to talk about their education plans. 
Both candidates have put academic achievement at the top of their education agenda. Both candidates call for a continued focus on the use of what’s called the science of reading, an evidence-based method of literacy education that was mandated in Minnesota by the 2023 READ Act.
Both candidates also call for using evidence-based math instruction. Demuth, the current Minnesota House speaker, advocates changing teacher preparation programs to focus on evidence-based practices. A key component of the READ Act changed how Minnesota’s teacher preparation programs teach educators how to teach reading. 
According to a recent New York Times survey of education experts that ranked cost-effective strategies for improving academic outcomes, the science of reading and high-quality curriculum were both ranked in their top five for cost-effective ways to improve educational outcomes.
Demuth and Klobuchar also both support an increase in tutoring for students who are currently below grade-level in reading and math. While Demuth specifically mentions expanding the existing Reading Corps and Math Corps tutoring programs, Klobuchar, who’s been in the U.S. Senate for 20 years, does not explain how she would expand tutoring. 
Neither candidate explains how they would pay for expanded tutoring. While tutoring can be effective at bringing students up to grade level, small-group tutoring is expensive relative to other policies that can improve academic outcomes for students.
Klobuchar’s plan includes several other strategies to improve academic outcomes, like banning cellphones and limiting screen time in the classroom, increasing student attendance, and requiring schools to automatically opt students into advanced courses when they qualify. All three strategies are considered low-cost ways to boost student achievement, with expanded access to advanced courses another cost-effective strategy.
Teacher pay
Demuth has proposed linking teacher pay to performance, but her plan doesn’t include details. The Q Comp program, which started in 2005, already allows districts that opt in and unions to collectively bargain for compensation that is not based on the traditional system of years of experience and credentials. While pay for performance is one of the allowed uses, Q Comp funding can also be spent on teacher professional development, teacher leadership positions and teacher evaluation. 
Klobuchar’s only reference to teacher pay is about making healthcare affordable for all educators. While higher educator compensation is one strategy for boosting academic outcomes for students, these strategies are expensive, and neither candidate provides details about how they would pay for their plans.
Linking teacher pay to performance metrics like student test scores has a similar impact on student outcomes as increased pay for all teachers, but it’s cheaper, according to the experts interviewed by The New York Times. 
For about the same cost as performance pay, paying teachers more to work in high-poverty schools could provide a larger boost to academic outcomes.  
Neither candidate has proposed this strategy.
School funding challenges
Neither candidate’s platform addresses major funding challenges facing Minnesota school districts. 
Without a change in state law, the state will reduce its special education funding by $250 million beginning next school year. This would reverse a boost to school funding the Legislature approved in 2023, when lawmakers sought to help districts with burgeoning special education costs. 
The gap between the what it costs school districts to provide legally mandated special education services and what the state pays for is called the cross-subsidy. The 2023 Legislature closed about half of that funding gap by expanding state cross-subsidy aid. Legislation passed in 2025 requires the $250 million cut to cross-subsidy aid, and would require legislative action to reverse.
Neither candidate addresses the reduction in what’s called compensatory revenue that some districts are dealing with as a result of the universal meals legislation, also passed in 2023. The state no longer accepts paper forms completed by parents to qualify students for federal free and reduced price meals. Instead, the state is now relying solely on administrative data already collected when children qualify for benefits like Medicaid or SNAP. For some districts, however, a significant number of students who meet low-income guidelines are not recorded as low-income because they’re not enrolled in those other programs. As a result, in some cases, those districts have missed out on millions of dollars of compensatory revenue funding this year.
More broadly, school districts are confronting rising labor costs — driven in part by skyrocketing health insurance premiums — and rising special education enrollment, which tends to be more expensive. Because state aid is dependent on student enrollment, some districts are also facing budget challenges due to population stagnation. 
Extra credit
Demuth includes several other policies in her education plan, including expanding funding for student safety to include private schools; opting Minnesota into a federal quasi-voucher scheme; allowing districts to opt-out of state mandates; and removing “woke standards” adopted during Walz’s tenure, though she hasn’t offered specifics other than anything that is “pushing our kids away from the basics of reading, math and science.” 
Klobuchar includes her education plan as part of a broader program for workforce development. She would expand access to the teaching profession for Minnesotans with non-traditional backgrounds, and automatic and direct admissions to Minnesota colleges for qualified high school students, i.e., if schools admit anyone with a high school diploma and a minimum GPA, the student wouldn’t have to apply, they would just receive an acceptance letter. 
Klobuchar also says she would also develop a statewide plan to address student homelessness.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Under attack: State looks to harden cybersecurity as AI changes the game
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Cyberattacks on government entities are increasing, the speed of attacks is accelerating and the impact could be far reaching thanks largely to artificial intelligence. 
February’s cyberattack on the University of Mississippi Medical Center demonstrated the damage that hackers can inflict. UMMC was without Wifi or phones and it’s regular computer system was down for more than a week. It canceled appointments and elective surgeries, and medical staff had to use paper charts to care for patients. 
On Tuesday, the Senate Cybersecurity Committee met with experts to learn about what the state should do to protect citizens and assets. 
READ MORE: UMMC revenue tumbled after February cyberattack
Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann created the committee in August to study the security of state and local government information systems and laws and penalties. The committee will develop recommendations for the Legislature’s 2027 session. 
Hosemann has said the state is “woefully inadequate” in cybersecurity.
In 2025, $77 billion in losses in the U.S. from cyber crimes were reported to the FBI. Hosemann said that due to underreporting, the actual cost could be in the hundreds of billions.
Speakers at the hearing on Tuesday emphasized the need for a collaborative, coordinated and centralized system for combatting cyber threats in state and local governments. 
According to Bobby Freeman, the director of the Cybersecurity Unit within the Department of Public Safety’s Office of Homeland Security, said that many cyberattacks are coming from outside of the U.S., requiring state agencies and local governments to work with federal agencies. 
To prepare for potential attacks, various agencies and local governments in Mississippi need to have a plan to work together. This could include common definitions, clear governance and crisis communications plans. 
“Coordination is key to all of this,” said Kevin Chin, a cybersecurity expert with Microsoft. 
Currently, cybersecurity and enforcement are dispersed. At the state level the Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services, the Cybersecurity Unit and the attorney general’s office are each responsible for different aspects of cybersecurity from providing services to state agencies to prosecuting crimes, and some departments have their own policies. Local governments are usually responsible for their own security resulting in a patchwork system that can make coordination and communication difficult. 
Doug Robinson, executive director of the National Association of State Chief Information Officers, told the committee he has seen a “march toward more consolidated and centralized models” across states.
Multiple speakers said that having a single centralized state cybersecurity resource would make collaboration and communication easier. A single system would also provide opportunities to eliminate duplicated work, share knowledge and save money. But speakers had different ideas about who the central agency or person should be.
A single system could also help the state respond quickly to cyberattacks. 
Cyberattacks are moving faster than ever thanks to AI and a rapid response is key to minimizing damage. Jon Tidwell, a government strategic services leader with Google, said that AI is making cyberattacks increasingly sophisticated and hackers are able to precisely time attacks to target a system. 
Some experts said that to be successful, the state needs more timely visibility into attacks on local governments. One proposal is to pass a law requiring local governments to report when they have data breaches within 24 hours. State agencies are already required to report incidents to state Information Technology Services
“You can’t protect what you don’t know about,” said Mark Butscher, a security specialist with Google. 
Cybersecurity tools and professionals are not cheap. Additionally, state and local governments are competing for these highly specialized personnel with private industry and the federal government, which often pay more. Suggestions included working with community colleges and universities to develop a pipeline and funding cybersecurity as a recurring expense in the state budget.
“Cybersecurity is no longer a back-office expense, it is a foundational requirement for public service continuity,” said Tidwell. 
The committee said it would first focus on policies around state agencies. This could include consolidation, increasing visibility of attacks and making sure state agencies are following policies. However, disparate and numerous city and county governments present a hard challenge. 
Legislators are also interested in how to enforce cybersecurity laws and punish crimes, although some speakers urged the committee to focus less on criminal laws and more on the organization and coordination of various groups.
Sen. Tyler McCaughn, a Republican from Newton and one of the committee’s chairmen, said he had more questions, including procurement, reporting and enforcement.
“I’m going to give you a heads up. We’re not done,” McCaughn said, “We’re not done with this year. We’re not done with these hearings. Because I feel really confident that an enforcement piece will be our next discussion.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Amendment 6 would remake balance of power between Missouri voters and lawmakers
text:
The Missouri House of Representatives on Feb. 19 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications). Missouri voters are being asked on Nov. 3 to fundamentally rewrite the balance of power between themselves and the state lawmakers they elect.
If Amendment 6 passes, future legislatures could no longer change laws enacted by voters through the initiative process on their own. Instead, at least 80% of both the House and Senate would have to agree to send any changes back to voters for another statewide election.
That would be a major departure from current law.
Today, lawmakers can amend or repeal a state law enacted through an initiative just as they can any other statute.
Voter-approved constitutional amendments are already protected from direct legislative changes, but a simple majority of each chamber can propose a new constitutional amendment and send it to voters.
Amendment 6 would require 80% support before lawmakers could propose changes to either.
And that is only part of the amendment.
It would also make initiative and referendum a “fundamental right,” preserve existing requirements for putting measures on the ballot and prohibit lawmakers from weakening the process.
The result would place Missouri among the states where laws enacted directly by voters receive the greatest protection from elected lawmakers.
“If the Missouri amendment passes, then Missouri would provide one of the highest levels of protection for voter-initiated measures that are found in any of the states,” said John Dinan, a Wake Forest University professor who studies state constitutions and direct democracy.
Supporters say that is precisely what Missouri needs after years of lawmakers attempting to revise, repeal or reverse decisions made by voters.
Opponents warn voters are being asked to trade one problem for another — protecting election results by making future governments far less able to respond when voter-written laws need to change.
At its heart is a question Missouri has wrestled with for years: When voters make law themselves, who should get the final word?
“Amendment 6 ensures that Missourians can be a check and balance on politicians when they are ignoring our voices,” said Jack Cardetti, a spokesman for the Yes on Amendment 6 campaign.
Republican state Sen. Joe Nicola of Grain Valley frames the choice differently.
“This is the most important amendment on the ballot,” Nicola recently wrote. “If it passes, it will begin to deconstruct our Constitutional Republic.”
His more practical concern is that initiatives lack the hearings, amendments, negotiations and opportunities for revision that accompany legislation. Under Amendment 6, he wrote, lawmakers could be unable to address problems even when “the change needed was substantial, a small technical change, an emergency or even just outdated over time.”
The Missouri Chamber of Commerce and Industry has raised a similar concern, warning that businesses need confidence the state can respond when a policy proves unworkable.
Missouri has a recent example of exactly the sort of legislative response Amendment 6 would make far more difficult.
Voters in November 2024 approved an initiative raising the minimum wage, requiring many employers to provide paid sick leave and tying future wage increases to inflation. Business groups, including the Chamber, opposed it.
‘Kicked a hornet’s nest’: Missouri GOP repeal of voter-approved laws inspires backlash

The sick leave requirement took effect May 1, 2025. Two weeks later, the Republican-controlled legislature passed a bill repealing it and eliminating future inflationary increases in the minimum wage. Gov. Mike Kehoe signed it in July 2025.
Under Amendment 6, lawmakers could not have done that themselves. They would have needed 80% support in both chambers just to ask voters to approve the changes.
That is a high bar even for Missouri’s Republican supermajority. Republicans won 111 of 163 House seats in 2024 and hold 24 of 34 Senate seats. Reaching 80% would take 131 House votes and 28 in the Senate, requiring Democratic support.
Cardetti argues the threshold is achievable when lawmakers broadly agree a change is needed. He noted that nearly one-third of the bills passed during the 2026 legislative session received support from at least 80% of lawmakers.
The amendment would also reach backward, covering initiatives adopted since Jan. 1, 2010. Lawmakers left the 2024 measure’s $15 minimum wage intact when they repealed sick leave. If Amendment 6 passes, changing that wage would require 80% of both chambers and another statewide vote.
But Amendment 6 does not stop at protecting voter-approved laws.
It also tries to prevent lawmakers from responding by making it substantially harder for citizens to put measures on the ballot in the first place.
 What happened in Arizona

Arizona voters approved the Voter Protection Act in 1998 after lawmakers altered a voter-approved drug policy initiative.
“They brought it on themselves,” said Chuck Coughlin, a veteran Republican political consultant in Arizona.
The amendment barred lawmakers from repealing voter-approved initiatives and allowed them to amend one only if three-fourths of each chamber agreed and the change furthered the purpose of the original measure.
The protections worked, Coughlin said.
“If you put something on the ballot and it passes,” he said, “they can’t monkey with it.”
But that did not end the struggle between lawmakers and initiative campaigns. Instead, Coughlin said, the fight moved to the front end.
Arizona lawmakers enacted rules making initiatives more difficult and expensive to qualify. Among them was a requirement that campaigns strictly comply with initiative laws rather than receive the more forgiving treatment they previously enjoyed.
Lawmakers were explicit about why. In adopting the strict-compliance standard in 2017, the Arizona Legislature said the Voter Protection Act “greatly impairs the ability of the legislature” to make changes or corrections to voter-approved initiatives.
Coughlin said the subsequent restrictions have blunted what was once a frequently used political tool, with initiatives becoming more expensive and difficult to qualify.
Amendment 6 would prohibit Missouri lawmakers from “weakening” initiative and referendum powers and preserve current signature requirements and the simple statewide majority needed for passage.
When the Missouri provisions were described to him, Coughlin said they appeared to reflect a lesson from Arizona.
“They’ve learned from our mistake out here,” he said.
Missouri lawmakers have already pursued the sort of front-end changes Coughlin described.
In August, voters overwhelmingly rejected a legislative proposal that would have required citizen-initiated constitutional amendments to win a majority in every congressional district rather than a simple statewide majority.
Nicola says the initiative process still “is not functioning well and needs to be adjusted.”
“However,” he wrote, “Amendment 6 is not what we need.”
Coughlin, meanwhile, said Arizona’s rigidity also forces initiative campaigns to be more careful because proponents know lawmakers may not be able to fix problems later.
“If you’re putting something on the ballot, you have to be very rigorous about what you’re doing,” he said.
That is essentially the same feature Nicola and Missouri business groups identify as a danger.
Opponents argue lawmakers need room to respond to mistakes and changing circumstances. Supporters argue giving them that freedom also gives them the power to substitute their judgment for a decision voters just made.
 More than a fight over one election

Missouri voters established the initiative and referendum process in 1908, giving citizens a way to bypass the legislature and make laws directly.
Conflict over that power has erupted repeatedly.
Voters approved restrictions on puppy mills in 2010, only to see lawmakers peel back key provisions the next year. Missourians increasingly turned instead to the state constitution, where lawmakers could not directly undo what voters enacted.
Voters have used constitutional amendments to create a new legislative redistricting system, expand Medicaid, legalize marijuana and sports betting and enshrine abortion rights. Lawmakers have at times resisted or sought to reverse those decisions, including by sending competing constitutional amendments back to voters.
Amendment 6 would largely erase the distinction between initiated statutes and initiated constitutional amendments when it comes to lawmakers’ ability to change them.
It would also restrict lawmakers from passing laws “similar in effect” to measures rejected through the referendum process — language that could have an almost immediate consequence.
Missouri Republicans scramble to launch late campaigns on two ballot measures

Voters on Nov. 3 will also decide whether to keep the congressional map Republicans passed last year. If they reject the map and approve Amendment 6, legal experts interviewed by The Independent believe lawmakers would likely need 80% support and another statewide vote to enact a similar map before the 2030 census.
The amendment does not define “similar in effect,” meaning any attempt could ultimately be tested in court.
Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians, the group that forced the map referendum, said Amendment 6 would constrain lawmakers but called that “a creature of the legislature’s own making through their own actions.”
The proposal would give courts another significant role, constitutionally requiring ballot summaries to be clear and unbiased and ensuring judges can rewrite language found to be misleading.
The politics surrounding Amendment 6 do not divide neatly along party lines.
Supporters include the Missouri AFL-CIO, former Republican U.S. Sen. Jack Danforth, former Democratic Secretary of State Jason Kander and former Republican state Sen. Bob Johnson.
The Amendment 6 campaign also has a large financial advantage. A committee called Vote Yes on Amendment 6 has reported more than $4.7 million in large contributions since Sept. 8. Much of that money has come from organized labor. The Missouri AFL-CIO has contributed more than $1.1 million, while the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council gave $500,000, IBEW Local 124 gave $400,000 and Sheet Metal Workers Local 36 contributed $300,000.
The organized opposition has operated on a far smaller scale, and only recently got off the ground. MO Protect PAC reported $14,870 on hand Oct. 1 and later received $10,000 each from political committees supporting Republican state Sens. Jason Bean and Brad Hudson.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Some of us never left Ukraine’s side — even if Washington did
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at Wheeler High School near Marietta, Georgia, on July 22. Trump spoke about Trump accounts for children and railed against his political opponents ( Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)I did not leave the Republican Party, and I am not going anywhere. But I am tired of watching most of my party’s leaders in Washington behave as if abandoning Ukraine to Vladimir Putin is simply the price of loyalty to this president.
President Donald Trump has never hidden his instinct to accommodate Putin, and we shouldn’t expect that to change. What can change, and what must change, is the silence of Republican officeholders who know better and say nothing while the administration does Moscow’s bidding.
On Friday, that silence got harder to defend. After a phone call with Putin, the president announced that Russia would immediately ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel, 500,000 more in November, and a million tons after that.
Within hours, the Treasury eased sanctions on Russian diesel for six months, the first such license since the invasion to run longer than the standard 30 days.
Just last month, the president signed a bipartisan sanctions law designed to choke off the oil and gas revenue that pays for Putin’s war. Republicans voted for that law. Now the administration is clearing the way for Russian diesel, announced while presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a peace proposal.
Diesel isn’t the only deal on the table. The New York Times reported this month that the administration’s Ukraine talks have widened to include a multibillion-dollar sale of Lukoil’s global oil fields, refineries and gas stations.
Putin himself reportedly raised that deal with Kushner and Witkoff at the Kremlin in September. Its investors include Middle Eastern business groups with ties to the envoys’ families and a co-owner of the Trump-linked World Liberty Financial.
The Times found no evidence that either envoy stands to profit personally. Still, a peace process that doubles as a deal-making venue for the president’s circle is not free-market capitalism. It is the crony kind, and conservatives should call it that.
Consider also Kushner’s recent remarks at a diplomatic forum in Kyiv, where he argued that Ukraine holds the last card between war and peace because Kyiv won’t hand over the territory Putin demands.
In Kushner’s telling, the “rest of the deal” is already assembled, and Ukraine needs to concede its own land. In the mouth of the president’s own son-in-law, the obstacle to peace is Ukraine’s refusal to surrender, not Russia’s decision to invade.
Then there is the company the Trump family keeps. ProPublica recently reported that Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch and Putin ally who runs a boxing federation financed by Gazprom, substantially bankrolled Donald Trump Jr.’s Bahamas wedding celebration this spring.
Kremlev is also closely involved with Healthy Fatherland, a Russian youth organization run by his wife’s twin sister. Ukraine has sanctioned that organization for its alleged role in abducting and forcibly relocating Ukrainian children from occupied territory. This is the man who helped pay for a Trump family celebration.
Put the wedding, the Kushner remarks, and the diesel deal side by side, and the optics aren’t a distraction from the policy. They are the policy, illustrated.
Here is what elected Republicans keep getting wrong: they assume the base has moved with the White House on Russia. It hasn’t.
YouGov’s most recent polling found that 52% of Republicans sympathize more with Ukraine than Russia, while barely 3% side with Moscow. Even among Trump’s most devoted MAGA supporters, 45% still side with Ukraine. Pew’s polling this spring found a growing share of Republicans now describe Russia as an enemy of the United States, not a partner or competitor.
We need to hear that from our own party’s elected officials, not just from Trump’s critics on the left.
Too many Republicans in Congress who privately understand what Putin is have decided that public silence is the safer play. It is not safe. It is a betrayal of a Republican tradition that once stood, unambiguously, against Russian aggression.
We cannot dictate what this president says about Putin. We can insist that the Republicans we elect to the House and Senate stop providing cover for it. Start with the sanctions law they passed just weeks ago. Every Republican who voted for it should be asked a simple question: will you defend your own law?
Our Republican Legacy exists to make that case inside our own party, not outside it. There are still Republicans, more than Washington seems to realize, who believe Ukraine deserves to win this war. It’s time our elected officials remembered they work for us, too.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Take it from a Floridian: You don’t want NextEra in South Carolina
text:
Under a timeline adopted in August 2026, the South Carolina Public Service Commission is scheduled to decide by Jan. 29, 2027, whether to approve a merger of NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy. The combined utility would serve 10 million customers across Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia. (File photo by Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)South Carolinians already know what it costs when a utility bets your money on something that never gets built.
You paid for it. You are still paying for it.
That spectacle should shape how South Carolina considers NextEra Energy’s $67 billion offer to buy Dominion Energy — a deal that would create the largest regulated electric utility in the world and put South Carolina inside it.
I am a native Floridian. I served on the staff of the Florida Public Service Commission, as counsel in the Florida Legislature, and later as an appointed commissioner of the Florida Public Service Commission.
SC utility regulators set January deadline for decision on Dominion, NextEra merger

I have watched NextEra operate in Florida from inside the room. What follows is not a prediction. It is a record.
Start with what a regulated utility actually sells. Its profits come less from the flow of electricity than from capital investments: the plants, poles, wires and substations it owns.
Regulators let it charge customers enough to recover prudent costs plus a return on that investment.
In exchange, it accepts an obligation: deliver fair, safe, reliable service at just and reasonable rates. That bargain is the regulatory compact, and it is the only thing standing between an electric monopoly and its customers.
Florida shows what happens when regulation fails and the bargain runs one way.
The national average authorized return on equity for capital investments by investor-owned utilities for 2024 and 2025 is about 9.8%.
Through settlement agreements in Florida that largely excluded residential and small-business voices, Florida Power & Light — NextEra’s flagship — secured a return of 10.95%, plus provisions letting it reach as high as 11.95%.
Every point above the national average is worth roughly $500 million a year, according to Timothy Devlin, the former executive director of the Florida Public Service Commission.
At the top of the range that Florida Power & Light will likely reach, it reaps about $1 billion a year above the national average, with households and small businesses bearing the heaviest burden.
The result is a company that in 2024 kept almost 30 cents of profit on every customer dollar, according to the utility’s own accounting records submitted to Florida regulators — against an industry average closer to 13 cents in 2024.
Thus, on a $200 monthly bill, more than $50 is profit, according to the Energy & Policy Institute’s utility tracker.
Here is what a utility profit margin of almost 30% looks like from a kitchen table: high bills and deep economic insecurity leaving working households in jeopardy.
Since the pandemic, Florida utilities have been among the worst actors in the nation for disconnections. In 2024 alone, Florida’s utilities shut off electricity to more than 2.1 million customers, and 60% of those shutoffs came from NextEra’s Florida Power & Light.
That means 23 of every 100 customers served by Florida Power & Light in 2024 lost power for unpaid bills, which is more than twice Dominion Energy’s 1 in 10 disconnections in South Carolina, according to an analysis by the Energy & Policy Institute.
Meanwhile, Florida Power & Light earned more than $5 billion, and NextEra CEO John Ketchum received about $24 million in compensation, according to NextEra Energy’s 2025 proxy statement.
When Floridians asked their local governments for relief from this economic onslaught, the utilities went to the Legislature and had local authority over energy choices preempted. There was nowhere left to appeal.
Now consider in this merger, where Dominion’s Virginia Power keeps about 18 cents of profit on the customer dollar, not 27%, in part because it operates inside a competitive wholesale market called PJM, where cheaper third-party power can beat utility-owned assets.
NextEra’s practice in Florida has been the opposite: wall off wholesale access and move as much generation as possible into the regulated rate base.
South Carolina’s municipal utilities, electric cooperatives and industrial customers buy from those same wholesale markets.
Other regulators have viewed the legacy of NextEra and said no. NextEra has failed to close at least five acquisitions — Oncor in Texas, Hawaiian Electric, Maryland’s Constellation Energy, and Jacksonville (Florida) Electric Authority — most under regulatory scrutiny.
In 2016, Hawaii’s commission found NextEra financially fit, willing and able, and yet rejected the deal anyway. Capacity to pay is not the same as commitment to the public interest.
South Carolina’s Public Service Commission does not have to consider this bid on faith, and it should not take it on promises. It can follow the wisdom of other informed leaders and reject it.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State Question 847 would cap Oklahomans’ property tax growth. At what cost?
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Oklahoma County Election Board on June 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state question on Oklahoma general election ballots could slow the growth of property taxes, but it has raised concerns about the financial impact on public services.
If State Question 847 passes on Nov. 3, the assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property could increase by no more than 1.75% per year, down from the current cap of 3%. The fair cash value of non-homestead properties could rise by a maximum of 4% annually rather than 5%.
The state question also would add similar caps ranging from 0.35% to 1.75% for Oklahomans age 65 or older who make too much income to qualify for the “senior freeze,” which locks recipients’ property taxes at the value of the time they apply.
The ballot measure wouldn’t cut Oklahomans’ property taxes, but it would limit the increased tax costs property owners could face over time, which supporters say would give needed relief as other expenses rise. 
Others say the state question would slowly drain millions of dollars from schools, CareerTech centers and other core services that depend on property tax revenue.
Although the ballot language states the exact fiscal impact is “unknown,” the Oklahoma Tax Commission projected local tax jurisdictions would lose $45.78 million in revenue the next fiscal year, if the state question passes.
When extending that over 10 years, local government entities could lose out on $457.8 million, the Oklahoma State School Boards Association estimated.
OSSBA executive director Shawn Hime acknowledged nobody likes to pay property taxes “until you start thinking about all the things that you receive and the core services that are offered based on those taxes.”
“We have to have the resources available for core services like emergency management, our roads and bridges, our police and fire,” Hime said. “All of those things cost money, along with resourcing our schools so that we can have high-quality teachers in the classroom with every student.”
Oklahoma State School Boards Association executive director Shawn Hime speaks at an Oklahoma City Board of Education meeting Feb. 29, 2024, at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma CareerTech state director Brent Haken estimated vocational learning centers alone would lose about $90 million over the next 10 years. Budgets would begin to constrict as inflation rises, he said, ultimately costing career training programs that help Oklahoma meet workforce demands.
“We will start to first be stagnant in program offerings, and then over time reduce because the cost of doing business will continue to rise while our cost of collections is not rising,” Haken said. “So, 10 years from now, you would expect to see less students enrolled in CareerTech than we do today if that measure were to pass.”
Local government entities still will receive more revenue than they did the year before, just at a lower rate, said House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow. 
Oklahomans have been asking their state lawmakers for relief from rising costs, which prompted the state Legislature to put SQ 847 up for a public vote, said Hilbert, who co-wrote the ballot measure.
Homeowners have been struggling under increasing home insurance costs and “through the roof” interest rates while “their house is getting hit with that maximum increase of 3% per year” in taxed valuation, he said.
“When you look at the national market of housing and interest rates, as a state government how much could we as a state do?” Hilbert said. “I’m not sure, but the one piece of that equation that we can certainly have an impact on is the property tax.”
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, left, debates a bill in the House chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 13. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Hilbert pointed to the expected $45.78 million decrease in property tax growth as an endorsement of the state question, not a drawback.
“At the end of the day, that’s $45 million that’s being saved to taxpayers, which I think is a good thing,” he said. “And so, I think that’s the crux of this argument, is the tax consumers who are against this bill are upset because they’re not going to be able to raise taxes by $45 million next year.”
The Oklahoma Farm Bureau, an organization representing farmers and ranchers, also has supported the state question. 
Agricultural properties sometimes lose money because of factors like drought, input costs, and fluctuating crop and livestock prices. Meanwhile, “property taxes on that land continue to steadily climb,” the Farm Bureau wrote in its voter guide. 
In Guthrie Public Schools, Superintendent Mike Simpson estimated property tax revenue generates about 30% of his district’s budget.
Bond issues, which also are paid through property tax collections, have been crucial in financing the construction of new school buildings, the cost of which has risen dramatically, Simpson said.
Guthrie Public Schools Superintendent Mike Simpson, right, attends an event in Edmond on Aug. 3. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Districts still paying back bond debt suddenly would have less revenue growth than expected, which Simpson said could cause a short-term increase in property tax millage rates. Hilbert said lawmakers considered this issue and adjusted the state question to mitigate it.
SQ 847 would limit districts’ long-term bonding capacity, Simpson said, and it would pinch school facility budgets that rely on property tax revenue.
“The relief (for taxpayers) will not be immediate at all,” he said. “It will be over time, and the net effect on the homeowner will be less advantageous to them than it will be a tremendous problem financially and a burden to the school districts and the entities that receive the property tax.”

title: The mountain elite: Wyoming mountains forged A.J. Cargill into a stylish ski champion
text:
When she was a kid, A.J. Cargill’s parents up and moved from the Midwest to the chic ski resort of Sun Valley, Idaho, setting her and two siblings afloat in a style-conscious culture the youths yearned to join.
Having skied only on 200-foot-high hills, the shy eighth grader was loosed onto the slopes of Bald Mountain, runs that regularly forged Olympic medalists. Competitive skiing, teenage insecurities, a cliquey society and the ski hill itself could have swallowed her up.
Instead, she became a world champion free skier, a 20-year ski patroller and the first woman to descend the Grand Teton on free-heel telemark skis. None of that was handed to her, she said. “I had to earn it all the hard way.”
As an impressionable child, just adapting to a new community was tough. “We were like really bad skiers in Sun Valley,” she said of herself, her brother and sister who were plopped into a challenging crucible. “And some of the other teenagers … like [future Olympic gold medalist] Picabo Street … were already on the U.S. development team.”
A lot of kids they circulated among were from cool, cool California. “We came from Michigan, so that was sort of intimidating,” she said. And nobody was cool unless they wore French Vuarnet cat-eye sunglasses. So the kids pleaded with their mother, hoping to fit in.
“We just begged and begged and begged until we got some Vuarnets,” she said. “It was a big deal.”
Cargill, a bookworm, absorbed a sense of Sun Valley slope style from her aunt who was well-settled in Idaho’s Wood River Valley before Cargill’s family arrived. She was a buyer for Snug Mountaineering, a landmark ski shop.
“She lived in an A-frame with shag carpet and a round fireplace,” Cargill said. “She had the big collars and she went on these sailing trips with her boyfriend. She was the epitome of cool.”
With an inside track, Cargill started to catch up with her peers and was among the first to don a Powderhorn jacket, designed in Jackson Hole, distinctly faddish and sporting a western leather yoke. Then came North Face and other brands.
Out of The Roundhouse
But clothes don’t ski and Cargill barely could. “I never knew what a race turn was at that time,” she said.
“The first race I had to do was a downhill,” she said, a long speed test with few turns. “It’s the same course that they used for pros for a while — right out of The Roundhouse,” a lodge perched midway up the mountain.
She became comfortable on her skis by the time she attended the University of Michigan. She tested the competitive moguls scene, but didn’t find her niche. A free-skiing competition in Crested Butte, Colorado, offered her a new challenge — unbridled skiing down large, gnarly faces where an athlete could show off her abilities.
She wanted access to more of those slopes. Jackson Hole’s geography “just drew me in,” she said, so she settled there in 1994.
The Tetons “taught me everything about humility,” she said. “These mountains shaped who I am, because you have to have tenacity. You’ve got to get back up and try it again to succeed around here.”
She competed in free-sking events in places as far away as Argentina and Alaska. But the women’s events were a sideshow, she said, paying her $500 for first place compared to the men’s prize of $2,500.
“I never made any money in a career as a competing athlete,” she said. She did make a name, however, and was crowned the women’s world free-skiing champion in 1997.
“There weren’t that many women living here doing what I was doing at the time,” Cargill said of Jackson Hole. She had to put up with discrimination and sexism.
“These mountains shaped who I am, because you have to have tenacity. You’ve got to get back up and try it again to succeed around here.”A.J. Cargill
Early in her Jackson Hole career she was invited onto the “Hollywood box,” the exclusive first aerial tram ride of the day at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, a ride once reserved for sponsored athletes, the beautiful people and their photographers.
“I was the only female to walk out there,” she said of her first morning at the tram loading dock. “My heart was beating hard, and I was super intimidated because everyone had these long skis, and they’re looking at you, and they’ve got, like, this moxie, this attitude.
“I’ve got my skis up on my ski boot so that my skis look longer,” she said. “They start giving Jason, the guy I’m with, a ton of shit that that we’re sleeping together,” she said. “And I’m standing right there.”
Only after she showed the men she could keep up, “they started slowly letting me in,” she said.
Slowly. Ski photographers at the time favored male models and gave them the first shots at pristine slopes. “I didn’t get that real opportunity to show people what I could do early on because of those types of things.”
Cargill’s off-slope mettle — she was a bartender who wouldn’t take guff at ski patrollers’ favorite pub — earned her an invitation to that elite cadre. She spent 20 years reducing avalanche risks and rescuing hapless skiers from Jackson Hole’s slopes.
Skiing the Grand
The Tetons turned Cargill on to telemark skiing with a free-heel binding that allowed her to get into the backcountry. The telemark gear at the time provided less control than a conventional ski-area binding and using it on steep slopes added a degree of risk.
No woman had descended the Grand Teton on telemark gear; it took Cargill three attempts before she even got to the summit of the 13,775-foot high peak. The ski route is unforgiving. If you fall, you die. The hardest part for Cargill was an ice-coated cliff where her team paused to use a rope to safeguard the short climb down.
“It was just hairball, hairball — taking my skis off, getting into crampons,” she said. “You’re barely on the edge of something. Don’t make a mistake with anything. Everything matters.”
Off piste, Cargill, now 60 (“I’ve always presented young for my age, and acted young,”) followed her aunt’s footsteps and got into the clothing business in Jackson Hole, becoming a buyer for a high-profile downtown sports store. The job fit her like an articulated ski glove.
“You get to go look at all the Patagonia stuff for next year, and you get to decide, like ‘what colors should we have in the store? How am I going to put them together?’” she said. “That’s when it really came alive for me.”
Even before she moved to stylish Sun Valley, what she wore on the modest Midwest hills made a difference to her outlook, she said. It’s part of the reason she and Heather Featherman started Alpine Revival, a sweater company that’s bringing back the bold colors and designs in functional, elegant cashmere wool.
“That sweater changed how I saw myself.”A.J. Cargill
She tells the story about how she was 7 when she got a ski sweater for Christmas. “It had personality, and it even had frogs on the sleeves,” she told an audience recently.
That it was an advertised label — Beconta — added to its luster. “It was a brand that was known and had some cachet,” she told WyoFile
“When I put it on, I stood a little taller,” she recently told an audience. “I felt like a skier, like I belonged to this world that was so much bigger than our little ski hill in Michigan.
“I started finding the courage to make turns, hit little jumps, and I even started trying the harder stuff. That sweater changed how I saw myself.”
In her journey — it even included a couple of seasons rowing a raft through the Grand Canyon — one decision stands out. Moving to Wyoming was “the best choice I ever made,” she said.
“It just welcomed me with open arms,” she said of the Equality State, despite the sexist remarks she had to endure. “That’s their problem,” she said of the men who made them.
“I do think it’s still true that women have to work harder just to get the same stuff,” she said of today’s world. Nevertheless, “we have it way better than they had it 100 years ago, way better. I really hope it doesn’t go backwards — the other direction.
“That’s the most terrifying and terrible thing about living right at this moment — seeing some of the backward steps that a lot of people, men and women, are willing to allow or choose. It doesn’t seem right or like progress or kind or thoughtful. Everything seems wrong about that.”
Women can hold on to what they’ve achieved, she believes. “So as long as I can keep earning my spot, I think I’m proving it for the younger generation.”

name: WyoFile
title: Once they’re gone, they’re gone forever
text:
Does anyone remember when Wyomingites spoke with one voice and our representatives in Washington said, “Screw you”? I do.

Opinion

Remember The One Big Beautiful Bill? It was designed to reward the rich and add to our massive deficit. It did both quite well. It was also designed to sell off our public lands, an idea that more than 90% of Wyomingites surveyed opposed. Lawmakers from Montana said, “hell no,” and threatened to vote against the bill. So, the sponsors of the bill took Montana’s public lands off the auction block. 
What did our three courageous representatives in Washington do? They voted for it, without even a squeak. Fortunately technical factors removed that part of the bill, but U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman has doubled down by leading the charge to get rid of our public lands and roadless areas in spite of massive public opposition from her constituents. And now she is on her way to becoming our U.S. senator, where she would continue her war against public lands and Wyoming sportsmen and sportswomen. Sen. John Barrasso will continue to sell us down the river in his own quiet way. If elected, U.S. Congress hopeful Chuck Gray will do whatever he is told by the Trump administration; what that will be remains to be seen. Our “true conservative” state legislators, like Sen. Bob Ide, are no better; they want all federal public lands gone. 
Do not be fooled by the argument that Wyoming should manage what are now Bureau of Land Management lands, national forests, parks and monuments. While the feds manage lands for many uses, including beauty and recreation, Wyoming manages state-owned lands through the five-person Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners following one constitutionally mandated goal: to maximize income from the property over which it has jurisdiction. Just look at what the board did when it granted Prism Logistics a gravel mine lease on the face of Casper Mountain. Those beautiful state lands are used by citizens for hiking and general enjoyment. While the Natrona County community banded against the mine, the board leased it without considering the community’s desires. (The board later flipped its stance in the face of major public opposition to the project.) With that vote, they tried to gift the community an eyesore that we can enjoy every new day for eternity. The issue is on appeal before the Wyoming Supreme Court. Fingers crossed. 
The state of Wyoming lacks the resources of the federal government to manage the vast properties it would acquire if the proponents of the transfer were to succeed. The only solution would be to turn the land into money and divest ownership. Prime recreational land would be sold to the highest bidder so that some wealthy landowner would be able to fence and sign it off from us ordinary people. The rich would rejoice, as would the powerful mineral extractors, who would no longer suffer under the yoke of federal regulations. Of course, the less-appealing properties would remain in state hands, unless and until the land board could turn a nickel with them.
One need only look at the occasions when wealthy out-of–state “ranchers” from California or Texas have traded lands they have purchased to the land board for school sections of lesser financial value, with the exclusive goal of blocking public access to national forests or other public lands. If Wyoming gains federal properties, they will sell them off or exploit them — especially the desirable ones —  to our detriment. Imagine, “Mr. Musk, may I hunt on your so-called ranch?” I have fished in Colorado, where most of the land is privately owned. One either pays for the “privilege” or stands elbow to elbow with other fishermen on the few public pieces of water. We are so spoiled in Wyoming, we don’t even appreciate what we have. There is a reason out-of-staters come to Wyoming to fish and hunt.
Everyone should take the time to read the opinion from the U.S. 10th Circuit Court authorizing corner crossing to access BLM land. The decision turns on the federal Unlawful Enclosures Act. If the state of Wyoming succeeds in acquiring that land, the act would no longer protect us and corner crossing will become illegal trespass: a crime, and a gift to the landed few. 
Of course, it is not even clear that our national representatives want to put the public lands into state hands. My belief is that Rep. Hageman wishes to sell them off at the federal level, “to balance the budget.” Bull. That wouldn’t be a drop in the bucket, but once those lands are gone, they are gone forever. I am not an unmitigated fan of the feds, but on this issue I trust them more than the other side.
Is this really part of the Trump agenda?  Why do our representatives disregard what us Wyomingites think? Who is their master? Only one explanation makes sense: money. Where do mystery out-of-state campaign dollars come from? Could it be from persons who have plans for our public lands?
Cowboy ethics: “Ride for the brand.” Our delegation is truly “riding for the brand,” just not our brand. Let’s cure that problem when we vote.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: PACs for and against Prop 1 raise more than $2.5 million in the last two weeks
text:
The groups opposing and supporting Proposition 1, the proposed abortion rights initiative that will be on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, collected more than $2.5 million total in just under two weeks. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)The political action committee opposing Idaho’s Proposition 1 abortion rights initiative collected nearly $1.5 million since the end of September, buoyed by two large donations from churches. 
The Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, reported the previously announced $1 million donation from the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on Oct. 8. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated another $300,000 to the PAC opposing the initiative the next day.
Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions

Since Sept. 29, Too Extreme for Idaho received $153,985 from 32 individual people and $1.3 million from four organizations, including the two churches. 
Too Extreme for Idaho has raised a total of just over $4 million, campaign finance data shows. 
As of Monday, the PAC supporting the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, brought in more than $630,000 since Sept. 29. The largest donation came from the federal Government that Works PAC, based out of Washington, D.C, which gave $250,000. 
Oklahoma-based billionaire philanthropist Lynn Schusterman donated $200,000 on Sept. 30, campaign finance data shows. Since Sept. 29, the PAC received $265,290 from 81 individuals and $370,000 from three organizations. 
In total, Idahoans United has collected more than $5.6 million. 
 Independent expenditures for and against Prop 1 total more than $2.5 million 

Groups and individuals spent more than $2.5 million combined to support and oppose Prop 1 in independent expenditures, which includes spending by organizations or individuals spent directly to support or oppose a ballot measure. 
The Idaho Secretary of State’s office in late September and early October began sharing a message with those filing campaign finance reports to request that any spending for or against a ballot initiative, constitutional amendment or advisory question be reported as an independent expenditure to help “voters more easily find and understand spending related to ballot measures.” 
The notice, first uploaded to the campaign finance reporting portal the last week of September and then updated on Oct. 7, also asked filers to amend previous campaign finance reports to classify spending related to ballot measures as independent expenditures. This request is likely why this category of election spending seemed to jump significantly from a previous Idaho Capital Sun analysis of campaign spending data.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
Groups, including several county-level Republican central committees, as of Monday have spent more than $1.4 million to oppose the measure, campaign finance data shows.
The anti-abortion group Right to Life Idaho PAC also reported spending more than $17,600 on advertising regarding the ballot measure, but reported its position as “N/A” in its campaign finance disclosure report. The same PAC reported a little over $1,000 in opposition to the measure, campaign finance data shows. 
Too Extreme for Idaho led independent expenditure spending with over $1.2 million spent in opposition. Idaho Chooses Life also reported spending more than $66,000 to oppose the initiative. 
Idahoans United reported spending $1.1 million in independent expenditures to support the initiative. Boise Democratic Socialists of America, Incorporated spent just under $760, and Planned Parenthood Votes Idaho PAC reported around $330 to support the initiative.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Families want meeting with UAB officials over organ harvesting of loved ones
text:
Families of loved ones whose organs were harvested after they died in Alabama prisons prepare to speak with reporters after a hearing on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Montgomery County Courthouse. The families want to meet with officials with the University of Alabama Birmingham. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Families of incarcerated Alabamians whose organs were harvested after their deaths demanded a meeting with University of Alabama Birmingham officials Tuesday as delays in their civil lawsuit continue to mount.
Speaking after a court hearing in Montgomery, in which UAB sought to have some counts dismissed, relatives said they wanted administrators to listen to stories of their relatives and demanded justice for their loved ones.
“If the attorneys for the Alabama Department of Corrections and UAB want to prolong this, they are the only ones who are benefitting financially,” said Simone Moore, whose brother Kelvin Moore died in Limestone Correctional Facility in 2023. “I don’t know what they are telling the trustees at UAB, but I believe the trustees should summon the attorneys and say to the attorneys, ‘Give us justification why you are prolonging this process and putting off the inevitable?’”
UAB declined comment on Tuesday.
In 2024, eight families sued the Alabama Department of Corrections, alleging that the department harvested the organs of their loved ones who died while in prison, and sent them to the University of Alabama Birmingham Heersink School of Medicine.
According to the lawsuit, a group of medical students from the school noticed that many of the specimens they worked with in the curriculum were taken from people who died while in Alabama’s prisons. The plaintiffs allege the organs were harvested without their permission, a violation of the law.
Montgomery Circuit Judge J.R. Gaines heard arguments Tuesday over UAB’s motion to dismiss but did not immediately rule on it. A trial in the case is tentatively scheduled to begin December 2027.
Since the original lawsuit, several other families have filed separate actions that have since been consolidated.
The university and the ADOC argued in February 2025 that state agencies enjoy absolute immunity and therefore cannot be held liable in civil lawsuits.
Gaines ruled against UAB and ADOC in April 2025 and allowed the case to proceed into discovery. However, defendants appealed the ruling for one of the lawsuits filed by the family of Charles Edward Singleton, 74, who died while in prison and whose organs were harvested without their permission.
Defense counsel appealed directly to the Alabama Supreme Court. In January 2026,  the justices dismissed six of the seven claims, and leaving one related to the Alabama Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (AUAGA). The justices wrote that attorneys for the defendants had not formally requested that it be dismissed in circuit court.
During the hearing Tuesday, UAB and ADOC attorneys argued that the statute of limitations to file a civil claim based on AUAGA had expired and that the officials who signed the agreement are individuals employed by the state and have immunity. Defense counsel also sought to dismiss the additional claims filed by plaintiffs against individuals on the grounds that the families filed their lawsuits after the two-year statute of limitations had expired.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs said defendants do not have immunity from their alleged wrongdoing and that the timeline on the statute of limitations did not begin until the family members knew they had a case, which did not happen until well after the autopsy had been done and was within the statute of limitations.
Several families Tuesday spoke about the grief they experienced knowing that their loved ones’ organs had been removed.
“It has been heartbreaking because every time we go to court, we get to live it and do not see that justice has been done,” said Tyrus Franklin, the brother of Kelvin Moore.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee GOP senator seeks one-month gas tax break
text:
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has approved a measure to allow farmers and loggers to use a lower-cost type of diesel through the October 2026 harvesting season, but now a state Senator wants a gas tax holiday for everyone. (Photo: John Partipilo/John Partipilo)A Tennessee Republican lawmaker is asking the governor to cut motorists some slack at the pump by calling for a one-month break on the state’s gas tax.
Sen. Tom Hatcher of Maryville sent a letter to Gov. Bill Lee requesting he suspend Tennessee’s 27.4-cent gas tax during November, with the average price of regular gas at about $3.90 per gallon in Tennessee.
“I believe the extraordinary circumstances facing Tennessee motorists warrant consideration of a temporary measure,” Hatcher said in an Oct. 7 letter to the governor.
The governor and lawmakers are likely leery about giving up a revenue stream as Tennessee struggles with a backlog of $58 billion to $87 billion in road and bridge construction projects over the next three decades and needs $3.6 billion annually to maintain and improve roads. But Hatcher said in his letter that he is seeking only a one-month suspension, which would allow for “minimal impact” on gas tax revenue, which “supports important transportation priorities” statewide. 
Hatcher told the Lookout the break would match the governor’s action on dyed diesel fuel, which is allowing farmers and loggers to use the cheaper, tax-exempt form of diesel normally allowed for off-road equipment on public roads during October’s harvest season and avoid record-high costs of more than $6 per gallon for regular diesel fuel. The diesel is dyed red to differentiate it from regular diesel for tax identification purposes.
The requested gas tax cut would take effect Nov. 1 and last 30 days, according to Hatcher.
“We’re allowing the farmers to use the different diesel that’s cheaper for them, and they need the help,” Hatcher said. “But also regular citizens need some help, and that would be right before Christmas time … and, hopefully, help them some also.”
Republican lawmakers asked Lee to allow the use of untaxed dyed diesel fuel on roads through Nov. 15, but he declined to extend the waiver past October. The ability to use dyed diesel for a full tank would save about $102 when filling up a 200-gallon semi truck tank.
House Democrats were rebuffed earlier this year when they urged the governor to put funds for a gas and diesel tax holiday in his budget. It’s unclear whether a Republican lawmaker will be heard. The governor’s office didn’t respond Tuesday to questions from the Lookout.
Lawmakers passed the IMPROVE Act in 2017, raising the gas tax by six cents and diesel by 10 cents over three years, a move designed to bring in hundreds of millions of dollars for road and bridge construction projects and put a dent in a $10 billion backlog. Simultaneously, the state decreased sales taxes on groceries to 4% as a way to ease the pain at the pump.
Despite that offset, the gas tax increase of nearly a decade ago has haunted lawmakers who supported it, costing Republican Rep. Barry Doss his seat in the following election and hurting veteran Republican Rep. Dennis Powers at the polls when he lost in this year’s primary.
