name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Teacher recruitment and retention a continuing problem, report suggests
text:
The number of teachers in the state has declined in the past 10 years. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)To enter the teaching profession in New Hampshire is to navigate a series of financial trade-offs. 
The median two-bedroom rent in the state in 2025 was $2,024 per month. The average monthly wage for a teacher? Several hundred dollars less.
And becoming a teacher means earning nearly 34% less than other New Hampshire professionals with similar educational backgrounds, according to estimates by the Economic Policy Institute. 
Those numbers are at the heart of a new report pointing to a continuing challenge. As New Hampshire public schools face declining enrollment, they are also contending with another long-term concern: recruiting and retaining teachers. 
And recent state projections suggest the gap is set to persist. 
The report, published Tuesday by the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, points to a steady decline in the number of teachers currently working in the state in the last 10 years, a decrease in the number of teaching students to replace those teachers, and a rising proportion of teachers who are in the later stages of their careers.
Together, the data suggest long-term headwinds for New Hampshire public schools that could affect student achievement and future economic growth in the state, the Fiscal Policy Institute report concludes.
“We really wanted to study … what the future of public education will look like,” said Ben Reynolds, a senior policy analyst at NHFPI. 
The report emerged as local school budgets enter the spotlight this election season. When New Hampshire residents vote in the Nov. 3 general election, they will face a ballot question asking whether they support imposing a tax cap on their school district to limit year-over-year tax increases to inflation. Under a state law passed this year, if at least 60% of voters in a school district approve that question, the cap will take effect for two years.
Democrats argue teacher pay is too low because of low state support for public schools; most public school funding comes from local property taxes. Republicans say school districts spend too much on administration and should spend more of their current budgets on teacher salaries. If passed, the November ballot measure would limit a district’s administrative spending to 6% of its overall budget. 
Continual decline and future challenges
The number of teachers in the state has declined in the past 10 years. In the 2025-2026 school year, there were 13,648 “full-time equivalent” educators in New Hampshire, a 5.7% drop from the 14,473 in 2015-2016. That metric is not the same as the true number of teachers — multiple part-time educators can constitute one full-time equivalent position — but it does show the overall decline in employment, the report notes.
The 5.7% drop in teachers took place as overall public school enrollment declined 12.8% in the same time period. Republican lawmakers have pointed to that enrollment drop as evidence that public schools should be scaling down in size, not expanding.
But Reynolds said the declining student population does not necessarily justify the loss of teachers. School districts still must hire specialty teachers to meet minimum state standards, and staffing levels cannot always drop proportionately, he noted
“You still need those teachers even if the classroom’s a little bit smaller,” he said. 
Despite projections that school enrollment will continue to decrease amid a nationwide drop in the birth rate, the state Department of Employment Security estimates that the number of teaching jobs in New Hampshire will increase between 2024 and 2034 by 3.5%, according to the report. 
The problem: Schools will likely struggle to fill those new jobs. 
While the number of teaching jobs could increase from 15,611 in 2024 to 16,164 in 2034, the state will face an average shortfall of 1,114 teachers per year, the department estimates. Across each public school grade level, the number of vacancies in New Hampshire will likely dwarf the number of prospective teachers, the data suggests.
Research suggests a higher turnover of teachers — and a lack of experience and effectiveness — leads to reduced student outcomes and can limit the earning potential of those students when they graduate.
But Reynolds notes that it also affects the teachers themselves. A constant churn means there are fewer opportunities for the mentorship and growth that can build effective educators, he said.
“Having that network and support there really helps improve young teachers,” he said.
And when teachers leave, he said: “The remaining teachers there (are) facing heavier workloads or additional responsibilities.”
Older teachers, fewer students
As the pool of teachers has shrunk in recent years, a larger share of New Hampshire’s teachers are nearing retirement, the data shows.
In 2004, 8,889 teachers were 55 or older. By 2025, that number had grown to 13,432, a 51% increase. Overall, 33.7% of New Hampshire teachers were in that older age group in 2025, up from 22.1% in 2004.
Meanwhile, the pipeline to replace the current crop of teachers is shrinking rapidly. The number of New Hampshire students earning a bachelor’s degree in teaching dropped from 442 in 2020 to 283 in 2025 — down from 567 in 2015. The state has seen a 47% drop in teaching graduates from 2010 to 2025, the report notes.
The aging challenges reflect broader demographic trends in New Hampshire, the second oldest state behind Maine. But for public schools, it will mean tougher recruitment battles.
“A smaller pool of graduates will likely make hiring teachers locally more difficult, particularly in rural or lower-paying school districts that have to compete with higher-paying districts,” the report states.
Teachers facing low salaries
In a Reaching Higher New Hampshire survey last month that asked teachers to pick “one change” to improve recruitment and retention, the frontrunner suggestion was clear: “increased pay.”
Tuesday’s report suggests New Hampshire’s public schools are far behind other industries when it comes to salaries. Though National Education Association data indicates the average teacher salary in New Hampshire in 2024-2025 was $69,432, the starting salary was $44,010. 
Those numbers are comparable to Maine, at $65,621 (average) and $44,152 (starting), and Vermont, at $71,871 and $46,963. But when compared to New Hampshire’s “minimum living wage” of $83,057, a number calculated by the Economic Policy Institute as the amount needed for an adult and a child to meet a “modest standard of living,” those numbers fall short. 
Meanwhile, U.S. Census American Community Survey data indicates that teachers have long made less than their counterparts with bachelor’s degrees — and the gap is widening. While weekly New Hampshire teacher wages were 29.6% below similar degree holders from 2005 to 2009, they were 34.5% below between 2015 and 2019, the report notes. 
A separate analysis by the Economic Policy Institute found that New Hampshire teachers in 2024-2025 earned 33.8% less than their similarly educated peers, even when adjusting for weeks worked to account for school summer vacation. 
Complicating the average wages, New Hampshire’s local property tax funding model allows high-property-value districts to offer far higher salaries to teachers than less resourced districts. The result: while a new teacher in New Castle made $59,396 in 2025-2026, a new teacher in Bath made $36,148, the report notes.
The disparity is one more factor in a broader, years-long problem, Reynolds notes. 
“They love to teach,” he said. “They’re very passionate about it, and they understand the importance of providing a high-quality education for these kids. But if the conversation doesn’t also happen about them, and they almost feel like they’re left behind, that could cause even more attrition than we’re already seeing.”

name: National
title: With fewer public defenders, indigent defendants pay the price
text:
A courtroom at the Placer County Superior Court in Roseville, California, earlier this year. In California and other states, the rosters of public defenders have been shrinking at an alarming rate, often leaving defendants in jail for days, weeks or months without access to an attorney. (Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr./ CalMatters)AUSTIN, Texas — It was a good day for the defense.
Standing in front of a judge in Austin’s Blackwell-Thurman Criminal Justice Center, attorney Matthew Shrum secured a ruling that spared his client from serious punishment on a shoplifting charge.
In the hallway immediately afterward, the defendant thanked Shrum with an appreciative hug.
“She walked out of there a free lady,” Shrum observed later. “It was Christmas in October.”
The 49-year-old Austin lawyer has spent most of his 20-year legal career as a defense attorney, and since 2023, he has been affiliated with the nonprofit Capital Area Private Defender Service, one of two entities in Travis County charged with representing indigent clients who can’t afford an attorney. The Travis County Public Defender’s Office performs a similar mission.
In 1963, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that under the Fourteenth Amendment, states must provide lawyers to criminal defendants who cannot afford one. But throughout Texas and many other states, the rosters of public defenders have been shrinking at an alarming rate, often leaving defendants in jail for days, weeks or months without access to an attorney.
Many public defenders are leaving, while those that remain are forced to juggle enormous caseloads. At one point, Shrum told Stateline, he had more than 500 cases. The overload facing him and other public defenders in Travis County, he said, results from “more indigent people than there were lawyers to take court-appointed cases.”
States put criminal justice, marijuana policies before voters in 2026

In a report to the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, which was created to monitor and partly fund county indigent defense programs, researchers from the Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M found that the state lost 1,345 attorneys tasked with representing indigent clients between 2014 and 2024 — nearly a fourth of all such attorneys. The decline occurred even as the total number of attorneys in Texas grew by more than 25,000.
A 2023 study by the Sixth Amendment Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, ranked Texas 46th nationally in per capita spending on indigent defense at $9.19. “Some states are struggling more than others,” said Aditi Goel, the center’s executive director.
Goel said there are no national statistics on the shortage of public defenders.
“It’s a complete black box,” she told Stateline. “We do not know as a country right now. There is absolutely no way to know whether every single person is getting their right to an attorney, and if not, how long they’re waiting for their right to an attorney.”
Problems across states
But there is plenty of evidence to suggest that jurisdictions across the nation are struggling to provide attorneys to the estimated 80%-90% of criminal defendants who cannot afford one.
Earlier this year, for example, the Oregon Supreme Court ruled that more than 1,400 criminal cases had to be dismissed because there weren’t enough lawyers to represent the defendants. A 2022 report by the American Bar Association found that Oregon would need an additional 1,296 attorneys — more than three times the number it had at the time — to meet its constitutional obligations.
In Pennsylvania, a 2024 study by the Quattrone Center for the Fair Administration of Justice at the University of Pennsylvania found that in a typical year, the state’s 850 public defenders are assigned cases that would require 1,200 lawyers to provide adequate representation. Sixty of Pennsylvania’s 66 counties don’t have enough attorneys, the study found.
Last year, a report by the Deason Criminal Justic Reform Center at Southern Methodist University in Dallas estimated that Kansas needed to add 277 public defenders to its roster of 123 lawyers to provide effective counsel to every indigent defendant. And a 2022 study found that New Mexico, which had 295 public defenders, needed an additional 602 full-time attorneys to provide effective counsel.
District attorney elections linked to more prison admissions during ‘tough on crime’ era

In Texas, the shrinking number of attorneys has been caused in large part by retirements and burnout among older defense attorneys and an accompanying shortage of younger lawyers or law school graduates willing to replace them. Instead, many younger lawyers are drawn to more financially rewarding jobs with private firms.
The growing complexity of evidence such as videos and body camera footage and increases in prosecution budgets also are contributing factors.
The indigent defense commission says one in three attorneys handling indigent defense in Texas is overburdened, carrying caseloads that exceed the commission’s caseload guidelines.
“It’s a big demographic problem of lawyers aging out, nobody to replace them,” said Keith Lauerman, another Austin public defender who is close to ending his 33-year legal career to become a Red Cross volunteer.  Lauerman, 70, says he’s enjoyed his years representing defendants but felt it was time to “pivot for a third act” after working as an attorney and school teacher.
Cited for contempt
A number of states and communities have been credited with taking steps to shore up support for public defenders while are others are embroiled in turmoil over the issue.
In California, San Francisco Public Defender Mano Raju was cited for contempt by Superior Court Judge Harry Dorfman after he announced that he would periodically stop taking “a very small percentage” of new cases because of “a dramatic increase” in active cases coming into his office.
“The pressure has been tremendous,” Raju told Stateline, citing a 78% increase in active misdemeanor cases and a 56% increase in active felony cases from 2019 to 2026.  Raju, the state’s only elected public defender, was also hit with $26,000 in sanctions by Dorfman but the fines haven’t gone into effect while the case is on appeal.
The Los Angeles County Public Defender, the largest public defense agency in the country, also made news following a study that defenders are carrying workloads more than double the volume that allows them to effectively represent their clients.
A new commission co-organized by former District Attorney of San Francisco Chesa Boudin has been empaneled to push California toward new standards and legal regulations for public defense.
“There was a crisis playing out in plain view and people weren’t paying attention,” said Boudin, who is the founding executive director of the Criminal Law & Justice Center at the UC Berkeley School of Law.
Texas is one of about 15 states in which counties bear the responsibility for representing indigent defendants, although the Texas Indigent Defense Commission provides limited state funds through grants partly reimbursing counties for their costs.
“Travis County, like a lot of counties, we have an attorney shortage,” said Geoff Burkhart, county executive for Community Legal Services, which oversees Travis County’s two indigent defense organizations. “We don’t have enough lawyers for public defense.”
Working miracles
Supporters of the Capital Area Public Defenders Service and the Travis County Public Defender’s Office turned out at a September budget hearing before Travis County Commissioners to urge a funding boost for the organizations. Kaylee Brilhart, who is in her third year as an attorney at the public defender’s office, warned that the “public defense system in Travis County is at capacity.” She said there are people in jail who have been “without attorneys for months.”
“I have clients who express gratitude just because I answer their calls from the jail or I respond to their texts or phone calls,” she said. “We work miracles in our office every day.”
The larger Capital Area Private Defender Service, known as CAPDS, was created in 2015 to manage and oversee appointments of private attorneys contracted to represent indigent clients.  The Travis County Public Defender’s Office, composed of staff attorneys and support personnel, was created in 2020 to further expand indigent services.
As of the 2024 fiscal year, the two organizations spent a total of $29 million on indigent defense services, handling 17,000 cases, with CAPDS shouldering the biggest caseload.
The leaders of both organizations say they are committed to the highest quality representation but acknowledge that the lingering shortage of attorneys is a constant challenge.  “You’re doing it because you believe in justice and want to help people,” said Adeola Ogunkeyede, the county’s chief public defender, while acknowledging that “there are not enough attorneys to represent people.”
Bradley Hargis, executive director of CAPDS, said the shortage has worsened over time.  “It started quietly,” he said. “There was an occasional shortage, an occasional day in which we were struggling to find the right attorney for each case, and then those occasional days became more regular, and then became chronic.
“It leads us, our attorneys, having caseloads greater than we would want, and really leads to overwork and burnout, and that’s what we are trying to guard against — overworking our attorneys,” he added.
Two of the state’s most populous counties — Travis, anchored by Austin, and Bexar, anchored by San Antonio —  have seen their indigent defense pools shrink by 50% over the past five years amid a 26% drop in the state’s urban counties.
In rural Texas counties, the number of public defenders has dropped by 29% in the past decade, from 1,926 to 1,371 attorneys.
Public Defenders Were Scarce Before COVID. It’s Much Worse Now.

After Bandera County Judge Richard Evans noticed an alarming absence of defense attorneys in his home county, he rallied leaders in neighboring jurisdictions to create the five-county Hill Country Public Defenders Office. Similar multicounty defense organizations have sprouted up elsewhere across the state.
“I really do believe we’ve improved indigent defense in the region,” said chief public defender Karli Kennell of Boerne, Texas.  The nearly six-year-old defense organization includes 20 attorneys and a staff of 30 charged with Kennell’s commitment “to go in and fight for our clients.”
“It’s important to me that my attorneys are advocates, that they’re not just a plea mill.  So now we don’t have as many people waiting in jail without an attorney,” she said.  “I do take pride in what we’ve done in this region because I think most of Texas is still struggling quite a bit.”
Pamela Metzger, executive director of the Deason Criminal Justice Reform Center at Southern Methodist University, said the stakes could not be higher.
“Every day that an arrested person doesn’t have a lawyer is a day that their constitutional rights are being violated — period, full stop,” she said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: What one broken New Hampshire bridge tells us about America
text:
The bridge on Windy Row in Hancock over the spillway for Halfmoon Pond, photographed in 2020. (Photo by Abbe Hamilton/Monadnock Ledger-Transcript)
I have a bridge that I’d like to sell you — maybe you’ve heard that one before. Actually, you’ve bought this bridge once before, long ago. I want you to buy it again. There’s a catch: this bridge has moved — not physically — but it’s in a different country. 
In 1936, Peterborough flooded. The New Hampshire town sits down low where the Nubanusit Brook runs into the Contoocook River, a good spot when the textile mills were powered by flowing water, but water power had its revenge in the wet spring of 1936. In the old black and white photos, the river is a torrent, flooding the main streets.
Peterborough wasn’t alone in these floods. After a snowy winter, weeks of heavy March rain and ice jams in the rivers led to flooding in much of New England. In places the Connecticut River jumped its banks, cresting at almost 38 feet in Hartford, the highest ever recorded. As many as 200 people across the Northeast died in the floods, and 14,000 were homeless.
In response Congress passed the Flood Control Act of 1936. Getting enough votes was a wrangle. Everyone wanted a piece of it — a needed dam or levee if it was in your district, pork if it was in someone else’s district. Peterborough would get the Edward MacDowell Dam, but not before the town flooded again in the great hurricane of 1938. It would take 12 years before the $2 million dam was built, creating a reservoir covering 165 acres linked to a spillway to the north of Peterborough’s downtown to discharge flood waters. It was a big, landscape-shifting project, one that is managed today by a full-time staff from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
As a small part of the dam, the Army Corps of Engineers built a bridge, just 224 feet long, to carry a dirt road over the spillway. In 1948, the Corps gifted the Windy Row Bridge to the town of Hancock and the town voted to accept it. “We thought we were getting a million-dollar bridge for free,” one old-timer told me.
All good in 1948, but today the bridge is closed. (You can still walk across or, if you dare, ride a horse.) The steel bridge has rusted into obsolescence, earning a troubling engineering score. The Windy Row Bridge is “structurally deficient.” On a scale in which nine is excellent and zero is failed, the concrete deck and the steel substructure (which distributes the weight to the foundation) rates a five, and the superstructure — the main load-bearing support — just a four. Recent inspections have found potholes in the concrete roadway, exposed rebar, missing nuts and bolts, “large holes” in the beams and bridge railing, broken welds, “hollow soundings” at the joints, peeling lead paint, and overall, extensive rust. This report card lands this deteriorating bridge in bottom 12% of all New Hampshire bridges. 
The spillway bridge joins 1,294 others in New England that are “red listed,” about 9% of all the bridges we may be driving over. (There are 42,000 bridges across the country that are “poor,” about 6.8% of the total.) It may cost $3 million to replace this short bridge and that may not happen for 20 years — or ever. It’s not even in line on any list. With a traffic load of only 243 cars daily, and another 180 bridges in the state needing work, it could be stuck in the back of the queue forever.
The U.S. economy is 10 times larger today than when the federal government stepped in to protect the small town of Peterborough, and yet today we say we can’t afford to repair thousands of bridges, dams, roads, schools, wastewater plants, drinking water plants, ports, railroads and public parks. Welcome to the land of the red-listed, white, and blue. 
We have moved to a triage model for public life. The public realm is shrinking. Consider, for example, the Rural Electrification Act of 1936. The goal was to bring power to every home. In our time, the build-out of broadband internet access in the 1990s created winners and losers. That’s how we proceed: Some schools, public parks and museums gleam with new construction, and the rest, serving the less fortunate, limp along on life-support. 
What you see in this rusting, broken bridge depends on your politics. Maybe you see government overreach, pork barrel projects c. 1936, or environmental overreach — you don’t like dams, even though this one saved Peterborough from flooding in 1987. Or you see the ghost of the American Century, the long-gone, ruined shell of the can-do industrial colossus that triumphed in World War II. 
I see a monument to our fractious republic as it stands, rotting away, and I see a different future. Imagine an America where all the bridges, roads and dams are in good order. There is no “red list.” An America where your flight leaves on time — every time — and where you can catch a train between cities, fast and frequent. But to get there, first we’d have to cross one “structurally deficient” bridge. We’d have to admit that this rusting bridge is us.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Cooke tries to pick off rural votes in second effort to flip Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District
text:
Democratic congressional candidate Rebecca Cooke and former U.S. Sen. Jon Tester (D-Montana) appear at an agricultural policy roundtable event at the Eau Claire-area farm Cooke grew up on. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)At a roundtable on her family’s Eau Claire area farm last week with former Montana Sen. Jon Tester, Democrat Rebecca Cooke argued that if she’s elected to represent Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, she’ll take on the issues that have been plaguing rural America for decades and work to undo the Trump administration policies that are making those problems worse. 
But Democrats all over the country, including in Wisconsin and the 3rd CD have had trouble winning rural support in the past. 
“We need people who are willing to stand up and speak. I come from an area that in the 1960s was solid blue, and now it’s solid red,” Tester said at the roundtable. That political shift happened, he said, “because Democrats don’t show up.” Nowadays, he added, “Republicans take it for granted” that rural areas are mainly red.  “So the opportunity here to help flip this situation around,” Tester said, “so we’ve got people in Washington D.C. that are working for us, everybody — not just rural America, but everybody — but making sure that rural America is at the table is really, really important.” 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Ron Kind represented Wisconsin’s 3rd CD for decades. After his retirement, state Sen. Brad Pfaff (D-Onalaska), the former state agriculture secretary, ran and lost to Derrick Van Orden in 2022. Cooke subsequently lost narrowly when she challenged Van Orden in 2024. 
“Derrick Van Orden has put rural America squarely last,” Cooke said after the event on her family’s farm. “He’s voted time and again for the war in Iran six times that has increased diesel prices, increased fertilizer prices … Farmers here in the 3rd Congressional District are reeling from the impact of reciprocal tariffs on our soybeans and our cranberries, are struggling because of the increased input costs from diesel and fertilizer prices with this war in Iran. And Congress’s failure to expand the ACA tax credit premium for three more years has really hurt a lot of farmers, too. They have seen their premiums go up from $400 to $1,800 a month. Derrick Van Orden has not delivered a successful farm bill out of this Congress. I don’t think that he’s really done very much at all to support our family farms or people in agriculture across this district.”
This year, with the national environment fueling Democratic hopes for victories up and down the ticket in states across the country as President Donald Trump’s approval ratings hit record lows, and diesel prices and tariffs on Canadian fertilizer hurt western Wisconsin farmers, Democrats are confident about their chances. The 3rd CD is at the top of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s list of 2026 targets. Both parties and a lineup of outside PACs have already spent nearly $30 million on the district with ads that have become increasingly negative. 
Van Orden, a former U.S. Navy SEAL, has often brought a combative personality, a penchant for social media trolling and an eagerness to support Trump to his role. A member of the House agriculture committee, he’s touted his work on the farm bill and legislative efforts to change visa programs for immigrant dairy workers. A spokesperson for Van Orden did not respond to a request for comment. 
At the Oct. 9 roundtable and during a Wisconsin Farmers Union town hall in Gays Mills the same day, area farmers said Van Orden has done little to help them or mischaracterized their problems while supporting large factory farms over the smaller family operations that define western Wisconsin’s cultural identity even as they struggle to make ends meet. 
The group of farmers at the roundtable complained that it has gotten harder for them to get healthcare coverage and that the Trump administration’s cuts to food programs such as SNAP hurt farmers. They also said that Trump’s crackdown on immigration, which spilled over into western Wisconsin during Operation Metro Surge in the nearby Twin Cities, has hurt the labor they depend on. They also worried that a food system oriented toward giving the biggest players a leg up will hasten the destruction of  their way of life. 
“We can identify the problems, like we know what the issues are, right?” Cooke told the group. “And we need to have people that are solutions-oriented going into Congress. There is a lot of finger-pointing to be had because these are bad things that are happening, but we also need to think about how do we move forward.”
If elected, Cooke will be a first-year Democrat during a Republican presidency but she said she hopes to get assigned to the agriculture committee and that one of her first priorities would be establishing a “right to repair” — which would allow farmers to work on their own machinery rather than paying high prices for repairs at dealerships. She also said she wants to push for a farm bill that “caters to small, mid-size ag,” provide a pathway to citizenship for the district’s immigrant laborers, create a health insurance public option and to expand Medicare to cover vision and dental.
A Rebecca Cooke campaign sign sits in a front yard in Gay Mills. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
In the August primary election, Cooke defeated former Eau Claire City Council president Emily Berge by about 20 points in a contentious race that left some local party activists and voters embittered. Cooke has had to work to try to win those voters back. 
Anthony Chergosky, a political science professor at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse, told the Wisconsin Examiner that a contentious general election with reams of negative ads can often help a candidate bring their team back together after a bruising primary. 
“I think coming out of divisive primaries, parties often confront the challenge of uniting their supporters for the general election,” he said. “There are different ways to go about doing that, but one of the most tried and true methods is a negative campaign against the opposition, because that can really motivate a party’s supporters.” 
At the roundtable on her family farm, a roster of invited guests expressed enthusiastic support for Cooke.
“We can get this woman elected. That’s what we can do by getting one neighbor that never voted before, getting one neighbor who don’t think it’s worth it. It is,” Phil Swanhorst, chair of the Eau Claire County Democratic Party, said. “Each and every one of us can make a difference if we work a little bit harder to get her elected than we did two years ago. We got to get this type of woman in Congress to turn this shit around. We got to do it.”
When Van Orden was first elected in 2022, he beat Pfaff by 3.7 points — a result that many Democrats in the state blamed on the disappearance of national money and support in the final weeks of the race. Critics of the national Democratic party’s decision to pull out of the race pointed to the fact that  Democratic Gov. Tony Evers won the district in his reelection campaign that year. 
Two years ago, Cooke outperformed Vice President Kamala Harris in the district, losing by only 2.7 points compared to Harris’ 7.4 point loss to Trump. This year national Democrats believe that the time is right for Cooke to get the job done. 
Chergosky said that the Cooke campaign doesn’t need to win a landslide among rural voters. Instead, Cooke’s path could involve picking off just enough rural Wisconsinites who vote for her or don’t vote at all — in addition to turning out the Democratic voters in the district’s urban centers of Eau Claire and La Crosse. 
“If Cooke can move the rural margins back in her favor even a little bit, then that would go a long way towards helping her win the district,” Chergosky said. “I guess the good news is that it can’t really get any worse for [Democrats] in many rural communities. And so, if they can turn the tide even a little bit, it could go a long way towards helping them win this district, and others like it.”
At the Farmers Union event in Gays Mills, Cooke was joined on the dais by three Democrats running for legislative seats and Alexander Kent, an independent running for the 3rd CD. None of the Republicans running in the area showed up — a fact that Cooke was quick to note. 
During his four years in office, Van Orden has developed a local reputation for avoiding his constituents. His debate appearance with Cooke next week, on Oct. 20,  will be his first since his 2020 campaign against Kind. He has neglected to hold open town halls with constituents and residents of the district often complain of being blown off by their congressional representative. 
“These are frustrating times for our agricultural communities,” Cooke said. “I’m running against somebody and an administration that has done little to help farmers … I’m here today and showing up because, unlike someone that doesn’t show up, I believe it’s important to have these conversations in our community.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: I updated my Kansas voter registration online. But the process left me with nagging questions.
text:
A voter fills out an advance ballot on July 29, 2022, at the Shawnee County Elections Office. (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Tuesday was the last day to update your voter registration for the November election.
I updated my voter registration because I have recently moved from Shawnee County to Douglas County and because I’m worried about the unfounded claims of large-scale voter fraud by immigrants. My vote matters, and we have seen attempts to remove voters. I still remember when Kris Kobach planned to remove 30,000 voter applications in 2015. His recent probe into voter fraud allegations in Kansas drew national attention. 
Maybe this column will let Kansas officials know that I tried to fill out the paperwork correctly on their poorly designed website before the deadline.
I did a quick Google search for “update Kansas voter registration.” The first result links to the Kansas Secretary of State Elections Voter Registration office, overseen by Secretary of State Scott Schwab, a Republican. I am already losing confidence in this application process after seeing the party. For years, Republicans have used allegations of voting fraud to discredit elections that don’t go their way and to make registration harder and voting more difficult.
The website states that a voter may update his or her registration for a name or address change, or to change party affiliation, by completing a new voter registration form. I’ve voted before. I am not a “new voter.” 
I clicked on the update voter registration icon on the homepage and it took me to the new voter registration page. The site warns: “Please allow time for processing. Your county election officer will notify you when your voter registration is completed successfully or when further action is needed. If you have questions, please call 1-800-262-8683.”
To register to vote online, you must do the following:
 Verify your voting eligibility. Verify that you have a valid driver’s license or non-driver’s identification card. Enter your personal information, review it and submit it. It also states if you do not have a valid driver’s license or non-driver’s identification card, you may register to vote using the following paper form. There’s an icon for the paper application that you click on so you can print off the paper application.
I proceeded with the online voter registration application. The questions are simple. Yes, I am a U.S. citizen. Yes, I will be 18 before Election Day. Yes, I am a resident of Kansas.
It asks whether you have a felony conviction. It says, “Please choose one.” No, I’ve never been convicted of a felony. No, I have not been convicted of a felony with all the terms of my sentence completed and my rights restored. No, I am not currently under sentence for a felony.
I pick “I have never been convicted of a felony.”
The next part of the process requires your name. It should match the name on your driver’s license or non-driver ID card. You enter your name, your date of birth and your driver’s license number, if you have one. To make sure, they ask you to enter your driver’s license number twice.

I’ve always been astounded that registering for a Kansas ID or a Kansas driver’s license doesn’t automatically register you to vote. It’s never made sense. Yes, some people who aren’t allowed to vote still receive a driver’s license or Kansas ID. This is easy to comprehend. But why there isn’t a process in place to automatically register Kansans who can lawfully vote when they get their ID? (State must offer the opportunity to register at motor vehicle agencies, but it’s not an automatic process.)

We can donate our organs after death at the DMV, but we can’t select a party affiliation. It would save everyone so much time and money. 
The form then asks for your voting residence address. It cannot be a P.O. Box. It asked me which county I reside in. I would assume at this point, in the age of artificial intelligence, that the combination of my address, state and ZIP code would auto-populate the county. Nonetheless, I entered my county: Douglas.
It asks whether my mailing address is different from my residential address. It asks whether my voting address has changed since my last registered vote. It asks for my previous street address. When entering data on the website, the previous street address field can only accommodate 20 characters, so I couldn’t enter my full apartment number. I hope the street address information will suffice. Again, I’m asked to enter the county I live in or previously lived in. It also asks my gender: female, male, or other.
The form asks for my party affiliation. I am not affiliated with a party. The options listed below are Democrat, Republican, Libertarian, United, Kansas and no party affiliation.
I haven’t seen a political party advocate for the party I believe I’m part of: the working class. The minimum wage in Kansas hasn’t changed since 2010, at $7.25, and we still haven’t expanded Medicaid. Republicans have controlled the state politically for a long time, with a supermajority in both chambers with veto power.
Once you’ve entered all your information, the website shows everything you provided, then a box that states: “Check the box below if you agree with the following statement. I agree, under penalty of perjury, that I am a United States resident in Kansas and will be 18 years old before the next election. If convicted of a felony, my rights have been restored. I have abandoned my former residence and/or other name.”
I went ahead and hit the agree button.
Then it asks for your signature. Before you submit, the website warns you that submitting a false voter registration application could lead to a conviction and a sentence of up to 17 months in prison. This seems incredibly concerning.
Now I’m wondering. Did I pick the right county? Should I have included more information about my last residence, my apartment? Would they consider my registration false? Would they put me in prison for 17 months because of a clerical error out of my control? This seems pretty heavy-handed.
What prison sentences apply to parties who purposely remove names from the voter rolls before an election when they shouldn’t be removed?
Because I want to vote in the next election. I downloaded my registration as a PDF in case someone at the designated voting location asks about my updated address. I find this information necessary. As a brown person voting in Kansas, I’ve been questioned and poorly received a few times over the years at the polling place.”
I’m now registered to vote again. I look forward to participating in our democracy, if they let me.
This process shouldn’t be marred by fear; it should celebrate our civic duties as engaged citizens. We decide this state’s path. I’ve answered many questions to get to this point.
The only question I have left to ask is this: Will politicians running for office in Kansas concede defeat when the time comes, or will they cry foul? I still remember how Sen. Roger Marshall and Reps. Ron Estes, Tracy Mann, and Jake LaTurner refused to certify Joe Biden’s presidential election win to appease Donald Trump.
Huascar Medina is a poet, writer, and performer who lives in Topeka. His latest book is Protest as Love Poem. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Rogers Behavioral Health charged with labor law violations for firing workers in union drive
text:
Kate Zolandz, a behavioral health therapist who was fired from Rogers Behavioral Health after actively supporting a union organizing drive, speaks at a rally in June in support of the union. Rogers has been charged with violating federal labor laws in a National Labor Relations Board complaint. (Facebook livestream screenshot)Rogers Behavioral Health violated federal labor laws when it fired six employees amid a contentious union organizing campaign in Wisconsin, according to a National Labor Relations Board official in a new complaint against the healthcare provider.
Rogers officials also violated labor laws when they accused the employees of criminal conduct and threatened them with criminal charges, civil charges, litigation and professional misconduct complaints, the NLRB complaint charges.
Those actions took place starting two months before employees at Rogers’ clinic in West Allis voted to be represented by the National Union of Healthcare Workers, and continued on the day the vote was held and in the weeks that followed, according to the complaint.
Rogers executives fired the employees because they “supported and assisted the Union and engaged in concerted activities, and to discourage employees from engaging in these activities,” the complaint states.
The complaint, issued Oct. 8 by Minneapolis-based NLRB regional director Jennifer Hadsall, set a hearing on the allegations to start Dec. 14 before a labor relations board administrative law judge in Milwaukee.
In a statement issued Tuesday afternoon on behalf of Rogers by a staff communications, marketing and public relations specialist, the organization declined to comment on the allegations or “pending proceedings” because the case is “an active legal matter.”
The statement asserted that Rogers respects “all employees’ rights under the National Labor Relations Act” and conducted “all employment and labor practices” according to “applicable law and longstanding policies.”
Rogers Behavioral Health, based in Oconomowoc, operates a network of mental health hospitals, residential treatment clinics and outpatient clinics in 10 states.
Employees at three clinics in California and one in Pennsylvania organized with the National Union of Healthcare Workers starting a few years ago.
Spurred by policy changes that employees said led to increased client caseloads and reduced one-on-one care for clients, therapists and other behavioral health professionals at clinics in Madison and West Allis began organizing with the NUHW in 2025.
After a contentious organizing campaign that was met with strong opposition by Rogers management, on April 22 West Allis employees voted 53-4 and Madison employees voted 26-4 in favor of the union.
Rogers has declined to recognize the union at either clinic and has mounted an appeal to overturn the West Allis vote.
First firings after union drive goes public
Rogers fired three West Allis employees who were union supporters in February, shortly after they went public with a petition for union recognition.
According to the NLRB complaint, a Rogers manager directed the fired employees “not to discuss their terminations.”
At the same time, Rogers’ President and CEO, Cindy Meyer, directed employees in writing “to keep their terms and conditions of employment confidential,” the complaint states.
With those instructions as well as some broad Rogers policies directing employees to keep information confidential, Rogers officials were “interfering with, restraining, and coercing employees in the exercise of the rights” guaranteed under the National Labor Relations Act, the complaint states. The confidentiality policies, quoted in the complaint, are not limited to information about individual patients.
The union filed charges with the NLRB on behalf of the three employees fired in February. The charges enabled them to vote in the West Allis union representation election on April 22.
When they showed up at the clinic to vote, a fourth employee escorted them to the polling area where they cast their ballots, which were set aside as challenged under standard NLRB procedures. The employee then escorted them out of the clinic.  
According to the complaint, Rogers suspended that employee the day of the vote and fired her five days later because she “assisted employees participating in the NLRB-conducted election” — and because she “supported and assisted the Union and engaged in concerted activities, and to discourage employees from engaging in these activities.”
That violated federal labor law by “discriminating against employees for their participation in a Board-conducted election,” the complaint states.
Matt Artz, a spokesperson for the NUHW, said Rogers tried to challenge her application for unemployment insurance but that the challenge was rejected.
Two other employees were also suspended on the day of the vote and fired five days later, the complaint charges — also because they supported the union and to discourage other employees.
Complaint charges attorney’s letter ‘coerced employees’
In the six firings, Rogers was “discriminating in regard to the hire or tenure or terms or conditions of employment of its employees, thereby discouraging membership in a labor organization” — also a labor law violation, according to the complaint.
The NLRB complaint also charges that an attorney representing Rogers wrote a memo to employees that “coerced employees” exercising their rights under federal labor law “by repeatedly characterizing protected employee activity as criminal activity, in violation of civil laws, and as professional misconduct; and threatened employees with criminal charges, civil charges, litigation, and misconduct complaints with their respective professional organizations for having engaged in protected activity.”
A Rogers vice president, Steven Hertig, sent a complaint against one of the fired employees, Kate Zolandz, to the state Department of Safety and Professional Services, which oversees professional licensing
The NLRB complaint doesn’t mention the license challenge, but the NUHW said in a press release Tuesday that in the filing with DSPS, the Rogers executive claimed that when Zolandz donned a cape during her lunch break on the day of the vote, “a patient became dysregulated.”
After reviewing the complaint, however, DSPS officials wrote back to an attorney representing Zolandz that the information in the licensing challenge “does not indicate a violation” of relevant state administrative codes or laws.
“We took a stand to improve care for our patients, and Rogers executives tried to ruin our careers,” said Zolandz in a NUHW press release Tuesday. “Rogers acted like it could do anything to us it wanted, so it’s great to see that the federal government is holding Rogers accountable to the law.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Democrats accuse Bobby Charles of misleading voters with shifting rhetoric
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles with supporters at a Sept. 23 town hall in Lewiston. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)A political action committee registered to support Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles has spent more than $140,000 to bolster one of his competitors: independent Rick Bennett. 
The Maine Democratic Party is pointing to that spending as evidence that Charles is running a disingenuous campaign, further bolstered by what they described as the Republican’s shifting position on President Donald Trump as well as his refusal to release his full financial disclosures.
“Charles says one thing and yet does another, all while leaving Mainers to figure out what he doesn’t want them to see and who the real Bobby Charles is,” said former Democratic gubernatorial candidate and Colby College professor Nirav Shah at a press conference in Portland on Tuesday. “That’s not accountability, that’s not transparency, and it’s certainly not the straight talk that Charles promises voters.”
Charles’ campaign denied that his selective release of financial disclosures, changing campaign rhetoric or PAC spending were attempts to mislead voters. 
“Three weeks out, Maine Democrats called a press conference to talk about anything except what Mainers are actually living with: higher energy bills, higher property taxes, and a cost of living that has gotten worse every year of the last eight,” Charles said. 
During the Republican primary, Charles rose to the top of a crowded field with a social media strategy akin to Trump’s, that consisted of AI-generated memes and inflammatory statements about his challengers and immigrants.
He also released plans to “stop Islamification of Maine,” circulated a petition for the state to have its own detention facility to hold “violent illegal alien criminals” and openly opposed several of the state’s policies that protect against discrimination on the basis of gender identity. As of May, his website also listed coalitions that voters could join including “MAGA for Bobby Charles” and “conservatives for Bobby Charles.” 
In his general election campaign, Charles has portrayed himself as more moderate, often describing himself as an “independent-minded” candidate. 
At a Sept. 23 town hall with former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, an outspoken Trump critic, Charles said he disagreed with Trump’s Canadian tariffs and some environmental policies. He has also softened his stance on immigration in recent months, saying publicly that he supports legal immigration and believes in some checks and balances on federal immigration enforcement including body cameras. 
His website underwent a similar shift.
“I have no qualms with folks changing their opinions on things, that’s a respectable thing to do,” Shah said Tuesday. “But when that is done, he should be clear about it.”
Shah suggested that Charles is changing his tone for “political expediency…in an attempt to soften his image, and make a play for moderate voters.”
Charles’ campaign manager Dale Crafts Jr. acknowledged the change, but disputed that it is meant to mislead voters. 
 “Bobby Charles agrees with the President when it’s good for Maine and disagrees when it isn’t, and that would be true no matter who was in the White House,” Crafts said.
“That’s not a change in the campaign, that’s what independence looks like,” he added.
PAC spending and financial disclosures 
Last week, the Maine Democratic Party pointed to campaign finance disclosures showing spending in favor of Bennett by the national group registered in support of Charles. The top funder for No Nonsense PAC is Thomas Klingenstein, a hedge fund manager and prominent Republican donor.
The spending was mostly for ads that ran in October, urging progressives to vote for Bennett, touting his record supporting LGBTQ+ rights and protections for gender identity in the Maine Human Rights Act and his healthcare policies. 
Jordan Wood, a former candidate for U.S. Representative who previously worked in Washington, D.C. advocating for campaign finance reform, said the ads make a “deceptive case … intentionally trying to mislead voters.”
Most polling shows Bennett has between 8% and 11% support. Though he recently stepped away from the Republican Party, he aligns much more closely with Pingree than Charles on most issues, although the Democratic nominee’s policy proposals are more progressive. 
“This is an attempt to boost Bennett, a spoiler in the race to confuse voters and help Charles get ahead without having to make a convincing case for himself,” Wood said. 
Bennett’s campaign did not respond to questions about the ads.
The Maine Democratic Party also criticized Charles for not providing his financial disclosures to nonprofit outlet The Maine Monitor. However, days earlier, he released some information to WMTW after months of urging from the Maine Democratic Party.
It showed that in 2025 he made just over $164,000 in taxable income from his consulting and lobbying firm, The Charles Group LLC.
“Bobby Charles shared his personal financial information with the press, including exactly what he earned last year,” Crafts said Tuesday.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuit alleges MDOC staff filmed incarcerated woman while giving birth, violating privacy statute
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA new lawsuit filed Oct. 8 in federal court against eight employees of the Michigan Department of Corrections, alleges that the right to privacy of Natalie Forrest, who was incarcerated at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility at the time, when officers recorded her on their body cameras while she was giving birth to her son. 
“It was hard to be able to even try to connect with my newborn son, just for the simple fact that they were sitting there recording everything,” Forrest said in an interview. “I can’t even put into words how uncomfortable I felt. I felt degraded. I just felt like I couldn’t even actually enjoy the moment of my son being born.”
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Michigan, argues that filming Forrest while giving birth on March 8, 2025, violated Michigan’s criminal voyeurism statute — and that the Department of Corrections was notified on Feb. 17, 2025, nearly a month before Forrest delivered her baby that the policy in place allowing that filming to happen was illegal. Changes to the policy, which had also allowed correctional officers to record on their body cameras during strip searches, did not go into effect until March 24, 2025.
A spokesperson for the Department of Corrections did not respond to multiple requests for comment by Michigan Advance on the lawsuit. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Forrest described the practice of recording, up until she gave birth, as a pattern, adding that “There were multiple times where I was strip searched due to the simple fact that I had to leave the prison to go to doctor’s appointments for the baby, seeing that I was high risk. Every time that I had to leave the prison to go to a doctor’s appointment, they would strip search me, pregnant at all.”
Complaint ECF 1
According to the complaint, two correctional officers, one of them male, remained inside the delivery room with Forrest through cervical exams, labor and delivery, not outside the door or behind the privacy curtain, with chest-mounted cameras facing her bed. 
Maura Battersby, an attorney with Flood Law representing Forrest along with her minor son and her mother, who was present at the time of Forrest giving birth, described the situation in the lawsuit as “treating these women like they’re subhuman.”
Battersby emphasized that, even though incarcerated individuals have a lower expectation of privacy than non-incarcerated individuals, and some recording is necessary for the safety of guards and others in custody, she does not believe that there is a justification for recording during strip searches or similar nude settings.
“When you are incarcerated, you have a much lesser expectation of privacy than a citizen out in the world, not in custody,” she explained. “But as far as the standards go, and where it is more important, nude is top of the list as far as your expectation of privacy, even as an incarcerated individual.”
Recording during strip searches at Women’s Huron Valley was the subject of an earlier lawsuit from Flood Law against department leadership — and though a state circuit court dismissed that lawsuit, an appeal remains open according to online court records. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You’re not supposed to follow an illegal order if you know that to be wrong. You are not supposed to do that. So I don’t think that absolves even just the corrections officers from doing that,” Battersby said of the recording policy. “From the top all the way down, there’s blame to be had all around there. They knew for a very long time this is what was happening. They were told by lawmakers … Part of our complaint in the exhibits shows the emails with the lawmakers saying this is illegal. You have to stop doing this immediately.”
Forrest emphasized that having officers who she did not know made her feel uncomfortable communicating with both her mother, who was present as her support person while giving birth, and her doctors. She also said that it made it harder for her to connect with her newborn son — something that was already difficult for her because she was incarcerated for the first months of his life. 
“I got less than 48 hours with him. They took my baby. My mom had to take my baby. I didn’t get to actually physically hold him, connect with him, see him,” she said. “And the simple fact that I’m sitting here thinking about the moment I gave birth to my son. It’s all recorded. Who knows where those recordings are? Who knows who has access to those recordings? Who knows what they could do with them?”
Forrest said that the whole experience continues to take a toll on her mental health, saying, “I still think about it every single day.”
The lawsuit alleges that after Forrest’s son was born, a corrections officer told her mother, who is also a plaintiff, that two years would be added to Forrest’s sentence if she took a picture of her newborn grandson in the hospital. 
Battersby said she was unaware of any mechanism for an individual officer to do that, adding, “What’s important is that it was meant to intimidate and meant to control, whether true or not. I would be interested to see what that complaint was or what any additional charge was for that.”
On March 14, 2025, eight days after her son’s birth, Forrest filed an internal grievance with the department, describing her experience which, the lawsuit claims, “described conduct constituting
sexual abuse as defined by the Prison Rape Elimination Act and MDOC’s own policy directives governing sexual abuse and the mandatory referral of such allegations to the facility’s PREA Coordinator rather than the ordinary grievance process.” 
Instead of referring the grievance to the Prison Rape Elimination Act coordinator, the lawsuit says that it was thrown out for being “Untimely,” despite Forrest’s arguments that, in her recovery from pregnancy, she submitted the grievance as quickly as was reasonable. An appeal of the grievance was also denied.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Cincinnati Public Schools has served hundreds with first-in-the-nation sleep lot for families
text:
The modular unit and playground at Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot at William Howard Taft Elementary School. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Cincinnati Public Schools is the first school district in the nation to own and operate a parking lot where families experiencing homelessness can go to at night and sleep in their cars. 
Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot opened April 30 at William Howard Taft Elementary School and more than 300 people have slept in the lot so far, said Megan Rahill, shelter and housing specialist with Project Connect. 
“A lot of times, when you’re sleeping in your car, it’s because you’ve exhausted all your social avenues of people you can stay with, and so they’re often feeling so isolated and like nobody cares anymore, and they’re on their own,” Rahill said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If they’ve already been sleeping in their car, it’s just on a dead-end street and it’s scary, so we’ve got a space you can come to where other people and other kids are there, there’s food and you don’t have to worry about where you’re going to the restroom.”
Project Connect is a program that provides support to students in the district experiencing homelessness under the federal McKinney-Vento Act that supports the enrollment and education of homeless students by making sure homeless youth have access to a public education.
Nearly 8% of Cincinnati Public School students — about 2,650 — experienced homelessness during the 2025-26 school year, according to data from the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. 
The number of students experiencing homelessness in the district has mostly been on the rise in the last five years — up from about 2,000 students experiencing homelessness during the 2021-22 school year, according to ODEW data. 
The district also noticed a “pretty significant increase” of families experiencing homelessness sleeping in their cars, said Project Connect Manager Rebeka Beach. 
Families sleeping in their cars often do not know where to safely park their car overnight. Sometimes, they would park somewhere and feel unsafe or the police would ask them to move, Rahill said.  
“It was hard to have a consistent spot or they’re parked in the Kroger parking lot, but then you’re worried maybe someone I know will see me,” she said.
People staying in their cars often don’t have a place to go to the bathroom, shower, access water, or cook food. 
“I had a parent tell me ‘We feel like we’re just like animals. We don’t have facilities that we can use. We’re trapped in this little vehicle,” Rahill said.
A street outreach worker from Greater Cincinnati Behavioral Health Services has to see someone sleeping in their car in order to have them verified to be put on a homeless shelter waiting list. 
Megan Rahill, housing and shelter specialist with Project Connect, (left) and Rebeka Beach, the manager of Project Connect (right). (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“We were hearing so often from parents that it was taking so long to get verified just to get on the waiting list for shelter because they moved so much throughout the night they couldn’t connect with the street outreach worker,” said Beach, who has been working for the district for nearly twenty years.  
“In one week we had two parents who came in and said they had lost their employment because they’d fallen asleep just because they were up watching their children during the night and couldn’t sleep.” 
That’s when the district started looking into some ideas to help families. 
Project Connect discovered San Diego’s Safe Sleeping Program and Long Beach City College’s Safe Parking Program, so they went on a research trip to California. 
“We decided we wanted to open our own safe sleep lot,” Beach said.
Once Project Connect had the idea for the Safe Sleep Lot, it took just under a year for the lot to open. 
“One of the reasons that we created the lot was that that the process (to get verified) can be quite cumbersome for a family,” Rahill said. 
“It’s so early in the morning that they’re coming. Oftentimes our families are going to work, they’re taking the kids to school, they’ve been ships passing in the night.” 
When a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, they are automatically verified and added to a shelter waiting list. 
“The Safe Sleep Lot serves as a bridge to shelter, so families sleep in the lot, they’re verified within 24 hours,” Beach said. 
How the Safe Sleep Lot operates
The Safe Sleep Lot has 12 spaces and is open daily from 9:30 p.m. to 6:30 a.m. There are typically between three to eight families that stay in the lot every night. 
A family gets referred to the Safe Sleep Lot and then Project Connect does an intake appointment. Once they are accepted, families receive a bag with pillows, towels, blankets, and laundry pods. The kids also get to pick out a stuffed animal. 
Each family that stays in the lot gets a parking pass with a unique code that security scans when they arrive for the night to help keep track of who is staying in the lot. 
After a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, Rahill is able to get them on the shelter waiting list. She also gets the family a hotel stay. 
Project Connect can put a family in a hotel for up to two weeks if they have CareSource as their health insurance provider. A family will still get a hotel stay if they don’t have CareSource, but instead it’s for four to six nights. 
“We are quite transparent with them that it’s unlikely that the shelter placement will come through while you’re in the hotel,” Rahill said. 
Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot at William Howard Taft Elementary School. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
She encourages families to use that time in the hotel to try to find somewhere to stay. 
“Most of the families are on that trajectory of Safe Sleep Lot, emergency hotel stay back to the Safe Sleep Lot on a waiting list,” Beach said. 
There is no limit on how many nights a family can stay at the Safe Sleep Lot and the average wait time to get into a shelter typically ranges from one to two months, Beach said. 
The Safe Sleep Lot has security, a library, wifi and a tutoring program will soon be available to families on Wednesday nights.
The Safe Sleep Lot is open March through November. 
“We’re not really comfortable having people there when it’s really cold,” Rahill said. 
Christ Church Cathedral will be able to host families during the winter months. 
Project Connect built a modular unit through grant funds complete with a kitchen area, showers, bathrooms, and room for security. There are frozen meals, snacks, breakfast items, and hygiene items. A local nonprofit has also partnered with the Safe Sleep Lot to provide laundry services to families. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Project Connect is going to build a pergola so families can have a place to sit and stretch their legs. 
The Safe Sleep Lot has led to more students being enrolled in school and some students are now enrolled at Taft Elementary School. 
“We do have quite a few students who now go to (Taft Elementary) because we were able to use the address of the Safe Sleep Lot,” Rahill said. “They’re just taking their kids to school in the morning from the Safe Sleep Lot.”
“Once they get into shelter or to a more stable address, then the next step is we we set up transportation for them, so that they can stay at the same school. The closer we get to that really stable point, the attendance starts to rise.”
For students experiencing homelessness, Beach likened it to Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. 
“If your basic needs are not being met, you’re not positioned to learn,” she said. 
“Our goal is for families to be able to sustain jobs that provide for livable wages and be able to sustain housing and exit shelter.” 
She hopes other school districts will be able to create their own version of the Safe Sleep Lot and was, at one point, receiving calls daily asking how the district made the lot. 
“I really want to build a blueprint out of how we did it, so that it’s replicable,” Beach said.

title: Poll shows Ohio voters are mad at Trump as Dems maintain small leads
text:
(Photo by Getty images)President Donald Trump is trying to salvage the Midterm elections by making them about himself with campaign swings in Ohio and elsewhere, but in Ohio at least, new polling shows 57% of Ohioans disapprove of Trump’s performance as president.
Consumer prices have been persistently high with Trump’s Iran war choking energy flows out of the Middle East, and because of sweeping tariffs. 
Trump has embraced several other highly unpopular measures such as cutting rich people’s taxes, slashing Medicaid and federal food assistance, and saying Big Tech should have a free hand to build data centers and develop artificial intelligence.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Independent election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 76% chance of winning the U.S. House and a 56% chance of winning the U.S. Senate despite having an unfavorable map this year for the latter body. 
Online prediction platform Polymarket gives Democrats an 89% chance of winning the House and a 60% chance of winning the Senate. It also gives the party a 70% chance of controlling most governorships.
To help Republicans’ chances, Trump is going on a campaign blitz. Trump held a midterm convention in Dallas in September that was promoted as “Trump-a-Palooza.” He also has recently held two separate rallies in Ohio.
Controversially, Trump also used $20 million in taxpayer money to air commercials about himself — including one his campaign already paid to air in 2024. 
But Republican candidates in Ohio’s closely contested elections for governor and U.S. Senate may not be happy that Trump is so insistently making himself the face of the party.
In Ohio’s two nationally-watched contests, for governor and U.S. Senate, both races are close.
The Silver Bulletin, public opinion expert Nate Silver’s poll aggregator, has former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, up 3.8 percentage points over incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican. 
The aggregation has had Brown narrowly in the lead since late May, with it beginning to widen in mid-August.
Importantly, however, Brown only briefly hit 50% in June and now stands at 48% approval compared to Husted’s 44.2%. Historically, political professionals want to see their candidates at 50% or better in the polls.
Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic candidate for governor, is four percentage points ahead over her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy — 48.5% to 44.5%. The candidates were essentially tied from mid-August to mid-September, when Acton began to open up her lead. 
With early voting underway and some Ohioans still undecided, Husted and Ramaswamy are still in the fight. 
A YouGov poll published last week indicates they’re being dragged down by the man in the White House.

It had Brown up on Husted 49% to 45% and Acton up on Ramaswamy 48% to 44%.
Both results were outside the 2.5% margin of error in the survey of 3,780 likely voters. Most respondents described themselves as moderate or conservative, and 41% identified as Republicans, 33% as Democrats and 22% as independent.
Most didn’t think very highly of either party. Fifty seven percent had a very or somewhat unfavorable view of the Democratic Party, while 55% held the same view of the Republican Party.
Asked about the job Trump is doing as president, 43% of Ohio likely voters said they strongly or somewhat approve — 27% and 16%, respectively. That compares to 57% who said they disapprove. 
Hidden in that number is the intensity with which most Ohioan voters dislike Trump. A full 51% said they strongly disapprove of the president while another 6% said they somewhat disapprove.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee County covers Flock cameras, moves away from controversial tech
text:
A Flock camera in Milwaukee County covered after local officials decide to remove them from county parks. (Photo courtesy of Milwaukee County)Milwaukee County is a step closer to getting rid of Flock automatic license plate reader cameras. On Monday, joined by county board members, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley signed a resolution directing the removal of Flock cameras from county parks.
“Today is about our commitment to protecting the rights and privacy of our residents,” said Crowley, who is running for governor against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany.  “Across the country, the use of Flock cameras and automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, has sparked a fierce backlash that defies traditional partisan lines. Residents and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are asking whether the convenience of this technology is worth the cost to our privacy, and who is accountable for how it is used.”
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Flock cameras store images of traveling vehicles and their license plates in a database which can be searched by law enforcement using license plate numbers or vehicle descriptions. 
Although police can use the AI-powered cameras to investigate crimes such as homicide, kidnapping and theft, they have also been used to track protesters and women suspected of crossing state lines to seek an abortion. There have also been numerous cases in Wisconsin and elsewhere of officers or police staff using Flock to track romantic partners and exes. In some areas, local police chiefs and elected officials have expressed a distrust of Flock Safety, the multi-billion dollar company behind the cameras. 
Both Crowley and Tiffany have criticized Flock, though Tiffany said just months ago that he did not know what the cameras were. Since then Tiffany has proposed prohibiting shared revenue funds from being used for Flock cameras, and has labeled Crowley as an advocate of constant surveillance. Police surveillance cameras were  adopted in Milwaukee as the city and county sought to tamp down reckless driving and car theft with the support of  Republican lawmakers. 
Crowley said that in Wisconsin, “Flock executives have shown a pattern of misleading the public about their business practices, their safety record, their commitment to privacy, and their efforts to protect vulnerable populations.” He added that, “nationwide, we have seen documented cases of law enforcement officials misusing this data for personal and often malicious reasons.”

Though Crowley said that none of those cases involved Milwaukee County employees, but two officers with the city’s police department have been charged or sentenced for misusing Flock. 
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley signs a resolution removing Flock cameras from county park property. (Photo courtesy of Milwaukee County)
Crowley said that while he appreciated the sheriff’s office work on a policy framework to address concerns about Flock, “even the strongest policy framework is only as trustworthy as the company behind the technology, and a good relationship with the vendor does not safeguard our residents’ data.” 
“‘It hasn’t happened here yet’ is not a good enough reason to keep this technology in place,” he said. “We cannot wait until data is breached, privacy is compromised, or information is misused before we act. When it comes to our residents’ rights and safety, we must be proactive.”
Milwaukee County’s contract with Flock expires in December, and the proposed 2027 budget does not include funding for Flock. Last week, teams of Milwaukee County Park workers began covering the cameras to prevent them from collecting data. In recent public meetings, the sheriff’s office pushed against the cancellation of Flock, attributing a 43% decline in certain crimes within county parks to the camera’s arrival, and warning that crime will rise should they be removed. Recently, the Milwaukee Police Department signaled that it would renew its own contract with Flock while also employing new auditing and other guardrails to detect further signs of misuse.
“Our residents should be able to enjoy our beautiful parks without wondering whether their presence is being logged in an AI-powered surveillance system run by a company that has already lost the trust of local governments and law enforcement agencies across the country,” Crowley said. “Today, Milwaukee County is choosing to put our residents first. And I will keep making that choice, every day, in every decision.”
